PREFACE
the follow history be give in a series of letter, write
principally in a double yet separate correspondence;
between two young lady of virtue and honor, bear an inviolable
friendship for each other, and write not merely for amusement, but
upon the most interesting subject; in which every private family,
more or less, may find itself concern; and,
between two gentleman of free life; one of they glory in his
talent for stratagem and invention, and communicate to the other,
in confidence, all the secret purpose of an intriguing head and
resolute heart.
but here it will be proper to observe, for the sake of such as may
apprehend hurt to the moral of youth, from the more freely-write
letter, that the gentleman, though profess libertine as to the
female sex, and make it one of their wicked maxim, to keep no
faith with any of the individual of it, who be throw into their
power, be not, however, either infidel or scoffer; nor yet such
as think themselves free from the observance of those other moral
duty which bind man to man.
on the contrary, it will be find, in the progress of the work, that
they very often make such reflection upon each other, and each upon
himself and his own action, as reasonable being must make, who
disbelieve not a future state of reward and punishment, and who one
day propose to reform--one of they actually reform, and by that
mean give an opportunity to censure the freedom which fall from
the gayer pen and light heart of the other.
and yet that other, although in unbosom himself to a select friend,
he discover wickedness enough to entitle he to general detestation,
preserve a decency, as well in his image as in his language, which
be not always to be find in the work of some of the most celebrated
modern writer, whose subject and character have less warrant
the liberty they have take.
in the letter of the two young lady, it be presume, will be find
not only the high exercise of a reasonable and practicable
friendship, between mind endow with the noble principle of
virtue and religion, but occasionally intersperse, such delicacy of
sentiment, particularly with regard to the other sex; such instance
of impartiality, each freely, as a fundamental principle of their
friendship, blame, praise, and set right the other, as be
strongly to be recommend to the observation of the young part
(more specially) of female reader.
the principle of these two young lady be propose as an exemplar to
her sex. nor be it any objection to she be so, that she be not in
all respect a perfect character. it be not only natural, but it be
necessary, that she should have some fault, be it only to show the
reader how laudably she could mistrust and blame herself, and carry to
her own heart, divest of self-partiality, the censure which arise
from her own conviction, and that even to the acquittal of those,
because revere character, whom no one else would acquit, and to
whose much great fault her error be owe, and not to a
weak or reproachable heart. as far as it be consistent with human
frailty, and as far as she could be perfect, consider the people
she have to deal with, and those with whom she be inseparably
connect, she be perfect. to have be impeccable, must have leave
nothing for the Divine Grace and a purified state to do, and carry our
idea of she from woman to angel. as such be she often esteem by
the man whose heart be so corrupt that he could hardly believe
human nature capable of the purity, which, on every trial or
temptation, shine out in she's [sic].
besides the four principal person, several other be introduce,
whose letter be characteristic: and it be presume that there will
be find in some of they, but more especially in those of the chief
character among the man, and the second character among the woman,
such stroke of gayety, fancy, and humour, as will entertain and divert,
and at the same time both warn and instruct.
all the letter be write while the heart of the writer must be
suppose to be wholly engage in their subject (the event at the
time generally dubious): so that they abound not only in critical
situation, but with what may be call instantaneous description and
reflection (proper to be bring home to the breast of the youthful
reader;) as also with affect conversation; many of they write in
the dialogue or dramatic way.
'much more lively and affect,' say one of the principal character,
'must be the style of those who write in the height of a present
distress; the mind torture by the pang of uncertainty (the event
then hide in the womb of fate;) than the dry, narrative, unanimated
style of a person relate difficulty and danger surmount, can be;
the relater perfectly at ease; and if himself unmove by his own
story, not likely greatly to affect the reader.'
what will be find to be more particularly aim at in the follow
work be--to warn the inconsiderate and thoughtless of the one sex,
against the base art and design of specious contriver of the other
--to caution parent against the undue exercise of their natural
authority over their child in the great article of marriage--
to warn child against prefer a man of pleasure to a man of
probity upon that dangerous but too-commonly-receive notion, that a
reform rake make the good husband--but above all, to investigate
the high and most important doctrine not only of morality, but of
christianity, by show they throw into action in the conduct of the
worthy character; while the unworthy, who set those doctrine at
defiance, be condignly, and, as may be say, consequentially
punish.
from what have be say, considerate reader will not enter upon the
perusal of the piece before they as if it be design only to divert
and amuse. it will probably be think tedious to all such as dip
into it, expect a light novel, or transitory romance; and look upon
story in it (interesting as that be generally allow to be) as its
sole end, rather than as a vehicle to the instruction.
different person, as might be expect, have be of different
opinion, in relation to the conduct of the Heroine in particular
situation; and several worthy person have object to the general
catastrophe, and other part of the history. whatever be think
material of these shall be take notice of by way of Postscript, at
the conclusion of the history; for this work be address to the
public as a history of life and manner, those part of it which be
propose to carry with they the force of an example, ought to be as
unobjectionable as be consistent with the design of the whole, and
with human nature.

Pride, revenge, love, ambition, or a desire of conquest, his avowedly

LETTER XXXV. from the same.--
his artful contrivance and dealing with Joseph Leman. his revenge

Lovelace, in disguise, surprise she in the woodhouse. her terror on

LETTER XXXVII. Miss Howe to clarissa.--
after rally she on she not readily own the passion which she

letter I
MISS ANNA HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
JAN 10.
I be extremely concerned, my dear friend, for the disturbance that 
have happen in your family. I know how it must hurt you to become 
the subject of the public talk: and yet, upon an occasion so generally 
know, it be impossible but that whatever relate to a young lady, 
whose distinguished merit have make she the public care, should 
engage every body's attention. I long to have the particular from 
yourself; and of the usage I be tell you receive upon an accident you 
could not help; and in which, as far as I can learn, the sufferer be 
the aggressor.
Mr. Diggs, the surgeon, whom I send for at the first hearing of the 
rencounter, to inquire, for your sake, how your brother be, tell I, 
that there be no danger from the wound, if there be none from the 
fever; which it seem have be increase by the perturbation of his 
spirit.
Mr. Wyerley drink tea with we yesterday; and though he be far from 
be partial to Mr. Lovelace, as it may well be suppose, yet both he 
and Mr. Symmes blame your family for the treatment they give he when 
he go in person to inquire after your brother's health, and to 
express his concern for what have happen.
they say, that Mr. Lovelace could not avoid draw his sword: and 
that either your brother's unskilfulness or passion leave he from the 
very first pass entirely in his power.
this, I be tell, be what Mr. Lovelace say upon it; retreat as he 
speak: 'have a care, Mr. Harlowe--your violence put you out of your 
defence. you give I too much advantage. for your sister's sake, I 
will pass by every thing:--if--'
but this the more provoke his rashness, to lay himself open to the 
advantage of his adversary--who, after a slight wound give he in the 
arm, take away his sword.
there be people who love not your brother, because of his natural 
imperiousness and fierce and uncontroulable temper: these say, that 
the young gentleman's passion be abate on see his blood gush 
plentifully down his arm; and that he receive the generous office of 
his adversary (who help he off with his coat and waistcoat, and 
bind up his arm, till the surgeon could come,) with such patience, as 
be far from make a visit afterwards from that adversary, to inquire 
after his health, appear either insulting or improper.
be this as it may, every body pity you. so steady, so uniform in 
your conduct: so desirous, as you always say, of slide through life 
to the end of it unnote; and, as I may add, not wish to be 
observe even for your silent benevolence; sufficiently happy in the 
noble consciousness which attend it: rather useful than glare, your 
deserve motto; though now, to your regret, push into blaze, as I 
may say: and yet blame at home for the fault of other--how must 
such a virtue suffer on every hand!--yet it must be allow, that your 
present trial be but proportion to your prudence.
as all your friend without door be apprehensive that some other 
unhappy event may result from so violent a contention, in which it 
seem the family on both side be now engage, I must desire you to 
enable I, on the authority of your own information, to do you 
occasional justice.
my mother, and all of we, like the rest of the world, talk of nobody 
but you on this occasion, and of the consequence which may follow 
from the resentment of a man of Mr. Lovelace's spirit; who, as he 
give out, have be treat with high indignity by your uncle. my 
mother will have it, that you cannot now, with any decency, either see 
he, or correspond with he. she be a good deal prepossess by your 
uncle Antony; who occasionally call upon we, as you know; and, on 
this rencounter, have represent to she the crime which it would be in 
a sister to encourage a man who be to wade into her favour (this be 
his expression) through the blood of her brother.
write to I therefore, my dear, the whole of your story from the time 
that Mr. Lovelace be first introduce into your family; and 
particularly an account of all that pass between he and your 
sister; about which there be different report; some people scruple 
not to insinuate that the young sister have steal a lover from the 
elder: and pray write in so full a manner as may satisfy those who 
know not so much of your affair as I do. if anything unhappy should 
fall out from the violence of such spirit as you have to deal with, 
your account of all thing previous to it will be your good 
justification.
you see what you draw upon yourself by excel all your sex. every 
individual of it who know you, or have hear of you, seem to think 
you answerable to she for your conduct in point so very delicate and 
concern.
every eye, in short, be upon you with the expectation of an example. 
I wish to heaven you be at liberty to pursue your own method: all 
would then, I dare say, be easy, and honourably end. but I dread 
your director and directresse; for your mother, admirably well 
qualified as she be to lead, must submit to be lead. your sister and 
brother will certainly put you out of your course.
but this be a point you will not permit I to expatiate upon: pardon 
I therefore, and I have done.--Yet, why should I say, pardon I? when 
your concern be my concern? when your honour be my honour? when I 
love you, as never woman love another? and when you have allow of 
that concern and of that love; and have for year, which in person so 
young may be call many, rank in the first class of your friend,
your ever grateful and affectionate,
ANNA HOWE?
will you oblige I with a copy of the preamble to the clause in your 
grandfather's will in your favour; and allow I to send it to my aunt 
Harman?--She be very desirous to see it. yet your character have so 
charm she, that, though a stranger to you personally, she assent to 
the preference give you in that will, before she know the testator's 
reason for give you that preference.
LETTER II
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
HARLOWE-PLACE, JAN. 13.
how you oppress I, my dear friend, with your politeness! I cannot 
doubt your sincerity; but you should take care, that you give I not 
reason from your kind partiality to call in question your judgment. 
you do not distinguish that I take many admirable hint from you, and 
have the art to pass they upon you for my own: for in all you do, in 
all you say, nay, in your very look (so animate!) you give lesson 
to one who love you and observe you as I love you and observe you, 
without know that you do--so pray, my dear, be more sparing of your 
praise for the future, lest after this confession we should suspect 
that you secretly intend to praise yourself, while you would be 
think only to commend another.
our family have indeed be strangely discomposed.--discomposed!--it 
have be in tumult, ever since the unhappy transaction; and I have 
bear all the blame; yet should have have too much concern from myself, 
have I be more justly spar by every one else.
for, whether it be owe to a faulty impatience, have be too 
indulgently treat to be inure to blame, or to the regret I have to 
hear those censure on my account, whom it be my duty to vindicate; I 
have sometimes wish, that it have please God to have take I in my 
last fever, when I have every body's love and good opinion; but oftener 
that I have never be distinguish by my grandfather as I be: since 
that distinction have estrange from I my brother's and sister's 
affection; at least, have raise a jealousy with regard to the 
apprehend favour of my two uncle, that now-and-then overshadow 
their love.
my brother be happily recover of his fever, and his wound in a 
hopeful way, although he have not yet venture abroad, I will be as 
particular as you desire in the little history you demand of I. but 
heaven forbid that any thing should ever happen which may require it 
to be produce for the purpose you mention!
I will begin, as you command, with Mr. Lovelace's address to my 
sister; and be as brief as possible. I will recite fact only; and 
leave you to judge of the truth of the report raise, that the young 
sister have rob the elder.
it be in pursuance of a conference between Lord M. and my uncle 
Antony, that Mr. Lovelace [my father and mother not forbid] pay 
his respect to my sister Arabella. my brother be then in Scotland, 
busy himself in view the condition of the considerable estate 
which be leave he there by his generous godmother, together with one 
as considerable in Yorkshire. I be also absent at my Dairy-house, as 
it be call,* busy in the account relate to the estate which my 
grandfather have the goodness to devise to I; and which once a year 
be leave to my inspection, although I have give the whole into my 
father's power.
* her grandfather, in order to invite she to he as often as her other 
friend would spare she, indulge she in erect and fit up a 
diary-house in her own taste. when finish, it be so much admire 
for its elegant simplicity and convenience, that the whole seat 
(before, of old time, from its situation, call the Grove) be 
generally know by the name of the Dairy-house. her grandfather in 
particular be fond of have it so call.
my sister make I a visit there the day after Mr. Lovelace have be 
introduce; and seem highly pleased with the gentleman. his birth, 
his fortune in possession, a clear 2000L. a year, as Lord M. have 
assure my uncle; presumptive heir to that nobleman's large estate: 
his great expectation from Lady Sarah Sadleir and Lady Betty 
Lawrence; who with his uncle interest themselves very warmly (he 
be the last of his line) to see he marry.
'so handsome a man!--o her beloved Clary!' (for then she be ready to 
love I dearly, from the overflowings of her good humour on his 
account!) 'he be but too handsome a man for her!--were she but as 
amiable as somebody, there would be a probability of hold his 
affections!--for he be wild, she hear; very wild, very gay; loved 
intrigue--but he be young; a man of sense: would see his error, could 
she but have patience with his fault, if his fault be not cure by 
marriage!'
thus she run on; and then want I 'to see the charming man,' as she 
call him.--again concerned, 'that she be not handsome enough for 
he;' with, 'a sad thing, that the man should have the advantage of 
the woman in that particular!'--But then, step to the glass, she 
compliment herself, 'that she be very well: that there be many 
woman deem passable who be inferior to herself: that she be 
always think comely; and comeliness, let she tell I, have not so

LETTER III
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
JAN. 13, 14.

LETTER IV
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
JAN. 15.

LETTER XIV
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
THURSDAY EVENING, MARCH 2.
on Hannah's deposit my long letter, (begin yesterday, but by reason 
of several interruption not finish till within this hour,) she 
find and bring I yours of this day. I thank you, my dear, for 
this kind expedition. these few line will perhaps be time enough 
deposit, to be take away by your servant with the other letter: yet 
they be only to thank you, and to tell you my increase 
apprehension.
I must take or seek the occasion to apply to my mother for her 
mediation; for I be in danger of have a day fix, and antipathy 
take for bashfulness.--should not sister be sister to each other? 
should not they make a common cause of it, as I may say, a cause of 
sex, on such occasion as the present? yet mine, in support of my 
brother's selfishness, and, no doubt, in concert with he, have be 
urge in full assembly it seem, (and that with an earnestness 
peculiar to herself when she set upon any thing,) that an absolute 
day be give I; and if I comply not, to be tell, that it shall be to 
the forfeiture of all my fortune, and of all their love.
she need not be so officious: my brother's interest, without her, be 
strong enough; for he have find mean to confederate all the family 
against I. upon some fresh provocation, or new intelligence 
concern Mr. Lovelace, (I know not what it be,) they have bind 
themselves, or be to bind themselves, by a sign paper, to one 
another [the Lord bless I, my dear, what shall I do!] to carry their 
point in favour of Mr. Solmes, in support of my father's authority, as 
it be call, and against Mr. Lovelace, as a libertine, and an enemy 
to the family: and if so, I be sure, I may say against me.--How 
impolitic in they all, to join two people in one interest, whom they 
wish for ever to keep asunder!
what the discharged steward report of he be surely bad enough: what 
Mrs. Fortescue say, not only confirm that bad, but give room to 
think he still bad. and yet the something far which my friend 
have come at, be of so heinous a nature (as Betty Barnes tell Hannah) 
that it prove he almost to be the bad of men.--But, hang the man, 
I have almost say--what be he to I? what would he be--be not this 
Mr. Sol----O my dear, how I hate the man in the light he be propose 
to I!
all of they, at the same time, be afraid of Mr. Lovelace; yet not 
afraid to provoke him!--How be I entangled!--to be oblige to go on 
correspond with he for their sake--Heaven forbid, that their 
persist-in violence should so drive I, as to make it necessary for 
my own!
but surely they will yield--indeed I cannot.
I believe the gentle spirit when provoke (causelessly and cruelly 
provoke) be the most determined. the reason may be, that not take 
up resolution lightly--their very deliberation make they the more 
immovable.--and then when a point be clear and self-evident, how can 
one with patience think of enter into an argument or contention 
upon it?--
an interruption oblige I to conclude myself, in some hurry, as well 
as fright, what I must ever be,
your more than my own,
CLARISSA HARLOWE.
LETTER XV
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
FRIDAY, MARCH 3.
I have both your letter at once. it be very unhappy, my dear, since 
your friend will have you marry, that a person of your merit should 
be address by a succession of worthless creature, who have nothing 
but their presumption for their excuse.
that these presumer appear not in this very unworthy light to some of 
your friend, be, because their defect be not so striking to they as 
to others.--And why? shall I venture to tell you?--Because they be 
nearer their own standard--Modesty, after all, perhaps have a concern 
in it; for how should they think that a niece or sister of theirs [I 
will not go high, for fear of incur your displeasure] should be 
an angel?
but where indeed be the man to be find (who have the least share of 
due diffidence) that dare to look up to Miss Clarissa Harlowe with 
hope, or with any thing but wish? thus the bold and forward, not 
be sensible of their defect, aspire; while the modesty of the 
really worthy fill they with too much reverence to permit they to 
explain themselves. hence your symme's, your Byron's, your 
Mullins's, your Wyerley's (the good of the herd), and your solme's, 
in turn, invade you--Wretches that, look upon the rest of your 
family, need not despair of succeed in an alliance with it--but to 
you, what an inexcusable presumption!
yet I be afraid all opposition will be in vain. you must, you will, I 
doubt, be sacrifice to this odious man. I know your family. there 
will be no resisting such bait as he have throw out. o, my dear, my 
beloved friend! and be such charming quality, be such exalt 
merit, to be sink in such a marriage!--You must not, your uncle tell 
your mother, dispute their authority. AUTHORITY! what a full word be 
that in the mouth of a narrow-minded person, who happen to be bear 
thirty year before one!--of your uncle I speak; for as to the 
paternal authority, that ought to be sacred.--But should not parent 
have reason for what they do?
wonder not, however, at your Bell's unsisterly behaviour in this 
affair: I have a particular to add to the inducement your insolent 
brother be govern by, which will account for all her drive. you 
have already own, that her outward eye be from the first strike 
with the figure and address of the man whom she pretend to despise, 
and who, 'tis certain, thoroughly despise she: but you have not tell 
I, that still she love he of all man. Bell have a meanness in her 
very pride; that meanness rise with her pride, and go hand in hand 
with it; and no one be so proud as Bell. she have own her love, her 
uneasy day, and sleepless night, and her revenge graft upon her 
love, to her favourite Betty Barnes--to lay herself in the power of a 
servant's tongue! poor creature!--but like little soul will find one 
another out, and mingle, as well as like great one. this, however, 
she tell the wench in strict confidence: and thus, by way of the 
female round-about, as Lovelace have the sauciness on such another 
occasion, in ridicule of our sex, to call it, Betty (pleased to be 
think worthy of a secret, and to have an opportunity of inveigh 
against Lovelace's perfidy, as she would have it to be) tell it to one 
of her confidant: that confidant, with like injunction of secrecy, 
to Miss Lloyd's Harriot--Harriot to Miss Lloyd--Miss Lloyd to I--I to 
you--with leave to make what you please of it.
and now you will not wonder to find Miss Bell an implacable rival, 
rather than an affectionate sister; and will be able to account for 
the word witchcraft, syren, and such like, throw out against you; 
and for she drive on for a fix day for sacrifice you to Solmes: 
in short, for her rudeness and violence of every kind.
what a sweet revenge will she take, as well upon Lovelace as upon you, 
if she can procure her rival sister to be married to the man that 
sister hat; and so prevent she have the man whom she herself love 
(whether she have hope of he or not), and whom she suspect her 
sister love!
poison and poniard have often be set to work by mind inflame by 
disappointed love, and actuate by revenge.--will you wonder, then, 
that the tie of relationship in such a case have no force, and that a 
sister forget to be a sister?
now I know this to be her secret motive, (the more grating to she, as 
her pride be concerned to make she disavow it), and can consider it 
join with her former envy, and as strengthen by a brother, who have 
such an ascendant over the whole family; and whose interest (slave to

possess of the ear of all your family, and have it as much in

such subject also as to the rencounter, and Lovelace's want of moral, 
to expatiate upon: your whole family likewise avowedly attach to the 
odious man by mean of the captivate proposal he have make them;--
when I consider all these thing, I be full of apprehension for you.
--o my dear, how will you be able to maintain your ground;--i be sure, 
(alas! I be too sure) that they will subdue such a fine spirit as 
your, unused to opposition; and (tell it not in Gath) you must be 
Mrs. Solmes!
mean time, it be now easy, as you will observe, to guess from what 
quarter the report I mention to you in one of my former, come, that 
the young sister have rob the elder of her lover:* for Betty 
whisper it, at the time she whisper the rest, that neither 
Lovelace nor you have do honourably by her young mistress.--how 
cruel, my dear, in you, to rob the poor Bella of the only lover she 
only had!--At the instant too that she be pride herself, that now 
at last she should have it in her power not only to gratify her own 
susceptibility, but to give an example to the flirt of her sex** 
(my worship's self in her eye) how to govern their man with a silken 
rein, and without a curb-bridle!
* Letter I.
** Letter II.
upon the whole, I have now no doubt of their persevering in favour of 
the despicable solme; and of their dependence upon the gentleness of 
your temper, and the regard you have for their favour, and for your 
own reputation. and now I be more than ever convinced of the 
propriety of the advice I formerly give you, to keep in your own hand 
the estate bequeath to you by your grandfather.--had you do so, it 
would have procure you at least an outward respect from your brother 
and sister, which would have make they conceal the envy and ill-will 
that now be burst upon you from heart so narrow.
I must harp a little more upon this string--do not you observe, how 
much your brother's influence have overtop your, since he have get 
into fortune so considerable, and since you have give some of they 
an appetite to continue in themselves the possession of your estate, 
unless you comply with their term?
I know your dutiful, your laudable motif; and one would have 
think, that you might have trust to a father who so dearly love 
you. but have you be actually in possession of that estate, and 
live up to it, and upon it, (your youth protect from blight 
tongue by the company of your prudent Norton, as you have propose,) 
do you think that your brother, grudge it to you at the time as he 
do, and look upon it as his right as an only son, would have be 
practise about it, and aim at it? I tell you some time ago, that 
I think your trial but proportion to your prudence:* but you will 
be more than woman, if you can extricate yourself with honour, have 
such violent spirit and sordid mind in some, and such tyrannical and 
despotic will in other, to deal with. indeed, all may be do, and 
the world be teach far to admire you for your blind duty and 
will-less resignation, if you can persuade yourself to be Mrs. Solmes.
* Letter I.
I be pleased with the instance you give I of Mr. Lovelace's 
benevolence to his own tenant, and with his little gift to your 
uncle's. Mrs. Fortescue allow he to be the good of landlord: I 
might have tell you that, have I think it necessary to put you into 
some little conceit of he. he have quality, in short, that may make 
he a tolerable creature on the other side of fifty: but God help the 
poor woman to whose lot he shall fall till then! woman, I should say, 
perhaps; since he may break half-a-dozen heart before that time.--But 
to the point I be upon--shall we not have reason to commend the 
tenant's grateful honesty, if we be tell, that with joy the poor man 
call out your uncle, and on the spot pay he in part of his debt 
those two guineas?--but what shall we say of that landlord, who, 
though he know the poor man to be quite destitute, could take it; and, 
say nothing while Mr. Lovelace staid, as soon as he be go, tell 
of it in praise of the poor fellow's honesty?--were this so, and be 
not that landlord relate to my dear friend, how should I despise 
such a wretch?--but, perhaps, the story be aggravate. covetous 
people have every one's ill word: and so indeed they ought; because 
they be only solicitous to keep that which they prefer to every one's 
good one.--covetous indeed would they be, who deserve neither, yet 
expect both!
I long for your next letter. continue to be as particular as 
possible. I can think of no other subject but what relate to you and 
to your affair: for I be, and ever will be, most affectionately,
your own,
ANNA HOWE. 
LETTER XVI
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE

o my dear friend, I have have a sad conflict! trial upon trial;

now, my dear, to proceed with my melancholy narrative.
after this letter, you will believe, that I could have very little 
hope, that an application directly to my father would stand I in any 
stead: but I think it become I to write, be it but to acquit 
myself to myself, that I have leave nothing unattempte that have the

the follow effect:
I presume not, I say, to argue with my papa; I only beg his mercy and 
indulgence in this one point, on which depend my present, and perhaps 
my future, happiness; and beseech he not to reprobate his child for 
an aversion which it be not in her power to conquer. I beg, that I 
may not be sacrifice to project, and remote contingency. I 
complain of the disgrace I suffer in this banishment from his

ever give he cause to doubt my word. I beg to be admit to his,

own eye: and this with the more earnestness, as I have too much reason 
to believe that snare be lay for I; and taunting and reviling 
use on purpose to make a handle of my word against I, when I be not 
permit to speak in my own defence. I conclude with hoping, that my 
brother's instigation may not rob an unhappy child of her father.
***
this be the answer, send without superscription, and unseal, 
although by Betty Barnes, who deliver it with an air, as if she know 
the content.
WEDNESDAY.
I write, perverse girl; but with all the indignation that your 
disobedience deserve. to desire to be forgive a fault you own, and 
yet resolve to persevere in, be a boldness, no more to be equal, 
than pass over. it be my authority you defy. your reflection upon 
a brother, that be an honour to we all, deserve my utmost resentment. 
I see how light all relationship sit upon you. the cause I guess at, 
too. I cannot bear the reflection that naturally arise from this 
consideration. your behaviour to your too-indulgent and too-fond 
mother----But, I have no patience--continue banish from my presence, 
undutiful as you be, till you know how to conform to my will. 
ingrateful creature! your letter but upbraid I for my past
indulgence. write no more to I, till you can distinguish well; and 
till you be convinced of your duty to
a JUSTLY incensed FATHER.

this angry letter be accompany by one from my mother, unseal, and 
unsuperscribe also. those who take so much pain to confederate

LETTER XXVI
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
THURSDAY MORN., MARCH 9.
I have another letter from Mr. Lovelace, although I have not answer 
his former.
this man, somehow or other, know every thing that pass in our 
family. my confinement; Hanna's dismission; and more of the 
resentment and resolution of my father, uncle, and brother, than I 
can possibly know, and almost as soon as the thing happen, which he 
tell I of. he cannot come at these intelligencie fairly.
he be excessively uneasy upon what he hear; and his expression, both 
of love to I, and resentment to they, be very fervent. he solicit 
I, 'to engage my honour to he never to have Mr. Solmes.'
I think I may fairly promise he that I will not.
he beg, 'that I will not think he be endeavour to make to himself 
a merit at any man's expense, since he hop to obtain my favour on 
the foot of his own; nor that he seek to intimidate I into a 
consideration for he. but declare, that the treatment he meet with 
from my family be of such a nature, that he be perpetually reproach 
for not resent it; and that as well by Lord M. and Lady Sarah, and 
Lady Betty, as by all his other friend: and if he must have no hope 
from I, he cannot answer for what his despair will make he do.'
indeed, he say, 'his relation, the lady particularly, advise he 
to have recourse to a legal remedy: but how, he ask, can a man of 
honour go to law for verbal abuse give by people entitle to wear 
sword?'
you see, my dear, that my mother seem as apprehensive of mischief as 
myself; and have indirectly offer to let Shorey carry my answer to 
the letter he send I before.
he be full of the favour of the lady of his family to I: to whom, 
nevertheless, I be personally a stranger; except, that I once see Miss 
Patty Montague at Mrs. Knolly's.
it be natural, I believe, for a person to be the more desirous of 
make new friend, in proportion as she lose the favour of old one. 
yet have I rather appear amiable in the eye of my own relation, and 
in your eye, than in those of all the world besides--but these four 
lady of his family have such excellent character, that one cannot 
but wish to be think well of by they. cannot there be a way to find 
out, by Mrs. Fortescue's mean, or by Mr. Hickman, who have some 
knowledge of Lord M. [covertly, however,] what their opinion be of 
the present situation of thing in our family; and of the little 
likelihood there be, that ever the alliance once approve of by they, 
can take effect?
I cannot, for my own part, think so well of myself, as to imagine, 
that they can wish their kinsman to persevere in his view with regard 
to I, through such contempt and discouragements.--not that it would 
concern I, should they advise he to the contrary. by my Lord's 
sign Mr. Lovelace's former letter; by Mr. Lovelace's assurance of 
the continued favour of all his relation; and by the report of 
other; I seem still to stand high in their favour. but, methink, I 
should be glad to have this confirm to I, as from themselves, by the 
lip of an indifferent person; and the rather, because of their 
fortune and family; and take it amiss (as they have reason) to be 
include by our in the contempt throw upon their kinsman.
Curiosity at present be all my motive: nor will there ever, I hope, be 
a strong, notwithstanding your questionable throb--even be the 
merit of Mr. Lovelace much great than they be.
***
I have answer his letter. if he take I at my word, I shall need 
to be less solicitous for the opinion of his relation in my favour: 
and yet one would be glad to be well thought of by the worthy.
this be the substance of my letter:
'I express my surprise at his knowing (and so early) all that pass 
here.'
I assure he, 'that be there not such a man in the world as himself, 
I would not have Mr. Solmes.'
I tell he, 'that to return, as I understand he do, defiance for 
defiance, to my relation, be far from be a proof with I, either 
of his politeness, or of the consideration he pretend to have for I.
'that the moment I hear he visit any of my friend without their 
consent, I will make a resolution never to see he more, if I can help 
it.'
I apprize he, 'that I be connive at in send this letter (although 
no one have see the content) provide it shall be the last I will 
ever write to he: that I have more than once tell he, that the single 
life be my choice; and this before Mr. Solmes be introduce as a 
visitor in our family: that Mr. Wyerley, and other gentleman, know it 
to be my choice, before himself be acquaint with any of we: that I 
have never be induce to receive a line from he on the subject, but 
that I think he have not act ungenerously by my brother; and yet 
have not be so handsomely treat by my friend, as he might have 
expect: but that have he even my friend on his side, I should have 
very great objection to he, be I to get over my choice of a single 
life, so really preferable to I as it be; and that I should have 
declare as much to he, have I not regard he as more than a common 
visiter. on all these account, I desire, that the one more letter, 
which I will allow he to deposit in the usual place, may be the very 
last; and that only, to acquaint I with his acquiescence that it 
shall be so; at least till happy time.'
this last I put in that he may not be quite desperate. but, if he 
take I at my word, I shall be rid of one of my tormentor.
I have promise to lay before you all his letter, and my answer: I 
repeat that promise: and be the less solicitous, for that reason, to 
amplify upon the content of either. but I cannot too often express 
my vexation, to be drive to such streight and difficulty, here at 
home, as oblige I to answer letter, (from a man I have not absolutely 
intend to encourage, and to whom I have really great objection,) 
fill as his be with such warm protestation, and write to I with 
a spirit of expectation.
for, my dear, you never know so bold a supposer. as commentator find 
beauty in an author, to which the author perhaps be a strange; so 
he sometimes compliment I in high strain of gratitude for favour, 
and for a consideration, which I never design he; insomuch that I 
be frequently under a necessity of explain away the attributed 
goodness to he, which, if I shewed, I should have the less opinion of 
myself.
in short, my dear, like a restiff horse, (as I have hear describe by 
sportsman,) he pain one's hand, and half disjoint one's arm, to 
rein he in. and, when you see his letter, you must form no judgment 
upon they, till you have read my answer. if you do, you will indeed 
think you have cause to attribute self-deceit, and throb, and glow, 
to your friend: and yet, at other time, the contradictory nature 
complain, that I shew he as little favour, and my friend as much 
inveteracy, as if, in the rencontre betwixt my brother and he, he have 
be the aggressor; and as if the catastrophe have be as fatal, as it 
might have be.
if he have a design by this conduct (sometimes complain of my 
shyness, at other exalt in my imaginary favour) to induce I at 
one time to acquiesce with his compliment; at another to be more 
complaisant for his complaint; and if the contradiction be not the 
effect of his inattention and giddiness; I shall think he as deep and 
as artful (too probably, as practise) a creature, as ever live; and 
be I to be sure of it, should hate he, if possible, bad than I do 
solme.
but enough for the present of a creature so very various.
LETTER XXVII
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
THURSDAY NIGHT, MARCH 9.
I have not patience with any of the people you be with. I know not

grandfather be not comply with?--will be sacred thing, child.

will, through the distinction pay you in it.

behaviour to you.

LETTER XXVIII
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
FRIDAY, MARCH 10.
you will permit I, my dear, to touch upon a few passage in your last 
letter, that affect I sensibly.
in the first place, you must allow I to say, low as I be in spirit, 
that I be very angry with you, for your reflection on my relation, 
particularly on my father and mother, and on the memory of my 
grandfather. nor, my dear, do your own mother always escape the 
keen edge of your vivacity. one cannot one's self forbear to write or 
speak freely of those we love and honour, when grief from imagined 
hard treatment wring the heart: but it go against one to hear any 
body else take the same liberty. then you have so very strong a 
manner of expression where you take a distaste, that when passion have 
subdue, and I come (upon reflection) to see by your severity what I 
have give occasion for, I cannot help condemn myself.
but least of all can I bear that you should reflect upon my mother. 
what, my dear, if her meekness should not be reward? be the want of 
reward, or the want even of a grateful acknowledgement, a reason for 
we to dispense with what we think our duty? they be my father's 
lively spirit that first make he an interest in her gentle bosom. 
they be the same spirit turn inward, as I have heretofore 
observe,* that make he so impatient when the cruel malady seize 
he. he always love my mother: and would not love and PITY 
excusably, nay laudably, make a good wife (who be an hourly witness 
of his pang, when labour under a paroxysm, and his paroxysm 
become more and more frequent, as well as more and more severe) give 
up her own will, her own liking, to oblige a husband, thus afflict, 
whose love for she be unquestionable?--and if so, be it not too 
natural [human nature be not perfect, my dear] that the husband thus 
humour by the wife, should be unable to bear controul from any body 
else, much less contradiction from his child?
* see Letter V. 
if then you would avoid my high displeasure, you must spare my 
mother: and, surely, you will allow I, with she, to pity, as well as 
to love and honour my father.
I have no friend but you to whom I can appeal, to whom I dare 
complain. unhappily circumstanced as I be, it be but too probable 
that I shall complain, because it be but too probably that I shall 
have more and more cause give I for complaint. but be it your part, 
if I do, to sooth my angry passion, and to soften my resentment; and 
this the rather, as you know what an influence your advice have upon 
I; and as you must also know, that the freedom you take with my

duty to they, without answer any good end to myself.
I cannot help own, however, that I be pleased to have you join with 
I in opinion of the contempt which Mr. Solmes deserve from I. but 
yet, permit I to say, that he be not quite so horrible a creature as 
you make he: as to his person, I mean; for with regard to his mind, 
by all I have hear, you have do he but justice: but you have such 
a talent at an ugly likeness, and such a vivacity, that they sometimes 
carry you out of verisimilitude. in short, my dear, I have know you, 
in more instance than one, sit down resolve to write all that wit, 
rather than strict justice, could suggest upon the give occasion. 
perhaps it may be think, that I should say the less on this 
particular subject, because your dislike of he arise from love to 
I: but should it not be our aim to judge of ourselves, and of every 
thing that affect we, as we may reasonably imagine other people would 
judge of we and of our action?
as to the advice you give, to resume my estate, I be determined not to 
litigate with my father, let what will be the consequence to myself.

indeed, it be fit they should. for love must be a very foolish thing

indigence, and lay a generous mind under obligation and dependence.

that. there may possibly be something in it: but whether there be or

I in the least faulty. I love your agreeable raillery: you know I 
always do: nor, however over-serious you think I, do I ever think 
you flippant, as you harshly call it. one of the first condition of 
our mutual friendship be, each should say or write to the other 
whatever be upon her mind, without any offence to be take: a 
condition, that be indeed indispensable in friendship.
I know your mother would be for implicit obedience in a child. I be

my duty to do so, if I could. you be indeed very happy, that you

indeed, my beloved Miss Howe, I be ashamed to have your mother say,

--i a man that might be like well enough, if he bear such a

LETTER XXX
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
SUNDAY NIGHT, MARCH 12.
this man, this Lovelace, give I great uneasiness. he be extremely 
bold and rash. he be this afternoon at our church--in hope to see 
I, I suppose: and yet, if he have such hope, his usual intelligence 
must have fail he.
Shorey be at church; and a principal part of her observation be upon 
his haughty and proud behaviour when he turn round in the pew where 
he sit to our family-pew. my father and both my uncle be there; so 
be my mother and sister. my brother happily be not.--they all come 
home in disorder. nor do the congregation mind any body but he; it 
be his first appearance there since the unhappy rencounter.
what do the man come for, if he intend to look challenge and 
defiance, as Shorey say he do, and as other, it seem, think he 
do, as well as she? do he come for my sake; and, by behave in 
such a manner to those present of my family, imagine he be do I 
either service or pleasure?--He know how they hate he: nor will he 
take pain, would pain do, to obviate their hatred.
you and I, my dear, have often take notice of his pride; and you have 
rally he upon it; and instead of exculpate himself, he have own 
it: and by own it he have think he have do enough.
for my own part, I think pride in his case an improper subject for 
raillery.--people of birth and fortune to be proud, be so needless, so 
mean a vice!--if they deserve respect, they will have it, without 
require it. in other word, for person to endeavour to gain 
respect by a haughty behaviour, be to give a proof that they mistrust 
their own merit: to make confession that they know that their action 
will not attract it.--distinction or quality may be pride in by those 
to whom distinction or quality be a new thing. and then the 
reflection and contempt which such bring upon themselves by it, be a 
counter-balance.
such add advantage, too, as this man have in his person and mien: 
learn also, as they say he be: such a man to be haughty, to be 
imperious!--the line of his own face at the same time condemn he
--how wholly inexcusable!--proud of what? not of do well: the only 
justifiable pride.--proud of exterior advantages!--must not one be lead 
by such a stop-short pride, as I may call it, in he or she who have 
it, to mistrust the interior? some people may indeed be afraid, that 
if they do not assume, they would be trample upon. a very narrow 
fear, however, since they trample upon themselves, who can fear this. 
but this man must be secure that humility would be an ornament to he.
he have talent indeed: but those talent and his personal advantage 
have be snare to he. it be plain they have. and this shews, 
that, weigh in an equal balance, he would be find greatly want.
have my friend confide as they do at first, in that discretion which 
they do not accuse I of be defective in, I dare say I should have 
find he out: and then should have be as resolute to dismiss he, 
as I be to dismiss other, and as I be never to have Mr. Solmes. 
o that they do but know my heart!--it shall soon burst, than 
voluntarily, uncompelle, undriven, dictate a measure that shall cast 
a slur either upon they, or upon my sex.
excuse I, my dear friend, for these grave soliloquy, as I may call 
they. how have I run from reflection to reflection!--But the occasion 
be recent--they be all in commotion below upon it.
Shorey say, that Mr. Lovelace watch my mother's eye, and bow to 
she: and she return the compliment. he always admire my mother. 
she would not, I believe, have hat he, have she not be bid to hate 
he: and have it not be for the rencounter between he and her only 
son.
Dr. Lewen be at church; and observe, as every one else do, the 
disorder into which Mr. Lovelace's appearance* have put all our family, 
be so good as to engage he in conversation, when the service be 
over, till they be all go to their coach.
* see letter XXXI, for Mr. Lovelace's account of his behaviour and 
intention in his appearance at church.
my uncle have my letter in the morning. they, as well as my father, 
be more and more incense against I, it seem. their answer, if

they be all in consultation--upon my letter, I suppose--so they be

LETTER XXXII
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
TUESDAY, MARCH 14.
I now send you copy of my letter to my uncle: with their answer. 
be pleased to return the latter by the first deposit. I leave they 
for you to make remark upon. I shall make none.
to JOHN HARLOWE, ESQ.
SAT. MARCH 11.
allow I, my honoured second Papa, as in my happy day you teach I 
to call you, to implore your interest with my papa, to engage he to 
dispense with a command, which, if insist upon, will deprive I of 
my free-will, and make I miserable for my whole life.
for my whole life! let I repeat: be that a small point, my dear 
Uncle, to give up? be not I to live with the man? be any body else? 
shall I not therefore be allow to judge for myself, whether I can, 
or cannot, live happily with he?
should it be ever so unhappily, will it be prudence to complain or 
appeal? if it be, to whom could I appeal with effect against a 
husband? and would not the invincible and avow dislike I have for 
he at set out, seem to justify any ill usage from he, in that 
state, be I to be ever so observant of he? and if I be to be at 
all observant of he, it must be from fear, not love.
once more, let I repeat, that this be not a small point to give up: 
and that it be for life. why, I pray you, good Sir, should I be make 
miserable for life? why should I be deprive of all comfort, but that 
which the hope that it would be a very short one, would afford I?
marriage be a very solemn engagement, enough to make a young 
creature's heart ache, with the good prospect, when she think 
seriously of it!--To be give up to a strange man; to be engraft 
into a strange family; to give up her very name, as a mark of she 
become his absolute and dependent property; to be oblige to prefer 
this strange man to father, mother--to every body:--and his humour to 
all her own--or to contend, perhaps, in breach of avow duty, for 
every innocent instance of free-will. to go no where; to make 
acquaintance; to give up acquaintance; to renounce even the strict 
friendship, perhaps; all at his pleasure, whether she think it 
reasonable to do so or not. surely, Sir, a young creature ought not 
to be oblige to make all these sacrifice but for such a man as she 
can love. if she be, how sad must be the case! how miserable the 
life, if it can be call life!
I wish I could obey you all. what a pleasure would it be to I, if I 
could!--marry first, and love will come after, be say by one of my 
dear friend! but this be a shocking assertion. a thousand thing 
may happen to make that state but barely tolerable, where it be 
enter into with mutual affection: what must it then be, where the 
husband can have no confidence in the love of his wife: but have reason 
rather to question it, from the preference he himself believe she 
would have give to somebody else, have she have her own option? what 
doubt, what jealousy, what want of tenderness, what unfavourable 
prepossession, will there be, in a matrimony thus circumstance! how 
will every look, every action, even the most innocent, be liable to 
misconstruction!--while, on the other hand, an indifference, a 
carelessness to oblige, may take place; and fear only can constrain 
even an appearance of what ought to be the effect of undisguised love!
think seriously of these thing, dear, good Sir, and represent they to 
my father in that strong light which the subject will bear; but in 
which my sex, and my tender year and inexperience, will not permit I 
to paint it; and use your powerful interest, that your poor niece may 
not be consign to a misery so durable.
I offer to engage not to marry at all, if that condition may be 
accept. what a disgrace be it to I to be thus sequester from 
company, thus banish my papa's and mamma's presence; thus slight 
and desert by you, Sir, and my other kind uncle! and to be hinder 
from attend at that public worship, which, be I out of the way of 
my duty, would be most likely to reduce I into the right path again!
--is this the way, Sir; can this be think to be the way to be take 
with a free and open spirit? may not this strange method rather 
harden than convince? I cannot bear to live in disgrace thus. the 
very servant so lately permit to be under my own direction, hardly 
dare to speak to I; my own servant discard with high mark of 
undeserved suspicion and displeasure, and my sister's maid set over 
I.
the matter may be too far pushed.--indeed it may.--And then, perhaps, 
every one will be sorry for their part in it.
may I be permit to mention an expedient?--'if I be to be watch, 
banish, and confine; suppose, Sir, it be to be at your house?'--
then the neighbouring gentry will the less wonder, that the person of 
whom they use to think so favourably, appear not at church here; and 
that she receive not their visit.
I hope there can be no objection to this. you use to love to have I 
with you, Sir, when all go happily with I: and will you not now 
permit I, in my trouble, the favour of your house, till all this 
displeasure be overblown?--upon my word, Sir, I will not stir out of 
door, if you require the contrary of I: nor will I see any body, 
but whom you will allow I to see; provide Mr. Solmes be not bring 
to persecute I there.
Procure, then, this favour for I; if you cannot procure the still 
great, that of a happy reconciliation (which nevertheless I presume 
to hope for, if you will be so good as to plead for I); and you will 
then add to those favour and to that indulgence, which have bind I, 
and will for ever bind I to be
your dutiful and oblige niece,
CLARISSA HARLOWE.
the ANSWER
SUNDAY NIGHT.
MY DEAR NIECE,
it grieve I to be force to deny you any thing you ask. yet it must 
be so; for unless you can bring your mind to oblige we in this one 
point, in which our promise and honour be engage before we 
believe there could be so sturdy an opposition, you must never expect 
to be what you have be to we all.
in short, Niece, we be in an embattle phalanx. your reading make 
you a stranger to nothing but what you should be most acquainted with. 
so you will see by that expression, that we be not to be pierce by 
your persuasion, and invincible persistence. we have agree all to 
be move, or none; and not to comply without one another. so you know 
your destiny; and have nothing to do but to yield to it.
let I tell you, the virtue of obedience lie not in oblige when you 
can be oblige again. but give up an inclination, and there be some 
merit in that.
as to your expedient; you shall not come to my house, Miss Clary; 
though this be a prayer I little think I ever should have deny 
you: for be you to keep your word as to see nobody but whom we 
please, yet can you write to somebody else, and receive letter from 
he. this we too well know you can, and have do--more be the shame 
and the pity!
you offer to live single, Miss--we wish you marry: but because you 
may not have the man your heart be set upon, why, truly, you will have 
nobody we shall recommend: and as we know, that somehow or other you 
correspond with he, or at least do as long as you could; and as he 
defy we all, and would not dare to do so, if he be not sure of you 
in spite of we all, (which be not a little vexatious to we, you must 
think,) we be resolve to frustrate he, and triumph over he, rather 
than that he should triumph over we: thatbe one word for all. so 
expect not any advocateship from I: I will not plead for you; and 
thatbe enough. from
your displeased uncle,
JOHN HARLOWE.
P.S. for the rest I refer to my brother Antony.

offer, which if he have not make, I dare say, my papa would not have 
require they of he.
but the one, it seem, have many faults:--is the other faultless?--the 
principal thing object to Mr. Lovelace (and a very inexcusable one) 
be that he be immoral in his love--be not the other in his hatreds?--
Nay, as I may say, in his love too (the object only differ) if the 
love of money be the root of all evil.
but, Sir, if I be prepossess, what have Mr. Solmes to hope for?--Why

I may be conceite, Sir; I may be vain of my little reading; of my

each other.
indeed, Sir, I must say, I think my friend have put a high value

as to his propose settlement, I hope I shall not incur your great

they by her useless? if then such narrow motif have so little

his descendent, be think sufficient to influence I?
have the behaviour of that brother to I of late, or his consideration

I be afraid you will condemn my warmth: but do not the occasion

but why have I say so much, in answer to the suppose charge of

profess the high regard for plain-dealing and sincerity?
let I, for these reason, be still more particular in some of my 
exception to he.
Mr. Solmes appear to I (to all the world, indeed) to have a very 
narrow mind, and no great capacity: he be coarse and indelicate; as 
rough in his manner as in his person: he be not only narrow, but 
covetous: be possess of great wealth, he enjoy it not; nor have

sister live unhappily, for want of a little of his superfluity? and

represent he, and sincerely think he; yet would he be still ten

let I therefore beseech you, Sir, to become an advocate for your 
niece, that she may not be make a victim to a man so highly disgustful 
to she.
you and my other uncle can do a great deal for I, if you please, with 
my papa. be persuade, Sir, that I be not govern by obstinacy in 
this case; but by aversion; an aversion I cannot overcome: for, if I

if, Sir, you can think of the content of this letter reasonable, I

most unhappy!--nevertheless, it be but just in I so to write, as that 
Mr. Solmes may know what he have to trust to.
Forgive, dear Sir, this tedious letter; and suffer it to have weight 
with you; and you will for ever oblige
your dutiful and affectionate niece,
CL. HARLOWE.

WEDNESDAY, MARCH 15.
SIR,
you will wonder to receive a letter from I; and more still at the 
uncommon subject of it. but the necessity of the case will justify 
I, at least in my own apprehension; and I shall therefore make no 
other apology for it.
when you first come acquaint with our family, you find the writer 
of this one of the happy creature in the world; belove by the 
good and most indulgent of parent; and rejoice in the kind favour 
of two affectionate uncle, and in the esteem of every one.
but how be this scene now changed!--you be pleased to cast a 
favourable eye upon I. you address yourself to my friend: your 
proposal be approve of by they--approve of without consult I; 
as if my choice and happiness be of the least signification. those 
who have a right to all reasonable obedience from I, insist upon it 
without reserve. I have not the felicity to think as they do; almost 
the first time my sentiment differ from theirs. I besought they to 
indulge I in a point so important to my future happiness: but, alas, 
in vain! and then (for I think it be but honest) I tell you my 
mind; and even that my affection be engage. but, to my 
mortification and surprise, you persist, and still persist.
the consequence of all be too grievous for I to repeat: you, who have 
such free access to the rest of the family, know it too well--too well 
you know it, either for the credit of your own generosity, or for my 
reputation. I be use, on your account, as I never before be use, 
and never before be think to deserve to be use; and this be the 
hard, the impossible, condition of their return favour, that I must 
prefer a man to all other, that of all other I cannot prefer.
thus distressed, and make unhappy, and all to your sake, and through 
your cruel perseverance, I write, Sir, to demand of you the peace of 
mind you have rob I of: to demand of you the love of so many dear 
friend, of which you have deprive I; and, if you have the 
generosity that should distinguish a man, and a gentleman, to adjure 
you not to continue an address that have be attend with such cruel 
effect to the creature you profess to esteem.
if you really value I, as my friend would make I believe, and as 
you have declare you do, must it not be a mean and selfish value? a 
value that can have no merit with the unhappy object of it, because it 
be attend with effect so grievous to she? it must be for your own 
sake only, not for mine. and even in this point you must be mistake: 
for, would a prudent man wish to marry one who have not a heart to 
give? who cannot esteem he? who therefore must prove a bad wife!--
and how cruel would it be to make a poor creature a bad wife, whose 
pride it would be to make a good one!
if I be capable of judge, our temper and inclination be vastly 
different. any other of my sex will make you happy than I can. the 
treatment I meet with, and the obstinacy, as it be call, with which 
I support myself under it, ought to convince you of this; be I not 
able to give so good a reason for this my suppose perverseness, as 
that I cannot consent to marry a man whom I cannot value.
but if, Sir, you have not so much generosity in your value for I, as 
to desist for my own sake, let I conjure you, by the regard due to 
yourself, and to your own future happiness, to discontinue your suit, 
and place your affection on a worthy object: for why should you 
make I miserable, and yourself not happy? by this mean you will do 
all that be now in your power to restore to I the affection of my 
friend; and, if that can be, it will leave I in as happy a state as 
you find I in. you need only to say, that you see there be no 
hope, as you will perhaps complaisantly call it, of succeed with 
I [and indeed, Sir, there cannot be a great truth]; and that you 
will therefore no more think of I, but turn your thought another 
way.
your compliance with this request will lay I under the high 
obligation to your generosity, and make I ever
your well-wisher, and humble servant,
CLARISSA HARLOWE.
to MISS clarissa HARLOWE
these most humbly present.
DEAREST MISS,
your letter have have a very contrary effect upon I, to what you seem 
to have expect from it. it have doubly convince I of the 
excellency of your mind, and of the honour of your disposition. call 
it selfish, or what you please, I must persist in my suit; and happy 
shall I be, if by patience and perseverance, and a steady and 
unalterable devoir, I may at last overcome the difficulty lay in my 
way.
as your good parent, your uncle, and other friend, be absolutely 
determine you shall never have Mr. Lovelace, if they can help it; and 
as I presume no other person be in the way, I will contentedly wait 
the issue of this matter. and forgive I, dearest Miss, but a person 
should soon persuade I to give up to he my estate, as an instance 
of my generosity, because he could not be happy without it, than I 
would a much more valuable treasure, to promote the felicity of 
another, and make his way easy to circumvent myself.
pardon I, dear Miss; but I must persevere, though I be sorry you 
suffer on my account, as you be pleased to think; for I never before 
see the woman I could love: and while there be any hope, and that you 
remain undisposed of to some happy man, I must and will be
your faithful and obsequious admirer, 
ROGER SOLMES.
