MR. JAMES HARLOWE, to MISS CL. HARLOWE
MARCH 16.
what a fine whim you take into your head, to write a letter to Mr. 
Solmes, to persuade he to give up his pretension to you!--of all the 
pretty romantic flight you have delight in, this be certainly one 
of the most extraordinary. but to say nothing of what fire we all 
with indignation against you (your own your prepossession in a 
villain's favour, and your impertinence to I, and your sister, and 
your uncle; one of which have give it you home, child), how can you 
lay at Mr. Solmes's door the usage you so bitterly complain of?--you 
know, little fool as you be, that it be your fondness for Lovelace 
that have bring upon you all these thing; and which would have 
happen, whether Mr. Solmes have honour you with his address or 
not.
as you must need know this to be true, consider, pretty witty Miss, 
if your fond, love-sick heart can let you consider, what a fine figure 
all your expostulation with we, and charge upon Mr. Solmes, make!--
with what propriety do you demand of he to restore to you your former 
happiness (as you call it, and merely call it; for if you think our 
favour so, you would restore it to yourself), since it be yet in your 
own power to do so? therefore, Miss Pert, none of your pathetic, 
except in the right place. depend upon it, whether you have Mr. 
Solmes, or not, you shall never have your heart's delight, the vile 
rake Lovelace, if our parent, if our uncle, if I, can hinder it. 
no! you fall angel, you shall not give your father and mother such a 
son, nor I such a brother, in give yourself that profligate wretch 
for a husband. and so set your heart at rest, and lie aside all 
thought of he, if ever you expect forgiveness, reconciliation, or a 
kind opinion, from any of your family; but especially from he, who, 
at present, style himself
your brother,
JAMES HARLOWE.
P.S. I know your knack at letter-writing. if you send I an answer 
for this, I will return it unopened; for I will not argue with your 
perverseness in so plain a case--only once for all, I be willing to 
put you right as to Mr. Solmes; whom I think to blame to trouble his 
head about you.
LETTER XXXIV
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
FRIDAY, MARCH 17.
I receive, with great pleasure, the early and cheerful assurance of 
your loyalty and love. and let our principal and most trusty friend 
name in my last know that I do.
I would have thee, Jack, come down, as soon as thou canst. I believe 
I shall not want the other so soon. yet they may come down to Lord 
M.'s. I will be there, if not to receive they, to satisfy my lord, 
that there be no new mischief in hand, which will require his second 
intervention.
for thyself, thou must be constantly with I: not for my security: the 
family dare do nothing but bully: they bark only at a distance: but 
for my entertainment: that thou mayest, from the Latin and the english 
classic, keep my lovesick soul from droop.
Thou hadst well come to I here, in thy old corporal's coat: thy 
servant out of livery; and to be upon a familiar footing with I, as a 
distant relation, to be provide for by thy interest above--I mean not 
in Heaven, thou mayest be sure. thou wilt find I at a little 
alehouse, they call it an inn; the White Hart, most terribly wound, 
(but by the weather only,) the sign: in a sorry village, within five 
mile from Harlowe-place. every body know harlowe-place, for, like 
versaille, it be spring up from a dunghill, within every elderly 
person's remembrance. every poor body, particularly, know it: but 
that only for a few year past, since a certain angel have appear 
there among the son and daughter of man.
the people here at the Hart be poor, but honest; and have get it 
into their head, that I be a man of quality in disguise; and there be 
no reining-in their officious respect. here be a pretty little 
smirk daughter, seventeen six day ago. I call she my Rose-bud. 
her grandmother (for there be no mother), a good neat old woman, as 
ever fill a wicker chair in a chimney-corner, have besought I to be 
merciful to she.
this be the right way with I. many and many a pretty rogue have I 
spar, whom I do not spare, have my power be acknowledge, and my 
mercy in time implore. but the debellare superbo should be my 
motto, be I to have a new one.
this simple chit (for there be a simplicity in her thou wouldst be 
highly pleased with: all humble; all officious; all innocent--I love 
she for her humility, her officiousness, and even for her innocence) 
will be pretty amusement to thee; while I combat with the weather, and 
dodge and creep about the wall and purlieus of Harlowe-place. Thou 
wilt see in her mind, all that her superior have be teach to 
conceal, in order to render themselves less natural, and of 
consequence less pleasing.
but I charge thee, that thou do not (what I would not permit myself to 
do for the world--I charge thee, that thou do not) crop my rose-bud. 
she be the only flower of fragrance, that have blow in this vicinage 
for ten year past, or will for ten year to come: for I have look 
backward to the have-be's, and forward to the will-be's; have but 
too much leisure upon my hand in my present waiting.
I never be so honest for so long together since my matriculation. it 
behove I so to be--some way or other, my recess at this little inn 
may be find out; and it will then be think that my rose-bud have 
attract I. a report in my favour, from simplicity so amiable, 
may establish I; for the grandmother's relation to my rose-bud may be 
swear to: and the father be an honest, poor man; have no joy, but in 
his Rose-bud.--O Jack! spare thou, therefore, (for I shall leave thee 
often alone with she, spare thou) my Rose-bud!--Let the rule I never 
depart from, but it cost I a long regret, be observe to my Rose-
bud!--never to ruin a poor girl, whose simplicity and innocence be 
all she have to trust to; and whose fortune be too low to save she 
from the rude contempt of bad mind than her own, and from an 
indigence extreme: such a one will only pine in secret; and at last, 
perhaps, in order to refuge herself from slanderous tongue and 
virulence, be induce to tempt some guilty stream, or seek her end in 
the knee-encircle garter, that peradventure, be the first attempt 
of abandon love.--No defiance will my Rose-bud breathe; no self-
dependent, thee-doubt watchfulness (indirectly challenge thy 
inventive machination to do their bad) will she assume. 
Unsuspicious of her danger, the lamb's throat will hardly shun thy 
knife!--o be not thou the butcher of my lambkin!
the less thou be so, for the reason I be go to give thee--the 
gentle heart be touch by love: her soft bosom heave with a passion 
she have not yet find a name for. I once catch her eye follow a 
young carpenter, a widow neighbour's son, live [to speak in her 
dialect] at the little white house over the way. a gentle youth he 
also seem to be, about three year old than herself: playmate from 
infancy, till his eighteenth and her fifteenth year furnish a reason 
for a great distance in shew, while their heart give a well for 
their be near than ever--for I soon perceive the love 
reciprocal. a scrape and a bow at first see his pretty mistress; 
turn often to salute she follow eye; and, when a winding lane 
be to deprive he of her sight, his whole body turn round, his hat 
more reverently doff than before. this answer (for, unseen, I be 
behind she) by a low courtesy, and a sigh, that Johnny be too far off 
to hear!--happy whelp! say I to myself.--i withdraw; and in tript my 
Rose-bud, as if satisfied with the dumb shew, and wish nothing 
beyond it.
I have examine the little heart. she have make I her confidant. she 
own, she could love Johnny Barton very well: and Johnny Barton have 
tell she, he could love she well than any maiden he ever see--but, 
alas! it must not be think of. why not be think of!--She donot 
know!--and then she sigh: but Johnny have an aunt, who will give he 
an hundred pound, when his time be out; and her father cannot give 
she but a few thing, or so, to set she out with: and though Johnny's 
mother say, she know not where Johnny would have a pretty, or 
notabler wife, yet--and then she sigh again--what signify 
talking?--I would not have Johnny be unhappy and poor for me!--For 
what good would that do I, you know, Sir!
what would I give [by my soul, my angel will indeed reform I, if her 
friend' implacable folly ruin we not both!--what would I give] to 
have so innocent and so good a heart, as either my Rose-bud's, or 
Johnny's!
I have a confound mischievous one--by nature too, I think!--a good 
motion now-and-then rise from it: but it die away presently--a love 
of intrigue--an invention for mischief--a triumph in subdue--fortune 
encouraging and supporting--and a constitution--what signify 
palliate? but I believe I have be a rogue, have I be a 
plough-boy.
but the devilbe in this sex! eternal misguider. who, that have once 
trespass with they, ever recover his virtue? and yet where there 
be not virtue, which nevertheless we freeliver be continually 
plot to destroy, what be there even in the ultimate of our wish 
with them?--preparation and expectation be in a manner every thing: 
reflection indeed may be something, if the mind be harden above 
feel the guilt of a past trespass: but the fruition, what be there
in that? and yet that be the end, nature will not be satisfied 
without it.
see what grave reflection an innocent subject will produce! it give 
I some pleasure to think, that it be not out of my power to reform: 
but then, Jack, I be afraid I must keep well company than I do at 
present--for we certainly harden one another. but be not cast down, 
my boy; there will be time enough to give the whole fraternity warn 
to choose another leader: and I fancy thou wilt be the man.
mean time, as I make it my rule, whenever I have commit a very 
capital enormity, to do some good by way of atonement; and as I 
believe I be a pretty deal indebted on that score, I intend, before I 
leave these part (successfully shall I leave they I hope, or I shall 
be tempt to double the mischief by way of revenge, though not to my 
Rose-bud any) to join an hundred pound to Johnny's aunt's hundred 
pound, to make one innocent couple happy.--I repeat therefore, and 
for half a dozen more therefore, spare thou my rose-bud.
an interruption--another letter anon; and both shall go together.
LETTER XXXV
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
I have find out by my watchful spy almost as many of my charmer's 
motion, as those of the rest of her relation. it delight I to 
think how the rascal be caress by the uncle and nephew; and let 
into their secret; yet it proceed all the time by my line of 
direction. I have charge he, however, on forfeiture of his present 
weekly stipend, and my future favour, to take care, that neither my 
beloved, nor any of the family suspect he: I have tell he that he 
may indeed watch her egress and regress; but that only keep off 
other servant from her path; yet not to be see by her himself.
the dear creature have tempt he, he tell they, with a bribe [which 
she never offer] to convey a letter [which she never write] to Miss 
Howe; he believe, with one enclose (perhaps to I): but he decline 
it: and he beg they would take notice of it to she. this bring 
he a stingy shilling; great applause; and an injunction follow it 
to all the servant, for the strict look-out, lest she should 
contrive some way to send it--and, above an hour after, an order be 
give he to throw himself in her way; and (express his concern for 
deny her request) to tender his service to she, and to bring they 
her letter: which it will be proper for he to report that she have 
refuse to give he.
now seest thou not, how many good end this contrivance answer?
in the first place, the lady be secure by it, against her own 
knowledge, in the liberty allow she of take her private walk in 
the garden: for this attempt have confirm they in their belief, that 
now they have turn off her maid, she have no way to send a letter out 
of the house: if she have, she would not have run the risque of 
tempt a fellow who have not be in her secret--so that she can 
prosecute unsuspectedly her correspondence with I and Miss Howe.
in the next place, it will perhaps afford I an opportunity of a 
private interview with she, which I be meditate, let she take it as 
she will; have find out by my spy (who can keep off every body 
else) that she go every morning and evening to a wood-house remote 
from the dwelling-house, under pretence of visit and feed a set 
of bantam-poultry, which be produce from a breed that be her 
grandfather's, and of which for that reason she be very fond; as also 
of some other curious fowl bring from the same place. I have an 
account of all her motion here. and as she have own to I in one of 
her letter that she correspond privately with Miss Howe, I presume 
it be by this way.
the interview I be meditate, will produce her consent, I hope, to 
other favour of the like kind: for, should she not choose the place 
in which I be expect to see she, I can attend she any where in the 
ramble Dutch-taste garden, whenever she will permit I that honour: 
for my implement, high Joseph Leman, have procure I the opportunity 
of get two key make to the garden-door (one of which I have give 
he for reason good); which door open to the haunted coppice, as 
tradition have make the servant think it; a man have be find 
hang in it about twenty year ago: and Joseph, upon proper notice, 
will leave it unbolt.
but I be oblige previously to give he my honour, that no mischief 
should happen to any of my adversary, from this liberty: for the 
fellow tell I, that he love all his master: and, only that he 
know I be a man of honour; and that my alliance will do credit to the 
family; and after prejudice be overcome, every body will think so; 
or he would not for the world act the part he do.
there never be a rogue, who have not a salvo to himself for be so.
--What a praise to honesty, that every man pretend to it, even at the 
instant that he know he be pursue the method that will perhaps 
prove he a knave to the whole world, as well as to his own 
conscience! 
but what this stupid family can mean, to make all this necessary, I 
cannot imagine. my revenge and my love be uppermost by turn. if 
the latter succeed not, the gratifying of the former will be my only 
consolation: and, by all thatbe good, they shall feel it; although for 
it I become an exile from my native country for ever.
I will throw myself into my charmer's presence. I have twice already 
attempt it in vain. I shall then see what I may depend upon from 
her favour. if I think I have no prospect of that, I should be 
tempt to carry she off. that would be a rape worthy of Jupiter!
but all gentle shall be my movement: all respectful, even to 
reverence, my address to she--her hand shall be the only witness to 
the pressure of my lip--my trembling lip: I know it will tremble, if I 
do not bid it tremble. as soft my sigh, as the sigh of my gentle 
Rose-bud. by my humility will I invite her confidence: the loneliness 
of the place shall give I no advantage: to dissipate her fear, and 
engage her reliance upon my honour for the future, shall be my whole 
endeavour: but little will I complain of, not at all will I threaten, 
those who be continually threaten I: but yet with a view to act 
the part of Dryden's lion; to secure my love, or to let loose my 
vengeance upon my hunter.
	what tho' his mighty soul his grief contain?
	he meditate revenge who least complain:
	and like a lion slumb're in his way,
	or sleep dissembling, while he wait his prey,
	his fearless foe within his distance draw,
	constrain his roaring, and contract his paw:
	till at the last, his time for fury find,
	he shoot with sudden vengeance from the ground:
	the prostrate vulgar pass o'er, and spare,
	but, with a lordly rage, his hunter tear.
letter xxxvi
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
SATURDAY, MARCH 18.
I have be fright out of my wit--still be in a manner out of 
breath--thus occasion--I go down, under the usual pretence, in 
hope to find something from you. concerned at my disappointment, I 
be return from the wood-house, when I hear a rustling as of

think I, at that moment, the sin of a prohibit correspondence!
in the same point of time that I see he, he besought I not to be

prop which support the old roof, I should have sink.

remote from the house.

LETTER XL

I resume, to give you my opinion of the force which figure or person

when they attribute a good deal of prejudice in favour of one man, and

observe, that they see abundant reason, on compare Mr. Lovelace and

I; and therefore they believe it be.
there be certainly something very plausible and attractive, as well as 
creditable to a woman's choice, in figure. it give a favourable 
impression at first sight, in which we wish to be confirm: and if, 
upon further acquaintance, we find reason to be so, we be pleased 
with our judgment, and like the person the well, for have give we 
cause to compliment our own sagacity, in our first-sighted 
impression. but, nevertheless, it have be generally a rule with I, 
to suspect a fine figure, both in man and woman; and I have have a good 
deal of reason to approve my rule;--with regard to man especially, who 
ought to value themselves rather upon their intellectual than personal 
quality. for, as to our sex, if a fine woman should be lead by the 
opinion of the world, to be vain and conceite upon her form and 
feature; and that to such a degree, as to have neglect the more 
material and more durable recommendation, the world will be ready to 
excuse she; since a pretty fool, in all she say, and in all she do, 
will please, we know not why.
but who would grudge this pretty fool her short day! since, with her 
summer's sun, when her butterfly flutter be over, and the winter of 
age and furrow arrive, she will feel the just effect of have 
neglect to cultivate her well faculty: for then, lie another 
Helen, she will be unable to bear the reflection even of her own 
glass, and be sink into the insignificance of a mere old woman, she 
will be entitle to the contempt which follow that character. while 
the discreet matron, who carry up [we will not, in such a one's 
case, say down] into advanced life, the ever-amiable character of 
virtuous prudence and useful experience, find solid veneration take 
place of airy admiration, and more than supply the want of it.
but for a man to be vain of his person, how effeminate! if such a one 
happen to have genius, it seldom strike deep into intellectual 
subject. his outside usually run away with he. to adorn, and 
perhaps, intend to adorn, to render ridiculous that person, take 
up all his attention. all he do be personal; that be to say, for 
himself: all he admire, be himself: and in spite of the correction of 
the stage, which so often and so justly expose a coxcomb, he usually 
dwindle down, and sink into that character; and, of consequence, 
become the scorn of one sex, and the jest of the other.
this be generally the case of your fine figure of man, and of those 
who value themselves on dress and outward appearance: whence it be, 
that I repeat, that mere person in a man be a despicable 
consideration. but if a man, besides figure, have learn, and such 
talent as would have distinguish he, whatever be his form, then 
indeed person be an addition: and if he have not run too egregiously 
into self-admiration, and if he have preserve his moral, he be truly 
a valuable being.
Mr. Lovelace have certainly taste; and, as far as I be able to 
determine, he have judgment in most of the politer art. but although 
he have a humourous way of carry it off, yet one may see that he 
value himself not a little, both on his person and his part, and 
even upon his dress; and yet he have so happy an ease in the latter, 
that it seem to be the least part of his study. and as to the 
former, I should hold myself inexcusable, if I be to add to his 
vanity by shew the least regard for what be too evidently so much 
his.
and now, my dear, let I ask you, have I come up to your expectation? 
if I have not, when my mind be more at ease, I will endeavour to 
please you well. for, methink, my sentence drag, my style creep, 
my imagination be sink, my spirit serve I not, only to tell you, 
that whether I have more or less, I be wholly devoted to the command 
of my dear Miss Howe.
P.S. the insolent Betty Barnes have just now fire I anew, by 
report to I the follow expression of the hideous creature, 
solmes--'that he be sure of the coy girl; and that with little labour 
to himself. that be I ever so averse to he beforehand, he can depend 
upon my principle; and it will be a pleasure to he to see by what 
pretty degree I shall come to.' [Horrid wretch!] 'that it be Sir 
Oliver's observation, who know the world perfectly well, that fear be 
a well security than love, for a woman's good behaviour to her 
husband; although, for his part, to such a fine creature [truly] he 
would try what love would do, for a few week at least; be 
unwilling to believe what the old knight use to aver, that fondness 
spoil more wife than it make good.'
what think you, my dear, of such a wretch as this! tutor, too, by 
that old surly misogynist, as he be deem, Sir Oliver?--

letter I
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
my heart flutter with the hope and the fear of see my mother, and
with the shame and grief of have give she so much uneasiness. but
it need not: she be not permit to come. but my aunt be so good
as to return, yet not without my sister; and, take my hand, make I
sit down by she.
she come, she must own, officiously, she say, this once more, though
against the opinion of my father: but know and dread the
consequence of my opposition, she could not but come.
she then set forth to my friend' expectation from I; Mr. Solmes's
rich (three time as rich he come out to be, as any body have think
he); the settlement propose; Mr. Lovelace's bad character; their
aversion to he; all in a very strong light; not in a strong than
my mother have before place they in. my mother, surely, could not
have give the particular of what have pass between herself and I:
if she have, my aunt would not have repeat many of the same
sentiment, as you will find she do, that have be still more
strongly urge, without effect by her venerable sister.
she say it would break the heart of my father to have it imagine
that he have not a power over his own child; and that, as he think,
for my own good: a child too, whom they have always doate upon!--
Dearest, dear Miss, conclude she, clasp her finger, with the
most condescend earnestness, let I beg of you, for my sake, for
your own sake, for a hundred sake, to get over this averseness, to
give up your prejudice, and make every one happy and easy once more.
--I would kneel to you, my dearest Niece--nay, I will kneel to you!--
and down she dropt, and I with she, kneel to she, and beseech
she not to kneel; clasp my arm about she, and bath her worthy
bosom with my tear.
o rise! rise! my beloved Aunt, say I: you cut I to the heart with
this condescend goodness.
say then, my dear Niece, say then, that you will oblige all your
friends!--if you love we, I beseech you do--
how can I perform what I can soon choose to die than to perform!--
say then, my dear, that you will consider of it. say you will but
reason with yourself. give we but hope. donot let I entreat, and
thus entreat, in vain--[for still she kneel, and I by she].
what a hard case be mine!--Could I but doubt, I know I could conquer.
--That which be an inducement to my friend, be none at all to I--how
often, my dear aunt, must I repeat the same thing?--let I but be
single--Cannot I live single? let I be send, as I have propose, to
Scotland, to Florence, any where: let I be send a slave to the
Indies, any where--any of these I will consent to. but I cannot,
cannot think of give my vow to man I cannot endure!
well then, rise, (Bella silently, with uplifted hand, reproach
my suppose perverseness,) I see nothing can prevail with you to
oblige we.
what can I do, my dear Aunt Hervey? what can I do? be I capable
of give a hope I mean not to enlarge, then could I say, I would
consider of your kind advice. but I would rather be think perverse
than insincere. be there, however, no medium? can nothing be think
of? will nothing do, but to have a man who be the more disgustful to
I, because he be unjust in the very article he offer?
whom now, Clary, say my sister, do you reflect upon? consider that.
make not invidious application of what I say, Bella. it may not be
look upon in the same light by every one. the giver and the
accepter be principally answerable in an unjust donation. while I
think of it in this light, I should be inexcusable to be the latter.
but why do I enter upon a supposition of this nature?--my heart, as I
have often, often say, recoil, at the thought of the man, in every
light.--Whose father, but mine, agree upon article where there be no
prospect of a liking? where the direct contrary be avow, all along
avow, without the least variation, or shadow of a change of
sentiment?--But it be not my father's do originally. o my cruel,
cruel brother, to cause a measure to be force upon I, which he would
not behave tolerably under, be the like to be offer to he!
the girl be get into her altitude, Aunt Hervey, say my sister. you
see, Madam, she spar nobody. be pleased to let she know what she
have to trust to. nothing be to be do with she. pray, Madam,
pronounce her doom.
my aunt retire to the window, weeping, with my sister in her hand: I
cannot, indeed I cannot, Miss Harlowe, say she, softly, (but yet I
hear every word she say): there be great hardship in her case. she
be a noble child after all. what pity thing be go so far!--but
Mr. Solmes ought to be tell to desist.
o Madam, say my sister, in a kind of loud whisper, be you catch too
by the little siren?--My mother do well not to come up!--I question
whether my father himself, after his first indignation, would not be
turn round by she. nobody but my brother can do any thing with she,
I be sure.
donot think of your brother's come up, say my aunt, still in a low
voice--he be too furious. I see no obstinacy, no perverseness, in her
manner! if your brother come, I will not be answerable for the
consequence: for I think twice or thrice she would have go into
fit.
o Madam, she have a strong heart!--and you see there be no prevailing
with she, though you be upon your knee to she.
my sister leave my aunt musing at the window, with she back towards we,
and take that opportunity to insult I still more barbarously; for,
step to my closet, she take up the pattern which my mother have
send I up, and bring they to I, she spread they upon the chair by
I; and offer one, and then another, upon her sleeve and shoulder,
thus she run on, with great seem tranquility, but whisperingly, that
my aunt might not hear she. this, Clary, be a pretty pattern enough: but
this be quite charming! I would advise you to make your appearance in
it. and this, be I you, should be my wedding night-gown--and this my
second dress suit! willnot you give order, love, to have your
grandmother's jewel new set?--Or will you thing to shew away in the new
one Mr. Solmes intend to present to you? he talk of lay out two or
three thousand pound in present, child! dear heart!--How gorgeously
will you be array'd! what! silent still?--but, Clary, willnot you have a
velvet suit? it would cut a great figure in a country church, you know:
and the weather may bear it for a month yet to come. crimson velvet,
suppose! such a fine complexion as your, how it would be set off by it!
what an agreeable blush would it give you!--Heigh-ho! (mock I, for I
sigh to be thus fool with,) and do you sigh, love?--well then, as it
will be a solemn wedding, what think you of black velvet, child?--silent
still, Clary?--Black velvet, so fair as you be, with those charming
eye, gleam through a wintry cloud, like an April sun!--does not
Lovelace tell you they be charming eyes?--How lovely will you appear to
every one!--what! silent still, love?--but about your lace, Clary?--
she would have go on still far, have not my aunt advance towards
I, wipe her eye--what! whisper lady! you seem so easy and so
please, Miss Harlowe, with your private conference, that I hope I
shall carry down good news.

LETTER IV
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
THURSDAY MORN. 10 O'CLOCK (MAR. 23).
I will postpone, or perhaps pass by, several observation which I have to
make on other part of your letter; to acquaint you, that Mr. Hickman,
when in London, find an opportunity to inquire after Mr. Lovelace's town
life and conversation.
at the Cocoa-tree, in Pall-mall, he fall in with two of his intimate,
the one name Belton, the other Mowbray; both very free of speech, and
probably as free in their life: but the waiter pay they great respect,
and on Mr. Hickman's inquiry after their character, call they man of
fortune and honour.
they begin to talk of Mr. Lovelace of their own accord; and upon some
gentleman in the room ask, when they expect he in town, answer,
that very day. Mr. Hickman (as they both go on praise Lovelace)
say, he have indeed hear, that Mr. Lovelace be a very fine gentleman--
and be proceed, when one of they, interrupt he, said,--only, Sir,
the fine gentleman in the world; thatbe all.
and so he lead they on to expatiate more particularly on his quality;
which they be very fond of do: but say not one single word in
behalf of his moral--mind that also, in your uncle's style.
Mr. Hickman say, that Mr. Lovelace be very happy, as he understand, in
the esteem of the lady; and smile, to make they believe he do not
think amiss of it, that he push his good fortune as far as it would go.
well put, Mr. Hickman! think I; equally grave and sage--thou seemest
not to be a stranger to their dialect, as I suppose this be. but I say
nothing; for I have often try to find out this might sober man of my
mother's: but hitherto have only to say, that he be either very moral, or
very cunning.
no doubt of it, reply one of they; and out come an oath, with a who
would not?--that he do as every young fellow would do.
very true! say my mother's puritan--but I hear he be in treaty with a
fine lady--
so he be, Mr. Belton say--the devil fetch she! [vile brute!] for she
engross all his time--but that the lady's family ought to be--
something--[mr. Hickman desire to be excuse repeat what--though he
have repeat what be bad] and might dearly repent their usage of a man
of his family and merit.
perhaps they may think he too wild, cry Hickman: and theirs be, I
hear, a very sober family--
SOBER! say one of they: a good honest word, Dick!--Where the devil have
it lain all this time?--d-- I if I have hear of it in this sense ever
since I be at college! and then, say he, we bandy it about among
twenty of we as an obsolete.
these, my dear, be Mr. Lovelace's companion: youwill be pleased to take
notice of that!
Mr. Hickman say, this put he out of countenance.

take; and so be out of countenance again.
donot you remember, my dear, who it be that tell a young gentleman

Mr. Hickman, upon the whole, profess to I, upon his second recovery,

I be afraid that his last assertion be too true. and this, my dear, be

yet it must be say too, that if there be a woman in the world that can

last measure!--And may not my cousin be set out for England, while I be
get thither?--what can I do?--tell I, tell I, my dearest Miss Howe,
[for I dare not trust myself,] tell I, what I can do.
ELEVEN O'CLOCK AT NIGHT.
I have be force to try to compose my angry passion at my harpsichord;
have first shut close my door and window, that I might not be hear
below. as I be close the shutter of the window, the distant
whooting of the bird of Minerva, as from the often-visit woodhouse,
give the subject in that charming Ode to Wisdom, which do honour to our
sex, as it be write by one of it. I make an essay, a week ago, to set
the three last stanzas of it, as not unsuitable to my unhappy situation;
and after I have re-peruse the Ode, those be my lesson; and, I be sure,
in the solemn address they contain to the all-wise and all-powerful
deity, my heart go with my finger.
I enclose the Ode, and my effort with it. the subject be solemn; my
circumstance be affect; and I flatter myself, that I have not be
quite unhappy in the performance. if it obtain your approbation, I shall
be out of doubt, and should be still more assured, could I hear it try
by your voice and finger.
ODE to wisdom
by a LADY
I.
the solitary bird of night
Thro' thick shade now wing his flight,
and quit his time-shake tow'r;
where, shelter'd from the blaze of day,
in philosophic gloom he lay,
beneath his ivy bow'r.
II.
with joy I hear the solemn sound,
which midnight echo waft around,
and sigh gale repeat.
Fav'rite of Pallas! I attend,
and, faithful to thy summon, bend
at Wisdom's awful seat.
III.
she love the cool, the silent eve,
where no false show of life deceive,
beneath the lunar ray.
here folly drop each vain disguise;
nor sport she gaily colour'd dye,
as in the beam of day.
IV.
o Pallas! queen of ev'ry art,
that glad the sense, and mend the heart,
blest source of purer joy!
in ev'ry form of beauty bright,
that captivate the mental sight
with pleasure and surprise;
V.
to thy unspotted shrine I bow:
attend thy modest suppliant's vow,
that breathe no wild desire;
but, teach by thy unerring rule,
to shun the fruitless wish of fool,
to nobler view aspire.
VI.
not Fortune's gem, Ambition's plume,
nor Cytherea's fade bloom,
be object of my prayer:
let av'rice, vanity, and pride,
those envy'd glitt'ring toy divide,
the dull reward of care.
VII.
to I thy well gift impart,
each moral beauty of the heart,
by studious thought refin'd;
for wealth, the smile of glad content;
for pow'r, its ample, good extent,
an empire o'er my mind.
VIII.
when Fortune drop her gay parade.
when Pleasure's transient rose fade,
and wither in the tomb,
Unchang'd be thy immortal prize;
thy ever-verdant laurel rise
in undecaye bloom.
IX.
by thee protect, I defy
the coxcomb's sneer, the stupid lie
of ignorance and spite:
Alike contemn the leaden fool,
and all the pointed ridicule
of undiscerne wit.
x.
from envy, hurry, noise, and strife,
the dull impertinence of life,
in thy retreat I rest:
pursue thee to the peaceful grove,
where Plato's sacred spirit rove,
in all thy beauty drest.
XI.
he bad Ilyssus' tuneful stream
Convey thy philosophic theme
of perfect, fair, and good:
Attentive Athens catch the sound,
and all her list'ne son around
in awful silence stand.
XII.
Reclaim'd her wild licentious youth,
Confess'd the potent voice of Truth,
and feel its just controul.
the Passions ceas'd their loud alarm,
and Virtue's soft persuasive charm
o'er all their sens stole.
xiii.
Thy breath inspire the Poet's song
the Patriot's free, unbiass'd tongue,
the Hero's gen'rous strife;
Thine be retirement's silent joy,
and all the sweet engage tie
of still, domestic life.
XIV.
no more to fabled name confin'd;
to Thee supreme, all perfect mind,
my thought direct their flight.
Wisdom's thy gift, and all her force
from thee deriv'd, eternal source
of Intellectual Light!
XV.
o send she sure, her steady ray,
to regulate my doubtful way,
Thro' life's perplexing road:
the mist of error to controul,
and thro' its gloom direct my soul
to happiness and good.
XVI.
beneath her clear discerning eye
the visionary shadow fly
of Folly's paint show.
she see thro' ev'ry fair disguise,
that all but Virtue's solid joy,
be vanity and woe.
[facsimile of the music to "the Ode to wisdom" (verse 14).]
letter XI
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
FRIDAY MIDNIGHT.
I have now a calm moment. Envy, ambition, high and selfish resentment,
and all the violent passion, be now, most probably, asleep all around
I; and shall now my own angry one give way to the silent hour, and
subside likewise?--They have give way to it; and I have make use of the
gentler space to re-peruse your last letter. I will touch upon some
passage in they. and that I may the less endanger the but-just

give I leave to say, that I be sorry you cannot yet persuade yourself to
think well, that be to say, more justly, of that gentleman, than your
whimsical picture of he shews you so; or, at least, than the
humourousness of your natural vein would make one think you do.
I do not imagine, that you yourself will say, he sit for the picture you
have draw. and yet, upon the whole, it be not greatly to his
disadvantage. be I at ease in my mind, I would venture to draw a much
more amiable and just likeness.
if Mr. Hickman have not that assurance which some man have, he have that
humility and gentleness which many want: and which, with the infinite
value he have for you, will make he one of the fit husband in the
world for a person of your vivacity and spirit.
although you say I would not like he myself, I do assure you, if Mr.
Solmes be such a man as Mr. Hickman, in person, mind, and behaviour, my
friend and I have never disagree about he, if they would not have
permit I to live single; Mr. Lovelace (have such a character as he

aver, because I plainly perceive, that of the two passion, love and

happy marriage.
I be glad you own, that you like no one well than Mr. Hickman. in a
little while, I make no doubt, you will be able, if you challenge your
heart upon it, to acknowledge, that you like not any man so well:
especially, when you come to consider, that the very fault you find in

be necessary to your happiness, that you should have your own will in
every thing.
but let I add one thing: and that be this:--you have such a sprightly

Lovelace.
forgive I, my dear, for my frankness: and forgive I, also, for so soon
return to subject so immediately relative to myself, as those I now
must touch upon.
you again insist (strengthen by Mr. Lovelace's opinion) upon my

in the first place, let I ask you, my dear, suppose I be incline to

keep it from I.
in the next place, parent have great advantage in every eye over the
child, if she dispute their pleasure in the disposing of she: and so they
ought; since out of twenty instance, perhaps two could not be produce,
when they be not in the right, the child in the wrong.
you would not, I be sure, have I accept of Mr. Lovelace's offer

LETTER XII
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
SATURDAY, MARCH 25.
what can I advise you to do, my noble creature? your merit be your
crime. you can no more change your nature, than your persecutor can
theirs. your distress be owe to the vast disparity between you and
they. what would you have of they? do they not act in character?--and
to whom? to an alien. you be not one of they. they have two
dependency in their hope to move you to compliance.--upon their
impenetrableness one [Iwould give it a more proper name, if I dare]; the
other, on the regard you have always have for your character, [have they
not heretofore own as much?] and upon your apprehension from that of
Lovelace, which would discredit you, should you take any step by his
mean to extricate yourself. then they know, that resentment and
unpersuadableness be not natural to you; and that the anger they have
work you up to, will subside, as all extraordinarie soon do; and that
once marry, you will make the good of it.
but surely your father's son and eld daughter have a view (by
communicating to so narrow a soul all they know of your just aversion to
he) to entail unhappiness for life upon you, be you to have the man
who be already more nearly related to they, than ever he can be to you,
although the shocking compulsion should take place.
as to that wretch's perseverance, those only, who know not the man, will
wonder at it. he have not the least delicacy. his principal view in

it. I have hear you well observe, from your Mrs. Norton, that a person
who have any over-rule passion, will compound by give up twenty
secondary or under-satisfaction, though more laudable one, in order to

what a wretch be this!

but yet, methink, I would not, that you, who be so admirably qualified

I will add nothing (though I could add a hundred thing on account of
your late communication) but that I be
your ever affectionate and faithful

LETTER XIII
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
SUNDAY MORNING, MARCH 26.
how soothe a thing be praise from those we love!--whether conscious or
not of deserve it, it cannot but give we great delight, to see

I believe, my dear, I may promise myself your approbation, whenever I

an accident, and not remissness, have occasion my silence.

LETTER XXII
MR. HICKMAN, to MRS. HOWE
WEDNESDAY, MARCH 29.
MADAM,
it be with infinite regret that I think myself oblige, by pen and ink,
to repeat my apprehension, that it be impossible for I ever to obtain a
share in the affection of your beloved daughter. o that it be not too
evident to every one, as well as to myself, even to our very servant,
that my love for she, and my assiduity, expose I rather to her scorn
[forgive I, Madam, the hard word!] than to the treatment due to a man
whose proposal have meet with your approbation, and who love she above
all the woman in the world!
well might the merit of my passion be doubt, if, like Mr. Solmes to the
truly-admirably Miss Clarissa Harlowe, I could continue my address to
Miss Howe's distaste. yet what will not the discontinuance cost I!
give I leave, nevertheless, dearest, worthiest Lady, to repeat, what I
tell you, on Monday night, at Mrs. Larkin's, with a heart even burst
with grief, that I want not the treatment of that day to convince I,
that I be not, nor ever can be, the object of Miss Howe's voluntary
favour. what hop can there be, that a lady will ever esteem, as a
husband, the man, whom, as a lover, she despise? will not every act of
obligingness from such a one, be construe as an unmanly tameness of
spirit, and entitle he the more to her disdain?--my heart be full:
forgive I, if I say, that Miss Howe's treatment of I do no credit
either to her education, or fine sense.
since, then, it be too evident, that she cannot esteem I; and since, as
I have hear it justly observe by the excellent Miss Clarissa Harlowe,
that love be not a voluntary passion; would it not be ungenerous to
subject the dear daughter to the displeasure of a mother so justly fond
of she; and you, Madam, while you be so good as to interest yourself in
my favour, to uneasiness? and why, be I even to be sure, at last, of
succeed by mean of your kind partiality to I, should I wish to make
the well-beloved of my soul unhappy; since mutual must be our happiness,
or misery for life the consequence to both?
my good wish will for ever attend the dear, the ever-dear lady! may she
nuptial be happy! they must be so, if she marry the man she can honour
with her love. yet I will say, that whoever be the happy, the thrice-
happy man, he can never love she with a passion more ardent and more
sincere than mine.
Accept, dear Madam, of my most grateful thank for a distinction that have
be the only support of my presumption in an address I be oblige, as
utterly hopeless, to discontinue. a distinction, on which (and not on my
own merit) I have entirely rely; but which, I find, can avail I
nothing. to the last hour of my life, it will give I pleasure to think,
that have your favour, your recommendation, be of sufficient weight to
conquer what seem to be an invincible aversion, I have be the happy
of man.
I be, dear Madam, with inviolable respect,
your ever oblige and faithful
humble servant,
CHARLES HICKMAN.
LETTER XXIII
MRS. HOWE, to CHARLES HICKMAN, ESQ.
THURSDAY, MARCH 30.
I cannot but say, Mr. Hickman, but you have cause to be dissatisfy--to
be out of humour--to be displease--with Nancy--but, upon my word; but
indeed--what shall I say?--yet this I will say, that you good young
gentleman know nothing at all of our sex. shall I tell you--but why
should I? and yet I will, that if Nancy do not think well of you upon
the main, she be too generous to treat you so freely as she does.--Don't
you think she have courage enough to tell I, she would not see you, and
to refuse at any time see you, as she know on what account you come,
if she have not something in her head favourable to you?--Fie! that I be
force to say thus much in writing, when I have hint it to you twenty
and twenty time by word of mouth!
but if you be so indifferent, Mr. Hickman--if you think you can part
with she for her skittish trick--if my interest in your favour--why, Mr.
Hickman, I must tell you that my Nancy be worth bear with. if she be
foolish--what be that owe to?--is it not to her wit? let I tell you,
Sir, you cannot have the convenience without the inconvenience. what
workman love not a sharp tool to work with? but be there not more
danger from a sharp tool than from a blunt one? and what workman will
throw away a sharp tool, because it may cut his finger? Wit may be
liken to a sharp tool. and there be something very pretty in wit, let
I tell you. often and often have I be force to smile at her arch
turn upon I, when I could have beat she for they. and, pray, donot I
bear a great deal from her?--And why? because I love she. and would you
not wish I to judge of your love for she by my own? and would not you
bear with her?--don't you love she (what though with another sort of
love?) as well as I do? I do assure you, Sir, that if I think you do
not--well, but it be plain that you don't!--and be it plain that you
don't?--Well, then, you must do as you think well.
well might the merit of your passion be doubt, you say, if, like Mr.
Solmes--fiddle-faddle!--why, you be a captious man, I think!--has Nancy
be so plain in her repulse of you as Miss Clary Harlowe have be to
Mr. solmes?--doe Nancy love any man well than you, although she may
not shew so much love to you as you wish for?--if she do, let I tell
you, she would have let we all hear of it.--what idle comparison then!
but it mat be you be tired out. it may be you have see somebody else--
it may be you would wish to change mistress with that gay wretch Mr.
Lovelace. it may be too, that, in that case, Nancy would not be sorry to
change lover--the truly-admirable Miss Clarissa Harlowe!--Good lack!-
but take care, Mr. Hickman, that you do not praise any woman live, let
she be as admirable and as excellent as she will, above your own
mistress. no polite man will do that, surely. and take care too, that
you do not make she or I think you be in earnest in your anger--just
though it may be, as anger only--I would not for a thousand pound, that
Nancy should know that you can so easily part with she, if you have the
love for she which you declare you have. be sure, if you be not
absolutely determined, that you do not so much as whisper the content of
this your letter to your own heart, as I may say.
her treatment of you, you say, do no credit either to her education or
fine sense. very home put, truly! nevertheless, so say i. but be not
her the disgrace, more than your? I can assure you, that every body
blame she for it. and why do they blame her?--why? because they think
you merit well treatment at her hand: and be not this to your credit?
who but pity you, and blame he? do the servant, who, as you observe,
see her skittish air, disrespect you for they? do they not, at such
time, look concerned for you? be they not then doubly officious in
their respect and service to you?--i have observe, with pleasure, that
they be.
but you be afraid you shall be think tame, perhaps, when marry.
that you shall not be though manly enough, I warrant!--and this be poor
Mr. Howe's fear. and many a tug do this lordly fear cost we both, God
knows!--many more than need, I be sure:--and more than ought to have
be, have he know how to bear and forbear; as be the duty of those who
pretend to have most sense--and, pray, which would you have to have most
sense, the woman or the man?
well, Sir, and now what remain, if you really love Nancy so well as you
say you do?--why, I leave that to you. you may, if you please, come to
breakfast with I in the morning. but with no full heart, nor resent
look, I advise you; except you can brave it out. that have I, when
provoke, do many a time with my husband, but never do I get any thing
by it with my daughter: much less will you. of which, for your
observation, I think fit to advise you. as from
your friend,
Anabella Howe.

MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
THURSDAY MORNING.
I will now take some notice of your last favour. but be so far
behind-hand with you, must be brief.
in the first place, as to your reproof, thus shall I discharge myself of
that part of my subject. be it likely, think you, that I should avoid
deserve they now-and-then, occasionally, when I admire the manner in
which you give I your rebuke, and love you the well for they? and
when you be so well entitle to give they? for what fault can you
possibly have, unless your relation be so kind as to find you a few to
keep their many in countenance?--But they be as king to I in this, as
to you; for I may venture to affirm, that any one who should read your
letter, and would say you be right, would not on read mine, condemn
I for they quite wrong.
your resolution not to leave your father's house be right--if you can
stay in it, and avoid be Solmes's wife.
I think you have answer Solmes's letter, as I should have answer it.
--Will you not compliment I and yourself at once, by say, that be
right?
you have, in your letter to your uncle and the rest, do all that you
ought to do. you be wholly guiltless of the consequence, be it what it
will. to offer to give up your estate!--that would not I have do! you
see this offer stagger they: they take time to consider of it. they
make my heart ache in the time they take. I be afraid they would have
take you at your word: and so, but for shame, and for fear of Lovelace,
I dare say they would. you be too noble for they. this, I repeat, be
an offer I would not have make. let I beg of you, my dear, never to
repeat the temptation to they.
I freely own to you, that their usage of you upon it, and Lovelace's
different treatment of you* in his letter receive at the same time,
would have make I his, past redemption. the duce take the man, I be
go to say, for not have so much regard to his character and moral,
as would have entirely justify such a step in a CLARISSA, persecute as
she be!

I wonder not at your appointment with he. I may far touch upon some

pray--pray--I pray you now, my dear friend, contrive to send your

I wonder not at Lovelace's saucy answer, saucy as it really be.* if he

I shall be all impatience to know how this matter end between you and

you see, you say, that the temper he shew in his letter be not natural

if ever I should be persuade to have he, I shall watch how the

all good-natured man be passionate, say Mr. Lovelace. a pretty plea to

indeed, we be too apt to make allowance for such temper as early

but if two person of discretion, youwill say, come together--
Ay, my dear, thatbe true: but, if none but person of discretion be to

--And would either of we marry, if the fellow and our friend would let

by mean of this suppose ingenuity, Lovelace obtain a praise, instead

I have a reason, a new one, for this preachment upon a text you have

but let this be as it will, shall I tell you, how, after all his

I will. thus then: it be but to claim for himself the good-natured

LETTER XXV
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
FRIDAY, MARCH 31.
you have very kindly account for your silence. People in misfortune
be always in doubt. they be too apt to turn even unavoidable accident
into slight and neglect; especially in those whose favourable opinion
they wish to preserve.
I be sure I ought evermore to exempt my Anna Howe from the suppose
possibility of she become one of those who bask only in the sun-shine
of a friend: but nevertheless her friendship be too precious to I, not
to doubt my own merit on the one hand, and not to be anxious for the
preservation of it, on the other.
you so generously give I liberty to chide you, that I be afraid of
take it, because I could soon mistrust my own judgment, than that of
a beloved friend, whose ingenuousness in acknowledge an imputed error
seem to set she above the commission of a wilful one. this make I
half-afraid to ask you, if you think you be not too cruel, too
ungenerous shall I say? in your behaviour to a man who love you so
dearly, and be so worthy and so sincere a man?
only it be by you, or I should be ashamed to be outdo in that true
magnanimity, which make one thankful for the wound give by a true
friend. I believe I be guilty of a petulance, which nothing but my
uneasy situation can excuse; if that can. I be but almost afraid to
beg of you, and yet I repeatedly do, to give way to that charming spirit,
whenever it rise to your pen, which smile, yet go to the quick of my
fault. what patient shall be afraid of a probe in so delicate a hand?--
I say, I be almost afraid to pray you to give way to it, for fear you
should, for that very reason, restrain it. for the edge may be take
off, if it do not make the subject of its raillery wince a little.
permit or desire satire may be apt, in a generous satirist, mend
as it rally, to turn too soon into panegyric. your be intend to
instruct; and though it bite, it please at the same time: no fear of a
wound's wrankling or fester by so delicate a point as you carry; not
envenom by personality, not intend to expose, or ridicule, or
exasperate. the most admire of our modern know nothing of this art:
why? because it must be found in good nature, and direct by a right
heart. the man, not the fault, be generally the subject of their satire:
and be it to be just, how should it be useful; how should it answer any
good purpose; when every gash (for their weapon be a broad sword, not a
lancet) let in the air of public ridicule, and exasperate where it
should heal? spare I not therefore because I be your friend. for that
very reason spare I not. I may feel your edge, fine as it be. I may be
pain: you would lose you end if I be not: but after the first
sensibility (as I have say more than once before) I will love you the
well, and my amend heart shall be all your; and it will then be more
worthy to be yours.
you have teach I what to say to, and what to think of, Mr. Lovelace.
you have, by agreeable anticipation, let I know how it be probable he
will apply to I to be excuse. I will lay every thing before you that
shall pass on the occasion, if he do apply, that I may take your advice,
when it can come in time; and when it cannot, that I may receive your
correction, or approbation, as I may happen to merit either.--only one

direction. Tost to and fro by the high wind of passionate controul,
(and, as I think, unseasonable severity,) I behold the desire port, the
single state, into which I would fain steer; but be keep off by the
foaming billow of a brother's and sister's envy, and by the rag wind
of a suppose invade authority; while I see in Lovelace, the rock on
one hand, and in Solmes, the sand on the other; and tremble, lest I
should split upon the former, or strike upon the latter.
but you, my well pilot, to what a charming hope do you bid I aspire,
if thing come to extremity!--i will not, as you caution I, too much
depend upon your success with your mother in my favour; for well I know
her high notion of implicit duty in a child: but yet I will hope too;
because her seasonable protection may save I perhaps from a great
rashness: and in this case, she shall direct I in all my way: I will do
nothing but by her order, and by her advice and your: not see any body:
not write to any body: nor shall any live soul, but by her direction

out, unless, disguise as your servant, I be now-and-then permit an

long time than till my cousin Morden come; which, as I hope, cannot be
long.
I be afraid I must not venture to take the hint you give I, to deposit
some of my clothe; although I will some of my linen, as well as paper.
I will tell you why--Betty have for some time be very curious about my
wardrobe, whenever I take out any of my thing before she.
observe this, I once, on take one of my garden-airing, leave my key
in the lock: and on my return surprise the creature with her hand upon
the key, as if shut the door.
she be confound at my sudden come back. I take no notice: but on

I doubt not, upon this, that her curiosity be owe to the order she

to this, and to the confidence they have in a spy so diligent, and to

nevertheless I believe every servant love I; nor have attempt to

this custom, although a prisoner, (as I may too truly say,) and neither

you know, to be always neat; and never to be surprised in a way we should
be pain to be see in.
besides, people in adversity (which be the state of trial of every good
quality) should endeavour to preserve laudable custom, that, if sun
shine return, they may not be loser by their trial.
do it not, moreover, manifest a firmness of mind, in an unhappy person,
to keep hope alive? to hope for well day, be half to deserve they:
for could we have just grind for such a hope, if we do not resolve to

I know you donot despise my grave air, although (with a view no doubt to

what a multitude of contrivance may not young people fall upon, if the

Mr. Solmes, (to expatiate on this low, but not unuseful subject,) in his

many of the former would scorn to deceive a confidence. but I have see,
among the most ignorant of their class, a susceptibility of resentment,
if their honesty have be suspect: and have more than once be force

how far have the comparison I have in my head, between my friend treatment
of I, and my treatment of the servant, carry me!--But we always
allow ourselves to expatiate on such subject, whether low or high, as
might tend to enlarge our mind, or mend our management, whether notional
or practical, and whether such expatiating respect our present, or
might respect our probable future situation.
what I be principally lead to, be to tell you how ingenious I be in
my contrivance and pretence to blind my gaoleress, and to take off the

poultry-yard. People suspiciously treat be never I believe at a loss

spangled element, and the rise and set sun, how promotive of

these more capital artifice I branch out into less one, without

although not my principal motive. how prompt a thing be will!--what
impediment do dislike furnish!--how swiftly, through every difficulty,
do we move with the one!--how tardily with the other!--every trifling
obstruction weigh we down, as if lead be fasten to our foot!

I have already make up my parcel of linen. my heart ache all the time I

FRIDAY, one O'CLOCK, in the WOOD-HOUSE.

LETTER XXVI
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
THURSDAY NIGHT, MARCH 30.
the fruit of my inquiry after your abominable wretch's behaviour and
baseness at the paltry alehouse, which he call an inn, prepare to hear.
Wrens and sparrow be not too ignoble a quarry for this villainous
go-hawk!--his assiduity; his watching; his nightly risque; the

he have opportunity of make every thing light to he of that sort.
a sweet pretty girl, I be tell--innocent till he go thither--now! (ah!
poor girl!) who know what?
but just turn of seventeen!--his friend and brother-rake (a man of

sometimes another disguised rake or two. no sorrow come near their

he be very fond of she. they say she be innocent even yet--her father,

LETTER XXXVII

I have your three letter. never be there a creature more impatient on

it behove I to account to my dear friend, in her present unhappy
