negligence or remissness on my part. I send Robin in the morning early,
in hope of a deposit. he loiter about the place till near ten to no
purpose; and then come away; my mother have give he a letter to carry
to Mr. Hunt's, which he be to deliver before three, when only, in the
day-time, that gentleman be at home; and to bring back an answer to it.
Mr. Hunt's house, you know, lie wide from Harlowe-place. Robin but just
save his time; and return not till it be too late to send he again.
I only could direct he to set out before day this morning; and if he get
any letter, to ride as for his life to bring it to I.
I lay by myself: a most uneasy night I have through impatience; and be
discompose with it, lie long than usual. just as I be rise, in came
Kitty, from Robin, with your three letter. I be not a quarter dress;
and only slipt on my morning sack; proceed no far till I have read
they all through, long as they be: and yet I often stop to rave aloud
(though by myself) at the devilish people you have to deal with.
how my heart rise at they all! how poorly do they design to trick you
into an encouragement of Solmes, from the extort interview!--I be very,
very angry at your aunt hervey--to give up her own judgment so tamely!--
and, not content to do so, to become such an active instrument in their
hands!--but it be so like the world!--so like my mother too!--next to her
own child, there be not any body live she value so much as you:--Yet
it be--why should we embroil ourselves, Nancy, with the affair of other
people?
other people!--how I hate the poor word, where friendship be concern,
and where the protection to be give may be of so much consequence to a
friend, and of so little detriment to one's self?
I be delighted with your spirit, however. I expect it not from you
nor do they, I be sure. nor would you, perhaps, have exert it, if
Lovelace's intelligence of Solmes's nursery-office have not set you up.
I wonder not that the wretch be say to love you the well for it. what
an honour would it be to he to have such a wife? and he can be even
with you when you be so. he must indeed be a savage, as you say.--yet
he be less to blame for his perseverance, than those of your own family,
whom most you reverence for theirs.
it be well, as I have often say, that I have not such provocation and
trial; I should perhaps long ago have take your cousin Dolly's advice--
yet dare I not to touch that key.--I shall always love the good girl for
her tenderness to you.
I know not what to say of Lovelace; nor what to think of his promise,
nor of his proposal to you. 'tis certain that you be highly esteemed
by all his family. the lady be person of unblemished honour. my
Lord M. be also (as man and peer go) a man of honour. I could tell what
to advise any other person in the world to do but you. so much expect
from you!--such a shin light!--your quit your father's house, and
throw yourself into the protection of a family, however honourable,
that have a man in it, whose person, part, declaration, and pretension,
will be think to have engage your warm esteem;--methink I be
rather for advise that you should get privately to London; and not to
let either he, or any body else but I, know where you be, till your
cousin Morden come.
as to go to your uncle's, that you must not do, if you can help it.
nor must you have solme, thatbe certain: not only because of his
unworthiness in every respect, but because of the aversion you have so
openly avow to he; which every body know and talk of; as they do of
your approbation of the other. for your reputation sake therefore, as
well as to prevent mischief, you must either live single, or have
Lovelace.
if you think of go to London, let I know; and I hope you will have
time to allow I a further concert as to the manner of your get away,
and thither, and how to procure proper lodging for you.
to obtain this time, you must palliate a little, and come into some
seem compromise, if you cannot do otherwise. drive as you be
drive, it will be strange if you be not oblige to part with a few of
your admirable punctilio's.
you will observe from what I have write, that I have not succeed with
my mother.
I be extremely mortified and disappointed. we have have very strong
debate upon it. but, besides the narrow argument of embroil
ourselves with other people's affair, as above-mention, she will have
it, that it be your duty to comply. she say, she be always of opinion
that daughter should implicitly submit to the will of their parent in
the great article of marriage; and that she govern herself accordingly
in marry my father; who at first be more the choice of her parent
than her own.
this be what she argue in behalf of her favourite Hickman, as well as
for solme in your case.
I must not doubt, but my mother always govern herself by this principle
--because she say she do. I have likewise another reason to believe
it; which you shall have, though it may not become I to give it--that
they do not live so happily together, as one would hope people might do
who marry prefer each other at the time to the rest of the world.
somebody shall fare never the well for this double-mean policy of my
mother, I do assure you. such a retrospection in her argument to he,
and to his address, it be but fit that he should suffer for my
mortification in fail to carry a point upon which I have set my whole
heart.
think, my dear, if in any way I can serve you. if you allow of it, I
protest I will go off privately with you, and we will live and die
together. think of it. improve upon my hint, and command I.
a little interruption.--what be breakfast to the subject I be upon?
***
London, I be tell, be the good hiding-place in the world. I have write
nothing but what I will stand in to at the word of command. woman love
to engage in knight-errantry, now-and-then, as well as to encourage it in
the man. but in your case, what I propose will not seem to have anything
of that nature in it. it will enable I to perform what be no more than
a duty in serve and comfort a dear and worthy friend, who labour
under undeserved oppression: and you will ennoble, as I may say, your
Anna Howe, if you allow she to be your companion in affliction.
I will engage, my dear, we shall not be in town together one month,
before we surmount all difficulty; and this without be beholden to
any man-fellow for their protection.
I must repeat what I have often say, that the author of your
persecution would not have presume to set on foot their selfish scheme
against you, have they not depend upon the gentleness of your spirit;
though now, have go so far, and have engage Old AUTHORITY in it,
[chide I if you will!] neither he nor they know how to recede.
when they find you out of their reach, and know that I be with you,
youwill see how theywill pull in their odious horn.
I think, however, that you should have write to your cousin Morden, the
moment they have begin to treat you disgracefully.
I shall be impatient to hear whether they will attempt to carry you to
your uncle's. I remember, that Lord M.'s dismiss bailiff report of
Lovelace, that he have six or seven companion as bad as himself; and that
the country be always glad when they leave it.* he actually have, as I
hear, such a knot of they about he now. and, depend upon it, he will
not suffer they quietly to carry you to your uncle's: and whose must you
be, if he succeed in take you from they?
* see Vol.I. Letter IV.
I tremble for you but upon suppose what may be the consequence of a
conflict upon this occasion. Lovelace owe some of they vengeance. this
give I a double concern, that my mother should refuse her consent to
the protection I have set my heart upon procure for you.
my mother will not breakfast without I. a quarrel have its conveniencie
sometimes. yet too much love, I think, be as bad as too little.
***
we have just now have another pull. upon my word, she be excessively--
what shall I say?--unpersuadable--I must let she off with that soft word.
who be the old Greek, that say, he govern Athens; his wife, he; and
his son, she?
it be not my mother's fault [I be write to you, you know] that she do
not govern my father. but I be but a daughter!--Yet I think I be not
quite so powerless when I be set upon carry a point, as I find myself
to be.
Adieu, my dear!--happier time must come--and that quickly too.--The
string cannot long continue to be thus overstrain. they must break or
be relax. in either way, the certainty must be preferable to the
suspense.
one word more:
I think in my conscience you must take one of these two alternative;
either to consent to let we go to London together privately; [in which
case, I will procure a vehicle, and meet you at your appointment at the
stile to which Lovelace propose to bring his uncle's chariot;] or, to
put yourself into the protection of Lord M. and the lady of his family.
you have another, indeed; and that be, if you be absolutely resolve
against Solmes, to meet and marry Lovelace directly.
Whichsoever of these you make choice of, you will have this plea, both to
yourself, and to the world, that you be conclude by the same uniform
principle that have govern your whole conduct, ever since the contention
between Lovelace and your brother have be on foot: that be to say, that
you have choose a less evil, in hope to prevent a great.
Adieu! and Heaven direct for the good my beloved creature, pray
her
ANNA HOWE.
LETTER XXXVIII
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
THURSDAY, APRIL 6.
I thank you, my dear friend, for the pain you have take in
accounting so affectionately for my paper not be take away
yesterday; and for the kind protection you would have procure for
I, if you could.
this kind protection be what I wish for: but my wish, raise at
first by your love, be rather govern by my despair of other refuge
[have before cast about, and not be able to determine, what I ought
to do, and what I could do, in a situation so unhappy] than by a
reasonable hope: for why indeed should any body embroil themselves for
other, when they can avoid it?
all my consolation be, as I have frequently say, that I have not, by my
own inadvertence or folly, bring myself into this sad situation. if I
have, I should not have dare to look up to any body with the expectation
of protection or assistance, nor to you for excuse of the trouble I give
you. but nevertheless we should not be angry at a person's not do
that for ourselves, or for our friend, which she think she ought not to
do; and which she have it in her option either to do, or to let it alone.
much less have you a right to be displeased with so prudent a mother, for
not engage herself so warmly in my favour, as you wish she would. if
my own aunt can give I up, and that against her judgment, as I may
presume to say; and if my father and mother, and uncle, who once love
I so well, can join so strenuously against I; can I expect, or ought
you, the protection of your mother, in opposition to they?
indeed, my dear love, [permit I to be very serious,] I be afraid I be
single out (either for my own fault, or for the fault of my family,
or perhaps for the fault of both) to be a very unhappy creature!--
signally unhappy! for see you not how irresistible the wave of
affliction come tumble down upon I?
we have be till within these few week, every one of we, too happy. no
cross, no vexation, but what we give ourselves from the pamperedness,
as I may call it, of our own will. surround by our heap and store,
hoard up as fast as acquire, we have seem to think ourselves out of
the reach of the bolt of adverse fate. I be the pride of all my
friend, proud myself of their pride, and glory in my standing. who
know what the justice of Heaven may inflict, in order to convince we,
that we be not out of the reach of misfortune; and to reduce we to a
well reliance, than what we have hitherto presumptuously make?
I should have be very little the well for the conversation-visit
with the good Dr. Lewen use to honour I with, and for the principle
work (as I may say) into my early mind by my pious Mrs. Norton,
found on her reverend father's experience, as well as on her own, if I
could not thus retrospect and argue, in such a strange situation as we
be in. strange, I may well call it; for donot you see, my dear, that we
seem all to be impel, as it be, by a perverse fate, which none of we
be able to resist?--and yet all arise (with a strong appearance of
self-punishment) from ourselves? do not my parent see the hopeful
child, from whom they expect a perpetuity of worldly happiness to
their branching family, now grow up to answer the till now distant hope,
set their angry face against each other, pull up by the root, as
I may say, that hope which be ready to be carry into a probable
certainty?
your partial love will be ready to acquit I of capital and intentional
faults:--but oh, my dear! my calamity have humble I enough to make I
turn my gaudy eye inward; to make I look into myself.--And what have I
discover there?--why, my dear friend, more secret pride and vanity than
I could have think have lain in my unexamined heart.
if I be to be single out to be the punisher of myself and family, who so
lately be the pride of it, pray for I, my dear, that I may not be leave
wholly to myself; and that I may be enable to support my character, so
as to be justly acquit of wilful and premeditated fault. the will of
Providence be resign to in the rest: as that lead, let I patiently
and unrepiningly follow!--i shall not live always!--May but my closing
scene be happy!
but I will not oppress you, my dear friend, with further reflection
of this sort. I will take they all into myself. surely I have a mind
that have room for they. my affliction be too sharp to last long. the
crisis be at hand. happy time you bid I hope for. I will hope.
***
but yet, I cannot be but impatient at time, to find myself thus drive,
and my character so depreciated and sink, that be all the future to be
happy, I should be ashamed to shew my face in public, or to look up. and
all by the instigation of a selfish brother, and envious sister--
but let I stop: let I reflect!--Are not these suggestion the
suggestion of the secret pride I have be censure? then, already so
impatient! but this moment so resign, so much well dispose for
reflection! yet 'tis hard, 'tis very hard, to subdue an embitter
spirit!--in the instant of its trial too!--O my cruel brother!--but now
it rise again.--I will lay down a pen I be so little able to govern.--
and I will try to subdue an impatience, which (if my affliction be send
I for corrective end) may otherwise lead I into still more punishable
errors.--
***
I will return to a subject, which I cannot fly from for ten minute
together--call upon especially, as I be, by your three alternative
state in the conclusion of your last.
as to the first; to wit, your advice for I to escape to London--let I
tell you, that the other hint or proposal which accompany it perfectly
frighten I--surely, my dear, (happy as you be, and indulgently treat
as your mother treat you,) you cannot mean what you propose! what a
wretch must I be, if, for one moment only, I could lend an ear to such a
proposal as this!--I, to be the occasion of make such a mother's
(perhaps shorten) life unhappy to the last hour of it!--Ennoble you, my
dear creature! how must such an enterprise (the rashness public, the
motif, be they excusable, private) debase you!--but I will not dwell
upon the subject--for your own sake I will not.
as to your second alternative, to put myself into the protection of Lord
M. and of the lady of that family, I own to you, (as I believe I have
own before,) that although to do this would be the same thing in the
eye of the world as put myself into Mr. Lovelace's protection, yet I
think I would do it rather than be Mr. Solmes's wife, if there be
evidently no other way to avoid be so.
Mr. Lovelace, you have see, propose to contrive a way to put I into
possession of my own house; and he tell I, that he will soon fill it
with the lady of his family, as my visiters;--upon my invitation,
however, to they. a very inconsiderate proposal I think it to be, and
upon which I cannot explain myself to he. what an exertion of
independency do it chalk out for I! how, be I to attend to he,
(and not to the natural consequence to which the following of his advice
would lead I,) might I be draw by gentle word into the penetration of
the most violent acts!--for how could I gain possession, but either by
legal litigation, which, be I inclined to have recourse to it, (as I
never can be,) must take up time; or by forcibly turn out the person
whom my father have place there, to look after the garden, the house,
and the furniture--person entirely attach to himself, and who, as I
know, have be lately instruct by my brother?
your third alternative, to meet and marry Mr. Lovelace directly; a man
with whose moral I be far from be satisfy--a step, that could not
be take with the least hope of ever obtain pardon from or
reconciliation with any of my friend; and against which a thousand
objection rise in my mind--that be not to be think of.
what appear to I, upon the full deliberation, the most eligible, if
I must be thus drive, be the escaping to London. but I would forfeit
all my hope of happiness in this life, rather than you should go away
with I, as you rashly, though with the kind intention, propose. if
I could get safely thither, and be private, methink I might remain
absolutely independent of Mr. Lovelace, and at liberty either to make
proposal to my friend, or, should they renounce I, (and I have no other
or well way,) to make term with he; suppose my cousin Morden, on
his arrival, be to join with my other relation. but they would then
perhaps indulge I in my choice of a single life, on give he up: the
renew to they this offer, when at my own liberty, will at least
convince they, that I be in earnest when I make it first: and, upon my
word, I would stand to it, dear as you seem to think, when you be
disposed to rally I, it would cost I, to stand to it.
if, my dear, you can procure a vehicle for we both, you can perhaps
procure one for I singly: but can it be do without embroil yourself
with your mother, or she with our family?--be it coach, chariot, chaise,
wagon, or horse, I matter not, provide you appear not to have a hand in
my withdrawing. only, in case it be one of the two latter, I believe I
must desire you to get I an ordinary gown and coat, or habit, of some
servant; have no concert with any of our own: the more ordinary the
well. they must be thrust on in the wood-house; where I can put they
on; and then slide down from the bank, that separate the wood-yard from
the green lane.
but, alas! my dear, this, even this alternative, be not without
difficulty, which, to a spirit so little enterprising as mine, seem in
a manner insuperable. these be my reflection upon it.
I be afraid, in the first place, that I shall not have time for the
requisite preparation for an escape.
should I be either detect in those preparation, or pursue and
overtaken in my flight, and so bring back, then would they think
themselves doubly warrant to compel I to have their solme: and,
conscious of an intend fault, perhaps, I should be the less able to
contend with they.
but be I even to get safely to London, I know nobody there but by name;
and those the tradesman to our family; who, no doubt, would be the first
write to and engage to find I out. and should Mr. Lovelace discover
where I be, and he and my brother meet, what mischief might ensue
between they, whether I be willing or not to return to Harlowe-place!
but suppose I could remain there conceal, to what might my youth, my
sex, and unacquaintedness of the way of that great, wicked town, expose
me!--I should hardly dare to go to church for fear of be discover.
People would wonder how I live. who know but I might pass for a kept
mistress; and that, although nobody come to I, yet, that every time I
go out, it might be imagine to be in pursuance of some assignation?
you, my dear, who alone would know where to direct to I, would be
watch in all your step, and in all your message; and your mother, at
present not highly pleased with our correspondence, would then have
reason to be more displeased: and might not difference follow between
she and you, that would make I very unhappy, be I to know they? and
this the more likely, as you take it so unaccountably (and, give I leave
to say, so ungenerously) into your head, to revenge yourself upon the
innocent Mr. Hickman, for all the displeasure your mother give you.
be Lovelace to find out my place of abode, that would be the same thing
in the eye of the world as if I have actually go off with he: for would
he, do you think, be prevail upon to forbear visit I? and then his
unhappy character (a foolish man!) would be no credit to any young
creature desirous of concealment. indeed the world, let I escape
whither, and to whomsoever I could, would conclude he to be the
contriver of it.
these be the difficulty which arise to I on revolve this scheme;
which, nevertheless, might appear surmountable to a more enterprising
spirit in my circumstance. if you, my dear, think they surmountable in
any one of the case put, [and to be sure I can take no course, but what
must have some difficulty in it,] be pleased to let I know your free and
full thought upon it.
have you, my dear friend, be marry, then should I have have no doubt
but that you and Mr. Hickman would have afford an asylum to a poor
creature more than half lose in her own apprehension for want of one kind
protect friend!
you say I should have write to my cousin Morden the moment I be
treat disgracefully: but could I have believe that my friend would
not have soften by degree when they see my antipathy to their Solmes?
I have thought indeed several time of writing to my cousin: but by the
time an answer could have come, I imagine all would have be over, as
if it have never be: so from day to day, from week to week, I hop on:
and, after all, I might as reasonably fear (as I have heretofore say)
that my cousin would be bring to side against I, as that some of those
I have name would.
and then to appeal a cousin [I must have write with warmth to engage
he] against a father; this be not a desirable thing to set about. then
I have not, you know, one soul on my side; my mother herself against I.
to be sure my cousin would have suspend his judgment till he could have
arrive. he might not have be in haste to come, hop the malady
would cure itself: but have he write, his letter probably would have
run in the qualifying style; to persuade I to submit, or they only to
relax. have his letter be more on my side than on theirs, they would
not have regard they: nor perhaps himself, have he come and be an
advocate for I: for you see how strangely determined they be; how they
have over-awed or get in every body; so that no one dare open their lip
in my behalf. and you have hear that my brother push his measure
with the more violence, that all may be over with I before my cousin's
expect arrival.
but you tell I, that, in order to gain time, I must palliate; that I
must seem to compromise with my friend: but how palliate? how seem to
compromise? you would not have I endeavour to make they believe, that I
will consent to what I never intend to consent to! you would not have
I to gain time, with a view to deceive!
to do evil, that good may come of it, be forbid: and shall I do evil,
yet know not whether good may come of it or not?
forbid it, heaven! that Clarissa Harlowe should have it in her thought to
serve, or even to save herself at the expense of her sincerity, and by a
study deceit!
and be there, after all, no way to escape one great evil, but by plunge
myself into another?--what an ill-fat creature be i!--pray for I, my
dear nancy!--my mind be at present so much disturbed, that I can
hardly pray for myself.
LETTER XXXIX
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
THURSDAY NIGHT.
this alarming hurry I mention under my date of last night, and Betty's
saucy dark hint, come out to be owe to what I guess they be; that
be to say, to the private intimation Mr. Lovelace contrive our family
should have of his insolent resolution [insolent I must call it] to
prevent my be carry to my uncle's.
I see at the time that it be as wrong with respect to answer his own
view, as it be insolent: for, could he think, as Betty (I suppose from
her better) justly observe, that parent would be insult out of their
right to dispose of their own child, by a violent man, whom they hate;
and who could have no pretension to dispute that right with they, unless
what he have from she who have none over herself? and how must this
insolence of his, aggravate as my brother be able to aggravate it,
exasperate they against I?
the rash man have indeed so far gain his point, as to intimidate they
from attempt to carry I away: but he have put they upon a surer and a
more desperate measure: and this have drive I also into one as
desperate; the consequence of which, although he could not foresee it,*
may perhaps too well answer his great end, little as he deserve to have
it answer.
* she be mistake in this. Mr. Lovelace do foresee this consequence.
all his contrivance lead to it, and the whole family, as he boast,
unknown to themselves, be but so many puppet dance by his wire. see
Vol.I. Letter XXXI.
in short, I have do, as far as I know, the most rash thing that ever I
do in my life.
but let I give you the motive, and then the action will follow of
course.
about six o'clock this evening, my aunt (who stay here all night, on my
account, no doubt) come up and tap at my door; for I be write; and
have lock myself in. I open it; and she enter, thus deliver
herself:
I come once more to visit you, my dear; but sorely against my will;
because it be to impart to you matter of the utmost concern to you, and
to the whole family.
what, Madam, be now to be do with I? say I, wholly attentive.
you will not be hurry away to your uncle's, child; let that comfort
you.--they see your aversion to go.--you will not be oblige to go to
your uncle Antony's.
how you revive I, Madam! this be a cordial to my heart!
I little think, my dear, what be to follow this suppose
condescension.
and then I run over with blessing for this good news, (and she permit
I so to do, by her silence); congratulate myself, that I think my
father could not resolve to carry thing to the last extremity.--
Hold, Niece, say she, at last--you must not give yourself too much joy
upon the occasion neither.--don't be surprised, my dear.--why look you
upon I, child, with so affect an earnestness?--but you must be Mrs.
Solmes, for all that.
I be dumb.
she then tell I, that they have undoubted information, that a certain
desperate ruffian (I must excuse she that word, she say) have prepare
armed man to way-lay my brother and uncle, and seize I, and carry I
off.--surely, she say, I be not consent to a violence that might be
follow by murder on one side or the other; perhaps on both.
I be still silent.
that therefore my father (still more exasperate than before) have change
his resolution as to my go to my uncle's; and be determine next
Tuesday to set out thither himself with my mother; and that (for it be
to no purpose to conceal a resolution so soon to be put into execution)--
I must not dispute it any long--on Wednesday I must give my hand--as
they would have I.
she proceed, that order be already give for a license: that the
ceremony be to be perform in my own chamber, in presence of all my
friend, except of my father and mother; who would not return, nor see
I, till all be over, and till they have a good account of my behaviour.
the very intelligence, my dear!--the very intelligence this, which
Lovelace give I!
I be still dumb--only sigh, as if my heart would break.
she go on, comfort I, as she think. 'she lay before I the
merit of obedience; and tell I, that if it be my desire that my
Norton should be present at the ceremony, it would be comply with: that
the pleasure I should receive from reconcile al my friend to I, and
in their congratulation upon it, must need overbalance, with such a one
as I, the difference of person, however preferable I might think the
one man to the other: that love be a fleeting thing, little well than
a name, where mortality and virtue do not distinguish the object of it:
that a choice make by its dictate be seldom happy; at least not durably
so: nor be it to be wonder at, when it naturally exalt the object
above its merit, and make the lover blind to fault, that be visible
to every body else: so that when a near intimacy stript it of its
imaginary perfection, it leave frequently both party surprise, that
they could be so grossly cheat; and that then the indifference become
strong than the love ever be. that a woman give a man great
advantage, and inspire he with great vanity, when she avow her love
for he, and preference of he; and be generally requite with insolence
and contempt: whereas the confessedly-oblige man, it be probable, would
be all reverence and gratitude'--and I cannot tell what.
'you, my dear, say she, believe you shall be unhappy, if you have Mr.
Solmes: your parent think the contrary; and that you will be undoubtedly
so, be you to have Mr. Lovelace, whose moral be unquestionably bad:

letter I
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
TUESDAY, NINE O'CLOCK.
I write, because you enjoin I to do so. love you still!--how can I help
it, if I would? you may believe how I stand aghast, your letter
communicate the first news--good God of Heaven and Earth!--But what
shall I say?--i be all impatient for particular.
Lord have mercy upon me!--But can it be?
my mother will indeed be astonished!--how can I tell it her!--it be but
last night (upon some jealousy put into her head by your foolish uncle)
that I assure she, and this upon the strength of your own assurance,
that neither man nor devil would be able to induce you to take a step
that be in the least derogatory to the most punctilious honour.
but, once more, can it be? what woman at this rate!--But, God preserve
you!
let nothing escape you in your letter. direct they for I, however, to
Mrs. Knolly's, till further notice.
***
Observe, my dear, that I donot blame you by all this--your relation only
be in fault!--Yet how you come to change your mind be the surprising
thing.
how to break it to my mother, I know not. yet if she hear it first from
any other, and find I know it before, she will believe it to be my
connivance!--Yet, as I hope to live, I know not how to break it to she.
but this be tease you.--i be sure, without intention.
let I now repeat my former advice--if you be not marry by this time,
be sure delay not the ceremony. since thing be as they be, I wish it
be think that you be privately marry before you go away. if
these man plead AUTHORITY to our pain, when we be their--why should we
not, in such a case as this, make some good out of the hat word, for
our reputation, when we be induce to violate a more natural one?
your brother and sister [that vex I almost as much as any thing!] have
now their end. now, I suppose, will go forward alteration of will, and
such-like spiteful doing.
***
Miss Lloyd and Miss Biddulph this moment send up their name. they be
out of breath, Kitty say, to speak to I--easy to guess their errand;--
I must see my mother, before I see they. I have no way but to shew she
your letter to clear myself. I shall not be able to say a word, till she
have run herself out of her first breath.--forgive I, my dear--surprise
make I write thus. if your messenger do not wait, and be not those
young lady below, I could write it over again, for fear of afflict
you.
I send what you write for. if there be any thing else you want that be
in my power, command without reserve
your ever affectionate
ANNA HOWE.

and will you, will you thus ungenerously, Mr. Lovelace, take advantage of
my fear? of my wish to prevent mischief? I, vain fool, to be
concerned for every one; nobody for I!
Dearest creature! interrupt he, hold my hand, as I tremblingly
offer to put the key to the lock--let I, if you will go, open the
door. but once more, consider, could you possibly obtain that delay
which seem to be your only dependence, whether you may not be close
confine? I know they have already have that in consideration. will you

if your hatred to Solmes continue!--but alas! that cannot continue. if
you go back, it must be from the impulse of a yielding (which youwill
call, a dutiful) heart, tired and tease out of your own will.
I have no patience, Sir, to be thus constrain. must I never be at
liberty to follow my own judgment? be the consequence what it may, I
will not be thus constrain.
and then, free my hand, I again offer the key to the door.
down the ready kneeler dropt between I and that: and can you, can you,
Madam, once more on my knee let I ask you, look with an indifferent eye
upon the evil that may follow? provoke as I have be, and triumph

lose not this only opportunity. my intelligence--
never, Mr. Lovelace, interrupt I, give so much credit to the word of a
traitor. your base intelligencer be but a servant. he may pretend to
know more than he have ground for, in order to earn the wage of

I be once more offer the key to the lock, when, start from his

o lord:--help, help, cry the fool, all in amaze and confusion, fright
beyond the power of controule.
now behind I, now before I, now on this side, now on that, turn I my

for, might I not have believe, that he, who think he have cause to

might throw I absolutely into his power, to avoid my own bad usage,

my friend and he meet?
but if it shall come out, that the person within the garden be his

I hope his heart cannot be so deep and so vile a one: I hope it cannot!

o why, why, my dear friends!--but wherefore blame I they, when I have

you know, my dear, that your Clarissa's mind be ever above justify

correspond with he.
o the vile encroacher! how my indignation, at time, rise at he! thus

how much more properly have I act, with regard to that correspondence,

tell I, my dear Miss Howe, tell I truly, if your unbiassed heart do

despise myself!--and well I may: for could the giddiest and most

you charge I to marry the first opportunity--ah! my dear! another of the
bless effect of my folly--thatbe as much in my power now as--as I be
myself!--and can I besides give a sanction immediately to his deluding
arts?--can I avoid be angry with he for trick I thus, as I may

my heart beat with expectation of find one from you!

this be the Wednesday morning I dread so much, that I once think of

LETTER III
MR. LOVELACE, to JOSEPH LEMAN
SAT. APRIL 8.
HONEST JOSEPH,
at length your beloved young lady have consent to free herself from the
cruel treatment she have so long bear. she be to meet I without the
garden-door at about four o'clock on Monday afternoon. I tell you she
have promise to do so. she have confirm her promise. thank Heaven she
have confirm her promise!
I shall have a chariot-and-six ready in the by-road front the private
path to harlowe-paddock; and several of my friend and servant not far
off, arm to protect she, if there be occasion: but every one charge to
avoid mischief. that, you know, have always be my principal care.
all my fear be, that, when she come to the point, the over-niceness of
her principle will make she waver, and want to go back: although she
honour be my honour, you know, and mine be she's. if she should, and
should I be unable to prevail upon she, all your past service will
avail nothing, and she will be lose to I for ever: the prey then of that
cursed Solmes, whose vile stinginess will never permit he to do good to
any of the servant of the family.
I have no doubt of your fidelity, honest Joseph; nor of your zeal to
serve an injure gentleman, and an oppressed young lady. you see by the
confidence I repose in you, that I have not; more particularly, on this
very important occasion, in which your assistance may crown the work:
for, if she waver, a little innocent contrivance will be necessary.
be very mindful, therefore, of the follow direction; take they into
your heart. this will probably be your last trouble, until my beloved
and I be join in holy wedlock: and then we will be sure to take care
of you. you know what I have promise. no man ever reproach I for
breach of word.
these, then, honest Joseph, be they:
Contrive to be in the garden, in disguise, if possible, and unseen by
your young lady. if you find the garden-door unbolt, you will know
that she and I be together, although you should not see she go out at
it. it will be lock, but my key shall be on the ground just without
the door, that you may open it with your's, as it may be needful.
if you hear our voice parley, keep at the door till I cry Hem, hem,
twice: but be watchful for this signal; for I must not hem very loud,
lest she should take it for a signal. perhaps, in struggle to prevail
upon the dear creature, I may have an opportunity to strike the door hard
with my elbow, or heel, to confirm you--then you be to make a violent
burst against the door, as if you would break it open, draw backward
and forward the bolt in a hurry: then, with another push, but with more
noise than strength, lest the lock give way, cry out (as if you see some
of the family) come up, come up, instantly!--here they be! here they
are!--hasten!--this instant! hasten! and mention sword, pistol, gun,
with as terrible a voice as you can cry out with. then shall I prevail
upon she, no doubt, if loth before, to fly. if I cannot, I will enter
the garden with she, and the house too, be the consequence what it will.
but, so affrighted, these be no question but she will fly.
when you think we at a sufficient distance [and I shall raise my voice
urge her swifter flight, that you may guess at that] then open the door
with your key: but you must be sure to open it very cautiously, lest we
should not be far enough off. I would not have she know you have a hand
in this matter, out of my great regard to you.
when you have open the door, take your key out of the lock, and put it
in your pocket: then, stoop for mine, put it in the lock on the
inside, that it may appear as if the door be open by herself, with a
key, which they will suppose to be of my procuring (it be new) and
leave open by we.
they should conclude she be go off by her own consent, that they may
not pursue we: that they may see no hope of tempt she back again. in
either case, mischief might happen, you know.
but you must take notice, that you be only to open the door with your
key, in case none of the family come up to interrupt we, and before we
be quite go: for, if they do, youwill find by what follow, that you
must not open the door at all. let they, on break it open, or by
get over the wall, find my key on the ground, if they will.
if they do not come to interrupt we, and if you, by help of your key,
come out, follow we at a distance; and, with uplifted hand, and wild
impatient gesture, (run backward and forward, for fear you should
come up too near we, and as if you see somebody come to your
assistance,) cry out for help, help, and to hasten. then shall we be soon
at the chariot.
tell the family that you see I enter a chariot with she: a dozen, or
more, man on horseback, attend we; all arm; some with blunderbuss,
as you believe; and that we take quite the contrary way to that we should
take.
you see, honest Joseph, how careful I be, as well as you, to avoid
mischief.
observe to keep at such a distance that she may not discover who you be.
take long stride, to alter your gait; and hold up your head, honest
Joseph; and shewill not know it to be you. man's air and gait be as
various and peculiar as their face. pluck a stake out of one of the
hedge: and tug at it, though it may come easy: this, if she turn back,
will look terrible, and account for your not follow we fast. then,
return with it, shoulder, to brag to the family what you would have
do, could you have overtake we, rather than your young lady should be
carry off by such a---- and you may call I name, and curse I. and
these air will make you look valiant, and in earnest. you see, honest
Joseph, I be always contrive to give you reputation. no man suffer by
serve I.
but, if our parley should last long than I wish; and if any of her
friend miss she before I cry, Hem, hem, twice; then, in order to save
yourself, (which be a very great point with I, I assure you,) make the
same noise as above: but as I direct before, open not the door with
your key. on the contrary, wish for a key with all your heart; but for
fear any of they should by accident have a key about they, keep in
readiness half a dozen little gravel-stone, no big than pea, and
thrust two or three slily into the key-hole; which will hinder their key
from turn round. it be good, you know, Joseph, to provide against
every accident in such an important case, as this. and let this be your
cry, instead of the other, if any of my enemy come in your sight, as
you seem to be try to burst the door open, Sir! Sir! or Madam!
Madam! o Lord, hasten! o Lord, hasten! Mr. Lovelace! Mr. Lovelace!--
and very loud--and that shall quicken I more than it shall those you
call to.--if it be Betty, and only Betty, I shall think bad of your art
of make love* than of your fidelity, if you cannot find a way to amuse
she, and put she upon a false scent.
* see Vol.II. Letter XXIX.
you must tell they that your young lady seem to run as fast off with I
as I with she. this will also confirm to they that all pursuit be in
vain. an end will hereby be put to Solmes's hope: and her friend,
after a while, will be more studious to be reconcile to she than to get
she back. so you will be a happy instrument of great good to all round.
and this will one day be acknowledge by both family. you will then be
every one's favourite; and every good servant, for the future, will be
proud to be liken to honest Joseph Leman.
if she should guess at you, or find you out, I have it already in my head
to write a letter for you to copy,* which, occasionally produce, will
set you right with she.
* see Vol.III. Letter XXI.
this one time be diligent, be careful: this will be the crown of all: and
once more, depend, for a recompense, upon the honour of
your assured friend,
R. LOVELACE.
you need not be so much afraid of go too far with Betty. if you
should make a match with she, she be a very likely creature, though a
vixen, as you say. I have an admirable receipt to cure a termagant wife.
--never fear, Joseph, but thou shalt be master of thine house. if she be
very troublesome, I can teach thee how to break her heart in a
twelvemonth; and honestly too;--or the precept would not be mine.
I enclose a new earnest of my future favour.
LETTER IV
to ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQUIER, his HONNER
SUNDAY MORNING, APRIL 9.
HONNERED SIR,
I must confesse I be infinitely oblige to your Honner's bounty. but
this last command!--it seem so intricket! Lord be merciful to I, how
have I be lead from littel stepps to grate stepps!--and if I should be
find out!--but your Honner say you will take I into your Honner's
sarvise, and protect I, if as I should at any time be find out; and
raise my wage besides; or set I upp in a good inne; which be my
ambishion. and you will be honnerable and kind to my dear young lady,
God love her.--but who can be unkind to she?
I wil do my good I be able, since your Honner will be apt to lose she, as
your Honner say, if I do not; and a man so stingie will be apt to gain
she. but mayhap my deareste young lady will not make all this trubble
needful. if she have promisse, she will stand to it, I dare to say.
I love your Honner for contrive to save mischiff so well. I think
till I know'd your Honner, that you be verry mischevous, and plese your
Honner: but find it to be clene contrary. your Honner, it be plane,
mean mighty well by every body, as far as I see. as I be sure I do
myself; for I be, althoff a very plane man, and all that, a very honnest
one, I thank my God. and have good principel, and have keep my young
lady's pressept always in mind: for she go no where, but save a soul
or two, more or less.
so, commend myself to your Honner's further favour, not forget the
inne, when your Honner shall so please, and good one offer; for plase
be no inherritanse now-a-day. and, I hope, your Honner will not think
I a dishonest man for sarve your Honner agenst my duty, as it may
look; but only as my conshence clear I.
be pleased, howsomever, if it like your Honner, not to call I honest
Joseph, so often. for, althoff I think myself verry honn, and all
that, yet I be touch a littel, for fear I should not do the quite right
thing: and too besides, your Honner have such a fesseshious way with you,
as that I hardly know whether you be in jest or earnest, when your
Honner call I honnest so often.
I be a very plane man, and seldom have writ to such honourable gentleman;
so you will be good enuff to pass by every thing, as I have often say,
and need not now say over again.
as to Mrs. Betty; I tho'te, indeed, she look above I. but she come
on vere well, natheless. I could like she well, iff she be well to
my young lady. but she have too much wit for so plane a man. Natheless,
if she be to angre I, althoff it be a shame to bete a woman, yet I
colde make shift to throe my hat at she, or so, your Honner.
but that same reseit, iff your Honner so please, to cure a shrewish wife.
it would more encurrege to wed, iff so be one know'd it before-hand, as
one may say. so likewise, if one knoe one could honnestly, as your
Honner say, and as of the handy-work of God, in one twelvemonth--
but, I shall grow impertinent to such a grate man.--And hereafter may do
for that, as she turn out: for one mought be loth to part with she,
mayhap, so verry soon too; espessially if she be to make the notable
landlady your Honner put into my head.
Butt wonce moer, beg your Honner's parden, and promisse all
dilligence and exsackness, I reste,
your Honner's dewtiful sarvant to command,
JOSEPH LEMAN.
LETTER V
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
ST. ALBAN'S, MONDAY NIGHT.
I snatch a few moment while my belove be retire, [as I hope, to rest,]
to perform my promise. no pursuit--nor have I apprehension of any;
though I must make my charmer dread that there will be one.
and now, let I tell thee, that never be joy so complete as mine!--But
let I inquire, be not the angel fly away?
***
o no! she be in the next apartment!--securely mine!--mine for ever!
o ecstasy!--My heart will burst my breast,
to leap into her bosom!
I know that the whole stupid family be in a combination to do my
business for I. I tell thee that they be all work for I, like so
many ground mole; and still more blind than the mole be say to be,
unknowing that they do so. I myself, the director of their principal
motion; which fall in with the malice of their little heart, they
take to be all their own.
but do I say my joy be perfect?--O no!--it receive some abatement from
my disgusted bride. for how can I endure to think that I owe more to her
relation' precaution than to her favour for me?--Or even, as far as I
know, to her preference of I to another man?
but let I not indulge this thought. be I to do so, it might cost my
charmer dear. let I rejoice, that she have pass the rubicon: that she
cannot return: that, as I have order it, the flight will appear to the
implacable to be altogether with her own consent: and that if I doubt
her love, I can put she to trial as mortify to her niceness, as
glorious to my pride.--For, let I tell thee, dearly as I love she, if I
think there be but the shadow of a doubt in her mind whether she
prefer I to any man live, I would shew she no mercy.
TUESDAY, DAY-DAWN.
but, on the wing of love, I fly to my charmer, who perhaps by this time
be rise to encourage the tardy dawn. I have not sleep a wink of the
hour and half I lay down to invite sleep. it seem to I, that I be not
so much body, as to require such a vulgar renovation.
but why, as in the chariot, as in the inn, at alight, all heart-
burst grief, my dearest creature? so persecute as thou wert
persecuted!--so much in danger of the most abhor compulsion!--yet
grief so unsuspectedly sincere for an escape so critical!--take care,
take care, o beloved of my soul! for jealous be the heart in which love
have erect a temple to thee.
yet, it must be allow, that such a sudden transition must affect she;
must ice she over. when a little more used to her new situation; when
her hurry be at an end; when she see how religiously I shall observe
all her injunction; she will undoubtedly have the gratitude to
distinguish between the confinement she have escape from, and the liberty
she have reason to rejoice in.
she come! she come! and the sun be just rise to attend she! Adieu!
be half as happy as I be (for all diffidencie, like night-fog before
the sun, disperse at her approach) and, next myself, thou wilt be the
happy man in the world.
LETTER VI
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
WEDNESDAY, APRIL 12.
I will pursue my melancholy story.
be thus hurry to the chariot, it would have be to no purpose to
have refuse enter into it, have he not in my fright lift I in, as
he do: and it instantly drive away a full gallop, and stop not till
it bring we to St. Alban's; which be just as the day shut in.
I think I should have faint several time by the way. with uplifted
hand and eye, God protect I! say I often to myself: can it be I, that
be here! my eye run over, and my heart ready to burst with sigh as
involuntarily as my flight.
how different, how inexpressibly different, the gay wretch; visibly
triumphing (as I could not be construe his almost rapturous joy) in the
success of his art! but overflow with complimental flourish, yet
respectfully distant his address, all the way we fly; for that, rather
than gallop, be the motion of the horse; which take, as I believe, a
round-about way, to prevent be trace.

LETTER ix
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE

I be infinitely concern, my ever dear and ever kind friend, that I be
the sad occasion of the displeasure between your mother and you.--how
many person have I make unhappy.
have I not to console myself, that my error be not owe to wicked

friend; to write to he.*
* see Vol. I. Letter III.

your affectionate
CL. HARLOWE.

LETTER XI
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
Mr. Lovelace, in continuation of his last letter, (no. VII.) give an
account to his friend (pretty much to the same effect with the lady's)

the people who come about we, as we alight, seem by their jaw-fall

assist hand, hurry into the house.***

mistress of the house I instantly change she into a sister, bring off

LETTER XV

I always love writing, and my unhappy situation give I now enough of

Mr. Lovelace. it bring on the subject which you advise I not to
decline, when it be handsomely offer. and I want to have either your

with he; and the more, as he have very quietly take up his quarter
here, without talk of remove, as he have promise.

why, Jack, thou need not make such a wonderment, as the girl say, if

LETTER XIX
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE

do not be so much concerned, my dear friend, at the bickering between

never do I hear of such a parcel of foolish toad as these Harlowes!--

one half of my contrivance.
he here relate the conversation between he and the Lady (upon the
subject of the noise and exclamation his agent make at the garden-

proceed exulting:
what a capacity for glorious mischief have thy friend!--Yet how near the
truth all of it! the only derivation, my assert that the fellow make

have she know the precise truth, her anger, to be so take in, would
never have let she forgive I.
have I be a military hero, I should have make gunpowder useless; for I
should have blow up all my adversary by dint of stratagem, turn
their own device upon they.
but these father and mother--Lord help 'em!--were not the power of
nature strong than those of discretion, and be not that busy dea bona
to afford her genial aid, till tardy prudence qualified parent to
manage their future offspring, how few people would have child!
James and Arabella may have their motif; but what can be say for a
father act as this father have act? what for a mother? what for an
aunt? what for uncles?--who can have patience with such fellow and
fellowesse?
soon will the fair one hear how high their foolish resentment run

trembling, as now, like a hungry hound, who see a delicious morsel
within his reach, (the froth hang upon his vermilion jaw,) yet dare
not leap at it for his life.
but I be originally a bashful mortal. indeed I be bashful still with

be the reason that I know it so well:--For, Jack, I have have abundant
cause, when I have look into myself, by way of comparison with the

a woman; and so, like Tiresias, can tell what they think, and what they
drive at, as well as themselves.
the modest one and I, particularly, be pretty much upon a par. the
difference between we be only, what they think, I act. but the immod
one out-do the bad of we by a bar's length, both in thinking and
act.
one argument let I plead in proof of my assertion; that even we rake

(that be to say, the sly,) love, and generally prefer, an impudent
man. whence can this be, but from a likeness in nature? and this make
the poet say, that ever woman be a rake in her heart. it concern they,
by their action, to prove the contrary, if they can.
thus have I read in some of the philosopher, that no wickedness be
comparable to the wickedness of a woman.* Canst thou tell I, Jack, who
say this? be it Socrates? for he have the devil of a wife--or who? or
be it solomon?--ke Solomon--Thou remembrest to have read of such a
king, dost thou not? SOL-O-MON, I learn, in my infant state [my mother
be a good woman] to answer, when ask, who be the wise man?--But my
indulgent questioner never ask I how he come by the uninspired part of
his wisdom.
* Mr. Lovelace be as much out in his conjecture of Solomon, as of
Socrates. the passage be in Ecclesiasticus, chap. xxv.
come, come, Jack, you and I be not so very bad, could we but stop where
we be.
he then give the particular of what pass between he and the Lady on
his menace relate to her brother and Mr. Solmes, and of his design
to punish Betty Barnes and Joseph Leman.
LETTER XXIV
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
FRIDAY, APR. 14.
I will now give you the particular of a conversation that have just
pass between Mr. Lovelace and I, which I must call agreeable.
it begin with his tell I, that he have just receive intelligence that
my friend be on a sudden come to a resolution to lay aside all
thought of pursue I, or of get I back: and that therefore he
attend I to know of my pleasure; and what I would do, or have he do?
I tell he, that I would have he leave I directly; and that, when it
be know to every body that I be absolutely independent of he, it
would pass, that I have leave my father's house because of my brother's ill
usage of I: which be a plea that I might make with justice, and to the
excuse of my father, as well as of myself.
he mildly reply, that if we could be certain that my relation would
adhere to this their new resolution, he could have no objection, since
such be my pleasure; but, as he be well assure that they have take it
only from apprehension, that a more active one might involve my brother
(who have breathe nothing but revenge) in some fatal misfortune, there
be too much reason to believe that they would resume their former
purpose the moment they should think they safely might.
this, Madam, say he, be a risque I cannot run. you would think it
strange if I could. and yet, as soon as I know they have so give out, I
think it proper to apprize you of it, and take your command upon it.
let I hear, say I, (willing to try if he have any particular view,) what
you think most advisable?
'tis very easy to say that, if I durst--if I might not offend you--if it
be not to break condition that shall be inviolable with I.
say then, Sir, what you would say. I can approve or disapprove, as I
think fit.
have not the man a fine opportunity here to speak out?--He have. and thus
he use it.
to wave, Madam, what I would say till I have more courage to speak out
[More courage,--mr. Lovelace more courage, my dear!]--i will only propose
what I think will be most agreeable to you--suppose, if you choose not to
go to Lady Betty's, that you take a turn cross the country to Windsor?
why to windsor?
because it be a pleasant place: because it lie in the way either to
Berkshire, to Oxford, or to London: Berkshire, where Lord M. be at
present: Oxford, in the neighbourhood of which live Lady Betty: London,
whither you may retire at your pleasure: or, if you will have it so,
whither I may go, you stay at Windsor; and yet be within an easy
distance of you, if any thing should happen, or if your friend should
change their new-take resolution.
this proposal, however, displease I not. but I say, my only objection
be, the distance of Windsor from Miss Howe, of whom I should be glad to
be always within two or three hour reach of by messenger, if possible.
if I have thought of any other place than Windsor, or near to Miss
Howe, he want but my command, and would seek for proper
accommodation: but, fix as I please, far or near, he have
servant, and they have nothing else to do but to obey I.
a grateful thing then he name to I--to send for my Hannah, as soon as I
shall be fix;* unless I would choose one of the young gentlewoman here
to attend I; both of whom, as I have acknowledge, be very obliging;
and he know I have generosity enough to make it worth their while.
* see his reason for propose Windsor, Letter XXV.--and her Hannah,
Letter XXVI.
this of Hannah, he might see, I take very well. I say I have thought of
send for she, as soon as I get to more convenient lodging. as to
these young gentlewoman, it be pity to break in upon that usefulness
which the whole family be of to each other; each have her proper
part, and perform it with an agreeable alacrity: insomuch, that I
like they all so well, that I could even pass my day among they, be
he to leave I; by which mean the lodging would be more convenient to
I than now they be.
he need not repeat his objection to this place, he say: but as to go
to Windsor, or wherever else I think fit, or as to his personal

that I could propose nothing in which I think my reputation, and even

since I be so much take up with my pen, he would instantly order his
horse to be get ready, and would set out.
not to be off my caution. have you any acquaintance at Windsor? say I.
--Know you of any convenient lodging there?
except the forest, reply he, where I have often hunt, I know the least
of Windsor of any place so noted and so pleasant. indeed I have
not a single acquaintance there.
upon the whole, I tell he, that I think his proposal of Windsor, not
amiss; and that I would remove thither, if I could get a lodging only for

please: and I should let every body know my independence.
he again propose himself, in very polite term, for my banker. but I,
as civilly, decline his offer.
this conversation be to be, all of it, in the main, agreeable. he ask

as near the castle, I say, as possible, for the convenience of go

I be agreeably surprised. I look at he, I believe, as if I doubt
my ear and my eye. his aspect however become his word.
I express my satisfaction in term so agreeable to he, that he say,

surely, my dear, the man must be in earnest. he could not have say

in the midst of my wild vagary, say he, I have ever preserve a

* that he propose one day to reform, and that he have sometimes good

and twenty thing of this sort I even preach to he; take care,

habitual evil change not on a sudden:

'tis else dissimulation--

how one evil bring on another, be sorrowfully witness to by

LETTER XXV
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
FRIDAY, APR. 14.
Thou hast often reproach I, Jack, with my vanity, without
distinguish the humourous turn that accompany it; and for which,
at the same time that thou robb I of the merit of it thou admirest I
highly. Envy give thee the indistinction: nature inspire the
admiration: unknown to thyself it inspire it. but thou art too clumsy
and too short-sight a mortal, to know how to account even for the
impulse by which thou thyself art move.
well, but this acquit thee not of my charge of vanity, Lovelace,
methink thou sayest.
and true thou sayest: for I have indeed a confounded parcel of it. but,
if man of part may not be allow to be in vain, who should! and yet,
upon second thought, man of part have the least occasion of any to be
vain; since the world (so few of they be there in it) be ready to find
they out, and extol they. if a fool can be make sensible that there be a
man who have more understanding than himself, he be ready enough to
conclude, that such a man must be a very extraordinary creature.
and what, at this rate, be the general conclusion to be draw from the
premises?--is it not, that no man ought to be vain? but what if a man
cannot help it!--thi, perhaps, may be my case. but there be nothing upon
which I value myself so much as upon my invention. and for the soul of
I, I cannot help let it be see, that I do. yet this vanity may be
a mean, perhaps, to overthrow I with this sagacious lady.
she be very apprehensive of I I see. I have study before she and Miss
Howe, as often as I have be with they, to pass for a giddy thoughtless
creature. what a folly then to be so expatiatingly sincere, in my answer
to her home put, upon the noise within the garden?--but such success
have attend that contrivance [success, Jack, have blow many a man
up!] my cursed vanity get uppermost, and keep down my caution. the
menace to have secrete solme, and that other, that I have thought to
run away with her foolish brother, and of my project to revenge she upon
the two servant, so much terrify the dear creature, that I be force
to sit down to muse after mean to put myself right in her opinion.
some favourable incident, at the time, tumble in from my agent in her
family; at least such as I be determined to make favourable: and
therefore I desire admittance; and this before she could resolve any
thing against I; that be to say, while her admiration of my intrepidity
keep resolution in suspense.
accordingly, I prepare myself to be all gentleness, all obligingness,
all serenity; and as I have now and then, and always have, more or less,
good motion pop up in my mind, I encourage and collect every thing of
this sort that I have ever have from novicehood to maturity, [not long in
recollect, Jack,] in order to bring the dear creature into good humour

may be able to lay a foundation fit to build my grand scheme upon!--love,
think I, be not naturally a doubter: fear be, I will try to banish the
latter: nothing then but love will remain. CREDULITY be the God of
Love's prime minister, and they never be asunder.
* he have say, Letter XVIII. that he would make reformation his stalking-
horse, &c.
he then acquaint his friend with what pass between he and the Lady,
in relation to his advice from Harlowe-place, and to his proposal
about lodging, pretty much to the same purpose as in her precede
Letter.
when he con to mention his proposal of the Windsor lodging, thus he
express himself:
now, Belford, can it enter into thy leaden head, what I mean by this
proposal!--i know it cannot. and so Iwill tell thee.
to leave she for a day or two, with a view to serve she by my absence,

then I want to inform myself, why I have not congratulatory letter from

word, might be make necessary to shew she as matter proceed.
as to Windsor, I have no design to carry she particularly thither: but

convenient nature, which I may pursue; or of an inconvenient nature,
which I may avoid.
always be careful of back door, be a maxim with I in all my exploit.
whoever know I, know that I be no proud man. I can talk as familiarly
to servant as to principal, when I have a mind to make it worth their
while to oblige I in any thing. then servant be but as the common

I be most apprehensive about Miss Howe. she have a confounded deal of

mongership--[I love to plague thee, who art a pretender to accuracy, and
a surface-skimmer in learn, with out-of-the-way word and phrase] I

Poor Hickman! I pity he for the prospect he have with such a virago!
but the fellowbe a fool, God wot! and now I think of it, it be
absolutely necessary for complete happiness in the married state, that
one should be a fool [an argument I once hold with this very Miss Howe.]
but then the fool should know the other's superiority; otherwise the
obstinate one will disappoint the wise one.
but my agent Joseph have help I to secure this quarter, as I have
hint to thee more than once.
LETTER XXVI
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
[in CONTINUATION.]
but be it not a confounded thing that I cannot fasten an obligation upon
this proud beauty? I have two motif in endeavour to prevail upon
she to accept of money and raiment from I: one; the real pleasure I
should have in the accommodating of the haughty maid; and to think there
be something near she, and upon she, that I could call mine: the other,
in order to abate her severity and humble she a little.
nothing more effectually bring down a proud spirit, than a sense of
lie under pecuniary obligation. this have always make I solicitous to
avoid lay myself under any such: yet, sometimes, formerly, have I be

your handsome husband, my dear, make a wife's heart ache very often: and

we have all our defect: we have often regret the particular fault,

LETTER XXXVII
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
WEDN. MORNING, APRIL 19.
I be glad, my dear friend, that you approve of my removal to London.
the disagreement between your mother and you give I inexpressible
affliction. I hope I think you both more unhappy than you be. but I
beseech you let I know the particular of the debate you call a very
pretty one. I be well acquainted with your dialect. when I be inform
of the whole, let your mother have be ever so severe upon I, I shall
be easy a great deal.--faulty people should rather deplore the occasion
they have give for anger than resent it.
if I be to be oblige to any body in England for money, it shall be to
you. your mother need not know of your kindness to I, you say--but she
must know it, if it be do, and if she challenge my beloved friend upon
it; for would you either falsify or prevaricate?--i wish your mother
could be make easy on this head--forgive I, my dear,--but I know--yet
once she have a well opinion of me.--O my inconsiderate rashness!--
excuse I once more, I pray you.--Pride, when it be native, will shew
itself sometimes in the midst of mortification--but my stomach be down
already.
***
I be unhappy that I cannot have my worthy Hannah. I be sorry for the
poor creature's illness as for my own disappointment by it. come, my
dear Miss Howe, since you press I to be beholden to you: and would think
I proud if I absolutely refuse your favour; pray be so good as to send
her two guineas in my name.
if I have nothing for it, as you say, but matrimony, it yield little
comfort, that his relation do not despise the fugitive, as person of
their rank and quality-pride might be suppose to do, for have be a
fugitive.
but o my cruel, thrice cruel uncle! to suppose--but my heart check my
pen, and will not let it proceed, on an intimation so extremely shocking
as that which he supposes!--Yet, if thus they have be persuade, no
wonder if they be irreconcilable.
this be all my hard-hearted brother's doings!--His surmisings:--god
forgive he--pray his injure sister!

to ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
TUESDAY NIGHT, APRIL 18.
DEAR SIR,
I be extremely rejoice to hear, that we shall so soon have you in town
after so long an absence. you will be the more welcome still, if what
report say, be true; which be, that you be actually married to the fair
lady upon whom we have hear you make such encomium. Mrs. Doleman, and
my sister, both wish you joy if you be; and joy upon your near prospect
if you be not.
I have be in town for this week past, to get help if I could, from my
paralytic complaint; and be in a course for they. which, nevertheless,
do not prevent I from make the desire inquiry. this be the
result.
you may have a first floor, well furnish, at a mercer's in Belford-
street, Covent-garden, with conveniencie for servant: and these either
by the quarter or month. the term accord to the convenience
require.
Mrs. Doleman have see lodging in Norfolk-street and other in cecil-
street; but though the prospect to the Thames and Surrey-hills look
invite from both these street, yet I suppose they be too near the
city.
the owner of those in Norfolk-street would have half the house go
together. it would be too much for your description therefore: and I
suppose, tat when you think fit to declare your marriage, you will
hardly be in lodging.
those in Cecil-street be neat and convenient. the owner be a widow of a
good character; and she insist, that you take they for a twelvemonth
certain.
you may have good accommodation in Dover-street, at a widow's, the
relict of an officer in the guard, who die soon after he have purchase
his commission (to which he have a good title by service, and which cost
he most part of what he have) she be oblige to let lodging.
this may possibly be an objection. but she be very careful, she say,
that she take no lodger, but of figure and reputation. she rent two
good house, distant from each other, only join by a large handsome
passage. the inner-house be the genteelest, and very elegantly
furnish; but you may have the use of a very handsome parlour in the
outer-house, if you choose to look into the street.
a little garden belong to the inner-house, in which the old gentlewoman
have display a true female fancy; have cram it with vas, flower-
pot, and figure, without number.
as these lodging seem to I the most likely to please you, I be more
particular in my inquiry about they. the apartment she have to let are
in the inner-house: they be a dining-room, two neat parlour, a
withdrawing-room, two or three handsome bedchamber, one with a pretty
light closet in it, which look into the little garden, all furnish in
taste.
a dignified clergyman, his wife, and maiden daughter be the last who
live in they. they have but lately quit they, on his be present
to a considerable church preferment in Ireland. the gentlewoman say
that he take the lodging but for three month certain; but like they

with regret, though on so good an account. she brag, that this be
the way of all the lodger she ever have, who staid with her four time as
long as they at first intended.
I have some knowledge of the colonel, who be always look upon as a man

people plump. she live reputably, and be, as I find, aforehand in the

if these, or any other of the lodging I have mention, be not
altogether to your lady's mind, she may continue in they the less while,
and choose other for herself.
the widow consent that you shall take they for a month only, and what of
they you please. the term, she say, she will not fall out upon, when
she know what your lady expect, and what her servant be to do, or
yours will undertake; for she observe that servant be generally bad
to deal with than their master or mistress.
the lady may board or not as she please.
as we suppose you be marry, but that you have reason, from family-
difference, to keep it private for the present, I think it not amiss
to hint as much to the widow (but as uncertainty, however); and ask

if none of these lodging please, you need not doubt very handsome one

let I add, that the lodging at the mercer's, those in Cecil-street,

I be, my dear Sir,
your sincere and affectionate friend and servant,
THO. DOLEMAN.
you will easily guess, my dear, when you have read the letter, which

and now, my dear, lest any thing should happen, in so variable, (which at

LETTER XXXIX
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.

he begin with communicate to he the letter he write to Mr. Doleman,
to procure suitable lodging in town, and which he send away by the

Thou know the widow; thou know her niece; thou know the

this of Tom Doleman? every possible objection anticipate! every
accident provide against! every tittle of it plot-proof!
who could forbear smile, to see my charmer, like a farcical dean and

no confidence in I, fair one! none at all, 'tis plain. thou wilt not,

but to see the charmer so far satisfied with my contrivance as to borrow
my friend's letter, in order to satisfy Miss Howe likewise!--
silly little rogue! to walk out into bye-path on the strength of their
own judgment!--When nothing but experience can enable they to disappoint
we, and teach they grandmother-wisdom! when they have it indeed, then
may they sit down, like so many Cassandras, and preach caution to other;
who will as little mind they as they do their instructress, whenever a
fine handsome confidant young fellow, such a one as thou know who,
come across they.
but, Belford, didst thou not mind that sly rogue Doleman's naming Dover-
street for the widow's place of abode?--what dost thou think could be
mean by that?--'Tis impossible thou shouldst guess, so, not to puzzle
thee about it, suppose the Widow Sinclair's in Dover-street should be
inquire after by some officious person, in order to come at character
[Miss Howe be as sly as the devil, and as busy to the full,] and neither
such a name, nor such a house, can be find in that street, nor a house
to answer the description; then will not the keenest hunter in England be
at a fault?
but how wilt thou do, methink thou askest, to hinder the lady from
resent the fallacy, and mistrust thee the more on that account,
when she find it out to be in another street?
Pho! never mind that: either I shall have a way for it, or we shall
thoroughly understand one another by that time; or if we donot, shewill
know enough of I, not to wonder at such a peccadilla.
but how wilt thou hinder the lady from apprize her friend of the real
name?
she must first know it herself, monkey, must she not?
well, but how wilt thou do to hinder she from know the street, and her
friend from direct letter thither, which will be the same thing as if
the name be know?
let I alone for that too.
if thou far objectest, that Tom Doleman, be too great a dunce to

order to save honest Tom all this trouble, I who know the town so well,
could send he a copy of what he should write, and leave he nothing to

what now sayest thou to I, Belford?
and suppose I have design this task of inquiry for thee; and suppose the

this it be to have leisure upon my hands!--what a matchless plotter thy

Ay, SINCLAIR, Jack!--Remember the name! SINCLAIR, I repeat. she have no
