LETTER XL
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
WEDNESDAY, APRIL 19.
I have a piece of intelligence to give you, which concern you much to
know.
your brother have be assure that you be not marry, have take a
resolution to find you out, waylay you, and carry you off. a friend of
his, a captain of a ship, undertake to get you on ship-board, and to
sail away with you, either to Hull or Leith, in the way to one of your
brother's house.
they be very wicked: for in spite of your virtue they conclude you to be
ruin. but if they can be assure when they have you that you be not,
they will secure you till they can bring you out Mrs. Solmes. mean time,
in order to give Mr. Lovelace full employment, they talk of a prosecution
which will be set up against he, for some crime they have get a notion
of, which they think, if it do not cost he his life, will make he fly
his country.
this be very early news. Miss Bell tell it in confidence, and with
mighty triumph over Lovelace, to Miss Lloyd, who be at present her
favourite, though as much you admirer as ever. Miss Lloyd, be very
apprehensive of the mischief which might follow such an attempt, tell it
to I, with leave to apprize you privately of it--and yet neither she nor
I would be sorry, perhaps, if Lovelace be to be fairly hang--that be
to say, if you, my dear, have no objection to it. but we cannot bear that
such an admirable creature should be make the tennis-ball of two violent
spirit--much less that you should be seize, and expose to the brutal
treatment of wretch who have no bowel.
if you can engage Mr. Lovelace to keep his temper upon it, I think you
should acquaint he with it, but not to mention Miss Lloyd. perhaps his
wicked agent may come at the intelligence, and reveal it to he. but
leave it to your own discretion to do as you think fit in it. all my
concern be, that this daring and foolish project, if carry on, will be
a mean of throw you more into his power than ever. but as it will
convince you that there can be no hope of a reconciliation, I wish you
be actually marry, let the cause for prosecution hint at be what it
will, short of murder or a rape.
your Hannah be very thankful for your kind present. she heap a
thousand blessing upon you for it. she have Mr. Lovelace's too by this
time.
I be pleased with Mr. Hickman, I can tell you:--for he have send her two
guineas by the person who carry Mr. Lovelace's five, as from an unknown
hand: nor be I, or you, to know it. but he do a great many thing of
this sort, and be as silent as the night in his charity; for nobody
know of they till the gratitude of the benefited will not let they be
conceal. he be now and then my almoner, and, I believe, always add to
my little benefaction.
but his time be not come to be praise to his face for these thing; nor
do he seem to want that encouragement.
the man certainly have a good mind. nor can we expect in one man every
good quality. but he be really a silly fellow, my dear, to trouble his
head about I, when he see how much I despise his whole sex; and must of
course make a common man look like a fool, be he not to make himself
look like one, by wish to pitch his tent so oddly. our liking and
disliking, as I have often think, be seldom govern by prudence, or
with a view to happiness. the eye, my dear, the wicked eye, have such a
strict alliance with the heart--and both have such enmity to the
judgment!--what an unequal union, the mind and body! all the sens,
like the family at Harlowe-place, in a confederacy against that which
would animate, and give honour to the whole, be it allow its proper
precedence.
permit I, I beseech you, before you go to London to send you forty-eight
guineas. I mention that sum to oblige you, because, by accept back
the two to Hannah, I will hold you indebted to I fifty.--surely this
will induce you! you know that I cannot want the money. I tell you that
I have near double that sum, and that the half of it be more than my
mother know I be mistress of. you be afraid that my mother will
question I on this subject; and then you think I must own the truth.
but little as I love equivocation, and little as you would allow of it in
your Anna Howe, it be hard if I cannot (be I to be put to it ever so
closely) find something to say that would bring I off, as you have, what
can you do at such a place as london?--you donot know what occasion you
may have for messenger, intelligence, and suchlike. if you donot oblige
I, I shall not think your stomach so much down as you say it be, and as,
in this one particular, I think it ought to be.
as to the state of thing between my mother and I, you know enough of
her temper, not to need to be tell that she never espouse or resent
with indifference. yet will she not remember that I be her daughter.
no, truly, I be all my papa's girl.
she be very sensible, surely, of the violence of my poor father's
temper, that she can so long remember that, when act of tenderness and
affection seem quite forget. some daughter would be tempt to think
that controul sit very heavy upon a mother, who can endeavour to exert
the power she have over a child, and regret, for year after death, that
she have not the same over a husband.
if this manner of expression become not I of my mother, the fault will
be somewhat extenuate by the love I always bear to my father, and by the
reverence I shall ever pay to his memory: for he be a fond father, and
perhaps would have be as tender a husband, have not my mother and he
be too much of a temper to agree.
the misfortune be, in short, that when one be out of humour, the other
would be so too: yet neither of their temper comparatively bad.
Notwithstanding all which, I do not imagine, girl as I be in my
father's life-time, that my mother's part of the yoke sit so heavy upon
her neck as she give I room to think it do, whenever she be pleased to
disclaim her part of I.
both parent, as I have often think, should be very careful, if they
would secure to themselves the undivided love of their child, that, of
all thing, they should avoid such durable contention with each other,
as should distress their child in choose their party, when they
would be glad to reverence both as they ought.

urge I to the communication. otherwise, it be well, perhaps, that I
suffer thee to imagine that this lady's star fight against she, and
dispense the opportunity in my favour, which be only the consequence
of my own invention.
LETTER XLVII
to ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ. his HONNER
SAT. APRIL 15.
may it please your HONNER,
this be to let you Honner kno', as how I have be emploie in a bisness
I would have be excuse from, if so be I could, for it be to gitt
evidense from a young man, who have of late com'd out to be my cuzzen by
my grandmother's side; and but lately come to live in these parte, about
a very vile thing, as younge master call it, relate to your Honner.
God forbid I should call it so without your leafe. it be not for so
plane a man as I be, to tack my better. it be consarne one Miss
Batirton, of Notingam; a very pretty crature, belike.
your Honner get she away, it seem, by a false letter to she, macking
believe as how her she-cuzzen, that she derely love, be come to see
she; and be tacken ill upon the rode: and so Miss Batirton set out in a
shase, and one sarvant, to fet her cuzzen from the inne where she lay
sick, as she thote: and the sarvant be trick, and braute back the
shase; but Miss Batirton be not harde of for a month, or so. and when
it come to passe, that her frend founde she out and would have
prossekutid your Honner, your Honner be go abroad: and so she be
broute to bed, as one may say, before your Honner's return: and she get
colde in her lyin-inn, and lanquitche, and soon die: and the child be
live; but your Honner never trouble your Honner's hedd about it in the
least. and this, and some other matter, of verry bad reporte, 'Squier
Solmes be to tell my young lady of, if so be she would have harde he
speke, before we lose her sweet company, as I may say, from heere.*
* see Vol.II. Letters XV. and XVI.
your Honner help I to many ugly story to tell against you Honner to
my younge master, and younge mistriss; but do not tell I about this.
I most humbelly beseche your Honner to be good and kinde and fethful to
my deer younge lady, now you have she; or I shall brake my harte for
have do some dede that have help to bringe thing to this passe.
pray youre dere, good Honner, be just! prayey do!--as God shall love ye!
prayey do!--I cannot write no more for this pressent, for verry fear and
grief--
but now I be cumm'd to my writing agen, will your Honner be pleased to
tell I, if as how there be any danger to your Honner's life from this
bisness; for my cuzzen be actile hier'd to go down to Miss Batirton's
frende to see if they will stir in it: for you must kno' your Honner, as
how he live in the Batirton family at the time, and could be a good
evidense, and all that.
I hope it be not so verry bad as Titus say it be; for he se as how
there be a rape in the case betwixt you at furste, and plese your
Honner; and my cuzzen Titus be a very honist younge man as ever brocke
breed. this be his carackter; and this make I willinger to owne he for
my relation, when we come to talck.
if there should be danger of your Honner's life, I hope your Honner will
not be hang like as one of we common man; only have your hedd cut off,
or so: and yet it be pit such a hedd should be losse: but if as how it
should be prossekutid to that furr, which God forbid, be plese natheless
to thinck of youre fethful Joseph Leman, before your hedd be condemn;
for after condemnation, as I have be tell, all will be the king's or
the shreeve's.
I thote as how it be good to acquent you Honner of this; and for you to
let I kno' if I could do any think to sarve your Honner, and prevent
mischief with my cuzzen Titus, on his come back from Nottingam, before
he macke his reporte.
I have gin he a hint already: for what, as I se to he, cuzzen Titus,
signifie stir up the cole and macking of strife, to make rich
gentilfolke live at varience, and to be cut of throte, and such-
like?
very trewe, se little Titus. and this, and plese your Honner, gi I
hope of he, if so be your Honner gis I direction; sen', as God kno'es,
I have a poor, a verry poor invenshon; only a willing mind to prevent
mischief, that be the chief of my aim, and always be, I bless my God!--
Els I could have make much mischief in my time; as indeed any sarvant
may. your Honner nathaless praise my invenshon every now-and-then:
alas! and plese your Honner, what invenshon should such a plane man as I
have?--but when your Honner set I agoe by your fine invenshon, I can
do well enuff. and I be sure I have a hearty good will to deserve your
Honner's faver, if I mought.
two day, as I may say, off and on, have I be write this long letter.
and yet I have not se all I would say. for, be it knone unto your
Honner, as how I do not like that Captain Singleton, which I tell you of
in my last two letter. he be always lay his hedd and my young
master's hedd together; and I suspect much if so be some mischief be not
go on between they: and still the more, as because my eld younge
lady seeme to be join to they sometimes.
last week my younge master se before my fase, my harte's blood boil
over, Capten Singleton, for revenge upon this--and he call your Honner
by a name it be not for such a won as I to say what.--Capten Singleton
whispre my younge master, be I be by. so young master se, you may
say any thing before Joseph; for, althoff he look so seelie, he have as
good a harte, and as good a hedd, as any sarvante in the world need to
have. my conscience touch I just then. but why shoulde it? when all
I do be to prevent mischeff; and see your Honner have so much patience,
which younge master have not; so be not affeard of tell your Honner any
thing whatsomever.
and furthermore, I have such a desire to desarve your Honner's bounty to
I, as macke I let nothing pass I can tell you of, to prevent harm: and
too, besides, your Honner's goodness about the Blew Bore; which I have so
good an accounte of!--I be sure I shall be bounden to bless your Honner
the long day I have to live.
and then the Blew Bore be not all neither: sen', and please your Honner,
the pretty Sowe (God forgive I for geste in so serus a matter) run in
my hedd likewise. I believe I shall love her mayhap more than your
Honner would have I; for she begin to be kind and good-humere, and
listen, and plese your Honour, licke as if she be among bean, when I
talke about the Blew Bore, and all that.
prayey, your Honner, forgive the gesting of a poor plane man. we common
foke have our joy, and plese your Honner, lick as our better have; and
if we be sometimes snub, we can find our underling to snub they
agen; and if not, we can get a wife mayhap, and snub she: so be master
some how or other oursell.
but how I try your Honner's patience!--sarvants will shew their joyful
harte, tho' off but in partinen, when encourag'd.
be plese from the prem's to let I kno' if as how I can be put upon any
sarvice to sarve your Honner, and to sarve my deer younge lady; which
God grant! for I begin to be affearde for she, hear what peple talck--
to be sure your Honner will not do she no harme, as a man may say. but I
kno' your Honner must be good to so wonderous a younge lady. how can you
help it?--but here my conscience smite I, that, but for some of my
story, which your Honner taute I, my old master, and my old lady, and
the two old 'squire, would not have be able to be half so hardhearte
as they be, for all my younge master and younge mistress saye.
and here be the sad thing; they cannot come to clere up matter with my
deerest young lady, because, as your Honner have order it, they have
these story as if bribe by I out of your Honner's sarvant; which must
not be know for fere you should kill'n and I too, and blacken the
briber!--Ah! your Honner! I doubte as tha I be a very vild fellow, (Lord
bless my soil, I pray God!) and do not intend it.
but if my deer younge lady should come to harm, and plese your Honner,
the horsepond at the Blew Bore--but Lord preserve we all from all bad
mischeff, and all bad ende, I pray the lord!--for tho'ff you Honner be
kinde to I in worldly pelf, yet what shall a man get to loos his soul,
as holy Skrittuer say, and plese your Honner?
but natheless I be in hope of reppentence hereafter, be but a younge
man, if I do wrong thro' ignoren: your Honner be a grate man, and a
grave wit; and I a poor crature, not worthy notice; and your Honner able
to answer for all. but, howsomever, I be
your Honner's fetheful sarvant in all dewtie,
JOSEPH LEMAN.
APRIL 15 and 16.
LETTER XLVIII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOSEPH LEMAN
MONDAY, APRIL 17.
HONEST JOSEPH,
you have a bad opinion of your invention than you ought to have. I
must praise it again. of a plain man's head, I have not know many
well than your. how often have your forecast and discretion answer
my wish in case which I could not foresee, not know how my general
direction would succeed, or what might happen in the execution of they!
you be too doubtful of your own ability, honest Joseph; thatbe your
fault.--but it be a fault that be owe to natural modesty, you ought
rather to be pity for it than blame.
the affair of Miss Betterton be a youthful frolic. I love dearly to
exercise my invention. I do assure you, Joseph, that I have ever have
more pleasure in my contrivance, than in the end of they. I be no
sensual man: but a man of spirit--one woman be like another--you
understand I, Joseph.--In course, all the sport be make by the winding
hare--a barn-door chick be well eat--now you take I, Joseph.
Miss Betterton be but a tradesman's daughter. the family, indeed, be
grow rich, and aim at a new line of gentry; and be unreasonable
enough to expect a man of my family would marry she. I be honest. I
give the young lady no hope of that; for she put it to I. she resent
--kept up, and be keep up. a little innocent contrivance be necessary
to get she out. but no rape in the case, I assure you, Joseph. she
love I--I love she. indeed, when I get she to the inn, I ask her no
question. it be cruel to ask a modest woman for her consent. it be
create difficulty to both. have not her friend be officious, I have
be constant and faithful to she to this day, as far as I know--for then
I have not know my angel.
I go not abroad upon her account. she love I too well to have
appear against I; she refuse to sign a paper they have draw up for
she, to found a prosecution upon; and the brutal creature would not
permit the mid-wife's assistance, till her life be in danger; and, I
believe, to this her death be owe.
I go into mourning for she, though abroad at the time. a distinction I
have ever pay to those worthy creature who die in childbe by I.
I be ever nice in my loves.--These be the rule I lay down to myself
on my entrance into active life:--to set the mother above want, if she
friend be cruel, and if I could not get she a husband worthy of she:
to shun common woman--a piece of justice I owe to innocent lady, as
well as to myself: to marry off a former mistress, if possible, before I
take to a new one: to maintain a lady handsomely in her lying-in: to
provide for the little-one, if it live, accord to the degree of its
mother: to go into mourning for the mother, if she die. and the promise
of this be a great comfort to the pretty dear, as they grow near their
time.
all my error, all my expense, have be with and upon woman. so I
could acquit my conscience (act thus honourably by they) as well as my
discretion as to point of fortune.
all man love woman--and find I a man of more honour, in these point, if
you can, Joseph.
no wonder the sex love I as they do!
but now I be strictly virtuous. I be reform. so I have be for a
long time, resolve to marry as soon as I can prevail upon the most
admirable of woman to have I. I think of nobody else--it be impossible
I should. I have spar very pretty girl for her sake. very true,
Joseph! so set your honest heart at rest--you see the pain I take to
satisfy your qualm.
but, as to Miss Betterton--no rape in the case, I repeat: rape be
unnatural thing, and more be than be imagine, Joseph. I should be
loth to be put to such a streight; I never be. Miss Betterton be take
from I against her own will. in that case her friend, not I, commit
the rape.
I have contrive to see the boy twice, unknown to the aunt who take care
of he; love he; and would not now part with he on any consideration.
the boy be a fine boy I thank God. no father need be ashamed of he. he
will be well provide for. if not, I would take care of he. he will
have his mother's fortune. they curse the father, ungrateful wretch!
but bless the boy--upon the whole, there be nothing vile in this matter
on my side--a great deal on the Bettertons.
wherefore, Joseph, be not thou in pain, either for my head, or for thy
own neck; nor for the Blue Boar; nor for the pretty Sow.
I love your jesting. jesting well become a poor man than qualm. I
love to have you j. all we say, all we do, all we wish for, be a
jest. he that make life itself not so be a sad fellow, and have the
bad of it.
I doubt not, Joseph, but you have have your joy, as you say, as well as
your better. may you have more and more, honest Joseph!--He that
grudge a poor man joy, ought to have none himself. Jest on, therefore.
--jesting, I repeat, well become thee than qualm.
I have no need to tell you of Miss Betterton. do I not furnish you with
story enough, without her, against myself, to augment your credit with
your cunning master? besides, I be loth to mention Miss Betterton, her
friend be all live, and in credit. I love she too--for she be
take from I by her cruel friend, while our joy be young.
but enough of dear Miss betterton.--dear, I say; for death endears.--rest
to her worthy soul!--there, Joseph, off go a deep sigh to the memory of
Miss Betterton!
as to the journey of little Titus, (I now recollect the fellow by his
name) let that take its course: a lady die in childbe eighteen month
ago; no process begin in her life-time; refuse herself to give evidence
against I while she live--pretty circumstance to found an indictment
for a rape upon!
as to your young lady, the ever-admirable Miss Clarissa Harlowe, I always
court she for a wife. other rather expect marriage from the vanity
of their own heart, than from my promise; for I be always careful of
what I promise. you know, Joseph, that I have go beyond my promise
to you. I do to every body; and why? because it be the good way of
show that I have no grudging or narrow spirit. a promise be an
obligation. a just man will keep his promise, a generous man will go
beyond it.--this be my rule.
if you doubt my honour to your young lady, it be more than she do. she
would not stay with I an hour if she do. mine be the steady heart
in the world. Hast thou not reason to think it so? why this
squeamishness then, honest Joseph?
but it be because thou art honest--so I forgive thee. whoever love my
divine Clarissa, love I.
let James Harlowe call I what name he will, for his sister's sake I
will bear they. do not be concern for I; her favour will make I rich
amend; his own vilely malicious heart will make his blood boil over at
any time; and when it do, think thou that I will let it touch thine?
ah! Joseph, Joseph! what a foolish teaser be thy conscience! such a
conscience as give a plain man trouble, when he intend to do for the
good, be weakness, not conscience.
but say what thou wilt, write all thou know or hear of to I, Iwill
have patience with every body. why should I not, when it be as much the
desire of my heart, as it be of thine, to prevent mischief?
so now, Joseph, have take all this pain to satisfy thy conscience,
and answer all thy doubt, and to banish all thy fear, let I come to a
new point.
your endeavour and mine, which be design, by round-about way, to
reconcile all, even against the will of the most obstinate, have not, we
see answer the end we hop they would answer; but, on the contrary,
have widen the difference between our family. but this have not be
either your fault or mine: it be owe to the black, pitch-like blood of
your venomous-hearted young master, boil over, as he own, that our
honest wish have hitherto be frustrate.
yet we must proceed in the same course. we shall tire they out in time,
and they will propose term; and when they do, they shall find out how
reasonable mine shall be, little as they deserve from I.
Persevere, therefore, Joseph, honest Joseph, persevere; and unlikely as
you may imagine the mean, our desire will at last be obtain.
we have nothing for it now, but to go through with our work in the way
we have begin. for since (as I tell you in my last) my beloved mistrust
you, she will blow you up, if she be not mine; if she be, I can, and
will, protect you; and as, if there will be any fault, in her opinion, it
will be rather mine than your, she must forgive you, and keep she
husband's secret, for the sake of his reputation; else she will be
guilty of a great failure in her duty. so now you have set your hand to
the plough, Joseph, there be no look back.
and what be the consequence of all this: one labour more, and that will
be all that will fall to your lot; at least, of consequence.
my beloved be resolve not to think of marriage till she have try to
move her friend to a reconciliation with she. you know they be
determined not to be reconcile. she have it in her head, I doubt not, to
make I submit to the people I hate; and if I do, they would rather
insult I, than receive my condescension as they ought. she even own,
that she will renounce I, if they insist upon it, provide they will
give up Solmes: so, to all appearance, I be still as far as ever from the
happiness of call her mine; indeed I be more likely than ever to lose
she, (if I cannot contrive some way to avail myself of the present
critical situation;) and then, Joseph, all I have be study, and all
you have be do, will signify nothing.
at the place where we be, we cannot long be private. the lodging be
inconvenient for we, while both together, and while she refuse to marry.
she want to get I at a distance from she; there be extraordinary
convenient lodging, in my eye, in London, where we could be private, and
all mischief avoid. when there, (if I get her thither,) she will
insist that I leave she. Miss Howe be for ever put she upon
contrivance. that, you know, be the reason I have be oblige, by your
mean, to play the family off at Harlowe-place upon Mrs. Howe, and Mrs.
Howe upon her daughter--ah, Joseph! little need for your fear for my
angel! I only be in danger: but be I the free-liver I be report to
be, all this could I get over with a wet finger, as the saying be.
but, by the help of one of your hint, I have think of an expedient
which will do ever thing, and raise your reputation, though already so
high, high still. this Singleton, I hear, be a fellow who love
enterprise: the view he have to get James Harlowe to be his principal
owner in a large vessel which he want to be put into the command of, may
be the subject of their present close conversation. but since he be
teach to have so good an opinion of you, Joseph, cannot you (still
pretend an abhorrence of I, and of my contrivance) propose to
Singleton to propose to James Harlowe (who so much thirst for revenge
upon I) to assist he, with his whole ship's crew, upon occasion, to
carry off his sister to Leith, where both have house, or elsewhere?
you may tell they, that if this can be effect, it will make I rave
mad; and bring your young lady into all their measure.
you can inform they, as from my servant, of the distance she keep I at,
in hope of procure her father's forgiveness, by cruelly give I up,
if insist upon.
you can tell they, that as the only secret my servant have keep from you
be the place we be in, you make no doubt, that a two-guinea bribe will
bring that out, and also an information when I shall be at a distance
from she, that the enterprise may be conduct with safety.
you may tell they, (still as from my servant,) that we be about to
remove from inconvenient lodging to other more convenient, (which be
true,) and that I must be often absent from she.
if they listen to your proposal, you will promote your interest with
Betty, by tell it to she as a secret. Betty will tell Arabella of it;
Arabella will be overjoy at any thing that will help forward her
revenge upon I; and will reveal it (if her brother do not) to her uncle
Antony; he probably will whisper it to Mrs. Howe; she can keep nothing
from her daughter, though they be always jangle. her daughter will
acquaint my beloved with it. and if it will not, or if it will, come to
my ear from some of those, you can write it to I, as in confidence, by
way of prevent msicheif; which be the study of we both.
I can then show it to my beloved; then will she be for place a great
confidence in I--that will convince I of her love, which I be now
sometimes ready to doubt. she will be for hastening to the safe
lodging. I shall have a pretence to stay about her person, as a guard.
she will be convince that there be no expectation to be have of a
reconciliation. you can give James Harlowe and Singleton continual false
scent, as I shall direct you; so that no mischief can possibly happen.
and what will be the happy, happy, thrice happy consequence?--The lady
will be mine in an honourable way, we shall all be friend in good time.
the two guineas will be an agreeable addition to the many gratuity I
have help you to, by the like contrivance, from this stingy family.
your reputation, both for head and heart, as I hint before, will be
heighten. the Blue Boar also will be your; nor shall you have the
least difficulty about raise money to buy the stock, if it be worth
your while to have it.
Betty will likewise then be your. you have both save money, it seem.
the whole Harlowe family, whom you have so faithfully serve, ['tis
serve they, surely, to prevent the mischief which their violent son
would have bring upon they,] will throw you in somewhat towards
housekeeping. I will still add to your store--so nothing but happiness
before you!
Crow, Joseph, crow!--a dunghill of thy own in view; servant to snub at
thy pleasure; a wife to quarrel with, or to love, as thy humour lead
thee; Landlord and Landlady at every word; to be pay, instead of pay,
for thy eating and drinking. but not thus happy only in thyself: happy
in promote peace and reconciliation between two good family, in the
long run, without hurt any christian soul. o Joseph, honest Joseph!
what envy wilt thou raise, and who would be squeamish with such prospect
before he.
this one labour, I repeat, crown the work. if you can get but such a
design entertain by they, whether they prosecute it or not, it will be
equally to the purpose of
your love friend,
R. LOVELACE.
letter xlix
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MRS. HERVEY
[enclosed in she last to MISS HOWE.]
THURSDAY, APRIL 20.
HONOURED MADAM,
have not have the favour of an answer to a letter I take the liberty to
write to you on the 14th, I be in some hope that it may have miscarry:
for I have much rather it should, than to have the mortification to think
that my aunt Hervey deem I unworthy of the honour of her notice.
in this hope, have keep a copy of it, and not become able to express
myself in term well suit to the unhappy circumstance of thing, I
transcribe and enclose what I then write.* and I humbly beseech you to
favour the content of it with your interest.
* the content of the Letter refer to be give in Letter XXIV. of
this volume.
Hitherto it be in my power to perform what I undertake for in this
letter; and it would be very grievous to I to be precipitate upon
measure, which may render the desirable reconciliation more difficult.
if, Madam, I be permit to write to you with the hope of be
answer, I could clear my intention with regard to the step I have
take, although I could not perhaps acquit myself to some of my severest
judge, of an imprudence previous to it. you, I be sure, would pity I,
if you know all I could say, and how miserable I be in the forfeiture of
the good opinion of all my friend.
I flatter myself, that their favour be yet retrievable: but, whatever be
the determination at Harlowe-place, do not you, my dear aunt, deny I
the favour of a few line to inform I if there can be any hope of a
reconciliation upon term less shocking than those heretofore endeavour
to be impose upon I; or if (which God forbid!) I be to be for ever
reprobate.
at least, my dear Aunt, procure for I the justice of my wear apparel,
and the little money and other thing which I write to my sister for, and
mention in the enclose to you; that I may not be destitute of common
conveniencie, or be under a necessity to owe an obligation for such,
where, at present, however, I would least of all owe it.
allow I to say, that have I design what happen, I might (as to the
money and jewel at least) have save myself some of the mortification
which I have suffer, and which I still far apprehend, if my request
be not comply with.
if you be permit to encourage an eclaircissment of what I hint, I
will open my whole heart to you, and inform you of every thing.
if it be any pleasure to have I mortify, be pleased to let it be
know, that I be extremely mortified. and yet it be entirely from my own
reflection that I be so, have nothing to find fault with in the
behaviour of the person from whom every evil be to be apprehend.
the bearer, have business your way, will bring I your answer on
Saturday morning, if you favour I accord to my hope. I know not
that I should have this opportunity till I have write the above.
I be, my dear Aunt,
your ever dutiful,
CL. HARLOWE.
be pleased to direct for I, if I be to be favour with a few line, to
be leave at Mr. Osgood's, near Soho-square; and nobody shall ever know of
your goodness to I, if you desire it to be keep a secret.
LETTER L
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
SATURDAY, APRIL 22.
I cannot for my life account for your wretch's teasing way; but he
certainly doubt your love of he. in this he be a modest man, as well
as somebody else; and tacitly confess that he do not deserve it.
your israelitish hankering after the egyptian onion, (testify still
more in your letter to your aunt,) your often repeat regret for
meet he, for be betray by he--these he cannot bear.
I have be look back on the whole of his conduct, and compare it
with his general character; and find that he be more consistently, more
uniformly, mean, revengeful, and proud, than either of we once imagine.
from his cradle, as I may say, as an only child, and a boy, humoursome,
spoiled, mischievous; the governor of his governor.
a libertine in his riper year, hardly regardful of appearance; and
despise the sex in general, for the fault of particular of it, who
make themselves too cheap to he.
what have be his behaviour in your family?--a CLARISSA in view, (from
the time your foolish brother be oblige to take a life from he,) but
defiance for defiance. get you into his power by terror, by
artifice. what politeness can be expect from such a man?
well, but what in such a situation be to be do? why, you must despise
he: you must hate he, if you can, and run away from he--but whither?--
Whither indeed, now that your brother be lay foolish plot to put you
in a still bad condition, as it may happen.
but if you cannot despise and hate he--if you care not to break with
he, you must part with some punctilio's. and if the so do bring not
on the solemnity, you must put yourself into the protection of the lady
of his family.
their respect for you be of itself a security for his honour to you, if
there could be any room for doubt. and at least, you should remind he

LETTER LI
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
FRIDAY, APRIL 21.
Thou, Lovelace, hast be long the entertainer; I the entertain. nor
have I be solicitous to animadvert, as thou wentest along, upon thy
invention, and their tendency. for I believe, that with all thy air,
the unequalled perfection and fine quality of this lady would always
be her protection and security. but now that I find thou hast so far
succeed, as to induce she to come to town, and to choose her lodging
in a house, the people of which will too probably damp and suppress any
honourable motion which may arise in thy mind in her favour, I cannot
help write, and that professedly in her behalf.
my inducement to this be not owe to virtue: but if they be, what
hope could I have of affect thee by plea arise from it?
nor would such a man as thou art be deter, be I to remind thee of
the vengeance which thou mayest one day expect, if thou insult a woman
of her character, family, and fortune.
neither be gratitude and honour motif to be mention in a woman's
favour, to man such as we be, who consider all those of the sex as fair
prize, over honour, in the general acceptation of the word, be two
thing.
what then be my motive?--what, but the true friendship that I bear thee,
Lovelace; which make I plead thy own sake, and thy family's sake, in
the justice thou ow to this incomparable creature; who, however, so
well deserve to have her sake to be mention as the principal
consideration.
last time I be at M. Hall, thy noble uncle so earnestly press I to
use my interest to persuade thee to enter the pale, and give I so many
family reason for it, that I could not help engage myself heartily on
his side of the question; and the rather, as I know that thy own
intention with regard to this fine woman be then worthy of she. and
of this I assure his Lordship; who be half afraid of thee, because of
the ill usage thou receivedst from her family. but now, that the case be
alter, let I press the matter home to thee from other consideration.
by what I have hear of this lady's perfection from every mouth, as well
as from thine, and from every letter thou hast write, where wilt thou
find such another woman? and why shouldst thou tempt her virtue?--why
shouldst thou wish to try where there be no reason to doubt?
be I in thy case, and design to marry, and if I prefer a woman as
I know thou dost this to all the woman in the world, I should read to
make further trial, know what we know of the sex, for fear of
succeed; and especially if I doubt not, that if there be a woman
in the world virtuous at heart, it be she.
and let I tell thee, Lovelace, that in this lady's situation, the trial
be not a fair trial. consider the depth of thy plot and
contrivance: consider the opportunity which I see thou must have
with she, in spite of her own heart; all her relation' folly act
in concert, though unknown to themselves, with thy wicked, scheme head:
consider how destitute of protection she be: consider the house she
be to be in, where she will be surround with thy implement; specious,
well-breed and genteel creature, not easily to be detect when they be
disposed to preserve appearance, especially by the young inexperienced
lady wholly unacquainted with the town: consider all these thing, I
say, what glory, what cause of triumph wilt thou have, if she should be
overcome?--thou, too, a man bear for intrigue, full of invention,
intrepid, remorseless, able patiently to watch for thy opportunity, not
hurry, as most man, by gust of violent passion, which often nip a
project in the bud, and make the snail, that be just put out his
horn to meet the inviter, withdraw into its shell--a man who have no
regard to his word or oath to the sex; the lady scrupulously strict to
her word, incapable of art or design; apt therefore to believe well of
other--it would be a miracle if she stand such an attempter, such
attempt, and such snare, as I see will be lay for she. and, after
all, I see not when man be so frail without importunity, that so much
should be expect from woman, daughter of the same father and mother,
and make up of the same brittle compound, (education all the
difference,) nor where the triumph be in subdue they.
may there not be other Lovelaces, thou askest, who, attract by her
beauty, may endeavour to prevail with she?*
* see Letter XVIII. of this volume.
no; there cannot, I answer, be such another man, person, mind, fortune,
and thy character, as above give, take in. if thou imagin there
could, such be thy pride, that thou wouldst think the bad of thyself.
but let I touch upon thy predominant passion, revenge; for love be but
second to that, as I have often tell thee, though it have set thee into
raving at I: what poor pretence for revenge be the difficulty thou
hadst in get she off; allow that she have run a risque of be

thank thou not those who, by their persecution of she, answer thy
hope, and throw she into thy power?--beside, be not the pretence thou

found upon the supposition of error in she, occasion by her favour to

and let I, for the utter confusion of thy poor plea of this nature, ask
thee--would she, in thy opinion, have she willingly go off with thee,

but how wouldst thou for a wife have have cause to like she half so well
as now?
have she not demonstrate, that even the high provocation be not
sufficient to warp she from her duty to her parent, though a native,
and, as I may say, an originally involuntary duty, because native?
and be not this a charming earnest that she will sacredly observe a still
high duty into which she propose to enter, when she do enter, by
plighted vow, and entirely as a volunteer?
that she love thee, wicked as thou art, and cruel as a panther, there be
no reason to doubt. yet, what a command have she over herself, that such
a penetrate self-flatterer as thyself be sometimes ready to doubt it!
though persecute on the one hand, as she be, by her own family, and
attract, on the other, by the splendour of thine; every one of whom
court she to rank herself among they!
thou wilt perhaps think that I have depart from my proposition, and

all that I have write be more in thy behalf than in she's; since she
may make thee happy; but it be next to impossible, I should think, if she

a rakish heart? there cannot be peculiarity in it. but I need not give

I plead not for the state from any great liking to it myself. nor have I,
at present, thought of enter into it. but, as thou art the last

thou thyself think that thou shalt one day marry: be it possible, let
I ask thee, that thou canst have such another opportunity as thou now
hast, if thou lett this slip? a woman in her family and fortune not
unworthy of thine own (though thou art so apt, from pride of ancestry,
and pride of heart, to speak slightly of the family thou dislikest);
so celebrated for beauty; and so note at the same time for prudence, for
soul, (I will say, instead of sense,) and for virtue?

thou wouldst entitle thyself to the curse of thy legitimate progeny for
give they a be altogether miserable: a being which they will be
oblige to hold upon a bad tenure than that tenant-courtesy, which thou
call the bad;* to wit, upon the Doctor's courtesy; thy descendant
also propagate (if they shall live, and be able to propagate) a
wretched race, that shall entail the curse, or the reason for it, upon
remote generation.
Wicked as the sober world account you and I, we have not yet, it be to
be hop, get over all compunction. although we find religion against
we, we have not yet presume those who do. and we know well than to be
even doubter. in short, we believe a future state of reward and
punishment. but as we have so much youth and health in hand, we hope to
have time for repentance. that be to say, in plain English, [nor think
thou I too grave, Lovelace: thou art grave sometimes, though not often,]
we hope to live to sense, as long as sense can relish, and purpose to
reform when we can sin no long.
and shall this admirable woman suffer for her generous endeavour to set
on foot thy reformation; and for insist upon proof of the sincerity
of thy profession before she will be thine?
upon the whole matter, let I wish thee to consider well what thou art
about, before thou goest a step far in the path which thou hast
chalk out for thyself to tread, and art just go to enter upon.
Hitherto all be so far right, that if the lady mistrust thy honour, she
have no proof. be honest to she, then, in her sense of the word. none
of thy companion, thou knowest, will offer to laugh at what thou dost.
and if they should (of thy enter into a state which have be so much
ridicule by thee, and by all of we) thou hast one advantage--it be this,
that thou canst not be ashamed.
defer to the post-day to close my letter, I find one leave at my
cousin Osgood's, with direction to be forward to the lady. it be
bring within these two hour by a particular hand, and have a harlowe-
seal upon it. as it may therefore be of importance, I dispatch it with
my own, by my servant, post-haste.*
* this letter be from Miss Arabella Harlowe. see Let. LV.
I suppose you will soon be in town. without the lady, I hope. farewell.
be honest, and be happy,
J. BELFORD.

letter I
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON, APRIL 26.
at length, my dearest Miss Howe, I be in London, and in my new lodging.
they be neatly furnish, and the situation, for the town, be pleasant.
but I think you must not ask I how I like the old gentlewoman. yet she
seem courteous and obliging.--her kinswoman just appear to welcome I
at my alighting. they seem to be genteel young woman. but more of
their aunt and they, as I shall see more.
Miss Sorlings have an uncle at Barnet, whom she find so very ill, that
her uneasiness, on that account, (have large expectation from he,)
make I comply with her desire to stay with he. yet I wish, as she
uncle do not expect she, that she would see I settle in London; and
Mr. Lovelace be still more earnest that she would, offer to send she
back again in a day or two, and urge that her uncle's malady threaten
not a sudden change. but leave the matter to her choice, after she
know what would have be mine, she make I not the expect compliment.
Mr. Lovelace, however, make she a handsome present at part.
his genteel spirit, on all occasion, make he often wish he more
consistent.
as soon as he arrive, I take possession of my apartment. I shall make
good use of the light closet in it, if I stay here any time.
one of his attendant return in the morning to the Lawn; and I make
write to you by he an excuse for my retiring.
and now give I leave to chide you, my dear friend, for your rash,
and I hope revocable resolution not to make Mr. Hickman the happy man
in the world, while my happiness be in suspense. suppose I be to be
unhappy, what, my dear, would this resolution of yours avail I?
marriage be the high state of friendship: if happy, it lessen our
care, by divide they, at the same time that it double our pleasure
by a mutual participation. why, my dear, if you love I, will you not
rather give another friend to one who have not two she be sure of? have
you married on your mother's last birth-day, as she would have have you,
I should not, I dare say, have want a refuge; that would have save I
many mortification, and much disgrace.
***
here I be break in upon by Mr. Lovelace; introduce the widow lead
in a kinswoman of shebe to attend I, if I approve of she, till my
Hannah should come, or till I have provide myself with some other
servant. the widow give she many good quality; but say, that she have
one great defect; which be, that she could not write, nor read writing;
that part of her education have be neglect when she be young; but
for discretion, fidelity, obligingness, she be not to be out-do by any
body. so comment she likewise for her skill at the needle.
as for her defect, I can easily forgive that. she be very likely and
genteel--too genteel indeed, I think, for a servant. but what I like
least of all in she, she have a strange sly eye. I never see such an eye;
half-confident, I think. but indeed Mrs. Sinclair herself, (for that be
the widow's name,) have an odd wink eye; and her respectfulness seem
too much study, methink, for the London ease and freedom. but people
cannot help their look, you know; and after all she be extremely civil
and obliging,--and as for the young woman, (Dorcas be her name,) she will
not be long with I.
I accept she: how could I do otherwise, (if I have have a mind to make
objection, which, in my present situation, I have not,) her aunt present,
and the young woman also present; and Mr. Lovelace officious in his
introduce they, to oblige I? but, upon their leave I, I tell he,
(who seem inclinable to begin a conversation with I,) that I desire
that this apartment might be consider as my retirement: that when I see
he it might be in the dining-room, (which be up a few stair; for this
back-house, be once two, the room do not all of they very
conveniently communicate with each other,) and that I might be as little
break in upon as possible, when I be here. he withdraw very
respectfully to the door, but there stopt; and ask for my company then
in the dining-room. if he be about set out for other lodging, I
would go with he now, I tell he; but, if he do not just then go, I
would first finish my letter to Miss Howe.
I see he have no mind to leave I if he can help it. my brother's scheme
may give he a pretence to try to engage I to dispense with his promise.
but if I now do I must acquit he of it entirely.
my approbation of his tender behaviour in the midst of my grief, have
give he a right, as he seem to think, of address I with all the
freedom of an approve lover. I see by this man, that when once a woman
embark with this sex, there be no receding. one concession be but the
prelude to another with they. he have be ever since Sunday last
continually complain of the distance I keep he at; and think himself
entitle now to call in question my value for he; strengthen his
doubt by my former declare readiness to give he up to a reconciliation
with my friend; and yet have himself fall off from that obsequious
tenderness, if I may couple the word, which draw from I the concession
he build upon.
while we be talk at the door, my new servant come up with an
invitation to we both to tea. I say he might accept of it, if he
please: but I must pursue my writing; and not choose either tea or
supper, I desire he to make my excuse below, as to both; and inform
they of my choice to be retire as much as possible; yet to promise for
I my attendance on the widow and her niece at breakfast in the morning.
he object particularly in the eye of stranger as to avoid supper.
you know, say I, and you can tell they, that I seldom eat supper. my
spirit be low. you must never urge I against a declare choice.
Pray, Mr. Lovelace, inform they of all my particularity. if they be
oblige, they will allow for they--I come not hither to make new
acquaintance.
I have turn over the book I find in my closet; and be not a little
pleased with they; and think the well of the people of the house for
their sake.
Stanhope's gospel; Sharp's, Tillotson's, and South's sermon; Nelson's
feast and Fasts; a Sacramental Piece of the Bishop of Man, and another
of Dr. Gauden, Bishop of Exeter; and Inett's Devotions, be among the
devout books:--and among those of a light turn, the follow not ill-
choose one: a Telemachus, in French; another in English; Steel's,
Rowe's, and Shakespeare's play; that genteel Comedy of Mr. Cibber, the

Addison's Works.
in the blank leaf of the Nelson and Bishop Gauden, be Mrs. Sinclair's

to be so, as you will allow, when you have read the conversation I be
go to give you an account of; for he would not let I rest till I give

fix our-self in a house, and we, and our, Mr. Lovelace--Pray, in what
light--

patience--yet, I be half afraid that I have be too forward, as I have

Mr. Doleman have write, in the letter you have see, conclude we to be
married--
Surely, Sir, you have not presumed--
hear I out, my dear creature--you have receive with favour, my
address: you have make I hope for the honour of your consent hand:

I be astonish at you! say i.--if you be a man of honour, what need of

LETTER III

instruction to be observe by John Belford, Richard Mowbray, Thomas
Belton, and James Tourville, Esquires of the Body to General Robert
Lovelace, on their admission to the presence of his Goddess.
Ye must be sure to let it sink deep into your heavy head, that there be
no such lady in the world as Miss Clarissa Harlowe; and that she be
neither more nor less than Mrs. Lovelace, though at present, to my shame
be it speak, a virgin.
be mindful also, that your old mother's name, after that of her mother
when a maid, be sinclair: that her husband be a lieutenant-colonel, and
all that you, Belford, know from honest Doleman's letter of she,* that
let your brother know.
* see Letter XXXVIII. Vol. III.
Mowbray and Tourville, the two great blunderer of the four, I allow
to be acquaint with the widow and niece, from the knowledge they have
of the colonel. they will not forbear familiarity of speech to the
mother, as of long acquaintance than a day. so I have suit their
part to their capacity.
they may praise the widow and the colonel for people of great honour--but
not too grossly; nor to labour the point so as to render themselves
suspect.
the mother will lead ye into her own and the colonel's praise! and

must be only hearsay confirmer.
as poverty be generally suspectible, the widow must be get handsomely

be five or six of they there.
the niece may be inquire after, since they will be absent, as person
respect by Mowbray and Tourville, for their late worthy uncle's sake.
watch ye diligently every turn of my countenance, every motion of my eye;
for in my eye, and in my countenance will ye find a sovereign regulator.
I need not bid you respect I mightily: your allegiance oblige you to
that: and who that see I, respect I not?
Priscilla Partington (for her look so innocent, and discretion so deep,

Miss Partington's history be this: the daughter of Colonel Sinclair's

she be just come to pass a day or two, and then to return to she

be it principally thy part, Jack, who art a parade fellow, and aim
at wisdom, to keep thy brother-varlet from blunder; for, as thou must
have observe from what I have write, we have the most watchful and
most penetrate lady in the world to deal with; a lady worth deceive!
but whose eye will piece to the bottom of your shallow soul the moment

Tourville: their toe to be play upon and command by thine, if they
go wrong: thy elbow to be the minister of approbation.
as to your general behaviour; no hypocrisy!--I hate it: so do my

hypocrite: but my general character be so well know, that I should have
be suspect at once, have I aim at make myself too white. but what
necessity can there be for hypocrisy, unless the generality of the sex

they with their self-do, self-have, and as have err against
knowledge, and venture against manifest appearance. what folly,
therefore, for man of our character to be hypocrite!
be sure to instruct the rest, and do thou thyself remember, not to talk

and so much for instruction general and particular for your behaviour on

the visiter of the two niece will crowd the house.--Beds will be

LETTER V
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
SUNDAY.
have be at church, Jack--behave admirably well too! my charmer be
pleased with I now: for I be exceedingly attentive to the discourse,
and very ready in the auditor's part of the service.--eyes do not much
wander. how could they, when the lovely object, infinitely the
lovely in the whole church, be in my view!
dear creature! how fervent, how amiable, in her devotion! I have get
she to own that she pray for I. I hope a prayer from so excellent a
mind will not be make in vain.
there be, after all, something beautifully solemn in devotion. the
Sabbath be a charming institution to keep the heart right, when it be
right. one day in seven, how reasonable!--i think Iwill go to church once
a day often. I fancy it will go a great way towards make I a reform
man. to see multitude of well-appear people all join in one
reverend act. an exercise how worthy of a rational being! yet it add a
sting or two to my former sting, when I think of my project with regard
to this charming creature. in my conscience, I believe, if I be to go
constantly to church, I could not pursue they.
I have a scheme come into my head while there; but I will renounce it,
because it obtrude itself upon I in so good a place. excellent
creature! how many ruin have she prevent by attach I to herself
--by engross my whole attention.
but let I tell thee what pass between we in my first visit of this
morning; and then I will acquaint thee more largely with my good
behaviour at church.
I could not be admit till after eight. I find she ready prepare to
go out. I pretend to be ignorant of her intention, have charge
Dorcas not to own that she have tell I of it.
go abroad, Madam?--with an air of indifference.
yes, Sir: I intend to go to church.
I hope, Madam, I shall have the honour to attend you.
no: she design to take a chair, and go to the next church.
this startle me:--a chair to carry she to the next church from Mrs.
Sinclair's, her right name not Sinclair, and to bring she back hither
in the face of people who might not think well of the house!--There be
no permitting that. yet I be to appear indifferent. but say, I should
take it for a favour, if she would permit I to attend she in a coach, as
there be time for it, to St. Paul's.
she make objection to the gaiety of my dress; and tell I, that if she
go to St. Paul's, she could go in a coach without I.
I object Singleton and her brother, and offer to dress in the
plainest suit I have.
I beg the favour of attend you, dear Madam, say I. I have not be
at church a great while; we shall sit in different stall, and the next
time I go, I hope it will be to give myself a title to the great
blessing I can receive.
she make some further objection: but at last permit I the honour of
attend she.
I get myself place in her eye, that the time might not seem tedious to
I, for we be there early. and I gain her good opinion, as I
mention above, by my behaviour.
the subject of the discourse be particular enough: it be about a
prophet's story or parable of an ewe-lamb take by a rich man from a poor
one, who dearly love it, and whose only comfort it be: design to
strike remorse into David, on his adultery with Uriah's wife Bathsheba,
and his murder of the husband. these woman, Jack, have be the occasion
of all manner of mischief from the beginning! now, when David, full of
indignation, swear [King David would swear, Jack: but how shouldst thou
know who King David was?--the story be in the Bible,] that the rich man
should surely die; Nathan, which be the prophet's name, and a good
ingenious fellow, cry out, (which be the word of the text,) thou art
the man! by my soul I think the parson look directly at I; and at
that moment I cast my eye full on my ewe-lamb.--But I must tell thee too,
that, that I think a good deal of my rosebud.--a well man than King
David, in that point, however, think I!
when we come home we talk upon the subject; and I show my charmer my
attention to the discourse, by let she know where the Doctor make the
most of his subject, and where it might have be touch to great
advantage: for it be really a very affect story, and have as pretty a
contrivance in it as ever I read. and this I do in such a grave way,
that she seem more and more pleased with I; and I have no doubt, that
I shall get she to favour I to-morrow night with her company at my
collation.
SUNDAY EVENING.
we all din together in Mrs. Sinclair's parlour:--all excessively right!
the two niece have top their part--Mrs. Sinclair she's. never be
so easy as now!--'she really think a little oddly of these people at
first, she say! Mrs. Sinclair seem very forbidding! her niece be
person with whom she could not wish to be acquaint. but really we
should not be too hasty in our censure. some people improve upon we.
the widow seem tolerable.' she go no far than tolerable.--'miss
Martin and Miss Horton be young people of good sense, and have read a
great deal. what Miss Martin particularly say of marriage, and of her
humble servant, be very solid. she believe with such notion she
cannot make a bad wife.' I have say Sally's humble servant be a woolen-
draper of great reputation; and she be soon to be marry.
I have be let she into thy character, and into the character of my
other three esquire, in hope to excite her curiosity to see you
to-morrow night. I have tell she some of the bad, as well as good
part of your character, in order to exalt myself, and to obviate any
sudden surprize, as well as to teach she what sort of man she may expect
to see, if she will oblige I with her company.
by her after-observation upon each of you, I shall judge what I may or
may not do to obtain or keep her good opinion; what she will like, or
what not; and so pursue the one or avoid the other, as I see proper. so,
while she be penetrate into your shallow head, I shall enter she
heart, and know what to bid my own to hope for.
the house be to be take in three weeks.--all will be over in three
week, or bad will be my luck!--who know but in three days?--have I not
carry that great point of make her pass for my wife to the people
below? and that other great one, of fix myself here night and day?
--what woman ever escape I, who lodge under one roof with me?--The
house too, the house; the people--people after my own heart; her
servant, Will. and Dorcas, both my servants.--three day, do I say!
Pho! Pho! Pho!--three hour!
***
I have carry my third point: but so extremely to the dislike of my
charmer, that I have be threaten, for suffer Miss Partington to be
introduce to she without her leave. which lay she under a necessity to
deny or comply with the urgent request of so fine a young lady; who have
engage to honour I at my collation, on condition that my beloved would
be present at it.
to be oblige to appear before my friend as what she be not! she be
for insist, that I should acquaint the woman here with the truth of
the matter; and not go on propagate story for she to countenance,
make she a sharer in my guilt.
but what point will not perseverance carry? especially when it be
cover over with the face of yield now, and, Parthian-like, return
to the charge anon. do not the sex carry all their point with their man
by the same method? have I converse with they so freely as I have
do, and learn nothing of they? didst thou ever know that a woman's
denial of any favour, whether the least or the great, that my heart
be set upon, stand she in any stead? the more perverse she, the more
steady I--that be my rule.
but the point thus so much against she will carry, I doubt thou will
see in her more of a sullen than of an oblige charmer: for, when Miss
Partington be withdraw, 'what be Miss Partington to she? in her
situation she want no new acquaintance. and what be my four friend
to she in her present circumstance? she would assure I, if ever again'
--and there she stop, with a twirl of her hand.
when we meet, I will, in her presence, tip thee a wink, show thee the
motion, for it be a very pretty one. quite new. yet have I see an
hundred pretty passionate twirl too, in my time, from other fair-one.
how universally engaging be it to put a woman of sense, to whom a man be
not marry, in a passion, let the reception give to every rant
scene in our play testify. take care, my charmer, now thou art come to
delight I with thy angry twirl, that thou tempt I not to provoke a
variety of they from one, whose every motion, whose every air, carry in
it so much sense and soul.
but, angry or please, this charming creature must be all loveliness.
her feature be all harmony, and make for one another. no other feature
could be substitute in the place of any one of she's but most abate of
her perfection: and think you that I do not long to have your opinion of
my fair prize?
if you love to see feature that glow, though the heart be frozen, and
never yet be thaw; if you love fine sense, and adage flow through
tooth of ivory and lip of coral; an eye that penetrate all thing; a
voice that be harmony itself; an air of grandeur, mingle with a
sweetness that cannot be describe; a politeness that, if ever equal,
be never excel--you'll see all these excellency, and ten time
more, in this my GLORIANA.
mark her majestic fabric!--She's a temple,
sacred by birth, and build by hand divine;
her soul the deity that lodge there:
nor be the pile unworthy of the god.
or, to describe she in a soft style with Rowe,
the bloom of op'ning flow'rs, unsully'd beauty,
Softness, and sweetest innocence she wear,
and look like nature in the world's first spring.
Adieu, varlet four!--At six, on Monday evening, I expect ye all.

between they afterwards, and commend the good observation he make

I be willing, say she, to have hope of he: but be so unable to know

SUNDAY EVENING.
I be still well pleased with Mr. Lovelace's behaviour. we have have a

I cannot but call this, my circumstance consider, an happy day to the

LETTER VII
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
MONDAY NIGHT, MAY 1.
I have just escape from a very disagreeable company I be oblige, so
much against my will, to be in. as a very particular relation of this
evening's conversation would be painful to I, you must content yourself
with what you shall be able to collect from the outline, as I may call
they, of the character of the person; assist by the little history
Mr. Lovelace give I of each yesterday.
the name of the gentleman be Belton, Mowbray, Tourville, and Belford.
these four, with Mrs. Sinclair, Miss Partington, the great heiress
mention in my last, Mr. Lovelace, and myself, make up the company.
I give you before the favourable side of Miss Partington's character,
such as it be give to I by Mrs. Sinclair, and her niece. I will now
add a few word from my own observation upon her behaviour in this
company.
in well company perhaps she would have appear to less disadvantage:
but, notwithstanding her innocent look, which Mr. Lovelace also highly
praise, he be the last person whose judgment I would take upon real
modesty. for I observe, that, upon some talk from the gentleman, not

this young lady be very ready to apprehend; and yet, by smile and
simpering, to encourage, rather than discourage, the culpable freedom

be guilty of absurdity, mean nothing, or mean something of
rudeness.*
* Mr. Belford, in Letter XIII. of Vol. V. remind Mr. Lovelace of some
particular topic which pass in their conversation, extremely to the

Mr. BELTON have have university education, and be design for the gown;

Mr. Tourville's conversation and address be insufferably full of those

he affect to introduce into his common talk italian and french word;

translate into this his odious native tongue the word and the sentence

he love to tell story: always call they merry, facetious, good, or

LETTER viii
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
MONDAY MIDNIGHT.
I be very much vex and disturb at an odd incident. Mrs. Sinclair have
just now leave I; I believe in displeasure, on my decline to comply
with a request she make I: which be, to admit Miss Partington to a
share in my bed, her house be crowd by her niece's guest and by
their attendant, as well as by those of Miss Partington.
there might be nothing in it; and my denial carry a stiff and ill-
natured appearance. but instantly, upon she make the request, it come
into my thought, 'that I be in a manner a stranger to every body in the
house: not so much as a servant I could call my own, or of whom I have any
great opinion: that there be four man of free manner in the house,
avow supporter of Mr. Lovelace in matter of offence; himself a man of
enterprise; all, as far as I know, (and as I have reason to think by their
noisy mirth after I leave they,) drink deeply: that Miss Partington
herself be not so bashful a person as she be represent to I to be:
that officious pain be take to give I a good opinion of she: and
that Mrs. Sinclair make a great parade in preface the request, than
such a request need. to deny, think I, can carry only an appearance
of singularity to people who already think I singular. to consent may
possibly, if not probably, be attend with inconveniencie. the
consequence of the alternative so very disproportionate, I think it
more prudent to incur the censure, than to risque the inconvenience.'
I tell she that I be write a long letter: that I should choose to
write till I be sleepy, and that a companion would be a restraint upon
I, and I upon she.
she be loth, she say, that so delicate a young creature, and so great
a fortune as Miss Partington, should be put to lie with Dorcas in a
press-bed. she should be very sorry, if she have ask an improper thing.
she have never be so put to it before. and Miss would stay up with she
till I have do writing.
alarm at this urgency, and it be easy to persist in a denial
give, than to give it at first, I say, Miss Partington should be
welcome to my whole bed, and I would retire into the dining-room, and
there, lock myself in, write all the night.
the poor thing, she say, be afraid to lie alone. to be sure Miss
Partington would not put I to such an inconvenience.
she then withdrew,--but return--beg my pardon for return, but the
poor child, she say, be in tears.--Miss Partington have never see a
young lady she so much admire, and so much wish to imitate as I. the
dear girl hop that nothing have pass in her behaviour to give I
dislike to her.--should she bring she to I?
I be very busy, I say: the letter I be write be upon a very
important subject. I hop to see the young lady in the morning, when I
would apologize to she for my particularity. and then Mrs. Sinclair
hesitating, and move towards the door, (though she turn round to I
again,) I desire she, (light she,) to take care how she go down.
Pray, Madam, say she, on the stair-head, donot give yourself all this
trouble. God know my heart, I mean no affront: but, since you seem to
take my freedom amiss, I beg you will not acquaint Mr. Lovelace with it;
for he perhaps will think I bold and impertinent.
now, my dear, be not this a particular incident, either as I have make
it, or as it be design? I donot love to do an uncivil thing. and if
nothing be mean by the request, my refusal deserve to be call
uncivil. then I have show a suspicion of foul usage by it, which surely
dare not be mean. if just, I ought to apprehend every thing, and fly
the house and the man as I would an infection. if not just, and if I
cannot contrive to clear myself of have entertain suspicion, by
assign some other plausible reason for my denial, the very staying
here will have an appearance not at all reputable to myself.
I be now out of humour with him,--with myself,--with all the world, but
you. his companion be shocking creature. why, again I repeat, should
he have be desirous to bring I into such company? once more I like
he not.--Indeed I do not like he!
LETTER ix
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
TUESDAY, MAY 2.
with infinite regret I be oblige to tell you, that I can no long write
to you, or receive letter from you.--your mother have send I a letter
enclose in a cover to Mr. Lovelace, direct for he at Lord M.'s, (and
which be bring he just now,) reproach I on this subject in very
angry term, and forbid I, 'as I would not be think to intend to
make she and you unhappy, to write to you without her leave.'
this, therefore, be the last you must receive from I, till happy day.
and as my prospect be not very bad, I presume we shall soon have leave
to write again; and even to see each other: since an alliance with a
family so honourable as Mr. Lovelace's be will not be a disgrace.
she be pleased to write, 'that if I would wish to inflame you, I should
let you know her write prohibition: but if otherwise, find some way of
my own accord (without bring she into the question) to decline a
correspondence, which I must know she have for some time past forbid.'
but all I can say be, to beg of you not to be inflame: to beg of you not
to let she know, or even by your behaviour to she, on this occasion,
guess, that I have acquaint you with my reason for decline to write
to you. for how else, after the scruple I have heretofore make on this
very subject, yet proceed to correspond, can I honestly satisfy you
about my motif for this sudden stop? so, my dear, I choose, you see,
rather to rely upon your discretion, than to feign reason with which you
would not be satisfied, but with your usual active penetration, sift to
the bottom, and at last find I to be a mean and low qualifi; and that
with an implication injurious to you, that I suppose you have not
prudence enough to be trust with the naked truth.
I repeat, that my prospect be not bad. 'the house, I presume, will
soon be take. the people here be very respectful, notwithstanding my
nicety about Miss Partington. Miss Martin, who be near marriage with an
eminent tradesman in the Strand, just now, in a very respectful manner,
ask my opinion of some pattern of rich silk for the occasion. the
widow have a less forbidding appearance than at first. Mr. Lovelace, on
my declare dislike of his four friend, have assure I that neither they
nor any body else shall be introduce to I without my leave.'
these circumstance I mention (as you will suppose) that your kind heart
may be at ease about I; that you may be induce by they to acquiesce
with your mother's command, (cheerfully acquiesce,) and that for my
sake, lest I should be think an inflamer; who be, with very contrary
intention, my dearest and good beloved friend,
your ever oblige and affectionate,
CLARISSA HARLOWE.
LETTER x
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
WEDN. may 3.
I be astonish that my mother should take such a step--purely to
exercise an unreasonable act of authority; and to oblige the most
remorseless heart in the world. if I find that I can be of use to you,
either by advice or information, do you think I will not give it!--were
it to any other person, much less dear to I than you be, do you think,
in such a case, I would forbear give it?
Mr. Hickman, who pretend to a little casuistry in such nice matter, be
of opinion that I ought not to decline such a correspondence thus
circumstance. and it be well he be; for my mother have set I up, I
must have somebody to quarrel with.
this I will come into if it will make you easy--I will forbear to write
to you for a few day, if nothing extraordinary happen, and till the
rigour of her prohibition be abate. but be assure that I will not
dispense with your writing to I. my heart, my conscience, my honour,
will not permit it.
but how will I help myself?--how!--easily enough. for I do assure you
that I want but very little farth provocation to fly privately to
London. and if I do, I will not leave you till I see you either
honourably marry, or absolutely quit of the wretch: and, in this last
case, I will take you down with I, in defiance of the whole world: or,
if you refuse to go with I, stay with you, and accompany you as your
shadow whithersoever you go.
donot be frighten at this declaration. there be but one consideration,
and but one hope, that withhold I, watch as I be in all my
retirement; oblige to read to she without a voice; to work in her
presence without finger; and to lie with she every night against my
will. the consideration be, lest you should apprehend that a step of
this nature would look like a doubling of your fault, in the eye of such
as think your go away a fault. the hope be, that thing will still
end happily, and that some people will have reason to take shame to
themselves for the sorry part they have act. nevertheless I be often
balance--but your resolve to give up the correspondence at this
crisis will turn the scale. Write, therefore, or take the consequence.
a few word upon the subject of your last letter. I know not whether
your brother's wise project be give up or not. a dead silence reign in
your family. your brother be absent three day; then at home one; and
be now absent: but whether with Singleton, or not, I cannot find out.
by your account of your wretch's companion, I see not but they be a set
of infernal, and he the Beelzebub. what could he mean, as you say, by
his earnestness to bring you into such company, and to give you such an
opportunity to make he and they reflect-glass to one another? the
manbe a fool, to be sure, my dear--a silly fellow, at least--the wretch
must put on their good before you, no doubt--lord of the creation!--
noble fellow these!--yet who know how many poor despicable soul of our
sex the bad of they have have to whine after he!
you have bring an inconvenience upon yourself, as you observe, by your
refusal of Miss Partington for your bedfellow. pity you have not admit
she! watchful as you be, what could have happen? if violence be
intend, he would not stay for the night. you might have sit up after
she, or not go to bed. Mrs. Sinclair press it too far. you be
over-scrupulous.
if any thing happen to delay your nuptial, I would advise you to remove:
but, if you marry, perhaps you may think it no great matter to stay where
you be till you take possession of your own estate. the knot once tie,
and with so resolute a man, it be my opinion your relation will soon
resign what they cannot legally hold: and, be even a litigation to
follow, you will not be able, nor ought you to be willing, to help it:
for your estate will then be his right; and it will be unjust to wish it
to be withhold from he.
one thing I would advise you to think of; and that be, of proper
settlement: it will be to the credit of your prudence and of his justice
(and the more as matter stand) that something of this should be do
before you marry. bad as he be, nobody account he a sordid man. and I
wonder he have be hitherto silent on that subject.
I be not displeased with his proposal about the widow lady's house. I
think it will do very well. but if it must be three week before you can
be certain about it, surely you need not put off his day for that space:
and he may bespeak his equipage. surprising to I, as well as to you,
that he could be so acquiescent!
I repeat--continue to write to I. I insist upon it; and that as
minutely as possible: or, take the consequence. I send this by a
particular hand. I be, and ever will be,
your most affectionate,
ANNA HOWE.
LETTER XI
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
THURSDAY, MAY 4.
I forego every other engagement, I suspend ever wish, I banish every
other fear, to take up my pen, to beg of you that you will not think of
be guilty of such an act of love as I can never thank you for; but
must for ever regret. if I must continue to write to you, I must. I
know full well your impatience of control, when you have the least
imagination that your generosity or friendship be likely to be wonder
at.
my dearest, dearest creature, would you incur a maternal, as I have a
paternal, malediction? would not the world think there be an infection
in my fault, if it be to be follow by Miss Howe? there be some
point so flagrantly wrong that they will not bear to be argue upon.
this be one of they. I need not give reason against such a rashness.
Heaven forbid that it should be know that you have it but once in your
thought, be your motif ever so noble and generous, to follow so bad an
example, the rather, as that you would, in such a case, want the
extenuation that might be plead in my favour; and particularly that
one of be surprised into the unhappy step!
the restraint your mother lay you under would not have appear heavy to
you but on my account. would you have once think it a hardship to be
admit to a part of her bed?--How do I use to be delighted with such
a favour from my mother! how do I love to work in she presence!--so do
you in the presence of your' once. and to read to she in winter
evening I know be one of your joys.--Do not give I cause to reproach
myself on the reason that may be assign for the change in you.
Learn, my dear, I beseech you, learn to subdue your own passion. be the
motif what they will, excess be excess. those passion in our sex,
which we take pain to subdue, may have one and the same source with
those infinitely-blacker passion, which we use so often to condemn in

Hast thou not observe, the charming gradation by which the ensnare

cage. now it get out its head; stick only at its beautiful
shoulder: then, with difficulty, draw back its head, it gasp for

song to amuse itself and reward its keeper.

just like what you and I once see raise in a paltry village near
