LETTER XVIII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
EDGEWARE, THURSDAY, MAY 4.
I know that thou art so abandon a man, that to give thee the good
reason in the world against what thou hast once resolve upon will be
but act the madman whom once we see try to buffet down a hurricane
with his hat. I hope, however, that the lady's merit will still avail she
with thee. but, if thou persist; if thou wilt avenge thyself on this
sweet lamb which thou hast single out from a flock thou hatest, for the
fault of the dog who keep it: if thou art not to be move by beauty, by
learning, by prudence, by innocence, all shin out in one charming
object; but she must fall, fall by the man whom she have choose for her
protector; I would not for a thousand world have thy crime to answer
for.
upon my faith, Lovelace, the subject stick with I, notwithstanding I
find I have no the honour of the lady's good opinion. and the more, when
I reflect upon her father's brutal curse, and the villainous hard-
heartedness of all her family. but, nevertheless, I should be desirous
to know (if thou wilt proceed) by what gradation, art, and contrivance
thou effectest thy ingrateful purpose. and, O Lovelace, I conjure thee,
if thou art a man, let not the specious devil thou have bring she among
be suffer to triumph over she; yield to fair seduction, if I may so
express myself! if thou canst raise a weakness in she by love, or by art
not inhuman; I shall the less pity she: and shall then conclude, that
there be not a woman in the world who can resist a bold and resolute
lover.
a messenger be just now arrive from my uncle. the mortification, it
seem, be get to his knee; and the surgeon declare that he cannot live
many day. he therefore send for I directly, with these shocking
word, that I will come and close his eye. my servant or his must of
necessity be in town every day on his case, or other affair; and one of
they shall regularly attend you for any letter or command. it will be
charity to write to I as often as you can. for although I be likely to
be a considerable gainer by the poor man's death, yet I cannot say that I
at all love these scene of death and the doctor so near I. the doctor
and death I should have say; for that be the natural order, and
generally speak, the one be but the harbinger to the other.
if, therefore, you decline to oblige I, I shall think you be displeased
with my freedom. but let I tell you, at the same, that no man have a
right to be displeased at freedom take with he for fault he be not
ashamed to be guilty of.
J. BELFORD.
LETTER XIX
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
I thank you and Mr. Hickman for his letter, send I with such kind
expedition; and proceed to obey my dear menacing tyranness.
[she then give the particular of what pass between herself and Mr.
Lovelace on Tuesday morning, in relation to his four friend, and to
Miss Partington, pretty much to the same effect as in Mr. Lovelace's
Letter, no. xiii. and then proceed:]
he be constantly accuse I of over-scrupulousness. he say, 'I be
always out of humour with he: that I could not have behave more
reservedly to Mr. Solmes: and that it be contrary to all his hope and
notion, that he should not, in so long a time, find himself able to
inspire the person, whom he hop so soon to have the honour to call his,
with the least distinguish tenderness for he before-hand.'
silly and partial encroacher! not to know to what to attribute the
reserve I be force to treat he with! but his pride have eat up his
prudence. it be indeed a dirty low pride, that have swallow up the true
pride which should have set he above the vanity that have overrun he.
yet he pretend that he have no pride but in oblige I: and be always
talk of his reverence and humility, and such sort of stuff: but of
this I be sure that he have, as I observe the first time I see he,* too
much regard to his own person, greatly to value that of his wife, marry
he whom he will: and I must be blind, if I do not see that he be
exceedingly vain of his external advantage, and of that address, which,
if it have any merit in it to an outward eye, be perhaps owe more to his
confidence that [sic] to any thing else.
* see Vol. I. Letter III.
have you not beheld the man, when I be your happy guest, as he walk to
his chariot, look about he, as if to observe what eye his specious
person and air have attract?
but indeed we have some homely coxcomb as proud as if they have person to
be proud of; at the same time that it be apparent, that the pain they
take about themselves but the more expose their defect.
the man who be fond of be think more or well than he be, as I have
often observe, but provoke a scrutiny into his pretension; and that
generally produce contempt. for pride, as I believe I have heretofore
say, be an infallible sign of weakness; of something wrong in the head
or in both. he that exalt himself insult his neighbour; who be
provoke to question in he even that merit, which, be he modest, would
perhaps be allow to be his due.
you will say that I be very grave: and so I be. Mr. Lovelace be
extremely sunk in my opinion since Monday night: nor see I before I any
thing that can afford I a pleasing hope. for what, with a mind so
unequal as his, can be my good hope?
I think I mention to you, in my former, that my clothe be bring
I. you flutter I so, that I be not sure I do. but I know I

you will the less wonder at my be so very solemn, when, add to the

COL. MORDEN, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
Florence, April 13.
I be extremely concerned to hear of a difference betwixt the rest of a
family so near and dear to I, and you still dearer to than any of the
rest.
my cousin James have acquaint I with the offer you have have, and with
your refusal. I wonder not at either. such charming promise at so
early an age as when I leave England; and those promise, as I have often
hear, so greatly exceed, as well in your person as mind; how much must
you be admire! how few must there be worthy of you!
your parent, the most indulgent in the world, to a child the most
deserve, have give way it seem to your refusal of several gentleman.
they have content themselves at last to name one with earnestness to
you, because of the address of another whom they cannot approve.
they have not reason, it seem, from your behaviour, to think you greatly
averse: so they proceed: perhaps too hastily for a delicacy like
your's. but when all be fix on their part, and most extraordinary
term conclude in your favour; term, which abundantly show the
gentleman's just value for you; you fly off with a warmth and vehemence
little suited to that sweetness which give grace to all your action.
I know very little of either of the gentleman: but of Mr. Lovelace I know
more than of Mr. Solmes. I wish I could say more to his advantage than I
can. as to every qualification but one, your brother own there be no
comparison. but that one outweigh all the rest together. it cannot be
think that Miss Clarissa Harlowe will dispense with moral in a
husband.
what, my dear cousin, shall I plead first to you on this occasion?
your duty, your interest, your temporal and your eternal welfare, do, and
may all, depend upon this single point, the morality of a husband. a
woman who hath a wicked husband may find it difficult to be good, and out
of her power to do good; and be therefore in a bad situation than the
man can be in, who hath a bad wife. you preserve all your religious
regard, I understand. I wonder not that you do. I should have wonder
have you not. but what can you promise youself, as to perseverance in
they, with an immoral husband?
if your parent and you differ in sentiment on this important occasion,
let I ask you, my dear cousin, who ought to give way? I own to you,
that I should have think there could not any where have be a more
suitable match for you than Mr. Lovelace, have he be a moral man. I
should have very little to say against a man, of whose action I be not
to set up myself as a judge, do he not address my cousin. but, on this
occasion, let I tell you, my dear Clarissa, that Mr. Lovelace cannot
possibly deserve you. he may reform, youwill say: but he may not. Habit
be not soon or easily shake off. libertine, who be libertine in
defiance of talent, of superior light, of conviction, hardly ever
reform but by miracle, or by incapacity. well do I know mine own sex.
well be I able to judge of the probability of the reformation of a
licentious young man, who have not be fasten upon by sickness, by
affliction, by calamity: who have a prosperous run of fortune before he:
his spirit high: his will uncontroulable: the company he keep, perhaps
such as himself, confirm he in all his course, assist he in
all his enterprise.
as to the other gentleman, suppose, my dear cousin, you do not like he
at present, it be far from be unlikely that you will hereafter:
perhaps the more for not like he now. he can hardly sink lower in
your opinion: he may rise. very seldom be it that high expectation be
so much as tolerably answer. how indeed can they, when a fine and
extensive imagination carry its expectation infinitely beyond reality,
in the high of our sublunary enjoyment? a woman adorn with such an
imagination see no defect in a favour object, (the less, if she be not
conscious of any wilful fault in herself,) till it be too late to rectify
the mistake occasion by her generous credulity.
but suppose a person of your talent be to marry a man of inferior
talent; who, in this case, can be so happy in herself as Miss Clarissa
Harlowe? what delight do you take in do good! how happily do you
devote the several portion of the day to your own improvement, and to
the advantage of all that move within your sphere!--and then, such be
your taste, such be your acquirement in the politer study, and in the
politer amusement; such your excellence in all the different part of
economy fit for a young lady's inspection and practice, that your friend
would wish you to be take off as little as possible by regard that may
be call merely personal.
but as to what may be the consequence respect yourself, respect a
young lady of your talent, from the preference you be suspect to give
to a libertine, I would have you, my dear cousin, consider what that may
be. a mind so pure, to mingle with a mind impure! and will not such a
man as this engross all your solitude? will he not perpetually fill you
with anxiety for he and for yourself?--the divine and civil power
defy, and their sanction break through by he, on every not merely
accidental but meditated occasion. to be agreeable to he, and to hope
to preserve an interest in his affection, you must probably be oblige
to abandon all your own laudable pursuit. you must enter into his
pleasure and distaste. you must give up your virtuous companion for
his profligate one--perhaps be forsake by your's, because of the
scandal he daily give. can you hope, cousin, with such a man as this to
be long so good as you now be? if not, consider which of your present
laudable delight you would choose to give up! which of his culpable one
to follow he in! how could you brook to go backward, instead of
forward, in those duty which you now so exemplarily perform? and how do
you know, if you once give way, where you shall be suffer, where you
shall be able, to stop?
your brother acknowledge that Mr. Solmes be not near so agreeable in
person as Mr. Lovelace. but what be person with such a lady as I have
the honour to be now write to? he own likewise that he have not the
address of Mr. Lovelace: but what a mere personal advantage be a
plausible address, without moral? a woman have well take a husband
whose manner she be to fashion, than to find they ready-fashioned to
her hand, at the price of her morality; a price that be often pay for
travel accomplishment. o my dear cousin, be you but with we here
at Florence, or at Rome, or at Paris, (where also I reside for many
month,) to see the gentleman whose suppose rough english manner at
set out be to be polish, and what their improvement be in their
return through the same place, you would infinitely prefer the man in
his first stage to the same man in his last. you find the difference on
their return--a fondness for foreign fashion, an attachment to foreign
vice, a supercilious contempt of his own country and countryman;
(himself more despicable than the most despicable of those he despise;)
these, with an unblushing effrontery, be too generally the attainment
that concur to finish the travelled gentleman!
Mr. Lovelace, I know, deserve to have an exception make in his favour;
for he really be a man of part and learning: he be esteem so both
here and at Rome; and a fine person, and a generous turn of mind, give
he great advantage. but you need not be tell, that a libertine of weak
part be able to do. and this I will tell you far, that it be Mr.
Lovelace's own fault that he be not still more respected than he be
among the literati here. there be, in short, some liberty in which
he indulge himself, that endanger his person and his liberty; and make
the good and most worthy of those who honour he with their notice give
he up, and his stay both at Florence and at Rome shorter than he
design.
this be all I choose to say of Mr. Lovelace. I have much rather have have
reason to give he a quite contrary character. but as to rakes or
libertine in general, I, who know they well, must be allow, because of
the mischief they have always in their heart, and too often in their
power, to do your sex, to add still a few more word upon this topic.
a libertine, my dear cousin, a plotting, an intriguing libertine, must be
generally remorseless--unjust he must always be. the noble rule of do
to other what he would have do to himself be the first rule he break;
and every day he break it; the oftener, the great his triumph. he have
great contempt for your sex. he believe no woman chaste, because he be
a profligate. every woman who favour he confirm he in his wicked
incredulity. he be always plot to extend the mischief he delight
in. if a woman love such a man, how can she bear the thought of
divide her interest in his affection with half the town, and that
perhaps the dreg of it? then so sensual!--how will a young lady of your
delicacy bear with so sensual a man? a man who make a jest of his vow?
and who perhaps will break your spirit by the most unmanly insult. to
be a libertine, be to continue to be every thing vile and inhuman.
Prayers, tear, and the most abject submission, be but fuel to his
pride: wager perhaps with lewd companion, and, not improbably, with
lewder woman, upon instance which he boast of to they of your patient
suffering, and broken spirit, and bring they home to witness both.
I write what I know have be.
I mention not fortune squander, estate mortgage or sell, and
posterity rob--nor yet a multitude of other evil, too gross, too
shocking, to be mention to a person of your delicacy.
all these, my dear cousin, to be shun, all the evil I have name to
be avoid; the power of do all the good you have be accustom to,
preserve, nay, increase, by the separate provision that will be make
for you: your charming diversion, and exemplary employment, all
maintain; and every good habit perpetuate: and all by one sacrifice,
the fade pleasure of the eye! who would not, (since every thing be not
to be meet with in one man, who would not,) to preserve so many
essential, give up to light, so unpermanent a pleasure!
weigh all these thing, which I might insist upon to more advantage, do
I think it needful to one of your prudence--weigh they well, my beloved
cousin; and if it be not the will of your parent that you should
continue single, resolve to oblige they; and let it not be say that the
power of fancy shall (as in many other of your sex) be too hard for
your duty and your prudence. the less agreeable the man, the more
oblige the compliance. remember, that he be a sober man--a man who have
reputation to lose, and whose reputation therefore be a security for his
good behaviour to you.
you have an opportunity offer you to give the high instance that can
be give of filial duty. embrace it. it be worthy of you. it be
expect from you; however, for your inclination-sake, we may be sorry
that you be call upon to give it. let it be say that you have be
able to lay an obligation upon your parent, (a proud word, my cousin!)
which you could not do, be it not lay against your inclination!--upon
parent who have lay a thousand upon you: who be set upon this point:
who will not give it up: who have give up many point to you, even of
this very nature: and in their turn, for the sake of their own authority,
as well as judgment, expect to be oblige.
I hope I shall soon, in person, congratulate you upon this your
meritorious compliance. to settle and give up my trusteeship be one of
the principal motif of my leave these part. I shall be glad to
settle it to every one's satisfaction; to yours particularly.
if on my arrival I find a happy union, as formerly, reign in a family so
dear to I, it will be an unspeakable pleasure to I; and I shall perhaps
so dispose my affair, as to be near you for ever.
I have write a very long letter, and will add no more, than that I be,
with the great respect, my dear cousin,
your most affectionate and faithful servant,
WM. MORDEN.

I will suppose, my dear Miss Howe, that you have read my cousin's letter.
it be now in vain to wish it have come soon. but if it have, I might
perhaps have be so rash as to give Mr. Lovelace the fatal meeting, as I
little thought of go away with he.
but I should hardly have give he the expectation of so do, previous
to the meeting, which make he come prepare; and the revocation of which
he so artfully make ineffectual.
persecute as I be, and little expect so much condescension, as my
aunt, to my great mortification, have tell I (and you confirm) I should
have meet with, it be, however, hard to say what I should or should not
have do as to meet he, have it come in time: but this effect I
verily believe it would have have--to have make I insist with all my
might on go over, out of all their way, to the kind writer of the
instructive letter, and on make a father (a protector, as well as a
friend) of a kinsman, who be one of my trustee. this, circumstance as
I be, would have be a natural, at least an unexceptionable protection!
--But I be to be unhappy! and how it cut I to the heart to think, that
I can already subscribe to my cousin's character of a libertine, so well
draw in the letter which I suppose you now to have read!
that a man of a character which ever be my abhorrence should fall to my
lot!--But, depend on my own strength; have no reason to apprehend
danger from headstrong and disgraceful impulse; I too little perhaps
cast up my eye to the Supreme Director: in whom, mistrust myself, I
ought to have place my whole confidence--and the more, when I see myself
so perserveringly address by a man of this character.
Inexperience and presumption, with the help of a brother and sister who
have low end to answer in my disgrace, have be my ruin!--a hard word,
my dear! but I repeat it upon deliberation: since, let the good happen
which now can happen, my reputation be destroy; a rake be my portion:
and what that portion be my cousin Morden's letter have acquaint you.
pray keep it by you till call for. I see it not myself (have not the
heart to inspect my trunk) till this morning. I would not for the world
this man should see it; because it might occasion mischief between the
most violent spirit, and the most settle brave one in the world, as my
cousin's be say to be.
this letter be enclose (open) in a blank cover. scorn and detest I
as they will, I wonder that one line be not send with it--be it but to
have more particularly point the design of it, in the same generous
spirit that send I the spira.
the sealing of the cover be with black wax. I hope there be no new
occasion in the family to give reason for black wax. but if there be,
it would, to be sure, have be mention, and lay at my door--perhaps
too justly!
I have begin a letter to my cousin; but lay it by, because of the
uncertainty of my situation, and expect every day for several day
past to be at a great certainty. you bid I write to he some time
ago, you know. then it be I begin it: for I have great pleasure in
obey you in all I may. so I ought to have; for you be the only
friend leave I. and, moreover, you generally honour I with your own
observance of the advice I take the liberty to offer you: for I pretend
to say, I give well advice than I have take. and so I have need. for,
I know not how it come about, but I be, in my own opinion, a poor lose
creature: and yet cannot charge myself with one criminal or faulty
inclination. do you know, my dear, how this can be?
yet I can tell you how, I believe--one devious step at set out!--
that must be it:--which pursue, have lead I so far out of my path, that I
be in a wilderness of doubt and error; and never, never, shall find my
way out of it: for, although but one pace awry at first, it have lead I
hundred and hundred of mile out of my path: and the poor estray have
not one kind friend, nor have meet with one direct passenger, to help she
to recover it.
but I, presumptuous creature! must rely so much upon my own knowledge of
the right path!--little apprehend that an ignus fatuus with its false
fire (and ye I have hear enough of such) would arise to mislead I! and
now, in the midst of fen and quagmire, it play around I, and around
I, throw I back again, whenever I think myself in the right track.
but there be one common point, in which all shall meet, err widely as
they may. in that I shall be lay quietly down at last: and then will
all my calamity be at an end.
but how I stray again; stray from my intention! I would only have say,
that I have begin a letter to my cousin Morden some time ago: but that now
I can never end it. you will believe I cannot: for how shall I tell he
that all his compliment be misbestowed? that all his advice be throw
away? all his warning vain? and that even my high expectation be to
be the wife of that free-liver, whom he so pathetically warn I to shun?
let I own, however, have your prayer join with my own, (my fate
depending, as it seem, upon the lip of such a man) 'that, whatever
shall be my destiny, that dreadful part of my father's malediction, that
I may be punish by the man in whom he suppose I put my confidence, may
not take place! that this for Mr. Lovelace's own sake, and for the sake
of human nature, may not be! or, if it be necessary, in support of the
parental authority, that I should be punish by he, that it may not be
by his premeditated or wilful baseness; but that I may be able to acquit
his intention, if not his action!' otherwise, my fault will appear to be
double in the eye of the event-judge world. and yet, methink, I
would be glad that the unkindness of my father and uncle, whose heart
have already be too much wound by my error, may be justify in every
article, except in this heavy curse: and that my father will be
pleased to withdraw that before it be generally know: at least the most
dreadful part of it which regard futurity!
I must lay down my pen. I must brood over these reflection. once more,
before I close my cousin's letter, I will peruse it. and then I shall
have it by heart.

MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE

when you reflect upon my unhappy situation, which be attend with so

LETTER XXI
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
TUESDAY, MAY 9.
I be a very unhappy man. this lady be say to be one of the sweetest-
temper creature in the world: and so I think she. but to I she be
one of the most perverse. I never be suppose to be an ill-natured
mortal neither. how can it be? I imagine, for a long while, that we

take notice of that; and observe upon it, that lover fall out
occasion lover fall in; and a well understanding of course. 'tis
natural that it should be so. but with we, we fall out so often, without
fall in once; and a second quarrel so generally happen before a first
be make up; that it be hard to guess what event our love will be
attend with. but perseverance be my glory, and patience my handmaid,
when I have in view an object worthy of my attempt. what be there in an
easy conquest? hudibra question well,
------what mad lover ever dy'd
to gain a soft and easy bride?
or, for a lady tender-hearte,

SATURDAY EVENING, MAY 13.
dear, good WOMAN,
your beloved's honour be inviolate!--must be inviolate! and will be so,
in spite of man and devil. could I have have hope of a reconciliation,
all my view be, that she should not have have this man.--all that can be
say now, be, she must run the risk of a bad husband: she of whom no man
living be worthy!
you pity her mother--so do not I! I pity no mother that put it out of
her power to show maternal love, and humanity, in order to patch up for
herself a precarious and sorry quiet, which every blast of wind shall
disturb.
I hate tyrant in ever form and shape: but paternal and maternal tyrant
be the bad of all: for they can have no bowel.
I repeat, that I pity none of they. our beloved friend only deserve
pity. she have never be in the hand of this man, but for they. she be
quite blameless. you donot know all her story. be I to tell you that
she have no intention to go off with this man, it would avail her nothing.
it would only deserve to condemn, with those who drive she to
extremity, he who now must be her refuge. I be
your sincere friend and servant,
ANNA HOWE.
LETTER XXVIII
MRS. HARLOWE, to MRS. NORTON
[not communicate till the letter come to be collect.]
SATURDAY, MAY 13.
I return an answer in writing, as I promise, to your communication. but
take no notice either to my Bella's Betty, (who I understand sometimes
visit you,) or to the poor wretch herself, nor to any body, that I do
write. I charge you donot. my heart be full: writing may give some vent
to my grief, and perhaps I may write what lie most upon my heart,
without confine myself strictly to the present subject.
you know how dear this ungrateful creature ever be to we all. you know
how sincerely we join with every one of those who ever have see she, or
converse with she, to praise and admire she; and exceed in our praise
even the bound of that modesty, which, because she be our own, should
have restrain we; be of opinion, that to have be silent in the
praise of so apparent a merit must rather have argue blindness or
affectation in we, than that we should incur the censure of vain
partiality to our own.
when therefore any body congratulate we on such a daughter, we receive
their congratulation without any diminution. if it be say, you be
happy in this child! we own, that no parent ever be happy in a
child. if, more particularly, they praise her dutiful behaviour to we,
we say, she know not how to offend. if it be say, Miss Clarissa
Harlowe have a wit and penetration beyond her year; we, instead of
disallow it, would add--and a judgment no less extraordinary than her
wit. if her prudence be praise, and a forethought, which every one see
supply what only year and experience give to other--nobody need to
scruple take lesson from Clarissa Harlowe, be our proud answer.
forgive I, o forgive I, my dear Norton--but I know you will; for your,
when good, be this child, and your glory as well as mine.
but have you not hear stranger, as she pass to and from church, stop
to praise the angel of a creature, as they call she; when it be enough
for those who know who she be, to cry, why, it be Miss Clarissa Harlowe!
--as if every body be oblige to know, or to have hear of Clarissa
Harlowe, and of her excellency. while, accustom to praise, it be
too familiar to she, to cause she to alter either her look or her pace.
for my own part, I could not stifle a pleasure that have perhaps a faulty
vanity for its foundation, whenever I be speak of, or address to, as
the mother of so sweet a child: Mr. Harlowe and I, all the time, love
each other the well for the share each have in such a daughter.
still, still indulge the fond, the overflowing heart of a mother! I
could dwell for ever upon the remembrance of what she be, would but that
remembrance banish from my mind what she be!
in her bosom, young as she be, could I repose all my grief--sure of
receive from her prudence and advice as well as comfort; and both
insinuate in so dutiful a manner, that it be impossible to take those
exception which the distance of year and character between a mother and
a daughter would have make one apprehensive of from any other daughter.
she be our glory when abroad, our delight when at home. every body be
even covetous of her company; and we grudge she to our brother Harlowe,
and to our sister and brother Hervey. no other contention among we,
then, but who should be next favour by she. no chiding ever know she
from we, but the chiding of lover, when she be for shut herself up
too long together from we, in pursuit of those charming amusement and
useful employment, for which, however, the whole family be the well.
our other child have reason (good child as they always be) to
think themselves neglect. but they likewise be so sensible of their
sister's superiority, and of the honour she reflect upon the whole
family, that they confess themselves eclipse, without envy the
eclipser. indeed, there be not any body so equal with she, in their own
opinion, as to envy what all aspire but to emulate. the dear creature,
you know, my Norton, give an eminence to we all!
then her acquirement. her skill in music, her fine needle-work, her
elegance in dress; for which she be so much admire, that the
neighbouring lady use to say, that they need not fetch fashion from
London; since whatever Miss Clarissa Harlowe wear be the good fashion,
because her choice of natural beauty set those of art far behind they.
her genteel ease, and fine turn of person; her deep reading, and these,
join to her open manner, and her cheerful modesty--o my good Norton,
what a sweet child be once my Clary Harlowe!
this, and more, you know she to be: for many of her excellency be
owe to yourself; and with the milk you give she, you give she what no
other nurse in the world could give she.
and do you think, my worthy woman, do you think, that the wilful lapse of
such a child be to be forgive? can she herself think that she deserve
not the severe punishment for the abuse of such talent as be
intrust to she?
her fault be a fault of premeditation, of cunning, of contrivance. she
have deceive every body's expectation. her whole sex, as well as the
family she spring from, be disgrace by it.
would any body ever have believe that such a young creature as this, who
have by her advice save even her over-lively friend from marry a fop,
and a libertine, would herself have go off with one of the vile and
most notorious of libertine? a man whose character she know; and know
it to be bad than the character of he from whom she save her friend;
a man against whom she be warn: one who have her brother's life in her
hand; and who constantly set our whole family at defiance.
think for I, my good Norton; think what my unhappiness must be both as a
wife and a mother. what restless day, what sleepless night; yet my own
rankle anguish endeavour to be smooth over, to soften the anguish
of fiercer spirit, and to keep they from blaze out to far
mischief! o this naughty, naughty girl, who know so well what she do;
and who could look so far into consequence, that we think she would
have die rather than have do as she have do!
her know character for prudence leave she absolutely without excuse.
how then can I offer to plead for she, if, through motherly indulgence,
I would forgive she myself?--And have we not moreover suffer all the
disgrace that can befall we? have not she?
if now she have so little like to his moral, have she not reason before
to have as little? or have she suffer by they in her own person?--O my
good woman, I doubt--I doubt--will not the character of the man make one
doubt an angel, if once in his power? the world will think the bad. I
be tell it do. so likewise her father fear; her brother hear; and
what can I do?
our antipathy to he she know before, as well as his character. these
therefore cannot be new motif without a new reason.--o my dear Mrs.
Norton, how shall I, how can you, support ourselves under the
apprehension to which these thought lead!
he continually press she, you say, to marry he: his friend likewise.
she have reason, no doubt she have reason, for this application to we: and
her crime be glossed over, to bring she to we with new disgrace!
Whither, whither, do one guilty step lead the misguided heart!--And
now, truly, to save a stubborn spirit, we be only to be sound, that
the application may be occasionally retract or deny!
upon the whole: be I inclined to plead for she, it be now the most
improper of all time. now that my brother Harlowe have discourage (as
he last night come hither on purpose to tell we) Mr. Hickman's insinuate
application; and be applaud for it. now, that my brother Antony be
intend to carry his great fortune, through her fault, into another
family:--she expect, no doubt, herself to be put into her
grandfather's estate, in consequence of a reconciliation, and as a reward
for her fault: and insist still upon the same term which she offer
before, and which be reject--not through my fault, I be sure,
reject!
from all these thing you will return such an answer as the case
require. it might cost I the peace of my whole life, at this time, to
move for she. God forgive she! if I do, nobody else will. and let it,
for your own sake, as well as mine, be a secret that you and I have
enter upon this subject. and I desire you not to touch upon it again
but by particular permission: for, o my dear, good woman, it set my
heart a bleeding in as many stream as there be vein in it!
yet think I not impenetrable by a proper contrition and remorse--but
what a torment be it to have a will without a power!
Adieu! adieu! God give we both comfort; and to the once dear--the ever-
dear creature (for can a mother forget her child?) repentance, deep
repentance! and as little suffering as may befit his bless will, and
her grievous fault, pray
your real friend,
CHARLOTTE HARLOWE.
LETTER xxix
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
SUNDAY, MAY 14.
how it be now, my dear, between you and Mr. Lovelace, I cannot tell.
but, wicke as the man be, I be afraid he must be your lord and master.
I call he by several very hard name in my last. I have but just hear
of some of his vileness, when I sit down to write; so my indignation
be raise. but on inquiry, and recollection, I find that the fact lay
to his charge be all of they commit some time ago--not since he have
have strong hope of your favour.
this be say something for he. his generous behaviour to the
innkeeper's daughter be a more recent instance to his credit; to say
nothing of the universal good character he have as a kind landlord. and
then I approve much of the motion he make to put you in possession of
Mrs. Fretchville's house, while he continue at the other widow's, till
you agree that one house shall hold you. I wish this be do. be sure
you embrace this offer, (if you do not soon meet at the altar,) and get
one of his cousin with you.
be you once marry, I should think you cannot be very unhappy, though
you may not be so happy with he as you deserve to be. the stake he have
in his country, and his reversion; the care he take of his affair; his
freedom from obligation; nay, his pride, with your merit, must be a
tolerable security for you, I should think. though particular of his
wickedness, as they come to my knowledge, hurt and incense I; yet, after
all, when I give myself time to reflect, all that I have hear of he to
his disadvantage be comprehend in the general character give of he
long ago, by Lord M.'s and his own dismiss bailiff,* and which be
confirm to I by Mrs. Fortescue, as I heretofore tell you,** and to you
by Mrs. Greme.***
* see Vol. I. Letter IV.
** ibid. Letter XII.
*** see Vol. III. Letter VI.
you can have nothing, therefore, I think, to be deeply concerned about,
but his future good, and the bad example he may hereafter set to his own
family. these indeed be very just concern: but be you to leave he
now, either with or without his consent, his fortune and alliance so
considerable, his person and address so engaging, (every one excuse you
now on those account, and because of your relation' folly,) it would
have a very ill appearance for your reputation. I cannot, therefore, on
the most deliberate consideration, advise you to think of that, while you
have no reason to doubt his honour. may eternal vengeance pursue the
villain, if he give room for an apprehension of this nature!
yet his teasing way be intolerable; his acquiescence with your slight
delay, and his resignedness to the distance you now keep he at, (for a
fault so much slighter, as he must think, than the punishment,) be
unaccountable: he doubt your love of he, that be very probable; but you
have reason to be surprised at his want of ardour; a blessing so great
within his reach, as I may say.
by the time you have read to this place, you will have no doubt of what
have be the issue of the conference between the two gentleman. I be
equally shocked, and enrage against they all. against they all, I say;
for I have try your good Norton's weight with your mother, (though at
first I do not intend to tell you so,) to the same purpose as the
gentleman sound your uncle. never be there such determined brute in
the world! why should I mince the matter? yet would I fain, methink,
make an exception for your mother.
your uncle will have it that you be ruin. 'he can believe every thing
bad of a creature, he say, who could run away with a man; with such a
one especially as Lovelace. they expect application from you, when
some heavy distress have fall upon you. but they be all resolve not
to stir an inch in your favour; no, not to save your life!'
my dear soul, resolve to assert your right. claim your own, and go
and live upon it, as you ought. then, if you marry not, how will the
wretch creep to you for your reversionary disposition!
you be accuse (as in your aunt's letter) 'of premeditation and
contrivance in your escape.' instead of pity you, the mediating
person be call upon 'to pity they; who once, your uncle say, doate
upon you: who take no joy but in your presence: who devour your word
as you speak they: who trod over again your footstep, as you walk

upon the whole, it be now evident to I, and so it must be to you, when
you read this letter, that you must be his. and the soon you be so

cannot have patience to suppose that.
I be concern, methink, to know how you will do to condescend, (now you
see you must be his,) after you have keep he at such a distance; and for
the revenge his pride may put he upon take for it. but let I tell
you, that if my go up, and share fortune with you, will prevent
such a noble creature from stoop too low; much more, be it likely to
prevent your ruin, I would not hesitate a moment about it. what be the
whole world to I, weigh against such a friend as you be? think you,
that any of the enjoyment of this life could be enjoyment to I, be

excuse my warmth of expression. the warmth of my heart want none. I be

there be yet, to a person of your fortune and independence, a good deal

donot find that he have once talk of settlement; nor yet of the
license. a foolish wretch!--But as your evil destiny have throw you out

for word leave no trace; they pass as breath; and mingle with air; and
may be explain with latitude. but the pen be a witness on record.

be her house to I? you talk of bring up your cousin Montague to

yourself to fetch she, you can write to she. I insist upon bring
these two point to an issue: off or on ought to be indifferent to I, if
so to they.'
such a declaration must bring all forward. there be twenty way, my dear,
that you would find out for another in your circumstance. he will
disdain, from his native insolence, to have it think he have any body to
consult. well then, will he not be oblige to declare himself? and if
he do, no delay on your side, I beseech you. give he the day. let
it be a short one. it would be derogate from your own merit, not to be

modesty'd away such opportunity as you ought not to have slip. as

this be my advice: mend it as circumstance offer, and follow your own.
but indeed, my dear, this, or something like it, would I do. and let he
tell I afterwards, if he dare or would, that he humble down to his
shoe-buckle the person it would have be his glory to exalt.
support yourself, mean time, with reflection worthy of yourself. though
trick into this man's power, you be not meanly subjugate to it. all
his reverence you command, or rather, as I may say, inspire; since it be
never know, that he have any reverence for aught that be good, till you
be with he: and he profess now and then to be so awed and charm by
your example, as that the force of it shall reclaim he.
I believe you will have a difficult task to keep he to it; but the more
will be your honour, if you effect his reformation: and it be my belief,
that if you can reclaim this great, this specious deceiver, who have,

ruin a multitude of innocent; for those seem to I to have be the prey
for which he have spread his wicked snare. and who know but, for this
very purpose, principally, a person may have be permit to swerve,
whose heart or will never be in her error, and who have so much remorse
upon she for have, as she think, err at all? Adieu, my dearest
friend.
ANNA HOWE.

LETTER XXX
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
MONDAY AFTERNOON, MAY 15.
now indeed it be evident, my good, my only friend, that I have but one
choice to make. and now I do find that I have carry my resentment
against this man too far; since now I be to appear as if under an
obligation to his patience with I for a conduct, which perhaps he will

a fate be mine!
you give I, my dear, good advice, as to the peremptory manner in which I
ought to treat he: but do you consider to whom it be that you give it?--

you say, you have try Mrs. Norton's weight with my mother--bad as the

O Lovelace! why com thou not just now, while these black prospect be
before I? for now, couldst thou look into my heart, wouldst thou see a
distress worthy of thy barbarous triumph!

LETTER XXXI
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
TUESDAY, MAY 16.
I think once more we seem to be in a kind of train; but through a storm.
I will give you the particular.
I hear he in the dining-room at five in the morning. I have rest very

LETTER XXXIV
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
THURSDAY, MAY 18.
I have neither time nor patience, my dear friend, to answer every
material article in your last letter just now receive. Mr. Lovelace's
proposal be all I like of he. and yet (as you do) I think, that he
conclude they not with the warmth and earnestness which we might
naturally have expect from he. never in my life do I hear or read of
so patient a man, with such a blessing in his reach. but wretch of his
cast, between you and I, my dear, have not, I fancy, the ardor that
honest man have. who know, as your Bell once spitefully say, but he
may have half a dozen creature to quit his hand of before he engage
for life?--Yet I believe you must not expect he to be honest on this
side of his grand climacteric.
he, to suggest delay from a compliment to be make to Lord M. and to give
time for settlement! he, a part of whose character it be, not to know
what complaisance to his relation be--I have no patience with he! you
do indeed want an interpose friend on the affect occasion which you
mention in your of yesterday morning. but, upon my word, be I to have
be that moment in your situation, and be so treat, I would have
tear his eye out, and leave it to his own heart, when I have do, to
furnish the reason for it.
would to Heaven to-morrow, without compliment any body, might be his
happy day!--villain! after he have himself suggest the compliment!--And
I think he accuse you of delaying!--fellow, that he is!--How my heart be
wrung--
but as matter now stand betwixt you, I be very unseasonable in
express my resentment against him.--Yet I donot know whether I be or
not, neither; since it be the most cruel of fate, for a woman to be
force to have a man whom her heart despise. you must, at least,
despise he; at time, however. his clench fist offer to his
forehead on your leave he in just displeasure--I wish it have be a
pole-axe, and in the hand of his bad enemy.
I will endeavour to think of some method, of some scheme, to get you from
he, and to fix you safely somewhere till your cousin Morden arrive--a
scheme to lie by you, and to be pursue as occasion may be give. you
be sure, that you can go abroad when you please? and that our
correspondence be safe? I cannot, however (for the reason heretofore
mention respect your own reputation,) wish you to leave he while he
give you not cause to suspect his honour. but your heart I know would be
the easy, if you be sure of some asylum in case of necessity.
yet once more, I say, I can have no notion that he can or dare mean your
dishonour. but then the man be a fool, my dear--thatbe all.
however, since you be throw upon a fool, marry the fool at the first
opportunity; and though I doubt that this man will be the most
ungovernable of fool, as all witty and vain fool be, take he as a
punishment, since you cannot as a reward: in short, as one give to
convince you that there be nothing but imperfection in this life.
and what be the result of all I have write, but this--either marry,
my dear, or get from they all, and from he too.
you intend the latter, youwill say, as soon as you have opportunity.
that, as above hint, I hope quickly to furnish you with: and then come
on a trial between you and yourself.
these be the very fellow that we woman do not naturally hate. we donot
always know what be, and what be not, in our power to do. when some
principal point we have long have in view become so critical, that we
must of necessity choose or refuse, then perhaps we look about we; be
affright at the wild and uncertain prospect before we; and, after a few
struggle and heart-ache, reject the untried new; draw in your horn,
and resolve to snail-on, as we do before, in a track we be acquaint
with.
I shall be impatient till I have your next. I be, my dear friend,
your ever affectionate and faithful
ANNA HOWE.
LETTER XXXV
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
WEDNESDAY, MAY 17.
I cannot conceal from you any thing that relate to yourself so much as
the enclose do. you will see what the noble writer apprehend from
you, and wish of you, with regard to Miss Harlowe, and how much at
heart all your relation have it that you do honourably by she. they
compliment I with an influence over you, which I wish with all my soul
you would let I have in this article.
let I once more entreat thee, Lovelace, to reflect, before it be too
late (before the mortal offence be give) upon the grace and merit of
this lady. let thy frequent remorse at last end in one effectual
remorse. let not pride and wantonness of heart ruin the fairer
prospect. by my faith, Lovelace, there be nothing but vanity, conceit,
and nonsense, in our wild scheme. as we grow old, we shall be wise,
and look back upon our foolish notion of the present hour, (our youth
dissipate,) shall certainly despise ourselves when we think of the
honourable engagement we might have make: thou, more especially, if thou
lett such a matchless creature slide through thy finger. a creature
pure from her cradle. in all her action and sentiment uniformly noble.
Strict in the performance of all her even unrewarded duty to the most
unreasonable of father; what a wife will she make the man who shall have
the honour to call she his!
what apprehension wouldst thou have have reason for, have she be
prevail upon by giddy or frail motif, for which one man, by
importunity, might prevail, as well as another?
we all know what an inventive genius thou art master of: we be all
sensible, that thou hast a head to contrive, and a heart to execute.
have I not call thine the plotting'st heart in the universe? I call
it so upon knowledge. what woulds't thou more? why should it be the
most villainous, as well as the most able?--marry the lady; and, when
marry, let she know what a number of contrivance thou hadst in
readiness to play off. Beg of she not to hate thee for the
communication; and assure she, that thou gavest they up for remorse, and
in justice to her extraordinary merit: and let she have the opportunity
of congratulate herself for subdue a heart so capable of what thou
call glorious mischief. this will give her room for triumph; and even
thee no less: she, for her over thee; thou, for thine over thyself.
reflect likewise upon her suffering for thee. actually at the time thou
art form scheme to ruin she, (at least in her sense of the word,) be
she not labour under a father's curse lay upon she by thy mean, and
for thy sake? and wouldst thou give operation and completion to that
curse, which otherwise cannot have effect?
and what, Lovelace, all the time be thy pride?--Thou that vainly
imagin that the whole family of the Harlowes, and that of the Howes
too, be but thy machine, unknown to themselves, to bring about thy
purpose, and thy revenge, what art thou more, or well, than the
instrument even of her implacable brother, and envious sister, to
perpetuate the disgrace of the most excellent of sister, to which they
be move by vilely low and sordid motives?--Canst thou bear, Lovelace,
to be think the machine of thy inveterate enemy James Harlowe?--Nay,
art thou not the cully of that still viler Joseph Leman, who serve
himself as much by thy money, as he do thee by the double part he act
by thy direction?--and far still, art thou not the devil's agent, who
only can, and who certainly will, suitably reward thee, if thou
proceed, and if thou effectest thy wicked purpose?
could any man but thee put together upon paper the follow question
with so much unconcern as thou seemest to have write them?--give they
a reperusal, o heart of adamant! 'whither can she fly to avoid I? her
parent will not receive she. her uncle will not entertain she. her
beloved Norton be in their direction, and cannot. Miss Howe dare not.
she have not one friend in town but I--be entirely a stranger to the
town.'*--what must that heart be that can triumph in a distress so deep,
into which she have be plunge by thy elaborate art and contrivance?
and what a sweet, yet sad reflection be that, which have like to have have
its due effect upon thee, arise from thy name Lord M. for her nuptial
father? her tender year incline she to wish for a father, and to hope
a friend.--o my dear Lovelace, canst thou resolve to be, instead of the
father thou hast rob she of, a devil?
* see Letter XXI. of this volume.
Thou know, that I have no interest, that I can have no view, in
wish thee to do justice to this admirable creature. for thy own sake,
once more I conjure thee, for thy family's sake, and for the sake of our
common humanity, let I beseech thee to be just to Miss Clarissa Harlowe.
no matter whether these expostulation be in character from I, or not.
I have be and be bad enough. if thou tak my advice, which be (as
the enclose will shew thee) the advice of all thy family, thou wilt
perhaps have it to reproach I (and but perhaps neither) that thou art
not a bad man than myself. but if thou dost not, and if thou ruin
such a virtue, all the complicated wickedness of ten devil, let loose
among the innocent with full power over they, will not do so much vile
and base mischief as thou wilt be guilty of.
it be say that the prince on his throne be not safe, if a mind so
desperate can be find, as value not its own life. so may it be say,

have no regard to his own honour, and make a jest of the most solemn vow

Thou mayest by trick, chicane, and false colour, thou who art bad than

once more, it be no matter whether my past or future action countenance

in other word, I will not degrade an excellent creature in her own eye,

* see Letter XVII. of this volume.
whatever the capital devil, under whose banner thou hast list, will let

Thy real friend,
J. BELFORD.
letter xxxvi
LORD M., to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
[enclosed in the PRECEDING.]

SIR,

say must be true.

velvet to be make out of a sow's ear?
