teach my nephew more mercy and compassion than be in his nature I doubt
to shew; which be this, that he who pity another, remember himself.
and this that be go to follow, I be sure he have prove the truth of a
hundred time, that he who do what he will seldom do what he ought.
nor be that unworthy of his notice, young man's frolic old man feel. my
devilish gout, God help I--but I will not say what I be go to say.
I remember, that you yourself, compliment I for my taste in pithy and
wise sentence, say a thing that give I a high opinion of you; and it
be this: 'man of talent,' say you, 'be soon to be convince by
short sentence than by long preachment, because the short sentence
drive themselves into the heart and stay there, while long discourse,
though ever so good, tire the attention; and one good thing drive out
another, and so on till all be forget.'
may your good counsel, Mr. Belford, found upon these hint which I have
give, pierce his heart, and incite he to do what will be so happy for
himself, and so necessary for the honour of that admirable lady whom I
long to see his wife; and, if I may, I will not think of one for myself.
should he abuse the confidence she have place in he, I myself shall
pray, that vengeance may fall upon his head--raro--I quite forget all my
Latin; but I think it be, raro antecedentem scelestum deseruit pede paean
claudo: where vice go before, vengeance (soon or later) will follow.
but why do I translate these thing for you?
I shall make no apology for this trouble. I know how well you love he
and I; and there be nothing in which you could serve we both more
importantly, than in forward this match to the utmost of your power.
when it be do, how shall I rejoice to see you at M. Hall! mean time, I
shall long to hear that you be likely to be successful with he; and be,
Dear Sir,
your most faithful friend and servant,
M.
[Mr. Lovelace have not return an answer to Mr. Belford's expostulary
letter so soon as Mr. Belford expect, he write to he, express
his apprehension that he have disoblige he by his honest freedom.
among other thing, he says--]
I pass my time here at Watford, attend my die uncle, very heavily.
I cannot therefore, by any mean, dispense with thy correspondence. and
why shouldst thou punish I, for have more conscience and more remorse
than thyself? Thou who never thoughtest either conscience or remorse an
honour to thee. and I have, besides, a melancholy story to tell thee, in
relation to Belton and his Thomasine; and which may afford a lesson to
all the keeping-class.
I have a letter from each of our three companion in the time. they have
all the wickedness that thou hast, but not the wit. some new roguery
do two of they boast of, which, I think, if complete, deserve the
gallow.
I be far from hat intrigue upon principle. but to have awkward
fellow plot, and commit their plot to paper, destitute of the
seasoning, of the acuman, which be thy talent, how extremely shocking
must their letter be!--But do thou, Lovelace, whether thou art, or art
not, determine upon thy measure with regard to the fine lady in thy
power, enliven my heavy heart by thy communication; and thou wilt oblige
Thy melancholy friend,
J. BELFORD.
LETTER XXXVII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
FRIDAY NIGHT, MAY 19.
when I have open my view to thee so amply as I have do in my former
letter; and have tell thee, that my principal design be but to bring
virtue to a trial, that, if virtue, it need not be afraid of; and that
the reward of it will be marriage (that be to say, if, after I have
carry my point, I cannot prevail upon she to live with I the life of
honour;* for that thou know be the wish of my heart); I be amazed at
the repetition of thy wambling nonsense.
* see Vol. III. Letter XVIII.
I be of opinion with thee, that some time hence, when I be grow wiser, I
shall conclude, that there be nothing but vanity, conceit, and nonsense,
in my present wild scheme. but what be this saying, but that I must
be first wise?
I do not intend to let this matchless creature slide through my finger.
art thou able to say half the thing in her praise, that I have say, and
be continually say or write?
her gloomy father curse the sweet creature, because she put it out of
his wicked power to compel she to have the man she hat. Thou know
how little merit she have with I on this score.--and shall I not try the
virtue I intend, upon full proof, to reward, because her father be a
tyrant?--why art thou thus eternally reflect upon so excellent a
woman, as if thou wert assure she would fail in the trial?--Nay, thou
declarest, every time thou writ on the subject, that she will, that
she must yield, entangle as she be: and yet makest her virtue the
pretence of thy solicitude for she.
an instrument of the vile James Harlowe, dost thou call me?--O Jack! how
could I curse thee!--i be instrument of that brother! of that sister!
but mark the end--and thou shalt see what will become of that brother,
and of that sister!
play not against I my own acknowledge sensibility, I desire thee.
sensibility, which at the same time that they contradict thy charge of
an adamantine heart in thy friend, thou hadst know nothing of, have I not
communicate they to thee.
if I ruin such a virtue, sayest thou!--eternal monotonist!--again; the
most immaculate virtue may be ruin by man who have no regard to their
honour, and who make a jest of the most solemn oath, &c. what must be
the virtue that will be ruin without oath? be not the world full of
these deception? and be not lover' oath a jest of hundred of year'
stand? and be not caution against the perfidy of our sex a
necessary part of the female education?
I do intend to endeavour to overcome myself; but I must first try, if I
cannot overcome this lady. have I not say, that the honour of her sex
be concerned that I should try?
whenever thou meet with a woman of but half her perfection, thou wilt
marry--do, Jack.
can a girl be degrade by trial, who be not overcome?
I be glad that thou tak crime to thyself, for not endeavour to
convert the poor wretch whom other have ruin. I will not
recriminate upon thee, Belford, as I might, when thou flatterest thyself
that thou never ruinedst the moral of any young creature, who otherwise
would not have be corrupt--the palliate consolation of an Hottentot
heart, determine rather to gluttonize on the garbage of other foul
feeder than to reform.--But tell I, Jack, wouldst thou have spar such
a girl as my Rosebud, have I not, by my example, engage thy generosity?
nor be my Rosebud the only girl I spared:--when my power be
acknowledge, who more merciful than thy friend?
it be resistance that inflame desire,
sharpen the dart of love, and blow its fire.
Love be disarm'd that meet with too much ease;
he languish, and do not care to please.
the woman know this as well as the man. they love to be address with
spirit:
and therefore 'tis their golden fruit they guard
with so much care, to make profession hard.
whence, for a by-reflection, the ardent, the complaisant gallant be so
often prefer to the cold, the unadore husband. and yet the sex do
not consider, that variety and novelty give the ardour and the
obsequiousness; and that, be the rake as much use to they as the
husband be, he would be [and be to his own wife, if marry] as
indifferent to their favour, as their husband be; and the husband, in
his turn, would, to another woman, be the rake. let the woman, upon the
whole, take this lesson from a lovelace--'alway to endeavour to make
themselves as new to a husband, and to appear as elegant and as oblige
to he, as they be desirous to appear to a lover, and actually be to
he as such; and then the rake, which all woman love, will last long in
the husband, than it generally do.'
but to return:--if I have not sufficiently clear my conduct to thee in
the above; I refer thee once more to mine of the 13th of last month.*
and pr'ythee, Jack, lie I not under a necessity to repeat the same
thing so often. I hope thou readest what I write more than once.
* see Vol. II. Letter XIV.
I be not displeased that thou art so apprehensive of my resentment, that
I cannot miss a day without make thee uneasy. thy conscience, 'tis
plain, tell thee, that thou have deserve my displeasure: and if it have
convince thee of that, it will make thee afraid of repeat thy fault.
see that this be the consequence. else, now that thou hast tell I how I
can punish thee, it be very likely that I do punish thee by my silence,
although I have as much pleasure in writing on this charming subject, as
thou canst have in read what I write.
when a boy, if a dog run away from I through fear, I generally look
about for a stone, or a stick; and if neither offer to my hand, I
skin my hat after he to make he afraid for something. what
signify power, if we do not exert it?
let my Lord know, that thou hast scribble to I. but give he not the
content of thy epistle. though a parcel of crude stuff, he would think
there be something in it. poor argument will do, when bring in
favour of what we like. but the stupid peer little think that this lady
be a rebel to love. on the contrary, not only he, but all the world
believe she to be a volunteer in his service.--so I shall incur blame,
and she will be pity, if any thing happen amiss.
since my Lord's heart be set upon this match, I have write already to
let he know, 'that my unhappy character have give my beloved an
ungenerous diffidence of I. that she be so mother-sick and father-fond,
that she have rather return to Harlowe-place than marry. that she be even
apprehensive that the step she have take of go off with I will make
the lady of a family of such rank and honour as ours think slightly of
she. that therefore I desire his lordship (though this hint, I tell he,
must be very delicately touch) to write I such a letter as I can shew
she; (let he treat I in it ever so freely, I shall not take it amiss, I
tell he, because I know his Lordship take pleasure in write to I in
a corrective style). that he may make what offer he please on the
marriage. that I desire his presence at the ceremony; that I may take
from his hand the great blessing that mortal man can give I.'
I have not absolutely tell the lady that I would write to his Lordship to
this effect; yet have give her reason to think I will. so that without
the last necessity I shall not produce the answer I expect from he: for
I be very loth, I own, to make use of any of my family's name for the
furthering of my design. and yet I must make all secure, before I pull
off the mask. be not this my motive for bring her hither?
thus thou seest that the old peer's letter come very seasonably. I thank
thee for that. but as to his sentence, they cannot possibly do I good.
I be early suffocated with his wisdom of nation. when a boy, I never
ask anything of he, but out fly a proverb; and if the tendency of
that be to deny I, I never could obtain the least favour. this give I
so great an aversion to the very word, that, when a child, I make it a
condition with my tutor, who be an honest parson, that I would not read
my Bible at all, if he would not excuse I one of the wise book in it:
to which, however, I have no other objection, than that it be call the
Proverbs. and as for Solomon, he be then a hat character with I, not
because of his polygamy, but because I have conceive he to be such
another musty old fellow as my uncle.
well, but let we leave old saw to old I. what signify thy tedious
whine over thy depart relation? be it not generally agree that he
cannot recover? will it not be kind in thee to put he out of his
misery? I hear that he be pester still with visit from doctor, and
apothecary, and surgeon; that they cannot cut so deep as the
mortification have go; and that in every visit, in every scarification,
inevitable death be pronounce upon he. why then do they keep
torment he? be it not to take away more of his live fleece than of
his dead flesh?--when a man be give over, the fee should surely be
refuse. be they not now rob his heirs?--what have thou to do, if
the will be as thou'dst have it?--he send for thee [do he not?] to close
his eye. he be but an uncle, be he?
let I see, if I mistake not, it be in the Bible, or some other good
book: can it be in herodotus?--o I believe it be in Josephus, a half-
sacred, and half-profane author. he tell we of a king of Syria put out
of his pain by his prime minister, or one who deserve to be so for his
contrivance. the story say, if I be right, that he spread a wet cloth
over his face, which kill he, he reign in his place. a notable
fellow! perhaps this wet cloth in the original, be what we now call
laudanum; a potion that overspread the faculty, as the wet cloth do
the face of the royal patient; and the translator know not how to render
it.
but how like forlorn varlet thou subscrib, 'thy melancholy friend, J.
BELFORD!' melancholy! for what? to stand by, and see fair play between
an old man and death? I think thou hadst be more of a man; that thou
art not afraid of an acute death, a sword's point, to be so plaugily
hip'd at the consequence of a chronical one!--what though the
scarificator work upon he day by day? itbe only upon a caput mortuum:
and pr'ythee go to, to use the stylum veterum, and learn of the royal
butcher; who, for sport, (an hundred time bad man than thy Lovelace,)
widow ten thousand at a brush, and make twice as many fatherless--learn
of they, I say, how to support a single death.
but art thou sure, Jack, it be a mortification?--My uncle once give
promise of such a root-and-branch distemper: but, alas! it turn to a
smart gout-fit; and I have the mortification instead of him.--I have hear
that bark, in proper dos, will arrest a mortification in its progress,
and at last cure it. let thy uncle's surgeon know, that it be worth more
than his ear, if he prescribe one grain of the bark.
I wish my uncle have give I the opportunity of set thee a well
example: thou shouldst have see what a brave fellow I have be. and have
I have occasion to write, my conclusion would have be this: 'I hope the
old Trojan's happy. in that hope, I be so; and
'thy rejoicing friend,
'R. LOVELACE.'
Dwell not always, Jack, upon one subject. let I have poor Belton's
story. the soon the well. if I can be of service to he, tell
he he may command I either in purse or person. yet the former with
a free will than the latter; for how can I leave my goddess? but
Iwill issue my command to my other vassal to attend thy summon.
if ye want head, let I know. if not, my quota, on this occasion, be
money.
LETTER XXXVIII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
SATURDAY, MAY 20.
not one word will I reply to such an abandon wretch, as thou hast shew
thyself to be in thine of last night. I will leave the lady to the
protection of that power who only can work miracle; and to her own
merit. still I have hope that these will save she.
I will proceed, as thou desir, to poor Belton's case; and the rather,
as it have throw I into such a train of think upon our past life,
our present course, and our future view, as may be of service to we
both, if I can give due weight to the reflection that arise from it.
the poor man make I a visit on Thursday, in this my melancholy
attendance. he begin with complaint of his ill health and spirit, his
hectic cough, and his increase malady of spit blood; and then lead to
his story.
a confound one it be; and which highly aggravate his other malady:
for it have come out, that his Thomasine, (who, truly, would be new
christen, you know, that her name might be near in sound to the
christian name of the man whom she pretend to doat upon) have for many
year carry on an intrigue with a fellow who have be hostler to her
father (an innkeeper at Darking); of whom, at the expense of poor Belton,
she have make a gentleman; and manage it so, that have the art to make
herself his cashier, she have be unable to account for large sum, which
he think forthcoming at demand, and have trust to her custody, in
order to pay off a mortgage upon his parental estate in Kent, which his
heart have run upon leave clear, but which now cannot be do, and will
soon be foreclose. and yet she have so long pass for his wife, that he
know not what to resolve upon about she; nor about the two boy he be
so fond of, suppose they to be his; whereas now he begin to doubt his
share in they.
so keep donot do, Lovelace. 'tis not the eligible wife. 'a man must
keep a woman, say the poor fellow to I, but not his estate!--two
interests!--then, my tottering fabric!' point to his emaciated
carcass.
we do well to value ourselves upon our liberty, or to speak more
properly, upon the liberty we take. we have need to run down matrimony
as we do, and to make that state the subject of our frothy jest; when we
frequently render ourselves (for this of Tom's be not a singular case)
the dupe and tool of woman who generally govern we (by art our wise
head penetrate not) more absolutely than a wife would attempt to do.
let we consider this point a little; and that upon our own principle, as
libertine, set aside what be exact from we by the law of our
country, and its custom; which, nevertheless, we cannot get over, till
we have get over almost all moral obligation, as member of society.
in the first place, let we consider (we, who be in possession of estate
by legal descent) how we should have like to have be such naked
destitute varlet, as we must have be, have our father be as wise as
ourselves; and despise matrimony as we do--and then let we ask
ourselves, if we ought not to have the same regard for our posterity, as
we be glad our father have for theirs?
but this, perhaps, be too moral a consideration.--to proceed therefore to
those consideration which will be more striking to we: how can we
reasonably expect economy or frugality (or anything indeed but riot and
waste) from creature who have an interest, and must therefore have
view, different from our own?
they know the uncertain tenure (our fickle humour) by which they hold:
and be it to be wonder at, suppose they to be provident harlot, that
they should endeavour, if they have the power, to lay up against a rainy
day? or, if they have not the power, that they should squander all they
can come at, when they be sure of nothing but the present hour; and when
the life they live, and the sacrifice they have make, put conscience and
honour out of the question?
whereas a wife, have the same family-interest with her husband, lie
not under either the same apprehension or temptation; and have not
break through (of necessity, at least, have not) those restraint which
education have fasten upon she: and if she make a private purse, which
we be tell by anti-matrimonialist, all wife love to do, and have
child, it go all into the same family at the long-run.
then as to the great article of fidelity to your bed--be not woman of
family, who be well-educate, under great restraint, than creature,
who, if they ever have reputation, sacrifice it to sordid interest, or to
more sordid appetite, the moment they give it up to you? do not the
example you furnish, of have succeed with she, give encouragement
for other to attempt she likewise? for with all her blandishment, can
any man be so credulous, or so vain, as to believe, that the woman he
could persuade, another may not prevail upon?
adultery be so capital a guilt, that even rake and libertine, if not
wholly abandon, and as I may say, invite by a woman's levity, disavow
and condemn it: but here, in a state of keeping, a woman be in no danger
of incur (legally, at least) that guilt; and you yourself have break
through and overthrow in she all the fence and boundary of moral
honesty, and the modesty and reserve of her sex: and what tie shall hold
she against inclination, or interest? and what shall deter an attempter?
while a husband have this security from legal sanction, that if his wife
be detect in a criminal conversation with a man of fortune, (the most
likely by bribe to seduce she,) he may recover very great damage, and
procure a divorce besides: which, to say nothing of the ignominy, be a
consideration that must have some force upon both party. and a wife
must be vicious indeed, and a reflection upon a man's own choice, who,
for the sake of change, and where there be no quality to seduce, nor
affluence to corrupt, will run so many hazard to injure her husband in
the tenderest of all point.
but there be difficulty in procure a divorce--[and so there ought]--
and none, say the rake, in part with a mistress whenever you suspect
she; or whenever you be weary of she, and have a mind to change she for
another.
but must not the man be a brute indeed, who can cast off a woman whom he
have seduce, [if he take she from the town, thatbe another thing,]
without some flagrant reason; something that will well justify he to
himself, as well as to she, and to the world, than mere power and
novelty?
but I donot see, if we judge by fact, and by the practice of all we have
be acquaint with of the keeping-class, that we know how to part with
they when we have they.
that we know we can if we will, be all we have for it: and this lead we
to bear many thing from a mistress, which we would not from a wife.
but, if we be good-natured and humane: if the woman have art: [and what
woman want it, who have fall by art? and to whose precarious situation
art be so necessary?] if you have give she the credit of be call by
your name: if you have a settle place of abode, and have receive and
pay visit in her company, as your wife: if she have bring you child
--you will allow that these be strong obligation upon you in the
world's eye, as well as to your own heart, against tear yourself from
such close connection. she will stick to you as your skin: and it will
be next to flay yourself to cast she off.
even if there be cause for it, by infidelity, she will have manage ill,
if she have not her defender. nor do I ever know a cause or a person
so bad, as to want advocate, either from ill-will to the one, or pity to
the other: and you will then be think a hard-hearted miscreant: and
even be she to go off without credit to herself, she will leave you as
little; especially with all those whose good opinion a man would wish to
cultivate.
well, then, shall this poor privilege, that we may part with a woman if
we will, be deem a balance for the other inconveniencie? shall it be
think by we, who be man of family and fortune, an equivalent for
give up equality of degree; and take for the partner of our bed, and
very probably more than the partner in our estate, (to the breach of all
family-rule and order,) a low-bear, a low-educate creature, who have not
bring any thing into the common stock; and can possibly make no return
for the solid benefit she receive, but those libidinous one, which a
man cannot boast of, but to his disgrace, nor think of, but to the shame
of both?
moreover, as the man advance in year, the fury of his libertinism will
go off. he will have different aim and pursuit, which will diminish
his appetite to range, and make such a regular life as the matrimonial
and family life, palatable to he, and every day more palatable.
if he have child, and have reason to think they his, and if his lewd
course have leave he any estate, he will have cause to regret the
restraint his boasted liberty have lay he under, and the valuable
privilege it have deprive he of; when he find that it must descend to
some relation, for whom, whether near or distant, he care not one
farthing; and who perhaps (if a man of virtue) have hold he in the
utmost contempt for his dissolute life.
and be we to suppose his estate in his power to bequeath as he please;
why should a man resolve, for the gratifying of his foolish humour only,
to bastardize his race? why should he wish to expose his child to the
scorn and insult of the rest of the world? why should he, whether they
be son or daughter, lie they under the necessity of comply with
proposal of marriage, either inferior as to fortune, or unequal as to
age? why should he deprive the child he love, who themselves may be
guilty of no fault, of the respect they would wish to have, and to
deserve; and of the opportunity of associate themselves with proper,
that be to say, with reputable company? and why should he make they think
themselves under obligation to every person of character, who will
vouchsafe to visit they? what little reason, in a word, would such
child have to bless their father's obstinate defiance of the law and
custom of his country; and for give they a mother, of whom they could
not think with honour; to whose crime it be that they owe their very
being, and whose example it be their duty to shun?
if the education and moral of these child be leave to chance, as too
generally they be, (for the man who have humanity and a feeling heart,
and who be capable of fondness for his offspring, I take it for grant
will marry,) the case be still bad; his crime be perpetuate, as I may
say, by his child: and the sea, the army, perhaps the highway, for the
boy; the common for the girl; too often point out the way to a bad
catastrophe.
what therefore, upon the whole, do we get by treading in these crooked
path, but danger, disgrace, and a too-late repentance?
and after all, do we not frequently become the cullie of our own
libertinism; slide into the very state with those half-wear-out doxy,
which perhaps we might have enter into with their lady; at least with
their superior both in degree and fortune? and all the time live
handsomely like ourselves; not sneak into hole and corner; and, when
we creep abroad with our woman, look about we, and at ever one that
pass we, as if we be confessedly accountable to the censure of all
honest people.
my cousin Tony Jenyns, thou knew. he have not the actively mischievous
spirit, that thou, Belton, Mowbray, Tourville, and myself, have: but he
imbibe the same notion we do, and carry they into practice.
how do he prate against wedlock! how do he strut about as a wit and a
smart! and what a wit and a smart do all the boy and girl of our
family (myself among the rest, then an urchin) think he, for the air he
give himself?--marry! no, not for the world; what man of sense would
bear the insolence, the petulance, the expensiveness of a wife! he
could not for the heart of he think it tolerable, that a woman of equal
rank and fortune, and, as it might happen, superior talent to his own,
should look upon herself to have a right to share the benefit of that
fortune which she bring he.
so, after he have flutter about the town for two or three year, in all
which time he have a well opinion of himself than any body else have,
what do he do, but enter upon an affair with his fencing-master's
daughter?
he succeed; take private lodging for she at Hackney; visit she by
stealth; both of they tender of reputation that be extremely tender,
but which neither have quite give up; for rake of either sex be always
the last to condemn or cry down themselves: visit by nobody, nor
visit: the life of a thief, or of a man best by creditor, afraid to
look out of his own house, or to be see abroad with she. and thus go
on for twelve year, and, though he have a good estate, hardly make both
end meet; for though no glare, there be no economy; and, beside, he have
ever year a child, and very fond of his child be he. but none of
they live above three year. and be now, on the death of the
dozenth, grow as dully sober, as if he have be a real husband, his good
Mrs. Thomas (for he have not permit she to take his own name) prevail
upon he to think the loss of their child a judgment upon the parent
for their wicked way of life; [a time will come, Lovelace, if we live to
advanced year, in which reflection will take hold of the enfeeble
mind;] and then it be not difficult for his woman to induce he, by way
of compound with Heaven, to marry she. when this be do, he have
leisure to sit down, and contemplate; an to recollect the many offer of
person of family and fortune to which he have decline in the prime of
life: his expense equal at least: his reputation not only less, but
lose: his enjoyment steal: his partnership unequal, and such as he have
always be ashamed of. but the woman say, that after twelve or
thirteen year' cohabitation, Tony do an honest thing by she. and that
be all my poor cousin get by make his old mistress his new wife--not a
drum, not a trumpet, not a fife, not a tabret, nor the expectation of a
new joy, to animate he on!
what Belton will do with his Thomasine I know not! nor care I to advise
he: for I see the poor fellow do not like that any body should curse
she but himself. this he do very heartily. and so low be he reduce,
that he blubber over the reflection upon his past fondness for her cub,
and upon his present doubt of their be his: 'what a damn'd thing be
it, Belford, if Tom and Hal should be the hostler dog's puppy and not
mine!'
very true! and I think the strong health of the chubby-face muscular
whelp confirm the too great probability.
but I say not so to he.
you, he say, be such a gay, lively mortal, that this sad tale would
make no impression upon you: especially now, that your whole heart be
engage as it be. Mowbray would be too violent upon it: he have not, he
say, a feeling heart. Tourville have no discretion: and, a pretty jest!
although he and his Thomasine live without reputation in the world,
(people guess that they be not marry, notwithstanding she go by
his name,) yet 'he would not too much discredit the curse ingrate
neither!'
could a man act a weak part, have he be really marry; and be he
sure he be go to separate from the mother of his own child?
I leave this as a lesson upon thy heart, without make any application:
only with this remark, 'that after we libertine have indulge our
licentious appetite, reflect, (in the conceit of our vain heart,)
both with our lip and by our life, upon our ancestor and the good old
way, we find out, when we come to year of discretion, if we live till
then (what all who know we find out before, that be to say, we find
out), our own despicable folly; that those good old way would have be
good for we, as well as for the rest of the world; and that in every step
we have deviate from they we have only expose our vanity and our
ignorance at the same time.'
J. BELFORD.

MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.

I be pleased with the sober reflection with which thou concludest thy

from such a woman as Miss Harlowe, a man be secure from all the

a blessing on thy heart, thou honest fellow! I think thou wert in

principle, I know, in thee: it could not be compassion--a little envy

say I, a blessing on thy heart, thou true friend, and very honest fellow!
now will I proceed with courage in all my scheme, and oblige thee with
the continued narrative of my progression towards bring they to
effect!--but I could not forbear to interrupt my story, to show my
gratitude.

MONDAY, MAY 15.
MADAM,
I do make a sort of resolution ten year ago never to marry. I see in
other family, where they live well, you will be pleased to mark that,
queerness I could not away with. then like well enough to live single
for the sake of my brother's family; and for one child in it more than
the rest. but that girl have turn we all off the hinge: and why should
I deny myself any comfort for they, as will not thank I for so do, I
donot know.
so much for my motif as from self and family: but the dear Mrs. Howe
make I go far.
I have a very great fortune, I bless God for it, all of my own getting,
or most of it; you will be pleased to mark that; for I be the young
brother of three. you have also, God be thank, a great estate, which
you have improve by your own frugality and wise management. frugality,
let I stop to say, be one of the great virtue in this mortal life,
because it enable we to do justice to all, and put it in our power to
benefit some by it, as we see they deserve.
you have but one child; and I be a bachelor, and have never a one--all
bachelor cannot say so: wherefore your daughter may be the well for
I, if she will keep up with my humour; which be never think bad:
especially to my equal. servant, indeed, I donot matter be angry
with, when I please; they be pay for bear it, and too-too often
deserve it; as we have frequently take notice of to one another. and,
moreover, if we keep not servant at distance, they will be familiar.
I always make it a rule to find fault, whether reasonable or not, that so
I might have no reason to find fault. young woman and servant in
general (as worthy Mr. Solmes observe) be well govern by fear than
love. but this my humour as to servant will not effect either you or
Miss, you know.
I will make very advantageous settlement; such as any common friend
shall judge to be so. but must have all in my own power, while I live:
because, you know, Madam, it be as creditable to the wife, as to the
husband, that it should be so.
I be not at fine word. we be not child; though it be hop we may
have some; for I be a very healthy sound man. I bless God for it: and
never bring home from my voyage and travel a worse constitution than
I take out with I. I be none of those, I will assure you. but this I
will undertake, that, if you be the survivor, you shall be at the least
ten thousand pound the well for I. what, in the contrary case, I
shall be the well for you, I leave to you, as you shall think my
kindness to you shall deserve.
but one thing, Madam, I shall be glad of, that Miss Howe might not live
with we then--[she need not know I write thus]--but go home to Mr.
Hickman, as she be upon the point of marriage, I hear: and if she behave
dutifully, as she should do, to we both, she shall be the well; for I
say so before.
you shall manage all thing, both mine and your own; for I know but
little of land-matter. all my opposition to you shall be out of love,
when I think you take too much upon you for your health.
it will be very pretty for you, I should think, to have a man of
experience, in a long winter's evening, to sit down by you, and tell you
story of foreign part, and the custom of the nation he have consort
with. and I have fine curiosity of the indian growth, such as lady
love, and some that even my niece Clary, when she be good, never see.
these, one by one, as you be kind to I, (which I make no question of,
because I shall be kind to you,) shall be all your. pretty
entertainment by much, than sit with a too smartish daughter,
sometimes out of humour; and thwarting, and vexing, as daughter will,
(when woman-grow especially, as I have hear you often observe;) and
think their parent old, without pay they the reverence due to
year; when, as in your case, I make no sort of doubt, they be young
enough to wipe their nose. you understand I, Madam.
as for I myself, it will be very happy, and I be delighted with the
thinking of it, to have, after a pleasant ride, or so, a lady of like
experience with myself to come home to, and but one interest betwixt we:
to reckon up our coming-in together; and what this day and this week have
produce--o how this will increase love!--most mightily will it increase
it!--and I believe I shall never love you enough, or be able to show you
all my love.
I hope, Madam, there need not be such maiden nicety and hanging-off,
as I may call they, between we, (for hang-off sake,) as that you will
deny I a line or two to this proposal, write down, although you would
not answer I so readily when I speak to you; your daughter be, I
suppose, hard by; for you look round you, as if not willing to be
overhear. so I resolve to write: that my writing may stand as upon
record for my upright meaning; be none of your Lovelaces; you will
mark that, Madam; but a downright, true, honest, faithful Englishman. so
hope you will not disdain to write a line or two to this my proposal: and
I shall look upon it as a great honour, I will assure you, and be proud
thereof. what can I say more?--for you be your own mistress, as I be my
own master: and you shall always be your own mistress, be pleased to mark
that; for so a lady of your prudence and experience ought to be.
this be a long letter. but the subject require it; because I would not
write twice where once would do. so would explain my sense and mean
at one time.
I have have writing in my head two whole month very near; but hardly know
how (be unpracticed in these matter) to begin to write. and now,
good lady, be favourable to
your most humble lover,
and obedient servant,
ANT. HARLOWE.

MRS. ANNABELLA HOWE, to ANTONY HARLY, ESQ.
MR. ANTONY HARLOWE,
FRIDAY, MAY 19.
SIR,
it be not usual I believe for our sex to answer by pen and ink the first
letter on these occasion. the first letter! how odd be that! as if I
expect another; which I do not. but then I think, as I do not judge
proper to encourage your proposal, there be no reason why I should not
answer in civility, where so great a civility be intend. indeed, I be
always of opinion that a person be entitle to that, and not to ill
usage, because he have a respect for I. and so I have often and often
tell my daughter.
a woman I think make but a poor figure in a man's eye afterwards, and
do no reputation to her sex neither, when she behave like a tyrant to
he beforehand.
to be sure, Sir, if I be to change my condition, I know not a gentleman
whose proposal could be more agreeable. your nephew and your niece have
enough without you: my daughter have a fine fortune without I, and I
should take care to double it, live or dying, be I to do such a
thing: so nobody need to be the bad for it. but Nancy would not think
so.
all the comfort I know of in child, be, that when young they do with
we what they will, and all be pretty in they to their very fault; and
when they be grow up, they think their parent must live for they only;
and deny themselves every thing for their sake. I know Nancy could not
bear a father-in-law. she would fly at the very thought of my be in
earnest to give her one. not that I stand in fear of my daughter
neither. it be not fit I should. but she have her poor papa's spirit.
a very violent one that be. and one would not choose, you know, Sir, to
enter into any affair, that, one know, one must renounce a daughter for,
or she a mother--except indeed one's heart be much in it; which, I
bless God, mine be not.
I have now be a widow these ten year; nobody to controul I: and I be
say not to bear controul: so, Sir, you and I be good as we be, I
believe: nay, I be sure of it: for we want not what either have; have
both more than we know what to do with. and I know I could not be in the
least accountable for any of my way.
my daughter indeed, though she be a fine girl, as girl go, (she have too
much sense indeed for one of her sex, and know she have it,) be more a
check to I than one would wish a daughter to be: for who would choose to
be always snap at each other? but she will soon be marry; and
then, not live together, we shall only come together when we be
pleased, and stay away when we be not; and so, like other lover, never
see any thing but the good side of each other.
I own, for all this, that I love she dearly; and she I, I dare say: so
would not wish to provoke she to do otherwise. besides, the girl be so
much regard every where, that have live so much of my prime a widow,
I would not lay myself open to her censure, or even to her indifference,
you know.
your generous proposal require all this explicitness. I thank you for
your good opinion of I. when I know you acquiesce with this my civil
refusal [and indeed, Sir, I be as much in earnest in it, as if I have
speak broader] I donot know but Nancy and I may, with your permission,
come to see your fine thing; for I be a great admirer of rarity that
come from abroad.
so, Sir, let we only converse occasionally as we meet, as we use to do,
without any other view to each other than good wish: which I hope may
not be lessen for this declining. and then I shall always think myself
your obliged servant,
ANNABELLA HOWE.
P.S. I send word by Mrs. Lorimer, that I would write an answer: but
would take time for consideration. so hope, Sir, you willnot think it a
slight, I do not write soon.
LETTER XLIV
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
SUNDAY, MAY 21.
I be too much disturb in my mind to think of any thing but revenge; or
I do intend to give thee an account of Miss Harlowe's observation on

whatbe the matter now? thou'lt ask.

LETTER XLVI
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
SUNDAY MORNING, seven O'CLOCK.
I be at the play last night with Mr. Lovelace and Miss Horton. it be,
you know, a deep and most affect tragedy in the reading. you have my
remark upon it, in the little book you make I write upon the principal
acting-play. you will not wonder, that Miss Horton, as well as I, be
greatly move at the representation, when I tell you, and have some
pleasure in tell you, that Mr. Lovelace himself be very sensibly
touch with some of the most affect scene. I mention this in praise
of the author's performance; for I take Mr. Lovelace to be one of the
most hard-hearted man in the world. upon my word, my dear, I do.
his behaviour, however, on this occasion, and on our return, be
unexceptionable; only that he would oblige I to stay to supper with the
woman below, when we come back, and to sit up with he and they till near
one o'clock this morning. I be resolve to be even with he; and indeed
I be not very sorry to have the pretence; for I love to pass the sunday
by myself.
to have the well excuse to avoid his teasing, I be ready dress to go
to church this morning. I will go only to St. James's church, and in a
chair; that I may be sure I can go out and come in when I please, without
be intrude upon by he, as I be twice before.
***
NEAR NINE O'CLOCK.
I have your kind letter of yesterday. he know I have. and I shall
expect, that he will be inquisitive next time I see he after your
opinion of his proposal. I doubt not your approbation of they, and
have write an answer on that presumption; which be ready for he. he
must study for occasion of procrastination, and to disoblige I, if now
any thing happen to set we at variance again.
he be very importunate to see I. he have desire to attend I to church.

should not have be at my own liberty if I have. I bid Dorcas tell he,
that I desire to have this day to myself. I would see he in the
morning as early as he please. she say, she know not what ail he,
but that he be out of humour with every body.
he have send again in a peremptory manner. he warn I of Singleton. I
send he word, that if he be not afraid of Singleton at the playhouse

playhouse. I have accept of his servant's propose attendance. but he
be quite displeased, it seem. I donot care. I will not be perpetually
at his insolent beck.--adieu my dear, till I return. the chair wait.
he willnot stop I, sure, as I go down to it.

what then can be do to make such a matchless creature get over the

by my faith, Jack, as I sit gaze upon she, my whole soul in my eye,

and must, think I, o creature so divinely excellent, and so beloved of my

there's ingenuousness!--how I lie myself open to thee!--but seest thou not,

what a surprisingly powerful effect, so much and so long in my power she!

how can this be account for in a Lovelace!
but what a heap of stuff have I written!--How have I be run away with!
--By what?--canst thou say by what?--O thou lurk varletess CONSCIENCE!

here I arise. I shake myself. the window be open. always the

and it be out of sight!--and once more I be

LETTER LII
LORD M. TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
TUESDAY, MAY 23.
it be a long lane that have no turning.--do not despise I for my proverb
--you know I be always fond of they; and if you have be so too, it
would have be the well for you, let I tell you. I dare swear, the
fine lady you be so likely to be soon happy with, will be far from
despise they; for I be tell, that she write well, and that all her
letter be full of sentence. God convert you! for nobody but he and
this lady can.
I have no manner of doubt but that you will marry, as your father, and
all your ancestor, do before you: else you would have have no title to
be my heir; nor can your descendant have any title to be your's, unless
they be legitimate; thatbe worth your remembrance, Sir!--No man be
always a fool, every man be sometimes.--But your folly, I hope, be now
at an end.
I know, you have vow revenge against this fine lady's family: but no
more of that, now. you must look upon they all as your relation; and
forgive and forget. and when they see you make a good husband and a good
father, [which God send, for all our sake!] they will wonder at their
nonsensical antipathy, and beg your pardon: but while they think you a
vile fellow, and a rake, how can they either love you, or excuse their
daughter?
and methink I could wish to give a word of comfort to the lady, who,
doubtless, must be under great fear, how she shall be able to hold in
such a wild creature as you have hitherto be. I would hint to she,
that by strong argument, and gentle word, she may do any thing with
you; for though you be apt to be hot, gentle word will cool you, and
bring you into the temper that be necessary for your cure.
would to God, my poor lady, your aunt, who be dead and go, have be a
proper patient for the same remedy! God rest her soul! no reflection
upon her memory! worth be well know by want! I know shebe now; and if
I have go first, she would by this time have know mine.
there be great wisdom in that saying, God send I a friend, that may tell
I of my fault: if not, an enemy, and he will. not that I be your
enemy; and that you well know. the more noble any one be, the more
humble; so bear with I, if you would be think noble.--am I not your
uncle? and do I not design to be well to you than your father could be?
Nay, I will be your father too, when the happy day come; since you
desire it: and pray make my compliment to my dear niece; and tell she, I
wonder much that she have so long defer your happiness.
pray let she know as that I will present she (not you) either my
Lancashire seat or the Lawn in Hertfordshire, and settle upon she a
thousand pound a year penny-rent; to show she, that we be not a family
to take base advantage: and you may have writing draw, and settle as
you will.--hon Pritchard have the rent-roll of both these estate; and
as he have be a good old servant, I recommend he to your lady's favour.
I have already consult he: he will tell you what be good for you, and
most pleasing to I.
I be still very bad with my gout, but will come in a litter, as soon as
the day be fix; it would be the joy of my heart to join your hand.
and, let I tell you, if you do not make the good of husband to so good
a young lady, and one who have have so much courage for your sake, I will
renounce you; and settle all I can upon she and shebe by you, and leave
you out of the question.
if any thing be want for your further security, I be ready to give it;
though you know, that my word have always be look upon as my bond.
and when the Harlowes know all this, let we see whether they be able to
blush, and take shame to themselves.
Lady Sarah and Lady Betty want only to know the day, to make all the
country round they blaze, and all their tenant mad. and, if any one of
mine be sober upon the occasion, Pritchard shall eject he. and, on the
birth of the first child, if a son, I will do something more for you, and
repeat all our rejoicing.
I ought indeed to have write soon. but I know, that if you think
I long, and be in haste as to your nuptial, you would write and tell
I so. but my gout be very troublesome: and I be but a slow writer, you
know, at good: for composing be a thing that, though formerly I be very
ready at it, (as my Lord Lexington use to say,) yet have leave it off a
great while, I be not so now. and I choose, on this occasion, to write
all out of my own hand and memory; and to give you my good advice; for I
may never have such an opportunity again. you have have [God mend you!] a
strange way of turn your back upon all I have say: this once, I hope,
you will be more attentive to the advice I give you for your own good.
I have still another end; nay, two other end.
the one be, that now you be upon the border of wedlock, as I may say,
and all your wild oats will be sow, I would give you some instruction
as to your public as well as private behaviour in life; which, intend
you so much good as I do, you ought to hear; and perhaps would never have
listen to, on any less extraordinary occasion.
the second be, that your dear lady-elect (who be it seem herself so fine
and so sententious a writer) will see by this, that it be not our fault,
nor for want of the good advice, that you be not a well man than you
have hitherto be.
and now, in a few word, for the conduct I would wish you to follow in
public, as well as in private, if you would think I worthy of advise.
--It shall be short; so be not uneasy.
as to the private life: love your lady as she deserve. let your action
praise you. be a good husband; and so give the lie to all your enemy;
and make they ashamed of their scandal. and let we have pride in
say, that Miss Harlowe have not do either herself or family any
discredit by come among we. do this; and I, and Lady Sarah, and Lady
Betty, will love you for ever.
as to your public conduct: this as follow be what I could wish: but I
reckon your lady's wisdom will put we both right--no disparagement, Sir;
since, with all your wit, you have not hitherto show much wisdom, you
know.
get into parliament as soon as you can: for you have talon to make a
great figure there. who so proper to assist in make new hold law,
as those whom no law in be could hold?
then, for so long as you will give attendance in St. Stephen's chapel--
its be call a chapel, I hope, will not disgust you: I be sure I have
know many a riot there--a speaker have a hard time of it! but we peer
have more decorum--but what be I go to say?--I must go back.
for so long as you will give your attendance in parliament, for so long
will you be out of mischief; out of private mischief, at least: and may
St. Stephen's fate be your's, if you wilfully do public mischief!
when a new election come, you will have two or three borough, you know,
to choose out of:--but if you stay till then, I have rather you be for
the shire.
you will have interest enough, I be sure; and be so handsome a man,
the woman will make their husband vote for you.
I shall long to read your speech. I expect you will speak, if occasion
offer, the very first day. you want no courage, and think highly enough
of yourself, and lowly enough of every body else, to speak on all
occasion.
as to the method of the house, you have spirit enough, I fear, to be too
much above they: take care of that.--I donot so much fear your want of
good-manner. to man, you want no decency, if they donot provoke you: as
to that, I wish you would only learn to be as patient of contradiction
from other, as you would have other people be to you.
although I would not have you to be a courtier; neither would I have you
to be a malcontent. I remember (for I have it down) what my old friend
Archibald Hutcheson say; and it be a very good saying--(to Mr.
Secretary Craggs, I think it was)--'I look upon an administration, as
entitle to every vote I can with good conscience give it; for a house of
common should not needlessly put drag upon the wheel of government:
and when I have not give it my vote, it be with regret: and, for my
country's sake, I wish with all my heart the measure have be such as I
could have approve.'
and another say he have, which be this: 'neither can an opposition,
neither can a ministry, be always wrong. to be a plumb man therefore
with either, be an infallible mark, that that man must mean more and
bad than he will own he do mean.'
be these saying bad, Sir? be they to be despised?--well, then, why
should I be despise for remember they, and quote they, as I love to
do? let I tell you, if you love my company more than you do, you would
not be the bad for it. I may say so without any vanity; since it be
other man's wisdom, and not my own, that I be so fond of.
but to add a word or two more on this occasion; and I may never have such
another; for you must read this through--love honest man, and herd with
they, in the house and out of the house; by whatever name they be
dignified or distinguish: keep good man company, and you shall be out
of their number. but do I, or do I not, write this before?--writing,
at so many different time, and such a quantity, one may forget.
you may come in for the title when I be dead and go--God help me!--So I
would have you keep an equilibrium. if once you get the name of be a
fine speaker, you may have any thing: and, to be sure, you have naturally
a great deal of elocution; a tongue that would delude an angel, as the
woman say--to their sorrow, some of they, poor creatures!--a lead man
in the house of commons be a very important character; because that house
have the giving of money: and money make the mare to go; ay, and queen
and king too, sometimes, to go in a manner very different from what they
might otherwise choose to go, let I tell you.
however, methink, I would not have you take a place neither--it will
double your value, and your interest, if it be believe, that you will
not: for, as you will then stand in no man's way, you will have no envy;
but pure sterling respect; and both side will court you.
for your part, you will not want a place, as some other do, to piece up
their break fortune. if you can now live reputably upon two thousand
pound a year, it will be hard if you cannot hereafter live upon seven or
eight--less you will not have, if you oblige I; as now, by marry so
fine a lady, very much you will--and all this, and above Lady Betty's and
Lady Sarah's favour! what, in the name of wonder, could possibly
possess the proud harlowes!--that son, that son of theirs!--But, for his
dear sister's sake, I will say no more of he.
I never be offer a place myself: and the only one I would have take,
have I be offer it, be master of the buckhound; for I love hunting
when I be young; and it carry a good sound with it for we who live in
the country. often have I think of that excellent old adage; he that
eat the king's goose, shall be choke with his feather. I wish to the
Lord, this be thoroughly consider by place-hunter! it would be well
for they, and for their poor family.
I could say a great deal more, and all equally to the purpose. but
really I be tired; and so I doubt be you. and besides, I would reserve
something for conversation.
my niece Montague, and Lady Sarah and Lady Betty, join in compliment to
my niece that be to be. if she would choose to have the knot tie among
we, pray tell she that we shall all see it securely do: and we will
make all the country ring and blaze for a week together. but so I
believe I say before.
if any thing far may be needful toward promote your reciprocal
felicity, let I know it; and how you order about the day; and all that.
the enclose bill be very much at your service. 'tis payable at sight,
as whatever else you may have occasion for shall be.
so God bless you both; and make thing as convenient to my gout as you
can; though, be it whenever it will, I will hobble to you; for I long to
see you; and still more to see my niece; and be (in expectation of that
happy opportunity)
your most affectionate Uncle
M.
LETTER LIII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
THURSDAY, MAY 25.
Thou seest, Belford, how we now drive before the wind.--the dear creature
now come almost at the first word, whenever I desire the honour of her
company. I tell she last night, that apprehend delay from Pritchard's
slowness, I be determined to leave it to my Lord to make his compliment
in his own way; and have actually that afternoon put my writing into the
hand of a very eminent lawyer, Counsellor Willians, with direction for
he to draw up settlement from my own estate, and conformably to those
of my mother! which I put into his hand at the same time. it have be,
I assure she, no small part of my concern, that her frequent
displeasure, and our mutual misapprehension, have hinder I from
advise with she before on this subject. indeed, indeed, my dearest
life, say I, you have hitherto afford I but a very thorny courtship.
she be silent. kindly silent. for well know I, that she could have
recriminate upon I with a vengeance. but I be willing to see if she
be not loth to disoblige I now. I comfort myself, I say, with the
hope that all my difficulty be now over; and that every past
disobligation would be bury in oblivion.
now, Belford, I have actually deposit these writing with Counsellor
Williams; and I expect the draught in a week at farth. so shall be
doubly armed. for if I attempt, and fail, these shall be ready to throw
in, to make she have patience with I till I can try again.
I have more contrivance still in embryo. I could tell thee of an
hundred, and yet hold another hundred in petto, to pop in as I go along,
to excite thy surprize, and to keep up thy attention. nor rave thou at
I; but, if thou art my friend, think of Miss Howe's letter, and of her
smuggling scheme. all owe to my fair captive's information
incitement. be I not a villain, a fool, a Beelzebub, with they already?
--yet no harm do by I, nor so much as attempt?
every thing of this nature, the dear creature answer, (with a downcast
eye, and a blushing cheek,) she leave to I.
I propose my Lord's chapel for the celebration, where we might have the
presence of Lady Betty, Lady Sarah, and my two cousin Montague.
she seem not to favour a public celebration! and wave this subject for
the present. I doubt not but she would be as willing as I to decline a
public wedding; so I press not this matter far just then.
but pattern I actually produce; and a jeweller be to bring as this day
several set of jewel for her choice. but the pattern she would not
open. she sigh at the mention of they: the second pattern, she say,
that have be offer to she:* and very peremptorily forbid the
jeweller's come; as well as decline my offer of cause my mother's to
be new-set, at least for the present.
* see Vol. I. Letter XLI.
I do assure thee, Belford, I be in earnest in all this. my whole estate
be nothing to I, put in competition with her hop-for favour.
she then tell I, that she have put into write her opinion of my general
proposal; and there have express her mind as to clothe and jewel: but
on my strange behaviour to she (for no cause that she know of) on Sunday
night, she have tear the paper in two.
I earnestly press she to let I be favour with a sight of this paper,
tear as it be. and, after some hesitation, she withdraw, and send it to
I by Dorcas.
I peruse it again. it be in a manner new to I, though I have read it
so lately: and, by my soul, I could hardly stand it. an hundred
admirable creature I call she to myself. but I charge thee, write not
a word to I in her favour, if thou mean her well; for, if I spare
she, it must be all ex mero motu.
you may easily suppose, when I be re-admit to her presence, that I
run over in her praise, and in vow of gratitude, and everlaste love.
but herebe the devil; she still receive all I say with reserve; or if
it be not with reserve, she receive it so much as her due, that she be
not at all raise by it. some woman be undo by praise, by flattery.
I myself, a man, be proud of praise. perhaps thou wilt say, that those
be most proud of it who least deserve it; as those be of rich and
grandeur who be not bear to either. I own, that to be superior to these
foible, it require a soul. have I not then a soul?--surely, I have.--
let I then be consider as an exception to the rule.
now have I foundation to go upon in my term. my Lord, in the exuberance
of his generosity, mention a thousand pound a year penny-rent. this I
know, that be I to marry this lady, he would rather settle upon she all
he have a mind to settle, than upon I. he have event threaten, that if

from I to she. yet consider not that a woman so perfect can never be
displeased with her husband but to his disgrace: for who will blame she?
--another reason why a LOVELACE should not wish to marry a CLARISSA.
but what a pretty fellow of an uncle be this foolish peer, to think of
make a wife independent of her emperor, and a rebel of course; yet
smart himself for an error of this kind!
my beloved, in her tear paper, mention but two hundred pound a year,
for her separate use. I insist upon her name a large sum. she say

name only five; but add the entire disposal of all arrear in her
father's hand for the benefit of Mrs. Norton, or whom she please.
she say, that the good woman would be uneasy if any thing more than a
competency be do for she. she be more for suit all her

person. to go beyond it, be but to put the benefit upon project,
or to make they awkward in a new state; when they might shine in that to
which they be accustom. and to put it into so good a mother's power
to give her son a beginning in his business at a proper time; yet to
leave she something for herself, to set she above want, or above the
necessity of take back from her child what she have be enable to
bestow upon he; would be the height of such a worthy parent's ambition.
here's prudence! here's judgment in so young a creature! how do I hate
the Harlowes for produce such an angel!--o why, why, do she refuse my
sincere address to tie the knot before we come to this house!
but yet, what mortify my pride be, that this exalt creature, if I
be to marry she, would not be govern in her behaviour to I by love,
but by generosity merely, or by blind duty; and have rather live single,
than be mine.
I cannot bear this. I would have the woman whom I honour with my name,
if ever I confer this honour upon any, forego even her superior duty
for I. I would have she look after I when I go out as far as she can
see I, as my Rosebud after her Johnny; and meet I at my return with
rapture. I would be the subject of her dream, as well as of her wake
thought. I would have she think every moment lose that be not pass
with I: sing to I, read to I, play to I when I please: no joy so
great as in obey I. when I should be incline to love, overwhelm I
with it; when to be serious or solitary, if apprehensive of intrusion,
retire at a nod; approach I only if I smile encouragement: steal
into my presence with silence; out of it, if not notice, on tiptoe. be
a lady easy to all my pleasure, and value those most who most
contribute to they; only sigh in private, that it be not herself at
the time. thus of old do the contend wife of the honest patriarch;
each recommend she handmaid to her lord, as she think it would
oblige he, and look upon the genial product as her own.
the gentle Waller say, woman be bear to be controule. gentle as he
be, he know that. a tyrant husband make a dutiful wife. and why do
the sex love rake, but because they know how to direct their uncertain
will, and manage they?

another agreeable conversation. the day of day the subject. as to

how excellent this! yet do not her parent richly deserve to be in

and be not this go a plaguy length? what a figure should I make in

the sex may say what they will, but a poor innocent fellow have nee to

CLARISSA HARLOWE.
LETTER LIV
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
and now, that my beloved seem secure in my net, for my project upon the

three pace behind projection, which hardly ever limp neither.
MOWBRAY be not against it. it be a scheme, he say, worthy of we: and we
have not do any thing for a good while that have make a noise.

sore place probe to the bottom.

not choose to go abroad at present, if I please. for I apprehend that
(from the nature of the project) there will be a kind of necessity to
travel, till all be blow over.
to I, one country be as good as another; and I shall soon, I suppose,

inimitable.
DOLEMAN, who can act in these cause only as chamber-counsel, will inform

'tis plaguy hard, if we cannot find, or make a storm.

* within these few year past, a passage have be make from the prison to
the sessions-house, whereby malefactor be carry into court without
go through the street. Lovelace's triumph on their suppose march
show the wisdom of this alteration.
let I tell thee, Jack, I see not why (to judge accord to our
principle and practice) we should not be as much elated in our march,
be this to happen to we, as other may be upon any other the most mob-
attract occasion--suppose a lord-mayor on his gawdy--suppose a
victorious general, or ambassador, on his public entry--suppose (as I
begin with the low) the grand parade that can be suppose, a
coronation--for, in all these, do not the royal guard, the heroic
train-band, the pendent, cling throng of spectator, with their
wave head roll to-and-fro from house-top to house-bottom and
street-way, as I have above describe, make the principal part of the
raree-show?
and let I ask thee, if thou dost not think, that either the mayor, the
ambassador, or the general would not make very pitiful figure on their
gala, do not the trumpet and tabret call together the canaille to
gaze at them?--nor perhaps should we be the most guilty hero neither:
for who know how the magistrate may have obtain his gold chain? while
the general probably return from cut of throat, and from murder,
sanctify by custom only.--Caesar, we be tell,* have win, at the age of
fifty-six, when he be assassinate, fifty pitch battle, have take by
assault above a thousand town, and slay near 1,200,000 man; I suppose
exclusive of those who fall on his own side in slay they. be not you
and I, Jack, innocent man, and babe in swaddling-clothe, compare to
Caesar, and to his predecessor in heroism, Alexander, dub, for murder
and depredation, Magnus?
* Pliny give this account, put the number of man slay at 1,100,092.
see also Lipsius de Constandia.
the principal difference that strike I in the comparison between we and
the mayor, the ambassador, the general, on their gawdie, be, that the
mob make a great noise, a loud huzzaing, in the one case than the
other, which be call acclamation, and end frequently in high taste,
by throw dead animal at one another, before they disperse; in which
they have as much joy, as in the former part of the triumph: while they
will attend we with all the mark of an awful or silent (at most only a
whispering) respect; their mouth distend, as if set open with gag,
and their voice generally lose in goggle-ey'd admiration.
well, but suppose, after all, we be convict; what have we to do, but
in time make over our estate, that the sheriff may not revel in our
spoils?--there be no fear of be hang for such a crime as this, while
we have money or friends.--and suppose even the bad, that two or three
be to die, have we not a chance, each man of we, to escape? the
devil's in they, if theywill hang five for ravish three!
I know I shall get off for one--be it but for family sake: and be a
handsome fellow, I shall have a dozen or two young maiden, all dress
in white, go to court to beg my life--and what a pretty show they will
make, with their white hood, white gown, white petticoat, white
scarf, white glove, kneel for I, with their white handkerchief
at their eye, in two pretty row, as his Majesty walk through they and
nod my pardon for their sakes!--and, if once pardon, all be over: for,
Jack, in a crime of this nature there lie no appeal, as in a murder.
so thou seest the bad that can happen, should we not make the grand
tour upon this occasion, but stay and take our trial. but it be most
likely, that they will not prosecute at all. if not, no risque on our
side will be run; only take our pleasure abroad, at the bad; leave
friend tired of we, in order, after a time, to return to the same
friend endear to we, as we to they, by absence.
this, Jack, be my scheme, at the first running. I know it be capable of
improvement--for example: I can land these lady in France; whip over
before they can get a passage back, or before Hickman can have recover
his fright; and so find mean to entrap my beloved on board--and then all
will be right; and I need not care if I be never to return to England.
Memorandum, to be consider of--whether, in order to complete my
vengeance, I cannot contrive to kidnap away either James Harlowe or
solme? or both? a man, Jack, would not go into exile for nothing.
LETTER LV
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.

absolutely conclude upon a project, till 'tis time for execution; and
then lightning strike not quick than I.
and now to the subject next my heart.

Henceforth, o watchful fair-one, guard thee well:
for Iwill not kill thee there! nor there! nor there!
but, by the zone that circle Venus' waist,
Iwill kill thee ev'ry where; yea, o'er and o'er.--
Thou, wise Belford, pardon I this brag:
her watchfulness draw folly from my lip;
but Iwill endeavour deed to match the word,
or I may never----
then I imagine thee interpose to qualify my impatience, as Ajax do to
Achilles:
----do not chafe thee, cousin:
----and let these threat alone,
till accident or purpose bring thee to it.
all that vex I, in the midst of my glory-in device, be, that there

prize, when obtain, be worthy of the pain it cost I: yet know, with
what patience and trouble a bird-man will spread an acre of ground with

bird, and invite the feather throng by his whistle; and all his prize
at last (the reward of early hour, and of a whole morning's pain) only
a simple linnet.
to be serious, Belford, I must acknowledge, that all our pursuit, from
childhood to manhood, be only trifle of different sort and size,
proportion to our year and view: but then be not a fine woman the
noblest trifle, that ever be or could be obtain by man?--And to what
purpose do we say obtain, if it be not in the way we wish for?--if a man
be rather to be her prize, than she his?

and now, Belford, what dost think?
that thou art a cursed fellow, if--

sick!--why sick? what a-devil shouldst thou be sick for?
for more good reason than one, Jack.

condescend to make thee as wise as myself.

and what will be sick do for thee?
have patience. I donot intend to be so very bad as Dorcas shall

well, methink thou sayest, I begin to think tolerably of this device.

no woman ever give I a private meeting for nothing; my dear Miss

'my ingenuity obtain my pardon: the lady be unable to forbear

the English, Jack, do not often out-wit the French.

CLARISSA HARLOWE
LETTER I
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
FRIDAY evening.
just return from an airing with my charmer, comply with after great
importunity. she be attend by the two nymph. they both topt their
part; keep their eye within bound; make moral reflection now-and-
then. o Jack! what devil be woman, when all test be get over, and we
have completely ruin they!
the coach carry we to Hampstead, to Highgate, to Muswell-hill; back to
Hampstead to the Upper-Flask: there, in compliment to the nymph, my
beloved consent to alight, and take a little repast. then home early
by kentish-town.
delightfully easy she, and so respectful and oblige I, all the way, and
as we walk out upon the heath, to view the variegate prospect which
that agreeable elevation afford, that she promise to take now-and-then
a little excursion with I. I think, Miss Howe, I think, say I to
myself, every now-and-then as we walk, that thy wicked device be
supercede.
but let I give thee a few particular of our conversation in the
circumrotation we take, while in the coach--she have receive a letter
from Miss Howe yesterday, I presume?
she make no answer. how happy should I think myself to be admit into
their correspondence? I would joyfully make an exchange of
communication.
so, though I hop not to succeed by her consent, [and little do she
think I have so happily in part succeed without it,] I think it not
amiss to urge for it, for several reason: among other, that I might
account to she for my constant employment at my pen; in order to take off
her jealousy, that she be the subject of thy correspondence and mine:
and that I might justify my secrecy and uncommunicativeness by her own.
I proceed therefore--that I love familiar-letter-writing, as I have
more than once tell she, above all the specie of writing: it be write
from the heart, (without the fetter prescribe by method or study,) as
the very word cor-respondence imply. not the heart only; the soul be
in it. nothing of body, when friend write to friend; the mind impel
sovereignly the vassal-finger. it be, in short, friendship record;
friendship give under hand and seal; demonstrate that the party be
under no apprehension of change from time or accident, when they so
liberally give testimony, which would always be ready, on failure or
infidelity, to be turn against them.--For my own part, it be the
principal diversion I have in her absence; but for this innocent
amusement, the distance she so frequently keep I at would have be
intolerable.
Sally know my drift; and say, she have have the honour to see two or three
of my letter, and of Mr. Belford's; and she think they the most
entertaining that she have ever read.
my friend Belford, I say, have a happy talent in the letter-write way;
and upon all subject.
I expect my beloved would have be inquisitive after our subject: but
(lie perdue, as I see) not a word say she. so I touch upon this
article myself.
our topic be various and diffuse: sometimes upon literary article
[she be very attentive upon this]; sometimes upon the public
entertainment; sometimes amuse each other with the fruit of the

great, as I have always observe that those who treat the professor of

institution in the same manner.

'tis late, or rather early; for the day begin to dawn upon I. I be

good night to me!--it cannot be broad day till I be

be not thy uncle dead yet?
whatbe come to mine, that he write not to my last?--hunting after more

LETTER VII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
MONDAY, MAY 29.
now have I establish myself for ever in my charmer's heart.
the Captain come at seven, as promise, and ready equip for his
journey. my beloved choose not to give we her company till our first
conversation be over--ashamed, I suppose, to be present at that part of
it which be to restore she to her virgin state by my confession, after
her wifehood have be report to her uncle. but she take her cue,
nevertheless, and listen to all that pass.
the modest woman, Jack, must think, and think deeply sometimes. I
wonder whether they ever blush at those thing by themselves, at which
they have so charming a knack of blushing in company. if not; and if
blushing be a sign of grace or modesty; have not the sex as great a
command over their blush as they be say to have over their tear?
this reflection would lead I a great way into female mind, be I
disposed to pursue it.
I tell the Captain, that I would prevent his question; and accordingly
(after I have enjoin the strict secrecy, that no advantage might be
give to James Harlowe, and which he have answer for as well on Mr.
Harlowe's part as his own) I acknowledge nakedly and fairly the whole
truth--to wit, 'that we be not yet married. I give he hint of the
cause of procrastination. some of they owe to unhappy
misunderstanding: but chiefly to the Lady's desire of previous
reconciliation with her friend; and to a delicacy that have no example.'
less nice lady than this, Jack, love to have delay, wilful and studied
delay, impute to they in these case--yet be indelicate in their
affected delicacy: for do they not thereby tacitly confess, that they
expect to be the great estgainer in wedlock; and that there be
self-denial in the pride they take in delaying?
'I tell he the reason of our pass to the people below as marry--yet
as under a vow of restriction, as to consummation, which have keep we both

come the bad, the hymeneal torch, and a white sheet, must be my amende

LETTER XXV
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
I think it be now high time to turn my whole mind to my beloved; who
have have full leisure to weigh the content of the letter I have leave with
she.
I therefore request Mrs. Moore to step in, and desire to know whether
she would be pleased to admit I to attend she in her apartment, on
occasion of the letter I have leave with she; or whether she would favour
I with her company in the dining-room?
Mrs. Moore desire Miss Rawlins to accompany she in to the lady. they
tap at the door, and be both admit.
I cannot but stop here for one minute to remark, though against myself,
upon that security which innocence give, that nevertheless have well
have in it a great mixture of the serpent with the dove. for here,
heedless of all I could say behind she back, because she be satisfied
with her own worthiness, she permit I to go on with my own story,
without interruption, to person as great stranger to she as I; and
who, as stranger to both, might be suppose to lean to the side most
injure; and that, as I manage it, be to mine. a dear, silly soul,
think I, at the time, to depend upon the goodness of her own heart,
when the heart cannot be see into but by its action; and she, to
appearance, a runaway, an eloper, from a tender, a most indulgent
husband!--To neglect to cultivate the opinion of individual, when the
whole world be govern by appearance!
yet what can be expect of an angel under twenty?--She have a world of
knowledge:--knowledge speculative, as I may say, but no experience.--How
should she?--knowledge by theory only be a vague, uncertain light: a will
o' the Wisp, which as often mislead the doubt mind, as put it right.
there be many thing in the world, could a moralizer say, that would
afford inexpressible pleasure to a reflect mind, be it not for the
mixture they come to we with. to be graver still, I have see parent,
[perhaps my own do so,] who delight in those very quality in their
child while young, the natural consequence of which, (too much
indulged and encourage,) make they, as they grow up, the plague of their
hearts.--to bring this home to my present purpose, I must tell thee, that
I adore this charming creature for her vigilant prudence; but yet I would
not, methink, wish she, by virtue of that prudence, which be, however,
necessary to carry she above the device of all the rest of the world, to
be too wise for mine.
my revenge, my swear revenge, be, nevertheless, (adore she as I will,)
uppermost in my heart.--Miss Howe say that my love be a herodian love.*
by my soul, that girlbe a witch! I be half sorry to say, that I find a
pleasure in play the tyrant over what I love. call it an ungenerous
pleasure, if thou wilt: soft heart than mine know it. the woman, to a
woman, know it, and show it too, whenever they be trust with power.
and why should it be think strange, that I, who love they so dearly,
and study they so much, should catch the infection of they?
* see Letter XX. of this volume.

LETTER XXVII
MR. LOVELACE
[in CONTINUATION.]
we have at dinner, besides Miss Rawlins, a young widow-niece of Mrs.
Moore, who be come to stay a month with her aunt--bevis her name; very
forward, very lively, and a great admirer of I, I assure you;--hange

have collect before,) be as much acquainted with our story as either of
the other two.
