from Miss Howe, I improve upon the hint I have throw out above-stair
against that mischief-make lady. I represent she to be an arrogant
creature, revengeful, artful, enterprising, and one who, have she be a
man, would have swear and curse, and commit rape, and play the
devil, as far as I know: [I have no doubt of it, Jack!] but who, by
advantage of a female education, and pride and insolence, I believe be
personally virtuous.
Mrs. Bevis allow, that there be a vast deal in education--and in
pride too, she say. while Miss Rawlins come with a prudish God forbid
that virtue should be owe to education only! however, I declare that
Miss Howe be a subtle contriver of mischief; one who have always be my
enemy: her motif I know not: but despise the man whom her mother be
desirous she should have, one Hickman; although I do not directly aver
that she would rather have have I; yet they all immediately imagine that
that be the ground of her animosity to I, and of her envy to my
beloved: and it be pity, they say, that so fine a young lady do not
see through such a pretended friend.
and yet nobody [add I] have more reason than she to know by experience
the force of a hatred found in envy; as I hint to you above, Mrs.
Moore, and to you, Miss Rawlins, in the case of her sister Arabella.
I have compliment make to my person and talent on this occasion: which
give I a singular opportunity of display my modesty, by disclaim
the merit of they, with a no, indeed!--i should be very vain, lady, if
I think so. while thus abuse myself, and exalt Miss Howe, I get
their opinion both for modesty and generosity; and have all the grace

SAT NIGHT, JUNE 10.
what will be the issue of all my plot and contrivance, devil take I if
I be able to divine. but I will not, as Lord M. would say, forestall my
own market.
at four, the appoint hour, I send up, to desire admittance in the
Captain's name and my own.
she would wait upon the Captain presently; [not upon I!] and in the
parlour, if it be not engage.
the dining-room be mine, perhaps that be the reason of her name the
parlour--mighty nice again, if so! no good sign for I, think I, this
stiff punctilio.
in the parlour, with I and the Captain, be Mrs. Moore, Miss Rawlins,
and Mrs. Bevis.
the woman say, they would withdraw when the lady come down.
Lovel. not, except she choose you should, Ladies.--People who be so
much above-board as I be, need not make secret of any of their affair.
besides, you three lady be now acquaint with all our concern.
Capt. I have some thing to say to your lady, that perhaps she would
not herself choose that any body should hear; not even you, Mr. Lovelace,
as you and her family be not upon such a good foot of understanding as
be to be wish.
Lovel. well, well, Captain, I must submit. give we a sign to withdraw,
and we will withdraw.
it be well that the exclusion of the woman should come from he, than
from I.
Capt. I will bow, and wave my hand, thus--when I wish to be alone with
the lady. her uncle dot upon she. I hope, Mr. Lovelace, you will not
make a reconciliation more difficult, for the earnestness which my dear
friend show to bring it to bear. but indeed I must tell you, as I tell
you more than once before, that I be afraid you have make light of the
occasion of this misunderstanding to I, than it ought to have be make.
Lovel. I hope, Captain Tomlinson, you do not question my veracity!
Capt. I beg your pardon, Mr. Lovelace--but those thing which we man
may think lightly of, may not be light to a woman of delicacy.--And then,
if you have bind yourself by a vow, you ought--
Miss Rawlins bridle, her lip close, (but her mouth stretch to a
smile of approbation, the long for not button,) tacitly show
herself pleased with the Captain for his delicacy.
Mrs. Moore could speak--very true, however, be all she say, with a
motion of her head that express the bow-approbatory.
for my part, say the jolly widow, star with eye as big as egg, I
know what I know.--But man and wife be man and wife; or they be not
man and wife.--i have no notion of stand upon such nicety.
but here she come! cry one, hear her chamber-door open--here she
come! another, hear it shut after she--and down dropt the angel among
we.
we all stand up, bow and courtesying, and could not help it; for she
enter with such an air as command all our reverence. yet the Captain
look plaguy grave.
Cl. pray keep your seat, lady--pray do not go, [for they make offer
to withdraw; yet Miss Rawlins would have burst have she be suffer to
retire.] before this time you have all hear my story, I make no doubt--
pray keep your seat--at least all Mr. Lovelace's.
a very saucy and whimsical beginning, think I.
Captain Tomlinson, your servant, address herself to he with
inimitable dignity. I hope you do not take amiss my decline your
visit yesterday. I be really incapable of talk upon any subject that
require attention.
Capt. I be glad to see you well now, Madam. I hope I do.

attend you some hour ago, but in hope I should have be well. I
beg your pardon, Sir, for the trouble I have give you; and shall the
rather expect it, as this day will, I hope, conclude it all.
thus set; thus determine; think i,--yet to have sleep upon it!--but,
as what she say be capable of a good, as well as a bad, construction, I
would not put an unfavourable one upon it.
Lovel. the Captain be sorry, my dear, he do not offer his attendance

Cl. perhaps I think that my uncle's friend might have wish to see
I as soon as he come, [how we stared!]--but, Sir, [to I,] it might be
convenient to you to detain he.
the devil, think I!--So there really be resentment as well as head-

honest gentleman.
Capt. you would detain I, Mr. Lovelace--I be for pay my respect

I frown--I bit my lip--I look at the woman--and shake my head.
Capt. I have nothing to offer, but what Mr. Lovelace be a party to, and

Cl. pray, lady, keep your seats.--thing be alter, Sir, since I

Capt. you surprise I, Madam! I be sorry to hear this!--sorry for your
uncle's sake!--Sorry for your sake!--sorry for Mr. Lovelace's sake!--And

Lovel. indeed, captain,--indeed, lady, I have tell you great part of

that consideration will comfort I for all.
Capt. God forbid that I should offer to plead in behalf of a crime,

Cl. do not blame I, Captain Tomlinson. I have a good opinion of you,

Capt. one word with you, Madam, if you please--offer to retire.

against I, I will reveal they.
Capt. Noble Lady! who can say as you say?
the woman hold up their hand and eye; each, as if she have said,--not I.

finely say, to be sure, say the widow Bevis, shrug her shoulder.

and then she burst into tear, which even affect that dog, who, bring

the woman, so used to cry without grief, as they be to laugh without
reason, by mere force of example, [confound their promptitude;] must
need pull out their handkerchief. the less wonder, however, as I
myself, between confusion, surprise, and concern, could hardly stand it.
whatbe a tender heart good for?--who can be happy that have a feeling

Capt. let I beg the favour of one word with you, Madam, in private;

the woman hereupon offer to retire. she insist that, if they go,

Capt. Sir, bow to I, shall I beg--
I hope, think I, that I may trust this solemn dog, instruct as he be.

Volume VI.
content of volume VI
LETTER I. II. Lovelace to belford.--
his conditional promise to Tomlinson in the lady's favour. his plea
and argument on their present situation, and on his darling and
hitherto-baffle view. his whimsical contest with his conscience. his
late adieu to it. his strange levity, which he call gravity, on the
death of Belford's uncle.
LETTER III. IV. from the same.--
she favour he with a meeting in the garden. her composure. her
conversation great and noble. but will not determine any thing in his
favour. it be however evident, he say, that she have still some
tenderness for he. his reason. an affect scene between they. her

LETTER viii. from the same.--
another conversation with the lady. his plausible argument to re-obtain

Copy of the license; with his observation upon it. his scheme for

CLARISSA HARLOWE
LETTER I
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
SAT. MIDNIGHT.
no rest, say a text that I once hear preach upon, to the wicked--and
I cannot close my eye (yet only want to compound for half an hour in
an elbow-chair)--so must scribble on.
I part with the Captain after another strong debate with he in
relation to what be to be the fate of this lady. as the fellow have an
excellent head, and would have make an eminent figure in any station of
life, have not his early day be taint with a deep crime, and he
detect in it; and as he have the right side of the argument; I have a
good deal of difficulty with he; and at last bring myself to promise,
that if I could prevail upon she generously to forgive I, and to
reinstate I in her favour, I would make it my whole endeavour to get off
of my contrivance, as happily as I could; (only that Lady Betty and
Charlotte must come;) and then substitute he for her uncle's proxy,
take shame to myself, and marry.
but if I should, Jack, (with the strong antipathy to the state that
ever man have,) what a figure shall I make in rakish annal? and can I
have take all this pain for nothing? or for a wife only, that, however
excellent, [and any woman, do I think I could make good, because I could
make any woman fear as well as love I,] might have be obtain without
the plague I have be at, and much more reputably than with it? and
hast thou not see, that this haughty woman [forgive I that I call she
haughty! and a woman! yet be she not haughty?] know not how to forgive
with graciousness? indeed have not at all forgive I? but hold my soul
in a suspense which have be so grievous to her own.
at this silent moment, I think, that if I be to pursue my former
scheme, and resolve to try whether I cannot make a great fault serve as
a sponge to wipe out the less; and then be forgive for that; I can
justify myself to myself; and that, as the fair invincible would say, be
all in all.
as it be my intention, in all my reflection, to avoid repeat, at
least dwell upon, what I have before write to thee, though the state
of the case may not have vary; so I would have thee to re-consider the
old reasoning (particularly those contain in my answer to thy last*
expostulatory nonsense); and add the new as they fall from my pen; and
then I shall think myself invincible;--at least, as argue rake to rake.
* see Vol. V. Letter XIV.
I take the gaining of this lady to be essential to my happiness: and be
it not natural for all man to aim at obtain whatever they think will
make they happy, be the object more or less considerable in the eye of
other?
as to the manner of endeavour to obtain she, by falsification of
oath, vow, and the like--do not the poet of two thousand year and
upwards tell we, that Jupiter laugh at the perjury of lover? and let
I add, to what I have heretofore mention on that head, a question or
two.
do not the mother, the aunt, the grandmother, the governess of the
pretty innocent, always, from their very cradle to riper year, preach
to they the deceitfulness of men?--That they be not to regard their
oath, vow, promises?--what a parcel of fibber would all these reverend
matron be, if there be not now and then a pretty credulous rogue take
in for a justification of their preachment, and to serve as a beacon
light up for the benefit of the rest?
do we not then see, that an honest prowl fellow be a necessary evil on
many account? do we not see that it be highly requisite that a sweet
girl should be now-and-then draw aside by him?--And the more eminent the
girl, in the grace of person, mind, and fortune, be not the example
likely to be the more efficacious?
if these postulata be grant I, who, I pray, can equal my charmer in
all these? who therefore so fit for an example to the rest of her sex?
--at bad, I be entirely within my worthy friend Mandeville's assertion,
that private vice be public benefit.
well, then, if this sweet creature must fall, as it be call, for the
benefit of all the pretty fool of the sex, she must; and therebe an end
of the matter. and what would there have be in it of uncommon or rare,
have I not be so long about it?--And so I dismiss all further
argumentation and debate upon the question: and I impose upon thee, when
thou writ to I, an eternal silence on this head.
Wafer'd on, as an after-write introduction to the paragraph which
follow, mark with turn comma, [thus, ']:
Lord, Jack, what shall I do now! how one evil bring on another!
dreadful news to tell thee! while I be meditate a simple robbery,
here have I (in my own defence indeed) be guilty of murder!--a bl--y
murder! so I believe it will prove. at her last gasp!--poor impertinent
opposer!--eternally resisting!--eternally contradict! there she lie
welter in her blood! her death's wound have I give her!--but she be
a thief, an impostor, as well as a tormentor. she have steal my pen.
while I be sullenly meditate, doubt, as to my future measure, she
steal it; and thus she write with it in a hand exactly like my own; and
would have face I down, that it be really my own hand-writing.
'but let I reflect before it be too late. on the manifold perfection
of this ever-amiable creature let I reflect. the hand yet be only hold
up. the blow be not strike. Miss Howe's next letter may blow thee up.
in policy thou shouldest be now at least honest. thou canst not live
without she. thou would rather marry she than lose she absolutely.
Thou mayest undoubtedly prevail upon she, inflexible as she seem to be,
for marriage. but if now she find thee a villain, thou may never
more engage her attention, and she perhaps will refuse and abhor thee.
'yet already have I not go too far? like a repentant thief, afraid of
his gang, and oblige to go on, in fear of hang till he come to be
hang, I be afraid of the gang of my cursed contrivance.
'as I hope to live, I be sorry, (at the present writing,) that I have
be such a foolish plotter, as to put it, as I fear I have do, out of
my own power to be honest. I hate compulsion in all form; and cannot
bear, even to be compel to be the wretch my choice have make I! so
now, Belford, as thou hast say, I be a machine at last, and no free
agent.
'upon my soul, Jack, it be a very foolish thing for a man of spirit to
have bring himself to such a height of iniquity, that he must proceed,
and cannot help himself, and yet to be next to certain, that this very
victory will undo he.
'why be such a woman as this throw into my way, whose very fall will
be her glory, and, perhaps, not only my shame but my destruction?
'what a happiness must that man know, who move regularly to some
laudable end, and have nothing to reproach himself with in his progress
to do it! when, by honest mean, he attain his end, how great and
unmixe must be his enjoyment! what a happy man, in this particular
case, have I be, have it be give I to be only what I wish to appear
to be!'
thus far have my conscience write with my pen; and see what a recreant
she have make of me!--I seize she by the throat--There!--There, say I,
thou vile impertinent!--take that, and that!--How often have I give thee
warning!--and now, I hope, thou intrude varletess, have I do thy
business!
Puling and low-voice, rear up thy detest head, in vain implor
thou my mercy, who, in thy day hast show I so little!--take that, for
a rise blow!--and now will thy pain, and my pain for thee, soon be
over. lie there!--Welter on!--had I not give thee thy death's wound,
thou would have rob I of all my joy. Thou could not have
mend I, 'tis plain. Thou could only have throw I into despair.
didst thou not see, that I have go too far to recede?--welter on, once
more I bid thee!--gasp on!--that thy last gasp, surely!--how hard di
thou!
ADIEU!--Unhappy man! ADIEU!
'tis kind in thee, however, to bid I, Adieu!
Adieu, Adieu, Adieu, to thee, o thou inflexible, and, till now,
unconquerable bosom intruder!--adieu to thee for ever!
LETTER II
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
SUNDAY MORN. (JUNE 11). four O'CLOCK.
a few word to the verbal information thou sentest I last night
concern thy poor old man; and then I rise from my seat, shake myself,
refresh, new-dress, and so to my charmer, whom, notwithstanding her
reserve, I hope to prevail upon to walk out with I on the Heath this
warm and fine morning.
the bird must have awaken she before now. they be in full song. she
always glory in accustom herself to behold the sun rise--one of
God's natural wonder, as once she call it.
her window salute the east. the valley must be gild by his ray, by
the time I be with she; for already have they make the up-land smile, and
the face of nature cheerful.
how unsuitable will thou find this gay preface to a subject so gloomy as
that I be now turn to!
I be glad to hear thy tedious expectation be at last answer.
Thy servant tell I that thou be plaguily grieve at the old fellow's
departure.
I cannot say, but thou mayest look as if thou wert; harass as thou hast
be for a number of day and night with a close attendance upon a die
man, behold his drawing-on hour--pretend, for decency's sake, to
whine over his excruciating pang; to be in the way to answer a thousand
impertinent inquiry after the health of a man thou wished to die--to
pray by he--for so once thou wrotest to me!--To read by he--to be
force to join in consultation with a crew of solemn and parading
doctor, and their officious zany, the apothecary, join with the
butcherly tribe of scarficator; all combine to carry on the physical
farce, and to cut out thong both from his flesh and his estate--to have
the superadded apprehension of divide thy interest in what he shall
leave with a crew of eager-hoping, never-to-be-satisfied relation,
legatee, and the devil know who, of private gratifier of passion
laudable and illaudable--in these circumstance, I wonder not that thou
look before servant, (as little grieve as thou after heirship,) as
if thou indeed wert grieve; and as if the most wry-fac'd woe have
befall thee.
then, as I have often think, the reflection that must naturally arise
from such mortifying object, as the death of one with whom we have be
familiar, must afford, when we be oblige to attend it in its slow
approach, and in its face-twist pang, that it will one day be our
own case, go a great way to credit the appearance of grief.
and that it be this, seriously reflect upon, may temporally give a fine
air of sincerity to the wailing of lively widow, heart-exult heir,
and residuary legatee of all denomination; since, by keep down the
inward joy, those interesting reflection must sadden the aspect, and add
an appearance of real concern to the assumed sable.
well, but, now thou art come to the reward of all thy watching,
anxiety, and close attendance, tell I what it be; tell I if it
compensate thy trouble, and answer thy hope?
as to myself, thou seest, by the gravity of my style, how the subject have
help to mortify I. but the necessity I be under of commit either
speedy matrimony, or a rape, have sadden over my gayer prospect, and,
more than the case itself, contribute to make I sympathize with the
present joyful-sorrow.
Adieu, Jack, I must be soon out of my pain; and my Clarissa shall be soon
out of her'--for so do the arduousness of the case require.
LETTER III
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
SUNDAY MORNING.
I have have the honour of my charmer's company for two complete hour. we
meet before six in Mrs. Moore's garden. a walk on the heath refuse I.
the sedateness of her aspect and her kind compliance in this meeting give
I hop. and all that either the Captain and I have urge yesterday to
obtain a full and free pardon, that re-urge I; and I tell she, besides,
that Captain Tomlinson be go down with hope to prevail upon her uncle
Harlowe to come up in person, in order to present to I the great
blessing that man ever receive.
but the utmost I could obtain be, that she would take no resolution in
my favour till she receive Miss Howe's next letter.
I will not repeat the argument I use; but I will give thee the
substance of what she say in answer to they.
she have consider of every thing, she tell I. my whole conduct be
before she. the house I carry she to must be a vile house. the people
early show what they be capable of, in the earnest attempt make to
fasten Miss Partington upon she; as she doubt not, with my approbation.
[surely, think I, she have not receive a duplicate of Miss Howe's
letter of detection!] they hear her cry. my insult be undoubtedly
premeditate. by my whole recollect behaviour to she, previous to it,
it must be so. I have the vilest of view, no question. and my treatment
of she put it out of all doubt.
Soul over all, Belford! she seem sensible of liberty that my passion
make I insensible of have take, or she could not so deeply resent.
she besought I to give over all thought of she. sometimes, she say,
she think herself cruelly treat by her near and dear relation;
at such time, a spirit of repine and even of resentment take place;
and the reconciliation, at other time so desirable, be not then so much
the favourite wish of her heart, as be the scheme she have formerly
plan--of take she good Norton for her directress and guide, and
live upon her own estate in the manner her grandfather have intend she
should live.
this scheme she doubt not that her cousin Morden, who be one of her
trustee for that estate, would enable she, (and that, as she hop,
without litigation,) to pursue. and if he can, and do, what, Sir, let
I ask you, say she, have I see in your conduct, that should make I
prefer to it an union of interest, where there be such a disunion in
mind?
so thou seest, Jack, there be reason, as well as resentment, in the
preference she make against me!--thou se, that she presume to think
that she can be happy without I; and that she must be unhappy with I!
I have beseech she, in the conclusion of my re-urged argument, to write
to Miss Howe before Miss Howe's answer could come, in order to lay before
she the present state of thing; and if she would pay a deference to her
judgment, to let she have an opportunity to give it, on the full knowledge
of the case--
so I would, Mr. Lovelace, be the answer, if I be in doubt myself,
which I would prefer--marriage, or the scheme I have mention. you
cannot think, Sir, but the latter must be my choice. I wish to part with
you with temper--don't put I upon repeating--
Part with I, Madam! interrupt I--I cannot bear those words!--but let
I beseech you, however, to write to Miss Howe. I hope, if Miss Howe be
not my enemy--
she be not the enemy of your person, Sir;--as you would be convince, if
you see her last letter* to I. but be she not an enemy to your
action, she would not be my friend, nor the friend of virtue. why will
you provoke from I, Mr. Lovelace, the harshness of expression, which,
however, which, however deserve by you, I be unwilling just now to use,
have suffer enough in the two past day from my own vehemence?
* the lady innocently mean Mr. Lovelace's forge one. see Vol. V.
Letter XXX.
I bite my lip for vexation. and be silent.
Miss Howe, proceed she, know the full state of matter already, Sir.
the answer I expect from her respect myself, not you. her heart be too
warm in the cause of friendship, to leave I in suspense one moment
long than be necessary as to what I want to know. nor do she answer
absolutely depend upon herself. she must see a person first, and that
person perhaps see other.
the cursed smuggler-woman, Jack!--Miss Howe's townsend, I doubt not--
plot, contrivance, intrigue, stratagem!--underground-mole these women--
but let the earth cover me!--let I be a mole too, think I, if they
carry their point!--and if this lady escape I now!
she frankly own that she have once think of embark out of all our
way for some one of our american colony. but now that she have be
compel to see I, (which have be her great dread), and which she
might be happy in the resumption of her former favourite scheme, if

Morden could come.--but if he come not soon, and if she have a difficulty
to get to a place of refuge, whether from her brother or from any body

MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.

LETTER VII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
I have begin another letter to thee, in continuation of my narrative: but

enclose thou wilt see, that neither of the correspondent deserve mercy

to MRS. HARRIOT LUCAS,

JUNE 10.
after the discovery I have make of the villanous machination of the
most abandon of man, particularize in my long letter of Wednesday*
last, you will believe, my dear friend, that my surprise upon peruse
your' of Thursday evening from Hampstead** be not so great as my
indignation. have the villain attempt to fire a city instead of a
house, I should not have wonder at it. all that I be amazed at be,
that he (whose boast, as I be tell, it be, that no woman shall keep he
out of her bed-chamber, when he have make a resolution to be in it) do
not discover his foot before. and it be as strange to I, that, have
get you at such a shocking advantage, and in such a horrid house, you
could, at the time, escape dishonour, and afterwards get from such a set
of infernal.
* see Vol. V. Letter XX.
** ibid. see Letter XXI.
I give you, in my long letter of Wednesday and Thursday last, reason why
you ought to mistrust that specious Tomlinson. that man, my dear, must
be a solemn villain. may lightne from Heaven blast the wretch, who have
set he and the rest of his REMORSELESS gang at work, to endeavour to
destroy the most consummate virtue!--heaven be praise! you have escape
from all their snare, and now be out of danger.--So I will not trouble
you at present with the particular I have far collect relate to
this abominable imposture.
for the same reason, I forbear to communicate to you some new story of
the abhor wretch himself which have come to my ear. one, in
particular, of so shocking a nature!--indeed, my dear, the manbe a devil.
the whole story of Mrs. Fretchville, and her house, I have no doubt to
pronounce, likewise, an absolute fiction.--Fellow!--How my soul spurn
the villain!
your thought of go abroad, and your reason for so do, most
sensibly affect I. but be comfort, my dear; I hope you will not be
under a necessity of quit your native country. be I sure that that
must be the cruel case, I would abandon all my well prospect, and soon
be with you. and I would accompany you whithersoever you go, and share
fortune with you: for it be impossible that I should be happy, if I know
that you be expose not only to the peril of the sea, but to the
attempt of other vile man; your personal grace attract every eye;
and expose you to those hourly danger, which other, less
distinguish by the gift of nature, might avoid.--All that I know that
beauty (so greatly coveted, and so greatly admire) be good for.
o my dear, be I ever to marry, and to be the mother of a CLARISSA,
[Clarissa must be the name, if promisingly lovely,] how often would my
heart ache for the dear creature, as she grow up, when I reflect that a
prudence and discretion, unexampled in woman, have not, in you, be a
sufficient protection to that beauty, which have draw after it as many
admirer as beholders!--how little should I regret the attack of that
cruel distemper, as it be call, which frequently make the great
ravage in the fine face!
SAT. AFTERNOON.
I have just part with Mrs. Townsend.* I think you have once see she
with I; but she say she never have the honour to be personally know to
you. she have a manlike spirit. she know the world. and her two
brother be in town, she be sure she can engage they in so good a
cause, and (if there should be occasion) both their ship' crew, in your
service.
* for the account of Mrs. Townsend, &c. see Vol. IV. Letter XLII.
give your consent, my dear; and the horrid villain shall be repay with
broken bone, at least, for all his vileness!
the misfortune be, Mrs. Townsend cannot be with you till Thursday next,
or Wednesday, at soon: be you sure you can be safe where you be till
then? I think you be too near London; and perhaps you have well be in
it. if you remove, let I, the very moment, know whither.
how my heart be tear, to think of the necessity so dear a creature be
drive to of hide herself! devilish fellow! he must have be
sportive and wanton in his invention--yet that cruel, that savage
sportiveness have save you from the sudden violence to which he have have
recourse in the violation of other, of name and family not
contemptible. for such the villain always glory to spread his snare.
the vileness of this specious monster have do more, than any other
consideration could do, to bring Mr. Hickman into credit with I. Mr.
Hickman alone know (from I) of your flight, and the reason of it. have
I not give he the reason, he might have think still bad of the vile
attempt. I communicate it to he by show he your letter from
Hampstead. when he have read it, [and he tremble and redden, as he
read,] he throw himself at my foot, and besought I to permit he to
attend you, and to give you the protection of his house. the
good-natured man have tear in his eye, and be repeatedly earnest on this
subject; propose to take his chariot-and-four, or a set, and in person,
in the face of all the world, give himself the glory of protect such
an oppressed innocent.
I could not but be pleased with he. and I let he know that I be. I
hardly expect so much spirit from he. but a man's passiveness to a
beloved object of our sex may not, perhaps, argue want of courage on
proper occasion.
I think I ought, in return, to have some consideration for his safety,
as such an open step would draw upon he the vengeance of the most
villanous enterpriser in the world, who have always a gang of fellow,
such as himself, at his call, ready to support one another in the vilest
outrage. but yet, as Mr. Hickman might have strengthen his hand by
legal recourse, I should not have stand upon it, have I not know your
delicacy, [since such a step must have make a great noise, and give
occasion for scandal, as if some advantage have be gain over you,] and
be there not the great probability that all might be more silently,
and more effectually, manage, by Mrs. Townsend's mean.
Mrs. Townsend will in person attend you--she hop, on Wednesday--her
brother, and some of their people, will scatteringly, and as if they
know nothing of you, [so we have contrive,] see you safe not only to
London, but to her house at Deptford.
she have a kinswoman, who will take your command there, if she herself
be oblige to leave you. and there you may stay, till the wretch's fury,
on lose you, and his search, be over.
he will very soon, 'tis likely, enter upon some new villany, which may
engross he: and it may be give out, that you be go to lay claim to
the protection of your cousin Morden at Florence.
possibly, if he can be make to believe it, he will go over, in hope to
find you there.
after a while, I can procure you a lodging in one of our neighbouring
village, where I may have the happiness to be your daily visiter. and
if this Hickman be not silly and apish, and if my mother do not do
unaccountable thing, I may the soon think of marrying, that I may,
without controul, receive and entertain the darling of my heart.
many, very many, happy day do I hope we shall yet see together; and as
this be my hope, I expect that it will be your consolation.
as to your estate, since you be resolve not to litigate for it, we will
be patient, either till Colonel Morden arrive, or till shame compel
some people to be just.
upon the whole, I cannot but think your prospect now much happy than
they could have be, have you be actually married to such a man as
this. I must therefore congratulate you upon your escape, not only from
a horrid libertine, but from so vile a husband, as he must have make to
any woman; but more especially to a person of your virtue and delicacy.
you hate he, heartily hate he, I hope, my dear--I be sure you do. it
would be strange, if so much purity of life and manner be not to abhor
what be so repugnant to itself.
in your letter before I, you mention one write to I for a feint.* I
have not receive any such. depend upon it, therefore, that he must have
it. and if he have, it be a wonder that he do not likewise get my long
one of the 7th. Heaven be praise that he do not; and that it come safe
to your hand!
* see Vol. V. Letters XXI. and XXII.
I send this by a young fellow, whose father be one of our tenant, with
command to deliver it to no other hand but your's. he be to return
directly, if you give he any letter. if not, he will proceed to London
upon his own pleasure. he be a simple fellow; but very honest. so you
may say anything to he. if you write not by he, I desire a line or
two, as soon as possible.
my mother know nothing of his go to you; nor yet of your abandon
the fellow. forgive I! but he be not entitle to good manner.
I shall long to hear how you and Mrs. Townsend order matter. I wish
she could have be with you soon. but I have lose no time in engage
she, as you will suppose. I refer to she, what I have far to say and
advise. so shall conclude with my prayer, that Heaven will direct and
protect my dear creature, and make your future day happy!
ANNA HOWE.
and now, Jack, I will suppose that thou hast read this cursed letter.
allow I to make a few observation upon some of its content.
it be strange to Miss Howe, that have get her friend at such a shocking
advantage, &c. and it be strange to I, too. if ever I have such
another opportunity give to I, the cause of both our wonder, I believe,
will cease.
so thou se Tomlinson be far detected.--No such person as Mrs.
fretchville.--may lightning from Heaven--o Lord, o Lord, o lord!--what a
horrid vixen be this!--my gang, my remorseless gang, too, be bring in--
and thou wilt plead for these girl again; wilt thou? heaven be praise,
she say, that her friend be out of danger--Miss Howe should be sure of
that, and that she herself be safe.--But for this termagant, (as I often
say,) I must surely have make a well hand of it.--
new story of I, jack!--what can they be?--i have not find that my
generosity to my rose-bud ever do I due credit with this pair of
friend. very hard, Belford, that credit cannot be set against debit,
and a balance strike in a rake's favour, as well as in that of every
common man!--but he, from whom no good be expect, be not allow the
merit of the good he do.
I ought to have be a little more attentive to character than I have
be. for, notwithstanding that the measure of right and wrong be say
to be so manifest, let I tell thee, that character bias and run away
with all mankind. let a man or woman once establish themselves in the
world's opinion, and all that either of they do will be sanctify. Nay,
in the very court of justice, do not character acquit or condemn as
often as fact, and sometimes even in spite of facts?--yet, [impolitic
that I have be and am!] to be so careless of mine!--and now, I doubt,
it be irretrievable.--but to leave moralize.
Thou, Jack, know almost all my enterprise worth remember. can
this particular story, which this girl hint at, be that of Lucy Villars?
--or can she have hear of my intrigue with the pretty gipsey, who meet I
in Norwood, and of the trap I catch her cruel husband in, [a fellow as
gloomy and tyrannical as old Harlowe,] when he pursue a wife, who would
not have deserve ill of he, if he have deserve well of her!--but he be
not quite drown. the man be alive at this day, and Miss Howe mention
the story as a very shocking one. besides, both these be a twelve-month
old, or more.
but evil fame and scandal be always new. when the offender have forget a
vile fact, it be often tell to one and to another, who, have never
hear of it before, trumpet it about as a novelty to other. but well
say the honest corregidor at Madrid, [a saying with which I encroach
Lord M.'s collection,]--good action be remember but for a day: bad
one for many year after the life of the guilty. such be the relish
that the world have for scandal. in other word, such be the desire which
every one have to exculpate himself by blacken his neighbour. you and
I, Belford, have be very kind to the world, in furnish it with
opportunity to gratify its devil.
[Miss Howe will abandon her own well prospect, and share fortune with
she, be she to go abroad.]--charme romancer!--i must set about this
girl, Jack. I have always have hope of a woman whose passion carry she
to such altitudes.--had I attack Miss Howe first, her passion,
(inflame and guide as I could have manage they,) would have bring
she into my lure in a fortnight.
but think thou, [and yet I think thou dost,] that there be any thing
in these high flight among the sex?--verily, Jack, these vehement
friendship be nothing but chaff and stubble, liable to be blow away by
the very wind that raise they. ape, mere ape of we! they think the
word friendship have a pretty sound with it; and it be much talk of--a
fashionable word. and so, truly, a single woman, who think she have a
soul, and know that she want something, would be think to have find
a fellow-soul for it in her own sex. but I repeat, that the word be a
mere word, the thing a mere name with they; a cork-bottom shuttle-cock,
which they be fond of strike to and fro, to make one another glow in
the frosty weather of a single-state; but which, when a man come in
between the pretend inseparable, be give up, like their music and
other maidenly amusement; which, nevertheless, may be necessary to keep
the pretty rogue out of active mischief. they then, in short, have
catch the fish, lie aside the net.*
* he allude here to the story of a pope, who, (once a poor fisherman,)
through every preferment he rise to, even to that of the cardinalate,
hang up in view of all his guest his net, as a token of humility. but,
when he arrive at the pontificate, he take it down, say, that there
be no need of the net, when he have catch the fish.
Thou hast a mind, perhaps, to make an exception for these two ladies.--
with all my heart. my Clarissa have, if woman have, a soul capable of
friendship. her flame be bright and steady. but Miss Howe's, be it
not keep up by her mother's opposition, be too vehement to endure. how
often have I know opposition not only cement friendship, but create
love? I doubt not but poor Hickman would fare the well with this
vixen, if her mother be as heartily against he, as she be for he.
thus much, indeed, as to these two lady, I will grant thee, that the
active spirit of the one, and the meek disposition of the other, may make
their friendship more durable than it would otherwise be; for this be
certain, that in every friendship, whether male or female, there must be
a man and a woman spirit, (that be to say, one of they must be a
forbear one,) to make it permanent.
but this I pronounce, as a truth, which all experience confirm, that
friendship between woman never hold to the sacrifice of capital
gratification, or to the endangering of life, limb, or estate, as it
often do in our nobler sex.
well, but next come an indictment against poor beauty! what have beauty
do that Miss Howe should be offend at it?--Miss Howe, Jack, be a
charming girl. she have no reason to quarrel with beauty!--didst ever see
her?--Too much fire and spirit in her eye, indeed, for a girl!--But
thatbe no fault with a man that can lower that fire and spirit at
pleasure; and I know I be the man that can.
for my own part, when I be first introduce to this lady, which be by
my goddess when she herself be a visiter at Mrs. Howe's, I have not be
half an hour with she, but I even hunger and thirst after a romping
'bout with the lively rogue; and, in the second or third visit, be more
deter by the delicacy of her friend, than by what I apprehend from
her own. this charming creature's presence, think I, awe we both.
and I wish her absence, though any other woman be present, that I
might try the difference in Miss Howe's behaviour before her friend's
face, or behind her back.
delicate woman make delicate woman, as well as decent man. with all Miss
Howe's fire and spirit, it be easy to see, by her very eye, that she
watch for lesson and fear reproof from the penetrate eye of her
milder dispositione friend;* and yet it be as easy to observe, in the
candour and sweet manner of the other, that the fear which Miss Howe
stand in of she, be more owing to her own generous apprehension that she
fall short of her excellency, than to Miss Harlowe's consciousness of
excellence over she. I have often since I come at Miss Howe's letter,
revolve this just and fine praise contain in one of they:** 'every one
see that the preference they give you to themselves exalt you not into
any visible triumph over they; for you have always something to say, on
every point you carry, that raise the yield heart, and leave every
one pleased and satisfied with themselves, though they carry not off
the palm.'
* Miss Howe, in Vol. III. Letter XIX. say, that she be always more
afraid of Clarissa than of her mother; and, in Vol. III. Letter XLIV.
that she fear she almost as much as she love she; and in many other
place, in her letter, verify this observation of Lovelace.
** see Vol. IV. letter XXXI.
as I propose, in a more advanced life, to endeavour to atone for my
useful freedom with individual of the sex, by give caution and
instruction to the whole, I have make a memorandum to enlarge upon this
doctrine;--to wit, that it be full as necessary to direct daughter in
the choice of their female companion, as it be to guard they against the
design of man.
I say not this, however, to the disparagement of Miss Howe. she have from
pride, what her friend have from principle. [the Lord help the sex, if

but it be time enough when I be old and joyless, to enlarge upon this

as to the comparison between the two lady, I will expatiate more on

I return to the consideration of a few more of its content, to justify

as to Mrs. Townsend,--her manlike spirit--her two brother--and the
ship' crew--I say nothing but this to the insolent threatening--let them

who can bear this porterly threatening!--broken bone, Jack!--D--n the

but these fellow be smuggler, it seem. and be not I a smuggler too?
--I am--and have not the least doubt but I shall have secure my good
before Thursday, or Wednesday either.
but do I want a plot, what a charming new one do this letter of Miss
Howe strike I out! I be almost sorry, that I have fix upon one.--For
here, how easy would it be for I to assemble a crew of swabber, and to
create a Mrs. Townsend (whose person, thou seest, my beloved know not)
to come on Tuesday, at Miss Howe's repeat solicitation, in order to

this, however, be my triumphant hope, that at the very time that these
ragamuffin will be at Hampstead (look for we) my dear Miss Harlowe
and I [so the Fates I imagine have ordain] shall be fast asleep in
each other's arm in town.--lie still, villain, till the time comes.--
my heart, Jack! my heart!--It be always thump away on the remotest

but it seem that the vileness of this specious monster [mean I,
Jack!] have bring Hickman into credit with she. so I have do some
good! but to whom I cannot tell: for this poor fellow, should I permit
he to have this termagant, will be punish, as many time we all be,
by the enjoyment of his own wish--nor can she be happy, as I take it,
with he, be he to govern himself by her will, and have none of his

but this honest fellow, it seem, with tear in his eye, and with humble

but dost think, Jack, that I in the like case (and equally affect with

but, 'tis good as it be. Honest Hickman may now sleep in a whole skin.

Miss Howe think I may be divert from pursue my charmer, by some

when sett thou out for the Isle of Wight, love?

LETTER VIII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
SUNDAY NIGHT--MONDAY morning.
I go down with revenge in my heart, the content of Miss Howe's letter
almost engross I, the moment that Miss Harlowe and Mrs. Moore
(accompany by Miss Rawlins) come in: but in my countenance all the
gentle, the placid, the serene, that the glass could teach; and in my
behaviour all the polite, that such an unpolite creature, as she have
often tell I I be, could put on.
Miss Rawlins be send for home almost as soon as she come in, to
entertain an unexpected visiter; to her great regret, as well as to the
disappointment of my fair-one, as I could perceive from the look of
both: for they have agree, it seem, if I go to town, as I say I
intend to do, to take a walk upon the heath, at least in Mrs. Moore's
garden; and who know, what might have be the issue, have the spirit of
curiosity in the one meet with the spirit of communication in the other?
Miss Rawlins promise to return, if possible: but send to excuse herself:
her visiter intending to stay with she all night.
I rejoice in my heart at her message; and, after much supplication,
obtain the favour of my beloved's company for another walk in the
garden, have, as I tell she, abundance of thing to say, to propose,
and to be inform of, in order ultimately to govern myself in my future
step.
she have vouchsafe, I should have tell thee, with eye turn from I,
and in a half-aside attitude, to sip two dish of tea in my company--
Dear soul!--How anger unpolishe the most polite! for I never see Miss
Harlowe behave so awkwardly. I imagine she know not how to be awkward.
when we be in the garden, I pour my whole soul into her attentive
ear; and besought she return favour.
she tell I, that she have form her scheme for her future life: that,
vile as the treatment be which she have receive from I, that be not
all the reason she have for reject my suit: but that, on the maturest
deliberation, she be convince that she could neither be happy with I,
nor make I happy; and she injoine I, for both our sake, to think no
more of she.
the Captain, I tell she, be rid down post, in a manner, to forward my
wish with her uncle.--lady Betty and Miss Montague be undoubtedly
arrive in town by this time. I would set out early in the morning to
attend they. they adore she. they long to see she. they would see
her.--they would not be deny her company in Oxfordshire. Whither could
she well go, to be free from her brother's insults?--whither, to be
absolutely make unapprehensive of any body else?--might I have any hope
of her return favour, if Miss Howe could be prevail upon to
intercede for I?
Miss Howe prevail upon to intercede for you! repeat she, with a
scornful bridle, but a very pretty one.--and there she stopt.
I repeat the concern it would be to I to be under a necessity of
mention the misunderstanding to Lady Betty and my cousin, as a
misunderstanding still to be make up; and as if I be of very little
consequence to a dear creature who be of so much to I; urge, that
these circumstance would extremely lower I not only in my own opinion,
but in that of my relation.
but still she refer to Miss Howe's next letter; and all the concession
I could bring she to in this whole conference, be, that she would wait
the arrival and visit of the two lady, if they come in a day or two, or
before she receive the expect letter from Miss Howe.
thank Heaven for this! think I. and now may I go to town with hope at
my return to find thee, dearest, where I shall leave thee.
but yet, as she may find reason to change her mind in my absence, I
shall not entirely trust to this. my fellow, therefore, who be in the
house, and who, by Mrs. Bevis's kind intelligence, will know every step
she can take, shall have Andrew and a horse ready, to give I immediate
notice of her motion; and moreover, go whither she will, he shall be one
of her retinue, though unknown to herself, if possible.
this be all I could make of the fair inexorable. should I be glad of
it, or sorry for it?--
Glad I believe: and yet my pride be confoundedly abate, to think that I
have so little hold in the affection of this daughter of the Harlowes.
donot tell I that virtue and principle be her guide on this occasion!
--'Tis pride, a great pride than my own, that govern she. love, she
have none, thou seest; nor ever have; at least not in a superior degree.
Love, that deserve the name, never be under the dominion of prudence,
or of any reasoning power. she cannot bear to be think a woman, I
warrant! and if, in the last attempt, I find she not one, what will she
be the bad for the trial?--No one be to blame for suffer an evil he
cannot shun or avoid.
be a general to be overpower, and rob by a highwayman, would he be
less fit for the command of an army on that account?--if indeed the
general, pretend great valour, and have boast that he never would
be rob, be to make but faint resistance when he be bring to the
test, and to yield his purse when he be master of his own sword, then
indeed will the highwayman who rob he be think the braver man.
but from these last conference be I furnish with one argument in
defence of my favourite purpose, which I never yet plead.
o Jack! what a difficulty must a man be allow to have to conquer a
predominant passion, be it what it will, when the gratifying of it be in
his power, however wrong he know it to be to resolve to gratify it!
reflect upon this; and then wilt thou be able to account for, if not to
excuse, a project crime, which have habit to plead for it, in a breast
as stormy as uncontroulable!
this that follow be my new argument--
should she fail in the trial; should I succeed; and should she refuse to
go on with I; and even resolve not to marry I (of which I can have no
notion); and should she disdain to be oblige to I for the handsome
provision I should be proud to make for she, even to the half of my
estate; yet cannot she be altogether unhappy--be she not entitle to an
independent fortune? will not Col. Morden, as her trustee, put she in
possession of it? and do she not in our former conference point out the
way of life, that she always prefer to the married life--to wit, 'to
take her good Norton for her directress and guide, and to live upon her

* see Letter III. of this volume.

be not this then the result of all, that Miss Clarissa Harlowe, if it be

and thus may her old nurse and she; an old coachman; and a pair of old
coach-horse; and two or three old maid-servant, and perhaps a very old
footman or two, (for every thing will be old and penitential about she,)

this have always be my notion, though Miss Howe grudge we rake the

Thou seest at bottom that I be not an abandon fellow; and that there be

LETTER XI
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.

Allbe right, as heart can wish!--in spite of all objection--in spite of a

A Lady take a great fancy to a young lion, or a bear, I forget

MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.

* see Letter IX. of this volume.
I will allow that her pride, in one sense, have suffer abasement: but

MONDAY, JUNE 19.
I then underwritten do hereby promise, that, on my come into possession
of my own estate, I will provide for Dorcas Martindale in a gentlewoman-
like manner, in my own house: or, if I do not soon obtain that

which I have show she. witness my hand this nineteenth day of June, in
the year above write.
CLARISSA HARLOWE.

LETTER XXVI
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.

contemplate the precarious situation I stand in with my beloved, I fall

dream; a fortunate dream; which, as I imagine, will afford my working

you must excuse I, Lovelace, from engage in the office you would have

at last by this much-injure lady.

not much confidence in the honour of a man, why by imitation of hand (I
will only call it) have show so little regard to the honour of his own
relation.
only that thou hast such jesuitical qualifying, or I should think thee
at last touch with remorse, and bring within view of be ashamed
of thy cursed invention by the ill success of thy last: which I heartily
congratulate thee upon.
o the divine lady!--But I will not aggravate!
nevertheless, when thou writ that, in thy present mood, thou think
of marrying, and yet canst so easily change thy mood; when I know thy
heart be against the state: that the four word thou court from the
lady be as much to thy purpose, as if she write forty; since it will
show she can forgive the high injury that can be offer to woman; and
when I recollect how easily thou canst find excuse to postpone; thou
must be more explicit a good deal, as to thy real intention, and future
honour, than thou art: for I cannot trust to temporary remorse; which
bring on by disappointment too, and not by principle, and the like of
which thou hast so often get over.
if thou canst convince I time enough for the day, that thou meanest to
do honourably by she, in her own sense of the word; or, if not time
enough, wilt fix some other day, (which thou ought to leave to her

most cheerfully undertake thy cause; by person, if she will admit I to
her presence; if she will not, by pen. but, in this case, thou must
allow I to be guarantee for thy family. and, if so, so much as I value
thee, and respect thy skill in all the qualification of a gentleman,
thou mayest depend upon it, that I will act up to the character of a
guarantee, with more honour than the prince of our day usually do----to
their shame be it speak.
mean time let I tell thee, that my heart bleed for the wrong this
angelic lady have receive: and if thou dost not marry she, if she will
have thee, and, when marry, make she the good and tender of
husband, I would rather be a dog, a monkey, a bear, a viper, or a toad,
than thee.
command I with honour, and thou shalt find none readier to oblige thee
than
Thy sincere friend,
JOHN BELFORD.

crisis now. but she must not be treat ill neither.
Thursday over, I shall know what to resolve upon.
if necessary, you must assume authority. the devil's in't, if such a
girl as this shall awe a man of your year and experience. you be not
in love with she as I be. fly out, if she doubt your honour. spirit
naturally soft may be beat out of their play and bear down (though ever
so much raise) by high anger. all woman be coward at bottom; only
violent where they may. I have often storm a girl out of her mistrust,
and make her yield (before she know where she be) to the point
indignantly mistrust; and that to make up with I, though I be the
aggressor.
if this matter succeed as Iwould have it, (or if not, and do not fail by
your fault,) I will take you off the necessity of pursue your curse
smuggling; which otherwise may one day end fatally for you.
we be none of we perfect, M'Donald. this sweet lady make I serious
sometimes in spite of my heart. but as private vice be less blamable
than public; an as I think smuggling (as it be call) a national evil;
I have no doubt to pronounce you a much bad man than myself, and as
such shall take pleasure in reform you.
I send you enclose ten guineas, as a small earnest of further favour.
Hitherto you have be a very clever fellow.
as to clothe for Thursday, Monmouth-street will afford a ready supply.
clothe quite new would make your condition suspect. but you may
defer that care, till you see if she can be prevail upon. your
riding-dress will do for the first visit. nor let your boot be over
clean. I have always tell you the consequence of attend to the
minutia, where art (or imposture, as the ill-mannered would call it) be
design--your linen rumple and soily, when you wait upon she--easy term
these--just come to town--remember (as formerly) to loll, to throw out
your leg, to stroke and grasp down your ruffle, as if of significance
enough to be careless. what though the presence of a fine lady would
require a different behaviour, be you not of year to dispense with
politeness? you can have no design upon she, you know. you be a father
yourself of daughter as old as she. Evermore be parade and
obsequiousness suspectable: it must show either a foolish head, or a
knavish heart. assume air of consequence therefore; and you will be
treat as a man of consequence. I have often more than half ruin
myself by my complaisance; and, be afraid of controul, have bring
controul upon myself.
I think I have no more to say at present. I intend to be at Slough, or
on the way to it, as by mine to the lady. adieu, honest M'Donald.
R.L.
LETTER XLV
to CAPTAIN TOMLINSON
[enclosed in the PRECEDING; to be show to the lady as in CONFIDENCE.]
M. HALL, TUESDAY MORN., JUNE 27.
DEAR CAPTAIN TOMLINSON,
an unhappy misunderstanding have arise between the dear lady in the
world and I (the particular of which she perhaps may give you, but I
will not, because I might be think partial to myself;) and she refuse
to answer my most pressing and respectful letter; I be at a most
perplexing uncertainty whether she will meet we or not next Thursday to
solemnize.
my Lord be so extremely ill, that if I think she would not oblige I,
I would defer go up to town for two or three day. he care not to
have I out of his sight: yet be impatient to salute my beloved as his
neice [sic] before he die. this I have promise to give he an
opportunity to do: intend, if the dear creature will make I happy,
to set out with she for this place directly from church.
with regret I speak it of the charmer of my soul, that irreconcilableness
be her family-fault--the less excusable indeed for she, as she herself
suffer by it in so high a degree from her own relation.
now, Sir, as you intend to be in town some time before Thursday, if
it be not too great an inconvenience to you, I could be glad you would
go up as soon as possible, for my sake: and this I the more boldly
request, as I presume that a man who have so many great affair of his
own in hand as you have, would be glad to be at a certainty as to the
day.
you, Sir, can so pathetically and justly set before she the unhappy
consequence that will follow if the day be postpone, as well with
regard to her uncle's disappointment, as to the part you have assure
I her mother be willing to take in the wish-for reconciliation, that
I have great hope she will suffer herself to be prevail upon. and a
man and horse shall be in wait to take your dispatch and bring they
to I.
but if you cannot prevail in my favour, you will be pleased to satisfy
your friend, Mr. John Harlowe, that it be not my fault that he be not
oblige. I be, dear Sir,
your extremely oblige
and faithful servant,
R. LOVELACE.

to ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
WEDN. JUNE 28, NEAR TWELVE O'CLOCK.
HONOURED SIR,
I receive your's, as your servant desire I to acquaint you, by ten

relater of the bad news; but so it be--the lady be go off! she be
miss but half an hour before I come.
her waiting-maid be run away, or hitherto be not to be find: so that
they conclude it be by her connivance.
they have send, before I come, to my honoured master Mr. Belton, Mr.
Mowbray, and Mr. Belford. Mr. Tourville be out of town.
high word be pass between Madam Sinclair, and Madam Horton, and

they have send to know if they can hear of Mabell, the waiting-maid, at

with whom she live last.
your messenger have just change his horse, be come back: so I will

Honoured Sir,

Dear Bobby, adieu. if Lord M. will die now, to comfort thee for this

RD. MOWBRAY.

these be the particular of Miss Harlowe's flight. thou'lt hardly think
I too minute.--How I long to triumph over thy impatience and fury on the
occasion!

where, Lovelace, can the poor lady be go? and who can describe the
distress she must be in?
by thy former letter, it may be suppose, that she can have very little
money: nor, by the suddenness of her flight, more clothe than those she
have on. and thou know who once say,* 'her parent will not receive
she. her uncle will not entertain she. her Norton be in their
direction, and cannot. Miss Howe dare not. she have not one friend or
intimate in town--entirely a stranger to it.' and, let I add, have be
despoiled of her honour by the man for whom she have make all these
sacrifice; and who stand bind to she by a thousand oath and vow, to
be her husband, her protector, and friend!
* see Vol. IV. Letter XXI.
how strong must be her resentment of the barbarous treatment she have
receive! how worthy of herself, that it have make she hate the man she
once love! and, rather than marry he, choose to expose her disgrace to
the whole world: to forego the reconciliation with her friend which her
heart be so set upon: and to hazard a thousand evil to which her youth
and her sex may too probably expose an indigent and friendly beauty!
Rememberest thou not that home push upon thee, in one of the paper
write in her delirium; of which, however it savour not?----
I will assure thee, that I have very often since most seriously reflect
upon it: and as thy intended second outrage convince I that it make no
impression upon thee then, and perhaps thou hast never think of it
since, I will transcribe the sentence.
'if, as religion teach we, God will judge we, in a great measure! by
our benevolent or evil action to one another--o wretch! bethink thee, in
time bethink thee, how great must be thy condemnation.'*
* see Vol. VI. Letter XVI.
and be this amiable doctrine the sum of religion? upon my faith,
believe it be. for, to indulge a serious thought, since we be not
atheist, except in practice, do God, the being of Beings, want any
thing of we for himself! and do he not enjoin we work of mercy to one
another, as the mean to obtain his mercy? a sublime principle, and
worthy of the SUPREME SUPERINTENDENT and FATHER of all things!--but if we
be to be judge by this noble principle, what, indeed, must be thy
condemnation on the score of this lady only? and what mine, and what all
our confraternity's, on the score of other woman: though we be none of
we half so bad as thou art, as well for want of inclination, I hope, as
of opportunity!
I must add, that, as well for thy own sake, as for the lady's, I wish ye
be yet to be married to each other. it be the only medium that can be
hit upon to salve the honour of both. all thatbe past may yet be

demonstration, that I be
Thy sincere friend,
J. BELFORD.

letter XLIX
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
FRIDAY, JUNE 30.
I be ruin, undo, blow up, destroy, and bad than annihilate,
thatbe certain!--but be not the news shock enough, dost thou think,
without thy throw into the too-weighty scale reproach, which thou
couldst have have no opportunity to make but for my own voluntary
communication? at a time too, when, as it fall out, I have another very
sensible disappointment to struggle with?
I imagine, if there be such a thing as future punishment, it must be none
of the small mortification, that a new devil shall be punish by a
worse old one. and, take that! and, take that! to have the old satyr
cry to the screaming sufferer, lay on with a cat-o'-nine-tail, with a
star of burn brass at the end of each: and, for what! for what!---why,
if the truth may be fairly tell, for not be so bad a devil as myself.
thou art, surely, casuist good enough to know, (what I have insist
upon* heretofore,) that the sin of seduce a credulous and easy girl, be
as great as that of bring to your lure an incredulous and watchful
one.
* see Vol. IV. letter XVII.
however ungenerous an appearance what I be go to say may have from my
pen, let I tell thee, that if such a woman as Miss Harlowe choose to
enter into the matrimonial state, [I be resolve to disappoint thee in
thy meditate triumph over my rage and despair!] and, accord to the
old patriarchal system, to go on contribute to get son and daughter,
with no other view than to bring they up piously, and to be good and
useful member of the commonwealth, what a devil have she to do, to let
her fancy run a gadding after a rake? one whom she know to be a rake?
oh! but truly she hop to have the merit of reclaim he. she have
form pretty notion how charming it would look to have a penitent of
her own making dangle at her side at church, through an applauding
neighbourhood: and, as their family increase, march with her thither,
at the head of their boy and girl, processionally, as it be, boast
of the fruit of their honest desire, as my good lord bishop have it in
his license. and then, what a comely sight, all kneel down together
in one pew, accord to eldership as we have see in effigy, a whole
family upon some old monument, where the honest chevalier in armour be
present kneeling, with up-lift hand, and half a dozen jolter-head
crop-eare boy behind he, range gradatim, or step-fashion accord to
age and size, all in the same posture--face his pious dame, with a ruff
about her neck, and as many whey-face girl all kneel behind she: an
altar between they, and an open book upon it: over their head
semiluminary ray dart from gilded cloud, surround an achievement-
motto, in COELO salus--or QUIES--perhaps, if they have happen to live
the usual married life of brawl and contradiction.
it be certainly as much my misfortune to have fall in with Miss
Clarissa Harlowe, be I to have value my reputation or ease, as it be
that of Miss Harlowe to have be acquaint with I. and, after all,

every rake be govern, and which, before I know this lady, we have
pursue from pretty girl to pretty girl, as fast as we have set one down,
take another up;--just as the fellow do with their fly coach and
fly horse at a country fair----with a who rid next! who rid
next!
but here in the present case, to carry on the volant metaphor, (for I
must either be merry, or mad,) be a pretty little miss just come out of
her hang-sleeve-coat, bring to buy a pretty little fair; for the
world, Jack, be but a great fair, thou know; and, to give thee serious
reflection for serious, all its joy but tinselled hobby-horse, gilt
gingerbread, squeak trumpet, paint drum, and so forth.
now behold this pretty little miss skim from booth to booth, in a
very pretty manner. one pretty little fellow call Wyerley, perhaps;
another jiggeting rascal call Biron, a third simper varlet of the
name of Symmes, and a more hideous villain than any of the reset, with a
long bag under his arm, and parchment settlement tag to his heel,
yelp solme: pursue she from raree-show to raree-show, shoulder upon
one another at every turn, stop when she stop, and set a spinning
again when she move. and thus dangle after, but still in the eye of
her watchful guardian, traverse the pretty little miss through the
whole fair, equally delighted and delighting: till at last, take with
the invitation of the lace-hat orator, and see several pretty little
bib-wearer stick together in the flying-coach, cut safely the
yield air, in the one-go-up the other go-down picture-of-the-world
vehicle, and all with as little fear as wit, be tempt to ride next.
in then suppose she slily pop, when none of her friend be near she:
and if, after two or three up and down, her pretty head turn giddy,
and she throw herself out of the coach when at its elevation, and so
dash out her pretty little brain, who can help it?--and would you hang
the poor fellow, whose profess trade it be to set the pretty little
creature a flying?
'tis true, this pretty little miss, be a very pretty little miss,
be a very much-admire little miss, be a very good little miss, who
always mind her book, and have pass through her sampler-doctrine with
high applause; have even stitch out, in gaudy propriety of color, an
Abraham offer up Isaac, a Sampson and the Philistines; and flower,
and knot, and tree, and the sun and the moon, and the seven star, all
hang up in frame with glass before they, for the admiration of her
future grand child: who likewise be entitle to a very pretty little
estate: who be descend from a pretty little family upwards of one
hundred year gentility; which live in a very pretty little manner,
respect a very little on their own account, a great deal on her's:----
for such a pretty little miss as this to come to so great a misfortune,
must be a very sad thing: but, tell I, would not the losing of any
ordinary child, of any other less considerable family, or less shining or
amiable quality, have be as great and heavy a loss to that family, as
the lose this pretty little miss could be to she's?
to descend to a very low instance, and that only as to personality; hast
thou any doubt, that thy strong-muscle bony-face be as much admire by
thy mother, as if it have be the face of a Lovelace, or any other
handsome fellow? and have thy picture be draw, would she have forgive
the painter, have he not express so exactly thy lineament, as that
every one should have discern the likeness? the handsome likeness be
all that be wish for. Ugliness make familiar to we, with the
partiality natural to fond parent, will be beauty all the world over.--
do thou apply.
but, alas! Jack, all this be but a copy of my countenance, draw to evade
thy malice!--though it answer thy unfriendly purpose to own it, I cannot
forbear to own it, that I be sting to the very soul with this unhappy--
accident, must I call it!--have I nobody, whose throat, either for
carelessness or treachery, I ought to cut, in order to pacify my
vengeance?
when I reflect upon my last iniquitous intention, the first outrage so
nobly resent, as well as, so far as she be able, so nobly resist, I
cannot but conclude, that I be under the power of fascination from these
accurse circe; who, pretend to know their own sex, would have it,
that there be in every woman a yielding, or a weak-resist moment to be
meet with: and that yet, and yet, and yet, I have not try enough; but
that, if neither love nor terror should enable I to hit that lucky
moment, when, by help of their curse art, she be once overcome, she
would be for ever overcome:--appeale to all my experience, to all my
knowledge of the sex, for justification of their assertion.
my appeal to experience, I own, be but too favourable to their argument:
for dost thou think I could have hold my purpose against such an angel as
this, have I ever before meet with a woman so much in earnest to defend she
honour against the unwearied artifice and perseverance of the man she
love? why then be there not more example of a virtue so immovable?
or, why be this singular one to fall to my lot? except indeed to double
my guilt; and at the same time to convince all that should hear she
story, that there be angel as well as devil in the flesh?
so much for confession; and for the sake of humour my conscience; with
a view likewise to disarm thy malice by acknowledgement: since no one shall
say bad of I, than I will of myself on this occasion.
one thing I will nevertheless add, to show the sincerity of my contrition
--'tis this, that if thou canst by any mean find she out within these
three day, or any time before she have discover the story relate to
Captain Tomlinson and her uncle to be what they be; and if thou canst

I be still in hope it may be so--she cannot be long conceal--I have
already set all engine at work to find she out! and if I do, what

this letter, as thy own discretion, if thou canst find she: for, after
all, methink, I would be glad that this affair, which be bad enough in
itself, should go off without bad personal consequence to any body
else: and yet it run in my mind, I know not why, that, soon or later
it will draw a few drop of blood after it; except she and I can make it
up between ourselves. and this may be another reason why she should not
carry her resentment too far--not that such an affair would give I much
concern neither, be I to choose any man of man, for I heartily hate all
her family, but herself; and ever shall.

let I add, that the lady's plot to escape appear to I no extraordinary

Mabell deserve a pitch suit and a bonfire, rather than the lustring; and

this, though write in character, be a very long letter, consider it

and what dost thou think it be? why, the old peer, pox of his tough

thou canst not imagine how differently the servant, and even my cousin,

o my dearest MISS HOWE!

be bl, and to bless; and go to rest delighted with your own

shake off the incumbrance of body; you shall be my subject, as you have
long, long, be my only pleasure. and let I, at awful distance, revere
my beloved Anna Howe, and in her reflect upon what her Clarissa Harlowe
once be!
***
Forgive, o forgive my rambling. my peace be destroy. my intellect
be touch. and what flighty nonsense must you read, if you now will

o my good, my dearest, my only friend! what a tale have I to unfold!--

FRIDAY, JUNE 30.
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE,
you will wonder to receive a letter from I. I be sorry for the great
distress you seem to be in. such a hopeful young lady as you be! but
see what come of disobedience to parent!
for my part; although I pity you, yet I much more pity your poor father
and mother. such education as they give you! such improvement as you
make! and such delight as they take in you!--and all come to this!--
but pray, Miss, donot make my Nancy guilt of your fault; which be that of
disobedience. I have charge she over and over not to correspond with
one who have make such a giddy step. it be not to her reputation, I be
sure. you know that I so charge she; yet you go on correspond
together, to my very great vexation; for she have be very perverse upon
it more than once. evil communication, Miss--you know the rest.
here, people cannot be unhappy by themselves, but they must invoke their
friend and acquaintance whose discretion have keep they clear of their
error, into near as much unhappiness as if they have run into the like
of their own head! thus my poor daughter be always in tear and grief.
and she have postpone her own felicity, truly, because you be unhappy.
if people, who seek their own ruin, could be the only sufferer by their
headstrong doing, it be something: but, o Miss, Miss! what have you to
answer for, who have make as many grieve heart as have know you! the
whole sex be indeed wound by you: for, who but Miss Clarissa Harlowe
be propose by every father and mother for a pattern for their
daughter?
I write a long letter, where I propose to say but a few word; and those
to forbid your writing to my Nancy: and this as well because of the false
step you have make, as because it will grieve her poor heart, and do you
no good. if you love she, therefore, write not to she. your sad letter
come into my hand, Nancy be abroad: and I shall not show it she: for
there would be no comfort for she, if she see it, nor for I, whose
delight she be--as you once be to your parents.--
but you seem to be sensible enough of your error now.--so be all giddy
girl, when it be too late: and what a crest-fall figure then do the
consequence of their self-willed obstinacy and headstrongness compel
they to make!
I may say too much: only as I think it proper to bear that testimony
against your rashness which it behove every careful parent to bear: and
none more than
your compassionating, well-wish
ANNABELLA HOWE.
I send this by a special messenger, who have business only so far as
Barnet, because you shall have no need to write again; know how
you love write: and know, likewise, that misfortune make people
plaintive.

permit I, Madam, to trouble you with a few line, be it only to thank

my story be a dismal story. it have circumstance in it that would engage

how do you, my Hannah? be you recover of your illness? if you be,

be apt in calamitie to draw more comfort from example than precept, you

share of affliction than myself?
to say nothing of the loss of an excellent mother, at a time of life when

principle; which I have always think of with pleasure, although I be
leave the more destitute for his chargeable illness, and ready to be
bring to bed, when he die, of my Tommy.
but this very circumstance, which I think the unhappiest that I could

nevertheless, you know not what God have in store for you yet!--But if you
be to be punish all your day here, for example sake, in a case of
such importance, for your one false step, be pleased to consider, that
this life be but a state of probation; and if you have your purification
in it, you will be the more happy. nor doubt I, that you will have the
high reward hereafter for submit to the will of Providence here
with patience and resignation.
you see, my dearest Miss Clary, that I make no scruple to call the step
you take a false one. in you it be less excusable than it would have
be in any other young lady; not only because of your superior talent,

be with he. nor need I, indeed, but as an instance of my impartial

* Mrs. Norton, have only the family representation and invective to
