LETTER LVII
MISS CL. HARLOWE, to LADY BETTY LAWRANCE
THURSDAY, JUNE 29.
MADAM,
I hope youwill excuse the freedom of this address, from one who have not
the honour to be personally know to you, although you must have hear
much of Clarissa Harlowe. it be only to beg the favour of a line from
your ladyship's hand, (by the next post, if convenient,) in answer to the
follow question:
1. whether you write a letter, date, as I have a memorandum, Wedn. June
7, congratulate your nephew Lovelace on his suppose nuptial, as
report to you by Mr. Spurrier, your ladyship's steward, as from one
Captain Tomlinson:--and in it reproach Mr. Lovelace, as guilty of
slight, &c. in not have acquaint your ladyship and the family
with his marriage?
2. whether your ladyship write to Miss Montague to meet you at Reading,
in order to attend you to your cousin Leeson's, in Albemarle-street;
on your being oblige to be in town on your old chancery affair, I
remember be the word? and whether you bespoke your nephew's
attendance there on Sunday night the 11th?
3. whether your ladyship and Miss Montague do come to town at that
time; and whether you go to Hampstead, on Monday, in a hire coach
and four, your own be repair, and take from thence to town with
the young creature whom you visit there?
your ladyship will probably guess, that the question be not ask for
reason favourable to your nephew Lovelace. but be the answer what it
will, it can do he no hurt, nor I any good; only that I think I owe it
to my former hope, (however deceive in they,) and even to charity, that
a person, of whom I be once willing to think well, should not prove so
egregiously abandon, as to be want, in every instance, to that
veracity which be indispensable in the character of a gentleman.
be pleased, Madam, to direct to I, (keep the direction a secret for
the present,) to be leave at the Belle-Savage, on Ludgate hill, till
call for. I be
your ladyship's most humble servant,
CLARISSA HARLOWE.
LETTER LVIII
LADY BETTY LAWRANCE, to MISS CL. HARLOWE
SATURDAY, JULY 1.
DEAR MADAM,
I find that all be not as it should be between you and my nephew
Lovelace. it will very much afflict I, and all his friend, if he have
be guilty of any design baseness to a lady of your character and
merit.
we have be long in expectation of an opportunity to congratulate you
and ourselves upon an event most earnestly wish for by we all; since
our hope of he be build upon the power you have over he: for if ever
man adore a woman, he be that man, and you, Madam, be that woman.
Miss Montague, in her last letter to I, in answer to one of mine,
inquire if she know from he whether he could call you his, or be
likely soon to have that honour, have these word: 'I know not what to
make of my cousin Lovelace, as to the point your ladyship be so earnest
about. he sometimes say he be actually married to Miss Cl. Harlowe: at
other time, that it be her own fault if he be not.--He speak of she not
only with love but with reverence: yet own, that there be a
misunderstanding between they; but confess that she be wholly
faultless. an angel, and not a woman, he say she be: and that no man
living can be worthy of she.'--
this be what my niece Montague write.
God grant, my dear young lady, that he may not have so heinously
offend you that you cannot forgive he! if you be not already
married, and refuse to be his, I shall lose all hope that he ever will
marry, or be the man I wish he to be. so will Lord M. so will Lady
Sarah Sadleir.
I will now answer your question: but indeed I hardly know what to write,
for fear of widen still more the unhappy difference between you. but
yet such a young lady must command every thing from I. this then be my
answer:
I write not any letter to he on or about the 7th of June.
neither I nor my steward know any such man as Captain Tomlinson.
I write not to my niece to meet I at Reading, nor to accompany I to my
cousin Leeson's in town.
my chancery affair, though, like most chancery affair, it be of long
standing, be, nevertheless, now in so good a way, that it cannot
give I occasion to go to town.
nor have I be in town these six month: nor at Hampstead for
year.
neither shall I have any temptation to go to town, except to pay my
congratulatory compliment to Mrs. Lovelace. on which occasion I
should go with the great pleasure; and should hope for the
favour of your accompany I to Glenham-hall, for a month at
least.
be what will the reason of your inquiry, let I entreat you, my dear
young lady, for Lord M.'s sake; for my sake; for this giddy man's sake,
soul as well as body; and for all our family's sake; not to suffer this
answer to widen difference so far as to make you refuse he, if he
already have not the honour of call you his; as I be apprehensive he
have not, by your signing by your family-name.
and here let I offer to you my mediation to compose the difference
between you, be it what it will. your cause, my dear young lady, cannot
be put into the hand of any body live more devoted to your service,
than into those of
your sincere admirer, and humble servant,
ELIZ. lawrance.
LETTER LIX
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MRS. HODGES
ENFIELD, JUNE 22.
MRS. HODGES,
I be under a kind of necessity to write to you, have no one among my
relation to whom I dare write, or hope a line from if I do. it be but
to answer a question. it be this:
whether you know any such man as Captain Tomlinson? and, if you do,
whether he be very intimate with my uncle Harlowe?
I will describe his person lest, possibly, he should go by another name
among you; although I know not why he should.
'he be a thin, tallish man, a little pock-fretten, of a sallowish
complexion. fifty year of age, or more. of good aspect when he look
up. he seem to be a serious man, and one who know the world. he
stoop a little in the shoulder. be of Berkshire. his wife of
Oxfordshire; and have several child. he remove lately into your part
form northamptonshire.'
I must desire you, Mrs. Hodges, that you will not let my uncle, nor any
of my relation, know that I write to you.
you use to say, that you would be glad to have it in your power to serve
I. that, indeed, be in my prosperity. but, I dare say, you will not
refuse I in a particular that will oblige I, without hurt yourself.
I understand that my father, mother, and sister, and I presume, my
brother, and my uncle Antony, be to be at my uncle Harlowe's this day.
God preserve they all, and may they rejoice in many happy birth-day!
you will write six word to I concern their health.
direct, for a particular reason, to Mrs. Dorothy Salcombe, to be leave
till call for, at the four Swans Inn, Bishopsgate-street.
you know my hand-writing well enough, be not the content of the letter
sufficient to excuse my name, or any other subscription, than that of
your friend.
LETTER LX
MRS. HODGES
[in ANSWER.]
SAT. JULY 2.
MADDAM,
I return you an anser, as you wish I to doe. Master be acquente with
no sitch man. I be shure no sitch ever come to our house. and master
stur very little out. he have no harte to stur out. for why? your
obstinacy make um not care to see one another. Master's birth-day never
be keep soe before: for not a sole heere: and nothing but sikeing and
sorrowin from master to think how it yuse to bee.
I ax master, if soe bee he know sitch a man as one Captain Tomlinson?
but say not whirfor I ax. he se, no, not he.
shure this be no trix nor forgery brue against master by one Tomlinson
--Won know not what company you may have be forse to keep, sen you
go away, you knoe, Maddam; but Lundon be a pestilent plase; and that
'Squire Luvless be a devil (for all he be sitch a like gentleman to look
to) as I hev herd every boddy say; and think as how you have find by
thiss.
I truste, Maddam, you wulde not let master cum to harme, if you knoe it,
by any body who may pretend to be acquente with he: but for fere, I
querid with myself if I shulde not tell he. but I be willin to show
you, that I wulde plessure you in advarsity, if advarsity be your lott,
as well as prosperity; for I be none of those that woulde doe otherwiss.
Soe no more from
your humble sarvent, to wish you well,
SARAH HODGES.
LETTER LXI
MISS CL. HARLOWE, to LADY BETTY LAWRANCE.
MONDAY, JULY 3.
MADAM,
I cannot excuse myself from give your ladyship this one trouble more;
to thank you, as I most heartily do, for your kind letter.
I must own to you, Madam, that the honour of be relate to lady as
eminent for their virtue as for their descent, be at first no small
inducement with I to lend an ear to Mr. Lovelace's address. and the
rather, as I be determine, have it come to effect, to do every thing in
my power to deserve your favourable opinion.
I have another motive, which I know would of itself give I merit with
your whole family; a presumptuous one, (a punishably presumptuous one, as
it have prove,) in the hope that I might be an humble mean in the hand of
Providence to reclaim a man, who have, as I think, good sense enough to
acknowledge the intend obligation, whether the generous hope be to
succeed or not.
but I have be most egregiously mistaken in Mr. Lovelace; the only man,
I persuade myself, pretend to be a gentleman, in whom I could have
be so much mistaken: for while I be endeavour to save a drown
wretch, I have be, not accidentally, but premeditatedly, and of set
purpose, draw in after he. and he have have the glory to add to the list
of those he have ruin, a name, that, I will be bold to say, would not
have disparage his own. and this, Madam, by mean that would shock
humanity to be make acquainted with.
my whole end be serve by your ladyship's answer to the question I take
the liberty to put to you in writing. nor have I a wish to make the
unhappy man more odious to you than be necessary to excuse myself for
absolutely decline your offer mediation.
when your ladyship shall be inform of the following particular:
that after he have compulsorily, as I may say, trick I into the act of
go off with he, he could carry I to one of the vile house, as it
prove, in London:
that he could be guilty of a wicked attempt, in resentment of which, I
find mean to escape from he to Hampstead:
that, after he have find I out there (I know not how) he could procure
two woman, dress out richly, to personate your ladyship and Miss
Montague; who, under pretence of engage I to make a visit in town to
your cousin Leeson, (promise to return with I that evening to
Hampstead,) betray I back again to the vile house: where, again make a
prisoner, I be first rob of my sens; and then of my honour. why
should I seek to conceal that disgrace from other which I cannot hide
from myself?
when your ladyship shall know, that, in the shocking progress to this
ruin, wilful falsehood, repeat forgery, (particularly of one letter
from your ladyship, another from Miss Montague, and a third from Lord M.)
and numberless perjury, be not the least of his crime: you will
judge, that I can have no principle that will make I worthy of an
alliance with lady of your' and your noble sister's character, if I
could not from my soul declare, that such an alliance can never now take
place.
I will not offer to clear myself entirely of blame: but, as to he, I
have no fault to accuse myself of: my crime be, the corresponding with
he at first, when prohibit so to do by those who have a right to my
obedience; make still more inexcusable, by give he a clandestine
meeting, which put I into the power of his art. and for this I be
content to be punish: thankful, that at last I have escape from he;
and have it in my power to reject so wicked a man for my husband: and
glad, if I may be a warning, since I cannot be an example: which once
(very vain, and very conceited, as I be) I propose to myself to be.
all the ill I wish he be, that he may reform; and that I may be the last
victim to his baseness. perhaps this desirable wish may be obtain,
when he shall see how his wickedness, his unmerited wickedness! to a poor
creature, make friendless by his cruel art, will end.
I conclude with my humble thank to your ladyship for your favourable
opinion of I; and with the assurance that I will be, while life be lend
I,
your ladyship's grateful and obliged servant,
CLARISSA HARLOWE.
LETTER LXII
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MRS. NORTON
SUNDAY EVENING, JULY 2.
how kindly, my beloved Mrs. Norton, do you soothe the anguish of a
bleed heart! surely you be mine own mother; and, by some
unaccountable mistake, I must have be lay to a family that, have
newly find out, or at least suspect, the imposture, cast I from their
heart, with the indignation that such a discovery will warrant.
oh! that I have be indeed your own child, bear to partake of your humble
fortune, an heiress only to that content in which you be so happy! then
should I have have a truly gentle spirit to have guide my ductile heart,
which force and ungenerous usage sit so ill upon: and nothing of what have
happen would have be.
but let I take heed that I enlarge not, by impatience, the breach
already make in my duty by my rashness! since, have I not err, my
mother, at least, could never have be think hard-hearted and
unforgiving. be I not then answerable, not only for my own fault, but
for the consequence of they; which tend to depreciate and bring disgrace
upon a maternal character never before call in question?
it be kind, however, in you to endeavour to extenuate the fault of one
so greatly sensible of it: and could it be wipe off entirely, it would
render I more worthy of the pain you have take in my education: for it
must add to your grief, as it do to my confusion, that, after such
promising beginning, I should have so behave as to be a disgrace
instead of a credit to you and my other friend.
but that I may not make you think I more guilty than I be, give I leave
briefly to assure you, that, when my story be know, I shall be
to more compassion than blame, even on the score of go away with Mr.
Lovelace.
as to all that happen afterwards, let I only say, that although I must
call myself a lose creature as to this world, yet have I this consolation
leave I, that I have not suffer either for want of circumspection, or
through careful credulity or weakness. not one moment be I off my
guard, or unmindful of your early precept. but (have be enable to
baffle many base contrivance) I be at last ruin by art the most
inhuman. but have I not be reject by every friend, this low-hearte
man have not dare, nor would have have opportunity, to treat I as he have
treat I.
More I cannot, at this time, nor need I say: and this I desire you to
keep to yourself, lest resentment should be take up when I be go,
that may spread the evil which I hope will end with I.
I have be misinform, you say, as to my principal relation be at
my uncle Harlowe's. the day, you say, be not keep. nor have my brother
and Mr. Solmes--astonishing!--what complicated wickedness have this
wretched man to answer for!--were I to tell you, you would hardly believe
that there could have be such a heart in man.--
but one day you may know the whole story!--At present I have neither
inclination nor word--o my bursting heart!--Yet a happy, a wished
relief!--were you present my tear would supply the rest!
***
I resume my pen!
and so you fear no letter will be receive from I. but don't grieve to
tell I so! I expect every thing bad--and such be my distress, that have
you not bid I hope for mercy from the throne of mercy, I should have
be afraid that my father's dreadful curse would be complete with
regard to both world.
for here, an additional misfortune!--in a fit of phrensical heedlessness,

yet you bid I not despond.--i will not, if I can help it. and, indeed,

but although your son should recover, I charge you, my dear Mrs. Norton,

but again, impatiency, found perhaps on self-partiality, that strange

then the people I be now with seem to be both honest and humane: and

when I reflect upon all that have happen to I, it be apparent, that
this generally-suppose thoughtless seducer have act by I upon a
regular and preconcerted plan of villany.
in order to set all his vile plot in motion, nothing be want, from

brief.
let I desire you to be secret in what I have communicate to you; at
least till you have my consent to divulge it.
God preserve to you your more faultless child!
I will hope for his mercy, although I should not obtain that of any
earthly person.
and I repeat my prohibition:--you must not think of come up to
your ever dutiful
CL. HARLOWE.
the oblige person, who leave your' for I this day, promise to call

LETTER LXIII
MRS. NORTON, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
MONDAY NIGHT, JULY 3.
o the barbarous villany of this detestable man! and be there a man in
the world who could offer violence to so sweet a creature!
and be you sure you be now out of his reach?
you command I to keep secret the particular of the vile treatment you
have meet with; or else, upon an unexpected visit which Miss Harlowe
favour I with, soon after I have receive your melancholy letter, I
should have be tempt to own I have hear from you, and to have
communicate to her such part of your two letter as would have
demonstrate your penitence, and your earnestness to obtain the
revocation of your father's malediction, as well as his protection from
outrage that may still be offer to you. but then your sister would
probably have expect a sight of the letter, and even to have be
permit to take they with she to the family.
yet they must one day be acquaint with the sad story:--and it be
impossible but they must pity you, and forgive you, when they know your
early penitence, and your unprecedented suffering; and that you have
fall by the brutal force of a barbarous ravisher, and not by the vile
art of a seducing lover.
the wicked man give it out at Lord M.'s, as Miss Harlowe tell I, that
he be actually married to you--yet she believe it not: nor have I the
heart to let she know the truth.
she put it close to I, whether I have not correspond with you from the
time of your go away? I could safely tell she, (as I do,) that I have
not: but I say, that I be well informed, that you take extremely to
heart your father's imprecation; and that, if she would excuse I, I
would say it would be a kind and sisterly part, if she would use she
interest to get you discharge from it.
among other severe thing, she tell I, that my partial fondness for you
make I very little consider the honour of the rest of the family: but,
if I have not hear this from you, she suppose I be set on by Miss Howe.
she express herself with a good deal of bitterness against that young
lady: who, it seem, every where, and to every body, (for you must think
that your story be the subject of all conversation,) rail against your
family; treat they, as your sister say, with contempt, and even with
ridicule.
I be sorry such angry freedom be take, for two reason; first, because
such liberty never do any good. I have hear you own, that Miss Howe
have a satirical vein; but I should hope that a young lady of her sense,
and right cast of mind, must know that the end of satire be not to
exasperate, but amend; and should never be personal. if it be, as my
good father use to say, it may make an impartial person suspect that the
satirist have a natural spleen to gratify; which may be as great a fault
in he, as any of those which he pretend to censure and expose in
other.
perhaps a hint of this from you will not be throw away.
my second reason be, that these freedom, from so warm a friend to you as
Miss Howe be know to be, be most likely to be charge to your account.
my resentment be so strong against this vilest of man, that I dare not
touch upon the shocking particular which you mention of his baseness.
what defence, indeed, could there be against so determined a wretch,
after you be in his power? I will only repeat my earnest supplication
to you, that, black as appearance be, you will not despair. your
calamity be exceed great; but then you have talent proportion to
your trial. this every body allow.
suppose the bad, and that your family will not be move in your favour,
your cousin Morden will soon arrive, as Miss Harlowe tell I. if he
should even be get over to their side, he will however see justice do
you; and then may you live an exemplary life, make hundred happy, and
teach young lady to shun the snare in which you have be so
dreadfully entangle.
as to the man you have lose, be an union with such a perjured heart as
his, with such an admirable one as your's, to be wish for? a base,
low-hearted wretch, as you justly call he, with all his pride of
ancestry; and more an enemy to himself with regard to his present and
future happiness than to you, in the barbarous and ungrateful wrong he
have do you: I need not, I be sure, exhort you to despise such a man as
this, since not to be able to do so, would be a reflection upon a sex to
which you have always be an honour.
your moral character be untainted: the very nature of your suffering, as
you will observe, demonstrate that. cheer up, therefore, your dear
heart, and do not despair; for be it not GOD who govern the world, and
permit some thing, and direct other, as he please? and will he not
reward temporary suffering, innocently incur, and piously support,
with eternal felicity?--and what, my dear, be this poor needle's point of
now to a boundless eternity?
my heart, however, labour under a double affliction: for my poor boy be
very, very bad--a violent fever--nor can it be bring to intermit.--Pray
for he, my dear Miss--for his recovery, if God see fit.--I hope God
will see fit--if not (how can I bear to suppose that!) pray for I, that
he will give I that patience and resignation which I have be wish
to you. I be, my dear young lady,
your ever affectionate
JUDITH NORTON.
LETTER LXIV
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MRS. JUDITH NORTON
THURSDAY, JULY 6.
I ought not, especially at this time, to add to your affliction--but yet
I cannot help communicate to you (who now be my only soothe friend)
a new trouble that have befall I.
I have but one friend in the world, beside you; and she be utterly
displeased with I.* it be grievous, but for one moment, to lie under a
beloved person's censure; and this through imputation that affect one's
honour and prudence. there be point so delicate, you know, my dear
Mrs. Norton, that it be a degree of dishonour to have a vindication of
one's self from they appear to be necessary. in the present case, my
misfortune be, that I know not how to account, but by guess (so subtle
have be the working of the dark spirit I have be unhappily entangle
by) for some of the fact that I be call upon to explain.
Miss Howe, in short, suppose she have find a flaw in my character. I
have just now receive her severe letter--but I shall answer it, perhaps,
in well temper, if I first consider yourbe: for indeed my patience be
almost at an end. and yet I ought to consider, that faithful be the
wound of a friend. but so many thing at once! o my dear Mrs. Norton,
how shall so young a scholar in the school of affliction be able to bear
such heavy and such various evil!
but to leave this subject for a while, and turn to your letter.
I be very sorry Miss Howe be so lively in her resentment on my account.
I have always blame she very freely for her liberty of this sort with
my friend. I once have a good deal of influence over her kind heart, and
she make all I say a law to she. but people in calamity have little
weight in any thing, or with any body. prosperity and independence be
charming thing on this account, that they give force to the counsel of
a friendly heart; while it be think insolence in the miserable to
advise, or so much as to remonstrate.
yet be Miss Howe an invaluable person: and be it to be expect that she
should preserve the same regard for my judgment that she have before I
forfeit all title to discretion? with what face can I take upon I to
reproach a want of prudence in she? but if I can be so happy as to
re-establish myself in her ever-value opinion, I shall endeavour to
enforce upon she your just observation on this head.
you need not, you say, exhort I to despise such a man as he, by whom I
have suffer--indeed you need not: for I would choose the cruell
death rather than to be his. and yet, my dear Mrs. Norton, I will own to
you, that once I could have love him.--ungrateful man!--had he permit
I to love he, I once could have love he. yet he never deserve
love. and be not this a fault?--but now, if I can but keep out of his
hand, and obtain a last forgiveness, and that as well for the sake of my
dear friend' future reflection, as for my own present comfort, it be
all I wish for.
Reconciliation with my friend I do not expect; nor pardon from they; at
least, till in extremity, and as a viaticum.
o my beloved Mrs. Norton, you cannot imagine what I have suffered!--but
indeed my heart be broken!--i be sure I shall not live to take possession
of that independence, which you think would enable I to atone, in some
measure, for my past conduct.
while this be my opinion, you may believe I shall not be easy till I can
obtain a last forgiveness.
I wish to be leave to take my own course in endeavour to procure this
grace. yet know I not, at present, what that course shall be.
I will write. but to whom be my doubt. calamity have not yet give I
the assurance to address myself to my FATHER. my UNCLES (well as they
once love I) be hard hearted. they never have their masculine passion
humanize by the tender name of FATHER. of my brother I have no hope. I
have then but my MOTHER, and my SISTER, to whom I can apply.--'And may I
not, my dear Mamma, be permit to lift up my trembling eye to your
all-cheering, and your once more than indulgent, your fond eye, in hope
of seasonable mercy to the poor sick heart that yet beat with life draw
from your own dearer heart?--especially when pardon only, and not
restoration, be implore?'
yet be I able to engage my mother's pity, would it not be a mean to
make she still more unhappy than I have already make she, by the
opposition she would meet with, be she to try to give force to that
pity?
to my SISTER, then, I think, I will apply--yet how hard-hearted have my
sister been!--but I will not ask for protection; and yet I be in hourly
dread that I shall want protection.--all I will ask for at present
(preparative to the last forgiveness I will implore) shall be only to be
free from the heavy curse that seem to have operate as far be it can
operate as to this life--and, surely, it be passion, and not intention,
that carry it so far as to the other!
but why do I thus add to your distresses?--it be not, my dear Mrs.
Norton, that I have so much feeling for my own calamity that I have none
for your's: since your's be indeed an addition to my own. but you have
one consolation (a very great one) which I have not:--that your
affliction, whether respect your more or your less deserving child,
rise not from any fault of your own.
but what can I do for you more than pray?--assure yourself, that in every
supplication I put up for myself, I will with equal fervour remember both
you and your son. for I be and ever will be
your truly sympathising and dutiful
CLARISSA HARLOWE.
LETTER LXV
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
[superscribe for MRS. RACHEL CLARK, &c.]
WEDNESDAY, JULY 5.
MY DEAR CLARISSA,
I have at last hear from you from a quarter I little expect.
from my mother!
she have for some time see I uneasy and grieving; and justly suppose it
be about you: and this morning dropt a hint, which make I conjecture
that she must have hear something of you more than I know. and when she
find that this add to my uneasiness, she own she have a letter in her
hand of your's, date the 29th of June, direct for I.
you may guess, that this occasion a little warmth, that could not be
wish for by either.
[it be surprising, my dear, mighty surprising! that know the
prohibition I lie under of correspond with you, you could send a
letter for I to our own house: since it must be fifty to one that it
would fall into my mother's hand, as you find it do.]
in short, she resent that I should disobey she: I be as much concerned
that she should open and withhold from I my letter: and at last she be
pleased to compromise the matter with I by give up the letter, and
permit I to write to you once or twice: she to see the content of
what I write. for, besides the value she have for you, she could not but
have great curiosity to know the occasion of so sad a situation as your
melancholy letter show you to be in.
[but I shall get she to be satisfied with hear I read what I write;
put in between hook, thus [], what I intend not to read to she.]
need I to remind you, Miss Clarissa Harlowe, of three letter I write to

a few line only, promise a letter at large, though you be well
enough, the day after you receive my second, to go joyfully back again
with he to the vile house? but more of these by-and-by. I must hasten
to take notice of your letter of Wednesday last week; which you could
contrive should fall into my mother's hand.
let I tell you, that that letter have almost break my heart. good God!
--What have you bring yourself to, Miss Clarissa harlowe?--could I have
believe, that after you have escape from the miscreant, (with such
mighty pain and earnestness escape,) and after such an attempt as he

be not proof against its inconsistent effect.
you your good self have not escaped!--indeed I see not how you could
expect to escape.
what a tale have you to unfold!--you need not unfold it, my dear: I would
have engage to prognosticate all that have happen, have you but tell I

take such pain to get out of it.
your peace be destroyed!--i wonder not at it: since now you must reproach
yourself for a credulity so ill-place.
your intellect be touched!--i be sure my heart bleed for you! but,
excuse I, my dear, I doubt your intellect be touch before you leave

he do, suffer he to prevail upon you to return to the horrid brothel.
I tell you, I send you three letter: the first of which, date the 7th

my dear--but nothing now will I ever wonder at!

the second, date June 10,* be give into your own hand at Hampstead, on

the third be date the 20th of June.* have not hear one word from

you have hear, that I have be ill, you say. I have a cold, indeed; but

but I remember once an argument you hold, on occasion of a censure pass

to have money, and will, and head, to be a villain, be too much for the

LETTER LXVI
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
THURSDAY, JULY 6.
few young person have be able to give more convincing proof than
myself how little true happiness lie in the enjoyment of our own wish.
to produce one instance only of the truth of this observation; what would
I have give for week past, for the favour of a letter from my dear Miss
Howe, in whose friendship I place all my remain comfort! little do
I think, that the next letter she would honour I with, should be in such
a style, as should make I look more than once at the subscription, that
I might be sure (the name not be write at length) that it be not
sign by another A.H. for surely, think I, this be my sister
Arabella's style: surely Miss Howe (blame I as she please in other
point) could never repeat so sharply upon her friend, word write in
the bitterness of spirit, and in the disorder of head; nor remind she,
with asperity, and with mingled stroke of wit, of an argument hold in
the gaiety of a heart elate with prosperous fortune, (as mine then
be,) and very little apprehensive of the severe turn that argument would
one day take against herself.
but what have I, sink in my fortune; my character forfeit; my honour
lose, [while I know it, I care not who know it;] destitute of friend,
and even of hope; what have I to do to show a spirit of repine and
expostulation to a dear friend, because she be not more kind than a
sister?----
you have till now, my dear, treat I with great indulgence. if it be
with great than I have deserve, I may be to blame to have build upon
it, on the consciousness that I deserve it now as much as ever. but I
find, by the rise bitterness which will mingle with the gall in my ink,
that I be not yet subdue enough to my condition.--I lie down my pen for
one moment.
***
pardon I, my Miss Howe. I have recollect myself: and will endeavour
to give a particular answer to your letter; although it will take I up
too much time to think of send it by your messenger to-morrow: he can
put off his journey, he say, till Saturday. I will endeavour to have
the whole narrative ready for you by Saturday.
but how to defend myself in every thing that have happen, I cannot tell:
since in some part of the time, in which my conduct appear to have be
censurable, I be not myself; and to this hour know not all the method
take to deceive and ruin I.
you tell I, that in your first letter you give I such an account of the
vile house I be in, and such caution about that Tomlinson, as make you
wonder how I could think of go back.
Alas, my dear! I be trick, most vilely trick back, as you shall
hear in its place.
without know the house be so very vile a house from your intended
information, I dislike the people too much, ever voluntarily to have
return to it. but have you really write such caution about
Tomlinson, and the house, as you seem to have purpose to do, they must,
have they come in time, have be of infinite service to I. but not one
word of either, whatever be your intention, do you mention to I, in
that first of the three letter you so warmly tell I you do send I. I
will enclose it to convince you.*
* the letter she enclose be Mr. Lovelace's forge one. see Vol. V.
Letter XXX.
but your account of your messenger's deliver to I your second
letter, and the description he give of I, as lie upon a couch, in a
strange way, bloated, and flush-colour; you donot know how, absolutely

Lord have mercy upon the poor Clarissa Harlowe! what can this mean!--who
be the messenger you send? be he one of Lovelace's creature too!--
could nobody come near I but that man's confederate, either set out

but indeed I know nothing of any messenger from you.

I wonder I have not hear from you: and be tell you be sick; and, at

it be on Sunday, June 11, you say, that the man give it I. I be at

CLARISSA HARLOWE.
LETTER LXVII
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
[refer to in LETTER XII.]
THURSDAY NIGHT.
he have find I out at Hampstead: strangely find I out; for I be still
at a loss to know by what mean.
I be loth, in my billet of the 6th,* to tell you so, for fear of give
you apprehension for I; and besides, I hop then to have a short and
happy issue to account to you for, through your assistance, than I meet
with.
* see Vol. V. Letter XXXI.
[she then give a narrative of all that pass at Hampstead between

Mr. Lovelace, find all he could say, and all Captain Tomlinson could

premeditate; rest all his hope on a visit which be to be pay I by

she could easily tell who be in fault, she say. and give he a look

he pretend to be awe into shame and silence.

LETTER LXXII
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
MONDAY, JULY 10.
I now, my dear friend, resume my pen, to obey my mother, in give you
her opinion upon your unhappy story.
she still harp upon the old string, and will have it that all your
calamity be owe to your first fatal step; for she believe, (what I
cannot,) that your relation have intend after one general trial more,
to comply with your aversion, if they have find it to be as rivet a
one, as, let I say, it be a folly to suppose it would not be find to
be, after so many ridiculously-repeat experiment.
as to your latter suffering from that vilest of miscreant, she be
unalterably of opinion that if all be as you have relate (which she
doubt not) with regard to the potion, and to the violence you have
sustain, you ought by all mean to set on foot a prosecution against
he, and against his devilish accomplice.
she ask, what murderer, what ravisher, would be bring to justice, if
modesty be to be a general plea, and allowable, against appear in a
court to prosecute?
she say, that the good of society require, that such a beast of prey
should be hunt out of it: and, if you do not prosecute he, she think
you will be answerable for all the mischief he may do in the course of
his future villanous life.
will it be think, Nancy, say she, that Miss Clarissa Harlowe can be in
earnest, when she say, she be not solicitous to have her disgrace
conceal from the world, if she be afraid or ashamed to appear in court,
to do justice to herself and her sex against he? will it not be rather
surmise, that she may be apprehensive that some weakness, or lurking
love, will appear upon the trial of the strange cause? if, infer she,
such complicated villany as this (where perjury, potion, forgery,
subornation, be all combine to effect the ruin of an innocent creature,
and to dishonour a family of eminence, and where the very crime, as may
be suppose, be proof of her innocence) be to go off with impunity,
what case will deserve to be bring into judgment? or what malefactor
ought to be hang?
then she think, and so do I, that the vile creature, his accomplice,
ought, by all mean, to be bring to condign punishment, as they must
and will be upon bring he to trial: and this may be a mean to blow up
and root out a whole nest of viper, and save many innocent creature.
she add, that if Miss Clarissa Harlowe could be so indifferent about
have this public justice do upon such a wretch for her own sake, she
ought to overcome her scruple out of regard to her family, her
acquaintance, and her sex, which be all highly injure and scandalize
by his villany to she.
for her own part, she declare, that be she your mother, she would
forgive you upon no other term: and, upon your compliance with these,
she herself will undertake to reconcile all your family to you.
these, my dear, be my mother's sentiment upon your sad story.
I cannot say but there be reason and justice in they: and it be my
opinion, that it would be very right for the law to oblige an injure
woman to prosecute, and to make seduction on the man's part capital,
where his studied baseness, and no fault in her will, appear.
to this purpose the custom in the Isle of Man be a very good one----
'if a single woman there prosecute a single man for a rape, the
ecclesiastical judge impannel a jury; and, if this jury find he guilty,
he be return guilty to the temporal court: where if he be convict,
the deemster, or judge, deliver to the woman a rope, a sword, and a
ring; and she have it in her choice to have he hang, behead, or to
marry he.'
one of the two former, I think, should always be her option.
I long for the particular of your story. you must have too much time
upon your hand for a mind so active as your's, if tolerable health and

the villany of the bad of man, and the virtue of the most excellent of

MONDAY, JULY 10.
I cannot, my dear friend, suffer the enclose to go unaccompanie by a
few line, to signify to you that they be both less tender in some
place than I would have write, have they not be to pass my mother's
inspection. the principal reason, however, of my writing thus separately
be, to beg of you to permit I to send you money and necessary, which
you must need want; and that you will let I know, if either I, or any
body I can influence, can be of service to you. I be excessively
apprehensive that you be not enough out of the villain's reach where you
be. yet London, I be persuade, be the place, of all other, to be
private in.
I could tear my hair for vexation, that I have it not in my power to
afford you personal protection!--I be
your ever devote
ANNA HOWE.

letter lxxiii
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
TUESDAY, JULY 11.
forgive you, my dear!--most cordially do I forgive you--will you forgive
I for some sharp thing I write in return to your' of the 5th? you
could not have love I as you do, nor have the concern you have always
show for my honour, if you have not be utterly displeased with I, on
the appearance which my conduct wear to you when you write that letter.
I most heartily thank you, my good and only love, for the opportunity you
give I of clear it up; and for be generously ready to acquit I of
intentional blame, the moment you have read my melancholy narrative.
as you be so earnest to have all the particular of my sad story before
you, I will, if life and spirit be lend I, give you an ample account of
all that have befall I, from the time you mention. but this, it be
very probable, you will not see, till after the close of my last scene:
and as I shall write with a view to that, I hope no other voucher will be
want for the veracity of the writer, be who will the reader.
I be far from think myself out of the reach of this man's further
violence. but what can I do? whither can I fly?--perhaps my bad state
of health (which must grow bad, as recollection of the past evil, and
reflection upon they, grow heavy and heavy upon I) may be my
protection. once, indeed, I think of go abroad; and, have I the
prospect of many year before I, I would go.--but, my dear, the blow be
given.--nor have you reason now, circumstance as I be, to be concern
that it be. what a heart must I have, if it be not break--and indeed,
my dear friend, I do so earnestly wish for the last closing scene, and
with so much comfort find myself in a decline way, that I even
sometimes ungratefully regret that naturally-healthy constitution, which
use to double upon I all my enjoyment.
as to the earnestly-recommend prosecution, I may possibly touch upon it
more largely hereafter, if ever I shall have well spirit; for they be
at present extremely sunk and low. but just now, I will only say, that I
would soon suffer every evil (the repetition of the capital one
except) than appear publicly in a court to do myself justice.* and I
be heartily grieve that your mother prescribe such a measure as the
condition of our future correspondence: for the continuance of your
friendship, my dear, and the desire I have to correspond with you to my
life's end, be all my remain hope and consolation. nevertheless,
as that friendship be in the power of the heart, not of the hand only, I
hope I shall not forfeit that.
* Dr. Lewen, in Letter XXIV. of Vol. VIII. press she to this public
prosecution, by argument worthy of his character; which she answer in a
manner worthy of she's. see Letter XXV. of that volume.
o my dear! what would I give to obtain a revocation of my father's
malediction! a reconciliation be not to be hop for. you, who never
love my father, may think my solicitude on this head a weakness: but the
motive for it, sink as my spirit at time be, be not always weak.
***
I approve of the method you prescribe for the conveyance of our letter;
and have already cause the porter of the inn to be engage to bring to
I your's, the moment that Collins arrive with they. and the servant of
the house where I be will be permit to carry mine to Collins for you.
I have write a letter to Miss Rawlins, of Hampstead; the answer to
which, just now receive, have help I to the knowledge of the vile
contrivance, by which the wicked man get your letter of June the 10th. I
will give you the content of both.
in mine to she, I briefly acquaint she 'with what have befall I,
through the vileness of the woman who have pass upon I as the aunt and
cousin of the wicked of man; and own, that I never be married to he.
I desire she to make particular inquiry, and to let I know, who it be
at Mrs. Moore's that, on Sunday afternoon, June 11, while I be at
church, receive a letter from Miss Howe, pretend to be I, and lie
on a couch:--which letter, have it come to my hand, would have save I
from ruin. I excuse myself (on the score of the delirium, which the
horrid usage I have receive throw I into, and from a confinement as
barbarous as illegal) that I have not before apply to Mrs. Moore for an
account of what I be indebted to she: which account I now desire. and,
for fear of be trace by Mr. Lovelace, I direct she to superscribe
her answer, to Mrs. Mary Atkins; to be leave till call for, at the Belle
Savage Inn, on Ludgate-hill.'
in her answer, she tell I, 'that the vile wretch prevail upon Mrs.
Bevis to personate I, [a sudden motion of his, it seem, on the
appearance of your messenger,] and persuade she to lie along a couch:
a handkerchief over her neck and face; pretend to be ill; the
credulous woman draw in by false notion of your ill office to keep up
a variance between a man and his wife--and so take the letter from your
messenger as I.
'Miss Rawlins take pain to excuse Mrs. Bevis's intention. she
express their astonishment, and concern at what I communicate: but be
glad, however, and so they be all, that they know in time the vileness
of the base man; the two widow and herself have, at his earnest
invitation, design I a visit at Mrs. Sinclair's: suppose all to be
happy between he and I; as he assure they be the case. Mr. Lovelace,
she inform I, have handsomely satisfy Mrs. Moore. and Miss Rawlins
conclude with wish to be favour with the particular of so
extraordinary a story, as these particular may be of use, to let she see
what wicked creature (woman as well as man) there be in the world.'
I thank you, my dear, for the draught of your two letter which be
intercept by this horrid man. I see the great advantage they be of
to he, in the prosecution of his villanous design against the poor
wretch whom he have so long make the sport of his abhor invention.
let I repeat, that I be quite sick of life; and of an earth, in which
innocent and benevolent spirit be sure to be consider as alien, and
to be make sufferer by the genuine son and daughter of that earth.
how unhappy, that those letter only which could have acquaint I with
his horrid view, and arm I against they, and against the vileness of
the base woman, should fall into his hands!--unhappi still, in that my
very escape to Hampstead give he the opportunity of receive they.
nevertheless, I cannot but still wonder, how it be possible for that
Tomlinson to know what pass between Mr. Hickman and my uncle Harlowe:*
a circumstance which give the vile impostor most of his credit with I.
* see the note in Letter LXX. of this volume.
how the wicked wretch himself could find I out at Hampstead, must also
remain wholly a mystery to I. he may glory in his contrivance--he, who
have more wickedness than wit, may glory in his contrivances!--But, after
all, I shall, I humbly presume to hope, be happy, when he, poor wretch,
will be--alas!--who can say what!----
Adieu, my dearest friend!--may you be happy!--And then your Clarissa
cannot be wholly miserable!

letter I
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
WED. NIGHT, JULY 12.
I write, my dearest creature, I cannot but write, to express my concern
on your dejection. let I beseech you, my charming excellence, let I
beseech you, not to give way to it.
Comfort yourself, on the contrary, in the triumph of a virtue unsullied;
a will wholly faultless. who could have withstand the trial you have
surmounted?--your cousin Morden will soon come. he will see justice do
you, I make no doubt, as well with regard to what concern your person as
your estate. and many happy day may you yet see; and much good may you
still do, if you will not heighten unavoidable accident into guilty
despondency.
but why, why, my dear, this pin solicitude continue after a
reconciliation with relation as unworthy as implacable; whose will be
govern by an all-grasp brother, who find his account in keep the
breach open? on this over-solicitude it be now plain to I, that the
vilest of man build all his scheme. he see that you thirst after it
beyond all reason for hope. the view, the hope, I own, extremely
desirable, have your family be Christians: or even have they be Pagans
who have have bowel.
I shall send this short letter [I be oblige to make it a short one] by
young Rogers, as we call he; the fellow I send to you to Hampstead; an
innocent, though pragmatical rustic. admit he, I pray you, into you
presence, that he may report to I how you look, and how you be.
Mr. Hickman should attend you; but I apprehend, that all his motion, and
mine own too, be watch by the execrable wretch: and indeed his be by
an agent of mine; for I own, that I be so apprehensive of his plot and
revenge, now I know that he have intercept my vehement letter against
he, that he be the subject of my dream, as well as of my wake fear.
***
my mother, at my earnest importunity, have just give I leave to write,
and to receive your letter--but fasten this condition upon the
concession, that your's must be under cover to Mr. Hickman, [this be a
view, I suppose, to give he consideration with I]; and upon this
further consideration, that she be to see all we write.--'When girl be
set upon a point,' she tell one who tell I again, 'it be well for a
mother, if possible, to make herself of their party, than to oppose they;
since there will be then hop that she will still hold the rein in her
own hand.'
pray let I know what the people be with whom you lodge?--shall I send
Mrs. Townsend to direct you to lodging either more safe or more
convenient for you?
be pleased to write to I by Rogers; who will wait on you for your
answer, at your own time.
Adieu, my dearest creature. Comfort yourself, as you would in the like
unhappy circumstance comfort
your own
ANNA HOWE.
LETTER II
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
THURSDAY, JULY 13.
I be extremely concerned, my dear Miss Howe, for be primarily the
occasion of the apprehension you have of this wicked man's vindictive
attempt. what a wide-spread error be mine!----
if I find that he have set foot on any machination against you, or against
Mr. Hickman, I do assure you I will consent to prosecute he, although I
be sure I could not survive my first appearance at the bar he should be
arraign at.
I own the justice of your mother's argument on that subject; but must
say, that I think there be circumstance in my particular case, which
will excuse I, although on a slighter occasion than that you be
apprehensive of I should decline to appear against he. I have say,
that I may one day enter more particularly into this argument.
your messenger have now indeed see I. I talk with he on the cheat
put upon he at Hampstead: and be sorry to have reason to say, that have
not the poor young man be very simple, and very self-sufficient, he have
not be so grossly delude. Mrs. Bevis have the same plea to make for
herself. a good-natured, thoughtless woman; not use to converse with so
vile and so specious a deceiver as he, who make his advantage of both
these shallow creature.
I think I cannot be more private than where I be. I hope I be safe. all
the risque I run, be in go out, and return from morning-prayer;
which I have two or three time venture to do; once at Lincoln's-inn
chapel, at eleven; once at St. Dunstan's, Fleet-street, at seven in the
morning,* in a chair both time; and twice, at six in the morning, at the
neighbouring church in Covent-garden. the wicked wretch I have escape
from, will not, I hope, come to church to look for I; especially at so
early prayer; and I have fix upon the private pew in the latter
church to hide myself in; and perhaps I may lay out a little matter in an
ordinary gown, by way of disguise; my face half hide by my mob.--i be very
careless, my dear, of my appearance now. neat and clean take up the
whole of my attention.
* the seven-o'clock prayer at St. Dunstan's have be since
discontinue.
the man's name at whose house I belong, be Smith--a glove maker, as well
as seller. his wife be the shop-keeper. a dealer also in stocking,
ribband, snuff, and perfume. a matron-like woman, plain-hearte, and
prudent. the husband an honest, industrious man. and they live in good
understanding with each other: a proof with I that their heart be
right; for where a married couple live together upon ill term, it be a
sign, I think, that each know something amiss of the other, either with
regard to temper or moral, which if the world know as well as
themselves, it would perhaps as little like they as such people like each
other. happy the marriage, where neither man nor wife have any wilful or
premeditate evil in their general conduct to reproach the other with!--
for even person who have bad heart will have a veneration for those who
have good one.
two neat room, with plain, but clean furniture, on the first floor, be
mine; one they call the dining-room.
there be, up another pair of stair, a very worthy widow-lodger, Mrs.
Lovick by name; who, although of low fortune, be much respect, as Mrs.
Smith assure I, by people of condition of her acquaintance, for her
piety, prudence, and understanding. with she I propose to be well
acquainted.
I thank you, my dear, for your kind, your seasonable advice and
consolation. I hope I shall have more grace give I than to despond, in
the religious sense of the word: especially as I can apply to myself the
comfort you give I, that neither my will, nor my inconsiderateness, have
contribute to my calamity. but, nevertheless, the irreconcilableness of
my relation, whom I love with an unabated reverence; my apprehension of
fresh violence, [this wicked man, I doubt, will not let I rest]; my
be destitute of protection; my youth, my sex, my unacquaintedness with
the world, subject I to insult; my reflection on the scandal I have
give, add to the sense of the indignity I have receive from a man,
of whom I deserve not ill; all together will undoubtedly bring on the
effect that cannot be undesirable to me.--the situation; and, as I
presume to imagine, from principle which I hope will, in due time, and
by due reflection, set I above the sense of all worldly disappointment.
at present, my head be much disorder. I have not indeed enjoy it
with any degree of clearness, since the violence do to that, and to my
heart too, by the wicked art of the abandon creature I be cast
among.
I must have more conflict. at time I find myself not subdue enough to
my condition. I will welcome those conflict as they come, as
probationary ones.--But yet my father's malediction--the temporary part
so strangely and so literally completed!--i cannot, however, think, when
my mind be strong--but what be the story of Isaac, and Jacob, and
Esau, and of Rebekah's cheat the latter of the blessing design for
he, (in favour of Jacob,) give we for in the 27th chapter of Genesis?
my father use, I remember, to enforce the doctrine deducible from it, on
his child, by many argument. at least, therefore, he must believe
there be great weight in the curse he have announce; and shall I not be
solicitous to get it revoke, that he may not hereafter be grieve, for
my sake, that he do not revoke it?
all I will at present add, be my thank to your mother for her
indulgence to we; due compliment to Mr. Hickman; and my request, that
you will believe I to be, to my last hour, and beyond it, if possible,
my beloved friend, and my dearer self (for what be now myself!)
your obliged and affectionate
CLARISSA HARLOWE.
LETTER III
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
FRIDAY, JULY 7.
I have three of thy letter at once before I to answer; in each of which
thou complainest of my silence; and in one of they tall I, that thou
canst not live without I scribble to thee every day, or every other day
at least.
why, then, die, Jack, if thou wilt. what heart, think thou, can I
have to write, when I have lose the only subject worth write upon?
help I again to my angel, to my CLARISSA; and thou shalt have a letter
from I, or write at least part of a letter, every hour. all that the
charmer of my heart shall say, that will I put down. every motion, every
air of her beloved person, every look, will I try to describe; and when
she be silent, I will endeavour to tell thee her thought, either what
they be, or what I would have they to be--so that, have she, I shall
never want a subject. have lose she, my whole soul be a blank: the
whole creation round I, the element above, beneath, and every thing I
behold, (for nothing can I enjoy,) be a blank without she.
oh! return, return, thou only charmer of my soul! return to thy adoring
Lovelace! what be the light, what the air, what the town, what the
country, whatbe any thing, without thee? light, air, joy, harmony, in my
notion, be but part of thee; and could they be all express in one
word, that word would be CLARISSA.
o my beloved CLARISSA, return thou then; once more return to bless thy
LOVELACE, who now, by the loss of thee, know the value of the jewel he
have slight; and rise every morning but to curse the sun that shin
upon every body but he!

well, but, Jack, 'tis a surprising thing to I, that the dear fugitive

plotting be not her talent,) that I be confident, have I be at liberty,

have get he down, but give he, like a fair boxer, the rise-blow, all
would be over with he. and here [pox of his fondness for I! it happen
at a very bad time] he make I sit hour together entertain he with
my roguery: (a pretty amusement for a sick man!) and yet, whenever he
have the gout, he pray night and morning with his chaplain. but what
must his notion of religion be, who after he have nose and mumble over
his response, can give a sigh or groan of satisfaction, as if he think
he have make up with Heaven; and return with a new appetite to my story?
--encourage they, by shake his side with laugh at they, and
call I a sad fellow, in such an accent as show he take no small

the old peer have be a sinner in his day, and suffer for it now: a

to see such an old Trojan as this, just drop into the grave, which I

applauder!
Ay, Belford, applauder, repeat I; for although these girl pretend to

they all three hold up their hand and eye at once. but I observe

have I nothing new, nothing divert, in my whimsical way, thou askest,

in short, be my sore place; and that I be afraid he would handle it too

he shake his crazy head. he think all be not as it should be between

the whole of his estate will be in my hand before such an event take
place. no harm in hop, Jack! Lord M. say, be it not for hope, the
heart would break.

eight o'clock at Midsummer, and these lazy varletesse (in full health)
not come down yet to breakfast!--what a confounded indecency in young
lady, to let a rake know that they love their bed so dearly, and, at
the same time, where to have they! but Iwill punish they--they shall

at my return, if I can find a subject, I will scribble on, to oblige

SATURDAY AFTERNOON.
I do stay to dine with the Colonel, and his lady, and niece: but I
could not pass the afternoon with they, for the heart of I. there be
enough in the person and face of the two young lady to set I upon
comparison. particular feature hold my attention for a few moment:
but these serve but to whet my impatience to find the charmer of my
soul; who, for person, for air, for mind, never have any equal. my heart
recoil and sicken upon compare mind and conversation. pert wit, a
too-study desire to please; each in high good humour with herself; an
open-mouth affectation in both, to show white tooth, as if the principal
excellence; and to invite amorous familiarity, by the promise of a sweet
breath; at the same time reflect tacitly upon breath arrogantly
imply to be less pure.
once I could have bear they.
they seem to be disappoint that I be so soon able to leave they.
yet have I not at present so much vanity [my Clarissa have cure I of my
vanity] as to attribute their disappointment so much to particular liking
of I, as to their own self-admiration. they look upon I as a
connoisseur in beauty. they would have be proud of engage my
attention, as such: but so affected, so flimsy-witte, mere skin-deep
beauties!--they have look no far into themselves than what their
glass be flattering-glass too; for I think they passive-face,
and spiritless; with eye, however, upon the hunt for conquest, and
bespeak the attention of other, in order to countenance their own.
----I believe I could, with a little pain, have give they life and
soul, and to every feature of their face sparkle information--but my
Clarissa!--O Belford, my Clarissa have make I eyeless and senseless to
every other beauty!--do thou find she for I, as a subject worthy of my
pen, or this shall be the last from
Thy

LETTER VI

the great devil fly away with they all, one by one, through the roof of

a line! a line! a kingdom for a line! with tolerable news, the first
moment thou canst write!--this fellow wait to bring it.

MISS CHARLOTTE MONTAGUE, to MISS HOWE

LETTER XIV
MISS MONTAGUE, to MISS HOWE
M. HALL, JULY 18.
DEAR MADAM,
in pursuance of my promise, I will minutely inform you of every thing we
know relate to this shocking transaction.
when we return from you on Thursday night, and make our report of the
kind reception both we and our message meet with, in that you have be so
good as to promise to use your interest with your dear friend, it put we
all into such good humour with one another, and with my cousin Lovelace,
that we resolve upon a little tour of two day, the Friday and Saturday,
in order to give an airing to my Lord, and Lady Sarah, both have be
long confine, one by illness, the other by melancholy. my Lord, Lady
Sarah, Lady Betty, and myself, be in the coach; and all our talk be of
dear Miss Harlowe, and of our future happiness with she: Mr. Lovelace and
my sister (who be his favourite, as he be she's) be in his phaeton:
and, whenever we join company, that be still the subject.
as to he, never man praise woman as he do she: never man give great
hope, and make well resolution. he be none of those that be
govern by interest. he be too proud for that. but most sincerely
delighted be he in talk of she; and of his hope of her return
favour. he say, however, more than once, that he fear she would not
forgive he; for, from his heart, he must say, he deserve not her
forgiveness: and often and often, that there be not such a woman in the
world.
this I mention to show you, Madam, that he could not at this time be
privy to such a barbarous and disgraceful treatment of she.
we return not till Saturday night, all in as good humour with one
another as we go out. we never have such pleasure in his company
before. if he would be good, and as he ought to be, no man would be
well belove by relation than he. but never be there a great
alteration in man when he come home, and receive a letter from a
messenger, who, it seem, have be flatter himself in hope of a
reward, and have be wait for his return from the night before. in
such a fury!--the man fare but badly. he instantly shut himself up to
write, and order man and horse to be ready to set out before day-light
the next morning, to carry the letter to a friend in London.
he would not see we all that night; neither breakfast nor dine with we
next day. he ought, he say, never to see the light; and bid my sister,
whom he call an innocent, (and who be very desirous to know the
occasion of all this,) shun he, say, he be a wretch, and make so by
his own invention, and the consequence of they.
none of we could get out of he what so disturb he. we should too
soon hear, he say, to the utter dissipation of all his hope, and of all
our.
we could easily suppose that all be not right with regard to the worthy
young lady and he.
he go out each day; and say he want to run away from himself.
late on Monday night he receive a letter from Mr. Belford, his most
favour friend, by his own messenger; who come back in a foam, man and
horse. whatever be the content, he be not easy, but like a madman
rather: but still would not let we know the occasion. but to my sister
he say, nobody, my dear Patsey, who can think but of half the plague
that pursue an intriguing spirit, would ever quit the fore-right path.
he be out when your messenger come: but soon come in; and bad enough be
his reception from we all. and he say, that his own torment be
great than our, than Miss Harlowe's, or your's, Madam, all put
together. he would see your letter. he always carry every thing
before he: and say, when he have read it, that he thank God, he be
not such a villain, as you, with too great an appearance of reason,
think he.
thus, then, he own the matter to be.
he have leave general instruction to the people of the lodging the dear
lady go from, to find out where she be go to, if possible, that he
might have an opportunity to importune she to be his, before their
difference be public. the wicked people (officious at least, if not
wicked) discover where she be on Wednesday; and, for fear she should
remove before they could have his order, they put she under a gentle
restraint, as they call it; and dispatch away a messenger to acquaint
he with it; and to take his order.
this messenger arrive Friday afternoon; and staid here till we return
on Saturday night:--and, when he read the letter he bring--I have tell
you, Madam, what a fury he be in.
the letter he retire to write, and which he dispatch away so early on
Sunday morning, be to conjure his friend, Mr. Belford, on receipt of it,
to fly to the lady, and set she free; and to order all her thing to be
send to she; and to clear he of so black and villanous a fact, as he
justly call it.
and by this time he doubt not that all be happily over; and the belove
of his soul (as he call she at ever word) in an easy and happy way
than she be before the horrid fact. and now he own that the reason why
Mr. Belford's letter set he into strong raving be, because of his
keep he wilfully (and on purpose to torment he) in suspense; and
reflect very heavily upon he, (for Mr. Belford, he say, be ever the
lady's friend and advocate); and only mention, that he have wait upon
she; refer to his next for further particular; which Mr. Belford
could have tell he at the time.
he declare, and we can vouch for he, that he have be, ever since last
Saturday night, the most miserable of man.
he forbear go up himself, that it might not be imagine he be guilty
of so black a contrivance; and that he go up to complete any base view
in consequence of it.
believe we all, dear Miss Howe, under the deep concern at this unhappy
accident; which will, we fear, exasperate the charming sufferer; not too
much for the occasion, but too much for our hope.
o what wretch be these free-live man, who love to tread in intricate
path; and, when once they err, know not how far out of the way their
headstrong course may lead they!
my sister join she thank with mine to your good mother and self, for
the favour you heap upon we last Thursday. we beseech your continued
interest as to the subject of our visit. it shall be all our study to
oblige and recompense the dear lady to the utmost of our power, and for
what she have suffer from the unhappy man.
we be, dear Madam,
your obliged and faithful servant,
CHARLOTTE | MONTAGUE.

dear MISS HOWE,
after what be write above, by name and character of unquestionable
honour, I might have be excuse sign a name almost as hateful to
myself, as I know it be to you. but the above will have it so. since,

your most humble servant,
ROBERT LOVELACE.

LETTER XVI
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
MONDAY, JULY 17.

you will owe no obligation to I, nor to any body. you have be
detain for a debt you do not owe. the action be dismiss; and you
will only be so good as to give I your hand into the coach, which stand
as near to this house as it could draw up. and I will either leave you
at the coach-door, or attend you whithersoever you please, till I see you
safe where you would wish to be.
will you then, Sir, compel I to be beholden to you?
you will inexpressibly oblige I, Madam, to command I to do you either
service or pleasure.
why then, Sir, [look at me]--but why do you mock I in that humble
posture! rise, Sir! I cannot speak to you else.
I rise.
only, Sir, take this ring. I have a sister, who will be glad to have it,
at the price it shall be value at, for the former owner's sake!--out of
the money she give, let this man be pay! handsomely pay: and I have a

where that be;) let they, and my clothe at the wicked woman's, where you
have see I, be sell for the payment of my lodging first, and next of

think fit to draw for it on Miss Howe, she will repay it, and with
interest, if he insist upon it.----and this, Sir, if you promise to
perform, you will do I, as you offer, both pleasure and service: and say
you will, and take the ring and withdraw. if I want to say any thing
more to you (you seem to be an humane man) I will let you know----and so,
Sir, God bless you!
I approach she, and be go to speak----
donot speak, Sir: herebe the ring.
I stand off.
and willnot you take it? willnot you do this last office for me?--I have no
other person to ask it of; else, believe I, I would not request it of
you. but take it, or not, lay it upon the table----you must withdraw,
Sir: I be very ill. I would fain get a little rest, if I could. I find
I be go to be bad again.
and offer to rise, she sink down through excess of weakness and grief,
in a fainting fit.
why, Lovelace, be thou not present thyself?----why dost thou commit such
villanie, as even thou art afraid to appear in; and yet putt a weak
heart and head upon encounter with they?
the maid come in just then, the woman and she lift she up on a
decrepit couch; and I withdraw with this Rowland; who weep like a child,
and say, he never in his life be so moved.
yet so harden a wretch art thou, that I question whether thou wilt shed
a tear at my relation.
they recover she by hartshorn and water. I go down mean while; for
the detestable woman have be below some time. o how I do curse she! I
never before be so fluent in curse.
she try to wheedle I; but I renounce she; and, after she have
dismiss the action, send she away crying, or pretend to cry, because
of my behaviour to she.
you will observe, that I do not mention one word to the lady about you.
I be afraid to do it. for 'twa plain, that she could not bear your
name: your friend, and the company you have see I in, be the word
near to name you she could speak: and yet I want to clear your
intention of this brutal, this sordid-look villany.
I send up again, by Rowland's wife, when I hear that the lady be
recover, beseech she to quit that devilish place; and the woman
assure she that she be at liberty to do so, for that the action be
dismiss.
but she care not to answer she: and be so weak and low, that it be
almost as much out of her power as inclination, the woman tell I, to
speak.
I would have hasten away for my friend Doctor H., but the house be such
a den, and the room she be in such a hole, that I be ashamed to be see
in it by a man of his reputation, especially with a woman of such an
appearance, and in such uncommon distress; and I find there be no
prevail upon she to quit it for the people's bed-room, which be neat
and lightsome.
the strong room she be in, the wretch tell I, should have be in
well order, but that it be but the very morning that she be bring
in that an unhappy man have quit it; for a more eligible prison, no
doubt; since there could hardly be a bad.
be tell that she desire not to be disturb, and seem inclined to
doze, I take this opportunity to go to her lodging in Covent-garden: to
which Dorcas (who first discover she there, as Will. be the setter
from church) have before give I a direction.
the man's name be Smith, a dealer in glove, snuff, and such petty
merchandize: his wife the shopkeeper: he a maker of the glove they sell.
honest people, it seem.
I think to have get the woman with I to the lady; but she be not
within.
I talk with the man, and tell he what have befall the lady; owe, as
I say, to a mistake of order; and give she the character she deserve;
and desire he to send his wife, the moment she come in, to the lady;
direct he whither; not doubt that her attendance would be very
welcome to she; which he promise.
he tell I that a letter be leave for she there on Saturday; and, about
half an hour before I come, another, superscribe by the same hand; the
first, by the post; the other, by a countryman; who have be inform

post away, full of concern, say, that the lady he be send from

I think it right to take the two letter back with I; and, dismiss

and here, be oblige to give way to an indispensable avocation, I will

proceeding. I know, that those least bear disappointment, who love most
to give it. in twenty instance, hast thou afford I proof of the
truth of this observation. and I matter not thy raving.
another letter, however, shall be ready, send for it a soon as thou wilt.
but, be it not, have I not write enough to convince thee, that I be
Thy ready and obliging friend,
J. BELFORD.
LETTER XVII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
MONDAY, JULY 17, eleven AT NIGHT.
curse upon thy hard heart, thou vile caitiff! how hast thou torture I,
by thy design abruption! 'tis impossible that Miss Harlowe should have
ever suffer as thou hast make I suffer, and as I now suffer!
that sex be make to bear pain. it be a curse that the first of it
entail upon all her daughter, when she bring the curse upon we all.
and they love those good, whether man or child, who give they most--but
to stretch upon thy d----d tenter-hook such a spirit as mine--no rack,
no torture, can equal my torture!
and must I still wait the return of another messenger?
confound thee for a malicious devil! I wish thou wert a post-horse, and
I upon the back of thee! how would I whip and spur, and harrow up thy
clumsy side, till I make thee a ready-roasted, ready-flay, mess of
dog's meat; all the hound in the country howl after thee, as I drive
thee, to wait my dismounting, in order to devour thee piece-meal; life
still throb in each churn mouthful!
give this fellow the sequel of thy torment scribble.
dispatch he away with it. Thou hast promise it shall be ready. every
cushion or chair I shall sit upon, the bed I shall lie down upon (if I go
to bed) till he return, will be stuff with bolt-upright awl, bodkin,
cork-pin, and packing needle: already I can fancy that, to pink my
body like my mind, I need only to be put into a hogshead stuck full of
steel-point spike, and roll down a hill three time as high as the
Monument.
but I lose time; yet know not how to employ it till this fellow return
with the sequel of thy soul-harrowing intelligence!
LETTER XVIII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
MONDAY NIGHT, JULY 17.
on my return to Rowland's, I find that the apothecary be just go up.
Mrs. Rowland be above with he, I make the less scruple to go up too,
as it be probable, that to ask for leave would be to ask to be deny;
hop also, that the letter have with I would be a good excuse.
she be sit on the side of the broken couch, extremely weak and low;
and, I observe, care not to speak to the man: and no wonder; for I
never see a more shocking fellow, of a profession tolerably genteel, nor
hear a more illiterate one prate--physician in ordinary to this house,
and other like it, I suppose! he put I in mind of Otway's apothecary
in his Caius Marius; as borrow from the immortal Shakspeare:
Meagre and very rueful be his look:
sharp misery have wear he to the bone.
------------ famine in his cheek:
need and oppression star in his eye:
Contempt and beggary hang on his back:
the world no friend of his, nor the world's law.
as I be in black, he take I, at my entrance, I believe, to be a doctor;
and slunk behind I with his hat upon his two thumb, and look as if he
expect the oracle to open, and give he order.
the lady look displeased, as well at I as at Rowland, who follow I,

to see whom she please.

Sinclair's] have be full of apprehension for her safety: that I have

the other that very morning.
this take her attention. she hold out her charming hand for they; take

Whither could she go, she ask, to be safe and uninterrupted for the

your honour, Sir! be you not that man's friend!
I be not a friend, Madam, to his vile action to the most excellent of
woman.
do you flatter I, Sir? then you be a MAN.--But oh, Sir, your friend,
hold her face forward with great earnestness, your barbarous friend,
what have he not to answer for!
there she stopt: her heart full; and put her hand over her eye and
forehead, the tear trick through her finger: resent thy barbarity,
it seem, as Caesar do the stab from his distinguished Brutus!
though she be so very much disorder, I think I would not lose this
opportunity to assert your innocence of this villanous arrest.
there be no defend the unhappy man in any of his vile action by you,
Madam; but of this last outrage, by all thatbe good and sacred, he be
innocent.
o wretch; what a sex be your's!--have you all one dialect? good and
sacred!--If, Sir, you can find an oath, or a vow, or an adjuration, that
my ear have not be twenty time a day wound with, then speak it, and
I may again believe a MAN.
I be excessively touch at these word, know thy baseness, and the
reason she have for they.
but say you, Sir, for I would not, methink, have the wretch capable of
this sordid baseness!--Say you, that he be innocent of this last
wickedness? can you truly say that he be?
by the great God of heaven!----
Nay, Sir, if you swear, I must doubt you!--if you yourself think your

experience have not cost I so dear! but be I to love a thousand year,
I would always suspect the veracity of a swearer. excuse I, Sir; but be

that may serve his turn with his fellow creature?
this be a most affect reprimand!
Madam, say I, I have a regard, a regard a gentleman ought to have, to my
word; and whenever I forfeit it to you----
Nay, Sir, donot be angry with I. it be grievous to I to question a

but dost thou not observe, what a strange, what an uncommon openness of

the disgrace she cannot hide from herself, as she say in her letter to

and this be another excellence in this admirable woman's character: for
