LETTER XIX
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
TUESDAY MORN. JULY 18, SIX O'CLOCK.
have sit up so late to finish and seal in readiness my letter to the
above period, I be disturb before I wish to have rise, by the
arrival of thy second fellow, man and horse in a foam.
while he bait, I will write a few line, most heartily to congratulate
thee on thy expect rage and impatience, and on thy recovery of mental
feeling.
how much do the idea thou givest I of thy deserved torment, by thy
upright awl, bodkin, pin, and packing-needle, by thy roll hogshead
with iron spike, and by thy macerated side, delight I!
I will, upon every occasion that offer, drive more spike into thy
hogshead, and roll thee down hill, and up, as thou recover to sense,
or rather returnest back to senselessness. Thou know therefore the
term on which thou art to enjoy my correspondence. be not I, who have
all along, and in time, protest against thy barbarous and ungrateful
perfidy to a woman so noble, entitle to drive remorse, if possible,
into thy hitherto-callous heart?
only let I repeat one thing, which perhaps I mention too slightly
before. that the lady be determined to remove to new lodging, where
neither you nor I should be able to find she, have I not solemnly assure
she, that she might depend upon be free from your visit.
these assurance I think I might give she, not only because of your
promise, but because it be necessary for you to know where she be, in
order to address yourself to she by your friend.
enable I therefore to make good to she this my solemn engagement; or
adieu to all friendship, at least to all correspondence, with thee for
ever.
J. BELFORD.
LETTER XX
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
TUESDAY, JULY 18. AFTERNOON.
I renew my inquiry after the lady's health, in the morning, by my
servant: and, as soon as I have din, I go myself.
I have but a poor account of it: yet send up my compliment. she return
I thank for all my good office; and her excuse, that they could not
be personal just then, be very low and faint: but if I give myself the
trouble of come about six this evening, she should be able, she hop,
to drink a dish of tea with I, and would then thank I herself.
I be very proud of this condescension; and think it look not amiss for
you, as I be your avow friend. methink I want fully to remove from
her mind all doubt of you in this last villanous action: and who know
then what your noble relation may be able to do for you with she, if you
hold your mind? for your servant acquaint I with their having
actually engage Miss Howe in their and your favour, before this curse
affair happen. and I desire the particular of all from yourself, that
I may the well know how to serve you.
she have two handsome apartment, a bed-chamber and dining-room, with
light closet in each. she have already a nurse, (the people of the house
having but one maid,) a woman whose care, diligence, and honesty, Mrs.
Smith highly commend. she have likewise the benefit of a widow
gentlewoman, Mrs. Lovick her name, who lodge over her apartment, and of
whom she seem very fond, have find something in she, she think,
resemble the quality of her worthy Mrs. Norton.
about seven o'clock this morning, it seem, the lady be so ill, that she
yield to their desire to have an apothecary send for--not the fellow,
thou mayest believe, she have have before at Rowland's; but one Mr.
Goddard, a man of skill and eminence; and of conscience too; demonstrate
as well by general character, as by his prescription to this lady: for
pronounce her case to be grief, he order, for the present, only
innocent julep, by way of cordial; and, as soon as her stomach should be
able to bear it, light kitchen-diet; tell Mrs. Lovick, that that, with
air, moderate exercise, and cheerful company, would do she more good than
all the medicine in his shop.
this have give I, as it seem it have the lady, (who also praise his
modest behaviour, paternal look, and genteel address,) a very good
opinion of the man; and I design to make myself acquainted with he, and,
if he advise to call in a doctor, to wish he, for the fair patient's
sake, more than the physician's, (who want not practice,) my worthy
friend Dr. H.--whose character be above all exception, as his humanity, I
be sure, will distinguish he to the lady.
Mrs. Lovick gratify I with an account of a letter she have write from
the lady's mouth to Miss Howe; she be unable to write herself with
steadiness.
it be to this effect; in answer, it seem, to her two letter, whatever
be the content of they:
'that she have be involve in a dreadful calamity, which she be sure,
when know, would exempt she from the effect of her friendly
displeasure, for not answer she first; have be put under an
arrest.--could she have believe it?--that she be release but the day
before: and be now so weak and so low, that she be oblige to account
thus for her silence to she [Miss Howe's] two letter of the 13th and
16th: that she would, as soon as able, answer they--beg of she, mean
time, not to be uneasy for she; since (only that this be a calamity
which come upon she when she be far from be well, a load lay upon
the shoulder of a poor wretch, ready before to sink under too heavy a
burden) it be nothing to the evil she have before suffer: and one
felicity seem likely to issue from it; which be, that she would be
at rest, in an honest house, with considerate and kind-hearted people;
have assurance give she, that she should not be molest by the
wretch, whom it would be death for she to see: so that now she, [Miss
Howe,] need not to send to she by private and expensive conveyance:
nor need Collins to take precaution for fear of be dog to her
lodging; nor need she write by a fictitious name to she, but by her
own.'
you can see I be in a way to oblige you: you see how much she depend
upon my engaging for your forbearing to intrude yourself into her
company: let not your flame impatience destroy all; and make I look
like a villain to a lady who have reason to suspect every man she see to
be so.--upon this condition, you may expect all the service that can
flow from
your sincere well-wisher,
J. BELFORD.
LETTER XXI
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
TUESDAY NIGHT, JULY 18.
I be just come from the lady. I be admit into the dining-room, where

I then mention your grief, your penitence, your resolution of make

I own I have.
she wish to see it.
this puzzle I horribly: for you must need think that most of the free

Thou rememberest the content, I suppose, of thy furious letter.* her

* see Letter XII. of this volume.

indeed I know not the person, man or woman, I should be so much afraid

at take my leave, I tender my good service to she, and besought she

she make I no answer, but by bow her head.
LETTER XXII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
WEDNESDAY, JULY 19.
this morning I take a chair to Smith's; and, be tell that the lady have
a very bad night, but be up, I send for her worthy apothecary; who, on
his come to I, approve of my proposal of call in Dr. H., I bid
the woman acquaint she with the design visit.
it seem she be at first displease; yet withdraw her objection: but,

Mrs. Lovick say, she have five guineas by she; they be at her service.

have be tell I be below with Mr. Goddard, she desire to speak one

she be sit in an elbow-chair, lean her head on a pillow; Mrs.

hartshorn, behind she; in her own hand her salt.

Lovelace.
I tell she no; and that I believe you never see he in your life.
be the Doctor my friend?
he be; and a very worthy and skilful man. I name he for his eminence

I have but one condition to make before I see the gentleman; that he

be under obligation, you may believe, Sir, I will not. I suffer this

leave, nor obstinate to such of my relation, as may some time hence, for
their private satisfaction, inquire after my behaviour in my sick hour.

ill! and cannot debate the matter.'

question as possible.

benignity which accompany she every graceful look.
I would have retire: but she forbid it.

three O'CLOCK, AFTERNOON.
I just now call again at Smith's; and be tell she be somewhat well;

ADIEU.
LETTER XXIII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
[in answer to letter XXI. of this volume.]
M. HALL, WED. NIGHT, JULY 19.
you might well apprehend that I should think you be play I booty in
communicate my letter to the lady.
you ask, who would think you might not read to she the least
exceptionable part of a letter write in my own defence?--I'll tell you
who--the man who, in the same letter that he ask this question, tell
the friend whom he expose to her resentment, 'that there be such an air
of levity run through his most serious letter, that those of this be
least fit to be see which ought to be most to his credit:' and now what
think thou of thyself-condemn folly? be, however, I charge thee,
more circumspect for the future, that so this clumsy error may stand
singly by itself.
'it be painful to she to think of I!' 'libertine froth!' 'so pernicious
and so despicable a plotter!' 'a man whose friendship be no credit to any
body!' 'hardened wretch!' 'the devil's counterpart!' 'a wicked, wicked
man!'--But do she, could she, dare she, to say, or imply all this?--and
say it to a man whom she praise for humanity, and prefer to myself for
that virtue; when all the humanity he show, and she know it too, be by
my direction--so rob I of the credit of my own work; admirably
entitle, all this show she, to thy refinement upon the word resentment
and revenge. but thou wert always aim and blunder at some thing
thou never couldst make out.
the praise thou givest to her ingenuousness, be another of thy peculiar.
I think not as thou dost, of her tell-tale recapitulation and
exclamations:--what end can they answer?--only that thou hast a holy love
for she, [the devil fetch thee for thy oddity!] or it be extremely
provoking to suppose one see such a charming creature stand upright
before a libertine, and talk of the sin against she, that cannot be
forgiven!--i wish, at my heart, that these chaste lady would have a
little modesty in their anger!--it would sound very strange, if I Robert
Lovelace should pretend to have more true delicacy, in a point that
require the utmost, than Miss Clarissa Harlowe.
I think I will put it into the head of her nurse Norton, and her Miss
Howe, by some one of my agent, to chide the dear novice for her
proclamation.
but to be serious: let I tell thee, that, severe as she be, and saucy,
in ask so contemptuously, 'what a man be your friend, Sir, to set
himself to punish guilty people!' I will never forgive the cursed woman,
who could commit this last horrid violence on so excellent a creature.
the barbarous insult of the two nymph, in their visit to she; the
choice of the most execrable den that could be find out, in order, no
doubt, to induce she to go back to theirs; and the still more execrable
attempt, to propose to she a man who would pay the debt; a snare, I make
no question, lay for her despairing and resent heart by that devilish
Sally, (think she, no doubt, a woman,) in order to ruin she with I;
and to provoke I, in a fury, to give she up to their remorseless
cruelty; be outrage, that, to express myself in her style, I never can,
never will forgive.
but as to thy opinion, and the two woman's at Smith's, that her heart be
break! that be the true woman's language: I wonder how thou cam into
it: thou who hast see and hear of so many female death and revival.
Iwill tell thee what make against this notion of theirs.
her time of life, and charming constitution: the good she ever delight
to do, and fancifie she be bear to do; and which she may still continue
to do, to as high a degree as ever; nay, high: since I be no sordid
varlet, thou know: her religious turn: a turn that will always teach
she to bear inevitable evil with patience: the contemplation upon she
last noble triumph over I, and over the whole crew; and upon she
succeed escape from we all: she will unviolate: and the inward pride
of have not deserve the treatment she have meet with.
how be it possible to imagine, that a woman, who have all these
consolation to reflect upon, will die of a broken heart?
on the contrary, I make no doubt, but that, as she recover from the
dejection into which this last scurvy villany (which none but wretch
of her own sex could have be guilty of) have throw she, return love
will re-enter her time-pacify mind: her thought will then turn once
more on the conjugal pivot: of course she will have lively notion in
her head; and these will make she perform all her circumvolution with
ease and pleasure; though not with so high a degree of either, as if the
dear proud rogue could have exalt herself above the rest of her sex, as
she turn round.
Thou askest, on recite the bitter invective that the lady make against
thy poor friend, (stand before she, I suppose, with thy finger in thy
mouth,) what couldst thou say for I?
have I not, in my former letter, suggest an hundred thing, which a
friend, in earnest to vindicate or excuse a friend, might say on such an
occasion?
but now to current topic, and the present state of matter here.--it be
true, as my servant tell thee, that Miss Howe have engage, before this
cursed woman's officiousness, to use her interest with her friend in my
behalf: and yet she tell my cousin, in the visit they make she, that it
be her opinion that she would never forgive I. I send to thee enclosed
copy of all that pass on this occasion between my cousin Montague,
Miss Howe, myself, Lady Betty, Lady Sarah, and Lord M.

MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE

what, my dearest creature, have be your sufferings!--what must have

LETTER XXV
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
THURSDAY AFTERNOON.
you pain I, Miss Howe, by the ardour of your noble friendship. I will
be brief, because I be not well; yet a good deal well than I be; and
because I be prepare an answer to your' of the 13th. but, before
hand, I must tell you, my dear, I will not have that man--don't be angry
with I. but indeed I willnot. so let he be ask no question about I,
I beseech you.
I do not despond, my dear. I hope I may say, I will not despond. be not
my condition greatly mend? I thank Heaven it be!
I be no prisoner now in a vile house. I be not now in the power of that
man's device. I be not now oblige to hide myself in corner for fear
of he. one of his intimate companion be become my warm friend, and
engage to keep he from I, and that by his own consent. I be among
honest people. I have all my clothe and effect restore to I. the
wretch himself bear testimony to my honour.
indeed I be very weak and ill: but I have an excellent physician, Dr. H.
and as worthy an apothecary, Mr. Goddard.--Their treatment of I, my
dear, be perfectly paternal!--my mind too, I can find, begin to
strengthen: and methink, at time, I find myself superior to my
calamity.
I shall have sinking sometimes. I must expect such. and my father's
maledict----But you will chide I for introduce that, now I be
enumerate my comfort.
but I charge you, my dear, that you do not suffer my calamity to sit
too heavily upon your own mind. if you do, that will be to new-point
some of those arrow that have be blunt and lose their sharpness.
if you would contribute to my happiness, give way, my dear, to your own;
and to the cheerful prospect before you!
you will think very meanly of your Clarissa, if you do not believe, that
the great pleasure she can receive in this life be in your prosperity
and welfare. think not of I, my only friend, but as we be in time
past: and suppose I go a great, great way off!--a long journey!----How
often be the dearest of friend, at their country's call, thus parted--
with a certainty for year--with a probability for ever.
love I still, however. but let it be with a weaning love. I be not what
I be, when we be inseparable lover, as I may say.--our view must now
be different--Resolve, my dear, to make a worthy man happy, because a
worthy man make you so.--and so, my dearest love, for the present adieu!
--adieu, my dear love!--but I shall soon write again, I hope!
LETTER XXVI
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
[in answer to LETTER XXIII. of this volume.]
THURDAY, JULY 20.
I read that part of your conclusion to poor Belton, where you inquire
after he, and mention how merrily you and the reset pass your time at
M. Hall. he fetch a deep sigh: you be all very happy! be his word.
--I be sorry they be his word; for, poor fellow, he be go very
fast. change of air, he hop, will mend he, join to the cheerful
company I have leave he in. but nothing, I dare say, will.
a consume malady, and a consume mistress, to an indulgent keeper, be
dreadful thing to struggle with both together: violence must be use to
get rid of the latter; and yet he have not spirit enough leave he to exert
himself. his house be Thomasine's house; not his. he have not be
within his door for a fortnight past. vagabond about from inn to
inn; enter each for a bait only; and stay two or three day without
power to remove; and hardly know which to go to next. his malady be
within he; and he cannot run away from it.
her boy (once he think they his) be sturdy enough to shoulder he in
his own house as they pass by he. side with the mother, they in a
manner expel he; and, in his absence, riot away on the remnant of his
break fortune. as to their mother, (who be once so tender, so
submissive, so studious to oblige, that we all pronounce he happy, and
his course of life the eligible,) she be now so termagant, so insolent,
that he cannot contend with she, without do infinite prejudice to his
health. a break-spirited defensive, hardly a defensive, therefore,
reduce to: and this to a heart, for so many year wag offensive war,
(not value whom the opponent,) what a reduction! now compare himself
to the superannuated lion in the fable, kick in the jaw, and lay
sprawling, by the spurning heel of an ignoble ass!
I have undertake his cause. he have give I leave, yet not without
reluctance, to put he into possession of his own house; and to place in
it for he his unhappy sister, whom he have hitherto slight, because
unhappy. it be hard, he tell I, (and wept, poor fellow, when he say
it,) that he cannot be permit to die quietly in his own house!--The
fruit of bless keeping these!----
Though but lately apprize of her infidelity, it now come out to have
be of so long continuance, that he have no room to believe the boy to
be his: yet how fond do he use to be of they!
to what, Lovelace, shall we attribute the tenderness which a repute
father frequently show to the child of another man?--what be that, I
pray thee, which we call nature, and natural affection? and what have man
to boast of as to sagacity and penetration, when he be as easily bring
to cover and rear, and even to love, and often to prefer, the product of
another's guilt with his wife or mistress, as a hen or a goose the egg,
and even young, of other of their kind?
Nay, let I ask, if instinct, as it be call, in the animal creation,
do not enable they to distinguish their own, much more easily than we,
with our boasted reason and sagacity, in this nice particular, can do?
if some man, who have wife but of doubtful virtue, consider this
matter duly, I believe their inordinate ardour after gain would be a good
deal cool, when they could not be certain (though their mate could)
for whose child they be elbow, bustling, griping, and perhaps
cheating, those with whom they have concern, whether friend,
neighbour, or more certain next-of-kin, by the mother's side however.
but I will not push this notion so far as it might be carry; because,
if propagate, it might be of unsocial or unnatural consequence; since
woman of virtue would perhaps be more liable to suffer by the mistrust
and caprice or bad-hearted and foolish-head husband, than those who
can screen themselves from detection by art and hypocrisy, to which a
woman of virtue cannot have recourse. and yet, be this notion duly and
generally consider, it might be attend with no bad effect; as good
education, good inclination, and establish virtue, would be the
principally-seek-after quality; and not money, when a man (not
bias by mere personal attraction) be look round he for a partner
in his fortune, and for a mother of his future child, which be to be
the heir of his possession, and to enjoy the fruit of his industry.
but to return to poor Belton.
if I have occasion for your assistance, and that of our compeer, in
re-instate the poor fellow, I will give you notice. mean time, I have
just now be tell that Thomasine declare she will not stir; for, it
seem, she suspect that measure will be fall upon to make she quit.
she be Mrs. Belton, she say, and will prove her marriage.
if she would give herself these air in his life-time, what would she
attempt to do after his death?
her boy threaten any body who shall presume to insult their mother.
their father (as they call poor Belton) they speak of as an unnatural
one. and their probably true father be for ever there, hostilely there,
pass for her cousin, as usual: now her protect cousin.
hardly ever, I dare say, be there a keeper that do not make
keeperess; who lavish away on her kept-fellow what she obtain from
the extravagant folly of he who keep she.
I will do without you, if I can. the case will be only, as I conceive,
that like of the ancient Sarmatians, their wife then in possession of
their slave. so that they have to contend not only with those wife,
conscious of their infidelity, and with their slave, but with the
child of those slave, grow up to manhood, resolute to defend their
mother and their long-manumit father. but the noble Sarmatians,
scorn to attack their slave with equal weapon, only provide
themselves with the same sort of whip with which they use formerly to
chastise they. and attack they with they, the miscreant flee before
them.--In memory of which, to this day, the device on the coin in
Novogrod, in Russia, a city of the antient Sarmatia, be a man on
horseback, with a whip in his hand.
the poor fellow take it ill, that you do not press he more than you
do to be of your party at M. Hall. it be owe to Mowbray, he be sure,
that he have so very slight an invitation from one whose invitation use
to be so warm.
Mowbray's speech to he, he say, he never will forgive: 'why, Tom,' say
the brutal fellow, with a curse, 'thou droop like a pip or
roup-cloak chicken. Thou shouldst grow perter, or submit to a
solitary quarantine, if thou wouldst not infect the whole brood.'
for my own part, only that this poor fellow be in distress, as well in
his affair as in his mind, or I should be sick of you all. such be the
relish I have of the conversation, and such my admiration of the
deportment and sentiment of this divine lady, that I would forego a
month, even of thy company, to be admit into she's but for one hour:
and I be highly in conceit with myself, greatly as I use to value thine,
for be able, spontaneously as I may say, to make this preference.
it be, after all, a devilish life we have live. and to consider how it
all end in a very few year--to see to what a state of ill health this
poor fellow be so soon reduce--and then to observe how every one of ye
run away from the unhappy being, as rat from a fall house, be fine
comfort to help a man to look back upon companion ill-choose, and a life
mis-spend!
it will be your turn by-and-by, every man of ye, if the justice of your
country interpose not.
thou art the only rake we have herd with, if thou wilt not except
thyself, who hast preserve entire thy health and thy fortune.
Mowbray indeed be indebted to a robust constitution that he have not yet
suffer in his health; but his estate be dwindle away year by year.
three-fourth of Tourville's very considerable fortune be already
dissipate; and the remain fourth will probably soon go after the
other three.
Poor Belton! we see how it be with him!--his own felicity be, that he
will hardly live to want.
thou art too proud, and too prudent, ever to be destitute; and, to do
thee justice, hath a spirit to assist such of thy friend as may be
reduce; and wilt, if thou shouldest then be live. but I think thou
must, much soon than thou imagin, be call to thy account--knock
on the head perhaps by the friend of those whom thou hast injure; for
if thou escap this fate from the Harlowe family, thou wilt go on
tempting danger and vengeance, till thou meet with vengeance; and
this, whether thou marriest, or not: for the nuptial life will not, I
doubt, till age join with it, cure thee of that spirit for intrigue which
be continually run away with thee, in spite of thy well sense, and
transitory resolution.
well, then, I will suppose thee lay down quietly among thy worthy
ancestor.
and now let I look forward to the end of Tourville and Mowbray, [Belton
will be crumble into dust before thee, perhaps,] suppose thy early
exit have save thee from gallow intervention.
reduce, probably, by riotous waste to consequential want, behold they
refuge in some obscene hole or garret; oblige to the careless care of
some dirty old woman, whom nothing but her poverty prevail upon to
attend to perform the last office for man, who have make such shocking
ravage among the young one.
then how miserably will they whine through squeaking organ; their big
voice turn into pule pity-beg lamentation! their now-offensive
paw, how helpless then!--their now-erect neck then deny support to
their ache head; those globe of mischief drop upon their quaking
shoulder. then what wry face will they make! their heart, and their
head, reproach each other!--distende their parch mouths!--sunk
their unmuscled cheeks!--dropt their under jaws!--each grunt like the
swine he have resemble in his life! oh! what a vile wretch have I be!
oh! that I have my life to come over again!--confessing to the poor old
woman, who cannot shrive they! imaginary ghost of deflower virgin,
and polluted matron, flit before their glassy eye! and old Satan,
to their apprehension, grin behind a look-glass hold up before
they, to frighten they with the horror visible in their own countenance!
for my own part, if I can get some good family to credit I with a sister
or daughter, as I have now an increase fortune, which will enable I to
propose handsome settlement, I will desert ye all; marry, and live a
life of reason, rather than a life of a brute, for the time to come.
LETTER XXVII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
THURSDAY NIGHT.
I be force to take back my twenty guineas. how the woman manage it I
cannot tell, (I suppose they too readily find a purchaser for the rich
suit;) but she mistrust, that I be the advancer of the money; and
would not let the clothe go. but Mrs. Lovick have actually sell, for
fifteen guineas, some rich lace worth three time the sum; out of which
she repay she the money she borrow for fee to the doctor, in an
illness occasion by the barbarity of the most savage of man. Thou
know his name!
the doctor call on she in the morning it seem, and have a short debate
with she about fee. she insist that he should take one every time he
come, write or not write; mistrust that he only give verbal direction
to Mrs. Lovick, or the nurse, to avoid take any.
he say that it would be impossible for he, have he not be a physician,
to forbear inquiry after the health and welfare of so excellent a
person. he have not the thought of pay she a compliment in decline
the offer fee: but he know her case could not so suddenly vary as to
demand his daily visit. she must permit he, therefore, to inquire of
the woman below after her health; and he must not think of come up, if
he be to be pecuniarily reward for the satisfaction he be so
desirous to give himself.
it end in a compromise for a fee each other time; which she unwillingly
submit to; tell he, that though she be at present desolate and in
disgrace, yet her circumstance be, of right, high; and no expense
could rise so as to be scruple, whether she live or die. but she
submit, she add, to the compromise, in hope to see he as often as
he have opportunity; for she really look upon he, and Mr. Goddard, from
their kind and tender treatment of she, with a regard next to filial.
I hope thou wilt make thyself acquainted with this worthy doctor when
thou com to town; and give he thy thank, for put she into
conceit with the sex that thou hast give she so much reason to execrate.
Farewell.
LETTER XXVIII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
M. HALL, FRIDAY, JULY 21.

LETTER XXIX
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
[in answer to letter XXII. XXVI. XXVII. of this volume.]
FRIDAY NIGHT, JULY 21.
I will throw away a few paragraph upon the content of thy last shocking
letter just bring I; and send what I shall write by the fellow who
carry mine on the interview with Hickman.
Reformation, I see, be come fast upon thee. Thy uncle's slow death,
and thy attendance upon he through every stage towards it, prepare thee
for it. but go thou on in thine own way, as I will in mine. happiness
consist in be pleased with what we do: and if thou canst find delight
in be sad, it will be as well for thee as if thou wert merry, though
no other person should join to keep thee in countenance.
I be, nevertheless, exceedingly disturb at the lady's ill health. it
be entirely owe to the curse arrest. she be absolutely triumphant
over I and the whole crew before. Thou believest I guiltless of that:
so, I hope, do she.--the rest, as I have often say, be a common case;
only a little uncommonly circumstanced; thatbe all: why, then, all these
severe thing from she, and from thee?
as to sell her clothe, and her lace, and so forth, it have, I own, a
shocking sound to it. what an implacable as well as unjust set of
wretch be those of her unkindredly kin, who have money of shebe in
their hand, as well as large arrear of her own estate; yet with-hold
both, avowedly to distress she! but may she not have money of that proud
and saucy friend of she's, Miss Howe, more than she wants?--and should
not I be overjoy, think thou, to serve her?----what then be there in
the parting with her apparel but female perverseness?--and I be not sure,
whether I ought not to be glad, if she do this out of spite to me.--
some disappointed fair-one would have hang, some drown themselves.
my beloved only revenge herself upon her clothe. different way of
working have passion in different bosom, as humour or complexion induce.
--beside, dost think I shall grudge to replace, to three time the
value, what she dispose of? so, Jack, there be no great matter in this.
Thou se how sensible she be of the soothing of the polite doctor:
this will enable thee to judge how dreadfully the horrid arrest, and her
gloomy father's curse, must have hurt she. I have great hope, if she
will but see I, that my behaviour, my contrition, my soothing, may have
some happy effect upon she.
but thou art too ready to give up. let I seriously tell thee that, all
excellence as she be, I think the earnest interposition of my relation;
the implored mediation of that little fury Miss Howe; and the commission
thou actest under from myself; be such instance of condescension and
high value in they, and such contrition in I, that nothing far can
be done.--So here let the matter rest for the present, till she consider
well of it.
but now a few word upon poor Belton's case. I own I be at first a
little startled at the disloyalty of his Thomasine. her hypocrisy to be
for so many year undetected!--i have very lately have some intimation
give I of her vileness; and have intend to mention they to thee when I
see thee. to say the truth, I always suspect her eye: the eye, thou
knowest, be the casement at which the heart generally look out. many
a woman, who will not show herself at the door, have tipt the sly, the
intelligible wink from the window.
but Tom. have no management at all. a very careless fellow. would never

LETTER XXX

LETTER XXXII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
SATURDAY, JULY 22.
what dost hate I for, Belford!--and why more and more! have I be
guilty of any offence thou knew not before?--if pathos can move such a
heart as thine, can it alter facts!--did I not always do this
incomparable creature as much justice as thou canst do she for the heart
of thee, or as she can do herself?----what nonsense then thy hatred, thy
augment hatred, when I still persist to marry she, pursuant to word
give to thee, and to faith plight to all my relation? but hate, if

do myself: and yet I know if thou really hatedst I, thou wouldst not
venture to tell I so.
well, but after all, what need of her history to these woman? she will

both.
Sickness pall every appetite, and make we hate what we love: but
renew health change the scene; dispose we to be pleased with
ourselves; and then we be in a way to be pleased with every one else.
every hope, then, rise upon we: every hour present itself to we on
dancing foot: and what Mr. Addison say of liberty, may, with still
great propriety, be say of health, for what be liberty itself without
health?
it make the gloomy face of nature gay;
give beauty to the sun, and pleasure to the day.
and I rejoice that she be already so much well, as to hold with
stranger such a long and interesting conversation.

mine, who offend she by act in character, while her parent act

even in common conversation, from the lip of this ever-charming

she not only bring I a father, but make I one: and then, be

into Navarre; I into Italy: both well inclined to propagate the good
lesson in which we have so well instruct each other.
but to return. one consolation arise to I, from the pretty regret
which this admirable creature seem to have in indulge reflection on
the people's wedding-day.--i ONCE!--thou makest she break off with
say.
she once! what--o Belford! why didst thou not urge she to explain what
she once hop?
what once a woman hop, in love matter, she always hop, while there
be room for hope: and be we not both single? can she be any man's but
mine? will I be any woman's but shebe?
I never will! I never can!--and I tell thee, that I be every day, every
hour, more and more in love with she: and, at this instant, have a more
vehement passion for she than ever I have in my life!--and that with view
absolutely honourable, in her own sense of the word: nor have I varied,
so much as in wish, for this week past; firmly fix, and work into my
very nature, as the life of honour, or of generous confidence in I, be,
in preference to the life of doubt and distrust. that must be a life of
doubt and distrust, surely, where the woman confide nothing, and tie up
a man for his good behaviour for life, take church-and-state sanction
in aid of the obligation she impose upon he.
I shall go on Monday to a kind of ball, to which Colonel Ambrose have
invite I. it be give on a family account. I care not on what: for
all that delight I in the thing be, that Mrs. and Miss Howe be to be
there;--Hickman, of course; for the old lady will not stir abroad without
he. the Colonel be in hope that Miss Arabella Harlowe will be there
likewise; for all the man and woman of fashion round he be invite.
I fall in by accident with the Colonel, who I believe, hardly think I
would accept of the invitation. but he know I not, if he think I be
ashamed to appear at any place, where woman dare show their face. yet
he hint to I that my name be up, on Miss Harlowe's account. but, to
allude to one of Lord M.'s phrase, if it be, I will not lie a bed when
any thing joyous be go forward.
as I shall go in my Lord's chariot, I would have have one of my cousin
Montague to go with I: but they both refuse: and I shall not choose to
take either of thy brother. it would look as if I think I want a
bodyguard: besides, one of they be too rough, the other too smooth, and
too great a fop for some of the staid company that will be there; and for
I in particular. man be know by their companion; and a fop [as
Tourville, for example] take great pain to hang out a sign by his dress
of what he have in his shop. Thou, indeed, art an exception; dress
like a coxcomb, yet a very clever fellow. nevertheless so clumsy a beau,
that thou seemest to I to owe thyself a double spite, make thy
ungracefulness appear the more ungraceful, by thy remarkable tawdriness,
when thou art out of mourning.
I remember, when I first see thee, my mind labour with a strong puzzle,
whether I should put thee down for a great fool, or a smatterer in wit.
something I see be wrong in thee, by thy dress. if this fellow, think
I, delight not so much in ridicule, that he will not spare himself, he
must be plaguy silly to take so much pain to make his ugliness more
conspicuous than it would otherwise be.
plain dress, for an ordinary man or woman, imply at least modesty, and
always procure a kind quarter from the censorious. who will ridicule a
personal imperfection in one that seem conscious, that it be an
imperfection? who ever say an anchoret be poor? but who would spare
so very absurd a wrong-head, as should bestow tinsel to make his
deformity the more conspicuous?
but, although I put on these lively air, I be sick at my soul!--my whole
heart be with my charmer! with what indifference shall I look upon all
the assembly at the Colonel's, my beloved in my ideal eye, and engross
my whole heart?

MISS HARLOWE,
I cannot help acquaint you (however it may be receive, come from

your humble servant,

I send you, enclose, copy of five letter that have pass between

only one we have to complain of; but we be silent on the other, as
they do not, as these have do, spread themselves out upon paper. we
only beg, that we may not be reflect upon by a young lady who know not
what we have suffer, and do suffer by the rashness of a naughty
creature who have bring ruin upon herself, and disgrace upon a family
which she have rob of all comfort. I offer not to prescribe to your
know wisdom in this case; but leave it to you to do as you think most
proper. I be, Madam,
your most humble servant,
charl. HARLOWE.
LETTER XXXIX
MRS. HOWE
[in ANSWER.]

DEAR MADAM,
I be highly offended with my daughter's letter to Miss Harlowe. I know
nothing at all of she have take such a liberty. these young creature
have such romantic notion, some of live, some of friendship, that there
be no govern they in either. nothing but time, and dear experience,
will convince they of their absurdity in both. I have chide Miss
Howe very severely. I have before so just a notion of what your whole
family's distress must be, that, as I tell your brother, Mr. Antony
Harlowe, I have often forbid she correspond with the poor fall angel
--for surely never do young lady more resemble what we imagine of
angel, both in person and mind. but, tired out with her headstrong
way, [I be sorry to say this of my own child,] I be force to give way
to it again. and, indeed, so sturdy be she in her will, that I be
afraid it would end in a fit of sickness, as too often it do in fit of
sullen.
none but parent know the trouble that child give. they be happy,
I have often think, who have none. and these woman-grow girl, bless
my heart! how ungovernable!
I believe, however, you will have no more such letter from my Nancy. I
have be force to use compulsion with she upon Miss Clary's illness,
[and it seem she be very bad,] or she would have run away to London, to
attend upon she: and this she call do the duty of a friend;
forget that she sacrifice to her romantic friendship her duty to her
fond indulgent mother.
there be a thousand excellency in the poor sufferer, notwithstanding
her fault: and, if the hint she have give to my daughter be true, she
have be most grievously abuse. but I think your forgiveness and her
father's forgiveness of she ought to be all at your own choice; and
nobody should intermeddle in that, for the sake of due authority in
parent: and besides, as Miss Harlowe write, it be what every body
expect, though Miss Clary would not believe it till she smart for her
credulity. and, fir these reason, I offer not to plead any thing in
alleviation of her fault, which be aggravate by her admirable sense, and
a judgment above her year.
I be, Madam, with compliment to good Mr. Harlowe, and all your afflict
family,
your most humble servant,
ANNABELLA HOWE.
I shall set out for the Isle of Wight in a few day, with my daughter. I
will hasten our set out, on purpose to break her mind from her
friend's distress; which afflict we as much, nearly, as Miss
Clary's rashness have do you.

what pain, my dear friend, do your kind solicitude for my welfare

(my dear and only love,) that I will do every thing I can to prolong my
life, till God, in mercy to I, shall be pleased to call for it. I have
reason to think my punishment be but the due consequence of my fault, and
I will not run away from it; but beg of Heaven to sanctify it to I.
when appetite serve, I will eat and drink what be sufficient to support
nature. a very little, you know, will do for that. and whatever my
physician shall think fit to prescribe, I will take, though ever so
disagreeable. in short, I will do every thing I can do to convince all
my friend, who hereafter may think it worth their while to inquire after
my last behaviour, that I possess my soul with tolerable patience; and
endeavour to bear with a lot of my own drawing; for thus, in humble
imitation of the sublime exemplar, I often say:--Lord, it be thy will;
and it shall be mine. thou art just in all thy dealing with the
child of man; and I know thou wilt not afflict I beyond what I can
bear: and, if I can bear it, I ought to bear it; and (thy grace assist
I) I will bear it.
'but here, my dear, be another reason; a reason that will convince you
yourself that I ought not to think of wedlock; but of a preparation for a
quite different event. I be persuade, as much as that I be now alive,
that I shall not long live. the strong sense I have ever have of my
fault, the loss of my reputation, my disappointment, the determine
resentment of my friend, aid the barbarous usage I have meet with
where I least deserve it, have seize upon my heart: seize upon it,
before it be so well fortify by religious consideration as I hope it
now be. donot be concern, my dear--but I be sure, if I may say it with
as little presumption as grief, that God will soon dissolve my substance;
and bring I to death, and to the house appoint for all live.'
and now, my dear friend, you know all my mind. and you will be
pleased to write to the lady of Mr. Lovelace's family, that I think
myself infinitely oblige to they for their good opinion of I; and that
it have give I great pleasure than I think I have to come in this
life, that, upon the little knowledge they have of I, and that not
personal, I be think worthy (after the ill usage I have receive) of
an alliance with their honourable family: but that I can by no mean
think of their kinsman for a husband: and do you, my dear, extract from
the above such reason as you think have any weight with they.
I would write myself to acknowledge their favour, have I not more
employment for my head, my heart, and my finger, than I doubt they will
be able to go through.
I should be glad to know when you set out on your journey; as also your
little stage; and your time of stay at your aunt Harman's; that my
prayer may locally attend you whithersoever you go, and wherever you
be.
CLARISSA HARLOWE.

LETTER XLIV
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MRS. NORTON
MONDAY NIGHT, JULY 24.
MY DEAR MRS. NORTON,
have I not fall into fresh trouble, which disable I for several day
from hold a pen, I should not have forborne inquire after your
health, and that of your son; for I should have be but too ready to
impute your silence to the cause to which, to my very great concern, I
find it be owe. I pray to Heaven, my dear good friend, to give you
comfort in the way most desirable to yourself.
I be exceedingly concerned at Miss Howe's writing about I to my friend.
I do assure you, that I be as ignorant of her intention so to do as of
the content of her letter. nor have she yet let I know (discourage, I
suppose, by her ill success) that she do write. it be impossible to
share the delight which such charming spirit give, without the
inconvenience that will attend their volatility.--So mixed be our good
enjoyment!
it be but yesterday that I write to chide the dear creature for freedom
of that nature, which her unseasonably-express love for I have make she
take, as you write I word in your former. I be afraid that all such
freedom would be attribute to I. and I be sure that nothing but my
own application to my friend, and a full conviction of my contrition,
will procure I favour. Least of all can I expect that either your
mediation or shebe (both of whose fond and partial love of I be so well
know) will avail I.
[she then give a brief account of the arrest: of her dejection under it:
of her apprehension of be carry to her former lodging: of
Mr. Lovelace's avow innocence as to that insult: of her release
by Mr. Belford: of Mr. Lovelace's promise not to molest she: of her
clothe be send she: of the earnest desire of all his friend,

now, my dear Mrs. Norton, you will be surprised, perhaps, that I should
have return such an answer: but when you have every thing before you,
you, who know I so well, will not think I wrong. and, besides, I be
upon a well preparation than for an earthly husband.
nor let it be imagine, my dear and ever venerable friend, that my
present turn of mind proceed from gloominess or melancholy; for although
it be bring on by disappointment, (the world show I early, even at
my first rush into it, its true and ugly face,) yet I hope that it have
obtain a well root, and will every day more and more, by its fruit,
demonstrate to I, and to all my friend, that it have.
I have write to my sister. last Friday I write. so the die be throw.
I hope for a gentle answer. but, perhaps, they will not vouchsafe I
any. it be my first direct application, you know. I wish Miss Howe have
leave I to my own working in this tender point.
it will be a great satisfaction to I to hear of your perfect recovery;
and that my foster-brother be out of danger. but why, say I, out of
danger?--When can this be justly say of creature, who hold by so
uncertain a tenure? this be one of those form of common speech, that
prove the frailty and the presumption of poor mortal at the same time.
donot be uneasy, you cannot answer your wish to be with I. I be
happy than I could have expect to be among mere stranger. it be
grievous at first; but use reconcile every thing to we. the people of
the house where I be be courteous and honest. there be a widow who
lodge in it [have I not say so formerly?] a good woman; who be the
well for have be a proficient in the school of affliction.
an excellent school! my dear Mrs. Norton, in which we be teach to know
ourselves, to be able to compassionate and bear with one another, and to
look up to a well hope.
I have as humane a physician, (whose fee be his least regard,) and as
worthy an apothecary, as ever patient be visit by. my nurse be
diligent, obliging, silent, and sober. so I be not unhappy without: and
within--I hope, my dear Mrs. Norton, that I shall be every day more and
more happy within.
no doubt it would be one of the great comfort I could know to have
you with I: you, who love I so dearly: who have be the watchful
sustainer of my helpless infancy: you, by whose precept I have be so
much benefited!--in your dear bosom could I repose all my grief: and by
your piety and experience in the way of Heaven, should I be strengthen
in what I be still to go through.
but, as it must not be, I will acquiesce; and so, I hope, will you: for
you see in what respect I be not unhappy; and in those that I be, they
lie not in your power to remedy.
then as I have tell you, I have all my clothe in my own possession. so
I be rich enough, as to this world, in common conveniencie.
you see, my venerable and dear friend, that I be not always turn the
dark side of my prospect, in order to move compassion; a trick impute

as to the day--I have pass it, as I ought to pass it. it have be a

how do they use to pass it!--what a festivity!--how have they now pass

suffer so much for my fault; and who, for eighteen year together,

think the rest!--adieu, my dearest Mrs. Norton!--
Adieu!

LETTER XLVI
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
[in answer to letter XXIX. XXXII. of this volume.]
EDGWARE, MONDAY, JULY 24.
what pain thou takest to persuade thyself, that the lady's ill health
be owe to the vile arrest, and to the implacableness of her friend.
both primarily (if they be) to be lay at thy door. what poor excuse
will good heart make for the evil they be put upon by bad hearts!--But
'tis no wonder that he who can sit down premeditatedly to do a bad
action, will content himself with a bad excuse: and yet what fool must
he suppose the rest of the world to be, if he imagine they as easy to be
impose upon as he can impose upon himself?
in vain dost thou impute to pride or wilfulness the necessity to which
thou hast reduce this lady of part with her clothe; for can she do
otherwise, and be the noble-minded creature she be?
her implacable friend have refuse she the current cash she leave behind
she; and wish, as her sister write to she, to see she reduce to want:
probably therefore they will not be sorry that she be reduce to such
straight; and will take it for a justification from Heaven of their
wicked hard heartedness. thou canst not suppose she would take supply
from thee: to take they from I would, in her opinion, be take they
from thee. Miss Howe's mother be an avaricious woman; and, perhaps, the
daughter can do nothing of that sort unknown to she; and, if she could,
be too noble a girl to deny it, if charge. and then Miss Harlowe be
firmly of opinion, that she shall never want nor wear the think she
dispose of.
have hear nothing from town that oblige I to go thither, I shall
gratify poor Belton with my company till to-morrow, or perhaps till
Wednesday. for the unhappy man be more and more loth to part with I.
I shall soon set out for Epsom, to endeavour to serve he there, and
re-instate he in his own house. poor fellow! he be most horribly low
spirit; mope about; and nothing divert he. I pity he at my heart;
but can do he no good.--what consolation can I give he, either from his
past life, or from his future prospect?
our friendship and intimacy, Lovelace, be only calculate for strong
life and health. when sickness come, we look round we, and upon one
another, like fright bird, at the sight of a kite ready to souse upon
they. then, with all our bravery, what miserable wretch be we!
Thou tall I that thou seest reformation be come swiftly upon I. I
hope it be. I see so much difference in the behaviour of this admirable
woman in her illness, and that of poor Belton in his, that it be plain to
I the sinner be the real coward, and the saint the true hero; and,
soon or later, we shall all find it to be so, if we be not cut off
suddenly.
the lady shut herself up at six o'clock yesterday afternoon; and intend
not to see company till seven or eight this; not even her nurse--impose
upon herself a severe fast. and why? it be her BIRTH-DAY!--Every
birth-day till this, no doubt, happy!--what must be her reflections!--
what ought to be thine!
what sport dost thou make with my aspiration, and my prostration, as
thou call they; and with my dropping of the banknote behind her chair!
I have too much awe of she at the time, to make it with the grace that
would well have become my intention. but the action, if awkward, be
modest. indeed, the fitter subject for ridicule with thee; who canst no
more taste the beauty and delicacy of modest obligingness than of modest
love. for the same may be say of inviolable respect, that the poet say
of unfeigned affection,
I speak! I know not what!--
speak ever so: and if I answer you
I know not what, it show the more of love.
Love be a child that talk in broken language;
yet then it speak most plain.
the like may be plead in behalf of that modest respect which make the
humble offerer afraid to invade the awful eye, or the revere hand; but
awkwardly to drop its incense behind the altar it should have be lay
upon. but how should that soul, which could treat delicacy itself
brutally, know any thing of this!
but I be still more amazed at thy courage, to think of throw thyself
in the way of Miss Howe, and Miss Arabella Harlowe!--Thou wilt not dare,
surely, to carry this thought into execution!
as to my dress, and thy dress, I have only to say, that the sum total of
thy observation be this: that my outside be the bad of I; and thine
the good of thee: and what gett thou by the comparison? do thou
reform the one, Iwill try to mend the other. I challenge thee to begin.
Mrs. Lovick give I, at my request, the copy of a meditation she show
I, which be extract by the lady from the scripture, while under
arrest at Rowland's, as appear by the date. the lady be not to know
that I have take a copy.
you and I always admire the noble simplicity, and natural ease and
dignity of style, which be the distinguish characteristic of these
book, whenever any passage from they, by way of quotation in the work
of other author, popt upon we. and once I remember you, even you,
observe, that those passage always appear to you like a rich vein of

try, Lovelace, if thou canst relish a divine beauty. I think it must

meditation
Saturday, July 15.
o that my grief be thoroughly weigh, and my calamity lay in the
balance together!
for now it would be heavy than the sand of the sea: therefore my word
be swallow up!
for the arrow of the Almighty be within I; the poison whereof drinketh
up my spirit. the terror of God do set themselves in array against I.
when I lie down, I say, when shall I arise? when will the night be go?
and I be full of tossing to and fro, unto the dawning of the day.
my day be swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and be spend without hope--
mine eye shall no more see good.
wherefore be light give to she that be in misery; and life unto the
bitter in soul?
who longeth for death; but it cometh not; and diggeth for it more than
for hid treasure?
why be light give to one whose way be hide; and whom God hath hedge in?
for the thing which I greatly fear be come upon I!
I be not in safety; neither have I rest; neither be I quiet; yet trouble
come.
but behold God be mighty, and despiseth not any.
he giveth right to the poor--and if they be find in fetter, and holden
in cord of affliction, then he showeth they their work and their
transgression.
I have a little leisure, and be in a scribbing vein: indulge I,
Lovelace, a few reflection on these sacred book.
we be teach to read the Bible, when child, as a rudiment only; and,
as far as I know, this may be the reason why we think ourselves above it
when at a mature age. for you know that our parent, as well as we,
wisely rate our proficiency by the book we be advanced to, and not by
our understanding of those we have pass through. but, in my uncle's
illness, I have the curiosity, in some of my dull hour, (light upon
one in his closet,) to dip into it: and then I find, wherever I turn,
that there be admirable thing in it. I have borrow one, on
receive from Mrs. Lovick the above meditation; for I have a mind to
compare the passage contain in it by the book, hardly believe they
could be so exceedingly apposite as I find they be. and one time or
another, it be very likely, that I shall make a resolution to give the
whole Bible a perusal, by way of course, as I may say.
this, meantime, I will venture to repeat, be certain, that the style be
that truly easy, simple, and natural one, which we should admire in each
other author excessively. then all the world join in an opinion of the
antiquity, and authenticity too, of the book; and the learn be fond of
strengthen their different argument by its sanction. indeed, I be
so much take with it at my uncle's, that I be half ashamed that it
appear so new to I. and yet, I cannot but say, that I have some of
the Old Testament history, as it be call, in my head: but, perhaps, be
more obliged for it to Josephus than to the Bible itself.
odd enough, with all our pride of learning, that we choose to derive the
little we know from the under current, perhaps muddy one too, when the
clear, the pellucid fountain-head, be much near at hand, and easy to
be come at--slight the more, possibly, for that very reason!
but man be a pragmatical, foolish creature; and the more we look into
he, the more we must despise he--lord of the creation!--who can
forbear indignant laughter! when we see not one of the individual of
that creation (his perpetually-eccentric self excepted) but act within
its own natural and original appointment: be of fancied and
self-dependent excellence, he be oblige not only for the ornament, but
for the necessary of life, (that be to say, for food as well as
raiment,) to all the other creature; strut with their blood and
spirit in his vein, and with their plumage on his back: for what have he
of his own, but a very mischievous, monkey-like, bad nature! yet think
himself at liberty to kick, and cuff, and elbow out every worthy
creature: and when he have none of the animal creation to hunt down and
abuse, will make use of his power, his strength, or his wealth, to
oppress the less powerful and weak of his own specie!
when you and I meet next, let we enter more largely into this subject:
and, I dare say, we shall take it by turn, in imitation of the two sage
of antiquity, to laugh and to weep at the thought of what miserable, yet
conceited being, man in general, but we libertine in particular, be.
I fall upon a piece at Dorrell's, this very evening, intitule, the
Sacred Classics, write by one Blackwell.
I take it home with I, and have not read a dozen page, when I be
convince that I ought to be ashamed of myself to think how greatly I
have admire less noble and less natural beauty in Pagan author; while
I have know nothing of this all-exciting collection of beauty, the
Bible! by my faith, Lovelace, I shall for the future have a well
opinion of the good sense and taste of half a score of parson, whom I
have fall in with in my time, and despise for magnifying, as I think
they do, the language and the sentiment to be find in it, in
preference to all the ancient poet and philosopher. and this be now a
convincing proof to I, and sham as much an infidel's presumption as
his ignorance, that those who know least be the great scoffer. a
pretty pack of would-be wit of we, who censure without knowledge, laugh
without reason, and be most noisy and loud against thing we know least
of!
LETTER XLVII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
WEDNESDAY, JULY 26.
I come not to town till this morning early: poor Belton cling to I,
as a man destitute of all other hold.
I hasten to Smith's, and have but a very indifferent account of the
lady's health. I send up my compliment; and she desire to see I in
the afternoon.
Mrs. Lovick tell I, that after I go away on Saturday, she actually
part with one of her good suit of clothe to a gentlewoman who be she
[Mrs. Lovick's] benefactress, and who buy they for a niece who be very
speedily to be marry, and whom she fit out and portion as her
intended heiress. the lady be so jealous that the money might come from
you or I, that she would see the purchaser: who own to Mrs. Lovick
that she buy they for half their worth: but yet, though her conscience
permit she to take they at such an under rate, the widow say she
friend admire the lady, as one of the lovely of her sex: and have
be let into a little of her story, could not help shed tear at
take away her purchase.
she may be a good sort of woman: Mrs. Lovick say she be: but self be an
odious devil, that reconcile to some people the most cruel and dishonest
action. but, nevertheless, it be my opinion, that those who can suffer
themselves to take advantage of the necessity of their
fellow-creature, in order to buy any thing at a less rate than would
allow they the legal interest of their purchase-money (suppose they
purchase before they want) be no well than robber for the difference.
--to plunder a wreck, and to rob at a fire, be indeed high degree of
wickedness: but do not those, as well as these, heighten the distress
of the distressed, and heap misery on the miserable, whom it be the duty
of every one to relieve?
about three o'clock I go again to Smith's. the lady be write when I
send up my name; but admit of my visit. I see a miserable alteration
in her countenance for the bad; and Mrs. Lovick respectfully accuse
she of too great assiduity to her pen, early and late, and of her
abstinence the day before, I take notice of the alteration; and tell she,

LETTER XLVIII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
THURSDAY, JULY 27.
I go this morning, accord to the lady's invitation, to breakfast,
and find Mr. Hickman with she.
a good deal of heaviness and concern hang upon his countenance: but he
receive I with more respect than he do yesterday; which, I presume,
be owe to the lady's favourable character of I.
he speak very little; for I suppose they have all their talk out
yesterday, and before I come this morning.
by the hint that drop, I perceive that Miss Howe's letter give an
account of your interview with she at Col. Ambrose's--of your profession
to Miss Howe; and Miss Howe's opinion, that marry you be the only way
now leave to repair her wrong.
Mr. Hickman, as I also gather, have press she, in Miss Howe's name, to
let she, on her return from the Isle of Wight, find she at a neighbouring
farm-house, where neat apartment would be make ready to receive she.
she ask how long it would be before they return? and he tell she, it
be propose to be no more than a fortnight out and in. upon which she
say, she should then perhaps have time to consider of that kind
proposal.
he have tender her money from Miss Howe; but could not induce she to
take any. no wonder I be refuse! she only say, that, if she have
occasion, she would be oblige to nobody but Miss Howe.
Mr. Goddard, her apothecary, come in before breakfast be over. at her

any consolation in relation to Miss Harlowe's recovery, to carry down to
a friend who love she as she love her own life?

herself. indeed you will, Madam. the doctor be entirely of this
opinion; and have order nothing for you but weak jelly and innocent
cordial, lest you should starve yourself. and let I tell you, Madam,
that so much watching, so little nourishment, and so much grief, as you
seem to indulge, be enough to impair the most vigorous health, and to
wear out the strong constitution.
what, Sir, say she, can I do? I have no appetite. nothing you call
nourishing will stay on my stomach. I do what I can: and have such kind
director in Dr. H. and you, that I should be inexcusable if I do not.
Iwill give you a regimen, Madam, reply he; which, I be sure, the doctor
will approve of, and will make physic unnecessary in your case. and that
be, 'go to rest at ten at night. rise not till seven in the morning.
let your breakfast be watergruel, or milk-pottage, or weak broth: your
dinner any thing you like, so you will but eat: a dish of tea, with milk,
in the afternoon; and sago for your supper: and, my life for your's, this
diet, and a month's country air, will set you up.'
we be much pleased with the worthy gentleman's disinterested regimen:
and she say, refer to her nurse, (who vouch for she,) pray, Mr.
Hickman, let Miss Howe know the good hand I be in: and as to the kind
charge of the gentleman, assure she, that all I promise to she, in the
long of my two last letter, on the subject of my health, I do and
will, to the utmost of my power, observe. I have engage, Sir, (to Mr.
Goddard,) I have engage, Sir, (to I,) to Miss Howe, to avoid all wilful
neglect. it would be an unpardonable fault, and very ill become the
character I would be glad to deserve, or the temper of mind I wish my
friend hereafter to think I mistress of, if I do not.
Mr. Hickman and I go afterwards to a neighbour coffee-house; and he
give I some account of your behaviour at the ball on Monday night, and
of your treatment of he in the conference he have with you before that;
which he represent in a more favourable light than you have do
yourself: and yet he give his sentiment of you with great freedom, but
with the politeness of a gentleman.
he tell I how very determined the lady be against marry you; that
she have, early this morning, set herself to write a letter to Miss Howe,
in answer to one he bring she, which he be to call for at twelve, it
be almost finish before he see she at breakfast; and that at three
he propose to set out on his return.
he tell I that Miss Howe, and her mother, and himself, be to begin

recover; and hop he should find it favourable.

can.
this gentleman be a little finical and formal. modest or diffident man

ever they have they, presently get above; because they be too confident
to doubt any thing. but I think Mr. Hickman be an agreeable, sensible
man, and not at all deserve of the treatment or the character you give

but you be really a strange mortal: because you have advantage in your
person, in your air, and intellect, above all the man I know, and a face
that would deceive the devil, you cannot think any man else tolerable.
it be upon this modest principle that thou deridest some of we, who, not
have thy confidence in their outside appearance, seek to hide their

sort of a sign must thou hang out, wert thou oblige to give we a clear
idea by it of the furniture of thy mind?
Mr. Hickman tell I, he should have be happy with Miss Howe some week
ago, (for all the settlement have be some time engross;) but that
she will not marry, she declare, while her dear friend be so unhappy.
this be truly a charming instance of the force of female friendship;
which you and I, and our brother rake, have constantly ridicule as a
chimerical thing in woman of equal age, and perfection.
but really, Lovelace, I see more and more that there be not in the
world, with our conceited pride, narrower-soule wretch than we rake
and libertine be. and Iwill tell thee how it come about.
our early love of roguery make we generally run away from instruction;
and so we become mere smatterer in the science we be put to learn;
and, because we will know no more, think there be no more to be know.
with an infinite deal of vanity, un-rein imagination, and no judgment
at all, we next commence half-wit, and then think we have the whole
field of knowledge in possession, and despise every one who take more
pain, and be more serious, than ourselves, as phlegmatic, stupid
fellow, who have no taste for the most poignant pleasure of life.
this make we insufferable to man of modesty and merit, and oblige we to
herd with those of our own cast; and by this mean we have no
opportunity of see or converse with any body who could or would
show we what we be; and so we conclude that we be the clever fellow
in the world, and the only man of spirit in it; and look down with
supercilious eye on all who give not themselves the liberty we take,
imagine the world make for we, and for we only.
thus, as to useful knowledge, while other go to the bottom, we only skim
the surface; be despise by people of solid sense, of true honour, and
superior talent; and shut our eye, move round and round, like so
many blind mill-horse, in one narrow circle, while we imagine we have
all the world to range in.

Pr'ythee tell I, thou vile Lovelace, if thou hast not a notion, even
from these jejune description of mine, that there must be a more exalted
pleasure in intellectual friendship, than ever thou couldst taste in the
gross fume of sensuality? and whether it may not be possible for thee,
in time, to give that preference to the infinitely preferable, which I
hope, now, that I shall always give?
I will leave thee to make the most of this reflection, from
thy true friend,
J. BELFORD.

LETTER LII

before the cry could go off the other: why may I not, therefore, curse
and applaud thee in the same moment? so take both in one: and what
follow, as it shall rise from my pen.

how often have I ingenuously confess my sin against this excellent

celebrate he.

have reason to compliment thyself on thy penetration.

I could make some pretty observation upon one or two place of the
lady's mediation: but, wicked as I be think to be, I never be so

sacre. I think it the high degree of ill manner to jest upon those
subject which the world in general look upon with veneration, and call
divine. I would not even treat the mythology of the heathen to a
heathen, with the ridicule that perhaps would fairly lie from some of the
absurdity that strike every common observer. nor, when at Rome, and in
other popish country, do I ever behave indecently at those ceremony
which I think very extraordinary: for I see some people affect, and
seemingly edify, by they; and I content myself to think, though they
be any good end to the many, there be religion enough in they, or
civil policy at least, to exempt they from the ridicule of even a bad man
who have common sense and good manner.
for the like reason I have never give noisy or tumultuous instance of
dislike to a new play, if I think it ever so indifferent: for I
conclude, first, that every one be entitle to see quietly what he pay

performance exhibit as would not please somebody in that mixed
multitude: and, if it do, those somebody have as much right to enjoy
their own judgment, undisturbedly, as I have to enjoy mine.
this be my way of show my disapprobation; I never go again. and as
a man be at his option, whether he will go to a play or not, he have not
the same excuse for express his dislike clamorously as if he be
compel to see it.
I have ever, thou know, declare against those shallow libertine, who

there again be preachment for thy preachment; and thou wilt be apt to

Iwill tell thee a short story, which I have from my tutor, admonish I
against expose myself by ignorant wonder, when I should quit college,

'the first time Dryden's Alexander's Feast fall into his hand, he tell
I, he be prodigiously charm with it: and, have never hear any body
speak of it before, think, as thou dost of the Bible, that he have make
a new discovery.
'he hasten to an appointment which he have with several wit, (for he
be then in town,) one of whom be a noted critic, who, accord to he,
have more merit than good fortune; for all the little nibbler in wit,
whose writing would not stand the test of criticism, make it, he say, a
common cause to run he down, as man would a mad dog.
'the young gentleman (for young he then be) set forth magnificently in
the praise of that inimitable performance; and give himself air of
second-hand merit, for find out its beauty.
'the old bard hear he out with a smile, which the collegian take for
approbation, till he speak; and then it be in these mortifying word:
'Sdeath, Sir, where have you live till now, or with what sort of company
have you converse, young as you be, that you have never before hear of
the fine piece in the English language?'
this story have such an effect upon I, who have ever a proud heart, and
want to be think a clever fellow, that, in order to avoid the like
disgrace, I lay down two rule to myself. the first, whenever I go
into company where there be stranger, to hear every one of they speak,
before I give myself liberty to prate: the other, if I find any of they
above my match, to give up all title to new discovery, content
myself to praise what they praise, as beauty familiar to I, though I
have never hear of they before. and so, by degree, I get the reputation
of a wit myself: and when I throw off all restraint, and book, and
learn conversation, and fall in with some of our brother who be now
wander in Erebus, and with such other as Belton, Mowbray, Tourville,
and thyself, I set up on my own stock; and, like what we have be tell
of Sir Richard, in his latter day, value myself on be the emperor of
the company; for, have fathom the depth of they all, and afraid of no
rival but thee, whom also I have get a little under, (by my gaiety and
promptitude at least) I proudly, like Addison's Cato, delight to give
law to my little senate.
proceed with thee by-and-by.

LETTER LIV
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE

FRIDAY NIGHT, JULY 28.
I will now, my dear friend, write to you all my mind, without reserve,
on your resolution not to have this vilest of man. you give I, in
your' of Sunday the 23d, reason so worthy of the pure mind of my
Clarissa, in support of this your resolution, that nothing but self-love,
lest I should lose my ever-amiable friend, could have prevail upon I

indeed, I think it be impossible there could be (however desirable) so
noble an instance give by any of our sex, of a passion conquer, when

be prevail upon by the solicitation of his friend, before you carry
your resentment to so great a height, that it would be more difficult

first.
but now, my dear, that I see you fix in your noble resolution; and that
it be impossible for your pure mind to join itself with that of so
perjure a miscreant; I congratulate you most heartily upon it; and beg
your pardon for but seem to doubt that theory and practice be not
the same thing with my beloved Clarissa.
I have only one thing that sadden my heart on this occasion; and that
be, the bad state of health Mr. Hickman (unwillingly) own you be in.
Hitherto you have well observe the doctrine you always lay down to I,
that a cursed person should first seek the world's opinion of she; and,

first to the last; and be, of consequence, well justify to your own
heart, as well as to your Anna Howe. let I therefore beseech you to

and this, as what, if it can be effect, will crown the work, and show
the world, that you be indeed get above the base wretch; and, though
put out of your course for a little while, could resume it again, and go
on blessing all within your knowledge, as well by your example as by your
precept.
for Heaven's sake, then, for the world's sake, for the honour of our sex,
and for my sake, once more I beseech you, try to overcome this shock:
and, if you can overcome it, I shall then be as happy as I wish to be;
for I cannot, indeed I cannot, think of part with you, for many, many
year to come.
the reason you give for discourage my wish to have you near we be

dear, when your mind be fully settle, as, (now you be so absolutely

LETTER LXI
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE

you have give I great pleasure, my dear friend, by your approbation
of my reasoning, and of my resolution found upon they, never to have

have be be she to be indifferent to he.

they be, and no doubt will long be, unhappy.

'here be my mother, one of the most prudent person of her sex, marry

LETTER LXII
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HARLOWE
SATURDAY, JULY 29.
I repine not, my dear Sister, at the severity you have be pleased to
express in the letter you favour I with; because that severity be
accompany with the grace I have petition for; and because the
reproach of mine own heart be strong than any other person's
reproach can be: and yet I be not half so culpable as I be imagine
to be: as would be allow, if all the circumstance of my unhappy story
be know: and which I shall be ready to communicate to Mrs. Norton, if
she be commission to inquire into they; or to you, my Sister, if you
can have patience to hear they.
I remember with a bleed heart what day the 24th of July be. I begin
with the eve of it; and I pass the day itself--as it be fit I should
pass it. nor have I any comfort to give to my dear and ever-honour
father and mother, and to you, my Bella, but this--that, as it be the
first unhappy anniversary of my birth, in all probability, it will be the
last.
believe I, my dear Sister, I say not this merely to move compassion, but
from the good ground. and as, on that account, I think it of the
high importance to my peace of mind to obtain one far favour, I
would choose to owe to your intercession, as my sister, the leave I beg,
to address half a dozen line (with the hope of have they answer as I
wish) to either or to both my honoured parent, to beg their last
blessing.
this blessing be all the favour I have now to ask: it be all I dare to
ask: yet be I afraid to rush at once, though by letter, into the presence
of either. and if I do not ask it, it might seem to be owe to
stubbornness and want of duty, when my heart be all humility
penitence. only, be so good as to embolden I to attempt this task--
write but this one line, 'Clary Harlowe, you be at liberty to write as
you desire.' this will be enough--and shall, to my last hour, be
acknowledge as the great favour, by
your truly penitent sister,
CLARISSA HARLOWE.
LETTER LXIII
MRS. NORTON, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
MONDAY, JULY 31.
my dearest YOUNG LADY,
I must indeed own that I take the liberty to write to your mother,
offer to enclose to she, if she give I leave, your' of the 24th: by
which I think she would see what be the state of your mind; what the
nature of your last trouble be from the wicked arrest; what the people

the term she write in, disturb you--but, as you have take the matter
