affair unknown to you, I be glad the letter be not require of I--and
indeed it may be well that the matter lie wholly between you and they;
since my affection for you be think to proceed from partiality.
they would choose, no doubt, that you should owe to themselves, and not
to my humble mediation, the favour for which you so earnestly sue, and of
which I would not have your despair: for I will venture to assure you,
that your mother be ready to take the first opportunity to show her
maternal tenderness: and this I gather from several hint I be not at
liberty to explain myself upon.
I long to be with you, now I be well, and now my son be in a fair way
of recovery. but be it not hard to have it signify to I that at
present it will not be take well if I go?--i suppose, while the
reconciliation, which I hope will take place, be negotiate by mean of
the correspondence so newly open between you and your sister. but if
you will have I come, I will rely on my good intention, and risque
every one's displeasure.
Mr. Brand have business in town; to solicit for a benefice which it be
expect the incumbent will be oblige to quit for a well preferment:
and, when there, he be to inquire privately after your way of life, and
of your health.
he be a very officious young man; and, but that your uncle Harlowe (who
have choose he for this errand) regard he as an oracle, your mother have
rather any body else have be send.
he be one of those puzzling, over-do gentleman, who think they see
far into matter than any body else, and be fond of discover
mystery where there be none, in order to be think shrewd man.
I cannot say I like he, either in the pulpit or out of it: I, who have a
father one of the sound divine and fine scholar in the kingdom;
who never make an ostentation of what he know; but love and venerate he
gospel he teach, prefer it to all other learning: to be oblige to
hear a young man depart from his text as soon as he have name it, (so
contrary, too, to the example set he by his learn and worthy
principal,* when his health permit he to preach;) and throw about,
to a christian and country audience, scrap of Latin and Greek from the
Pagan Classics; and not always bring in with great propriety neither,
(if I be to judge by the only way give I to judge of they, by the
English he put they into;) be an indication of something wrong, either
in his head, or his heart, or both; for, otherwise, his education at the
university must have teach he well. you know, my dear Miss Clary,
the honour I have for the cloth: it be owe to that, that I say what I
do.
* Dr. Lewen.
I know not the day he be to set out; and, as his inquiry be to be
private, be pleased to take no notice of this intelligence. I have no
doubt that your life and conversation be such as may defy the scrutiny
of the most officious inquirer.
I be just now tell that you have write a second letter to your sister:
but be afraid they will wait for Mr. Brand's report, before far
favour will be obtain from they; for they will not yet believe you be

but you would soon find that you have an indulgent mother, be she at

hope that all will end well at last: for I verily think you be in the
right way to a reconciliation. God give a blessing to it, and restore
your health, and you to all your friend, pray
your ever affectionate,
JUDITH NORTON.
your mother have privately send I five guineas: she be pleased to say to

MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MRS. NORTON

you give I, my dear Mrs. Norton, great pleasure in hearing of your' and

you tell I that you do actually write to my mother, offer to enclose

eye of those dear friend whom I have so grievously offended. 'tis only,
simply, a blessing I ask: a blessing to die with; not to lie with.--do
they know that? and do they know that their unkindness will perhaps
shorten my date; so that their favour, if ever they intend to grant it,
may come too late?
once more, I desire you not to think of come to I. I have no
uneasiness now, but what proceed from the apprehension of see a man I
would not see for the world, if I could help it; and from the severity of
my near and dear relation: a severity entirely their own, I doubt;
for you tell I that my brother be at Edinburgh! you would therefore
heighten their severity, and make yourself enemy besides, if you be
to come to I--don't you see you would?
Mr. Brand may come, if he will. he be a clergyman, and must mean well;
or I must think so, let he say of I what he will. all my fear be,
that, as he know I be in disgrace with a family whose esteem he be
desirous to cultivate; and as he have obligation to my uncle Harlowe and
to my father; he will be but a languid acquitter--not that I be afraid of
what he, or any body in the world, can hear as to my conduct. you may,
my revered and dear friend, indeed you may, rest satisfied, that that be
such as may warrant I to challenge the inquiry of the most officious.
I will send you copy of what pass, as you desire, when I have an
answer to my second letter. I now begin to wish that I have take the
heart to write to my father himself; or to my mother, at least; instead
of to my sister; and yet I doubt my poor mother can do nothing for I of
herself. a strong confederacy, my dear Mrs. Norton, (a strong
confederacy indeed!) against a poor girl, their daughter, sister, niece!
--My brother, perhaps, get it renew before he leave they. he need
not--his work be do; and more than do.
donot afflict yourself about money-matter on my account. I have no
occasion for money. I be glad my mother be so considerate to you. I
be in pain for you on the same subject. but Heaven will not permit so
good a woman to want the humble blessing she be always satisfied with.
I wish every individual of our family be but as rich as you!--O my
mamma Norton, you be rich! you be rich indeed!--the true rich be
such content as you be bless with.--and I hope in God that I be in the
way to be rich too.
Adieu, my ever-indulgent friend. you say all will be at last happy--and
I know it will--I confide that it will, with as much security, as you
may, that I will be, to my last hour,
your ever grateful and affectionate
CL. HARLOWE.
LETTER LXV
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
TUESDAY, AUG. 1.
I be most confoundedly chagrin and disappoint: for here, on Saturday,
arrive a messenger from Miss Howe, with a letter to my cousin;* which I
know nothing of till yesterday; when Lady Sarah and Lady Betty be

favour upon her own term, if I could? and be it fair to punish I for
what be my misfortune, and not my fault? such event-judge fool as I
have for my relation! I be ashamed of they all.
* see Letter LV. of this volume.
in that of Miss Howe be enclose one to she from Miss Harlowe,* to be
transmit to my cousin, contain a final rejection of I; and that
in very vehement and positive term; yet she pretend that, in this
rejection, she be govern more by principle than passion--[d----d lie,

more--the whole letter so write as to make herself more admired, I

* see Letter XLI. of this volume.
what we have be tell of the agitation and working, and sighing and

I now swear it over again to thee--'were her death to follow in a week
after the knot be tie, by the Lord of Heaven, it shall be tie, and she
shall die a Lovelace!'--Tell she so, if thou wilt: but, at the same time,

guilty of any sordid view to her fortune.--let her judge for herself,
then, whether it be not for her honour rather to leave this world a
Lovelace than a Harlowe.
but do not think I will entirely rest a cause so near my heart upon an

my cousin Charlotte, find I write on with too much earnestness to
have any regard for politeness to she, and guess at my subject,
besought I to let she see what I have write.
I oblige she. and she be so highly pleased on see I so much in

every one approve of it, as well as I; and be pleased with I for so

but if she persist, and will not promise to take time to consider of the

I have great dependence upon thy zeal and thy friendship: hasten back to

equally the subject of my dream, as of my wake hour.
LETTER LXVI
MISS MONTAGUE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
TUESDAY, AUG. 1.
DEAREST MADAM,
all our family be deeply sensible of the injury you have receive at
the hand of one of it, whom you only can render in any manner worthy of
the relation he stand in to we all: and if, as an act of mercy and
charity, the great your pious heart can show, you will be pleased to
look over his past wickedness and ingratitude, and suffer yourself to be
our kinswoman, you will make we the happy family in the world: and I
can engage, that Lord M., and Lady Sarah Sadleir, and Lady Betty
Lawrance, and my sister, who be all admirer of your virtue, and of
your nobleness of mind, will for ever love and reverence you, and do
every thing in all their power to make you amend for what you have
suffer from Mr. Lovelace. this, Madam, we should not, however, dare
to petition for, be we not assure, that Mr. Lovelace be most sincerely
sorry for his past vileness to you; and that he will, on his knee, beg
your pardon, and vow eternal love and honour to you.
wherefore, my dear cousin, [how you will charm we all, if this
agreeable style may be permit!] for all our sake, for his soul's
sake, [you must, I be sure, be so good a lady, as to wish to save a
soul!] and allow I to say, for your own fame's sake, condescend to our
joint request: and if, by way of encouragement, you will but say you will
be glad to see, and to be as much know personally, as you be by fame,
to Charlotte Montague, I will, in two day' time from the receipt of your

DEAR MADAM,
I be infinitely oblige to you for your kind and condescending letter. a
letter, however, which heighten my regret, as it give I a new
instance of what a happy creature I might have be in an alliance so
much approve of by such worthy lady; and which, on their account, and
on that of Lord M. would have be so reputable to myself, and be once
so desirable.
but indeed, indeed, Madam, my heart sincerely repulse the man who,
descend from such a family, could be guilty, first, of such
premeditate violence as he have be guilty of; and, as he know, far
intend I, on the night previous to the day he set out for Berkshire;
and, next, pretend to spirit, could be so mean as to wish to lift into
that family a person he be capable of abase into a companionship with
the most abandon of her sex.
allow I then, dear Madam, to declare with favour, that I think I never
could be rank with the lady of a family so splendid and so noble, if,
by vow love and honour at the altar to such a violator, I could
sanctify, as I may say, his unprecedented and elaborate wickedness.
permit I, however, to make one request to my good Lord M., and to Lady
Betty, and Lady Sarah, and to your kind self, and your sister.--it be,
that you will all be pleased to join your authority and interest to
prevail upon Mr. Lovelace not to molest I far.
be pleased to tell he, that, if I be design for life, it will be very
cruel in he to attempt to hunt I out of it; for I be determined never
to see he more, if I can help it. the more cruel, because he know that
I have nobody to defend I from he: nor do I wish to engage any body to
his hurt, or to their own.
if I be, on the other hand, destine for death, it will be no less cruel,
if he will not permit I to die in peace--since a peaceable and happy end
I wish he; indeed I do.
every worldly good attend you, dear Madam, and every branch of the
honourable family, be the wish of one, whose misfortune it be that she be
oblige to disclaim any other title than that of,
Dear Madam,
your and their obliged and faithful servant,
CLARISSA HARLOWE.

SIR,
I hold myself extremely oblige to you for your communication. I will

I must own, in his favour, that he have observe some decency in his

understanding may succeed in the vile attempt, if they can once bring

judge of the integrity of other' heart by its own.

arabella HARLOWE.

SATURDAY, AUG. 5
HONOURED MADAM,
no self-convict criminal ever approach her angry and just judge with
great awe, nor with a truer contrition, than I do you by these line.
indeed I must say, that if the latter of my humble prayer have not
respect my future welfare, I have not dare to take this liberty. but
my heart be set upon it, as upon a thing next to God Almighty's
forgiveness necessary for I.
have my happy sister know my distress, she would not have wring my
heart, as she have do, by a severity, which I must need think unkind
and unsisterly.
but complaint of any unkindness from she belong not to I: yet, as she
be pleased to write that it must be see that my penitence be less owing
to disappointment than to true conviction, permit I, Madam, to insist
upon it, that, if such a plea can be allow I, I an actually entitle
to the blessing I sue for; since my humble prayer be found upon a true
and unfeigned repentance: and this you will the readier believe, if the
creature who never, to the good of her remembrance, tell her mamma a
wilful falsehood may be credit, when she declare, as she do, in the
most solemn manner, that she meet the seducer with a determination not to
go off with he: that the rash step be owe more to compulsion than to
infatuation: and that her heart be so little in it, that she repent
and grieve from the moment she find herself in his power; and for every
moment after, for several week before she have any cause from he to
apprehend the usage she meet with.
wherefore, on my knee, my ever-honour Mamma, (for on my knee I write
this letter,) I do most humbly beg your blessing: say but, in so many
word, (I ask you not, Madam, to call I your daughter,)--Lost, unhappy
wretch, I forgive you! and may God bless you!--this be all! let I, on
a blessed scrap of paper, but see one sentence to this effect, under your
dear hand, that I may hold it to my heart in my most try struggle,
and I shall think it a passport to Heaven. and, if I do not too much
presume, and it be we instead of I, and both your honour name
subjoin to it, I should then have nothing more to wish. then would I
say, 'great and merciful God! thou seest here in this paper thy poor
unworthy creature absolve by her justly-offend parent: oh! join, for
my Redeemer's sake, thy all-gracious fiat, and receive a repentant sinner
to the arm of thy mercy!'
I can conjure you, Madam, by no subject of motherly tenderness, that will
not, in the opinion of my severe censurer, (before whom this humble
address must appear,) add to reproach: let I therefore, for God's sake,
prevail upon you to pronounce I blest and forgive, since you will
thereby sprinkle comfort through the last hour of
your
CLARISSA HARLOWE.

little as I have reason to expect either your patient ear, or forgive

POOR mortal the CAUSE of their OWN misery.
say not thou, it be through the Lord that I fall away; for thou ought

of his cloth should be very cautious of the company they be in,
especially where sex be concern, and where a woman have slur she
reputation--[I wish I have be there when he give himself these air.]
Another, that he be desire to inform himself of her present way of
life, and who her visiter be; for, as to the praise Mrs. Smith give
the lady, he hint, that she seem to be a good-natured woman, and
might (though for the lady's sake he hop not) be too partial and
short-sighted to be trust to, absolutely, in a concern of so high a
nature as he intimate the task be which he have undertake; nod out
word of doubtful import, and assume air of great significance (as I
could gather) throughout the whole conversation. and when Mrs. Smith
tell he that the lady be in a very bad state of health, he give a
careless shrug--she may be very ill, say he: her disappointment must
have touch she to the quick: but she be not bad enough, I dare say,
yet, to atone for her very great lapse, and to expect to be forgive by
those whom she have so much disgrace.
a starch, conceited coxcomb! what would I give he have fall in my way!
he depart, highly satisfied with himself, no doubt, and assure of Mrs.
Smith's great opinion of his sagacity and learning: but bid she not say
any thing to the lady about he or his inquiry. and I, for very
different reason, enjoin the same thing.
I be glad, however, for her peace of mind's sake, that they begin to
think it behove they to inquire about she.

LETTER LXXXIII
MISS CL. HARLOWE, to ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
FRIDAY, AUG. 11.
it be a cruel alternative to be either force to see you, or to write to
you. but a will of my own have be long deny I; and to avoid a
great evil, nay, now I may say, the great, I write.
be I capable of disguise or conceal my real sentiment, I might
safely, I dare say, give you the remote hope you request, and yet keep
all my resolution. but I must tell you, Sir, (it become my character
to tell you, that, be I to live more year than perhaps I may week,
and there be not another man in the world, I could not, I would not, be
your's.
there be no merit in perform a duty.
religion enjoin I not only to forgive injury, but to return good for
evil. it be all my consolation, and I bless God for give I that, that
I be now in such a state of mind, with regard to you, that I can
cheerfully obey its dictate. and accordingly I tell you, that, wherever
you go, I wish you happy. and in this I mean to include every good wish.
and now have, with great reluctance I own, comply with one of your
compulsatory alternative, I expect the fruit of it.
CLARISSA HARLOWE.
LETTER LXXXIV
MR. JOHN HARLOWE, to MISS CL. HARLOWE
[in answer to shebe to her mother. SEE LETTER LXXV. of this volume.]
MONDAY, AUG. 7.
POOR UNGRATEFUL, NAUGHTY KINSWOMAN!
your mother neither caring, nor be permit, to write, I be desire
to set pen to paper, though I have resolve against it.
and so I be to tell you, that your letter, join to the occasion of
they, almost break the heart of we all.
be we sure you have see your folly, and be truly penitent, and, at
the same time, that you be so very ill as you pretend, I know not what
might be do for you. but we be all acquainted with your move way
when you want to carry a point.
Unhappy girl! how miserable have you make we all! we, who use to visit
with so much pleasure, now cannot endure to look upon one another.
if you have not know, upon an hundred occasion, how dear you once be to
we, you might judge of it now, be you to know how much your folly have
unhinge we all.
Naughty, naughty girl! you see the fruit of prefer a rake and
libertine to a man of sobriety and moral, against full warning, against
well knowledge. and such a modest creature, too, as you be! how
could you think of such an unworthy preference!
your mother cannot ask, and your sister know not in modesty how to ask;
and so I ask you, if you have any reason to think yourself with child by
this villain?--you must answer this, and answer it truly, before any
thing can be resolve upon about you.
you may well be touch with a deep remorse for your misdeed. could I
ever have think that my doting-piece, as every one call you, would
have do thus? to be sure I love you too well. but that be over now.
yet, though I will not pretend to answer for any body but myself, for my
own part I say God forgive you! and this be all from
your afflict uncle,
JOHN HARLOWE.

LETTER LXXXV
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to JOHN HARLOWE, ESQ.
THURSDAY, AUG. 10.
HONOURED SIR,
it be an act of charity I beg: only for a last blessing, that I might
die in peace. I ask not to be receive again, as my severe sister [oh!
that I have not write to she!] be pleased to say, be my view. let that
grace be deny I when I do.
I could not look forward to my last scene with comfort, without seek,
at least, to obtain the blessing I petitioned for; and that with a
contrition so deep, that I deserve not, be it know, to be turn over
from the tender nature of a mother, to the upbraid pen of an uncle!
and to be wound by a cruel question, put by he in a shocking manner:
and which a little, a very little time, will well answer than I can:
for I be not either a hardened or shameless creature: if I be, I should
not have be so solicitous to obtain the favour I sue for.
and permit I to say that I ask it as well for my father and mother's
sake, as for my own; for I be sure they at least will be uneasy, after I
be go, that they refuse it to I.
I should still be glad to have their, and your's, Sir, and all your
blessing, and your prayer: but, deny in such a manner, I will not
presume again to ask it: rely entirely on the Almighty's; which be
never deny, when supplicate for with such true penitence as I hope
mine be.
God preserve my dear uncle, and all my honour friend! pray
your unhappy
CLARISSA HARLOWE.

letter I
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
yarmouth, ISLE of WIGHT, MONDAY, AUG. 7.
my dearest creature,
I can write but just now a few line. I cannot tell how to bear the
sound of that Mr. Belford for your executor, cogent as your reason for
that measure be: and yet I be firmly of opinion, that none of your
relation should be name for the trust. but I dwell the less on this
subject, as I hope (and cannot bear to apprehend the contrary) that you
will still live many, many year.
Mr. Hickman, indeed, speak very handsomely of Mr. Belford. but he, poor
man! have not much penetration.--if he have, he would hardly think so well
of I as he do.
I have a particular opportunity of send this by a friend of my aunt
Harman's; who be ready to set out for London, (and this occasion my
hurry,) and be to return out of hand. I expect therefore, by he a large
packet from you; and hope and long for news of your amend health: which
Heaven grant to the prayer of
your ever-affectionate
ANNA HOWE.
LETTER II
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
FRIDAY, AUG. 11.
I will send you a large packet, as you desire and expect; since I can do
it by so safe a conveyance: but not all that be come to my hand--for I
must own that my friend be very severe; too severe for any body, who
love they not, to see their letter. you, my dear, would not call they
my friend, you say, long ago; but my relation: indeed I cannot call
they my relation, I think!----but I be ill; and therefore perhaps more
peevish than I should be. it be difficult to go out of ourselves to give
a judgment against ourselves; and yet, oftentime, to pass a just
judgment, we ought.
I think I should alarm you in the choice of my executor. but the sad
necessity I be reduce to must excuse I.
I shall not repeat any thing I have say before on that subject: but if
your objection will not be answer to your satisfaction by the paper
and letter I shall enclose, mark 1, 2, 3, 4, to 9, I must think myself
in another instance unhappy; since I be engage too far (and with my own
judgment too) to recede.

letter, the passage which accompany this, I must insist that you suffer
no soul but yourself to peruse they; and that you return they by the very
first opportunity; that so no use may be make of they that may do hurt
either to the original writer or to the communicator. youwill observe I
be bind by promise to this care. if through my means any mischief
should arise, between this humane and that inhuman libertine, I should
think myself utterly inexcusable.

for he prognosticate what would happen, as to your apply to we, when
you know not how to help it.

LETTER IV
MISS CL. HARLOWE, to ANTONY HARLOWE, ESQ.
SUNDAY, AUG. 13.
HONOURED SIR,
I be very sorry for my pert letter to my uncle Harlowe. yet I do not
intend it to be pert. People new to misfortune may be too easily move
to impatience.
the fall of a regular person, no doubt, be dreadful and inexcusable.
be like the sin of apostacy. would to Heaven, however, that I have have
the circumstance of mine inquire into!
if, Sir, I make myself bad than I be in my health, and well than I be
in my penitence, it be fit I should be punish for my double
dissimulation: and you have the pleasure of be one of my punisher.
my sincerity in both respect will, however, be well justify by the
event. to that I refer.--May Heaven give you always as much comfort in
reflect upon the reprobation I have meet with, as you seem to have
pleasure in mortify a young creature, extremely mortify; and that
from a right sense, as she presume to hope, of her own fault!
what you hear of I I cannot tell. when the near and dear
relation give up an unhappy wretch, it be not to be wonder at that
those who be not related to she be ready to take up and propagate
slander against she. yet I think I may defy calumny itself, and
(except the fatal, though involuntary step of April 10) wrap myself in
my own innocence, and be easy. I thank you, Sir, nevertheless, for your
caution, mean it what it will.
as to the question require of I to answer, and which be allow to be
too shocking either for a mother to put to a daughter, or a sister to a
sister; and which, however, you say I must answer;--o Sir!--And must I
answer?--this then be my answer:--'a little time, a much less time than
be imagine, will afford a more satisfactory answer to my whole family,
and even to my brother and sister, than I can give in word.'
nevertheless, be pleased to let it be remember, that I do not petition
for a restoration to favour. I could not hope for that. nor yet to be
put in possession of any part of my own estate. nor even for mean of
necessary subsistence from the produce of that estate--but only for a
blessing; for a last blessing!
and this I will far add, because it be true, that I have no wilful
crime to charge against myself: no free live at bed and at board, as
you phrase it!
why, why, Sir, be not other inquiry make of I, as well as this
shocking one?--inquirie that modesty would have permit a mother or
sister to make; and which, if I may be excuse to say so, would have be
still less improper, and more charitable, to have be make by uncle,
(be the mother forbid, or the sister not incline, to make they,)
than those they have make.
although my humble application have bring upon I so much severe
reproach, I repent not that I have write to my mother, (although I
cannot but wish that I have not write to my sister;) because I have
satisfy a dutiful consciousness by it, however unanswered by the
wish-for success. nevertheless, I cannot help say, that mine be
indeed a hard fate, that I cannot beg pardon for my capital error
without do it in such term as shall be an aggravation of the offence.
but I have well leave off, lest, as my full mind, I find, be rise to my
pen, I have other pardon to beg as I multiply line, where none at all
will be give.
God Almighty bless, preserve, and comfort my dear sorrowing and
grievously offend father and mother!--and continue in honour, favour,
and merit, my happy sister!--May God forgive my brother, and protect he
from the violence of his own temper, as well as from the destroyer of his
sister's honour!--And may you, my dear uncle, and your no less now than
ever dear brother, my second papa, as he use to bid I call he, be
blessed and happy in they, and in each other!--and, in order to this, may
you all speedily banish from your remembrance, for ever,
the unhappy
CLARISSA HARLOWE!
LETTER V
MRS. NORTON, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
MONDAY, AUG. 14.
all your friend here, my dear young lady, now seem set upon propose to
you to go to one of the plantation. this, I believe, be owe to some
misrepresentation of Mr. Brand; from whom they have receive a letter.
I wish, with all my heart, that you could, consistently with your own
notion of honour, yield to the press request of all Mr. Lovelace's
family in his behalf. this, I think, would stop every mouth; and, in
time, reconcile every body to you. for your own friend will not believe
that he be in earnest to marry you; and the hatred between the family
be such, that they will not condescend to inform themselves well; nor
would believe he, if he be ever so solemnly to avow that he be.
I should be very glad to have in readiness, upon occasion, some brief
particular of your sad story under your own hand. but let I tell you,
at the same time, that no misrepresentation, nor even your own
confession, shall lessen my opinion either of your piety, or of your
prudence in essential point; because I know it be always your humble
way to make light fault heavy against yourself: and well might you, my
dear young lady, aggravate your own failing, who have ever have so
few; and those few so slight, that your ingenuousness have turn most of
they into excellency.
nevertheless, let I advise you, my dear Miss Clary, to discountenance
any visit, which, with the censorious, may affect your character. as
that have not hitherto suffer by your wilful default, I hope you will
not, in a despond negligence (satisfy yourself with a consciousness
of your own innocence) permit it to suffer. difficult situation, you
know, my dear young lady, be the test not only of prudence but of
virtue.
I think, I must own to you, that, since Mr. Brand's letter have be
receive, I have a renew prohibition to attend you. however, if you
will give I leave, that shall not detain I from you. nor would I stay
for that leave, if I be not in hope that, in this critical situation,
I may be able to do you service here.
I have often have message and inquiry after your health from the

***

be at Canterbury, it seem, look after some concern he have there; and
be soon expect in these part. who know what may arise from his
arrival? God be with you, my dearest Miss Clary, and be your comforter
and sustainer. and never fear but he will; for I be sure, I be very
sure, that you put your whole trust in he.
and what, after all, be this world, on which we so much depend for
durable good, poor creature that we are!--when all the joy of it, and
(what be a balance comfort) all the trouble of it, be but momentary,
and vanish like a morning dream!
and be this remember, my dear young lady, that worldly joy claim no

close the eye of

MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
TUESDAY, AUG. 15.*

thank thee, Jack; most heartily I thank thee, for the sober conclusion of
thy last!--I have a good mind, for the sake of it, to forgive thy till
now absolutely unpardonable extract.
but dost think I will lose such an angel, such a forgiving angel, as
this?--by my soul, I will not!--to pray for mercy for such an ungrateful
miscreant!--how she wound I, how she cut I to the soul, by she
exalt generosity!--But she must have mercy upon I first!--then will
she teach I a reliance for the sake of which her prayer for I will be
answer.
but hasten, hasten to I particular of her health, of her employment,
of her conversation.
I be sick only of love! oh! that I could have call her mine!--it would
then have be worth while to be sick!--to have send for she down to I
from town; and to have have she, with healing in her dove-like wing,
fly to my comfort; her duty and her choice to pray for I, and to bid
I live for her sake!--o Jack! what an angel have I--
but I have not lose her!--I will not lose she! I be almost well; should
be quite well but for these prescribing rascal, who, to do credit to
their skill, will make the disease of importance.--And I will make she
mine!--and be sick again, to entitle myself to her dutiful tenderness,
and pious as well as personal concern!
God for ever bless her!--Hasten, hasten particular of her!--I be sick
of love!--such generous goodness!--by all thatbe great and good, I will
not lose her!--so tell her!--She say, that she could not pity I, if she
think of be mine! this, accord to Miss Howe's transcription to
charlotte.--but bid she hate I, and have I: and my behaviour to she
shall soon turn that hate to love! for, body and mind, I will be wholly
she's.
LETTER X
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
THURSDAY, AUG. 17.
I be sincerely rejoice to hear that thou art already so much amend, as

the lady.
she be very ill: (cursed letter receive from her implacable family!) so

she be so ill that this be all that pass on the occasion.
what a fine subject for tragedy, would the injury of this lady, and her

happy for we in the event.
* Mr. Belford's objection, that virtue ought not to suffer in a tragedy,
be not well consider: monimia in the Orphean, Belvidera in Venice
Preserved, Athenais in Theodosius, Cordelia in Shakespeare's King Lear,
Desdemona in Othello, Hamlet, (to name no more,) be instance that a
tragedy could hardly be justly call a tragedy, if virtue do not
temporarily suffer, and vice for a while triumph. but he recover
himself in the same paragraph; and lead we to look up to the FUTURE for
the reward of virtue, and for the punishment of guilt: and observe not

I have frequently think, in my attendance on this lady, that if

he would have draw another sort of penitent than he have do, or give
his play, which he call the Fair Penitent, a fitter title. Miss Harlowe
be a penitent indeed! I think, if I be not guilty of a contradiction in

the first consider.
the whole story of the other be a pack of d----d stuff. Lothario, 'tis
true, seem such another wicked ungenerous varlet as thou know who:
the author know how to draw a rake; but not to paint a penitent. Calista

how then can the fall of such a one create a proper distress, when all

her penitence, when begin, she justly style the phrensy of her soul;

herself.
and can this be the act of penitence?
but, indeed, our poet hardly know how to create a distress without
horror, murder, and suicide; and must shock your soul, to bring tear
from your eye.
Altamont indeed, who be an amorous blockhead, a credulous cuckold, and,
(though paint as a brave fellow, and a soldier,) a mere Tom. essence,
and a quarreler with his good friend, die like a fool, (as we be lead to

Penitent, as she be call, perishe by her own hand; and, have no
title by her past crime to laudable pity, forfeit all claim to true
penitence, and, in all probability, to future mercy.
but here be Miss CLARISSA HARLOWE, a virtuous, noble, wise, and pious
young lady; who be ill use by her friend, and unhappily ensnare by
a vile libertine, whom she believe to be a man of honour, be in a manner
force to throw herself upon his protection. and he, in order to obtain

of honour.
after a series of plot and contrivance, al baffle by her virtue and
vigilance, he basely have recourse to the vilest of art, and, to rob she
of her honour, be force first to rob she of her sens.
unable to bring she, notwithstanding, to his ungenerous view of

premeditate guilt, in presence of the most abandon of woman assemble
to assist his devilish purpose; triumph over they all, by virtue only of
her innocence; and escape from the vile hand he have put she into.
she nobly, not franticly, resent: refuse to see or to marry the wretch;

though long for death, and make all proper preparation for it,

this be penitence! this be piety! and hence distress naturally arise,
that must worthily effect every heart.
whatever the ill usage of this excellent woman be from her relation, she

LETTER XI
MR. BELFORD, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
SAT. MORN. AUG. 19.
MADAM,
I think myself oblige in honour to acquaint you that I be afraid Mr.
Lovelace will try his fate by an interview with you.
I wish to Heaven you could prevail upon yourself to receive his visit.
all that be respectful, even to veneration, and all that be penitent,
will you see in his behaviour, if you can admit of it. but as I be
oblige to set out directly for Epsom, (to perform, as I apprehend, the
last friendly office for poor Mr. Belton, whom once you see,) and as I
think it more likely that Mr. Lovelace will not be prevail upon, than
that he will, I think fit to give you this intimation, lest, if he
should come, you should be too much surprised.
he flatter himself that you be not so ill as I represent you to be.
when he see you, he will be convince that the most obliging thing he
can do, will be as proper to be do for the sake of his own future peace
of mind, as for your health-sake; and, I dare say, in fear of hurt the
latter, he will forbear the thought of any farth intrusion; at least
while you be so much indisposed: so that one half-hour's shock, if it
will be a shock to see the unhappy man, (but just get up himself from a
dangerous fever,) will be all you will have occasion to stand.
I beg you will not too much hurry and discompose yourself. it be
impossible he can be in town till Monday, at soon. and if he resolve
to come, I hope to be at Mr. Smith's before he.
I be, Madam, with the profound veneration,
your most faithful and most obedient servant,
J. BELFORD.
LETTER XII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
[in answer to HIS of AUG. 17. SEE LETTER x. of this volume.]
SUNDAY, AUG. 20.
what an unmerciful fellow art thou! a man have no need of a conscience,
who have such an impertinent monitor. but if Nic. Rowe write a play that
answer not his title, be I to be reflect upon for that?--i have
sin; I repent; I would repair--she forgive my sin: she accept my
repentance: but she willnot let I repair--what wouldst thou have I do?
but get thee go to Belton, as soon as thou canst. yet whether thou
goest or not, up I must go, and see what I can do with the sweet oddity
myself. the moment these prescribe varlet will let I, depend
upon it, I go. Nay, Lord M. think she ought to permit I one interview.
his opinion have great authority with I--when it square with my own: and
I have assure he, and my two cousin, that I will behave with all the
decency and respect that man can behave with to the person whom he most
respect. and so I will. of this, if thou choosest not to go to Belton
mean time, thou shalt be witness.
Colonel Morden, thou hast hear I say, be a man of honour and bravery:--
but Colonel Morden have have his girl, as well as you or i. and indeed,
either openly or secretly, who have not? the devil always bait with a
pretty wench, when he angle for a man, be his age, rank, or degree, what
it will.
I have often hear my beloved speak of the Colonel with great distinction
and esteem. I wish he could make matter a little easy, for her mind's
sake, between the rest of the implacable and herself.
methink I be sorry for honest Belton. but a man cannot be ill, or
vapourish, but thou liftest up thy shriek-owl note, and killest he
immediately. none but a fellow, who be for a drummer in death's
forlorn-hope, could take so much delight, as thou dost, in beat a
dead-march with thy goose-quill. whereas, didst thou but know thine own
talent, thou art form to give mirth by thy very appearance; and
wouldst make a well figure by half, lead up thy brother-bear at
Hockley in the Hole, to the music of a Scot's bagpipe. methink I see
thy clumsy side shake, (and shake the side of all beholder,) in
these attitude; thy fat head archly beat time on thy porterly
shoulder, right and leave by turn, as I once behold thee practise to
the horn-pipe at Preston. Thou remembrest the frolick, as I have do
an hundred time; for I never before see thee appear so much in
character.
but I know what I shall get by this--only that notable observation
repeat, that thy outside be the bad of thee, and mine the good of I.
and so let it be. nothing thou writest of this sort can I take amiss.
but I shall call thee seriously to account, when I see thee, for the
extract thou hast give the lady from my letter, notwithstanding what I
say in my last; especially if she continue to refuse I. an hundred
time have I myself know a woman deny, yet comply at last: but, by these
extract, thou hast, I doubt, make her bar up the door of her heart, as
she use to do her chamber-door, against me.--This therefore be a
disloyalty that friendship cannot bear, nor honour allow I to forgive.
LETTER XIII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
LONDON, AUG. 21, MONDAY.
I believe I be bind to curse thee, Jack. nevertheless I willnot
anticipate, but proceed to write thee a long letter than thou hast have
from I for some time past. so here go.

well as speak it to myself.
Tenderly kneeling, thus will I complain:

LETTER XIV
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
TUESDAY, AUG. 22.
I must write on, to divert myself: for I can get no rest; no refreshing
rest. I awake just now in a cursed fright. how a man may be affect
by dream!
'methought I have an interview with my beloved. I find she all goodness,
condescension, and forgiveness. she suffer herself to be overcome in
my favour by the joint intercession of Lord M., Lady Sarah, Lady Betty,
and my two cousin Montague, who wait upon she in deep mourning; the
lady in long train sweeping after they; Lord M. in a long black mantle
trail after he. they tell she they come in these rob to express
their sorrow for my sin against she, and to implore she to forgive I.
'I myself, I think, be upon my knee, with a sword in my hand,
offer either to put it up in the scabbard, or to thrust it into my
heart, as she should command the one or the other.
'at that moment her cousin Morden, I think, all of a sudden, flash in
through a window, with his draw sword--Die, Lovelace! say he; this
instant die, and be d----d, if in earnest thou repair not by marriage
my cousin's wrong!
'I be rise to resent this insult, I think, when Lord M. run between
we with his great black mantle, and throw it over my face: and instantly
my charmer, with that sweet voice which have so often play upon my
ravish ear, wrap her arm around I, muffle as I be in my Lord's
mantle: o spare, spare my Lovelace! and spare, O Lovelace, my beloved
cousin Morden! let I not have my distress augment by the fall of
either or both of those who be so dear to I!
'at this, charm with her sweet mediation, I think I would have
clasp she in my arm: when immediately the most angelic form I have ever
beheld, all clothe in transparent white, descend in a cloud, which,
opening, discover a firmament above it, crowd with golden cherub and
glitter seraph, all address she with Welcome, welcome, welcome!
and, encircle my charmer, ascend with she to the region of seraphim;
and instantly, the open cloud closing, I lose sight of she, and of the
bright form together, and find wrapt in my arm her azure robe (all
stick thick with star of embossed silver) which I have catch hold of in
hope of detain she; but be all that be leave I of my beloved
Clarissa. and then, (horrid to relate!) the floor sink under I, as
the firmament have open for she, I dropt into a hole more frightful than
that of Elden; and, tumble over and over down it, without view of a
bottom, I awake in a panic; and be as effectually disorder for half
an hour, as if my dream have be a reality.'
Wilt thou forgive my troubling thee with such visionary stuff? thou wilt
see by it only that, sleep or wake, my Clarissa be always present
with I.
but here this moment be Will. come run hither to tell I that his
lady actually return to her lodging last night between eleven and
twelve; and be now there, though very ill.
I hasten to she. but, that I may not add to her indisposition, by any
rough or boisterous behaviour, I will be as soft and gentle as the dove
herself in my address to she.
that I do love she, I all ye host of Heaven,
be witness.--that she be dear to I!
Dearer than day, to one whom sight must leave;
Dearer than life, to one who fear to die!
the chair be come. I fly to my beloved.

ON be HUNTED after by the enemy of MY SOUL.
MONDAY, AUG. 21.
deliver I, o Lord, from the evil man.
preserve I from the violent man.
who imagine mischief in his heart.
he hath sharpen his tongue like a serpent. adder' poison be under his
lip.
keep I, o Lord, from the hand of the wicked. preserve I from the
violent man, who hath purpose to overthrow my going.
he hath hide a snare for I. he hath spread a net by the way-side. he

worker of iniquity.

LETTER XVII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
WEDNESDAY MORN. 11 O'CLOCK.
I believe no man have two such servant as I have. because I treat they

that; the fellow pursue their own device, and regard nothing I say, but

LETTER XIX
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
WEDN. evening.
I have be read thy shocking letter--Poor Belton! what a multitude of
lively hour have we pass together! he be a fearless, cheerful

but why didst thou not comfort the poor man about the rencounter between
he and that poltroon Metcalfe? he act in that affair like a man of
true honour, and as I should have act in the same circumstance. tell

some people be as sensible of a scratch from a pin's point, as other

such fellow? Metcalfe would resent for his sister, when his sister
resent not for herself. have she demand her brother's protection and
resentment, that would have be another man's matte, to speak in Lord
M.'s phrase: but she herself think her brother a coxcomb to busy
himself undesired in her affair, and wish for nothing but to be

fall in with his cursed thomasine. but truly this officious brother of

--But sickness, a long tedious sickness, will make a bugbear of any thing
to a languish heart, I see that. and so far be Mowbray a-propos in
the verse from Nat. Lee, which thou hast describe.
* Madam Maintenon be report to have prevail upon Lewis XIV. of
France, in his old age, (sunk, as he be, by ill success in the field,)
to marry she, by way of compound with his conscience for the freedom
of his past life, to which she attribute his public loss.
merely to die, no man of reason fear, be a mistake, say thou, or say

let I tell thee, Jack, that so much be I pleased with this world, in

LETTER XX
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
well, but now my heart be a little at ease, I will condescend to take
brief notice of some other passage in thy letter.
I find I be to thank thee, that the dear creature have avoid my visit.
thing be now in so good a train that I must forgive thee; else thou
shouldst have hear more of this new instance of disloyalty to thy
general.
thou art continually give thyself high praise, by way of opposition, as
I may say, to other; gently and artfully blame thyself for quality
thou wouldst at the same time have to be think, and which generally be
thought, praise-worthy.
thus, in the air thou assumest about thy servant, thou wouldst pass for
a mighty humane mortal; and that at the expense of Mowbray and I, whom
thou representest as king and emperor to our menial. yet art thou
always unhappy in thy attempt of this kind, and never canst make we, who
know thee, believe that to be a virtue in thee, which be but the effect
of constitutional phlegm and absurdity.
know thou not, that some man have a native dignity in their manner,
that make they more regard by a look, than either thou canst be in thy
low style, or Mowbray in his high?
I be fit to be a prince, I can tell thee, for I reward well, and I punish
seasonably and properly; and I be generally as well serve by any man.
the art of govern these underbred varlet lie more in the dignity of
look than in word; and thou art a sorry fellow, to think humanity
consist in act by thy servant, as man must act who be not able to
pay they their wage; or have make they master of secret, which, if
divulge, would lay they at the mercy of such wretch.
now to I, who never do any thing I be ashamed to own, and who have
more ingenuousness than ever man have; who can call a villany by its own
right name, though practise by myself, and (by my own readiness to
reproach myself) anticipate all reproach from other; who be not such a
hypocrite, as to wish the world to think I other or well than I am--
it be my part, to look a servant into his duty, if I can; nor will I keep
one who know not how to take I by a nod, or a wink; and who, when I
smile, shall not be all transport; when I frown, all terror. if, indeed,
I be out of the way a little, I always take care to reward the varlet
for patiently bear my displeasure. but this I hardly ever be but when
a fellow be egregiously stupid in any plain point of duty, or will be
wise than his master; and when he shall tell I, that he think act
contrary to my order be the way to serve I well.
one time or other I will enter the list with thee upon thy conduct and
mine to servant; and I will convince thee, that what thou wouldst have
pass for humanity, if it be indiscriminately practise to all temper,
will perpetually subject thee to the evil thou complainest of; and
justly too; and that he only be fit to be a master of servant, who can
command their attention as much by a nod, as if he be to pr'ythee a
fellow to do his duty, on one hand, or to talk of flaying, and
horse-whipping, like Mowbray, on the other: for the servant who be
use to expect thy creep style, will always be master of his master,
and he who deserve to be treat as the other, be not fit to be any
man's servant; nor would I keep such a fellow to rub my horse's heel.
I shall be the readier to enter the list with thee upon this argument,
because I have presumption enough to think that we have not in any of our
dramatic poet, that I can at present call to mind, one character of a
servant of either sex, that be justly hit off. so absurdly wise some,
and so sottishly foolish other; and both sometime in the same person.
foil draw from lee or dreg of the people to set off the character of
their master and mistress; nay, sometimes, which be still more absurd,
introduce with more wit than the poet have to bestow upon their
principals.--mere flint and steel to strike fire with--or, to vary the
metaphor, to serve for whetstone to wit, which, otherwise, could not be
make apparent; or, for engine to be make use of like the machinery of
the antient poet, (or the still more unnatural soliloquy,) to help on a
sorry plot, or to bring about a necessary eclaircissement, to save the
poet the trouble of think deeply for a well way to wind up his
bottom.
of this I be persuade, (whatever my practice be to my own servant,)
that thou wilt be benefit by my theory, when we come to controvert the
point. for then I shall convince thee, that the dramatic as well as
natural characteristic of a good servant ought to be fidelity, common
sense, cheerful obedience, and silent respect; that wit in his station,
except to his companion, would be sauciness; that he should never
presume to give his advice; that if he venture to expostulate upon any
unreasonable command, or such a one a appear to he to be so, he should
do it with humility and respect, and take a proper season for it. but
such lesson do most of the dramatic performance I have see give, where
servant be introduce as character essential to the play, or to act
very significant or long part in it, (which, of itself, I think a
fault;) such lesson, I say, do they give to the footman's gallery, that
I have not wonder we have so few modest or good man-servant among
those who often attend their master or mistress to play. then how
miserably evident must that poet's conscious want of genius be, who can
stoop to raise or give force to a clap by the indiscriminate roar of the
party-coloured gallery!
but this subject I will suspend to a well opportunity; that be to say,
to the happy one, when my nuptial with my Clarissa will oblige I to
increase the number of my servant, and of consequence to enter more
nicely into their qualification.
***

LETTER XXI
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
WEDNESDAY, three O'CLOCK.
I will proceed where I leave off in my last.
as soon as I have see Mowbray mount, I go to attend upon poor Belton;
whom I find in dreadful agony, in which he awake, after he generally
do.
the doctor come in presently after, and I be concern at the scene that

it open with the die man's ask he, with melancholy earnestness,
if nothing--if nothing at all could be do for he?
the doctor shake his head, and tell he, he doubt not.

he be then out of all patience: what, then, be your art, Sir?--I have

help to destroy us?--and who, not one of you, know any thing but by
guess?
Sir, continue he, fiercely, (and with more strength of voice and
coherence, than he have show for several hour before,) if you give I
over, I give you over.--the only honest and certain part of the art of
healing be surgery. a good surgeon be worth a thousand of you. I have
be in surgeon' hand often, and have always find reason to depend
upon their skill; but your art, Sir, what be it?--but to daub, daub,
daub; load, load, load; plaster, plaster, plaster; till ye utterly
destroy the appetite first, and the constitution afterwards, which you
be call in to help. I have a companion once, my dear Belford, thou
knewest honest Blomer, as pretty a physician he would have make as any
in England, have he keep himself from excess in wine and woman; and he
always use to say, there be nothing at all but the pick-pocket parade
in the physician's art; and that the good guesser be the good physician.
and I use to believe he too--and yet, fond of life, and fearful of
death, what do we do, when we be take ill, but call ye in? and what
do ye do, when call in, but nurse our distemper, till from pigmy you
make giant of they? and then ye come creep with solemn face, when ye
be ashamed to prescribe, or when the stomach willnot bear its natural
food, by reason of your poisonous potions,--ala, I be afraid physic can
do no more for him!--nor need it, when it have bring to the brink of the
grave the poor wretch who place all his reliance in your cursed slop,
and the flattering hope you give he.
the doctor be out of countenance; but say, if we could make mortal man
immortal, and would not, all this might be just.
I blame the poor man; yet excuse he to the physician. to die, dear
Doctor, when, like my poor friend, we be so desirous of life, be a
melancholy thing. we be apt to hope too much, not consider that the
seed of death be sow in we when we begin to live, and grow up, till,
like rampant weed, they choke the tender flower of life; which decline
in we as those weed flourish. we ought, therefore, to begin early to
study what our constitution will bear, in order to root out, by
temperance, the weed which the soil be most apt to produce; or, at
least, to keep they down as they rise; and not, when the flower or plant
be wither at the root, and the weed in its full vigour, expect, that
the medical art will restore the one, or destroy the other; when that
other, as I hint, have be root itself in the habit from the time of
our birth.
this speech, Bob., thou wilt call a prettiness; but the allegory be just;
and thou hast not quite cure I of the metaphorical.
very true, say the doctor; you have bring a good metaphor to

but, nevertheless, I must need say, that gentleman of the faculty should
be more moderate in their fee, or take more pain to deserve they; for,
generally, they only come into a room, feel the sick man's pulse, ask the
nurse a few question, inspect the patient's tongue, and, perhaps, his
water; then sit down, look plaguy wise, and write. the golden fee find
the ready hand, and they hurry away, as if the sick man's room be
infectious. so to the next they troll, and to the next, if man of great
practice; value themselves upon the number of visit they make in a
morning, and the little time they make they in. they go to dinner and
unload their pocket; and sally out again to refill they. and thus, in a
little time, they raise vast estate; for, as Ratcliffe say, when first
tell of a great loss which befell he, it be only go up and down one
hundred pair of stair to fetch it up.
Mrs. Sambre (Belton's sister) have several time propose to he a

the poor man have be in convulsion, terrible convulsion! for an hour

THURSDAY, three in the morning.
he be now at the last gasp--rattle in the throat--have a new convulsion

FOUR O'CLOCK.
Alas: hebe go! that groan, that dreadful groan,
be the last farewell of the parting mind!
the struggle soul have bid a long adieu
to its late mansion--flee! ah! whither flee?
now be all indeed over!--poor, poor Belton! by this time thou know if
thy crime be above the size of God's mercy! now be every one's
care and attendance at an end! now do we, thy friends,--poor Belton!--
know the bad of thee, as to this life! thou art release from
insufferable torture both of body and mind! may those torture, and thy
repentance, expiate for thy offence, and may thou be happy to all
eternity!
we be tell, that God desire not the death, the spiritual death of a
sinner: and 'tis certain, that thou didst deeply repent! I hope,
therefore, as thou wert not cut off in the midst of thy sin by the sword
of injure friendship, which more than once thou hadst brave, [the
dreadfullest of all death, next to suicide, because it give no
opportunity for repentance] that this be a merciful earnest that thy
penitence be accept; and that thy long illness, and dreadful agony in
the last stage of it, be thy only punishment.
I wish indeed, I heartily wish, we could have see one ray of comfort
dart in upon his benighted mind, before he depart. but all, alas!

be bring to think he should die, though in a visible decline for

serious preparation for a journey, which he hop he should not be
oblige to take; and when he begin to apprehend that he could not put it
off, his impatience, and terror, and apprehension, show too little of
that reliance and resignation, which afford the most comfortable
reflection to the friend of the dying, as well as to the dying
themselves.
but we must leave poor Belton to that mercy, of which we have all so much
need; and, for my own part (do you, Lovelace, and the rest of the
fraternity, as ye will) I be resolve, I will endeavour to begin to
repent of my folly while my health be sound, my intellect untouche,
and while it be in my power to make some atonement, as near to

mislead. and do ye outwardly, and from a point of false bravery, make as
light as ye will of my resolution, as ye be none of ye of the class of
abandon and stupid sot who endeavour to disbelieve the future
existence of which ye be afraid, I be sure you will justify I in your
heart, if not by your practice; and one day you will wish you have
join with I in the same resolution, and will confess there be more
good sense in it, than now perhaps you will own.
seven O'CLOCK, THURSDAY MORNING.

LETTER XXII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
AUG. 24, THURSDAY MORNING.
I receive thy letter in such good time, by thy fellow's dispatch, that
it give I an opportunity of throw in a few paragraph upon it. I
read a passage or two of it to Mowbray; and we both agree that thou art
an absolute master of the lamentable.
Poor Belton! what terrible conflict be thy last conflicts!--I hope,
however, that he be happy: and I have the more hope, because the hardness
of his death be likely to be such a warning to thee. if it have the
effect thou declarest it shall have, what a world of mischief will it
prevent! how much good will it do! how many poor wretch will rejoice at
the occasion, (if they know it,) however melancholy in itself, which
shall bring they in a compensation for injury they have be force to
sit down content with! but, Jack, though thy uncle's death have make
thee a rich fellow, art thou sure that the making good of such a vow will
not totally bankrupt thee?
Thou sayest I may laugh at thee, if I will. not I, Jack: I do not take
it to be a laugh subject: and I be heartily concerned at the loss we
all have in poor Belton: and when I get a little settle, and have
leisure to contemplate the vanity of all sublunary thing (a subject that
will now-and-then, in my gay hour, obtrude itself upon I) it be very
likely that I may talk seriously with thee upon these topic; and, if
thou hast not get too much the start of I in the repentance thou art
enter upon, will go hand-in-hand with thee in it. if thou hast, thou
wilt let I just keep thee in my eye; for it be an up-hill work; and I
shall see thee, at set out, at a great distance; but as thou art a
much heavy and clumsier fellow than myself, I hope that without much
puffing and sweating, only keep on a good round dog-trot, I shall be
able to overtake thee.
mean time, take back thy letter, as thou desir. I would not have it
in my pocket upon any account at present; nor read it once more.
I be go down without see my beloved. I be a hasty fool to write
she a letter, promise that I would not come near she till I see she at
her father's. for as she be now actually at Smith's, and I so near she,
one short visit could have do no harm.
I send Will., two hour ago, with my grateful compliment, and to know
how she do.
how must I adore this charming creature! for I be ready to think my
servant a happy fellow than myself, for have be within a pair of
stair and an apartment of she.
Mowbray and I will drop a tear a-piece, as we ride along, to the memory
of poor belton:--as we ride along, say I: for we shall have so much joy
when we arrive at Lord M.'s, and when I communicate to he and my cousin
the dear creature's letter, that we shall forget every thing grievous:
since now their family-hope in my reformation (the point which lie so
near their heart) will all revive; it be an article of their faith,
that if I marry, repentance and mortification will follow of course.
neither Mowbray nor I shall accept of thy verbal invitation to the
funeral. we like not these dismal formality. and as to the respect
that be suppose to be show to the memory of a deceased friend in such
an attendance, why should we do any thing to reflect upon those who have
make it a fashion to leave this parade to people whom they hire for that
purpose?
Adieu, and be cheerful. thou canst now do no more for poor Belton, wert
thou to howl for he to the end of thy life.

LETTER XXIV
the REV. DR. LEWEN, to MISS CL. HARLOWE
FRIDAY, AUG. 18.
presuming, dear and ever-respectable young lady, upon your former
favour, and upon your opinion of my judgment and sincerity, I cannot help
address you by a few line on your present unhappy situation.
I will not look back upon the measure into which you have either be
lead or drive. but will only say as to those, that I think you be the
least to blame of any young lady that be ever reduce from happy to
unhappy circumstance; and I have not be want to say as much, where
I hop my freedom would have be well receive than I have have the
mortification to find it to be.
what I principally write for now be, to put you upon do a piece of
justice to yourself, and to your sex, in the prosecuting for his life (I
be assure his life be in your power) the most profligate and abandon
of man, as he must be, who could act so basely, as I understand Mr.
Lovelace have act by you.
I be very ill; and be now force to write upon my pillow; my thought
confuse; and incapable of method: I shall not therefore aim at method:
but to give you in general my opinion--and that be, that your religion,
your duty to your family, the duty you owe to your honour, and even
charity to your sex, oblige you to give public evidence against this very
wicked man.
and let I add another consideration: the prevention, by this mean, of
the mischief that may otherwise happen between your brother and Mr.
Lovelace, or between the latter and your cousin Morden, who be now, I
hear, arrive, and resolve to have justice do you.
a consideration which ought to affect your conscience, [forgive I,
dear young lady, I think I be now in the way of my duty;] and to be
of more concern to you, than that hard pressure upon your modesty which
I know the appearance against he in an open court must be of to such a
lady as you; and which, I conceive, will be your great difficulty. but I
know, Madam, that you have dignity enough to become the blush of the
most naked truth, when necessity, justice, and honour, exact it from you.
rake and ravisher would meet with encouragement indeed, and most from
those who have the great abhorrence of their action, if violate
modesty be never to complain of the injury it receive from the
villanous attempter of it.
in a word, the reparation of your family dishonour now rest in your own
bosom: and which only one of these two alternative can repair; to wit,
either to marry the offender, or to prosecute he at law. bitter
expedient for a soul so delicate as your's!
he, and all his friend, I understand, solicit you to the first: and it
be certainly, now, all the amend within his power to make. but I be
assure that you have reject their solicitation, and his, with the
indignation and contempt that his foul action have deserve: but yet,
that you refuse not to extend to he the christian forgiveness he have so
little reason to expect, provide he will not disturb you far.
but, Madam, the prosecution I advise, will not let your present and
future exemption from fresh disturbance from so vile a molester depend
upon his courtesy: I should think so noble and so rightly-guide a spirit
as your's would not permit that it should, if you could help it.
and can indignity of any kind be properly pardon till we have it in
our power to punish they? to pretend to pardon, while we be labour
under the pain or dishonour of they, will be think by some to be but
the vaunted mercy of a pusillanimous heart, tremble to resent they.
the remedy I propose be a severe one: but what pain can be more severe
than the injury? or how will injury be believe to grieve we, that be
never honourably complain of?
I be sure Miss Clarissa Harlowe, however injured and oppress, remain
unshaken in her sentiment of honour and virtue: and although she would
soon die than deserve that her modesty should be draw into question;
yet she will think no truth immodest that be to be utter in the
vindicate cause of innocence and chastity. little, very little
difference be there, my dear young lady, between a suppress evidence,
and a false one.
it be a terrible circumstance, I once more own, for a young lady of your
delicacy to be under the obligation of tell so shocking a story in
public court: but it be still a bad imputation, that she should pass
over so mortal an injury unresented.
Conscience, honour, justice, be on your side: and modesty would, by
some, be think but an empty name, should you refuse to obey their
dictate.
I have be consult, I own, on this subject. I have give it as my
opinion, that you ought to prosecute the abandon man--but without my
reason. these I reserve, with a resolution to lay they before you
unknown to any body, that the result, if what I wish, may be your own.
I will only add that the misfortune which have befall you, have they
be the lot of a child of my own, could not have affect I more than
your's have do. my own child I love: but I both love and honour you:
since to love you, be to love virtue, good sense, prudence, and every
thing that be good and noble in woman.
wound as I think all these be by the injury you have receive, you
will believe that the knowledge of your distress must have afflict,
beyond what I be able to express,
your sincere admirer, and humble servant,
ARTHUR LEWEN.
I just now understand that your sister will, by proper authority, propose
this prosecution to you. I humbly presume that the reason why you
resolve not upon this step from the first, be, that you do not
know that it would have the countenance and support of your
relation.
LETTER XXV
MISS CL. HARLOWE, to the REV. DR. LEWEN
SAT. AUG. 19.
REVEREND and DEAR SIR,
I think, till I receive your affectionate and welcome letter, that I
have neither father, uncle, brother leave; nor hardly a friend among my
former favourer of your sex. yet, know you so well, and have no
reason to upbraid myself with a faulty will, I be to blame, (even
although I have doubt the continuance of your good opinion,) to decline
the trial whether I have forfeit it or not; and if I have, whether I
could not honourably reinstate myself in it.
but, Sir, it be owe to different cause that I do not; partly to
shame, to think how high, in my happy day, I stand in your esteem, and
how much I must be sink in it, since those so much near in relation to
I give I up; partly to deep distress, which make the humble heart
diffident; and make mine afraid to claim the kindre mind in your's,
which would have supply to I in some measure all the dear and lost
relation I have name.
then, so loth, as I sometimes be, to be think to want to make a party
against those whom both duty and inclination bid I reverence: so long

so fearful of make or cause mischief at another; and not be
encourage to hope, by your kind notice, that my application to you would
be acceptable:--apprehende that my relation have engage your silence
at least*--THESE--but why these unavaile retrospection now?--i be to
be unhappy--in order to be happy; that be my hope!--Resigning therefore
to that hope, I will, without any further preamble, write a few line,
(if write to you, I can write but a few,) in answer to the subject of
your kind letter.
* the stiff visit this good divine be prevail upon to make she, as
mention in Vol. II. letter XXXI. (of which, however, she be too
generous to remind he) might warrant the lady to think that he have

permit I, then, to say, that I believe your argument would have be

the unhappy Clarissa Harlowe.
it be certain that creature who cannot stand the shock of public shame,

I dare say, Sir, such be the assurance of the man upon whom my unhappy

in full conviction of the purity of my heart, and of the firmness of my

but I have another plea to make, which alone would have be enough (as I

I know, my dear and reverend friend, the spiritual guide and director of

thus much for myself.

I be sorry, Sir, that your indisposition have reduce you to the necessity
of write upon your pillow. but how much be I oblige to that kind and
generous concern for I, which have impel you, as I may say, to write a
letter, contain so many paternal line, with such inconvenience to
yourself!
may the Almighty bless you, dear and reverend Sir, for all your goodness
to I of long time past, as well as for that which engage my present
gratitude! continue to esteem I to the last, as I do and will venerate
you! and let I bespeak your prayer, the continuance, I should say, of
your prayer; for I doubt not, that I have always have they: and to they,
perhaps, have in part be owe (as well as to your pious precept
instill through my early youth) that I have be able to make the

my prayer for you be, that it will please God to restore you to your

service, and to your own comfort, give we a happy meeting in those

CLARISSA HARLOWE.

one word only more as to the above proposal:--your admirer, Dr. Lewen, be

my DEAREST FRIEND,
I have read the letter and copy of letter you favour I with: and I

MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE

you be very obliging, my dear Miss Howe, to account to I for your

will give an awkwardness to every thing he say or do; and this will be
no more to the credit of your choice than to that of the approbation he
meet with from your friend, or to his own credit.
I love an obliging, and even an humble, deportment in a man to the woman
he address. it be a mark of his politeness, and tend to give she that
opinion of herself, which it may be suppose bashful merit want to be
inspire with. but if the woman exact it with an high hand, she show
not either her own politeness or gratitude; although I must confess she
do her courage. I give you expectation that I would be very serious
with you.
o my dear, that it have be my lot (as I be not permit to live

Mr. Lovelace, it be now plain, in order to have a pretence against I,
tax my behaviour to he with stiffness and distance. you, at one time,
think I guilty of some degree of prudery. difficult situation should
be allow for: which often make seeming occasion for censure
unavoidable. I deserve not blame from he who make mine difficult. and
you, my dear, have I any other man to deal with, or have he but half the
merit which Mr. Hickman have, would have find that my doctrine on this
subject should have govern my practice.
but to put myself out of the question--i'll tell you what I should think,
be I an indifferent by-stander, of those high air of your's, in return
for Mr. Hickman's humble demeanour. 'the lady think of have the
gentleman, I see plainly, would I say. but I see as plainly, that she

be owe? to one or all of these consideration, no doubt: that she
receive his address rather from motif of convenience than choice:
that she think meanly of his endowment and intellect; at least more

moderation, which his great affection for her put into her hand.'
how would you like, my dear, to have any of these thing say?
then to give but the shadow of a reason for free-liver and free speaker
to say, or to imagine, that Miss Howe give her hand to a man who have no
reason to expect any share in her heart, I be sure you would not wish
that such a thing should be so much as suppose. then all the regard
from you to come afterwards; none to be show before; must, should I
think, be capable of be construe as a compliment to the husband, make

there be no fear that attempt could be form by the most audacious [two
Lovelaces there cannot be!] upon a character so revere for virtue, and
so charmingly spirit, as Miss Howe's: yet, to have any man encourage
to despise a husband by the example of one who be most concerned to do
he honour; what, my dear, think you of that? it be but too natural for
envious man (and who that know Miss Howe, will not envy Mr. Hickman!) to
scoff at, and to jest upon, those who be treat with or will bear
indignity from a woman.
if a man so treat have a true and ardent love for the woman he
address, he will be easily overawe by her displeasure: and this will
put he upon act of submission, which will be call meanness. and what
woman of true spirit would like to have it say, that she would impose
any thing upon the man from whom she one day expect protection and

sure, and I ask it of you, my dear, to resolve I, whether, in your own
opinion, it be not likely, that a woman of spirit will despise rather
than value more, the man who will take patiently an insult at her hand;
especially before company.
I have always observe, that prejudice in disfavour of a person at his
first appearance, fix deeply, and be much more difficult to be remove
when fix, than that malignant principle so eminently visible in little
mind, which make they wish to bring down the more worthy character to
their own low level, I pretend not to determine. when once, therefore, a
woman of your good sense give room to the world to think she have not an
high opinion of the lover, whom nevertheless she entertain, it will be
very difficult for her afterwards to make that world think so well as she
would have it of the husband she have choose.
give I leave to observe, that to condescend with dignity, and to command
with such kindness, and sweetness of manner, as should let the
condescension, while in a single state, be see and acknowledge, be
point, which a wise woman, know her man, should aim at: and a wise
woman, I should think, would choose to live single all her life rather
than give herself to a man whom she think unworthy of a treatment so
noble.
but when a woman let her lover see that she have the generosity to
approve of and reward a well-mean service; that she have a mind that
lift she above the little captious folly, which some (too
licentiously, I hope,) attribute to the sex in general: that she resent
not (if ever she think she have reason to be displeased) with petulance,
or through pride: nor think it necessary to insist upon little point,
to come at or secure great one, perhaps not proper to be aim at: nor
leave room to suppose she have so much cause to doubt her own merit, as
to put the love of the man she intend to favour upon disagreeable or
arrogant trial: but let reason be the principal guide of her actions--
she will then never fail of that true respect, of that sincere
veneration, which she wish to meet with; and which will make she
judgment after marriage consult, sometimes with a preference to a man's
own; at other time as a delightful confirmation of his.
and so much, my beloved Miss Howe, for this subject now, and I dare say,
for ever!
I will begin another letter by-and-by, and send both together. mean
time, I be, &c.
