LETTER XXXIV
MR. WYERLEY, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
WEDNESDAY, AUG. 23.
DEAREST MADAM,
you will be surprised to find renew, at this distance of time, an
address so positively though so politely discourage: but, however it be
receive, I must renew it. every body have hear that you have be
vilely treat by a man who, to treat you ill, must be the vilest of man.
every body know your just resentment of his base treatment: that you be
determined never to be reconcile to he: and that you persist in these
sentiment against all the entreaty of his noble relation, against all
the prayer and repentance of his ignoble self. and all the world that
have the honour to know you, or have hear of he, applaud your
resolution, as worthy of yourself; worthy of your virtue, and of that
strict honour which be always attribute to you by every one who speak
of you.
but, Madam, be all the world to have be of a different opinion, it
could never have alter mine. I ever love you; I ever must love you.
yet have I endeavour to resign to my hard fate. when I have so many
way, in vain, seek to move you in my favour, I sit down seemingly
content. I even write to you that I would sit down content. and I
endeavour to make all my friend and companion think I be. but
nobody know what pang this self-denial cost I! in vain do the chace,
in vain do travel, in vain do lively company, offer themselves, and
be embrace in their turn: with redoubled force do my passion for you
renew my unhappiness, when I look into myself, into my own heart; for
there do your charming image sit enthrone; and you engross I all.
I truly deplore those misfortune, and those suffering, for your own
sake; which nevertheless encourage I to renew my old hope. I know not
particular. I dare not inquire after they; because my suffering would
be increase with the knowledge of what your's have be. I therefore
desire not the know more than what common report wound my ear with; and
what be give I to know, by your absence from your cruel family, and
from the sacred place, where I, among number of your reject admirer,
use to be twice a week sure to behold you do credit to that service
of which your example give I the high notion. but whatever be those
misfortune, of whatsoever nature those suffering, I shall bless the
occasion for my own sake (though for your's curse the author of they,) if
they may give I the happiness to know that this my renew address may
not be absolutely rejected.--only give I hope, that it may one day meet
with encouragement, if in the interim nothing happen, either in my moral
or behaviour, to give you fresh offence. give I but hope of this--not
absolutely to reject I be all the hope I ask for; and I will love you,
if possible, still more than I ever love you--and that for your
suffering; for well you deserve to be love, even to adoration, who can,
for honour's and for virtue's sake, subdue a passion which common spirit
[I speak by cruel experience] find invincible; and this at a time when
the black offender kneel and supplicate, as I be well assured he do,
(all his friend likewise supplicate for he,) to be forgive.
that you cannot forgive he, not forgive he so as to receive he again
to favour, be no wonder. his offence be against virtue: this be a part
of your essence. what magnanimity be this! how just to yourself, and to
your spotless character! be it any merit to admire more than ever a lady
who can so exaltedly distinguish? it be not. I cannot plead it.
what hope have I leave, may it be say, when my address be before
reject, now, that your suffering, so nobly bear, have, with all the
good judge, exalt your character? yet, Madam, I have to pride myself
in this, that while your friend (not look upon you in the just light
I do) persecute and banish you; while your estate be withhold from you,
and threaten (as I know,) to be withhold, as long as the chicane law,
or rather the chicanery of its practiser, can keep it from you: while
you be destitute of protection; every body standing aloof, either
through fear of the injurer of one family, or of the hard-hearted of the
other; I pride myself, I say, to stand forth, and offer my fortune, and
my life, at your devotion. with a selfish hope indeed: I should be too
great an hypocrite not to own this! and I know how much you abhor
insincerity.
but, whether you encourage that hope or not, accept my good service, I
beseech you, Madam: and be pleased to excuse I for a piece of honest
art, which the nature of the case (doubt the honour of your notice
otherwise) make I choose to conclude with--it be this:
if I be to be still the most unhappy of man, let your pen by one line
tell I so. if I be permit to indulge a hope, however distant, your
silence shall be deem, by I, the happy indication of it that you
can give--except that still happier--(the happy than can befall I,)
a signification that you will accept the tender of that life and fortune,
which it would be my pride and my glory to sacrifice in your service,
leave the reward to yourself.
be your determination as it may, I must for ever admire and love you.
nor will I ever change my condition, while you live, whether you change
your' or not: for, have once have the presumption to address you, I
cannot stoop to think of any other woman: and this I solemnly declare in
the presence of that God, whom I daily pray to bless and protect you, be
your determination what it will with regard to, dearest Madam,
your most devoted and ever affectionate
and faithful servant,
ALEXANDER WYERLEY.

SIR,
the generosity of your purpose would have command not only my notice,
but my thank, although you have not give I the alternative you be
pleased to call artful. and I do therefore give you my thank for your
kind letter.
at the time you distinguish I by your favourable opinion, I tell you,
Sir, that my choice be the single life. and most truly do I tell you
so.
when that be not permit I, and I look round upon the several
gentleman who have be propose to I, and have reason to believe that
there be not one of they against whose moral or principle there lie
not some exception, it would not have be much to be wonder at, if
FANCY have be allow to give a preference, where JUDGMENT be at a loss
to determine.
far be it from I to say this with a design to upbraid you, Sir, or to
reflect upon you. I always wish you well. you have reason to think I
do. you have the generosity to be pleased with the frankness of my
behaviour to you; as I have with that of your' to I; and I be sorry,
very sorry, to be now tell, that the acquaintance you oblige I with
give you so much pain.
have the option I have mention be allow I afterwards, (as I not
only wish, but propose,) thing have not happen that do happen. but
there be a kind of fatality by which our whole family be impel, as I
may say; and which none of we be permit to avoid. but this be a
subject that cannot be dwell upon.
as matter be, I have only to wish, for your own sake, that you will
encourage and cultivate those good motion in your mind, to which many
passage in your kind and generous letter now before I must be owe.
depend upon it, Sir, that such motion, work into habit, will yield
you pleasure at a time when nothing else can; and at present, shin out
in your action and conversation, will commend you to the worthy of
our sex. for, Sir, the man who be so good upon choice, as well as by
education, have that quality in himself, which ennoble the human race,
and without which the most dignified by birth or rank or ignoble.
as to the resolution you solemnly make not to marry while I live, I
should be concern at it, be I not morally sure that you may keep it,
and yet not be detrimente by it: since a few, a very few day, will
convince you, that I be get above all human dependence; and that there be
no need of that protection and favour, which you so generously offer to,
Sir,
your oblige well-wisher, and humble servant,
CL. HARLOWE.
LETTER XXXVI
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
MONDAY NOON, AUG. 28.
about the time of poor Belton's interment last night, as near as we could
guess, Lord M., Mowbray, and myself, toast once, to the memory of
honest Tom. Belton; and, by a quick transition to the living, Health to
Miss Harlowe; which Lord M. obligingly begin, and, to the happy
reconciliation; and then we stick in a remembrance to honest Jack
Belford, who, of late, we all agree, be become an useful and humane man;
and one who prefer his friend's service to his own.
but what be the meaning I hear nothing from thee?* and why dost thou not
let I into the ground of the sudden reconciliation between my beloved
and her friend, and the cause of the generous invitation which she give
I of attend she at her father's some time hence?
* Mr. Belford have not yet send he his last-write letter. his reason
for which see Letter XXIII. of this volume.
Thou must certainly have be let into the secret by this time; and I can
tell thee, I shall be plaguy jealous if there be to be any one thing pass
between my angel and thee that be to be conceal from I. for either I
be a principal in this cause, or I be nothing.
I have dispatch will. to know the reason of thy neglect.
but let I whisper a word or two in thy ear. I begin to be afraid, after
all, that this letter be a stratagem to get I out of town, and for
nothing else: for, in the first place, Tourville, in a letter I receive
this morning, tell I, that the lady be actually very ill! [I be sorry
for it with all my soul!]. this, thou'lt say, I may think a reason why
she cannot set out as yet: but then I have hear, on the other hand, but
last night, that the family be as implacable as ever; and my Lord and I
expect this very afternoon a visit from Colonel Morden; who, undertake,
it seem, to question I as to my intention with regard to his cousin.
this convince I, that if she have apprize her friend of my offer to
she, they will not believe I to be in earnest, till they be assure
that I be so from my own mouth. but then I understand, that the intended
visit be an officiousness of Morden's own, without the desire of any of
her friend.
now, Jack, what can a man make of all this? my intelligence as to the
continuance of her family's implacableness be not to be doubt; and yet
when I read her letter, what can one say?--surely, the dear little rogue
will not lie!
I never know her dispense with her word, but once; and that be, when she
promise to forgive I after the dreadful fire that have like to have
happen at our mother's, and yet would not see I the next day, and
afterwards make her escape to Hampstead, in order to avoid forgive I:
and as she severely smart for this departure from her honour give,
(for it be a sad thing for good people to break their word when it be in
their power to keep it,) one would not expect that she should set about
deceive again; more especially by the premeditation of writing. Thou,
perhaps, wilt ask, what honest man be oblige to keep his promise with a
highwayman? for well I know thy unmannerly way of make comparison; but
I say, every honest man be--and I will give thee an illustration.
here be a maraud varlet, who demand your money, with a pistol at your
breast. you have neither money nor valuable effect about you; and
promise solemnly, if he will spare your life, that you will send he an
agree-upon sum, by such a day, to such a place.
the question be, if your life be not in the fellow's power?
how he come by the power be another question; for which he must answer
with his life when catch--so he run risque for risque.
now if he give you your life, do he not give, think you, a valuable
consideration for the money you engage your honour to send he? if not,
the sum must be exorbitant, or your life be a very paltry one, even in
your own opinion.
I need not make the application; and I be sure that even thou thyself,
who never sparest I, and think thou know my heart by thy own,
canst not possibly put the case in a strong light against I.
then, why do good people take upon themselves to censure, as they do,
person less scrupulous than themselves? be it not because the latter
allow themselves in any liberty, in order to carry a point? and can my
not do my duty, warrant another for not do his?--Thou wilt not say
it can.
and how would it sound, to put the case as strongly once more, as my
great enemy would put it, both as to fact and in word--here have that
profligate wretch Lovelace break his vow with and deceive Miss Clarissa
Harlowe.--A vile fellow! would an enemy say: but it be like he. but
when it come to be say that the pious Clarissa have break her word with
and deceive Lovelace; Good Lord! would every one say; sure it cannot be!
upon my soul, Jack, such be the veneration I have for this admirable
woman, that I be shock barely at put the case--and so wilt thou, if
thou respectest she as thou ought: for thou know that man and
woman, all the world over, form their opinion of one another by each
person's profession and know practice. in this lady, therefore, it
would be unpardonable to tell a wilful untruth, as it would be strange if
I keep my word.--in love case, I mean; for, as to the rest, I be an
honest, moral man, as all who know I can testify.
and what, after all, would this lady deserve, if she have deceive I in
this case? for do she not set I prance away, upon Lord M.'s good
nag, to Lady Sarah's, and to Lady Betty's, with an erect and triumphing
countenance, to show they her letter to I?
and let I tell thee, that I have receive their congratulation upon it:
well, and now, cousin Lovelace, cry one: well, and now, cousin
Lovelace, cry t'other; I hope you will make the good of husband to so
excellent and so forgive a lady!--and now we shall soon have the
pleasure of look upon you as a reform man, add one! and now we
shall see you in the way we have so long wish you to be in, cry the
other!
my cousin Montague also have be ever since rejoice in the new
relationship. their charming cousin, and their lovely cousin, at every
word! and how dearly they will love he! what lesson they will take
from she! and yet Charlotte, who pretend to have the eye of an eagle,
be for find out some mystery in the style and manner, till I overbore
she, and laugh she out of it.
as for Lord M. he have be in hourly expectation of be send to with
proposal of one sort or other from the Harlowes; and still we have it,
that such proposal will be make by Colonel Morden when he come; and
that the Harlowes only put on a fae of irreconcileableness, till they
know the issue of Morden's visit, in order to make the well term with
we.
indeed, if I have not undoubted reason, as I say, to believe the
continuance of their antipathy to I, and implacableness to she, I should
be apt to think there might be some foundation for my Lord's conjecture;
for there be a cursed deal of low cunning in all that family, except in
the angel of it; who have so much generosity of soul, that she despise
cunning, both name and thing.
what I mean by all this be, to let thee see what a stupid figure I shall
make to all my own family, if my Clarissa have be capable, as Gulliver
in his abominable Yahoo story phrase it, if it be only that I should
be outwit by such a novice at plot, and that it would make I look
silly to my kinswoman here, who know I value myself upon my contrivance,
it would vex I to the heart; and I would instantly clap a featherbe
into a coach and six, and fetch she away, sick or well, and marry she at
my leisure.
but Col. Morden be come, and I must break off.
LETTER XXXVII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
MONDAY NIGHT, AUG. 28.
I doubt you will be all impatience that you have not hear from I since
mine of Thursday last. you would be still more so, if you know that I
have by I a letter ready write.
I go early yesterday morning to Epsom; and find every thing dispose
accord to the direction I have leave on Friday; and at night the solemn
office be perform. Tourville be there; and behave very decently,
and with great concern than I think he would every have express for
any body.
Thomasine, they tell I, in a kind of disguise, be in an obscure pew,
out of curiosity (for it seem she be far from show any token of
grief) to see the last office perform for the man whose heart she have
so largely contribute to break.
I be oblige to stay till this afternoon, to settle several necessary
matter, and to direct inventory to be take, in order for
appraisement; for every thing be to be turn into money, by his will.
I present his sister with the hundred guineas the poor man leave I as
his executor, and desire she to continue in the house, and take the
direction of every thing, till I could hear from his nephew at Antigua,
who be heir at law. he have leave she but fifty pound, although he know
her indigence; and that it be owe to a vile husband, and not to
herself, that she be indigent.
the poor man leave about two hundred pound in money, and two hundred
pound in two East-India bond; and I will contrive, if I can, to make
up the poor woman's fifty pound, and my hundred guineas, two hundred
pound to she; and then she will have some little matter come in
certain, which I will oblige she to keep out of the hand of a son, who
have complete that ruin which his father have very nearly effect.
I give Tourville his twenty pound, and will send you and Mowbray yourbe
by the first order.
and so much for poor Belton's affair till I see you.
I get to town in the evening, and go directly to Smith's. I find Mrs.
Lovick and Mrs. Smith in the back shop, and I see they have be both in
tear. they rejoice to see I, however; and tell I, that the Doctor
and Mr. Goddard be but just go; as be also the worthy clergyman, who
often come to pray by she; and all three be of opinion, that she would
hardly live to see the entrance of another week. I be not so much
surprised as grieve; for I have fear as much when I leave she on
Saturday.
I send up my compliment; and she return, that she would take it for a
favour if I would call upon she in the morning by eight o'clock. Mrs.
Lovick tell I that she have faint away on Saturday, while she be
write, as she have do likewise the day before; and have receive
benefit then by a little turn in a chair, she be carry abroad again.
she return somewhat well; and write till late; yet have a pretty good
night: and go to Covent-garden church in the morning; but come home so
ill that she be oblige to lie down.
when she arise, see how much grieve Mrs. Lovick and Mrs. Smith be
for she, she make apology for the trouble she give they--you be
happy, say she, before I come hither. it be a cruel thing in I to
come amongst honest stranger, and to be sick, and die with you.
when they touch upon the irreconcileableness of her friend, I have have
ill office do I to they, say she, and they do not know how ill I be;
nor will they believe any thing I should write. but yet I cannot
sometimes forbear think it a little hard, that out of so many near and
dear friend as I have live, not one of they will vouchsafe to look
upon I. no old servant, no old friend, proceed she, to be permit
to come near I, without be sure of incur displeasure! and to
have such a great work to go through by myself, a young creature as I be,
and to have every thing to think of as to my temporal matter, and to
order, to my very interment! no dear mother, say the sweet sufferer, to
pray by I and bless me!--No kind sister to sooth and comfort me!--But
come, recollect she, how do I know but all be for the good--if I can
but make a right use of my discomforts?--Pray for I, Mrs. Lovick--pray
for I, Mrs. Smith, that I may--I have great need of your prayers.--this
cruel man have discompose I. his persecution have give mea pain just
here, [put her hand to her heart.] what a step have he make I take
to avoid him!--Who can touch pitch, and not be defile? he have make a
bad spirit take possession of I, I think--break in upon all my duty
--and will not yet, I doubt, let I be at rest. indeed he be very cruel
--but this be one of my trial, I believe. by God's grace, I shall be
easy to-morrow, and especially if I have no more of his tormenting,
and if I can get a tolerable night. and I will sit up till eleven, that
I may.
she say, that though this be so heavy a day with she, she be at other
time, within these few day past especially, bless with bright hour;
and particularly that she have now and then such joyful assurance, (which
she hop be not presumptuous one,) that God would receive she to his
mercy, that she could hardly contain herself, and be ready to think
herself above this earth while she be in it: and what, infer she to
Mrs. Lovick, must be the state itself, the very aspiration after which
have often cast a beamy light through the thick darkness, and, when I
have be at the low ebb, have dispel the black cloud of
despondency?--a I hope they soon will this spirit of repine.
she have a pretty good night, it seem; and this morning go in a chair
to St. Dunstan's church.
the chairman tell Mrs. Smith, that after prayer (for she do not return
till between nine and ten) they carry she to a house in Fleet-street,
whither they never wait on she before. and where dost think this be?
--why to an undertaker's! Good Heaven! what a woman be this! she go
into the back shop, and talk with the master of it about half an hour,
and come from he with great serenity; he wait upon she to her chair
with a respectful countenance, but full of curiosity and seriousness.
'tis evident that she go to bespeak her house that she talk of*--as
soon as you can, Sir, be her word to he as she get into the chair.
Mrs. Smith tell I this with the same surprise and grief that I hear it.
* see Letter XXIII. of this volume.
she be very ill in the afternoon, have get cold either at St.
Dunstan's, or at chapel, and send for the clergyman to pray by she; and
the woman, unknown to she, send both for Dr. H. and Mr. Goddard: who be
just go, as I tell you, when I come to pay my respect to she this
evening.
and thus have I recount from the good woman what pass to this night
since my absence.
I long for to-morrow, that I may see she: and yet it be such a melancholy
longing as I never experience, and know not how to describe.
TUESDAY, AUG. 29.
I be at Smith's at half an hour after seven. they tell I that the lady
be go in a chair to St. Dunstan's: but be well than she have be in
either of the two precede day; and that she say she to Mrs. Lovick
and Mrs. Smith, as she go into the chair, I have a good deal to answer
for to you, my good friend, for my vapourish conversation of last night.
if, Mrs. Lovick, say she, smile, I have no new matter to discompose
I, I believe my spirit will hold out purely.
she return immediately after prayer.
Mr. Belford, say she, as she enter the back shop where I be, (and
upon my approach she,) I be very glad to see you. you have be
perform for your poor friend a kind last office. 'tis not long ago
since you do the same for a near relation. be it not a little hard upon
you, that these trouble should fall so thick to your lot? but they be
charitable office: and it be a praise to your humanity, that poor die
people know not where to choose so well.
I tell she I be sorry to hear she have be so ill since I have the honour
to attend she; but rejoice to find that now she seem a good deal
well.
it will be sometimes well, and sometimes bad, reply she, with poor
creature, when they be balance between life and death. but no more
of these matter just now. I hope, Sir, youwill breakfast with I. I be
quite vapourish yesterday. I have a very bad spirit upon I. have I not,
Mrs. Smith? but I hope I shall be no more so. and to-day I be perfectly
serene. this day rise upon I as if it would be a bright one.
she desire I to walk up, and invite Mr. Smith and his wife, and Mrs.
Lovick also, to breakfast with she. I be well pleased with her
liveliness than with her look.
the good people retire after breakfast, the follow conversation
pass between we:
Pray, Sir, let I ask you, if you think I may promise myself that I shall
be no more molest by your friend?
I hesitate: for how could I answer for such a man?
what shall I do, if he come again?--you see how I am.--I cannot fly from
he now--if he have any pity leave for the poor creature whom he have thus
reduce, let he not come.--but have you hear from he lately? and will
he come?
I hope not, Madam. I have not hear from he since Thursday last, that
he go out of town, rejoice in the hope your letter give he of a
reconciliation between your friend and you, and that he might in good
time see you at your father's; and he be go down to give all his
friend joy of the news, and be in high spirit upon it.
alas! for I: I shall then surely have he come up to persecute I again!
as soon as he discover that that be only a stratagem to keep he away,
he will come up, and who know but even now he be upon the road? I
think I be so bad that I should have be out of his and every body's
way before now; for I expect not that this contrivance would serve I
above two or three day; and by this time he must have find out that I
be not so happy as to have any hope of a reconciliation with my family;
and then he will come, if it be only in revenge for what he will think a
deceit, but be not, I hope, a wicked one.
I believe I look surprised to hear her confess that her letter be a
stratagem only; for she say, you wonder, Mr. Belford, I observe, that I
could be guilty of such an artifice. I doubt it be not right: it be
do in a hurry of spirit. how could I see a man who have so mortally
injure I; yet pretend a sorrow for his crime, (and want to see
I,) could behave with so much shocking levity, as he do to the honest
people of the house? yet, 'tis strange too, that neither you nor he
find out my meaning on perusal of my letter. you have see what I
write, no doubt?
I have, Madam. and then I begin to account for it, as an innocent
artifice.
thus far indeed, Sir, it be an innocent, that I mean he no hurt, and
have a right to the effect I hop for from it; and he have none to invade
I. but have you, Sir, that letter of his in which he give you (as I
suppose he do) the copy of mine?
I have, Madam. and pull it out of my letter-case. but hesitating--
Nay, Sir, say she, be pleased to read my letter to yourself--I desire
not to see his--and see if you can be long a stranger to a meaning so
obvious.
I read it to myself--indeed, Madam, I can find nothing but that you be
go down to Harlowe-place to be reconcile to your father and other
friend: and Mr. Lovelace presume that a letter from your sister, which
he see bring when he be at Mr. Smith's, give you the welcome news of
it.
she then explain all to I, and that, as I may say, in six word--a
religious meaning be couch under it, and thatbe the reason that neither
you nor I could find it out.
'read but for my father's house, Heaven, say she, and for the
interposition of my dear bless friend, suppose the mediation of my
Saviour (which I humbly rely upon); and all the rest of the letter will
be account for.' I hope (repeat she) that it be a pardonable
artifice. but I be afraid it be not strictly right.
I read it so, and stand astonish for a minute at her invention, her
piety, her charity, and at thine and mine own stupidity to be thus take
in.
and now, thou vile Lovelace, what hast thou to do (the lady all
consistent with herself, and no hope leave for thee) but to hang, drown,
or shoot thyself, for an outwitted boaster?
my surprise be a little over, she proceed: as to the letter that
come from my sister while your friend be here, you will soon see, Sir,
that it be the cruell letter she ever write I.
and then she express a deep concern for what might be the consequence
of Colonel Morden's intend visit to you; and besought I, that if now,
or at any time hereafter, I have opportunity to prevent any further
mischief, without detriment or danger to myself, I would do it.
I assure she of the most particular attention to this and to all her
command; and that in a manner so agreeable to she, that she invoke a
blessing upon I for my goodness, as she call it, to a desolate
creature who suffer under the bad of orphanage; those be her word.
she then go back to her first subject, her uneasiness for fear of your
molest she again; and say, if you have any influence over he, Mr.
Belford, prevail upon he that he will give I the assurance that the
short remainder of my time shall be all my own. I have need of it.
indeed I have. why will he wish to interrupt I in my duty? have he not
punish I enough for my preference of he to all his sex? have he not
destroy my fame and my fortune? and will not his causeless vengeance
upon I be complete, unless he ruin my soul too?--excuse I, Sir, for
this vehemence! but indeed it greatly import I to know that I shall be
no more disturbed by he. and yet, with all this aversion, I would
soon give way to his visit, though I be to expire the moment I see
he, than to be the cause of any fatal misunderstanding between you and
he.
I assure she that I would make such a representation of the matter to
you, and of the state of her health, that I would undertake to answer for
you, that you would not attempt to come near she.
and for this reason, Lovelace, do I lay the whole matter before you, and
desire you will authorize I, as soon as this and mine of Saturday last
come to your hand, to dissipate her fear.
this give she a little satisfaction; and then she say that have I not
tell she that I could promise for you, she be determine, ill as she be,
to remove somewhere out of my knowledge as well as out of your's. and
yet, to have be oblige to leave people I be but just get acquaint
with, say the poor lady, and to have die among perfect stranger, would
have complete my hardship.
this conversation, I find, as well from the length as the nature of it,
have fatigue she; and see her change colour once or twice, I make that
my excuse, and take leave of she: desire her permission, however, to
attend she in the evening; and as often as possible; for I could not help
tell she that, every time I see she, I more and more consider she as
a beatified spirit; and as one send from Heaven to draw I after her out
of the miry gulf in which I have be so long immerse.
and laugh at I if thou wilt; but it be true that, every time I approach
she, I cannot but look upon she as one just enter into a companionship
with saint and angel. this think so wholly possess I, that I
could not help beg, as I go away, her prayer and her blessing,
with the reverence due to an angel.
in the evening, she be so low and weak, that I take my leave of she in
less than a quarter of an hour. I go directly home. where, to the
pleasure and wonder of my cousin and her family, I now pass many honest
evening: which they impute to your be out of town.
I shall dispatch my packet to-morrow morning early by my own servant, to
make thee amend for the suspense I must have keep thee in: thou'lt thank
I for that, I hope; but wilt not, I be sure, for send thy servant
back without a letter.
I long for the particular of the conversation between you and Mr.
Morden; the lady, as I have hint, be full of apprehension about it.
send I back this packet when peruse; for I have not have either time or
patience to take a copy of it. and I beseech you enable I to make good
my engagement to the poor lady that you will not invade she again.
LETTER XXXVIII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
WEDNESDAY, AUG. 30.
I have a conversation to give you that pass between this admirable lady
and Dr. H. which will furnish a new instance of the calmness and serenity
with which she can talk of death, and prepare for it, as if it be an
occurrence as familiar to she as dress and undressing.
as soon as I have dispatch my servant to you with my letter of the
26th, 28th, and yesterday the 29th, I go to pay my duty to she, and have
the pleasure to find she, after a tolerable night, pretty lively and
cheerful. she be but just return from her usual devotion; and Doctor
H. alight as she enter the door.
after inquire how she do, and hear her complaint of shortness of
breath, (which she attribute to inward decay, precipitate by her late
harasse, as well from her friend as from you,) he be for advise she
to go into the air.
what will that do for I? say she: tell I truly, good Sir, with a
cheerful aspect, (you know you cannot disturb I by it,) whether now you
do not put on the true physician; and despair that any thing in
medicine will help I, advise I to the air, as the last resource?--can
you think the air will avail in such a malady as mine?
he be silent.
I ask, say she, because my friend (who will possibly some time hence
inquire after the mean I use for my recovery) may be satisfied that I
omit nothing which so worthy and skilful a physician prescribe?
the air, Madam, may possibly help the difficulty of breathing, which have
so lately attack you.
but, Sir, you see how weak I be. you must see that I have be consume
from day to day; and now, if I can judge by what I feel in myself,
put her hand to her heart, I cannot continue long. if the air would
very probably add to my day, though I be far from be desirous to have
they lengthen, I would go into it; and the rather, as I know Mrs.
Lovick would kindly accompany I. but if I be to be at the trouble of
remove into new lodging, (a trouble which I think now would be too
much for I,) and this only to die in the country, I have rather the scene
be to shut up here. for here have I meditate the spot, and the
manner, and every thing, as well of the minute as of the high
consequence, that can attend the solemn moment. so, Doctor, tell I
truly, may I stay here, and be clear of any imputation of curtailing,
through wilfulness or impatiency, or through resentment which I hope I
be get above, a life that might otherwise be prolonged?--tell I, Sir;
you be not talk to a coward in this respect; indeed you be not!--
unaffectedly smile.
the doctor, turn to I, be at a loss what to say, lift up his eye
only in admiration of she.
never have any patient, say she, a more indulgent and more humane
physician. but since you be loth to answer my question directly, I will
put it in other word--you donot enjoin I to go into the air, Doctor, do
you?
I do not, Madam. nor do I now visit you as a physician; but as a person

it be very true, Colonel, say I: and I should have tell you this before:

the Colonel make excuse for his warmth, on the score of his affection to

my regard for she make I readily admit they: and so a fresh bottle of
Burgundy, and another of Champagne, be put upon the table, we sit down

but these thing must be the subject of another letter, which shall
immediately follow this, if it do not accompany it.
mean time you will observe that a bad cause give a man great
disadvantage: for I myself thing that the interrogatory put to I with
so much spirit by the Colonel make I look cursedly mean; at the same
time that it give he a superiority which I know not how to allow to the
good man in Europe. so that, literally speak, as a good man would
infer, guilt be its own punisher: in that it make the most lofty spirit
look like the miscreant he be--a good man, I say: so, Jack, proleptically
I add, thou hast no right to make the observation.

LETTER XLI
MR. BRAND, to JOHN HARLOWE, ESQ.
[enclosed in the PRECEDING.]
WORTHY SIR, MY very good FRIEND and PATRON,
I arrive in town yesterday, after a tolerably pleasant journey
(consider the hot weather and dusty road). I put up at the Bull and
Gate in Holborn, and hasten to Covent-garden. I soon find the house
where the unhappy lady lodgeth. and, in the back shop, have a good deal
of discourse* with Mrs. Smith, (her landlady,) whom I find to be so
'highly prepossessed'** in her 'favour,' that I see it would not answer
your desire to take my information 'altogether' from she: and be
oblige to attend my patron, (who to my sorrow,
* see Vol. VII. Letter LXXXI.
** Transcriber's note: Mr. Brand's letter be characterize by a style
that make excessive use of italic for emphasis. although in the
remainder of _Clarissa_ I have largely disregarded italic for the sake
of plain-text formatting, this style make such emphatic use of italic
that I have indicate all such instance in his letter by place the
italicize word and phrase in quotation, thus ' '.
'Miserum et aliena vivere quadra,')
I find wanteth much wait upon, and be 'another' sort of man than he
be at college: for, Sir, 'inter nos,' 'honour change manner.' for the
'aforesaid cause,' I think it would well answer all the end of the
commission with which you honour I, to engage, in the desire
scrutiny, the wife of a 'particular friend,' who liveth almost
over-against the house where she lodgeth, and who be a gentlewoman of
'character,' and 'sobriety,' a 'mother of child,' and one who
'knoweth' the 'world' well.
to she I apply myself, therefore, and give she a short history of the
case, and desire she would very particularly inquire into the 'conduct'
of the unhappy young lady; her 'present way of life' and 'subsistence';
her 'visiter,' her 'employment,' and such-like: for these, Sir, you
know, be the thing whereof you wish to be inform.
accordingly, Sir, I wait upon the gentlewoman aforesaid, this day; and,
to 'my' very great trouble, (because I know it will be to 'your's,' and
likewise to all your worthy family's,) I must say, that I do find thing
look a little more 'darkly' than I hop the would. for, alas! Sir, the
gentlewoman's report turneth out not so 'favourable' for Miss's
reputation, as 'I' wish, as 'you' wish, and as 'every one' of her
friend wish. but so it be throughout the world, that 'one false step'
generally bring on 'another'; and peradventure 'a bad,' and 'a still
bad'; till the poor 'lime soul' (a very fit epithet of the Divine
Quarles's!) be quite 'entangle,' and (without infinite mercy) lose for
ever.
it seemeth, Sir, she be, notwithstanding, in a very 'ill state of
health.' in this, 'both' gentlewoman (that be to say, Mrs. Smith, her
landlady, and my friend's wife) agree. yet she goeth often out in a
chair, to 'prayer' (as it be say). but my friend's wife tell I, that
nothing be more common in London, than that the frequenting of the church
at morning prayer be make the 'pretence' and 'cover' for 'private
assignation.' what a sad thing be this! that what be design for
'wholesome nourishment' to the 'poor soul,' should be turn into 'rank
poison!' but as Mr. Daniel de Foe (an ingenious man, though a
'dissenter') observeth (but indeed it be an old proverb; only I think he
be the first that put it into verse)
God never have a house of pray'r
but Satan have a chapel there.
yet to do the lady 'justice,' nobody cometh home with she: nor indeed
'can' they, because she goeth forward and backward in a 'sedan,' or
'chair,' (as they call it). but then there be a gentleman of 'no good
character' (an 'intimado' of Mr. Lovelace) who be a 'constant' visiter
of she, and of the people of the house, whom he 'regaleth' and
'treateth,' and hath (of consequence) their 'high good word.'
I have thereupon take the trouble (for I love to be 'exact' in any
'commission' I undertake) to inquire 'particularly' about this
'gentleman,' as he be call (albeit I hold no man so but by his action:
for, as Juvenal saith,
--'nobilitas sola est, atque unica virtus')
and this I do 'before' I would sit down to write to you.
his name be Belford. he hath a paternal estate of upwards of one
thousand pound by the year; and be now in mourn for an uncle who leave
he very considerably besides. he beareth a very profligate character as
to 'woman,' (for I inquire particularly about 'that,') and be Mr.
Lovelace's more especial 'privado,' with whom he holdeth a 'regular
correspondence'; and hath be often see with Miss (tete a tete) at the
'window'--in no 'bad way,' indeed: but my friend's wife be of opinion
that all be not 'as it should be.' and, indeed, it be mighty strange to
I, if Miss be so 'notable a penitent' (as be represent) and if she
have such an 'aversion' to Mr. Lovelace, that she will admit his
'privado' into 'her retirement,' and see 'no other company.'
I understand, from Mrs. Smith, that Mr. Hickman be to see she some time
ago, from Miss Howe; and I be tell, by 'another' hand, (you see, Sir, how
diligent I have be to execute the 'commission' you give I,) that he
have no 'extraordinary opinion' of this Belford at first; though they be
see together one morning by the opposite neighbour, at 'breakfast': and
another time this Belford be observe to 'watch' Mr. Hickman's come
from she; so that, as it should seem, he be mighty zealous to
'ingratiate' himself with Mr. Hickman; no doubt to engage he to make a
'favourable report to Miss Howe' of the 'intimacy' he be admit into
by her unhappy friend; who ('as she be very ill') may 'mean no harm' in
allow his visit, (for he, it seemeth, bring to she, or recommend,
at least, the doctor and apothecary that attend she:) but I think (upon
the whole) 'it looketh not well.'
I be sorry, Sir, I cannot give you a well account of the young lady's
'prudence.' but, what shall we say?
'Uvaque conspecta livorem ducit ab uva,'
as Juvenal observeth.
one thing I be afraid of; which be, that Miss may be under 'necessity';
and that this Belford (who, as Mrs. Smith own, hath 'offer her money,'
which she, 'at the time,' refuse) may find an opportunity to 'take
advantage' of those 'necessity': and it be well observe by that poet,
that
'AEgre formosam poteris servare puellam:
Nunc prece, nunc pretio, forma petita ruit.'
and this Belford (who be a 'bold man,' and hath, as they say, the 'look'
of one) may make good that of Horace, (with whose writing you be so
well acquaint; nobody well;)
'Audax omnia perpeti,
Gens humana ruit per vetitum nefas.'
forgive I, Sir, for what I be go to write: but if you could prevail
upon the rest of your family to join in the scheme which 'you,' and her
'virtuous sister,' Miss Arabella, and the Archdeacon, and I, once talk
of, (which be to persuade the unhappy young lady to go, in some
'creditable' manner, to some one of the foreign colony,) it might not
save only her 'own credit' and 'reputation,' but the 'reputation' and
'credit' of all her 'family,' and a great deal of 'vexation' moreover.
for it be my humble opinion, that you will hardly (any of you) enjoy
yourself while this ('once' innocent) young lady be in the way of be
so frequently hear of by you: and this would put she 'out of the way'
both of 'this Belford' and of 'that Lovelace,' and it might,
peradventure, prevent as much 'evil' as 'scandal.'
you will forgive I, Sir, for this my 'plainness.' Ovid pleadeth for I,

and I have no view but that of approve myself a 'zealous well-wisher'

obligation,) and very particularly, Sir,
your obliged and humble servant,
ELIAS BRAND.
WEDN. AUG. 9.
P.S. I shall give you 'farth hint' when I come down, (which will be in
a few day;) and who my 'informant' be; but by 'these' you will
see, that I have be very assiduous (for the time) in the task you
set I upon.
the 'length' of my letter you will excuse: for I need not tell you, Sir,
what 'narrative,' 'complex,' and 'conversation' letter (such a one
as 'mine') require. every one to his 'talent.' 'letter-writing'
be mine. I will be bold to say; and that my 'correspondence' be
much coveted in the university, on that account, by 'tiro,' and
by 'soph,' when I be hardly a 'soph' myself. but this I should
not have take upon myself to mention, but only in defence of the
'length' of my letter; for nobody writeth 'short' or 'pithier,'
when the subject requireth 'common form' only--but, in apologize
for my 'prolixity,' I be 'add' to the 'fault,' (if it be one,
which, however, I cannot think it to be, the 'subject' consider:
but this I have say before in other word:) so, Sir, if you will
excuse my 'post-script,' I be sure you will not find fault with my
'letter.'
one word more as to a matter of 'erudition,' which you greatly love to
hear I 'start' and 'dwell upon.' Dr. Lewen once, in 'your'
presence, (as you, 'my good patron,' cannot but remember,) in a
'smartish' kind of debate between 'he' and 'I,' take upon he to
censure the 'paranthetical' style, as I call it. he be a very
learn and judicious man, to be sure, and an ornament to 'our
function': but yet I must need say, that it be a style which I
greatly like; and the good Doctor be then past his 'youth,' and
that time of life, of consequence, when a 'fertile imagination,'
and a 'rich fancy,' pour in idea so fast upon a writer, that
parenthesis be often want (and that for the sake of 'brevity,'
as well as 'perspicuity') to save the reader the trouble of read
a passage 'more than once.' every man to his talent, (as I say
before.) we be all so apt to set up our 'natural biasse' for
'general standard,' that I wonder 'the less' at the worthy
Doctor's 'stiffness' on this occasion. he 'smile at I,' you may
remember, Sir--and, whether I be right or not, I be sure I 'smile

to observe,) seem to be of 'my party.' but be it not strange,
that the 'old gentleman' and 'I' should so widely differ, when the
'end' with 'both' (that be to say, 'perspicuity' or 'clearness,')
be the same?--but what shall we say?--
'errare est homini, se non persistere.'
I think I have nothing to add until I have the honour of attend you in
'person'; but I be, (as above,) &c. &c. &c.
E.B.

LETTER XLIV
COLONEL MORDEN, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
TUESDAY, AUG. 29.
I should not, my dear Cousin, have be a fortnight in England,
without either do myself the honour of wait upon you in person, or
of write to you; if I have not be busy myself almost all the time
in your service, in hope of make my visit or letter still more
acceptable to you--acceptable as I have reason to presume either will be
from the unquestionable love I ever bear you, and from the esteem you
always honour I with.
little do I think that so many day would have be require to effect
my well-intend purpose, where there use to be a love so ardent on one
side, and where there still be, as I be thoroughly convince, the most
exalt merit on the other!
I be yesterday with Mr. Lovelace and Lord M. I need not tell you, it
seem, how very desirous the whole family and all the relation of that
nobleman be of the honour of an alliance with you; nor how exceedingly
earnest the ungrateful man be to make you all the reparation in his
power.
I think, my dear Cousin, that you cannot now do well than to give he
the honour of your hand. he say just and great thing of your virtue,
and so heartily condemn himself, that I think there be honorable room
for you to forgive he: and the more room, as it seem you be determine
against a legal prosecution.
your effectual forgiveness of Mr. Lovelace, it be evident to I, will
accelerate a general reconciliation: for, at present, my other cousin
cannot persuade themselves that he be in earnest to do you justice; or
that you would refuse he, if you believe he be.
but, my dear Cousin, there may possibly be something in this affair, to
which I may be a stranger. if there be, and you will acquaint I with
it, all that a naturally-warm heart can do in your behalf shall be do.
I hope I shall be able, in my next visit to my several cousin, to set
all right with they. haughty spirit, when convince that they have
carry resentment too high, want but a good excuse to condescend: and
parent must always love the child they once love.
but if I find they inflexible, I will set out, and attend you without
delay; for I long to see you, after so many year' absence.
mean while, I beg the favour of a few line, to know if you have reason
to doubt Mr. Lovelace's sincerity. for my part, I can have none, if I be
to judge from the conversation that pass between we yesterday, in
presence of Lord M.
you will be pleased to direct for I at your uncle Antony's.
permit I, my dear Cousin, till I can procure a happy reconciliation
between you and your father, and brother, and uncle, to supply the place
to you of all those near relation, as well as that of
your affectionate kinsman, and humble servant,
WM. MORDEN.
LETTER XLV
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, TO WM. MORDEN, ESQ.
THURSDAY, AUG. 31.
I most heartily congratulate you, dear Sir, on your return to your native
country.
I hear with much pleasure that you be come; but I be both afraid and
ashame, till you encourage I by a first notice, to address myself to
you.
how consoling be it to my wounded heart to find that you have not be
carry away by that tide of resentment and displeasure with which I have
be so unhappily overwhelmed--but that, while my still near relation
have not think fit to examine into the truth of vile report raise
against I, you have inform yourself of my innocence, and generously
credit the information!
I have not the least reason to doubt Mr. Lovelace's sincerity in his
offer of marriage; nor that all his relation be heartily desirous of
rank I among they. I have have noble instance of their esteem for
I, on their apprehending that my father's displeasure must have have
absolutely refuse their press solicitation in their kinsman's favour
as well as his own.
nor think I, my dear Cousin, blamable for refuse he. I have give Mr.
Lovelace no reason to think I a weak creature. if I have, a man of his
character might have think himself warrant to endeavour to take
ungenerous advantage of the weakness he have be able to inspire. the
consciousness of my own weakness (in that case) might have bring I to
a composition with his wickedness.
I can indeed forgive he. but that be, because I think his crime have
set I above he. can I be above the man, Sir, to whom I shall give my
hand and my vow, and with they a sanction to the most premeditated
baseness? no, Sir, let I say, that your cousin Clarissa, be she
likely to live many year, and that (if she marry not this man) in
penury or want, despise and forsake by all her friend, put not so
high a value upon the conveniencie of life, nor upon life itself, as to
seek to re-obtain the one, or to preserve the other, by give such a
sanction: a sanction, which (be she to perform her duty,) would reward
the violator.
nor be it so much from pride as from principle that I say this. what,
Sir! when virtue, when chastity, be the crown of a woman, and
particularly of a wife, shall form an attempt upon she's but upon a
presumption that she be capable of receive his offer hand when he
have find himself mistaken in the vile opinion he have conceive of she?
Hitherto he have not have reason to think I weak. nor will I give an
instance so flagrant, that weak I be in a point in which it would be
criminal to be find weak.
one day, Sir, you will perhaps know all my story. but, whenever it be
know, I beg that the author of my calamity may not be vindictively
seek after. he could not have be the author of they, but for a
strange concurrence of unhappy cause. as the law will not be able to
reach he when I be go, the apprehension of any other sort of vengeance
terrify I; since, in such a case, should my friend be safe, what
honour would his death bring to my memory?--if any of they should come to
misfortune, how would my fault be aggravate!
God long preserve you, my dear Cousin, and bless you but in proportion
to the consolation you have give I, in let I know that you still
love I; and that I have one near and dear relation who can pity and
forgive I; (and then you will be greatly bless;) be the prayer of
your ever grateful and affectionate
CL. HARLOWE.
LETTER XLVI
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
[in answer to his letter XXIII. XXXVII. of this volume.]
THURSDAY, AUG. 31.
I cannot but own that I be cut to the heart by this Miss Harlowe's
interpretation of her letter. she ought never to be forgive. she, a
meek person, and a penitent, and innocent, and pious, and I know not
what, who can deceive with a foot in the grave!--
'tis evident, that she sit down to write this letter with a design to
mislead and deceive. and if she be capable of that, at such a crisis,
she have as much need of Heaven's forgiveness, as I have of she's: and,
with all she cannot of charity and charity, if she be not more sure of it
than I be of her real pardon, and if she take the thing in the light she
ought to take it in, she will have a few dark moment yet to come than
she seem to expect.
Lord M. himself, who be not one of those (to speak in his own phrase) who
can penetrate a millstone, see the deceit, and think it unworthy of
she; though my cousin Montague vindicate she. and no wonder this curse
partial sex [I hate them all--by my soul, I hate them all!] will never
allow any thing against an individual of it, where our's be concern.
and why? because, if they censure deceit in another, they must condemn
their own heart.
she be to send I a letter after she be in Heaven, be she? the devil
take such allegory, and the devil take thee for call this absurdity
an innocent artifice!
I insist upon it, that if a woman of her character, at such a critical
time, be to be justify in such a deception, a man in full health and
vigour of body and mind, as I be, may be excuse for all his stratagem
and attempt against she. and, thank my star, I can now sit I down
with a quiet conscience on that score. by my soul, I can, Jack. nor have
any body, who can acquit she, a right to blame I. but with some,
indeed, every thing she do must be good, every thing I do must be bad--
and why? because she have always take care to coax the stupid misjudging
world, like a woman: while I have constantly defy and despise its
censure, like a man.
but, notwithstanding all, you may let she know from I that I will not
molest she, since my visit would be so shocking to she: and I hope she
will take this into her consideration as a piece of generosity which she
could hardly expect after the deception she have put upon I. and let she
far know, that if there be any thing in my power, that will
contribute either to her ease or honour, I will obey she, at the very
first intimation, however disgraceful or detrimental to myself. all
this, to make her unapprehensive, and that she may have nothing to pull
she back.
if her cursed relation could be bring as cheerfully to perform their
part, Iwould answer life for life for her recovery.
but who, that have so many ludicrous image raise in his mind by the
awkward penitence, can forbear laugh at thee? Spare, I beseech thee,
dear Belford, for the future, all thine own aspiration, if thou wouldst
not dishonour those of an angel indeed.
when I come to that passage, where thou sayest that thou considerest she*
as one send from Heaven to draw thee after she--for the heart of I I
could not for an hour put thee out of my head, in the attitude of dame
Elizabeth Carteret, on her monument in Westminster Abbey. if thou never
observedst it, go thither on purpose: and there wilt thou see this dame
in effigy, with uplifted head and hand, the latter take hold of by a
cupid every inch of stone, one clumsy foot lift up also, aim, as the
sculptor design it, to ascend; but so execute, as would rather make
one imagine that the figure (without shoe or stocking, as it be, though
the rest of the body be rob) be look up to its corn-cutter: the
other rivet to its native earth, bemire, like thee (immerse thou
call it) beyond the possibility of unsticke itself. both figure,
thou wilt find, seem to be in a contention, the big, whether it should
pull down the less about its ear--the less (a chubby fat little
varlet, of a fourth part of the other's bigness, with wing not much
large than those of a butterfly) whether it should raise the large to a
Heaven it point to, hardly big enough to contain the great toe of
either.
* see Letter XXXVII. of this volume.

LETTER XLVII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.

when I conclude my last, I hop that my next attendance upon this

LETTER XLVIII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
FRIDAY MORN. SEPT. 1.
it be surprising, that I, a man, should be so much affect as I be, at
such an object as be the subject of my former letter; who also, in my

give I by Mrs. Smith) run in my head.
however, not be able to keep away from Smith's, I go thither about

I be prevail upon by Mrs. Smith and her nurse Shelburne (Mrs. Lovick

since show I a copy of the draught by which all be order; and I will
give thee a sketch of the symbol.
the principal device, neatly etch on a plate of white metal, be a

of eternity: and in the circle make by it be this inscription:
CLARISSA HARLOWE.
April x.
[then the year.]
AETAT. XIX.
for ornament: at top, an hour-glass, wing. at bottom, an urn.
under the hour-glass, on another plate, this inscription:
here the wicked cease from troubling: and here the
weary be at rest. Job. iii. 17.
over the urn, near the bottom:
turn again unto thy rest, o my soul! for the Lord hath

over this be the head of a white lily snapt short off, and just fall

the day of man be but as grass. for he flourisheth as a

use to draw for her needlework, for have show more fancy than would
perhaps be think suitable on so solemn an occasion.
the date, April 10, she account for, as not be able to tell what her
closing-day would be; and as that be the fatal day of she leave she

pride leave not poor mortal to the last: but indeed she do not know but

'to person in health, say she, this sight may be shocking; and the
preparation, and my unconcernedness in it, may appear affect: but to
I, who have have so gradual a weaning-time from the world, and so much
reason not to love it, I must say, I dwell on, I indulge, (and, strictly

believe I, my good friend, it do what nothing else can do: it teach

the injury I have receive; and shut out the remembrance of past evil

and now let I ask thee, Lovelace, Dost thou think that, when the time
shall come that thou shalt be oblige to launch into the boundless ocean

part with such true heroism, as this sweet and tender blossom of a woman
have manifest, and continue to manifest!
oh! no! it cannot be!--and why cannot it be?--the reason be evident: she
have no wilful error to look back upon with self-reproach--and her mind
be strengthen by the consolation which flow from that religious
rectitude which have be the guide of all her action; and which have
teach she rather to choose to be a sufferer than an aggressor!
this be the support of the divine Socrates, as thou hast read. when lead
to execution, his wife lament that he should suffer be innocent,
Thou fool, say he, wouldst thou wish I to be guilty!
LETTER XLIX
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
FRIDAY, SEPT. 1.
how astonishing, in the midst of such affect scene, be thy mirth on
what thou call my own aspiration! never, surely, be there such
another man in this world, thy talent and thy levity take together!--
surely, what I shall send thee with this will affect thee. if not,
nothing can, till thy own hour come: and heavy will then thy reflection
be!
I be glad, however, that thou enablest I to assure the lady that thou
wilt no more mol she; that be to say, in other word, that, after
have ruin her fortune, and all her worldly prospect, thou wilt be
so gracious, as to let she lie down and die in peace.
Thy give up to poor Belton's sister the little legacy, and thy
undertaking to make Mowbray and Tourville follow thy example, be, I must
say to thy honour, of a piece with thy generosity to thy Rose-bud and her
Johnny; and to a number of other good action in pecuniary matter:
although thy Rose-bud's be, I believe, the only instance, where a pretty
woman be concern, of such a disinterested bounty.
upon my faith, Lovelace, I love to praise thee; and often and often, as
thou know, have I study for occasion to do it: insomuch that when,
for the life of I, I could not think of any thing do by thee that
deserve praise, I have take pain to applaud the not ungraceful manner
in which thou hast perform action that merit the gallow.
now thou art so near, I will dispatch my servant to thee, if occasion
require. but, I fear, I shall soon give thee the news thou art
apprehensive of. for I be just now send for by Mrs. Smith; who have
order the messenger to tell I, that she know not if the lady will be
alive when I come.

I could not close my letter in such an uncertainty as must have add to

she be tolerably recover by the time I cane; and the doctor make she

LETTER L
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
UXBRIDGE, SEPT. 1, TWELVE O'CLOCK AT NIGHT.
I send you the paper with this. you must account to I honestly and
fairly, when I see you, for the earnestness with which you write for
they. and then also will we talk about the content of your last
dispatch, and about some of your severe and unfriendly reflection.
mean time, whatever thou dost, donot let the wonderful creature leave we!
Set before she the sin of her preparation, as if she think she could
depart when she please. shewill persuade herself, at this rate, that she
have nothing to do, when all be ready, but to lie down, and go to sleep:
and such a lively fancy as she's will make a reality of a jest at any
time.
a jest I call all that have pass between she and I; a mere jest to die
for--for have not her triumph over I, from first to last, be infinitely
great than her suffering from I?
would the sacred regard I have for her purity, even for her personal as
well as intellectual purity, permit, I could prove this as clear as the
sun. Tell, therefore, the dear creature that she must not be wicked in
her piety. there be a too much, as well as too little, even in
righteousness. perhaps she do not think of that.--oh! that she would
have permit my attendance, as obligingly as she do of thine!--the
dear soul use to love humour. I remember the time that she know how to
smile at a piece of apropos humour. and, let I tell thee, a smile upon
the lip, or a sparkling in the eye, must have have its correspondent
cheerfulness in a heart so sincere as she's.
tell the doctor I will make over all my possession, and all my
reversion, to he, if he will but prolong her life for one twelvemonth
to come. but for one twelvemonth, Jack!--He will lose all his reputation
with I, and I shall treat he as Belton do his doctor, if he cannot do
this for I, on so young a subject. but nineteen, belford!--nineteen
cannot so soon die of grief, if the doctor deserve that title; and so
blooming and so fine a constitution as she have but three or four month
ago!
but what need the doctor to ask her leave to write to her friend? could
he not have do it without let she know any thing of the matter?
that be one of the likeli mean that could be think of to bring
some of they about she, since she be so desirous to see they. at least
it would have induce they to send up her favourite Norton. but these
plaguy solemn fellow be great trader in parade. theywill cram down
your throat their poisonous drug by wholesale, without ask you a
question; and have the assurance to own it to be prescribe: but when
they be to do good, they be to require your consent.
how the dear creature's character rise in every line of thy letter!
but it be owe to the uncommon occasion she have meet with that she
blaze out upon we with such a meridian lustre. how, but for those
occasion, could her noble sentiment, her prudent consideration, her
forgiving spirit, her exalt benevolence, and her equanimity in view of
the most shocking prospect (which set she in a light so superior to all
her sex, and even to the philosopher of antiquity) have be manifest?
I know thou wilt think I be go to claim some merit to myself, for
have give she such opportunity of signalize her virtue. but I be
not; for, if I do, I must share that merit with her implacable
relation, who would justly be entitle to two-third of it, at least:
and my soul disdain a partnership in any thing with such a family.
but this I mention as an answer to thy reproach, that I could be so
little edify by perfection, to which, thou supposest, I be for so
long together daily and hourly a personal witness--when, admirable as she
be in all she say, and in all she do, occasion have not at that time
ripen, and call forth, those amazing perfection which now astonish
and confound I.
hence it be that I admire she more than ever; and that my love for she be
less personal, as I may say, more intellectual, than ever I think it
could be to a woman.
hence also it be that I be confident (would it please the Fates to spare
she, and make her mine) I could love she with a purity that would draw on
my own future, as well as ensure her TEMPORAL, happiness.--And hence, by
necessary consequence, shall I be the most miserable of all man, if I be
deprive of she.
Thou severely reflect upon I for my levity: the Abbey instance in
thine eye, I suppose. and I will be ingenuous enough to own, that as
thou se not my heart, there may be passage, in every one of my
letter, which (the melancholy occasion consider) deserve thy most
point rebuke. but faith, Jack, thou art such a tragi-comical mortal,
with thy leaden aspiration at one time, and thy fly hour-glass and
dream terror at another, that, as Prior say, what serious be, thou
turn'st to farce; and it be impossible to keep within the bound of
decorum or gravity when one read what thou writest.
but to restrain myself (for my constitutional gayety be ready to run
away with I again) I will repeat, I must ever repeat, that I be most
egregiously affect with the circumstance of the case: and, be this
paragon actually to quit the world, should never enjoy myself one hour
together, though I be to live to the age of Methusalem.
indeed it be to this deep concern, that my levity be owe: for I
struggle and struggle, and try to buffet down my cruel reflection as
they rise; and when I cannot, I be force, as I have often say, to try
to make myself laugh, that I may not cry; for one or other I must do: and
be it not philosophy carry to the high pitch, for a man to conquer
such tumult of soul as I be sometimes agitate by, and, in the very
height of the storm, to be able to quaver out an horse-laugh?
your seneca's, your Epictetus's, and the rest of your stoical tribe, with
all their apathy nonsense, could not come up to this. they could forbear
wry face: bodily pain they could well enough seem to support; and that
be all: but the pang of their own smitten-down soul they could not
laugh over, though they could at the folly of other. they read grave
lecture; but they be grave. this high point of philosophy, to laugh
and be merry in the midst of the most soul-harrowing woe, when the
heart-string be just burst asunder, be reserve for thy Lovelace.
there be something owe to constitution, I own; and that this be the
laugh-time of my life. for what a woe must that be, which for an hour
together can mortify a man six or seven and twenty, in high blood and
spirit, of a naturally gay disposition, who can sing, dance, and
scribble, and take and give delight in they all?--But then my grief, as
my joy, be sharper-pointed than most other man's; and, like what dolly
Welby once tell I, describe the parturient throe, if there be not
lucid interval, if they do not come and go, there would be no bearing
they.
***
after all, as I be so little distant from the dear creature, and as she
be so very ill, I think I cannot excuse myself from make her one visit.
nevertheless, if I think she so near--[what word shall I use, that my
soul be not shock at!] and that she would be too much discompose by a
visit, I would not think of it.--yet how can I bear the recollection,
that, when she last go from I (her innocence so triumphant over my
premeditate guilt, as be enough to reconcile she to life, and to set
she above the sense of injury so nobly sustain, that) she should then
depart with an incurable fracture in her heart; and that that should be
the last time I should ever see her!--How, how, can I bear this
reflection!
o Jack! how my conscience, that give edge even to thy blunt reflection,
tear me!--even this moment would I give the world to push the cruel
reproacher from I by one ray of my usual gayety!--sick of myself!--sick
of the remembrance of my vile plot; and of my light, my momentary
ecstacy [villanous burglar, felon, thief, that I be!] which have bring
on I such durable and such heavy remorse! what would I give that I have
not be guilty of such barbarous and ungrateful perfidy to the most
excellent of God's creature!
I would end, methink, with one sprightly line!--but it will not be.--
let I tell thee then, and rejoice at it if thou wilt, that I be
inexpressibly miserable!

LETTER LII
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE
TUESDAY, AUG. 29.
my DEAREST FRIEND,
we be at length return to our own home. I have intend to wait on you
in London: but my mother be very ill--Alas! my dear, she be very ill
indeed--and you be likewise very ill--I see that by your' of the 25th--
what shall I do, if I lose two such near, and dear, and tender friend?
she be take ill yesterday at our last stage in our return home--and have
a violent surfeit and fever, and the doctor be doubtful about she.
if she should die, how will all my pertness to her fly in my face!--
why, why, do I ever vex she? she say I have be all duty and
obedience!--she kindly forget all my fault, and remember every thing I
have be so happy as to oblige she in. and this cut I to the heart.
I see, I see, my dear, that you be very bad--and I cannot bear it. do,
my beloved Miss Harlowe, if you can be well, do, for my sake, be
well; and send I word of it. let the bearer bring I a line. be sure

LETTER LIII
MISS HOWE, to MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE

the Colonel think fit once, in praise of Lovelace's generosity, to say,
that (as a man of honour ought) he take to himself all the blame, and

mighty generous, I say, (be it as he suppose,) in such insolent

you the bright of innocent.

I urge your apprehension on this head from your last letter to I: but

this sex from the gentleman down to the peasant.
upon the whole, I find that Mr. Morden have a very slender notion of

I never know a man who deserve to be well thought of himself for his

for if, from the difference of temperament and education, modesty,
chastity, and piety too, be not to be find in our sex preferably to

he even hint (as from your relation indeed) that it be impossible
but there most be some will where there be much love.
these sort of reflection be enough to make a woman, who have at heart
her own honour and the honour of her sex, to look about she, and consider
what she be do when she enter into an intimacy with these wretch;
since it be plain, that whenever she throw herself into the power of a

she must take into her own bosom a share of his guilty baseness.
I be write to general case. you, my dear, be out of the question.
your story, as I have heretofore say, will afford a warning as well as
an example:* for who be it that will not infer, that if a person of your
fortune, character, and merit, could not escape ruin, after she have put

creature expect?
* see Vol. IV. Letter XXIII.
every man, they will say, be not a LOVELACE--true: but then, neither be

example must be of general use.

LETTER LIV
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
SUNDAY EVENING, SEPT. 3.
I wonder not at the impatience your servant tell I you express to hear
from I. I be design to write you a long letter, and be just
return from Smith's for that purpose; but, since you be urgent, you
must be content with a short one.
I attend the lady this morning, just before I set out for Edgware. she
be so ill over-night, that she be oblige to leave unfinished her
letter to Miss Howe. but early this morning she make an end of it, and
just seal it up as I come. she be so fatigued with writing, that she
tell I she would lie down after I be go, and endeavour to recruit her
spirit.
they have send for Mr. Goddard, when she be so ill last night; and not
be able to see he out of her own chamber, he, for the first time, see
her house, as she call it. he be extremely shocked and concerned at
it; and chid Mrs. Smith and Mrs. Lovick for not persuade she to have
such an object remove form her bed-chamber: and when they excuse
themselves on the little authority it be reasonable to suppose they must
have with a lady so much their superior, he reflect warmly on those who
have more authority, and who leave she to proceed with such a shocking and
solemn whimsy, as he call it.
it be place near the window, like a harpsichord, though cover over to
the ground: and when she be so ill that she cannot well go to her closet,
she write and read upon it, as other would upon a desk or table. but
(only as she be so ill last night) she choose not to see any body in
that apartment.
I go to Edgware; and, return in the evening, attend she again.
she have a letter bring she from Mrs. Norton (a long one, as it seem by
its bulk,) just before I come. but she have not open it; and say, that
as she be pretty calm and compose, she be afraid to look into the
content, lest she should be ruffle; expect now to hear of nothing
that could do she good or give her pleasure from that good woman's dear
hard-hearted neighbour, as she call her own relation.
see she so weak and ill, I withdraw; nor do she desire I to tarry,
as sometimes she do, when I make a motion to depart.
I have some hint, as I go away, from Mrs. Smith, that she have
appropriate that evening to some office, that be to save trouble, as
she call it, after her departure; and have be give order to her
nurse, and to Mrs. Lovick, and Mrs. Smith, about what she would have do
when she be go; and I believe they be of a very delicate and
affect nature; but Mrs. Smith descend not to particular.
the doctor have be with she, as well as Mr. Goddard; and they both
join with great earnestness to persuade she to have her house remove
out of her sight; but she assure they that it give her pleasure and
spirit; and, be a necessary preparation, she wonder they should be
surprised at it, when she have not any of her family about she, or any old
acquaintance, on whose care and exactness in these punctilio, as she
call they, she could rely.
the doctor tell Mrs. Smith, that he believe she would hold out long
enough for any of her friend to have notice of her state, and to see
she; and hardly long; and since he could not find that she have any
certainty of see her cousin Morden, (which make it plain that her
relation continue inflexible,) he would go home, and write a letter to
her father, take it as she would.
she have spend great part of the day in intense devotion; and to-morrow
morning she be to have with she the same clergyman who have often attend
she; from whose hand she will again receive the sacrament.
Thou se, Lovelace, that all be prepare, that all will be ready; and
I be to attend she to-morrow afternoon, to take some instruction from
she in relation to my part in the office to be perform for she. and
thus, omit the particular of a fine conversation between her and
Mrs. Lovick, which the latter acquaint I with, as well as another
between she and the doctor and apothecary, which I have a design this
evening to give you, they be of a very affect nature, I have
yield to your impatience.
I shall dispatch Harry to-morrow morning early with her letter to Miss
Howe: an offer she take very kindly; as she be extremely
solicitous to lessen that young lady's apprehension for she on
not hear from she by Saturday's post: and yet, if she write
truth, as no doubt but she will, how can her apprehension be
lessen?
LETTER LV
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MISS HOWE
SATURDAY, SEPT. 2.
I write, my beloved Miss Howe, though very ill still: but I could not by
the return of your messenger; for I be then unable to hold a pen.
your mother's illness (as mention in the first part of your letter,)
give I great distress for you, till I read far. you bewail it as
become a daughter so sensible. may you be bless in each other for
many, very many year to come! I doubt not, that even this sudden and
grievous indisposition, by the frame it have put you in, and the
apprehension it have give you of lose so dear a mother, will contribute
to the happiness I wish you: for, alas! my dear, we seldom know how to
value the blessing we enjoy, till we be in danger of lose they, or
have actually lose they: and then, what would we give to have they
restore to we!
what, I wonder, have again happen between you and Mr. Hickman? although
I know not, I dare say it be owe to some petty petulance, to some
half-ungenerous advantage take of his obligingness and assiduity. will
you never, my dear, give the weight you and all our sex ought to give to
the quality of sobriety and regularity of life and manner in that sex?
must bold creature, and forward spirit, for ever, and by the good and
wise of we, as well as by the indiscreet, be the most kindly
treat?
my dear friend know not that I have actually suffer within less than
an inch of my life.
poor Mr. Brand! he mean well, I believe. I be afraid all will turn
heavily upon he, when he probably imagine that he be take the good
method to oblige. but be he not to have be so light of belief, and
so weakly officious; and have give a more favourable, and, it would be
strange if I could not say, a juster report; thing would have be,
nevertheless, exactly as they be.
I must lay down my pen. I be very ill. I believe I shall be well
by-and-by. the bad writing would betray I, although I have a mind to
keep from you what the event must soon--
***

I have want no money: so donot be angry about such a trifle as money.

it, I have already dispose of a good part of it; and could only hope they
would be willing to give it up at my last request. and now how rich
shall I think myself in this my last stage!--and yet I do not want
before--indeed I do not--for who, that have many superfluity, can be
say to want!
do not, my dear friend, be concerned that I call it my last stage; for
what be even the long life which in high health we wish for? what, but,
as we go along, a life of apprehension, sometimes for our friend,
oftener for ourselves? and at last, when arrive at the old age we
covet, one heavy loss or deprivation have succeed another, we see
ourselves stript, as I may say, of every one we love; and find ourselves
expose, as uncompanionable poor creature, to the slight, to the
contempt, of jostle youth, who want to push we off the stage, in hope
to possess what we have:--and, superadde to all, our own infirmity
every day increase: of themselves enough to make the life we wish for
the great disease of all! donot you remember the line of Howard,
which once you read to I in my ivy-bower?*
* these be the line the lady refer to:
from death we rise to life: 'tis but the same,
through life to pass again from whence we come.
with shame we see our passion can prevail,
where reason, certainty, and virtue fail.
HONOUR, that empty name, can death despise; |
SCORN'D love to death, as to a refuge, fly; |
and SORROW wait for death with long eye. |
HOPE triumph o'er the thought of death; and FATE
Cheats fool, and flatter the unfortunate.
we fear to lose, what a small time must waste,
till life itself grow the disease at last.
beg for life, we beg for more decay,
and to be long a die only pray.
in the disposition of what belong to I, I have endeavour to do every
thing in the justest and good manner I could think of; put myself in
my relation' place, and, in the great point, order my matter as
if no misunderstanding have happen.

my cousin, you tell I, think I be off my guard, and that I be take

I should hope that my cousin have not take the liberty which you (by an

but we woman be to often to blame on this head; since the most virtuous
among we seldom make virtue the test of their approbation of the other
sex; insomuch that a man may glory in his wickedness of this sort without
be reject on that account, even to the face of woman of
unquestionable virtue. hence it be, that a libertine seldom think
himself concern so much as to save appearance: and what be it not that
our sex suffer in their opinion on this very score? and what have I,
