may my story be a warning to all, how they prefer a libertine to a man of
true honour; and how they permit themselves to be mislead (where they mean
the good) by the specious, yet foolish hope of subdue riveted habit,
and, as I may say, of alter natures!--the more foolish, as constant
experience might convince we, that there be hardly one in ten, of even

husband's affection, which she have in the lover's. what influence then
can she hope to have over the moral of an avow libertine, who marry
perhaps for conveniency, who despise the tie, and whom, it be too
probable, nothing but old age, or sickness, or disease, (the consequence
of ruinous riot,) can reclaim?

SUNDAY MORNING, SEPT. 3, SIX O'CLOCK.
Hither I have write, and be force to quit my pen. and so much weak
and bad I grow, that have I resume it, to have close here, it must
have be with such trembling unsteadiness, that it would have give you
more concern for I, than the delay of send it away by last night's

of my letter, which I will pursue as currently as if I have not leave off.

impression of Mr. Belford; since, otherwise, some misunderstanding might

altered man, and in time will be a reform one, yet be he one of those
high spirit that have be accustom to resent imaginary indignity to

offence to other; man of this cast act as if they think all the
world be make to bar with they, and they with nobody in it.
Mr. Lovelace, you tell I, think fit to intrust my cousin with the copy

Mr. Lovelace be for his baseness, and how freely he accuse himself to my
cousin. this show, that the true bravery of spirit be to be above do
a vile action; and that nothing subject the human mind to so much
meanness, as the consciousness of have do wilful wrong to our fellow
creature. how low, how sordid, be the submission which elaborate
baseness compel! that that wretch could treat I as he do, and then
could so poorly creep to I for forgiveness of crime so wilful, so
black, and so premeditate! how my soul despise he for his meanness on
a certain occasion, of which you will one day be inform!* and he whose
action one's heart despise, it be far from be difficult to reject,
have one ever so partially favour he once.
* mean his meditated second violence (see Vol. VI. Letter XXXVI.) and
his succeed letter to she, supplicate for her pardon.
yet be I glad this violent spirit can thus creep; that, like a poisonous
serpent, he can thus coil himself, and hide his head in his own narrow
circlet; because this stoop, this abasement, give I hope that no
farth mischief will ensue.
all my apprehension be, what may happen when I be go; lest then my
cousin, or any other of my family, should endeavour to avenge I, and
risk their own more precious life on that account.
if that part of Cain's curse be Mr. Lovelace's, to be a fugitive and
vagabond in the earth; that be to say, if it mean no more harm to he
than that he should be oblige to travel, as it seem he intend, (though
I wish he no ill in his travel;) and I could know it; then should I be
easy in the hop-for safety of my friend from his skilful violence--oh!
that I could hear he be a thousand mile off!
when I begin this letter, I do not think I could have run to such a
length. but 'tis to you, my dear friend, and you have a title to the
spirit you raise and support; for they be no long mine, and will
subside the moment I cease write to you.
but what do you bid I hope for, when you tell I that, if your mother's
health will permit, you will see I in town? I hope your mother's health
will be perfect as you wish; but I dare not promise myself so great a
favour; so great a blessing, I will call it--and indeed I know not if I

yet one comfort it be in your power to give I; and that be, let I know,
and very speedily it must be, if you wish to oblige I, that all matter
be make up between you and Mr. Hickman; to whom, I see, you be
resolve, with all your bravery of spirit, to owe a multitude of
obligation for his patience with your flightiness. think of this, my
dear proud friend! and think, likewise, of what I have often tell you,
that PRIDE, in man or woman, be an extreme that hardly ever fail, soon
or later, to bring forth its mortifying CONTRARY.
may you, my dear Miss Howe, have no discomfort but what you make to
yourself! as it will be in your own power to lessen such as these, they
ought to be your punishment if you do not. there be no such thing as
perfect happiness here, since the busy mind will make to itself evil,
be it to find none. you will, therefore, pardon this limited wish,
strange as it may appear, till you consider it: for to wish you no
infelicity, either within or without you, be to wish you what can never
happen in this world; and what perhaps ought not to be wish for, if by
a wish one could give one's friend such an exemption; since we be not to
live here always.
we must not, in short, expect that our rose will grow without thorn:
but then they be useful and instructive thorn: which, by prick the
finger of the too-hasty plucker, teach future caution. and who know
not that difficulty give poignancy to our enjoyment; which be apt to
lose their relish with we when they be over easily obtain?
I must conclude--
God for ever bless you, and all you love and honour, and reward you here
and hereafter for your kindness to
your ever oblige and affectionate
CLARISSA HARLOWE.

FRIDAY MORNING.
Betty be with I just now. she tell I, that your cousin Morden be so

what noble fortune still, my dear young lady, await you! I be

see many happy day.

with you.

I hear that Miss Howe have obtain leave from her mother to see you; and

to buy clothe for her approach nuptial.
Mr. Hickman's mother-in-law be lately dead. her jointure of 600L. a-year
be fall to he; and she have, moreover, as an acknowledgement of his
good behaviour to she, leave he all she be worth, which be very
considerable, a few legacy except to her own relation.
these good man be uniformly good: indeed could not else be good; and
never fare the bad for be so. all the world agree he will make

much agree in she make he an excellent wife. but I hope a woman of
her principle would not encourage his address, if, whether she at
present love he or not, she think she could not love he; or if she
prefer any other man to he.
Mr. Pocock undertake to deliver this; but fear it will be Saturday
night first, if not Sunday morning.
may the Almighty protect and bless you!--I long to see you--my dearest
young lady, I long to see you; and to fold you once more to my fond
heart. I dare to say happy day be come. be but cheerful. give way
to hope.
whether for this world, or the other, you must be happy. wish to live,

they prolong? which God grant, if it be his blessed will, to the
prayer of
your
JUDITH NORTON
LETTER LVII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
MONDAY, SEPT. 4.
the lady would not read the letter she have from Mrs. Norton till she have

while we be thus solemnly engage, a servant come with a letter from

she break it open; but every line, she say, appear two to she: so
that, be unable to read it herself, she desire I would read it to
she. I do so; and wish it be more consolatory to she: but she be
all patient attention: tear, however, often trickle down her cheek.
by the date, it be write yesterday; and this be the substance of it.
he tell she, 'that the Thursday before he have procure a general meeting
of her principal relation, at her father's; though not without
difficulty, her haughty brother oppose it, and, when meet, render all
his endeavour to reconcile they to her ineffectual. he censure he, as
the most ungovernable young man he ever know: some great sickness, he
say, some heavy misfortune, be want to bring he to a knowledge of
himself, and of what be due from he to other; and he wish that he
be not her brother, and his cousin. nor doe he spare her father and
uncle for be so implicitly lead by he.'
he tell she, 'that he part with they all in high displeasure, and
think never more to darken any of their door: that he declare as much
to her two uncle, who come to he on Saturday, to try to accommodate
with he; and who find he prepare to go to London to attend she; and
that, notwithstanding their press entreaty, he determine so to do,
and not to go with they to Harlowe-place, or to either of their own
house; and accordingly dismiss they with such an answer.
'but that her noble letter,' as he call it, of Aug. 31,* 'be bring
he about an hour after their departure, he think it might affect they
as much as it do he; and give they the exalt opinion of her virtue
which be so well deserve; he therefore turn his horse's head back
to her uncle Antony's, instead of forward toward London.
* see Letter XLV. of this volume.
'that accordingly arrive there, and find she two uncle together, he
read to they the affect letter; which leave none of the three a dry
eye: that the absent, as be usual in such case, bear all the load,
they accuse her brother and sister; and besought he to put off his
journey to town, till he could carry with he the blessing which she have
formerly in vain solicit for; and (as they hop) the happy tiding of
a general reconciliation.
'that not doubt but his visit would be the more welcome to she, if
these good end could be obtain, he the more readily comply with
their desire. but not be willing to subject himself to the
possibility of receive fresh insult from her brother, he have give she
uncle a copy of her letter, for the family to assemble upon; and desire
to know, as soon as possible, the result of their deliberation.
'he tell she, that he shall bring she up the account relate to the
produce of her grandfather's estate, and adjust they with she; have
actually in his hand the arrear due to she from it.
'he highly applaud the noble manner in which she resent your usage of
she. it be impossible, he own, that you can either deserve she, or to
be forgive. but as you do justice to her virtue, and offer to make she
all the reparation now in your power; and as she be so very earnest with
he not to resent that usage; and declare, that you could not have be
the author of her calamity but through a strange concurrence of unhappy
cause; and as he be not at a loss to know how to place to a proper
account that strange concurrence; he desire she not to be apprehensive
of any vindictive measure from he.'
nevertheless (as may be expect) 'he inveigh against you; as he find
that she give you no advantage over she. but he forbear to enter
far into this subject, he say, till he have the honour to see she;
and the rather, as she seem so much determined against you. however, he
cannot but say, that he think you a gallant man, and a man of sense; and
that you have the reputation of be think a generous man in every
instance but where the sex be concern. in such, he own, that you have
take inexcusable liberty. and he be sorry to say, that there be very
few young man of fortune but who allow themselves in the same. both
sex, he observe, too much love to have each other in their power: yet
he hardly ever know man or woman who be very fond of power make a right
use of it.
'if she be so absolutely determined against marry you, as she declare
she be, he hop, he say, to prevail upon she to take (as soon as she
health will permit) a little tour abroad with he, as what will probably
establish it; since travel be certainly the good physic for all those
disorder which owe their rise to grief or disappointment. an absence of
two or three year will endear she to every one, on her return, and every
one to she.
'he express his impatience to see she. he will set out, he say, the
moment he know the result of her family's determination; which, he
doubt not, will be favourable. nor will he wait long for that.'
when I have read the letter through to the languish lady, and so, my
friend, say she, have I hear of a patient who actually die, while
five or six principal physician be in a consultation, and not agree

emperor Joseph, I think.
I ask, if I should write to her cousin, as he know not how ill she be,
to hasten up?
by no mean, she say; since, if he be not already set out, she be
persuade that she should be so low by the time he could receive my

and afflict he.
I hope, however, she be not so very near her end. and without say any
more to she, when I retire, I write to Colonel Morden, that if he
expect to see his beloved cousin alive, he must lose no time in set
out. I send this letter by his own servant.
Dr. H. send away his letter to her father by a particular hand this
morning.
Mrs. Walton the milliner have also just now acquaint Mrs. Smith, that
her husband have a letter bring by a special messenger from Parson
Brand, within this half hour, enclose the copy of one he have write to
Mr. John Harlowe, recant his officious one.
and as all these, and the copy of the lady's letter to Col. Morden, will

not strike with a remorse that shall burst open the double-bar door
of their heart.
will. engage to reach you with this (late as it will be) before you go
to rest. he beg that I will testify for he the hour and the minute I

I pretend to be (now by use) the swift short-hand writer in England,

before they be write or send.
LETTER LVIII
DR. H. TO JAMES HARLOWE, SENIOR, ESQ.
LONDON, SEPT. 4.
SIR,
if I may judge of the heart of other parent by my own, I cannot doubt
but you will take it well to be inform that you have yet an opportunity
to save yourself and family great future regret, by dispatch hither
some one of it with your last blessing, and your lady's, to the most
excellent of her sex.
I have some reason to believe, Sir, that she have be represent to you
in a very different light from the true one. and this it be that induce
I to acquaint you, that I think she, on the good ground, absolutely
irreproachable in all her conduct which have pass under my eye, or come
to my ear; and that her very misfortune be make glorious to she, and
honourable to all that be relate to she, by the use she have make of
they; and by the patience and resignation with which she support herself
in a painful, lingering, and dispirit decay! and by the greatness of
mind with which she view her approach dissolution. and all this from
proper motif; from motif in which a die saint might glory.
she know not that I write. I must indeed acknowledge, that I offer to
do so some day ago, and that very pressingly: nor do she refuse I from
obstinacy--she seem not to know what that be--but desire I to forbear
for two day only, in hope that her newly-arrive cousin, who, as she
hear, be solicit for she, would be able to succeed in her favour.
I hope I shall not be think an officious man on this occasion; but, if
I be, I cannot help it, be drive to write, by a kind of parental and
irresistible impulse.
but, Sir, whatever you think fit to do, or permit to be do, must be
speedily do; for she cannot, I verily think, live a week: and how long
of that short space she may enjoy her admirable intellect to take
comfort in the favour you may think proper to confer upon she cannot be
say. I be, Sir,
your most humble servant,
R.H.
LETTER LIX
MR. BELFORD, to WILLIAM MORDEN, ESQ.
LONDON, SEPT. 4.
SIR,
the urgency of the case, and the opportunity by your servant, will
sufficiently apologize for this trouble from a stranger to your person,
who, however, be not a stranger to your merit.
I understand you be employ your good office with the parent of
Miss Clarissa Harlowe, and other relation, to reconcile they to the most
meritorious daughter and kinswoman that ever family have to boast of.
Generously as this be intend by you, we here have too much reason to
think all your solicitude on this head will be unnecessary: for it be
the opinion of every one who have the honour of be admit to she
presence, that she cannot lie over three day: so that, if you wish to
see she alive, you must lose no time to come up.
she know not that I write. I have do it soon, if I have have the least
doubt that before now she would not have receive from you some news of
the happy effect of your kind mediation in her behalf. I be, Sir,
your most humble servant,
J. BELFORD.
LETTER LX
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
[in answer to LETTER LVII.]
UXBRIDGE, TUESDAY MORN, between 4 and 5.
and can it be, that this admirable creature will so soon leave this
cursed world! for cursed I shall think it, and more cursed myself, when
she be go. o, Jack! thou who canst sit so cool, and, like Addison's
Angel, direct, and even enjoy, the storm, that tear up my happiness by
the root; blame I not for my impatience, however unreasonable! if thou
know, that already I feel the torment of the damned, in the remorse
that wring my heart, on look back upon my past action by she, thou
wouldst not be the devil thou art, to halloo on a worrying conscience,
which, without my merciless aggravation, be altogether intolerable.
I know not what to write, nor what I would write. when the company that
use to delight I be as uneasy to I as my reflection be painful, and
I can neither help nor divert myself, must not every servant about I
partake in a perturbation so sincere!
shall I give thee a faint picture of the horrible uneasiness with which
my mind struggle? and faint indeed it must be; for nothing but
outrageous madness can exceed it; and that only in the apprehension of
other; since, as to the sufferer, it be certain, that actual distraction
(take it out of its lucid interval) must be an infinitely more happy
state than the state of suspense and anxiety, which often bring it on.
forbid to attend the dear creature, yet long to see she, I would
give the world to be admit once more to her beloved presence. I ride
towards London three or four time a day, resolve pro and con, twenty
time in two or three mile; and at last ride back; and, in view of
Uxbridge, loathe even the kind friend, and hospitable house, turn my
horse's head again towards the town, and resolve to gratify my humour,
let she take it as she will; but, at the very entrance of it, after
infinite canvassing, once more alter my mind, dread to offend and
shock she, lest, by that mean, I should curtail a life so precious.
yesterday, in particular, to give you an idea of the strength of that
impatience, which I cannot avoid suffer to break out upon my servant,
I have no soon dispatch Will., than I take horse to meet he on his
return.
in order to give he time, I loiter about on the road, rid up this
lane to the one highway, down that to the other, just as my horse
point; all the way curse my very being; and though so lately look
down upon all the world, wish to change condition with the poor
beggar that cry to I for charity as I ride by he--and throw he
money, in hope to obtain by his prayer the blessing my heart pant
after.
after I have saunter about an hour or two, (which seem three or four
tedious one,) fear I have slipt the fellow, I inquire at every
turnpike, whether a servant in such a livery have not pass through in
his return from London, on a full gallop; for woe have be to the dog,
have I meet he on a sluggish trot! and lest I should miss he at one end
of Kensingtohn, as he might take either the Acton or Hammersmith road; or
at the other, as he might come through the Park, or not; how many score
time do I ride backwards and forwards from the Palace to the Gore,
make myself the subject of observation to all passenger whether on
horseback or on foot; who, no doubt, wonder to see a well-dress and
well-mount man, sometimes amble, sometimes prance, (as the beast
have more fire than his master) backwards and forwards in so short a
compass!
yet all this time, though long to espy the fellow, do I dread to meet
he, lest he should be charge with fatal tiding.
when at distance I see any man gallop towards I, my
resemblance-form fancy immediately make it to be he; and then my
heart choke I. but when the person's near approach undeceive I,
how do I curse the varlet's delay, and thee, by turn! and how ready
be I to draw my pistol at the stranger, for have the impudence to
gallop; which none but my messenger, I think, have either right or
reason to do! for all the business of the world, I be ready to imagine,
should stand still on an occasion so melancholy and so interesting to I.
Nay, for this week past, I could cut the throat of any man or woman I see
laugh, while I be in such dejection of mind.
I be now convinced that the wretch who fly from a heavy scene, labour
under ten time more distress in the intermediate suspense and
apprehension, than they could have, be they present at it, and to see
and know the bad: so capable be fancy or imagination, the more
immediate offspring of the soul, to outgo fact, let the subject be either
joyous or grievous.
and hence, as I conceive, it be, that all pleasure be great in the
expectation, or in the reflection, than in fruition; as all pain, which
press heavy upon both part of that unequal union by which frail
mortality hold its precarious tenure, be ever most acute in the time of
suffering: for how easy sit upon the reflection the heavy misfortune,
when surmounted!--but most easy, I confess, those in which body have more
concern than soul. this, however, be a point of philosophy I have
neither time nor head just now to weigh: so take it as it fall from a
madman's pen.
Woe be to either of the wretch who shall bring I the fatal news that
she be no more! for it be but too likely that a shriek-owl so hat will
never hoot or scream again; unless the shock, that will probably disorder
my whole frame on so sad an occasion, (by unsteadye my hand,) shall
divert my aim from his head, heart, or bowel, if it turn not against my
own.
but, surely, she will not, she cannot yet die! such a matchless
excellence,
----whose mind
contain a world, and seem for all thing fram'd,
could not be lend to be so soon demand back again!
but may it not be, that thou, Belford, art in a plot with the dear
creature, (who will not let I attend she to convince myself,) in order
to work up my soul to the deep remorse; and that, when she be
convinced of the sincerity of my penitence, and when my mind be make such
wax, as to be fit to take what impression she please to give it, she
will then raise I up with the joyful tiding of her return health and
acceptance of I!
what would I give to have it so! and when the happiness of hundred, as
well as the peace and reconciliation of several eminent family, depend
upon her restoration and happiness, why should it not be so?
but let I presume it will. let I indulge my former hope, however
improbable--I will; and enjoy it too. and let I tell thee how ecstatic
my delight would be on the unravelling of such a plot as this!
do, dear Belford, let it be so!--And, o, my dearest, and ever-dear
Clarissa, keep I no loner in this cruel suspense; in which I suffer a
thousand time more than ever I make thee suffer. nor fear thou that I
will resent, or recede, on an ecclaircissement so desirable; for I will
adore thee for ever, and without reproach thee for the pang thou hast
torture I with, confess thee as much my superior in virtue and honour!
but once more, should the bad happen--say not what that bad be--and I
be go from this hat island--go for ever--and may eternal--but I be
craze already--and will therefore conclude myself,
thine more than my own,
(and no great compliment neither)
R.L.
LETTER LXI
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
TUES. SEPT. 9 in the MORN. AT MR. SMITH'S.
when I read yours of this morning, I could not help pity you for the
account you give of the dreadful anxiety and suspense you labour under.
I wish from my heart all be to end as you be so willing to hope: but
it will not be; and your suspense, if the bad part of your torment, as
you say it be, will soon be over; but, alas! in a way you wish not.
I attend the lady just now. she be extremely ill: yet be she aim
at an answer to her Norton's letter, which she begin yesterday in her own
chamber, and have write a good deal: but in a hand not like her own fine
one, as Mrs. Lovick tell I, but large, and the line crook.
I have accept of the offer of a room adjoining to the widow Lovick's,
till I see how matter go; but unknown to the lady; and I shall go home
every night, for a few hour. I would not lose a sentence that I could
gain from lip so instructive, nor the opportunity of receive any
command from she, for an estate.
in this my new apartment I now write, and shall continue to write, as
occasion offer, that I may be the more circumstantial: but I depend upon
the return of my letter, or copy of they, on demand, that I may have
together all that relate to this affecting story; which I shall
re-peruse with melancholy pleasure to the end of my life.
I think I will send thee Brand's letter to Mr. John Harlowe, recant
his base surmise. it be a matchless piece of pedantry; and may perhaps
a little divert thy deep chagrin: some time hence at least it may, if not
now.
what wretched creature be there in the world! what strangely mixed
creatures!--so sensible and so silly at the same time! what a various,
what a foolish creature be man!--
three O'CLOCK.
the lady have just finish her letter, and have entertain Mrs. Lovick,
Mrs. Smith, and I, with a noble discourse on the vanity and brevity of
life, to which I cannot do justice in the repetition: and indeed I be so
grieve for she, that, ill as she be, my intellect be not half so clear
as she's.
a few thing which make the strong impression upon I, as well from
the sentiment themselves as from her manner of utter they, I
remember. she introduce they thus:
I be think, say she, what a gradual and happy death God Almighty
(bless be his name) afford I! who would have think, that, suffer
what I have suffer, and abandon as I have be, with such a
tender education as I have have, I should be so long a dying!--but see now
by little and little it have come to this. I be first take off from the
power of walk; then I take a coach--a coach grow too violent an
exercise: then I take up a chair--the prison be a large DEATH-STRIDE
upon I--I should have suffer long else!--next, I be unable to go to
church; then to go up or down stair; now hardly can move from one room
to another: and a less room will soon hold me.--My eye begin to fail I,
so that at time I cannot see to read distinctly; and now I can hardly
write, or hold a pen.--next, I presume, I shall know nobody, nor be able
to thank any of you; I therefore now once more thank you, Mrs. Lovick,
and you, Mrs. Smith, and you, Mr. Belford, while I can thank you, for all
your kindness to I. and thus by little and little, in such a gradual
sensible death as I be bless with, God die away in we, as I may say,
all human satisfaction, in order to subdue his poor creature to himself.
Thou mayest guess how affected we all be at this move account of her
progressive weakness. we hear it with wet eye; for what with the
woman's example, and what with her move eloquence, I could no more help
it than they. but we be silent nevertheless; and she go on apply
herself to I.
o Mr. Belford! this be a poor transitory life in the good enjoyment.
we flutter about here and there, with all our vanity about we, like
paint butterfly, for a gay, but a very short season, till at last we
lie ourselves down in a quiescent state, and turn into vile worm: and
who know in what form, or to what condition we shall rise again?
I wish you would permit I, a young creature, just turn of nineteen
year of age, blooming and healthy as I be a few month ago, now nipt by
the cold hand of death, to influence you, in these my last hour, to a
life of regularity and repentance for any past evil you may have be
guilty of. for, believe I, Sir, that now, in this last stage, very few
thing will bear the test, or be pass as laudable, if pardonable, at
our own bar, much less at a more tremendous one, in all we have do, or
delight in, even in a life not very offensive neither, as we may think!
--ought we not then to study in our full day, before the dark hour
approach, so to live, as may afford reflection that will soften the
agony of the last moment when they come, and let in upon the depart
soul a ray of divine mercy to illuminate its passage into an awful
eternity?
she be ready to faint, and choose to lie down, I withdraw; I need not
say with a melancholy heart: and when I get to my new-take apartment, my
heart be still more affected by the sight of the solemn letter the
admirable lady have so lately finish. it be communicate to I by Mrs.
Lovick; who have it to copy for I; but it be not to be deliver to I
till after her departure. however, I trespass so far, as to prevail
upon the widow to let I take a copy of it; which I do directly in
character.
I send it enclose. if thou canst read it, and thy heart not blee at
thy eye, thy remorse can hardly be so deep as thou hast incline I to
think it be.
LETTER LXII
MISS CLARISSA HARLOWE, to MRS. NORTON
[in answer to LETTER LVI.*]
* Begun on Monday Sept. 4, and by piecemeal finish on Tuesday; but not
send till the Thursday follow.
my DEAREST MRS. NORTON,
I be afraid I shall not be able to write all that be upon my mind to say
to you upon the subject of your last. yet I will try.
as to my friend, and as to the sad breakfasting, I cannot help be
afflict for they. what, alas! have not my mother, in particular,
suffer by my rashness!--Yet to allow so much for a son!--so little for
a daughter!--but all now will soon be over, as to I. I hope they will
bury all their resentment in my grave.
as to your advice, in relation to Mr. Belford, let I only say, that the
unhappy reprobation I have meet with, and my short time, must be my
apology now.--i wish I could have write to my mother and my uncle as
you advise. and yet, favour come so slowly from they.
the granting of one request only now remain as a desirable one from
they. which nevertheless, when grant, I shall not be sensible of. it
be that they will be pleased to permit my remain to be lay with those
of my ancestor--place at the foot of my dear grandfather, as I have
mention in my will. this, however, as they please. for, after all,
this vile body ought not so much to engage my care. it be a weakness--
but let it be call a natural weakness, and I shall be excuse;
especially when a reverential gratitude shall be know to be the
foundation of it. you know, my dear woman, how my grandfather love I.
and you know how much I honour he, and that from my very infancy to
the hour of his death. how often since have I wish, that he have not
love I so well!
I wish not now, at the writing of this, to see even my cousin Morden.
O, my blessed woman! my dear maternal friend! I be enter upon a
well tour than to France or Italy either!--or even than to settle at my
once-beloved Dairy-house!--all these prospect and pleasure, which use
to be so agreeable to I in health, how poor seem they to I now!--
indeed, indeed, my dear Mamma Norton, I shall be happy! I know I shall!
--I have charming foreboding of happiness already!--tell all my dear
friend, for their comfort, that I shall!--who would not bear the
punishment I have bear, to have the prospect and assurance I rejoice
in!--assurance I might not have have, be my own wish to have be
grant to I!
neither do I want to see even you, my dear Mrs. Norton. nevertheless I
must, in justice to my own gratitude, declare, that there be a time,
could you have be permit to come, without incur displeasure from
those whose esteem it be necessary for you to cultivate and preserve,
that your presence and comforting would have be balm to my wounded
mind. but be you now, even by consent, and with reconciliatory
tiding, to come, it would but add to your grief; and the sight of one I
so dearly love, so happily fraught with good news, might but draw I back
to wish I have have great struggle to get above. and let I tell you
for your comfort, that I have not leave undo any thing that ought to be
do, either respect mind or person; no, not to the minute
preparation: so that nothing be leave for you to do for I. every one have
her direction as to the last offices.--And my desk, that I now write upon
--O my dearest Mrs. Norton, all be provided!--all be ready! and all will
be as decent as it should be!
and pray let my Miss Howe know, that by the time you will receive this,
and she your signification of the content of it, will, in all
probability, be too late for she to do I the inestimable favour, as I
should once have think it, to see I. God will have no rival in the
heart of those he sanctify. by various method he deaden all other
sensation, or rather absorb they all in the love of he.
I shall nevertheless love you, my Mamma Norton, and my Miss Howe, whose
love to I have pass the love of woman, to my late hour!--but yet, I
be now above the quick sense of those pleasure which once delight I,
and once more I say, that I do not wish to see object so dear to I,
which might bring I back again into sense, and rival my supreme love.

twice have I be force to leave off. I wish, that my last writing
might be to you, or to Miss Howe, if it might not be to my dear ma----
Mamma, I would have write--be the word distinct?--my eye be so misty!--
if, when I apply to you, I break off in half-word, do you supply them--
the kind be your due.--be sure take the kind, to fill up chasm
with, if any chasm there be--
***
another break off!--but the new day seem to rise upon I with healing
in its wing. I have get, I think, a recruit of strength: spirit, I
bless God, I have not of late want.
let my dear Miss Howe purchase her wedding-garment--and may all
temporal blessing attend the charming preparation!--blessings will, I
make no question, notwithstanding the little cloudiness that Mr. Hickman
encounter with now and then, which be but prognostication of a future
golden day to he: for her heart be good, and her head not wrong.--But
great merit be coy, and that coyness have not always its foundation in
pride: but if it should seem to be pride, take off the skin-deep
covering, and, in she, it be noble diffidence, and a love that want but
to be assure!
tell Mr. Hickman I write this, and write it, as I believe, with my last
pen; and bid he bear a little at first, and forbear; and all the future
will be crown gratitude, and rewarding love: for Miss Howe have great
sense, fine judgment, and exalt generosity; and can such a one be
ungrateful or easy under those obligation which his assiduity and
obligingness (when he shall be so happy as to call she his) will lay she
under to he?
as for I, never bride be so ready as I be. my wedding garment be
buy---and though not fine or gawdy to the sight, though not adorn
with jewel, and set off with gold and silver, (for I have no beholder'
eye to wish to glitter in,) yet will they be the easy, the happy
suit, that ever bridal maiden wear--for they be such as carry with they
a security against all those anxiety, pain, and perturbation, which
sometimes succeed to the most promising outsetting.
and now, my dear Mrs. Norton, do I wish for no other.
o hasten, good God, if it be thy blessed will, the happy moment that I be
to be deck out in his all-quiet garb! and sustain, comfort, bless,
and protect with the all-shadow wing of thy mercy, my dear parent, my
uncle, my brother, my sister, my cousin Morden, my ever-dear and
ever-kind Miss Howe, my good Mrs. Norton, and every deserve person to
whom they wish well! be the ardent prayer, first and last, of every
beginning hour, as the clock tell it I, (hour now be day, nay,
year,) of
your now not sorrow or afflict, but happy,
CLARISSA HARLOWE.
LETTER LXIII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
WED. MORN. SEPT. 6, HALF an hour after three.
I be not the savage which you and my bad enemy think I. my soul be
too much penetrate by the content of the letter which you enclose in
your last, to say one word more to it, than that my heart have bleed over
it from every vein!--i will fly from the subject--but what other can I
choose, that will not be as grievous, and lead into the same?
I could quarrel with all the world; with thee, as well as the rest;
oblige as thou supposest thyself for write to I hourly. how dar
thou, (though unknown to she,) to presume to take an apartment under the
sane roof with her?--i cannot bear to think that thou shouldest be see,
at all hour pass to and repasse from her apartment, while I, who
have so much reason to call her mine, and one be prefer by she to all
the world, be force to keep aloof, and hardly dare to enter the city
where she be!
if there be any thing in Brand's letter that will divert I, hasten it to
I. but nothing now will ever divert I, will ever again give I joy or
pleasure! I can neither eat, drink, nor sleep. I be sick of all the
world.
surely it will be well when all be over--when I know the bad the
Fates can do against I--yet how shall I bear that worst?--O Belford,
Belford! write it not to me!--but if it must happen, get somebody else to
write; for I shall curse the pen, the hand, the head, and the heart,
employ in communicate to I the fatal tiding. but what be this
saying, when already I curse the whole world except she--myself most?
in fine, I be a most miserable be. life be a burden to I. I would
not bear it upon these term for one week more, let what would be my lot;
for already be there a hell begin in my own mind. never more mention it
to I, let she, or who will say it, the prison--I cannot bear it--May
d----n----n seize quick the cursed woman, who could set death upon take
that large stride, as the dear creature call it!--I have no hand in it!--
but her relation, her implacable relation, have do the business. all
else would have be get over. never persuade I but it would. the fire
of youth, and the violence of passion, would have plead for I to good
purpose, with an individual of a sex, which love to be address with
passionate ardour, even to tumult, have it not be for that cruelty and
unforgivingness, which, (the object and the penitence consider,) have
no example, and have aggravate the heinousness of my fault.
unable to rest, though I go not to bed till two, I dispatch this ere
the day dawn--who know what this night, this dismal night, may have
produce!
I must after my messenger. I have tell the varlet I will meet he,
perhaps at Knightsbridge, perhaps in Piccadilly; and I trust not myself
with pistol, not only on his account, but my own--for pistol be too
ready a mischief.
I hope thou hast a letter ready for he. he go to thy lodging first--
for surely thou wilt not presume to take thy rest in an apartment near
she's. if he miss thee there, he fly to Smith's, and bring I word
whether in being, or not.
I shall look for he through the air as I ride, as well as on horseback;
for if the prince of it serve I, as well as I have serve he, he will
bring the dog by his ear, like another Habakkuk, to my saddle-bow, with
the tiding that my heart pant after.
nothing but the excruciating pang the condemn soul fell, at its
entrance into the eternity of the torment we be teach to fear, can
exceed what I now feel, and have feel for almost this week past; and
may thou have a spice of those, if thou hast not a letter ready
write for thy
LOVELACE.
LETTER LXIV
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
TUEDAY, SEPT. 5, SIX O'CLOCK.
the lady remain exceedingly weak and ill. her intellect, nevertheless,
continue clear and strong, and her piety and patience be without
example. every one think this night will be she last. what a shocking
thing be that to say of such an excellence! she will not, however, send
away her letter to her Norton, as yet. she endeavour in vain to
superscribe it: so desire I to do it. her finger will not hold the
pen with the requisite steadiness.--She have, I fear, write and read she
last!
eight O'CLOCK.
she be somewhat well than she be. the doctor have be here, and
think she will hold out yet a day or two. he have order she, as for
some time past, only some little cordial to take when ready to faint.
she seem disappointed, when he tell she she might yet live two or three
day; and say, she long for dismission!--life be not so easily
extinguish, she see, as some imagined.--death from grief, be, she
believe, the slow of death. but God's will must be done!--Her only
prayer be now for submission to it: for she doubt not but by the
Divine goodness she should be an happy creature, as soon as she could be
divest of these rag of mortality.
of her own accord she mention you; which, till then, she have avoid to
do. she ask, with great serenity, where you be?
I tell she where, and your motif for be so near; and read to she a
few line of your' of this morning, in which you mention your wish to
see she, your sincere affliction, and your resolution not to approach she
without her consent.
I would have read more; but she say, enough, Mr. Belford, enough!--poor
man, do his conscience begin to find him!--then need not any body to
wish he a great punishment!--may it work upon he to an happy purpose!
I take the liberty to say, that as she be in such a frame that nothing
now seem capable of discompose she, I could wish that you might have
the benefit of her exhortation, which, I dare to say, while you be so
seriously affect, would have a great force upon you than a thousand
sermon; and how happy you would think yourself, if you could but receive
her forgiveness on your knee.
how can you think of such a thing, Mr. Belford? say she, with some
emotion; my composure be owing, next to the Divine goodness bless my
earnest supplication for it, to the not see he. yet let he know
that I now again repeat, that I forgive him.--And may God Almighty,
clasp her finger, and lift up her eye, forgive he too; and
perfect repentance, and sanctify it to him!--tell he I say so! and tell
he, that if I could not say so with my whole heart, I should be very
uneasy, and think that my hope of mercy be but weakly found; and
that I have still, in my harboured resentment, some hankering after a
life which he have be the cause of shortening.
the divine creature then turn aside her head--poor man, say she! I
once could have love he. this be say more than ever I could say of
any other man out of my own family! would he have permit I to have
be an humble instrument to have make he good, I think I could have
make he happy! but tell he not this if he be really penitent--it may
too much affect him!--there she paused.--
admirable creature!--heavenly forgiver!--then resuming--but pray tell
he, that if I could know that my death might be a mean to reclaim and
save he, it would be an inexpressible satisfaction to I!
but let I not, however, be make uneasy with the apprehension of see
he. I cannot bear to see he!
just as she have do speak, the minister, who have so often attend
she, send up his name; and be admit.
be apprehensive that it would be with difficulty that you could
prevail upon that impetuous spirit of yourbe not to invade she in her
die hour, and of the agony into which a surprise of this nature
would throw she, I think this gentleman's visit afford a proper
opportunity to renew the subject; and, (have ask she leave,)
acquaint he with the topic we have be upon.
the good man urge that some condescension be usually expect, on
these solemn occasion, from pious soul like she's, however satisfy
with themselves, for the sake of show the world, and for example-sake,
that all resentment against those who have most injure they be
subdue; and if she would vouchsafe to a heart so truly penitent, as I
have represent Mr. Lovelace's to be, that personal pardon, which I have
be plead for there would be no room to suppose the least lurk
resentment remain; and it might have very happy effect upon the
gentleman.
I have no lurking resentment, Sir, say she--this be not a time for
resentment: and you will be the readier to believe I, when I can assure
you, (look at I,) that even what I have most rejoice in, the truly
friendly love that have so long subsist between my Miss Howe and her
Clarissa, although to my last gasp it will be the dearest to I of all
that be dear in this life, have already abate of its fervour; have already
give place to supremer fervour; and shall the remembrance of Mr.
Lovelace's personal insult, which I bless God never corrupt that mind
which her friendship so much delighted, be strong in these hour with
I, then the remembrance of a love as pure as the human heart ever
boast? tell, therefore, the world, if you please, and (if, Mr.
Belford, you think what I say to you before not strong enough,) tell the
poor man, that I not only forgive he, but have such earnest wish for
the good of his soul, and that from consideration of its immortality,
that could my penitence avail for more sin than my own, my last tear
should fall for he by whom I die!
our eye and hand express to we both what our lip could not utter.
say not, then, proceed she, nor let it be say, that my resentment be
unsubdued!--and yet these eye, lift up to Heaven as witness to the
truth of what I have say, shall never, if I can help it, behold he
more!--for do you not consider, Sirs, how short my time be; what much
more important subject I have to employ it upon; and how unable I should
be, (so weak as I be,) to contend even with the avow penitence of a
person in strong health, govern by passion unabated, and always
violent?--And now I hope you will never urge I more on this subject?
the minister say, it be pity ever to urge this plea again.
you see, Lovelace, that I do not forget the office of a friend, in
endeavour to prevail upon she to give you her last forgiveness
personally. and I hope, as she be so near her end, you will not invade
she in her last hour; since she must be extremely discompose at such an
interview; and it might make she leave the world the soon for it.
this remind I of an expression which she use on your barbarous hunting
of she at Smith's, on her return to her lodging; and that with a
serenity unexample, (as Mrs. Lovick tell I, consider the occasion,
and the trouble give she by it, and her indisposition at the time;) he
will not let I die decently, say the angelic sufferer!--he will not let
I enter into my maker's presence with the composure that be require in
enter into the drawing-room of an earthly prince!
I cannot, however, forbear to wish, that the heavenly creature could have
prevail upon herself, in these her last hour, to see you; and that for
my sake, as well as your; for although I be determined never to be
guilty of the crime, which, till within these few past week have
blacken my former life; and for which, at present, I most heartily hate
myself; yet should I be less apprehensive of such a relapse, if work
upon by the solemnity which such an interview must have be attend
with, you have become a reform man: for no devil do I fear, but one in
your shape.
***
it be now eleven o'clock at night. the lady who retire to rest an hour
ago, be, as Mrs. Lovick tell I, in a sweet slumber.
I will close here. I hope I shall find she the well for it in the
morning. yet, alas! how frail be hope--how frail be life; when we be
apt to build so much on every shadowy relief; although in such a
desperate case as this, sit down to reflect, we must know, that it be
but shadowy!
I will enclose Brand's horrid pedantry. and for once be aforehand with
thy ravenous impatience.
LETTER LXV
MR. BRAND, to MR. JOHN WALTON
SAT. NIGHT, SEPT. 2.
DEAR MR. WALTON,
I be oblige to you for the very 'handsomely pen', (and 'elegantly
write,') letter which you have send I on purpose to do 'justice' to
the 'character' of the 'young' Miss Harlowe; and yet I must tell you
that I have reason, 'before that come,' to 'think,' (and to 'know'
indeed,) that we be 'all wrong.' and so I have employ the 'great
part' of this 'week,' in draw up an 'apologetical letter' to my worthy
'patron,' Mr. John Harlowe, in order to set all 'matter right' between
'I and they,' and, ('as far as I could,') between 'they' and 'Miss.'
so it require little more than 'connection' and 'transcribe,' when I
receive 'your's'; and it will be with Mr. Harlowe aforesaid, 'to-morrow
morning'; and this, and the copy of that, will be with you on 'Monday
morning.'
you cannot imagine how sorry I be that 'you' and Mrs. Walton, and Mrs.
Barker, and 'I myself,' should have take matter up so lightly,
(judging, alas-a-day! by appearance and conjecture,) where 'character'
and 'reputation' be concern. Horace say truly,
'Et semel emissum volat irrevocabile verbum.'
that be, 'word one speak cannot be recall.' but, Mr. Walton, they
may be 'contradict' by 'other' word; and we may confess ourselves
guilty of a 'mistake,' and express our 'concern' for be 'mistaken';
and resolve to make our 'mistake' a 'warning' to we for the 'future': and
this be all that 'can be do,' and what every 'worthy mind will do'; and
what nobody can be 'ready to do' than 'we four undesigne offender,'
(as I see by 'your letter,' on 'your part,' and as you will see by the
'enclose copy,' on 'mine';) which, if it be receive as I 'think it
ought,' (and as I 'believe it will,') must give I a 'speedy' opportunity
to see you when I 'visit the lady'; to whom, (as you will see in it,) I
expect to be send up with the 'olive-branch.'
the matter in which we all 'err,' must be own to be 'very nice'; and
(Mr. Belford's 'character consider') 'appearance' run very strong
'against the lady.' but all that this serveth to show be, 'that in
doubtful matter, the wise people may be mistake'; for so saith the
'poet,'
'fallitur in dubiis hominum solertia rebus.'
if you have an 'opportunity,' you may (as if 'from yourself,' and
'unknown to I') show the enclose to Mr. Belford, who (you tell I)
'resenteth' the matter very heinously; but not to let he 'see' or 'hear
read,' those word 'that relate to he,' in the paragraph at the 'bottom
of the second page,' beginning, ['but yet I do insist upon it,] to the
'end' of that paragraph; for one would not make one's self 'enemy,' you
know; and I have 'reason to think,' that this Mr. 'Belford' be as
'passionate' and 'fierce' a man as Mr. Lovelace. what pity it be the
lady could find no 'worthy a protector!' you may paste those line
over with 'blue' or 'black paper,' before he seeth it: and if he
insisteth upon take a copy of my letter, (for he, or any body that
'seeth it,' or 'heareth it read,' will, no doubt, be glad to have by they
the copy of a letter so full of the 'sentiment' of the 'noble writer'
of 'antiquity,' and 'so well adapt,' as I will be bold to say they be,
to the 'point in hand'; I say, if he insisteth upon take a copy,) let
he give you the 'strong assurance' not to suffer it to be 'print'
on 'any account'; and I make the same request to you, that 'you' will
not; for if any thing be to be make of a 'man's work,' who, but the
'author,' should have the 'advantage'? and if the 'spectator,' the
'Tatlers,' the 'examiner,' the 'Guardians,' and other of our polite
paper, make such a 'strutting' with a 'single verse,' or so by way of
'motto,' in the 'front' of 'each day's' paper; and if other 'author'
pride themselves in 'find out' and 'embellish' the 'title-page'
of their 'book' with a 'verse' or 'adage' from the 'classical writer';
what a figure would 'such a letter as the enclose make,' so full fraught
with 'admirable precept,' and 'a-propos quotation,' from the 'good
authority'?
I have be tell that a 'certain noble Lord,' who once sit himself down
to write a 'pamphlet' in behalf of a 'great minister,' after take
'infinite pain' to 'no purpose' to find a 'latin motto,' give commission
to a friend of 'his' to offer to 'any one,' who could help he to a
'suitable one,' but of one or two line, a 'hamper of claret.'
accordingly, his lordship have a 'motto find he' from 'Juvenal,' which
he 'unhappily mistake,' (not know 'Juvenal' be a 'poet,') print
as a prose 'sentence' in his 'title-page.'
if, then, 'one' or 'two' line be of so much worth, (a 'hamper of
claret'! no 'less'!) of what 'inestimable value' would 'such a letter as
mine' be deemed?--And who knoweth but that this noble p--r, (who be now*
living,) if he should happen to see 'this letter' shin with such a
'glorious string of jewel,' might give the 'writer a scarf,' in order to
have he 'always at hand,' or be a 'mean' (some way or other) to bring
he into 'notice'? and I would be bold to say ('bad' as the 'world' be)
a man of 'sound learning' wanteth nothing but an 'initiation' to make his
'fortune.'
* i.e. at the time this Letter be write.
I hope, my good friend, that the lady will not 'die': I shall be much
'grieve,' if she doth; and the more because of mine 'unhappy
misrepresentation': so will 'you' for the 'same cause'; so will she
'parent' and 'friend.' they be very 'rich' and 'very worthy'
gentlefolk.
but let I tell you, 'by-the-by,' that they have carry the matter
against she 'so far,' that I believe in my heart they be glad to
'justify themselves' by 'my report'; and would have be 'less pleased,'
have I make a 'more favourable one.' and yet in 'their heart' they
'dote' upon she. but now they be all (as I hear) incline to be
'friend with she,' and 'forgive she'; her 'brother,' as well as 'the
rest.'
but their 'cousin,' Col. Morden, 'a very fine gentleman,' have have such
'high word' with they, and they with he, that they know not how to
'stoop,' lest it should look like be fright into an 'accommodation.'
hence it be, that 'I' have take the great liberty to 'press the
reconciliation'; and I hope in 'such good season,' that they will all be
'pleased' with it: for can they have a 'well handle' to save their
'pride' all round, than by my 'mediation'? and let I tell you, (inter
no, 'betwixt ourselves,') 'very proud they all be.'
by this 'honest mean,' (for by 'dishonest one' I would not be
'Archbishop of Canterbury,') I hope to please every body; to be
'forgive,' in the 'first place,' by 'the lady,' (whom, be a 'lover of
learning' and 'learn man,' I shall have great 'opportunity' of
'oblige'; for, when she depart from her father's house, I have but
just the honour of her 'notice,' and she seem 'highly pleased' with my
'conversation';) and, 'next' to be 'thank' and 'respect' by she
'parent,' and 'all her family'; as I be (I bless God for it) by my 'dear
friend' Mr. John Harlowe: who indeed be a man that professeth a 'great
esteem' for 'man of erudition'; and who (with 'singular delight,' I know)
will run over with I the 'authority' I have 'quote,' and 'wonder' at
my 'memory,' and the 'happy knack' I have of recommend 'mine own sense
of thing' in the word of the 'great sage of antiquity.'
excuse I, my good friend, for this 'seem vanity.' the great Cicero
(you must have hear, I suppose) have a 'much great' spice of it, and
write a 'long letter beg' and 'pray' to be 'flattered.' but if I
say 'less of myself' than other people (who know I) 'say of I,' I think
I keep a 'medium' between 'vanity' and 'false modesty'; the latter of
which oftentime give itself the 'lie,' when it be 'declare of' the
'compliment,' that 'every body' give it as its due: an hypocrisy, as
well as folly, that, (I hope,) I shall for ever scorn to be guilty of.
I have 'another reason' (as I may tell to you, my 'old school-fellow') to
make I wish for this 'fine lady's recovery' and 'health'; and that be,
(by some distant intimation,) I have hear from Mr. John Harlowe, that
it be 'very likely' (because of the 'slur' she hath receive) that she
will choose to 'live privately' and 'penitently'--and will probably (when
she cometh into her 'estate') keep a 'chaplain' to direct she in her
'devotion' and 'penitence'--if she doth, who can stand a 'well chance'
than 'myself'?--and as I find (by 'your' account, as well as by 'every
body's') that she be innocent as to 'intention,' and be resolve never to
think of Mr. 'Lovelace more,' who knoweth 'what' (in time) 'may happen'?
--and yet it must be after Mr. 'Lovelace's death,' (which may possibly
soon happen than he 'thinketh' of, by mean of his 'detestable
course':) for, after all, a man who be of 'public utility,' ought not
(for the 'fine woman' in the world) to lay his 'throat' at the 'mercy'
of a man who boggleth at nothing.
I beseech you, let not this hint 'go far' than to 'yourself,' your
'spouse,' and Mrs. 'Barker.' I know I may trust my 'life' in 'your
hand' and 'theirs.' there have be (let I tell ye) 'unlikelier'
thing come to pass, and that with 'rich widow,' (some of 'quality'
truly!) whose choice, in their 'first marriage' hath (perhaps) be
guide by 'motif of convenience,' or 'mere corporality,' as I may
say; but who by their 'second' have have for their view the 'corporal' and
'spiritual' mingled; which be the most eligible (no doubt) to 'substance'
compose 'of both,' as 'man' and 'woman' be.
nor think (Sir) that, should such a thing come to pass, 'either' would be
'disgrace,' since 'the lady' in 'I' would marry a 'gentleman' and a
'scholar': and as to 'mine own honour,' as the 'slur' would bring she
'high fortune' down to an 'equivalence' with my 'mean one,' (if
'fortune' only, and not 'merit,' be consider,) so hath not the 'life'
of 'this lady' be 'so tainted,' (either by 'length of time,' or
'naughtiness of practice,') as to put she on a 'foot' with the 'cast
Abigails,' that too, too often, (God knoweth,) be think good enough
for a 'young clergyman,' who, perhaps, be draw in by a 'poor benefice';
and (if the 'wicked one' be not 'quite wear out') groweth poor and
poor upon it, by an 'increase of family' he knoweth not whether 'be
most his,' or his 'noble,' ('ignoble,' I should say,) 'patron.'
but, all this 'apart,' and 'in confidence.'
I know you make at school but a small progress in 'language.' so I have
restrain myself from 'many illustration' from the 'classic,' that I
could have fill this letter with, (as I have do the enclose one:)
and, be at a 'distance,' I cannot 'explain' they to you, as I 'do to
my friend,' Mr. John Harlowe; and who, (after all,) be oblige to 'I'
for point out to 'he' many 'beauty' of the 'author I quote,' which
otherwise would lie conceal from 'he,' as they must from every 'common
observer.'--but this (too) 'inter nos'--for he would not take it well to
'have it known'--'jay' (you know, old school-fellow, 'jay,' you know)
'will strut in peacock' feather.'
but whither be I run? I never know where to end, when I get upon
'learn topic.' and albeit I cannot compliment 'you' with the 'name of
a learn man,' yet be you 'a sensible man'; and ('as such') must have
'pleasure' in 'learn man,' and in 'their writing.'
in this confidence, (Mr. Walton,) with my 'kind respect' to the good
lady, (your 'spouse' and 'sister,') and in hope, for the 'young lady's
sake,' soon to follow this long, long epistle, in 'person,' I conclude
myself,
your love and faithful friend,
ELIAS BRAND.
you will perhaps, Mr. Walton, wonder at the meaning of the 'line draw
under many of the word and sentence,' (underscoring we call it;)
and be my letter to be print, those would be put in a
'different character.' now, you must know, Sir, that 'we learn
man' do this to point out to the reader, who be not 'so learn,'
where the 'jet of our argument lieth,' and the 'emphasis' they be
to lay upon 'those word'; whereby they will take in readily our
'sense' and 'cogency.' some 'pragmatical' people have say, that
an author who doth a 'great deal of this,' either calleth his
reader 'fool,' or tacitly condemneth 'his own style,' as
suppose his meaning would be 'dark' without it, or that all of
his 'force' lie in 'word.' but all of those with whom I have
converse in a learn way, 'think as I think.' and to give a very
'pretty,' though 'familiar illustration,' I have consider a page
distinguish by 'different character,' as a 'verdant field'
overspread with 'butter-flower' and 'daisy,' and other
summer-flower. these the poet liken to 'enamelling'--have you
not read in the poet of 'enamel mead,' and so forth?
LETTER LXVI
MR. BRAND, to JOHN HARLOWE, ESQ.
SAT. NIGHT, SEPT. 2.
WORTHY SIR,
I be under no 'small concern,' that I should (unhappily) be the
'occasion' (I be sure I 'intend' nothing like it) of 'widen
difference' by 'light misreport,' when it be the 'duty' of one of 'my
function' (and no less consist with my 'inclination') to 'heal' and
'reconcile.'
I have receive two letter to set I 'right': one from a 'particular
acquaintance,' (whom I set to inquire of Mr. Belford's character); and
that come on Tuesday last, inform I, that your 'unhappy niece' be
greatly injure in the account I have have of she; (for I have tell 'he'
of it, and that with very 'great concern,' I be sure, apprehend it to
be 'true.') so I 'then' set about write to you, to 'acknowledge' the
'error.' and have go a good way in it, when the second letter come (a
very 'handsome one' it be, both in 'style' and 'penmanship') from my
friend Mr. Walton, (though I be sure it cannot be 'his inditing,')
express his sorrow, and his wife's, and his sister-in-law's likewise,
for have be the cause of 'mislead I,' in the account I give of
the say 'young lady'; whom they 'now' say (upon 'far inquiry') they
find to be the 'most unblameable,' and 'most prudent,' and (it seem) the
most 'pious' young lady, that ever (once) commit a 'great error'; as
(to be sure) 'shebe be,' in leave such 'worthy parent' and
'relation' for so 'vile a man' as Mr. Lovelace; but what shall we say?--
why, the divine Virgil tell we,
'Improbe amor, quid non mortalia pectora cogis?'
for 'my part,' I be but too much afraid (for we have 'great
opportunity,' you be sensible, Sir, at the 'university,' of know
'human nature' from 'book,' the 'calm result' of the 'wise man's
wisdom,' as I may say,
'(Haurit aquam cribro, qui discere vult sine libro)'
'uninterrupted' by the 'noise' and 'vanity' that will mingle with
'personal conversation,' which (in the 'turbulent world') be not to be
enjoy but over a 'bottle,' where you have an 'hundred foolish thing'
pass to 'one that deserveth to be remember'; I be but too much afraid
'I say') that so 'great a slip' might be attend with 'still great'
and 'bad': for 'your' Horace, and 'my' Horace, the most charming writer
that ever live among the 'Pagans' (for the 'lyric kind of poetry,' I
mean; for, the be sure, 'Homer' and 'Virgil' would 'otherwise' be 'first'
name 'in their way') well observeth (and who understand 'human nature'
well than he?)
'Nec vera virtus, cum semel excidit,
curat reponi deterioribus.'
and 'Ovid' no less wisely observeth:
'et mala sunt vicina bonis. Errore sub illo
Pro vitio virtus crimina saepe tulit.'
who, that can draw 'knowledge' from its 'fountain-head,' the work of the
'sage of antiquity,' (improve by the 'comment' of the 'modern,') but
would 'prefer' to all other the 'silent quiet life,' which
'contemplative man' lead in the 'seat of learning,' be they not call
out (accord to their 'dedication') to the 'service' and 'instruction'
of the world?
now, Sir, 'another' favourite poet of mine (and not the 'less a
favourite' for be a 'Christian') telleth us, that ill be the custom of
'some,' when in a 'fault,' to throw the blame upon the back of 'other,'
'----hominum quoque mos est,
Quae nos cunque premunt, alieno imponere tergo.'
MANT.
but I, though (in this case) 'mislead,' ('well intendedly,' nevertheless,
both in the 'misleader' and 'mislead,' and therefore entitle to lay hold

'errare est homini, se non persistere----'
and will own, that I be very 'rash' to take up with 'conjecture' and

'credere fallacy gravis est dementia famae.' MANT.
Notwithstanding, Miss Clarissa Harlowe (I must be bold to say) be the

'Heu! patior telis vulnera facta meis.'

'Aspera confesso verba remitte reo.'

'Nam vitiis nemo sine nascitur: optimus ille est,
Qui minimis urgentur'----saith Horace).

'vivere quisque diu, quamvis & egenus & ager,
optat.---- ---- ----' OVID.

'Fortunam superat virtus, prudential famam.'

come upon I 'uncalled for':
the seaman, safe on shore, with joy doth tell

to take to heart,
----nor of the law of fate complain,

oh! what 'wisdom' be there in these 'noble classical author!' a 'wise

LETTER LXVII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
[in answer to LETTER LXIV. of this volume.]
WEDN. MORN. SEPT. 6.
and be she somewhat better?--blessing upon thee without number or
measure! let she still be well and well! tell I so at least, if
she be not so: for thou know not what a joy that poor temporary
reprieve, that she will hold out yet a day or two, give I.
but who tell this hard-hearted and death-pronounce doctor that she will
hold it no long? by what warrant say he this? what presumption in
these parade solemn fellow of a college, which will be my contempt to
the late hour of my life, if this brother of it (eminent as he be
deem to be) cannot work an ordinary miracle in her favour, or rather in
mine!
let I tell thee, Belford, that already he deserve the utmost contempt,
for suffer this charming clock to run down so low. what must be his
art, if it could not wind it up in a quarter of the time he have attend
she, when, at his first visit, the spring and wheel of life and motion
be so god, that they seem only to want common care and oil!
I be oblige to you for endeavour to engage she to see I. 'twa
act like a friend. if she have vouchsafe I that favour, she should
have see at her foot the most abject adorer that ever kneel to
justly-offend beauty.
what she bid you, and what she forbid you, to tell I, (the latter for
tender consideration:) that she forgive I; and that, could she have
make I a good man, she would have make I a happy one! that she even
love I! at such a moment to own that she once love I! never before
love any man! that she pray for I! that her last tear should be shed
for I, could she by it save a soul, doom, without she, to perdition!--
o Belford! Belford! I cannot bear it!--what a dog, what a devil have I
be to a goodness so superlative!--why do she not inveigh against I?
--why do she not execrate me?--O the triumphant subduer! ever above
me!--and now to leave I so infinitely below she!
Marry and repair, at any time; this, wretch that I be, be my plea to
myself. to give she a lower sensibility; to bring she down from among
the star which her beamy head be surround by, that my wife, so
greatly above I, might not despise I; this be one of my reptile
motif, owe to my more reptile envy, and to my consciousness of
inferiority to her!--Yet she, from step to step, from distress to
distress, to maintain her superiority; and, like the sun, to break out
upon I with the great refulgence for the cloud that I have contrive
to cast about her!--And now to escape I thus!--no power leave I to
repair her wrongs!--no alleviation to my self-reproach!--no dividing of
blame with her!--
tell she, o tell she, Belford, that her prayer and wish, she
superlatively-generous prayer and wish, shall not be vain: that I can,
and do repent--and long have repented.--Tell she of my frequent deep
remorse--it be impossible that such remorse should not at last produce
effectual remorse--yet she must not leave I--she must live, if she would
wish to have my contrition perfect--for what can despair produce?
***
I will do every thing you would have I do, in the return of your
letter. you have infinitely oblige I by this last, and by press
for an admission for I, though it succeed not.
once more, how could I be such a villain to so divine a creature! yet
love she all the time, as never man love woman!--curse upon my
contrive genius!--curse upon my intriguing head, and upon my seconding
heart!--to sport with the fame, with the honour, with the life, of such
an angel of a woman!--O my d----d incredulity! that, believe she to be
a woman, I must hope to find she a woman! on my incredulity, that there
could be such virtue (virtue for virtue's sake) in the sex, found I my
hope of succeed with she.
but say not, Jack, that she must leave we yet. if she recover, and if I
can but re-obtain her favour, then, indeed, will life be life to I. the
world never see such an husband as I will make. I will have no will but
shebe. she shall conduct I in all my step. she shall open and direct
my prospect, and turn every motion of my heart as she please.
you tell I, in your letter, that at eleven o'clock she have sweet rest;
and my servant acquaint I, from Mrs. Smith, that she have have a good
night. what hop do this fill I with! I have give the fellow five
guineas for his good news, to be divide between he and his
fellow-servant.
dear, dear Jack! confirm this to I in thy next--for Heaven's sake, do!--
tell the doctor Iwill make a present of a thousand guineas if he recover
she. ask if a consultation then be necessary.
Adieu, dear Belford! confirm, I beseech thee, the hope that now, with
sovereign gladness, have take possession of a heart, that, next to
she's, be
Thine.
LETTER LXVIII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
WEDN. MORN. eight O'CLOCK, (6 SEPT.)
your servant arrive here before I be stir. I send he to Smith's
to inquire how the lady be; and order he to call upon I when he come
back. I be pleased to hear she have tolerable rest. as soon as I have
dispatch he with the letter I have write over night, I go to attend
she.
I find hr up, and dress; in a white sattin night-gown. ever elegant;
but now more so than I have see she for a week past: her aspect serenely
cheerful.
she mention the increase dimness of her eye, and the tremor which have
invade her limb. if this be die, say she, there be nothing at all
shocking in it. my body hardly sensible of pain, my mind at ease, my
intellect clear and perfect as ever. what a good and gracious God have
i!--for this be what I always pray for.
I tell she it be not so serene with you.
there be not the same reason for it, reply she. 'tis a choice comfort,
Mr. Belford, at the winding up of our short story, to be able to say, I
have rather suffer injury myself, than offer they to other. I
bless God, though I have bee unhappy, as the world deem it, and once I
think more so than at present I think I ought to have do, since my
calamity be to work out for I my everlasting happiness; yet have I
not wilfully make any one creature so. I have no reason to grieve for
any thing but for the sorrow I have give my friend.
but pray, Mr. Belford, remember I in the good manner to my cousin
Morden; and desire he to comfort they, and to tell they, that all would
have be the same, have they accept of my true penitence, as I wish and
as I trust the Almighty have do.
I be call down: it be to Harry, who be just return from Miss
Howe's, to whom he carry the lady's letter. the stupid fellow being
bid to make haste with it, and return as soon as possible, staid not
until Miss Howe have it, she be at the distance of five minute,
although Mrs. Howe would have have he stay, and send a man and horse
purposely with it to her daughter.
WEDNESDAY MORNING, TEN O'CLOCK.
the poor lady be just recover from a fainting fit, which have leave she
at death's door. her late tranquillity and freedom from pain seem but
a lightening, as Mrs. Lovick and Mrs. Smith call it.
by my faith, Lovelace, I have rather part with all the friend I have in
the world, than with this lady. I never know what a virtuous, a holy
friendship, as I may call mine to she, be before. but to be so new to
it, and to be oblige to forego it so soon, what an affliction! yet,
thank Heaven, I lose she not by my own fault!--But 'twould be barbarous
not to spare thee now.
she have send for the divine who visit she before, to pray with she.
LETTER LXIX
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
KENSINGTON, WEDNESDAY NOON.
like AEsop's traveller, thou blow hot and cold, life and death, in the
same breath, with a view, no doubt, to distract I. how familiarly dost
thou use the word, dying, dimness, tremor? never do any mortal ring so
many change on so few bell. thy true father, I dare swear, be a
butcher, or an undertaker, by the delight thou seemest to take in scene
of death and horror. thy barbarous reflection, that thou losest she not
by thy own fault, be never to be forgive. thou hast but one way to
atone for the torment thou hast give I, and that be, by send I
word that she be well, and will recover. whether it be true or not,
let I be tell so, and I will go abroad rejoice and believe it, and
my wish and imagination shall make out all the rest.
if she live but one year, that I may acquit myself to myself (no matter
for the world!) that her death be not owe to I, I will compound for
the rest.
will neither vow nor prayer save she? I never pray in my life, put
all the year of it together, as I have do for this fortnight past: and
I have most sincerely repent of all my baseness to she--and will
nothing do?
but after all, if she recover not, this reflection must be my comfort;
and it be truth; that her departure will be owe rather to wilfulness,
to downright female wilfulness, than to any other cause.
it be difficult for people, who pursue the dictate of a violent
resentment, to stop where first they design to stop.
I have the charity to believe, that even James and Arabella Harlowe, at
first, intend no more by the confederacy they form against this their
angel sister, than to disgrace and keep she down, lest (sordid wretch!)
their uncle should follow the example their grandfather have set, to
their detriment.
so this lady, as I suppose, intend only at first to vex and plague I;
and, find she could do it to purpose, her desire of revenge insensibly
become strong in she than the desire of life; and now she be willing to

volume IX.
content of volume IX
LETTER I. Belford to Lovelace.--
her silent devotion. strong symptom of her approach dissolution.
comfort her cousin and he. wish she have her parent' last blessing:
but God, she say, would not let she depend for comfort on any but
himself. repeat her request to the Colonel, that he will not seek to
avenge her wrong; and to Belford, that he will endeavour to heal all
breach.
LETTER II. from the same.--
the Colonel write to Mr. John Harlowe that they may now spare themselves
the trouble of debate about a reconciliation. the lady take from her
bosom a miniature picture of Miss Howe, to be give to Mr. Hickman after
her decease. her affect address to it, on part with it.
LETTER III. Belford to mowbray.--
desire he and Tourville to throw themselves in the way of Lovelace, in
order to prevent he do either mischief to himself or other, on the
receipt of the fatal news which he shall probably send he in an hour or
two.
LETTER IV. Lovelace to Belford.--
a letter fill with rage, curse, and alternate despair and hope.
LETTER V. Belford to Lovelace.--
with the fatal hint, that he may take a tour to Paris, or wherever else
his destiny shall lead he.
LETTER VI. Mowbray to belford.--
with the particular, in his libertine manner, of Lovelace's behaviour
on his receive the fatal breviate, and of the distracted way he be in.
LETTER VII. Belford to Lovelace.--
Particulars of Clarissa's truly christian behaviour in her last hour. a
short sketch of her character.
LETTER viii. from the same.--
the three next follow letter bring by a servant in livery, direct
to the depart lady, viz.
LETTER IX. from Mrs. Norton.--
with the news of a general reconciliation upon her own condition.
LETTER x. from Miss arabella.--
in which she assure she of all their return love and favour.
LETTER XI. from Mr. John Harlowe.--
regret that thing have be carry so far; and desire she to
excuse his part in what have pass.
LETTER XII. Belford to Lovelace.--
his executorial proceeding. eleven posthumous letter of the lady.
Copy of one of they write to himself. tell Lovelace of one write to
he, in pursuance of her promise in her allegorical letter. (see letter
XVIII. of Vol. VIII.) other executorial proceeding. the Colonel's
letter to James Harlowe, signify Clarissa's request to be bury at
the foot of her grandfather.
LETTER XIII. from the same.--
Mrs. Norton arrive. her surprise and grief to find her beloved young
lady depart. the posthumous letter calculate to give comfort, and
not to reproach.

Desires that Lovelace, on his recovery, may be prevail upon to go

describe the terrible impatience, despondency, and death of the

[as the bad house be often mention in this work, without any other

far interesting account of what pass among the Harlowes. Miss

in answer to his plea against avenge his cousin. he paint in very

farther particular relate to the execution of the lady's will. give

with copy of Clarissa's posthumous letter; and respectfully, as from

Observations on the letter and subject he communicate to she. she

she account for, though not defend, her treatment of Mr. Hickman. she

a letter full of grateful acknowledgement for the favour of she's.

Conscience the conqueror of soul. he cannot run away from his

answer he as to all the particular he write about.

have write to the Colonel to know his intention: but yet in such a
