LETTER I
MR. BELFORD
[in CONTINUATION.]
SOHO, SIX O'CLOCK, SEPT. 7.
the lady be still alive. the Colonel have just send his servant to let
I know that she inquire after I about an hour ago, I be dress to
attend she. Joel beg of I to dispatch he back, though but with one
line to gratify your present impatience. he expect, he say, to find
you at Knightsbridge, let he make what haste he can back; and, if he have
not a line or two to pacify you, he be afraid you will pistol he; for he
apprehend that you be hardly yourself. I therefore dispatch this, and
will have another ready, as soon as I can, with particulars.--but you
must have a little patience; for how can I withdraw myself every half
hour to write, if I be admit to the lady's presence, or if I be with
the Colonel?
SMITH's, eight in the morning.
the lady be in a slumber. Mrs. Lovick, who sit up with she, say she have
a well night than be expect; for although she sleep little, she
seem easy; and the easy for the pious frame she be in; all her
wake moment be take up in devotion, or in an ejaculatory silence;
her hand and eye often lift up, and her lip move with a fervour
worthy of these her last hour.
TEN O'CLOCK.
the Colonel be earnest to see his cousin as soon as she awake, we be
both admit. we observe in she, as soon as we enter, strong
symptom of her approach dissolution, notwithstanding what the woman
have flatter we with from her last night's tranquillity.--The Colonel
and I, each loth to say what we think, look upon one another with
melancholy countenance.
the Colonel tell she he should send a servant to her uncle Antony's for
some paper he have leave there; and ask if she have any command that
way.
she think not, she say, speak more inwardly than she do the day
before. she have indeed a letter ready to be send to her good Norton; and
there be a request intimate in it. but it be time enough, if the
request be signify to those whom it concern when all be over.
--However, it might be send they by the servant who be go that way.
and she cause it to be give to the Colonel for that purpose.
her breath be very short, she desire another pillow. have two
before, this make she in a manner sit up in her bed; and she speak then
with more distinctness; and, see we greatly concern, forget her own
suffering to comfort we; and a charming lecture she give we, though a
brief one, upon the happiness of a timely preparation, and upon the
hazard of a late repentance, when the mind, as she observe, be so much
weaken, as well as the body, as to render a poor soul hardly able to
contend with its natural infirmity.
I beseech ye, my good friend, proceed she, mourn not for one who
mourn not, nor have cause to mourn, for herself. on the contrary,
rejoice with I, that all my worldly trouble be so near to their end.
believe I, Sirs, that I would not, if I might, choose to live, although
the pleasantest part of my life be to come over again: and yet eighteen
year of it, out of nineteen, have be very pleasant. to be so much
expose to temptation, and to be so liable to fail in the trial, who
would not rejoice that all her danger be over?--all I wish be pardon
and blessing from my dear parent. easy as my departure seem promise
to be, it would have be still easy, have I that pleasure. but GOD
ALMIGHTY would not let I DEPEND for COMFORT UPON ANY but HIMSELF.
she then repeat her request, in the most earnest manner, to her cousin,
that he would not heighten her fault, by seek to avenge her death; to
I, that I would endeavour to make up all breach, and use the power I
have with my friend, to prevent all future mischief from he, as well as
that which this trust might give I to prevent any to he.
she make some excuse to her cousin, for not have be able to alter
her will, to join he in the executorship with I; and to I, for the
trouble she have give, and yet should give I.
she have fatigue herself so much, (grow sensibly weak) that she sink
her head upon her pillow, ready to faint; and we withdraw to the window,
look upon one another; but could not tell what to say; and yet both
seem inclinable to speak: but the motion pass over in silence. our
eye only speak; and that in a manner neither's be use to--mine, at
least, not till I know this admirable creature.
the Colonel withdraw to dismiss his messenger, and send away the letter
to Mrs. Norton. I take the opportunity to retire likewise; and to write
thus far. and Joel return to take it, I now close here.
ELEVEN O'CLOCK.
LETTER II
MR. BELFORD
[in CONTINUATION.]
the Colonel tell I that he have write to Mr. John Harlowe, by his
servant, 'that they might spare themselves the trouble of debate about
a reconciliation; for that his dear cousin would probably be no more
before they could resolve.'
he ask I after his cousin's mean of subsist; and whether she have
accept of any favour from I; he be sure, he say, she would not from
you.
I acquaint he with the truth of she part with some of her apparel.
this wring his heart; and bitterly do he exclaim as well against you as
against her implacable relation.
he wish he have not come to England at all, or have come soon; and
hop I would apprize he of the whole mournful story, at a proper
season. he add, that he have thought, when he come over, of fix
here for the remainder of his day; but now, as it be impossible his
cousin could recover, he would go abroad again, and re-settle himself at
Florence or Leghorn.
the lady have be give order, with great presence of mind, about her
body! direct her nurse and the maid of the house to put she in the
coffin as soon as she be cold. Mr. Belford, she say, would know the
rest by her will.
***
she have just now give from her bosom, where she always wear it, a
miniature picture, set in gold, of Miss Howe. she give it to Mrs.
Lovick, desire she to fold it up in white paper, and direct it, to
Charles Hickman, Esq. and to give it to I, when she be depart, for
that gentleman.
she look upon the picture, before she give it she--sweet and
ever-amiable friend!--companion!--sister!--lover! say she--and kiss
it four several time, once at each tender appellation.
***
your other servant be come.--Well may you be impatient!--well may you!
--but do you think I can leave off, in the middle of a conversation, to
run and set down what offer, and send it away piece-meal as I write?
--if I could, must I not lose one half, while I put down the other?
this event be nearly as interesting to I as it be to you. if you be
more grieved than I, there can be but one reason for it; and thatbe at
your heart!--i have rather lose all the friend I have in the world,
(yourself in the number,) than this divine lady; and shall be unhappy
whenever I think of her suffering, and of her merit; though I have
nothing to reproach myself by reason of the former.
I say not this, just now, so much to reflect upon you as to express my
own grief; though your conscience I suppose, will make you think
otherwise.
your poor fellow, who say that he beg for his life, in desire to be
dispatch back with a letter, tear this from I--else, perhaps, (for
I be just send for down,) a quarter of an hour would make you--not easy
indeed--but certain--and that, in a state like your's, to a mind like
your's, be a relief.
THURSDAY AFTERNOON, FOUR O'CLOCK.
LETTER III
MR. BELFORD, TO RICHARD MOWBRAY, ESQ.
THURSDAY AFTERNOON.
DEAR MOWBRAY,
I be glad to hear you be in town. throw yourself the moment this come
to your hand, (if possible with Tourville,) in the way of the man who
least of all man deserve the love of the worthy heart; but most that of
thine and Tourville; else the news I shall most probably send he within
an hour or two, will make annihilation the great blessing he have to
wish for.
you will find he between Piccadilly and Kensington, most probably on
horseback, rid backwards and forwards in a crazy way; or put up,
perhaps, at some inn or tavern in the way--a waiter possibly, if so,
watch for his servant's return to he from I.
***
his man Will. be just come to I. he will carry this to you in his way
back, and be your director. hie away in a coach, or any how. your being
with he may save either his or a servant's life. see the blessed
effect of triumphant libertinism! soon or later it come home to we,
and all conclude in gall and bitterness!
Adieu.
J. BELFORD.
LETTER IV
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
curse upon the Colonel, and curse upon the writer of the last letter I
receive, and upon all the world! thou to pretend to be as much
interested in my Clarissa's fate as myself!--'tis well for one of we that
this be not say to I, instead of written.--living or die, she be
mine--and only mine. have I not earn her dearly?--is not d----n----n
likely to be the purchase to I, though a happy eternity will be she's?
an eternal separation!--o God! o god!--how can I bear that thought!--but
yet there be life!--Yet, therefore, hope--enlarge my hope, and thou shalt
be my good genius, and I will forgive thee every thing.
for this last time--but it must not, shall not be the last--let I hear,
the moment thou receivest this--what I be to be--for, at present, I be
the most miserable of Men.
ROSE, AT KNIGHTSBRIDGE, five O'CLOCK.
my fellow tell I that thou art send Mowbray and Tourville to me:--i
want they not--my soul's sick of they, and of all the world--but most of
myself. yet, as they send I word they will come to I immediately, I
will wait for they, and for thy next. o Belford, let it not be--but
hasten it, be what it may!
LETTER V
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
seven O'CLOCK, THURSDAY EVENING, SEPT. 7.
I have only to say at present--thou wilt do well to take a tour to
Paris; or wherever else thy destiny shall lead thee!----
JOHN BELFORD.
LETTER VI
MR. MOWBRAY, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
UXBRIDGE, SEPT. 7, between ELEVEN and TWELVE AT NIGHT.
DEAR JACK,
I send by poor Lovelace's desire, for particular of the fatal breviate
thou sentest he this night. he cannot bear to set pen to paper; yet
want to know every minute passage of Miss Harlowe's departure. yet why
he should, I cannot see: for if she be go, she be go; and who can
help it?
I never hear of such a woman in my life. what great matter have she
suffer, that grief should kill she thus?
I wish the poor fellow have never know she. from first to last, what
trouble she have cost he! the charming fellow have be half lose to we
ever since he pursue she. and what be there in one woman more than
another, for matter of that?
it be well we be with he when your note come. your show your true
friendship in your foresight. why, Jack, the poor fellow be quite
beside himself--mad as any man ever be in Bedlam.
will. bring he the letter just after we have join he at the Bohemia
Head; where he have leave word at the Rose at Knightsbridge he should be;
for he have be saunter up and down, backwards and forwards, expect
we, and his fellow. will., as soon as he deliver it, get out of his
way; and, when he open it, never be such a piece of scenery. he
tremble like a devil at receive it: fumble at the seal, his finger
in a palsy, like Tom. Doleman's; his hand shake, shake, shake, that he
tear the letter in two, before he could come at the content: and, when
he have read they, off go his hat to one corner of the room, his wig to
the other--D--n--n seize the world! and a whole volley of such-like
excratious wish; run up and down the room, and throw up the
sash, and pull it down, and smite his forehead with his double fist,
with such force as would have fell as ox, and stamp and tearing,
that the landlord run in, and fast out again. and this be the
distraction scene for some time.
in vain be all Jemmy or I could say to he. I offer once to take hold
of his hand, because he be go to do himself a mischief, as I
believe, look about for his pistol, which he have lay upon the
table, but which will., unseen, have take out with he, [a faithful,
honest dog, that will.! I shall for ever love the fellow for it,] and he
hit I a d--d dowse of the chop, as make my nose bleed. 'twas well
'twa he, for I hardly know how to take it.
Jemmy rave at he, and tell he, how wicked it be in he, to be so
brutish to abuse a friend, and run mad for a woman. and then he say he
be sorry for it; and then will. venture in with water and a towel; and
the dog rejoice, as I could see by his look, that I have it rather than
he.
and so, by degree, we bring he a little to his reason, and he
promise to behave more like a man. and so I forgave he: and we ride on
in the dark to here at Doleman's. and we all try to shame he out of
his mad, ungovernable foolishness: for we tell he, as how she be but a
woman, and an obstinate perverse woman too; and how could he help it?
and you know, Jack, (as we tell he, moreover,) that it be a shame to
manhood, for a man, who have serve twenty and twenty woman as bad or
bad, let he have serve Miss Harlowe never so bad, should give himself
such obstropulous air, because she would die: and we advise he never
to attempt a woman proud of her character and virtue, as they call it,
any more: for why? the conquest do not pay trouble; and what be there
in one woman more than another? Hay, you know, Jack!--And thus we
comfort he, and advise he.
but yet his d--d addled pate run upon this lady as much now shebe dead
as it do when she be live. for, I suppose, Jack, it be no joke: she
be certainly and bona fide dead: i'n't she? if not, thou deservest to be
doubly d--d for thy fooling, I tell thee that. so he will have I write
for particular of her departure.
he willnot bear the word dead on any account. a squeamish puppy! how love
unman and soften! and such a noble fellow as this too! rot he for an
idiot, and an oaf! I have no patience with the foolish duncical dog
--upon my soul, I have not!
so send the account, and let he howl over it, as I suppose he will.
but he must and shall go abroad: and in a month or two Jemmy, and you,
and I, will join he, and hewill soon get the well of this
chicken-hearte folly, never fear; and will then be ashamed of himself:
and then wewill not spare he; though now, poor fellow, it be pity to
lay he on so thick as he deserve. and do thou, till then, spare all
reflection upon he; for, it seem, thou hast work he unmercifully.
I be willing to give thee some account of the hand we have have with the
tear fellow, who have certainly be a lost man, have we not be with
he; or he would have kill somebody or other. I have no doubt of it.
and now he be but very middling; sit grin like a man in straw;
curse and swear, and be confound gloomy; and creep into hole and
corner, like an old hedge-hog hunt for his grease.
and so, adieu, Jack. Tourville, and all of we, wish for thee; for no one
have the influence upon he that thou hast.
R. MOWBRAY.
as I promise he that I would write for the particular abovesaid, I
write this after all be go to bed; and the fellow be set out
with it by day-break.
LETTER VII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
THURSDAY NIGHT.
I may as well try to write; since, be I to go to bed, I shall not
sleep. I never have such a weight of grief upon my mind in my life, as
upon the demise of this admirable woman; whose soul be now rejoice
in the region of light.
you may be glad to know the particular of her happy exit. I will try
to proceed; for all be hush and still; the family retire; but not one
of they, and least of all her poor cousin, I dare say, to rest.
at four o'clock, as I mention in my last, I be send for down; and,
as thou usedst to like my description, I will give thee the woeful scene
that present itself to I, as I approach the bed.
the Colonel be the first that take my attention, kneel on the side of
the bed, the lady's right hand in both his, which his face cover,
bath it with his tear; although she have be comfort he, as the
woman since tell I, in elevated strain, but broken accent.
on the other side of the bed sit the good widow; her face overwhelm
with tear, lean her head against the bed's head in a most
disconsolate manner; and turn her face to I, as soon as she see I,
o Mr. Belford, cry she, with folded hand--the dear lady--a heavy sob
permit she not to say more.
Mrs. Smith, with clasped finger, and uplifted eye, as if implore help
from the only power which could give it, be kneel down at the bed's
foot, tear in large drop trickle down her cheek.
her nurse be kneel between the widow and Mrs. Smith, her arm
extend. in one hand she hold an ineffectual cordial, which she have
just be offer to her die mistress; her face be swoln with weeping
(though use to such scene as this); and she turn her eye towards I,
as if she call upon I by they to join in the helpless sorrow; a fresh
stream burst from they as I approach the bed.
the maid of the house with her face upon her fold arm, as she stand
lean against the wainscot, more audibly expr her grief than any of
the other.
the lady have be silent a few minute, and speechless, as they think,
move her lip without utter a word; one hand, as I say, in her
cousin's. but when Mrs. Lovick, on my approach, pronounce my name, O
Mr. Belford, say she, with a faint inward voice, but very distinct
nevertheless--now!--now! [in broken period she spoke]--I bless God for
his mercy to his poor creature--all will soon be over--a few--a very
few moment--will end this strife--and I shall be happy!
Comfort here, Sir--turn her head to the Colonel--comfort my cousin
--see! the blame--able kindness--he would not wish I to be happy
--so soon!
here she stopt for two or three minute, earnestly look upon he.
then resume, my dear Cousin, say she, be comfort--what be die
but the common lot?--the mortal frame may seem to labour--but that be
all!--It be not so hard to die as I believe it to be!--the preparation
be the difficulty--I bless God, I have have time for that--the rest be
bad to beholder, than to me!--I be all bless hope--hope itself. she
look what she say, a sweet smile beam over her countenance.
after a short silence, once more, my dear Cousin, say she, but still in
broken accent, commend I most dutifully to my father and mother--there

uncle--and tell they, I bless they with my parting breath--for all their
goodness to I--even for their displeasure, I bless they--most happy have
be to I my punishment here! happy indeed!
she be silent for a few moment, lift up her eye, and the hand she
cousin hold not between his. then, O death! say she, where be thy
sting! [the word I remember to have hear in the burial-service read
over my uncle and poor Belton.] and after a pause--it be good for I
that I be afflict! word of scripture, I suppose.
then turn towards we, who be lose in speechless sorrow--o dear, dear
gentleman, say she, you know not what foretaste--what assurance--and
there she again stop, and look up, as if in a thankful rapture,
sweetly smile.
then turn her head towards I--do you, Sir, tell your friend that I
forgive him!--and I pray to God to forgive him!--Again pausing, and
lift up her eye as if pray that he would. let he know how
happily I die:--and that such as my own, I wish to be his last hour.
she be again silent for a few moment: and then resume--my sight

divine frame, though in accent as break as her own]; and the voice of
grief be alike in all. be not this Mr. Morden's hand? press one of
his with that he have just let go. which be Mr. Belford's? hold out
the other. I give her mine. God Almighty bless you both, say she, and
make you both--in your last hour--for you must come to this--happy as I
be.
she pause again, her breath grow short; and, after a few minute
--and now, my dear Cousin, give I your hand--nearer--still nearer

lover; and an heavenly crown hereafter; and such assurance of it, as I
have, through the all-satisfy merit of my blessed Redeemer.
her sweet voice and broken period methink still fill my ear, and never
will be out of my memory.
after a short silence, in a more broken and faint accent--and you, Mr.
Belford, press my hand, may God preserve you, and make you sensible of
all your error--you see, in I, how all end--may you be--and down sink
her head upon her pillow, she faint away, and draw from we her
hand.
we think she be then go; and each give way to a violent burst of
grief.
but soon show sign of return life, our attention be again
engage; and I besought she, when a little recover, to complete in my
favour her half-pronounce blessing. she wave her hand to we both, and
bow her head six several time, as we have since recollect, as if
distinguish every person present; not forget the nurse and the
maid-servant; the latter have approach the bed, weeping, as if
crowd in for the divine lady's blessing; and she speak falter and
inwardly--Bless--bless--bless--you all--and--now--and now--[holde up
she almost lifeless hand for the last time] come--o come--bless Lord
--JESUS!
and with these word, the last but half-pronounce, expired:--such a
smile, such a charming serenity overspread her sweet face at the
instant, as seem to manifest her eternal happiness already begin.
o Lovelace!--But I can write no more!
***
I resume my pen to add a few line.
while warm, though pulseless, we press each her hand with our lip;
and then retire into the next room.
we look at each other, with intent to speak: but, as if one motion
govern, as one cause affect both, we turn away silent.
the Colonel sigh as if his heart would burst: at last, his face and
hand uplifted, his back towards I, Good Heaven! say he to himself,
support me!--and be it thus, o flower of nature!--then pausing--and must
we no more--never more!--my bless, bless Cousin! utter some other
word, which his sigh make inarticulate.--And then, as if recollect
himself--forgive I, Sir!--Excuse I, Mr. Belford! and slide by I,
Anon I hope to see you, Sir--and down stair he go, and out of the
house, leave I a statue.
when I recover, I be ready to repine at what I then call an unequal
dispensation; forget her happy preparation, and still happy
departure; and that she have but draw a common lot; triumph in it, and
leave behind she every one less assured of happiness, though equally
certain that the lot would one day be their own.
she depart exactly at forty minute after six o'clock, as by her watch
on the table.
and thus die Miss CLARISSA HARLOWE, in the blossom of her youth and
beauty: and who, her tender year consider, have not leave behind her her
superior in extensive knowledge and watchful prudence; nor hardly she
equal for unblemished virtue, exemplary piety, sweetness of manner,
discreet generosity, and true christian charity: and these all set off by
the most graceful modesty and humility; yet on all proper occasion,
manifest a noble presence of mind, and true magnanimity: so that she
may be say to have be not only an ornament to her sex, but to human
nature.
a well pen than mine may do her full justice. Thine, I mean, O
Lovelace! for well dost thou know how much she excel in the grace of
both mind and person, natural and acquire, all that be woman. and thou
also can well account for the cause of her immature death, through those
calamity which in so short a space of time, from the high pitch of
felicity, (every one in a manner adore she,) bring he to an exit so
happy for herself, but, that it be so early, so much to be deplore by
all who have the honour of her acquaintance.
this task, then, I leave to thee: but now I can write no more, only that
I be a sympathizer in every part of thy distress, except (and yet it be
cruel to say it) in that which arise from thy guilt.
one O'CLOCK, FRIDAY morning.

to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.

SIR,
I take this last and solemn occasion to repeat to you my thank for all
your kindness to I at a time when I most need countenance and
protection.
a few consideration I beg leave, as now at your perusal of this, from
the dead, to press upon you, with all the warmth of a sincere friendship.
by the time you will see this, you will have have an instance, I humbly
trust, of the comfortable importance of a pacified conscience, in the
last hour of one, who, to the last hour, will wish your eternal welfare.
the great Duke of Luxemburgh, as I have hear, on his death-bed,
declare, that he would then much rather have have it to reflect upon,
that he have administer a cup of cold water to a worthy poor creature in
distress, than that he have win so many battle as he have triumph for.
and, as one well observe, all the sentiment of worldly grandeur vanish
at that unavoidable moment which decide the destiny of man.
if then, Sir, at the tremendous hour it be thus with the conqueror of
army, and the subduer of nation, let I in a very few word (many be
not need,) ask, what, at that period, must be the reflection of those,
(if capable of reflection,) who have live a life of sense and offence;
whose study and whose pride most ingloriously have be to seduce the
innocent, and to ruin the weak, the unguarded, and the friendless; make
still more friendless by their base seductions?--O Mr. Belford, weigh,
ponder, and reflect upon it, now that, in health, and in vigour of mind
and body, the reflection will most avail you--what an ungrateful, what
an unmanly, what a mean than reptile pride be this!
in the next place, Sir, let I beg of you, for my sake, who be, or, as
now you will well read it, have be, drive to the necessity of apply

LETTER XVI
to JAMES HARLOWE, JUN. ESQ.
SIR,
there be but one time, but one occasion, after the rash step I be
precipitate upon, that I would hope to be excuse look up to you
in the character of a brother and friend. and now be that time, and
this the occasion. now, at read this, will you pity your late unhappy
sister! now will you forgive her fault, both suppose and real! and
now will you afford to her memory that kind concern which you refuse to
she before!
I write, my Brother, in the first place, to beg your pardon for the
offence my unhappy step give to you, and to the rest of a family so dear
to I.
Virgin purity should not so behave as to be suspect, yet, when you come
to know all my story, you will find farth room for pity, if not more
than pity, for your late unhappy sister!
o that passion have not be deaf! that misconception would have give
way to inquiry! that your rigorous heart, if it could not itself be
soften (moderate the power you have obtain over every one) have
permit other heart more indulgently to expand!
but I write not to give pain. I have rather you should think I faulty
still, than take to yourself the consequence that will follow from
acquit I.
abandon therefore a subject which I have not intend to touch upon,
(for I hope, at the writing of this, I be above the spirit of
recrimination,) let I tell you, Sir, that my next motive for write to
you in this last and most solemn manner be, to beg of you to forego any
active resentment (which may endanger a life so precious to all your
friend) against the man to whose elaborate baseness I owe my worldly
ruin.
for, ought an innocent man to run an equal risque with a guilty one?--
a more than equal risque, as the guilty one have be long inure to act
of violence, and be skilled in the art of offence?
you would not arrogate to yourself God's province, who have say,
Vengeance be mine, and I will repay it. if you would, I tremble for the
consequence: for will it not be suitable to the divine justice to punish
the presumptuous innocent (as you would be in this case) in the very
error, and that by the hand of the self-defend guilty--reserve he
for a future day of vengeance for his accumulate crime?
leave then the poor wretch to the divine justice. let your sister's
fault die with she. at least, let it not be revive in blood. life be a
short stage where long. a little time hence, the now-green head will
be grey, if it live this little time: and if Heaven will afford he time
for repentance, why should not you?
then think, my Brother, what will be the consequence to your dear
parent, if the guilty wretch, who have occasion to they the loss of a
daughter, should likewise deprive they of their good hope, and only son,
more worth in the family account than several daughter?
would you add, my Brother, to those distress which you hold your sister
so inexcusable for have (although from involuntary and undersigned
cause) give?
seek not then, I beseech you, to extend the evil consequence of your
sister's error. his conscience, when it shall please God to touch it,
will be sharp than your sword.
I have still another motive for write to you in this solemn manner: it
be, to entreat you to watch over your passion. the principal fault I
know you to be guilty of be, the violence of your temper when you think
yourself in the right; which you would oftener be, but for that very
violence.
you have several time bring your life into danger by it.
be not the man guilty of a high degree of injustice, who be more apt
to give contradiction, than able to bear it? how often, with you, have
impetuosity bring on abasement? a consequence too natural.
let I then caution you, dear Sir, against a warmth of temper, an
impetuosity when move, and you so ready to be move, that may hurry you
into unforeseen difficulty; and which it be in some measure a sin not
to endeavour to restrain. God enable you to do it for the sake of your
own peace and safety, as well present as future! and for the sake of your
family and friend, who all see your fault, but be tender of speak to
you of it!
as for I, my Brother, my punishment have be seasonable. God give I
grace to make a right use of my suffering. I early repent. I never
love the man half so much as I hat his action, when I see what he be
capable of. I give up my whole heart to a well hope. God bless my
penitence and my reliance upon he. and now I presume to say, I AM
HAPPY.
May Heave preserve you in safety, health, and honour, and long continue
your life for a comfort and stay to your honoured parent! and may you,
in that change of your single state, meet with a wife as agreeable to
every one else as to yourself, and be happy in a hopeful race, and not
have one Clarissa among they, to embitter your comfort when she should
give you most comfort! but may my example be of use to warn the dear
creature whom once I hop to live to see and to cherish, of the evil
with which the deceitful world abound! be the prayer of
your affectionate sister,

LETTER XIX
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
SAT. AFTERNOON, SEPT. 9.
I understand, that thou breath nothing but revenge against I, for
treat thee with so much freedom; and against the cursed woman and her
infernal crew. I be not at all concerned for thy menace against myself.
it be my design to make thee feel. it give I pleasure to find my
intention answer. and I congratulate thee, that thou hast not lose
that sense.
as to the cursed crew, well do they deserve the fire here, that thou
threaten they with, and the fire hereafter, that seem to await they.
but I have this moment receive news which will, in all likelihood, save
thee the guilt of punish the old wretch for her share of wickedness as
thy agent. but if that happen to she which be likely to happen, wilt
thou not tremble for what may befal the principal?
not to keep thee long in suspense; last night, it seem, the infamous
woman get so heartily intoxicate with her beloved liquor, arrack punch,
at the expense of Colonel Salter, that, mistake her way, she fall down
a pair of stair, and break her leg: and now, after a dreadful night, she
lie foam, raving, roar, in a burn fever, that want not any
other fire to scorch she into a feeling more exquisite and durable than
any thy vengeance could give she.
the wretch have request I to come to she; and lest I should refuse a
common messenger, send her vile associate, Sally Martin; who not find
I at Soho, come hither; another part of her business be to procure
the divine lady's pardon for the old creature's wickedness to she.
this devil incarnate, Sally, declare that she never be so shocked in
her life, as when I tell she the lady be dead.
she take out her salt to keep from fainting; and when a little recover
she accuse herself for her part of the injury the lady have sustain;
as she say Polly Horton would do for she's; and shed tear,
declare, that the world never produce such another woman. she call
she the ornament and glory of her sex; acknowledge, that her ruin be
owe more to their instigation, than even (savage as thou art) to thy
own vileness; since thou wert incline to have do her justice more than
once, have they not keep up thy profligate spirit to its height.
this wretch would fain have be admit to a sight of the corpse; but I

she could forgive herself, she say, for every thing but her insult upon
the admirable lady at Rowland's, since all the rest be but in pursuit of
a livelihood, to which she have be reduce, as she boast, from well
expectation, and which hundred follow as well as she. I do not ask

at go away, she tell I, that the old monster's bruise be of more

apprehend, and that the vile wretch have so much compunction of heart,

all these thing I leave upon thy reflection.

to WILLIAM MORDEN, ESQ.
SATURDAY, SEPT. 9.
DEAR COUSIN,

my sister Arabella (but, alas! I have now no other sister) be prepare

be so near her end?--why, as every body say, do he not send sooner?--
or, why at all?

be with her!--ala! Sir, I fear my mother will never get over this shock.
--She have be in hourly fit ever since she receive the fatal news. my
poor father have the gout throw into his stomach; and Heaven know--o
Cousin!--O Sir!--I mean nothing but the honour of the family; yet have I
all the weight throw upon me--[o this curse Lovelace!--may I perish if
he escape the deserved vengeance!]*
* the word thus enclose [] be omit in the transcript to Mr.
Lovelace.
we have begin to please ourselves that we should soon see she here--Good
Heaven! that her next entrance into this house, after she abandon we so
precipitately, should be in a coffin.
we can have nothing to do with her executor, (another strange step of the
dear creature's!)--He cannot expect we will--nor, if he be a gentleman,

will you not, dear Sir, favour we with your presence at this melancholy
time? pray do--and pity and excuse, with the generosity which be natural
to the brave and the wise, what pass at our last meeting. every one's
respect attend you. and I be, Sir,
your inexpressibly afflict cousin and servant,
JA. HARLOWE, JUN.
every thing thatbe fit or reasonable to be perform! [repeat I to the

LETTER XXI
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
SUNDAY MORN. eight O'CLOCK, SEPT. 10.
I staid at Smith's till I see the last of all that be mortal of the
divine lady.
as she have direct ring by her will to several person, with her hair
to be set in crystal, the afflict Mrs. Norton cut off, before the

between four and five in the morning, the corpse be put into the hearse;
the coffin before be fill, as intend, with flower and aromatic
herb, and proper care take to prevent the corpse suffering (to the eye)

Poor Mrs. Norton be extremely ill. I give particular direction to Mrs.

chariot) to take care of she. the Colonel, who rid with his servant

when the hearse move off, and be out of sight, I lock up the lady's

LETTER XXII
MR. MOWBRAY, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
UXBRIDGE, SUNDAY MORN. nine O'CLOCK.
DEAR JACK,
I send you enclose a letter from Mr. Lovelace; which, though write in
the cursed Algebra, I know to be such a one as will show what a queer way
he be in; for he read it to we with the air of a tragedian. you will see
by it what the mad fellow have intend to do, if we have not all of we
interpose. he be actually set out with a surgeon of this place, to
have the lady open and embalmed.--rot I if it be not my full
persuasion that, if he have, her heart would have be find to be either
iron or marble.
we have get Lord M. to he. his Lordship be also much afflict at the
lady's death. his sister and niece, he say, will be ready to break
their heart. what a routbe here about a woman! for after all she be
no more.
we have take a pailful of black bull's blood from he; and this have
lower he a little. but he threaten Col. Morden, he threaten you for
your cursed reflection, [curse reflection indeed, Jack!] and curse
all the world and himself still.
last night his mourning (which be full as deep as for a wife) be bring
home, and his fellow' mourning too. and, though eight o'clock, he would
put it on, and make they attend he in theirs.
every body blame he on this lady's account. but I see not for why.
she be a vixen in her virtue. what a pretty fellow she have ruin--hey,
jack!--and her relation be ten time more to blame than he. I will
prove this to the tooth of they all. if they could use her ill, why
should they expect he to use her well?--you, or I, or Tourville, in his
shoe, would have do as he have do. be not all the girl forewarn?
--'Has he do by she as that caitiff Miles do to the farmer's daughter,
whom he trick up to town, (a pretty girl also, just such another as
Bob.'s Rosebud,) under a notion of wait on a lady?--drille she on,
pretend the lady be abroad. drank her light-hearted--then carry
she to a play--then it be too late, you know, to see the pretend lady
--then to a bagnio--ruin she, as they call it, and all this the same
day. keep she on (an ugly dog, too!) a fortnight or three week, then
leave she to the mercy of the people of the bagnio, (never pay for any
thing,) who stript she of all her clothe, and because she would not take
on, throw she into prison; where she die in want and despair!'--a true
story, thou know, Jack.--This fellow deserve to be d----d. but have
our Bob. be such a villain as this?--and would he not have marry this
flinty-hearted lady?--So he be justify very evidently.
why, then, should such cursed qualm take him?--who would have think he
have be such poor blood? now [rot the puppy!] to see he sit silent in a
corner, when he have tire himself with his mock majesty, and with his
argumentation, (who so fond of argue as he?) and teach his shadow to
make mouth against the wainscot--the devil fetch I if I have patience
with he!
but he have have no rest for these ten day--thatbe the thing!--You must
write to he; and pr'ythee coax he, Jack, and send he what he write
for, and give he all his way--there will be no bear he else. and
get the lady bury as fast as you can; and donot let he know where.
this letter should have go yesterday. we tell he it do. but be in
hope he would have inquire after it again. but he rave as he have not
any answer.
what he vouchsafe to read of other of your letter have give my Lord
such a curiosity as make he desire you to continue your account. pray
do; but not in your hellish Arabic; and we will let the poor fellow only
into what we think fitting for his present way.
I live a cursed dull poking life here. what with I so lately see of poor
Belton, and what I now see of this charming fellow, I shall be as crazy
as he soon, or as dull as thou, Jack; so must seek for well company in
town than either of you. I have be force to read sometimes to divert
I; and you know I hate read. it presently set I into a fit of
drowsiness; and then I yawn and stretch like a devil.
yet in Dryden's Palemon and Arcite have I just now meet with a passage,
that have in it much of our Bob.'s case. these be some of the line.
Mr. Mowbray then recite some line from that poem, describe a
distracted man, and run the parallel; and then, pride himself
in his performance, say:
let I tell you, that have I begin to write as early as you and Lovelace,
I might have cut as good a figure as either of you. why not? but boy or
man I ever hat a book. 'tis folly to lie. I love action, my boy. I
hat droning; and have lead in former day more boy from their book,
than ever my master make to profit by it. Kicking and cuffing, and
orchard-robbing, be my early glory.
but I be tired of writing. I never write such a long letter in my life.
my wrist and my finger and thumb ache d----n----y. the pen be an
hundred weight at least. and my eye be ready to drop out of my head
upon the paper.--The cramp but this minute in my finger. rot the goose
and the goose-quill! I will write no more long letter for a
twelve-month to come. yet one word; we think the mad fellow come to.
Adieu.
LETTER XXIII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
UXBRIDGE, SAT. SEPT. 9.
JACK,
I think it absolutely right that my ever-dear and beloved lady should be
open and embalm. it must be do out of hand this very afternoon.
your acquaintance, Tomkins, and old Anderson of this place, I will bring
with I, shall be the surgeon. I have talk to the latter about it.
I will see every thing do with that decorum which the case, and the
sacred person of my beloved require.
every thing that can be do to preserve the charmer from decay shall
also be do. and when she will descend to her original dust, or cannot
be keep long, I will then have she lay in my family-vault, between my
own father and mother. myself, as I be in my soul, so in person, chief
mourner. but her heart, to which I have such unquestionable pretension,
in which once I have so large a share, and which I will prize above my
own, I will have. I will keep it in spirit. it shall never be out of
my sight. and all the charge of sepulture too shall be mine.
surely nobody will dispute my right to she. whose be she living?--whose
be she dead but mine?--her cursed parent, whose barbarity to she, no
doubt, be the true cause of her death, have long since renounce she.
she leave they for I. she choose I therefore; and I be her husband.
what though I treat she like a villain? do I not pay for it now?
would she not have be mine have I not? nobody will dispute but she
would. and have she not forgive me?--i be then in statu quo prius with
she, be I not? as if I have never offended?--whose then can she be but
mine?
I will free you from your executorship, and all your care.
take notice, Belford, that I do hereby actually discharge you, and every
body, from all care and trouble relate to she. and as to her last
testament, I will execute it myself.
there be no article between we, no settlement; and she be mine, as
you see I have prove to a demonstration; nor could she dispose of
herself but as I pleased.--D----n----n seize I then if I make not good
my right against all opposer!
her bowel, if her friend be very solicitous about they, and very
humble and sorrowful, (and none have they of their own,) shall be send
down to they--to be lay with her ancestor--unless she have order
otherwise. for, except that, she shall not be commit to the unworthy
earth so long as she can be keep out of it, she will shall be perform
in every thing.
I send in the mean time for a lock of her hair.
I charge you stir not in any part of she will but by my express
direction. I will order every thing myself. for be I not her husband?
and, be forgive by she, be I not the choose of her heart? what else
signify her forgiveness?
the two insufferable wretch you have send I plague I to death, and
would treat I like a babe in strings.--D--n the fellow, what end can
they mean by it? yet that crippled monkey Doleman join with they. and,
as I hear they whisper, they have send for Lord M.--to controul I, I
suppose.
what I write to you for be,
1. to forbid you intermeddle with any thing relate to she. to
forbid Morden intermeddling also. if I remember right, he have threaten
I, and curse I, and use I ill--and let he be go from she, if he
would avoid my resentment.
2. to send I a lock of her hair instantly by the bearer.
3. to engage tomkin to have every thing ready for the opening and
embalming. I shall bring Anderson with I.
4. to get her will and every thing ready for my perusal and
consideration.
I will have possession of her dear heart this very night; and let tomkin
provide a proper receptacle and spirit, till I can get a golden one make
for it.
I will take her paper. and, as no one can do her memory justice equal
to myself, and I will not spare myself, who can well show the world
what she be, and what a villain he that could use her ill? and the
world shall also see what implacable and unworthy parent she have.
all shall be set forth in word at length. no mincing of the matter.
name undisguise as well as fact. for, as I shall make the bad
figure in it myself, and have a right to treat myself as nobody else
shall, who shall controul I? who dare call I to account?
let I know, if the d----d mother be yet the subject of the devil's own
vengeance--if the old wretch be dead or alive? some exemplary mischief
I must yet do. my revenge shall sweep away that devil, and all my
opposer of the cruel Harlowe family, from the face of the earth. whole
hecatomb ought to be offer up to the mane of my Clarissa Lovelace.
although her will may in some respect cross mine, yet I expect to be
observe. I will be the interpreter of she's.
next to mine, shebe shall be observe: for she be my wife, and shall be
to all eternity.--i will never have another.
Adieu, Jack, I be prepare to be with you. I charge you, as you value
my life or your own, do not oppose I in any thing relate to my
Clarissa Lovelace.
my temper be entirely alter. I know not what it be to laugh, or smile,
or be pleasant. I be grow choleric and impatient, and will not be
controule.
I write this in character as I use to do, that nobody but you should
know what I write. for never be any man plague with impertinent as
I be.
R. LOVELACE.
in a separate paper enclosed in the ABOVE.
let I tell thee, in character still, that I be in a dreadful way just
now. my brain be all boil like a cauldron over a fiery furnace. what
a devil be the matter with I, I wonder! I never be so strange in my
life.
in truth, Jack, I have be a most execrable villain. and when I
consider all my action to the angel of a woman, and in she the piety,
the charity, the wit, the beauty, I have help to destroy, and the good
to the world I have thereby be a mean of frustrating, I can pronounce
d----n----n upon myself. how then can I expect mercy any where else?
I believe I shall have no patience with you when I see you. your d----d
sting and reflection have almost turn my brain.
but here Lord M. they tell I, be come!--D----n he, and those who send
for he!
I know not what I have write. but her dear heart and a lock of her
hair I will have, let who will be the gainsayer! for be she not mine?
whose else can she be? she have no father nor mother, no sister, no
brother, no relation but I. and my beloved be mine, and I be her's--
and thatbe enough.--but Oh!--
shebe out. the damp of death have quench'd she quite!
those spicy door, her lip, be shut, close lock'd,
which never gale of life shall open more!
and be it so?--is it indeed so?--Good God!--Good god!--but they will not

LETTER XXIV
MR. BELFORD, TO RICHARD MOWBRAY, ESQ.
SUNDAY, SEPT. 10. four in the AFTERNOON.
I have your's, with our unhappy friend's enclosed. I be glad my Lord be
with he. as I presume that his phrensy will be but of short
continuance, I most earnestly wish, that on his recovery he could be
prevail upon to go abroad. Mr. Morden, who be inconsolable, have see
by the will, (as indeed he suspect before he read it,) that the case
be more than a common seduction; and have dropt hint already, that he
look on himself, on that account, as free from his promise make to the
die lady, which be, that he would not seek to avenge her death.
you must make the recovery of his health the motive for urge he on
this head; for, if you hint at his own safety, he will not stir, but
rather seek the Colonel.
as to the lock of hair, you may easily pacify he, (as you once see the
angel,) with hair near the colour, if he be intent upon it.
at my Lord's desire I will write on, and in my common hand; that you may
judge what be, and what be not, fit to be read to Mr. Lovelace at
present. but as I shall not forbear reflection as I go along, in hope
to reach his heart on his recovery, I think it well to direct myself to
he still, and that as if he be not disorder.
as I shall not have leisure to take copy, and yet be willing to have
the whole subject before I, for my own future contemplation, I must
insist upon a return of my letter some time hence. Mr. Lovelace know
that this be one of my condition; and have hitherto comply with it.
Thy letter, Mowbray, be an inimitable performance. thou art a strange
impenetrable creature. but let I most earnestly conjure thee, and the
idle flutterer, Tourville, from what you have see of poor Belton's exit;
from our friend Lovelace's phrensy, and the occasion of it; and from the
terrible condition in which the wretched Sinclair lie; to set about an
immediate change of life and manner. for my own part, I be determine,
be your resolution what they may, to take the advice I give.
as witness,
J. BELFORD.
LETTER XXV
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
O Lovelace! I have a scene to paint in relation to the wretched Sinclair,
that, if I do it justice, will make thee seriously ponder and reflect, or
nothing can. I will lead thee to it in order; and that in my usual hand,
that thy compeer may be able to read it as well as thyself.
when I have write the precede letter, not know what to do with
myself, recollect, and in vain wish for that delightful and
improve conversation, which I have now for ever lose; I think I have as
good begin the task, which I have for some time past resolve to begin;
that be to say, to go to church; and see if I could not reap some benefit
from what I should hear there. accordingly I determine to go to hear
the celebrated preacher at St. James's church. but, as if the devil (for
so I be then ready to conclude) think himself concerned to prevent my
intention, a visit be make I, just as I be dress, which take I off
from my purpose.
from whom should this visit be, but from Sally Martin, accompany by
Mrs. Carter, the sister of the infamous Sinclair! the same, I suppose I
need not tell you, who keep the bagnio near Bloomsbury.
these tell I that the surgeon, apothecary, and physician, have all give
the wretched woman over; but that she say, she should not die, nor be at
rest, till she see I; and they besought I to accompany they in the
coach they come in, if I have one spark of charity, of christian charity,
as they call it, left.
I be very loth to be divert from my purpose by a request so unwelcome,
and from people so abhor; but at last went, and we get thither by ten;
where a scene so shocking present itself to I, that the death of poor
despond Belton be not, I think, to be compare with it.
the old wretch have once put her leg out by her rage and violence, and have
be cry, scold, cursing, ever since the precede evening, that
the surgeon have tell she it be impossible to save she; and that a
mortification have begin to show itself; insomuch that, purely in
compassion to their own ear, they have be force to send for another
surgeon, purposely to tell she, though against his judgment, and (be a
friend of the other) to seem to convince he, that he mistake the case;
and that if she would be patient, she might recover. but, nevertheless,
her apprehension of death, and her antipathy to the thought of dying,
be so strong, that their imposture have not the intended effect, and she
be rave, crying, cursing, and even howl, more like a wolf than a
human creature, when I come; so that as I go up stair, I say, surely
this noise, this howling, cannot be from the unhappy woman! Sally say
it be; and assure I, that it be note to the noise she have make all
night; and step into her room before I, dear Madam Sinclair, say
she, forbear this noise! it be more like that of a bull than a woman!--
here come Mr. Belford; and youwill fright he away if you bellow at this
rate.
there be no less than eight of her cursed daughter surround her bed
when I enter; one of her partner, Polly Horton, at their head; and now
Sally, her other partner, and Madam Carter, as they call she, (for they
be all Madams with one another,) make the number ten; all in shocking
dishabille, and without stay, except Sally, Carter, and Polly; who, not
dare to leave she, have not be in bed all night.
the other seven seem to have be but just up, rise perhaps from their
customer in the fore-house, and their nocturnal orgy, with face,
three or four of they, that have run, the paint lie in streaky seam not
half blowze off, discover coarse wrinkle skin: the hair of some of
they of diver colour, oblige to the black-lead comb where black be
affect; the artificial jet, however, yield apace to the natural
brindle: that of other plaster with oil and powder; the oil
predominating: but every onebe hang about her ear and neck in broken
curl, or ragged end; and each at my entrance take with one motion,
stroke their matted lock with both hand under their coif, mob, or
pinner, every one of which be awry. they be all slip-shoed;
stockingless some; only under-petticoate all; their gown, make to cover
straddling hoop, hang trollopy, and tangle about their heel; but
hastily wrapt round they, as soon as I come up stair. and half of they
(unpadde, shoulder-bent, pallid-lip, limber-joint wretch)
appear, from a bloom nineteen or twenty perhaps over-night, haggard
well-wear strumpet of thirty-eight or forty.
I be the more particular in describe to thee the appearance these
creature make in my eye when I come into the room, because I believe
thou never saw any of they, much less a group of they, thus unprepared
for be see.* I, for my part, never do before; nor have I now, but
upon this occasion, be thus favour. if thou hadst, I believe thou
wouldst hate a profligate woman, as one of Swift's yahoo, or Virgil's
obscene harpy, squirt their ordure upon the Trojan trench; since
the person of such in their retirement be as filthy as their minds.--
hate they as much as I do; and as much as I admire, and next to adore, a
truly virtuous and elegant woman: for to I it be evident, that as a neat
and clean woman must be an angel of a creature, so a sluttish one be the
impure animal in nature. but these be the veteran, the choose band;
for now-and-then flit in to the number of half a dozen or more, by
turn, subordinate sinner, under-graduate, young than some of the
choose phalanx, but not less obscene in their appearance, though indeed
not so much beholden to the plastering focus; yet unpropt by stay,
squalid, loose in attire, sluggish-haired, uner-petticoate only as the
former, eye half-open, wink and pinking, mispatched, yawning,
stretching, as if from the unworn-off effect of the midnight revel; all
arm in succession with supply of cordial (of which every one present
be either taster or partaker) under the direction of the busy Dorcas,
who frequently popt in, to see her slop duly give and take.
* whoever have see Dean Swift's Lady's Dressing room, will think this
description of Mr. Belford's not only more natural, but more decent
painting, as well as well justify by the design, and by the use that
may be make of it.
but when I approach the old wretch, what a spectacle present itself
to my eye!
her misfortune have not at all sink, but rather, as I think, increase
her flesh; rage and violence perhaps swell her muscular feature.
Behold she, then, spread the whole troubled bed with her huge quaggy
carcase: her mill-post arm hold up; her broad hand clench with
violence; her big eye, goggle and flame ready as we may suppose
those of a salamander; her matted griesly hair, make irreverend by her
wickedness (her clouted head-dress being half off, spread about her fat

her broad chin in convulsive motion; her wide mouth, by reason of the
contraction of her forehead (which seem to be half-lose in its own
frightful furrow) split her face, as it be, into two part; and
her huge tongue hideously roll in it; heaving, puff as if four
breath; her bellow-shaped and various-colour breast ascend by
turn to her chin, and descend out of sight, with the violence of her
gasping.
this be the spectacle, as recollection have enable I to describe it,
that this wretch make to my eye, by her suffragan and daughter, who
survey she with scoule fright attention, which one might easily
see have more in it of horror and self-concern (and self-condemnation too)
than of love or pity; as who should say, see! what we ourselves must one
day be!
as soon as she see I, her naturally-big voice, more hoarsened by her
raving, break upon I: o Mr. Belford! o Sir! see what I be come to!--
see what I be bring to!--To have such a cursed crew about I, and not
one of they to take care of I! but to let I tumble down stair so
distant from the room I go from! so distant from the room I mean to go
to!--Cursed, curse be every careless devil!--may this or bad be their
fate every one of they!
and then she curse and swear most vehemently, and the more, as two or
three of they be excuse themselves on the score of their be at
that time as unable to help themselves as she. as soon as she have

to bemoan herself. and here, say she--Heaven grant I patience!
[clench and unclenche her hand] be I to die thus miserably!--of a
break leg in my old age!--snatche away by mean of my own intemperance!
self-do! self-undone!--no time for my affair! no time to repent!--and
in a few hour (oh!--oh!--with another long howl O--h!--U--gh--o! a
kind of scream key terminate it) who know, who can tell where I
shall be?--oh! that indeed I never, never, have have a being!
what could one say to such a wretch as this, whose whole life have be
spend in the most diffusive wickedness, and who no doubt have number of
soul to answer for? yet I tell she, she must be patient: that her
violence make she bad: and that, if she would compose herself, she
might get into a frame more proper for her present circumstance.
who, I? interrupt she: I get into a well frame! I, who can neither
cry, nor pray! yet already feel the torment of the d----d! what mercy
can I expect? what hope be leave for me?--then, that sweet creature! that
incomparable Miss Harlowe! she, it seem, be dead and go! o that
cursed man! have it not be for he! I have never have this, the most
crying of all my sin, to answer for!
and then she set up another howl.
and be she dead?--indeed dead? proceed she, when her howl be over--o
what an angel have I be the mean of destroy! for though it be
that it be mine, and your's, and your's, and your's, devil as we all
be [turn to Sally, to Polly, and to one or two more] that he do not
do her justice! and that, that be my curse, and will one day be your!
and then again she howl.
I still advise patience. I say, that if her time be to be so short
as she apprehend, the more ought she to endeavour to compose herself:
and then she would at least die with more ease to herself--and
satisfaction to her friend, I be go to say--but the word die put she
into a violent raving, and thus she break in upon I. die, do you say,
Sir?--Die!--I will not, I cannot die!--i know not how to die!--die, Sir!
--And must I then die?--leave this world?--i cannot bear it!--And who
bring you hither, Sir?--[her eye strike fire at I] who bring you
hither to tell I I must die, Sir?--I cannot, I will not leave this
world. let other die, who wish for another! who expect a better!--i
have have my plague in this; but would compound for all future hope, so
as I may be nothing after this!
and then she howl and bellow by turn.
by my faith, Lovelace, I tremble in every joint; and look upon she
who speak this, and roar thus, and upon the company round I, I more
than once think myself to be in one of the infernal mansion.
yet will I proceed, and try, for thy good, if I can shock thee but half

how unlike my honest english friend tomkin, a plain serious, intelligent

O, Lovelace! what life do most of we rake and libertine lead! what
company do we keep! and, for such company, what society renounce, or
endeavour to make like these!
what woman, nice in her person, and of purity in her mind and manner,
do she know what miry wallower the generality of man of our class be
in themselves, and constantly trough and sty with, but would detest the
thought of associate with such filthy sensualist, whose favourite
taste carry they to mingle with the dreg of stew, brothel, and
common sewer?
yet, to such a choice be many worthy woman betray, by that false and
inconsiderate notion, raise and propagate, no doubt, by the author of
all delusion, that a reform rake make the good husband. we rake,
indeed, be bold enough to suppose, that woman in general be as much
rake in their heart, as the libertine some of they suffer themselves
to be take with be in their practice. a supposition, therefore, which
it behove person of true honour of that sex to discountenance, by
reject the address of every man, whose character will not stand the
test of that virtue which be the glory of a woman: and indeed, I may
say, of a man too: why should it not?
how, indeed, can it be, if this point be duly weigh, that a man who
think alike of all the sex, and know it to be in the power of a wife
to do he the great dishonour man can receive, and doubt not she will
to do it, if opportunity offer, and importunity be not want: that such
a one, from principle, should be a good husband to any woman? and,
indeed, little do innocent think, what a total revolution of manner,
what a change of fix habit, nay, what a conquest of a bad nature, and
what a portion of Divine GRACE, be require, to make a man a good
husband, a worthy father, and true friend, from principle; especially
when it be consider, that it be not in a man's own power to reform when
he will. this, (to say nothing of my own experience,) thou, Lovelace,
hast find in the progress of thy attempt upon the divine Miss Harlowe.
for whose remorse could be deep, or more frequent, yet more transient
than thine!
now, Lovelace, let I know if the word grace can be read from my pen
without a sneer from thee and thy associate? I own that once it sound
oddly in my ear. but I shall never forget what a grave man once say on
this very word--that with he it be a rake's sibboleth.* he have always
hope of one who could bear the mention of it without ridicule it; and
ever give he up for an abandon man, who make a jest of it, or of he
who use it.
* see Judges xii. 6.
donot be disgust, that I mingle such grave reflection as these with my
narrative. it become I, in my present way of thinking, to do so, when
I see, in Miss Harlowe, how all human excellence, and in poor Belton, how
all inhuman libertinism, and be near see in this abandon woman, how
all diabolical profligacy, end. and glad should I be for your own sake,
for your splendid family's sake, and for the sake of all your intimate
and acquaintance, that you be labour under the same impression,
that so we who have be companion in (and promoter of one another's)
wickedness, might join in a general atonement to the utmost of our power.
I come home reflect upon all these thing, more edify to I than
any sermon I could have hear preach: and I shall conclude this long

be herself, as it be call, what must be her reflection upon her past

business, devil-like, to make other as wicked as herself! what must she
terror be (a hell already begin in her mind!) on look forward to the
dreadful state she be now upon the verge of!--But I drop my trembling
pen.
to have do with so shocking a subject at once, we shall take notice,
that Mr. Belford, in a future letter, write, that the miserable
woman, to the surprise of the operator themselves, (through hourly
increase torture of body and mind,) hold out so long as till
Thursday, Sept. 21; and then die in such agony as terrify into
a transitory penitence all the wretch about she.
LETTER XXVI
colonel MORDEN, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
SUNDAY NIGHT, SEPT. 10.
DEAR SIR,

wonder they could not be present!'
Several express their astonishment, as people do every hour, 'that a
man could live whom such perfection could not engage to be just to she;'
--to be humane I may say. and who, her rank and fortune consider,
could be so disregardful of his own interest, have he have no other motive
to be just!--
the good divine, lead by his text, just touch upon the unhappy step that
be the cause of her untimely fate. he attribute it to the state of
thing below, in which there could not be absolute perfection. he very
politely touch upon the noble disdain she show (though earnestly
solicit by a whole splendid family) to join interest with a man whom
she find unworthy of her esteem and confidence: and who court she with
the utmost earnestness to accept of he.
what he most insist upon be, the happy end she make; and thence draw
consolation to her relation, and instruction to the auditory.
in a word, his performance be such as heighten the reputation which he
have before in a very eminent degree obtain.
when the corpse be to be carry down into the vault, (a very spacious
one, within the church,) there be great crowding to see the coffin-lid,
and the device upon it. particularly two gentleman, muffle up in
cloke, press forward. these, it seem, be Mr. Mullins and Mr.
Wyerley; both of they profess admirer of my dear cousin.
when they come near the coffin, and cast their eye upon the lid, 'in
that little space,' say Mr. Mullins, 'be include all human excellence!'
--And then Mr. Wyerley, unable to contain himself, be force to quit the
church, and we hear be very ill.
it be say that Mr. Solmes be in a remote part of the church, wrap
round in a horseman's coat; and that he shed tear several time. but I
see he not.
another gentleman be there incognito, in a pew near the entrance of the
vault, who have not be take notice of, but for his great emotion when
he look over his pew, at the time the coffin be carry down to its
last place. this be Miss Howe's worthy Mr. Hickman.
my cousin John and Antony and their nephew James choose not to descend
into the vault among their depart ancestor.
Miss Harlowe be extremely affected. her conscience, as well as she
love, be concern on the occasion. she would go down with the corpse
of her dear, her only sister, she say; but her brother would not permit
it. and her overwhelmed eye pursue the coffin till she could see no
more of it; and then she throw herself on the seat, and be near faint
away.
I accompany it down, that I might not only satisfy myself, but you,
Sir, her executor, that it be deposit, as she have direct, at the
foot of her grandfather.
Mr. Melvill come down, contemplate the lid, and shed a few tear over
it. I be so well satisfied with his discourse and behaviour, that I
present he on the solemn spot with a ring of some value; and thank
he for his performance.
and here I leave the remain of my beloved cousin; have bespeak my own
place by the side of her coffin.
on my return to Harlowe-place, I content myself with send my
compliment to the sorrow parent, and retire to my chamber. nor be
I ashame to own, that I could not help give way to a repeat fit of
humanity, as soon as I enter it. I be, Sir,
your most faithful and obedient servant,
WM. MORDEN.
P.S. you will have a letter from my cousin James, who hop to prevail
upon you to relinquish the executorship. it have not my
encouragement.
LETTER XXXI
MR. BELFORD, to WILLIAM MORDEN, ESQ.
SATURDAY, SEPT. 16.
DEAR SIR,
I once have thought to go down privately, in order, disguised, to see the
last solemnity perform. but there be no need to give myself this
melancholy trouble, since your last letter so naturally describe all
that pass, that I have every scene before my eye.
you crowd I, Sir, methink, into the silent slow procession--now with
the sacred bier, do I enter the awful porch; now measure I, with solemn
pace, the venerable aisle; now, ambitious of a relationship to she,
place in a pew near to the eye-attract coffin, do I listen to the
moving eulogy; now, through the buz of gap, eye-swoln crowd, do I
descend into the clammy vault, as a true executor, to see that part of
she will perform with my own eye. there, with a soul fill with
musing, do I number the surround monument of mortality, and
contemplate the present stillness of so many once busy vanity, crowd
all into one poor vaulted nook, as if the live grudge room for the
corpse of those for which, when animate, the earth, the air, and the
water, could hardly find room. then see she place at the foot of
he whose earthly delight she be; and who, as I find, ascribe to the
pleasure she give he the prolongation of his own life;* sigh, and
with avert face, I quit the solemn mansion, the symbolic coffin, and,
for ever, the glory of her sex; and ascend with those, who, in a few
year, after a very short blaze of life, will fill up other space of the
same vault, which now (while they mourn only for she, whom they jointly
persecute) they press with their foot.
* see Vol. I. Letter V.
nor do your affect description permit I here to stop; but, ascend,
I mingle my tear and my praise with those of the numerous spectator.
I accompany the afflict mourner back to their uncomfortable mansion;
and make one in the general concert of unavaile woe; till retire as I
imagine, as they retire, like they, in reality, I give up to new scene
of solitary and sleepless grief; reflect upon the perfection I have
see the end of; and have no relief but from an indignation, which
make I approve of the resentment of other against the unhappy man,
and those equally unhappy relation of she's, to whom the irreparable
loss be owe.
forgive I, Sir, these reflection, and permit I, with this, to send you
what you decline receive till the funeral be over.
[he give he then an account of the money and effect, which he send
he down by this opportunity, for the legatee at Harlowe-place,
and in its neighbourhood; which he desire he to dispose of
accord to the will.
he also send he an account of other step he have take in pursuance of
the will; and desire to know if Mr. Harlowe expect the discharge
of the funeral-expense from the effect in his hand; and the
re-imbursement of the sum advance to the testatrix since her
grandfather's death.]
these expeditious proceeding, say he, will convince Mr. James Harlowe
that I be resolve to see the will completely execute; and yet, by my
manner of do it, that I desire not to give unnecessary mortification
to the family, since every thing that relate to they shall pass through
your hand.

SIR,

will.
we shall all think ourselves extremely oblige to you, if you please to

pleading for our own expectation of this favour from you:
first, because she never would have have the thought of trouble you,

upon themselves.
secondly, I understand that she recommend to you in the will to trust
to the honour of any of our family, for the performance of such of the
article as be of a domestic nature. we be, any of we, and all of we,

all you can desire, as a man of honour, be, that the trust be execute.
we be the more concerned, Sir, to wish you to decline this office,
because of your short and accidental knowledge of the dear testatrix, and
long and intimate acquaintance with the man to whom she owe her ruin,
and we the great loss and disappointment (her manifold excellency
consider) that ever befell a family.
you will allow due weight, I dare say, to this plea, if you make our case
your own; and so much the readier, when I assure you, that your
interfering in this matter, so much against our inclination, (excuse,
Sir, my plain dealing,) will very probably occasion an opposition in some
point, where otherwise there might be none.
what, therefore, I propose be, not that my father should assume this
trust; he be too much afflict to undertake it--nor yet myself--I might
be think too much concerned in interest; but that it might be allow
to devolve upon my two uncle; whose know honour, and whose affection to
the dear deceased, nobody every doubt; and they will treat with you,
Sir, through my cousin Morden, as to the point they will undertake to

the trouble you have already have will well entitle you to the legacy she
bequeath you, together with the re-imbursement of all the charge you
have be at, and allowance of the legacy you have discharge, although
you should not have qualify yourself to act as an executor, as I
presume you have not yet do, nor will now do.
your compliance, Sir, will oblige a family, (who have already distress
enough upon they,) in the circumstance that occasion this application to
you, and more particularly, Sir,
your most humble servant,
JAMES HARLOWE, JUN.

SIR,
you will excuse my plain-deal in turn: for I must observe, that if I

to MY EXECUTOR
'I hope I may be excuse for expatiating, in diver part of this solemn
last act, upon subject of importance. for I have hear of so many
instance of confusion and disagreement in family, and so much doubt
and difficulty, for want of absolute clearness in the testament of
depart person, that I have often conclude, (be there to be no other
reason but those which respect the peace of survive friend,) that
this last act, as to its designation and operation, ought not to be the
last in its composition or making; but should be the result of cool
deliberation, and (as be more frequently than justly say) of a sound
mind and memory; which too seldom be to be meet with but in sound health.
all pretence of insanity of mind be likewise prevent, when a testator
give reason for what he will; all cavil about word be obviate; the
oblige be assure; and they enjoy the benefit for whom the benefit be
intend. hence have I, for some time past, employ myself in pen
down head of such a disposition; which, as reason offer, I have
alter and add to, so that I be never absolutely destitute of a will,
have I be take off ever so suddenly. these minute and imperfect
sketch enable I, as God have graciously give I time and sedateness,
to digest they into the form in which they appear.'
I, CLARISSA HARLOWE, now, by strange melancholy accident, lodge in the
parish of St. Paul, Covent-garden, be of sound and perfect mind and
memory, as I hope these present, draw up by myself, and write with my
own hand, will testify, do, [this second day of September,*] in the year
of our Lord ----,** make and publish this my last will and testament, in
manner and form follow:

day. see Vol. VIII. Letter LI.
** the date of the year be leave blank for particular reason.
in the first place, I desire that my body may lie unburied three day

any account that it be open; and it be my desire, that it shall not be

excellent Miss Clarissa Harlowe will be attend with far bad

be alike; and they perhaps will accompany he.

induce I to press the matter. I think no time should be lose.

paragraph.
