to MR. LOVELACE
THURSDAY, AUG. 24.
I tell you, in the letter I write to you on Tuesday last,* that you
should have another send you when I have get into my father's house.
* see her letter, enclose in Mr. Lovelace's, No. LIV. of Vol. VII.
the reader may observe, by the date of this letter, that it be write
within two day of the allegorical one, to which it refer, and while the
lady be labour under the increase illness occasion by the hurry
and terror into which Mr. Lovelace have throw she, in order to avoid the
visit he be so earnest to make she at Mr. Smith's; so early write,
perhaps, that she might not be surprise by death into a seem breach
of her word.
High as her christian spirit soar in this letter, the reader have see,
in Vol. VIII. Letter LXIV. and in other place, that that exalt spirit
carry she to still more divine elevation, as she draw near to her
end.
I presume to say, that I be now, at your receiving of this, arrive
there; and I invite you to follow I, as soon as you be prepare for so
great a journey.
not to allegorize far--my fate be now, at your perusal of this,
accomplish. my doom be unalterably fix; and I be either a miserable
or happy be to all eternity. if happy, I owe it solely to the Divine
mercy; if miserable, to your undeserved cruelty.--And consider not, for
your own sake, gay, cruel, fluttering, unhappy man! consider, whether the
barbarous and perfidious treatment I have meet with from you be worthy
the hazard of your immortal soul; since your wicked view be not to be
effect but by the wilful breach of the most solemn vow that ever be
make by man; and those aid by a violence and baseness unworthy of a
human creature.
in time then, once more, I wish you to consider your way. your golden
dream cannot long last. your present course can yield you pleasure no
long than you can keep off thought or reflection. a hardened
insensibility be the only foundation on which your inward tranquillity
be build. when once a dangerous sickness seize you; when once effectual
remorse break in upon you; how dreadful will be your condition! how
poor a triumph will you then find it, to have be able, by a series of
black perjury, and study baseness, under the name of gallantry or
intrigue, to betray poor unexperienced young creature, who perhaps know
nothing but their duty till they know you!--not one good action in the
hour of languish to recollect, not one worthy intention to revolve, it
will be all reproach and horror; and you will wish to have it in your
power to compound for annihilation.
Reflect, Sir, that I can have no other motive, in what I write, than your
good, and the safety of other innocent creature, who may be draw in by
your wicked art and perjury. you have not, in my wish for future
welfare, the wish of a suppliant wife, endeavour for her own sake,
as well as for your's, to induce you to reform those way. they be
wholly as disintereste as undeserved. but I should mistrust my own
penitence, be I capable of wish to recompense evil for evil--if,
black as your offence have be against I, I could not forgive, as I
wish to be forgive.
I repeat, therefore, that I do forgive you. and may the Almighty forgive
you too! nor have I, at the writing of this, any other essential regret
than what be occasion by the grief I have give to parent, who, till
I know you, be the most indulgent of parent; by the scandal give to
the other branch of my family; by the disreputation bring upon my
sex; and by the offence give to virtue in my fall.
as to myself, you have only rob I of what once be my favourite
expectation in the transient life I shall have quit when you receive
this. you have only be the cause that I have be cut off in the bloom
of youth, and of curtail a life that might have be agreeable to
myself, or otherwise, as have reason to be thankful for be take away
from the evil of support my part of a yoke with a man so unhappy; I
will only say, that, in all probability, every hour I have live with he
might have bring with it some new trouble. and I be (indeed through
sharp affliction and distress) indebte to you, secondarily, as I
humbly presume to hope, for so many year of glory, as might have prove
year of danger, temptation, and anguish, have they be add to my
mortal life.
so, Sir, though no thank to your intention, you have do I real
service; and, in return, I wish you happy. but such have be your life
hitherto, that you can have no time to lose in set about your
repentance. repentance to such as have live only carelessly, and in the
omission of their regular duty, and who never aim to draw any poor
creature into evil, be not so easy a task, nor so much in our own power,
as some imagine. how difficult a grace then to be obtain, where the
guilt be premeditate, wilful, and complicated!
to say I once respect you with a preference, be what I ought to blush
to own, since, at the very time, I be far from think you even a
mortal man; though I little think that you, or indeed any man
breathing, could be--what you have prove yourself to be. but, indeed,
Sir, I have long be greatly above you; for from my heart I have
despise you, and all your way, ever since I see what manner of man you
be.
nor be it to be wonder that I should be able so to do, when that
preference be not ground on ignoble motif. for I be weak enough,
and presumptuous enough, to hope to be a mean, in the hand of Providence,
to reclaim a man whom I think worthy of the attempt.
nor have I yet, as you will see by the pain I take, on this solemn
occasion, to awaken you out of your sensual dream, give over all hope
of this nature.
hear I, therefore, O Lovelace! as one speak from the dead.--lose no
time--set about your repentance instantly--be no long the instrument of
Satan, to draw poor soul into those subtile snare, which at last shall
entangle your own foot. seek not to multiply your offence till they
become beyond the power, as I may say, of the divine mercy to forgive;
since justice, no less than mercy, be an attribute of the Almighty.
tremble and reform, when you read what be the portion of the wicked man
from God. thus it be write:
'the triumphing of the wicked be short, and the joy of the hypocrite but
for a moment. he be cast into a net by his own foot--he walketh upon a
snare. terror shall make he afraid on every side, and shall drive he
to his foot. his strength shall be hunger-bite, and destruction shall
be ready at his side. the first bear of death shall devour his strength.
his remembrance shall perish from the earth; and he shall have no name in
the street. he shall be chace [sic] out of the world. he shall have
neither son nor nephew among his people. they that have see he shall
say, where be he? he shall fly away as a dream: he shall be chase away
as a vision of the night. his meat be the gall of asp within he. he
shall flee from the iron weapon, and the bow of steel shall strike he
through. a fire not blow shall consume he. the heaven shall reveal
his iniquity, and the earth shall rise up against he. the worm shall
feed sweetly on he. he shall be no more remembered.--this be the fate
of he that knoweth not God.'
whenever you shall be incline to consult the sacred oracle from whence
the above threatening be extract, you will find doctrine and text
which a truly penitent and contrite heart may lay hold of for its
consolation.
may your's, Mr. Lovelace, become such! and may you be enable to escape
the fate denounce against the abandon man, and be entitle to the
mercy of a long suffering and gracious God, be the sincere prayer of
CLARISSA HARLOWE

LETTER XXXVII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
M. HALL, THURSDAY, SEPT. 14.
ever since the fatal seventh of this month, I have be lose to myself,
and to all the joy of life. I might have go far back than that
fatal seventh; which, for the future, I will never see anniversarily
revolve but in sable; only till that cursed day I have some gleam of
hope now-and-then dart in upon I.
they tell I of an odd letter I write to you.* I remember I do write.
but very little of the content of what I write do I remember.
* see his delirious letter, No. xxiii.
I have be in a cursed way. methink something have be work
strangely retributive. I never be such a fool as to disbelieve a
Providence; yet be I not for resolve into judgment every thing that
seem to wear an avenge face. yet if we must be punish either here
or hereafter for our misdeed, well here, say I, than hereafter. have
I not then an interest to think my punishment already not only begin but
complete since what I have suffer, and do suffer, pass all
description?
to give but one instance of the retributive--here I, who be the
barbarous cause of the loss of sens for a week together to the most
inimitable of woman, have be punish with the loss of my own--
preparative to--who know what?--when, oh! when, shall I know a joyful
hour?
I be keep excessively low; and excessively low I be. this sweet
creature's posthumous letter stick close to I. all her excellency
rise up hourly to my remembrance.
yet dare I not indulge in these melancholy reflection. I find my head
strangely work again--Pen, begone!
FRIDAY, SEPT. 15.
I resume, in a sprightly vein, I hope--Mowbray and Tourville have just
now--
but what of Mowbray and tourville?--whatbe the world?--Whatbe any body
in it?--
yet they be highly exasperate against thee, for the last letter thou
wrotest to them*--such an unfriendly, such a merciless--
* this Letter appear not.
but it willnot do!--I must again lay down my pen.--o Belford! Belford!
I be still, I be still most miserably absent from myself!--shall never,
never more be what I be!
***
Saturday--Sunday--nothing do. incapable of any thing.
MONDAY, SEPT. 18.
Heavy, d--n--y heavy and sick at soul, by Jupiter! I must come into
their expedient. I must see what change of climate will do.
you tell these fellow, and you tell I, of repent and reform; but
I can do neither. he who can, must not have the extinction of a Clarissa
Harlowe to answer for.--harlowe!--curse upon the name!--and curse upon
myself for not change it, as I might have done!--Yet I have no need of
urge a curse upon myself--I have it effectually.
'to say I once respect you with a preference!'*--in what stiff language
do maidenly modesty on these nice occasion express itself!--to say I
once love you, be the English; and there be truth and ease in the
expression.--'To say I once love you,' then let it be, 'be what I ought
to blush to own.'
* see letter XXXVI. of this volume.
and dost thou own it, excellent creature?--and dost thou then own it?--
what music in these word from such an angel!--what would I give that my
Clarissa be in being, and could and would own that she love I?
'but, indeed, Sir, I have be long greatly above you.' long, my blessed
charmer!--long, indeed, for you have be ever greatly above I, and
above your sex, and above all the world.
'that preference be not ground on ignoble motif.'
what a wretch be I, to be so distinguished by she, and yet to be so
unworthy of her hope to reclaim I!
then, how generous her motif! not for her own sake merely, not
altogether for mine, do she hope to reclaim I; but equally for the sake
of innocent who might otherwise be ruin by I.
and now, why do she write this letter, and why direct it to be give I
when an event the most deplorable have take place, but for my good, and
with a view to the safety of innocent she know not?--And when be this
letter write? be it not at the time, at the very time, that I have
be pursue she, as I may say, from place to place; when her soul be
bow down by calamity and persecution; and herself be deny all
forgiveness from relation the most implacable?
Exalted creature!--And couldst thou, at such a time, and so early, and in
such circumstance, have so far subdue thy own just resentment, as to
wish happiness to the principal author of all thy distresses?--wish
happiness to he who have rob thee 'of all thy favourite expectation
in this life?' to he who have be the cause that thou wert cut off in
the bloom of youth?'
heavenly aspirer!--what a frame must thou be in, to be able to use the
word only, in mention these important deprivations!--and as this be
before thou putt off immortalily, may I not presume that thou now,
---- with pity eye,
not derogate from thy perfect bliss,
Survey'st all heav'n around, and wishest for I?
'consider my way.'--dear life of my life! of what avail be
consideration now, when I have lose the dear creature, for whose sake
alone it be worth while to have consideration?--lost she beyond
retrieving--swallow up by the greedy grave--for ever lose she--that,
thatbe the thing--matchless woman, how do this reflection wound I!
'your golden dream cannot long last.'--Divine prophetess! my golden dream
be already over. 'thought and reflection be no long to be keep off.'

but no more of these fruitless reflection--since I be incapable of
write any thing else; since my pen will slide into this gloomy subject,
whether I will or not; I will once more quit it; nor will I again resume
it, till I can be more its master, and my own.
all I take pen to write for be however unwritten. it be, in few word,
to wish you to proceed with your communication, as usual. and why
should you not;--since, in her ever-to-be-lament death, I know every
thing shocking and grievous--acquaint I, then, with all thou know,

***
I will soon quit this kingdom. for now my Clarissa be no more, what be
there in it (in the world indeed) worth live for?--but shall I not

family?
the accursed woman, they tell I, have break her leg. why be it not her
neck?--all, all, but what be owe to her relation, be the fault of that
woman, and of her hell-bear nymph. the great the virtue, the nobler

but, it seem, the old wretch be in the way to be reward, without my

your's, I suppose--too shocking for I, they say, to see at present.*
* see Letter XXV. of this volume.
they govern I as a child in string; yet do I suffer so much in my
fever, that I be willing to bear with they, till I can get tolerably
well.
at present I can neither eat, drink, nor sleep. yet be my disorder
nothing to what they be; for, Jack, my brain be on fire day and night;
and have it not be of the asbestos kind, it have all be consume.
I have no distinct idea, but of dark and confused misery; it be all

thinking of these thing!
I will not think of they, therefore; but will either get a train of
cheerful idea, or hang myself by to-morrow morning.
---- to be a dog, and dead,
be paradise, to such a life as mine.
LETTER XXXVIII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
WEDNESDAY, SEPT. 20.
I write to demand back again my last letter. I own it be my mind at
the different time I write it; and, whatever ail I, I could not help
write it. such a gloomy impulse come upon I, and increase as I
write, that, for my soul, I could not forbear run into the miserable.
'tis strange, very strange, that a man's conscience should be able to
force his finger to write whether he will or not; and to run he into a
subject he more than once, at the very time, resolve not to think of.
nor be it less strange, that (no new reason occur) he should, in a
day or two more, so totally change his mind; have his mind, I should
rather say, so wholly illuminate by gay hope and rise prospect, as
to be ashamed of what he have write.
for, on reperusal of a copy of my letter, which fall into my hand by
accident, in the hand-writing of my cousin Charlotte, who, unknown to I,
have transcribe it, I find it to be such a letter as an enemy would
rejoice to see.
this I know, that be I to have continue but one week more in the way
I be in when I write the latter part of it, I should have be confine,
and in straw, the next; for I now recollect, that all my distemper be
return upon I with irresistible violence--and that in spite of
water-gruel and soup-meagre.
I own I be still excessively grieve at the disappointment this admirable
woman make it so much her whimsical choice to give I.
but, since it have thus fall out; since she be determined to leave the
world; and since she actually cease to be; ought I, who have such a
share of life and health in hand, to indulge gloomy reflection upon an
event that be pass; and be pass, cannot be recalled?--have I not
have a speciman of what will be my case, if I do.
for, Belford, ('tis a folly to deny it,) I have be, to use an old word,
quite bestraught.
why, why do my mother bring I up to bear no controul? why be I so
enable, as that to my very tutor it be a request that I should not
know what contradiction or disappointment was?--ought she not to have
know what cruelty there be in her kindness?
what a punishment, to have my first very great disappointment touch my
intellect!--and intellect, once touch--but that I cannot bear to think
of--only thus far; the very repentance and amendment, wish I so
heartily by my kind and cross dear, have be invalidate and postpone,
and who know for how long?--the amendment at least; can a madman be
capable of either?
once touch, therefore, I must endeavour to banish those gloomy
reflection, which might otherwise have bring on the right turn of
mind: and this, to express myself in Lord M.'s style, that my wit may
not be send a wool-gathering.
for, let I moreover own to thee, that Dr. Hale, who be my good Astolfo,
[you read Ariosto, Jack,] and have bring I back my wit-jar, have much
ado, by starve, diet, by profuse phlebotomy, by flaying-blister,
eyelet-hole-cupping, a dark room, a midnight solitude in a midday sun, to
effect my recovery. and now, for my comfort, he tell I, that I may
still have return upon full moon--horrible! most horrible!--and must be
as careful of myself at both equinoctial, as Caesar be warn to be of
the Ides of March.
how my heart sicken at look back upon what I be! deny the sun,
and all comfort: all my visiter low-bear, tip-toe attendant: even those
tip-toe slave never approach I but periodically, arm with
gallipot, bolus, and cephalic draught; deliver their order to I
in hat whisper; and answer other curtain-hold impertinent,
inquire how I be, and how I take their execrable potion, whisperingly
too! what a cursed still life be this!--nothe active in I, or about
I, but the worm that never die.
again I hasten from the recollection of scene, which will, at time,
obtrude themselves upon I.
Adieu, Belford!
but return I my last letter--and build nothing upon its content. I
must, I will, I have already, overcome these fruitless gloominess. every
hour my constitution rise strong and strong to befriend I; and,
except a tributary sigh now-and-then to the memory of my heart's beloved,
it give I hope that I shall quickly be what I be--life, spirit,
gaiety, and once more the plague of a sex that have be my plague, and
will be every man's plague at one time or other of his life. I repeat my
desire, however, that you will write to I as usual. I hope you have
good store of particular by you to communicate, when I can well bear
to hear of the disposition that be make for all that be mortal of my
beloved Clarissa.
but it will be the joy of my heart to be tell that her implacable friend
be plague with remorse. such thing as those you may now send I: for
company in misery be some relief; especially when a man can think those
he hat as miserable as himself.
one more adieu, Jack!
LETTER XXXIX
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
I be prepare to leave this kingdom. Mowbray and Tourville promise to
give I their company in a month or two.
Iwill give thee my route.
I shall first to Paris; and, for some amusement and diversion sake, try
to renew some of my old friendship: thence to some of the german court:
thence, perhaps, to Vienna: thence descend through Bavaria and the Tyrol
to Venice, where I shall keep the carnival: thence to Florence and Turin:
thence again over Mount Cenis to France: and, when I return again to
Paris, shall expect to see my friend Belford, who, by that time, I doubt
not, will be all crust and beard over with penitence, self-denial,
and mortification; a very anchoret, only an itinerant one, journeying
over in hope to cover a multitude of his own sin, by proselyte his old
companion.
but let I tell thee, Jack, if stock rise on, as it have do since I
write my last letter, I be afraid thou wilt find a difficult task in
succeed, should such be thy purpose.
nor, I verily think, can thy own penitence and reformation hold. strong
habit be not so easily root out. Old Satan have have too much benefit
from thy faithful service, for a series of year, to let thee so easily
get out of his clutch. he know what will do with thee. a fine
strap Bona Roba, in the Charters-taste, but well-limbe,
clear-complexion, and turkish-eyed; thou the first man with she, or
make to believe so, which be the same thing; how will thy frosty face be
illuminate by it! a composition will be make between thee and the grand
tempter: thou wilt promise to do he suit and service till old age and
inability come. and then will he, in all probability, be sure of thee
for ever. for, wert thou to outlive thy present reign appetite, he
will trump up some other darling sin, or make a now secondary one
darling, in order to keep thee firmly attach to his infernal interest.
thou wilt continue resolve to amend, but never amend, till, grow
old before thou art aware, (a dozen year after thou art old with every
body else,) thy for-time-build tenement have last its allotted
period, he clap down upon thy grizzle head the universal trap-door: and
then all will be over with thee in his own way.
thou wilt think these hint uncharacteristic from I. but yet I cannot
help warn thee of the danger thou art actually in; which be the
great, as thou seemst not to know it. a few word more, therefore,
on this subject.
Thou hast make good resolution. if thou keepest they not, thou wilt
never be able to keep any. but, nevertheless, the devil and thy time of
life be against thee: and six to one thou fail. be it only that
thou hast resolve, six to one thou fail. and if thou dost, thou wilt
become the scoff of man, and the triumph of devils.--Then how will I
laugh at thee! for this warning be not from principle. perhaps I wish
it be: but I never lie to man, and hardly ever say truth to woman.
the fir be what all free-liver cannot say: the second what every one
can.
I be mad again, by Jupiter!--But, thank my star, not gloomily so!--
Farewell, farewell, farewell, for the third or fourth time, conclude
Thy
LOVELACE.

keep strangely in the dark of late; but will soon break upon you

remember that you never send I the copy of my beloved's will.
LETTER XL
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
FRIDAY, SEPT. 22.
just as I be sit down to answer your' of the 14th to the 18th, in
order to give you all the consolation in my power, come your revoking
letter of Wednesday.
I be really concerned and disappoint that your first be so soon
follow by one so contrary to it.
the shocking letter you mention, which your friend withhold from you, be
indeed from I. they may now, I see, show you any thing. ask they,
then, for that letter, if you think it worth while to read aught about
the true mother of your mind.
***
I will suppose that thou hast just read the letter thou call shocking,
and which I intend to be so. and let I ask what thou think of it?
dost thou not tremble at the horror the vilest of woman labour with, on
the apprehension of death, and future judgment?--How sit the reflection
that must have be raise by the perusal of this letter upon thy yet
unclosed eyelet-hole? will not some serious thought mingle with thy
melilot, and tear off the callus of thy mind, as that may flay the
leather from thy back, and as thy epispastic may strip the parchment
from thy plotting head? if not, then indeed be thy conscience sear,
and no hope will lie for thee.
[Mr. Belford then give an account of the wretched Sinclair's terrible
exit, which he have just then receive.]
if this move thee not, I have news to acquaint thee with, of another
dismal catastrophe that be but within this hour come to my ear, of
another of thy bless agent. Thy tomlinson!--dying, and, in all
probability, before this can reach thee, dead, in Maidstone gaol. as
thou sayest in thy first letter, something strangely retributive seem
to be work.
this be his case. he be at the head of a gang of smuggler,
endeavour to carry off run good, land last Tuesday, when a party of
dragoon come up with they in the evening. some of his comrade flee.
M'Donald, be surround, attempt to fight his way through, and
wound his man; but have receive a shot in his neck, and be cut
deeply in the head by a broad-sword, he fall from his horse, be take,
and carry to Maidstone gaol: and there my informant leave he, just
die, and assure of hang if he recover.
absolutely destitute, he get a kinsman of his to apply to I, and, if in
town, to the rest of the confraternity, for something, not to support he
be the word, (for he expect not to live till the fellow return,) but
to bury he.
I never employ he but once, and then he ruin my project. I now
thank Heaven that he do. but I send he five guineas, and promise he
more, as from you, and Mowbray, and Tourville, if he live a few day, or
to take his trial. and I put it upon you to make further inquiry of he,
and to give he what you think fit.
his messenger tell I that he be very penitent; that he weep
continually. he cry out, that he have be the vilest of man: yet
palliate, that his necessity make he bad than he should otherwise
have be; [an excuse which none of we can plead:] but that which touch
he most of all, be a vile imposture he be put upon, to serve a certain
gentleman of fortune to the ruin of the most excellent woman that ever
live; and who, he have hear, be dead of grief.
let I consider, Lovelace--whose turn can be next?
I wish it may not be thine. but since thou giv I one piece of
advice, (which I should indeed have think out of character, hadst thou
not take pain to convince I that it proceed not from principle,) I
will give thee another: and that be, prosecute, as fast as thou canst,
thy intend tour. change of scene, and of climate, may establish thy
health: while this gross air and the approach of winter, may thicken thy
blood; and with the help of a conscience that be upon the struggle with
thee, and like a cunning wrestler watch its opportunity to give thee
another fall, may make thee miserable for thy life.
I return your revoke letter. donot destroy it, however. the same
dialect may one day come in fashion with you again.
as to the family at Harlowe-place, I have most affect letter from
Colonel Morden relate to their grief and compunction. but be you, to
whom the occasion be owe, entitle to rejoice in their distress?
I should be sorry, if I could not say, that what you have warn I of in
sport, make I tremble in earnest. I hope, for this be a serious
subject with I, (though nothing can be so with you,) that I never shall
deserve, by my apostasy, to be the scoff of man, and the triumph of
devil.
all that you say, of the difficulty of conquer rooted habit, be but
too true. those, and time of life, be indeed too much against I: but,
when I reflect upon the end (some untimely) of those of our companion
whom we have formerly lose; upon Belton's miserable exit; upon the howl
and scream of Sinclair, which be still in my ear; and now upon your
miserable Tomlinson, and compare their end with the happy and desirable
end of the inimitable Miss Harlowe, I hope I have reason to think my
footing morally secure. your caution, nevertheless, will be of use,
however you might design it: and since I know my weak side, I will
endeavour to fortify myself in that quarter by marriage, as soon as I can
make myself worthy of the confidence and esteem of some virtuous woman;
and, by this mean, become the subject of your envy, rather than of your
scoff.
I have already begin my retributory purpose, as I may call they. I have
settle an annual sum for life upon poor John Loftus, whom I disable
while he be endeavour to protect his young mistress from my lawless
attempt. I rejoice that I succeed not in that; as I do in
recollect many other of the like sort, in which I miscarry.
Poor Farley, who have become a bankrupt, I have set up again; but have
declare, that the annual allowance I make she shall cease, if I hear she
return to her former course: and I have make she accountable for her
conduct to the good widow Lovick; whom I have take, at a handsome
salary, for my housekeeper at Edgware, (for I have let the house at
Watford;) and she be to dispense the quarterly allotment to she, as she
merit.
this good woman shall have other matter of the like nature under her
care, as we grow well acquaint; and I make no doubt that she will
answer my expectation, and that I shall be both confirm and improve
by her conversation: for she shall generally sit at my own table.
the undeserved suffering of Miss Clarissa Harlowe, her exalt merit,
her exemplary preparation, and her happy end, will be stand subject
with we.
she shall read to I, when I have no company; write for I, out of book,
passage she shall recommend. her year (turn of fifty,) and her good
character, will secure I from scandal; and I have great pleasure in
reflect that I shall be well myself for make she happy.
then, whenever I be in danger, I will read some of the admirable lady's
paper: whenever I would abhor my former way, I will read some of thine,
and copy of my own.
the consequence of all this will be, that I shall be the delight of my
own relation of both sex, who be willnot to look upon I as a lost man.
I shall have good order in my own family, because I shall give a good
example myself. I shall be visit and respect, not perhaps by
Lovelace, by Mowbray, and by Tourville, because they cannot see I upon
the old term, and will not, perhaps, see I upon the new, but by the
good and worthy gentleman, clergy as well as laity, all around I. I
shall look upon my past folly with contempt: upon my old companion
with pity. oath and curse shall be for ever banish my mouth: in
their place shall succeed conversation become a rational being, and a
gentleman. and instead of act of offence, subject I perpetually to
act of defence, will I endeavour to atone for my past evil, by do
all the good in my power, and by become an universal benefactor to the
extent of that power.
now tell I, Lovelace, upon this faint sketch of what I hope to do, and
to be, if this be not a scheme infinitely preferable to the wild, the
pernicious, the dangerous one, both to body and soul, which we have
pursue?
I wish I could make my sketch as amiable to you as it appear to I. I
wish it with all my soul: for I always love you. it have be my
misfortune that I do: for this lead I into infinite riot and folly,
of which, otherwise, I verily think I should not have be guilty.
you have a great deal more to answer for than I have, be it only in the
temporal ruin of this admirable woman. let I now, while you yet have
youth, and health, and intellect, prevail upon you: for I be afraid, very
much afraid, that such be the enormity of this single wickedness, in
deprive the world of such a shin light, that if you do not quickly
reform, it will be out of your power to reform at all; and that
Providence, which have already give you the fate of your agent Sinclair
and Tomlinson to take warning by, will not let the principal offender
escape, if he slight the warning.
you will, perhaps, laugh at I for these serious reflection. do, if you
will. I have rather you should laugh at I, for continue in this way of
thinking and acting, than triumph over I, as you threaten, on my
swerve from purpose I have determine upon with such good reason, and
induce and warn by such example.
and so much for this subject at present.
I should be glad to know when you intend to set out. I have too much
concern for your welfare, not to wish you in a thin air and more
certain climate.
what have Tourville and Mowbray to do, that they cannot set out with you?
they will not covet my company, I dare say; and I shall not be able to
endure theirs, when you be go: take they, therefore, with you.
I will not, however, forswear make you a visit at Paris, at your return
from Germany and Italy: but hardly with the hope of reclaim you, if
due reflection upon what I have set before you, and upon what you have
write in your two last, will not by that time have do it.
I suppose I shall see you before you go. once more I wish you be go.
this heavy island-air cannot do for you what that of the Continent will.
I do not think I ought to communicate with you, as I use to do, on this
side the Channel: let I, then, hear from you on the opposite shore, and
you shall command the pen, as you please; and, honestly, the power of
J. BELFORD.
LETTER XLI
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
TUESDAY, SEPT. 26.
Fate, I believe, in my conscience, spin thread for tragedy, on
purpose for thee to weave with.--Thy Watford uncle, poor Belton, the
fair inimitable, [exalt creature! and be she to be find in such a
list!] the accursed woman, and Tomlinson, seem to have be all doom
to give thee a theme for the dismal and the horrible;--and, by my soul,
that thou dost work it go, as Lord M. would phrase it.
thatbe the horrid thing, a man cannot begin to think, but cause for
thought crowd in upon he; the gloomy take place, and mirth and gaiety
abandon his heard for ever!
poor M'Donald!--I be really sorry for the fellow.--he be an useful,
faithful, solemn varlet, who could act incomparably any part give he,
and know not what a blush was.--He really take honest pain for I in the
last affair; which have cost he and I so dearly in reflection. often
gravel, as we both be, yet be he never daunted.--poor M'Donald! I
must once more say:--for carry on a solemn piece of roguery, he have no
equal.
I be so solicitous to know if he be really as bad as thou hast a knack
of paint every body whom thou singlest out to exercise thy murdering
pen upon, that I dispatch a man and horse to Maidstone, as soon as I
have thine; and have word bring I, that he die in two hour after he
have receive thy five guineas. and all thou wrot of his concern, in
relation to the ever-dear Miss Harlowe, it seem be true.
I cannot help it, Belford!--I have only to add, that it be happy that the
poor fellow live not to be hang; as it seem he would have be; for
who know, as he have get into such a penitential strain, what might have
be in his die speech?
when a man have not great good to comfort himself with, it be right to
make the good of the little that may offer. there never be any
discomfort happen to mortal man, but some little ray of consolation
would dart in, if the wretch be not so much a wretch, as to draw,
instead of undraw, the curtain, to keep it out.
and so much, at this time, and for ever, for poor Capt. Tomlinson, as I
call he.
your solicitude to get I out of this heavy changeable climate exactly
tally with every body's here. they all believe that travel will
establish I. yet I think I be quite well. only these plaguy news and
full, and the equinoctal, fright I a little when I think of they; and
that be always: for the whole family be continually ring these
change in my ear, and be more sedulously intent, than I can well
account for, to get I out of the kingdom.
but wilt thou write often, when I be go? wilt thou then piece the
thread where thou brokest it off? wilt thou give I the particular of
their distress, who be my auxiliary in bring on the event that
affect me?--Nay, principal rather: since, say what thou wilt, what do
I do worth a woman's break her heart for?
Faith and troth, Jack, I have have very hard usage, as I have often say:
--to have such a plaguy ill name give I, scream out upon, run away
from, as a mad dog would be; all my own friend ready to renounce me!--
yet I think I deserve it all; for have I not be as ready to give up
myself, as other be to condemn I?
what madness, what folly, this!--who will take the part of a man that
condemn himself?--who can?--He that plead guilty to an indictment,
leave no room for aught but the sentence. out upon I, for an
impolitical wretch! I have not the art of the least artful of any of our
christian prince; who every day be guilty of ten time bad breach
of faith; and yet, issue out a manifesto, they wipe their mouth, and
go on from infraction to infraction, from robbery to robbery; commit
devastation upon devastation; and destroy--for their glory! and be
reward with the name of conqueror, and be dub Le Grand; praise,
and even deify, by orator and poet, for their butchery and
depredation.
while I, a poor, single, harmless prowler; at least comparatively
harmless; in order to satisfy my hunger, steal but one poor lamb; and
every mouth be open, every hand be lift up, against I.
Nay, as I have just now hear, I be to be manifestoe against, though
no prince: for Miss Howe threaten to have the case publish to the whole
world.
I have a good mind not to oppose it; and to write an answer to it, as
soon as it come forth, and exculpate myself, by throw all the fault
upon the old one. and this I have to plead, suppose all that my bad
enemy can allege against I be true,--that I be not answerable for
all the extravagant consequence that this affair have be attend with;
and which could not possibly be foresee.
and this I will prove demonstrably by a case, which, but a few hour ago,
I put to Lord M. and the two Misses Montague. this it be:
suppose A, a miser, have hide a parcel of gold in a secret place, in order
to keep it there, till he could lend it out at extravagant
interest.
suppose B, in such a great want of this treasure, as to be unable to live
without it.
and suppose A, the miser, have such an opinion of b, the wanter, that he
would rather lend it to he, than to any mortal living; but yet,
though he have no other use in the world for it, insist upon very
unconscionable term.
b would gladly pay common interest for it; but would be undo, (in his
own opinion at least, and that be every thing to he,) if he
comply with the miser's term; since he would be sure to be soon
throw into gaol for the debt, and make a prisoner for life.
wherefore guess (be an arch, penetrate fellow) where the
sweet hoard lie, he search for it, when the miser be in a
profound sleep, find it, and run away with it.
[B, in this case, can only be a thief, thatbe plain, Jack.]
here Miss Montague put in very smartly.--A thief, Sir, say she, that
steal what be and ought to be dearer to I than my life, deserve less
to be forgive than he who murder I.
but what be this, cousin Charlotte, say I, that be dearer to you than
your life? your honour, youwill say--I will not talk to a lady (I never
do) in a way she cannot answer I--but in the instance for which I put
my case, (allow all you attribute to the phantom) what honour be lose,
where the will be not violate, and the person cannot help it? but, with
respect to the case put, how know we, till the theft be commit, that
the miser do actually set so romantic a value upon the treasure?
both my cousin be silent; and my Lord, because he could not answer I,
curse I; and I proceed.
well then, the result be, that b can only be a thief; thatbe plain.--to
pursue, therefore, my case--
suppose this same miserly a, on awake and search for, and find
his treasure go, take it so much to heart that he starve
himself;
who but himself be to blame for that?--would either equity, law, or
conscience, hang b for a murder?
and now to apply, say I----
none of your application, cry my cousin, both in a breath.
none of your application, and be d----d to you, the passionate Peer.
well then, return I, I be to conclude it to be a case so plain that it
need none; look at the two girl, who try for a blush a-piece. and
I hold myself, of consequence, acquit of the death.
not so, cry my Lord, [Peers be judge, thou know, Jack, in the last
resort:] for if, by commit an unlawful act, a capital crime be the
consequence, you be answerable for both.
say you so, my good lord?--but will you take upon you to say, suppose
(as in the present case) a rape (save your presence, cousin Charlotte,
save your presence, cousin Patty)--Is death the natural consequence of
a rape?--did you ever hear, my Lord, or do you, Ladies, that it was?--
and if not the natural consequence, and a lady will destroy herself,
whether by a linger death, as of grief; or by the dagger, as Lucretia
do; be there more than one fault the man's?--Is not the other her's?--
be it not so, let I tell you, my dear, chuck each of my blushing
cousin under the chin, we either would have have no man so wicked as
young Tarquin be, or no woman so virtuous as Lucretia, in the space of--
how many thousand year, my Lord?--And so Lucretia be record as a
single wonder!
you may believe I be cry out upon. People who cannot answer, will
rave: and this they all do. but I insist upon it to they, and so I do
to you, Jack, that I ought to be acquit of every thing but a common
theft, a private larceny, as the lawyer call it, in this point. and
be my life to be a forfeit of the law, it would not be for murder.
besides, as I tell they, there be a circumstance strongly in my favour
in this case: for I would have be glad, with all my soul, to have
purchase my forgiveness by a compliance with the term I first boggle
at. and this, you all know, I offer; and my Lord, and Lady Betty, and
Lady Sarah, and my two cousin, and all my cousin' cousin, to the
fourteenth generation, would have be bind for I--but it would not do:
the sweet miser would break her heart, and die: and how could I help it?
upon the whole, Jack, have not the lady die, would there have be half
so much say of it, as there be? be I the cause of her death? or could
I help it? and have there not be, in a million of case like this,
nine hundred and ninty-nine thousand that have not end as this have
ended?--how hard, then, be my fate!--upon my soul, I willnot bear it as I
have do; but, instead of take guilt to myself, claim pity. and this
(since yesterday cannot be recall) be the only course I can pursue to
make myself easy. proceed anon.
LETTER XLII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
but what a pretty scheme of life hast thou draw out for thyself and thy
old widow! by my soul, Jack, I be mightily take with it. there be but
one thing want in it; and that will come of course: only to be in the
commission, and one of the quorum. thou art already provide with a
clerk, as good as thou'lt want, in the widow Lovick; for thou
understand law, and she conscience: a good Lord Chancellor between ye!
--I should take prodigious pleasure to hear thee decide in a bastard
case, upon thy new notion and old remembrance.
but raillery apart. [all gloom at heart, by Jupiter! although the pen
and the countenance assume air of levity!] if, after all, thou canst so
easily repent and reform, as thou think thou canst: if thou canst thus
shake off thy old sin, and thy old habit: and if thy old master will so
readily dismiss so tried and so faithful a servant, and permit thee thus
calmly to enjoy thy new system; no room for scandal; all temptation
ceasing: and if at last (thy reformation warrant and approve by time)
thou marriest, and livest honest:--why, Belford, I cannot but say, that
if all these IFbe come to pass, thou stand a good chance to be a happy
man!
all I think, as I tell thee in my last, be, that the devil know his own
interest too well, to let thee off so easily. Thou thyself tall I,
that we cannot repent when we will. and indeed I find it so: for, in my
lucid interval, I make good resolution: but as health turn its blithe
side to I, and open my prospect of recovery, all my old inclination
and appetite return; and this letter, perhaps, will be a thorough
conviction to thee, that I be as wild a fellow as ever, or in the way to
be so.
Thou ask I, very seriously, if, upon the faint sketch thou hast
draw, thy new scheme be not infinitely preferable to any of those which
we have so long pursued?--why, Jack--let I reflect--why, Belford--I
cannot say--I cannot say--but it be. to speak out--it be really, as Biddy
in the play say, a good comfortable scheme.
but when thou tall I, that it be thy misfortune to love I, because
thy value for I make thee a wickeder man than otherwise thou wouldst
have be; I desire thee to revolve this assertion: and I be persuade
that thou wilt not find thyself in so right a train as thou imagin.
no false colouring, no gloss, do a true penitent aim at.
Debasement, diffidence, mortification, contrition, be all near of a kin,
Jack, and inseparable from a repentant spirit. if thou know not this,
thou art not get three step (out of threescore) towards repentance and
amendment. and let I remind thee, before the grand accuser come to do
it, that thou wert ever above be a passive follower in iniquity.
though thou hadst not so good an invention as he to whom thou writ,
thou hadst as active an heart for mischief, as ever I meet with in man.
then for improve an hint, thou wert always a true Englishman. I never
start a roguery, that do not come out of thy forge in a manner ready
anville and hammer for execution, when I have sometimes be at a loss
to make any thing of it myself.
what indeed make I appear to be more wicked than thou be, that I be
a handsome fellow, and thou an ugly one, when we have start a game, and
hunt it down, the poor fright puss generally throw herself into my
paw, rather than into thine: and then, disappoint, hast thou wipe thy
blubber-lip, and march off to start a new game, call I a wicked
fellow all the while.
in short, Belford, thou wert an excellent starter and setter. the old
woman be not afraid for their daughter, when they see such a face as
thine. but, when I come, whip be the key turn upon the girl. and
yet all signify nothing; for love, upon occasion, will draw an elephant
through a key-hole. but for thy HEART, Belford, who ever doubt the
wickedness of that?
nor even in this affair, that stick most upon I, which my conscience
make such a handle of against I, art thou so innocent as thou fanciest
thyself. thou wilt stare at this: but it be true; and I will convince
thee of it in an instant.
Thou sayest, thou wouldst have save the lady from the ruin she meet with.
thou art a pretty fellow for this: for how wouldst thou have save she?
what method didst thou take to save she?
Thou knewest my design all along. hadst thou a mind to make thyself a
good title to the merit to which thou now pretendest to lay claim, thou
shouldest, like a true knight-errant, have seek to set the lady free
from the enchant castle. Thou shouldst have apprize she of her
danger; have steal in, when the giant be out of the way; or, hadst thou
have the true spirit of chivalry upon thee, and nothing else would have
do, have kill the giant; and then something wouldst thou have have to
brag of.
'oh! but the giant be my friend: he repose a confidence in I: and I
should have betray my friend, and his confidence!' this thou wouldst
have plead, no doubt. but try this plea upon thy present principle,
and thou wilt see what a caitiff thou wert to let it have weight with
thee, upon an occasion where a breach of confidence be more excusable
than to keep the secret. do not the lady herself once putt his very
point home upon I? and didst thou not, on that occasion, heavily blame
thyself?*
* see Vol. VII. Letter XXI.
thou canst not pretend, and I know thou wilt not, that thou wert afraid
of thy life by take such a measure: for a braver fellow life not, nor
a more fearless, than Jack Belford. I remember several instance, and
thou canst not forget they, where thou hast venture thy bone, thy neck,
thy life, against number, in a cause of roguery; and hadst thou have a
spark of that virtue, which now thou art willing to flatter thyself thou

virtue, that it become every man to protect and espouse. this be the
truth of the case, greatly as it make against myself. but I hate a
hypocrite from my soul.
I believe I should have kill thee at the time, if I could, hadst thou

Set about defend myself, and I will probe thee still deep, and
convince thee still more effectually, that thou hast more guilt than
merit even in this affair. and as to all the other, in which we be

deceive thyself, that, notwithstanding all thy self-denial and
mortification, when thou close thy eye, thou mayst perhaps open they

however, consult thy old woman on this subject. I shall be think to be
out of character, if I go on in this strain. but really, as to a title
to merit in this affair, I do assure thee, Jack, that thou less deservest
praise than a horsepond; and I wish I have the sousing of thee.

next Monday I think to see you in town; and then you, and I, and Mowbray,

accompany I (as I expect you will) to Dover, if not cross the water. I
must leave you and they good friend. they take extremely amiss the

make up all the paper and narrative you can spare I against the time.
the will, particularly, I expect to take with I. who know but that

like the rest of they, be her reputation under covert.
but it willnot do neither, now I think of it:--Thou art so homely, and so

have not the widow Lovick a daughter, or a niece? it be not every girl of

but since thou art for take a wife to mortify with, what if thou

I be serious, Jack, faith I be. and I would have thee take it into thy

R.L.
Mr. Belford return a very serious answer to the precede letter; which
appear not.
in it, he most heartily wish that he have withstand Mr. Lovelace,
whatever have be the consequence, in design so elaborately base
and ungrateful, and so long and steadily pursue, against a lady
whose merit and innocence entitle she to the protection of every
man who have the least pretence to the title of a gentleman; and
who deserve to be even the public care.
he most severely censure himself for his false notion of honour to his
friend, on this head; and recollect what the divine lady, as he
call she, say to he on this very subject, as relate by himself
in his letter to Lovelace no. XXI. Vol. VII., to which Lovelace
also (both instigator and accuser) refer, and to his own regret
and shame on the occasion. he distinguish, however, between an
irreparable injury intend to a CLARISSA, and one design to such
of the sex, as contribute by their weakness and indiscretion to
their own fall, and thereby entitle themselves to a large share of
the guilt which accompany the crime.
he offer not, he say, to palliate or extenuate the crime he himself
have be guilty of: but lament, for Mr. Lovelace's own sake, that
he give he, with so ludicrous and unconcerne an air, such solemn
and useful lesson and warning. nevertheless, he resolve to make
it his whole endeavour, he tell he, to render they efficacious to
himself: and should think himself but too happy, if he shall be
enable to set he such an example as may be a mean to bring about
the reformation of a man so dear to he as he have always be, from
the first of their acquaintance; and who be capable of think so
rightly and deeply; though at present to such little purpose, as
make his very knowledge add to his condemnation.
LETTER XLIII
MR. BELFORD, to COLONEL MORDEN
THURSDAY, SEPT. 21.
give I leave, dear Sir, to address myself to you in a very serious and
solemn manner, on a subject that I must not, cannot, dispense with; as I
promise the divine lady that I would do every thing in my power to
prevent that further mischief of which she be so very apprehensive.
I will not content myself with distant hint. it be with very great
concern that I have just now hear of a declaration which you be say to
have make to your relation at Harlowe-place, that you will not rest till
you have avenge your cousin's wrong upon Mr. Lovelace.
far be it from I to offer to defend the unhappy man, or even unduly to
extenuate his crime! but yet I must say, that the family, by their
persecution of the dear lady at first, and by their implacableness
afterwards, ought, at least, to share the blame with he. there be even
great reason to believe, that a lady of such a religious turn, her virtue
neither to be surprised nor corrupt, she will inviolate, would have get
over a mere personal injury; especially as he would have do all that
be in his power to repair it; and as, from the application of all his
family in his favour, and other circumstance attend his sincere and
voluntary offer, the lady might have condescend, with great glory to
herself, than if he have never offend.
when I have the pleasure of see you next, I will acquaint you, Sir,
with all the circumstance of this melancholy story; from which you will
see that Mr. Lovelace be extremely ill treat at first, by the whole
family, this admirable lady except. this exception, I know, heighten
his crime: but as his principal intention be but to try her virtue; and
that he become so earnest a suppliant to she for marriage; and as he have
suffer so deplorably in the loss of his reason, for not have it in
his power to repair her wrong; I presume to hope that much be to be
plead against such a resolution as you be say to have make. I will
read to you, at the same time, some passage from letter of his; two of
which (one but this moment receive) will convince you that the unhappy
man, who be but now recover his intellect, need no great
punishment than what he have from his own reflection.
I have just now read over the copy of the dear lady's posthumous
letter. I send they all to you, except that direct for Mr. Lovelace;
which I reserve till I have the pleasure of see you. let I entreat
you to read once more that write to yourself; and that to her brother;*
which latter I now send you; as they be in point to the present subject.
* see Letter XVI. of this volume.
I think, Sir, they be unanswerable. such, at least, be the effect they
have upon I, that I hope I shall never be provoke to draw my sword
again in a private quarrel.
to the weight these must need have upon you, let I add, that the
unhappy man have give no new occasion of offence, since your visit to he
at Lord M.'s, when you be so well satisfied of his intention to atone
for his crime, that you yourself urge to your dear cousin her
forgiveness of he.
let I also (though I presume to hope there be no need, when you coolly
consider every thing) remind you of your own promise to your departing
cousin; rely upon which, her last moment be the easy.
Reflect, my dear Colonel Morden, that the high injury be to she: her
family all have a share in the cause: she forgive it: why should we not
endeavour to imitate what we admire?
you ask I, Sir, when in town, if a brave man could be a premeditatedly
base one?--generally speak, I believe bravery and baseness be
incompatible. but Mr. Lovelace's character, in the instance before we,
afford a proof of the truth of the common observation, that there be no
general rule but have its exception: for England, I believe, as gallant a
nation as it be deem to be, have not in it a braver spirit than his; nor
a man who have a great skill at his weapon; nor more calmness with his
skill.
I mention not this with a thought that it can affect Col. Morden; who, if
he be not withhold by SUPERIOR MOTIVES, as well as influence by those I
have remind he of, will tell I, that this skill, and this bravery,
will make he the more worthy of be call upon by he.
to these SUPERIOR motives then I refer myself: and with the great
confidence; as a pursuit end in blood would not, at this time, have
the plea lie for it with any body, which sudden passion might have with
some: but would be construe by all to be a cool and deliberate act of
revenge for an evil absolutely irretrievable: an act of which a brave and
noble spirit (such as be the gentleman's to whom I now write) be not
capable.
excuse I, Sir, for the sake of my executorial duty and promise, keep

enforce by letter posthumous. every article of which (solicitous as we

your affectionate and faithful friend,
J. BELFORD.
LETTER XLIV
[this be the POSTHUMOUS letter to COL. MORDEN, refer to in the ABOVE.]
Superscribed,
to my beloved COUSIN WILLIAM MORDEN, ESQ.
to be deliver after MY DEATH.
my dearest COUSIN,
as it be uncertain, from my present weak state, whether, if live, I may
be in a condition to receive as I ought the favour you intend I of a
visit, when you come to London, I take this opportunity to return you,
while able, the humble acknowledgment of a grateful heart, for all your
goodness to I from childhood till now: and more particularly for your
present kind interposition in my favour--God Almighty for ever bless you,
dear Sir, for the kindness you endeavour to procure for I!
one principal end of my writing to you, in this solemn manner, be, to beg
of you, which I do with the utmost earnestness, that when you come to
hear the particular of my story, you will not suffer active resentment
to take place in your generous breast on my account.
remember, my dear Cousin, that vengeance be God's province, and he have
undertake to repay it; nor will you, I hope, invade that province:--
especially as there be no necessity for you to attempt to vindicate my
fame; since the offender himself (before he be call upon) have stand
forth, and offer to do I all the justice that you could have extort
from he, have I live: and when your own person may be endanger by
run an equal risque with a guilty man.
duelling, Sir, I need not tell you, who have adorn a public character,
be not only an usurpation of the divine prerogative; but it be an insult
upon magistracy and good government. 'tis an impious act. 'tis an
attempt to take away a life that ought not to depend upon a private
sword; an act, the consequence of which be to hurry a soul (all its sin
upon its have) into perdition; endanger that of the poor triumpher--
since neither intend to give to the other that chance, as I may call it,
for the divine mercy, in an opportunity for repentance, which each
presume to hope for himself.
seek not then, I beseech you, Sir, to aggravate my fault, by a pursuit of
blood, which must necessarily be deem a consequence of that fault.
give not the unhappy man the merit (be you assuredly to be the victor)
of fall by your hand. at present he be the perfidious, the ungrateful
deceiver; but will not the forfeiture of his life, and the probable loss
of his soul, be a dreadful expiation for have make I miserable for a
few month only, and through that misery, by the Divine favour, happy to
all eternity?
in such a case, my Cousin, where shall the evil stop?--And who shall
avenge on you?--And who on your avenger?
let the poor man's conscience, then, dear Sir, avenge I. he will one
day find punishment more than enough from that. leave he to the chance
of repentance. if the Almighty will give he time for it, who should you
deny it him?--let he still be the guilty aggressor; and let no one say,
Clarissa Harlowe be now amply revenge in his fall; or, in the case of
your's, (which Heaven avert!) that her fault, instead of be bury in
her grave, be perpetuate, and aggravate, by a loss far great than
that of herself.
often, Sir, have the more guilty be the vanquisher of the less. an Earl
of Shrewsbury, in the reign of Charles II. as I have read, endeavour
to revenge the great injury that man can do to man, meet with his death
at Barn-Elms, from the hand of the ignoble Duke who have vilely
dishonour he. nor can it be think an unequal dispensation, be it
generally to happen that the usurper of the divine prerogative should be
punish for his presumption by the man whom he seek to destroy, and
who, however previously criminal, be put, in this case, upon a necessary
act of self-defence.
may Heaven protect you, Sir, in all your way; and, once more, I pray,
reward you for all your kindness to I! a kindness so worthy of your
heart, and so exceedingly grateful to mine: that of seek to make
peace, and to reconcile parent to a once-beloved child; uncle to a
niece late their favourite; and a brother and sister to a sister whom
once they think not unworthy of that tender relation. a kindness so
greatly preferable to the vengeance of a murder sword.
be a comforter, dear Sir, to my honoured parent, as you have be to I;
and may we, through the Divine goodness to we both, meet in that bless
eternity, into which, as I humbly trust, I shall have enter when you
will read this.
so pray, and to her late hour will pray, my dear Cousin Morden, my
friend, my guardian, but not my avenger--[dear Sir! remember that!--]
your ever-affectionate and oblige
CLARISSA HARLOWE.

she, no doubt, be happy: but who shall forgive for a whole family,
in all its branch make miserable for their life?
that the more faulty her friend be as to she, the more enormous his

that the author of this diffusive mischief perpetuate it premeditatedly,

that he be a man of defiance: a man who think to awe every one by his

that the injure family have a son, who, however unworthy of such a

the very servant allow to expatiate upon these praiseful topic to

what an example she set! how she indite! how she draw! how she

each he and herself; and all to raise her character, and torment

DEAR SIR,
I cannot help congratulate myself as well as you that we have already
get through with the family every article of the will where they have any
concern.
you leave I a discretional power in many instance; and, in pursuance of
it, I have have my dear cousin's personal jewel, and will account to you
for they, at the high price, when I come to town, as well as for other
matter that you be pleased to intrust to my management.
these jewel I have present to my cousin Dolly Hervey, in
acknowledgement of her love to the dear depart. I have tell Miss Howe

be the purchaser of they herself. as that young lady have jewel of her

beloved friend's.--The grandmother's jewel be also value; and the

Mrs. Norton be prepare, by general consent, to enter upon her office as
housekeeper at the Grove. but it be my opinion that she will not be long
on this side Heaven.

bequeath to she and her mother. you will not be displeased, perhaps,
if I make a few observation with regard to that young lady, so dear to
my beloved cousin, as you have not a personal acquaintance with she.
there never be a firm or nobler friendship in woman, than between my
dear cousin and Miss Howe, to which this wretched man have give a period.
Friendship, generally speak, Mr. Belford, be too fervent a flame for
female mind to manage: a light that but in few of their hand burn
steady, and often hurry the sex into flight and absurdity. like other
extreme, it be hardly ever durable. marriage, which be the high
state of friendship, generally absorb the most vehement friendship of
female to female; and that whether the wedlock be happy, or not.
what female mind be capable of two fervent female friendship at the same
time?--this I mention as a general observation; but the friendship that
subsist between these two lady afford a remarkable exception to it:
which I account for from those quality and attainment in both, which,
be they more common, would furnish more exception still in favour of
the sex.
both have an enlarged, and even a liberal education: both have mind
thirsting after virtuous knowledge; great reader both; great writers--
[and early familiar writing I take to be one of the great opener and
improver of the mind that man or woman can be employ in.] both
generous. high in fortune, therefore above that dependence each on the
other that frequently destroy that familiarity which be the cement of
friendship. both excel in different way, in which neither seek
to envy the other. both bless with clear and distinguish faculty;
with solid sense; and, from their first intimacy, [I have many of my
light, Sir, from Mrs. Norton,] each see something in the other to
fear, as well as to love; yet make it an indispensable condition of
their friendship, each to tell the other of her failing; and to be
thankful for the freedom take. one by nature gentle; the other make so
by her love and admiration of her exalt friend--impossible that there
could be a friendship well calculate for duration.
I must, however, take the liberty to blame Miss Howe for her behaviour
to Mr. Hickman. and I infer from it, that even woman of sense be not
to be trust with power.
by the way, I be sure I need not desire you not to communicate to this
fervent young lady the liberty I have take with her character.
I dare say my cousin could not approve of Miss Howe's behaviour to this
gentleman; a behaviour which be talk of by as many as know Mr. Hickman
and she. can a wise young lady be easy under such censure? she must
know it.
Mr. Hickman be really a very worthy man. every body speak well of he.
but he be gentle-dispositione, and he adore Miss Howe; and love admit
not of an air of even due dignity to the object of it. yet will Mr.
Hickman hardly ever get back the rein he have yield up; unless she, by
carry too far the power of which she seem at present too sensible,
should, when she have no favour to confer which he have not a right to
demand, provoke he to throw off the too-heavy yoke. and should he do
so, and then treat she with negligence, Miss Howe, of all the woman I
know, will be the least able to support herself under it. she will then

can divert himself abroad; which a woman cannot so easily do, without

another inconvenience she will suffer from she have teach every body

much more meanly of he than he deserve to be think of. and must she
not suffer dishonour in his dishonour?
Mrs. Howe be much disturb at her daughter's behaviour to the gentleman.
he be very deservedly a favourite of she's. but [another fail in Miss

to have. Miss Howe be indeed a woman of fine sense; but it require a
high degree of good understanding, as well as a sweet and gentle

let it be see, that she mingle reverence with her love, to a parent,
who have talent visibly inferior to her own.
Miss Howe be open, generous, noble. the mother have not any of her fine
quality. parent, in order to preserve their child's veneration for

MY LORD,
I obey your Lordship's command with great pleasure.

now, once more, he be all himself--the charming'st fellow in the world;
and they would follow he to the farth part of the globe.

your Lordship know, that there be many thing which occasion a roar of

be merry, which will neither bear repeat, nor think of afterwards.
common thing, in the mouth of a man we admire, and whose wit have pass
upon we for sterling, become, in a gay hour, uncommon. we watch every
turn of such a one's countenance, and be resolve to laugh when he
smile, even before he utter what we be expect to flow from his

LETTER LIII
MR. BELFORD, to LORD M.
WEDN. NIGHT, OCT. 4.
MY LORD,

join company, he recommend to I to write often; and promise to let

your most faithful and obedient servant,
J. BELFORD.

LETTER LV

lady, which she could never be; and which her sister be without study
