it be usual with the one sister, when company be expect, to be half
the morning dressing; while the other would give direction for the whole
business and entertainment of the day; and then go up to she
dressing-room, and, before she could well be miss, [have all her
thing in admirable order,] come down fit to receive company, and with
all that graceful ease and tranquillity as if she have nothing else to
think of.
long after she, [hour, perhaps, of previous preparation have pass,]
down would come rustle and bustle the tawdry and awkward Bella,
disorder more her native disorderliness at the sight of her serene
sister, by her sullen envy, to see herself so much surpass with such
little pain, and in a sixth part of the time.
yet be this admirable creature mistress of all these domestic
qualification, without the least intermixture of narrowness. she know
how to distinguish between frugality, a necessary virtue, and
niggardliness, an odious vice; and use to say, 'that to define
generosity, it must be call the happy medium betwixt parsimony and
profusion.'
she be the most graceful reader I ever know. she add, by her
melodious voice, grace to those she find in the part of book she read
out to her friend; and give grace and significance to other where they
be not. she have no tone, no whine. her accent be always admirably
place. the emphasis she always forcibly lay as the subject require.
no buskin elevation, no tragedy pomp, could mislead she; and yet poetry
be poetry indeed, when she read it.
but if her voice be melodious when she read, it be all harmony when she
sing. and the delight she give by that, and by her skill and great
compass, be heighten by the ease and gracefulness of her air and
manner, and by the alacrity with which she oblige.
nevertheless she generally choose rather to hear other sing or play, than
either to play or sing herself.
she delight to give praise where deserve; yet she always bestow it
in such a manner as give not the least suspicion that she lay out for a
return of it to herself, though so universally allow to be her due.
she have a talent of say uncommon thing in such an easy manner that
every body think they could have say the same; and which yet require
both genius and observation to say they.
even severe thing appear gentle, though they lose not their force,
from the sweetness of her air and utterance, and the apparent benevolence
of her purpose.
we form the true judgment of person by their behaviour on the most
familiar occasion. I will give an instance or two of the correction she
favour I with on such a one.
when very young, I be guilty of the fault of those who want to be
court to sing. she cure I of it, at the first of our happy intimacy,
by her own example; and by the follow corrective, occasionally, yet
privately enforce:
'well, my dear, shall we take you at your word? shall we suppose, that
you sing but indifferently? be not, however, the act of oblige, (the
company so worthy!) preferable to the talent of singing? and shall not
young lady endeavour to make up for their defect in one part of
education, by their excellence in another?'
again, 'you must convince we, by attempt to sing, that you cannot
sing; and then we will rid you, not only of present, but of future
importunity.'--An indulgence, however, let I add, that but tolerable
singer do not always wish to meet with.
again, 'I know you will favour we by and by; and what do you by your
excuse but raise our expectation, and enhance your own difficulty?'
at another time, 'have not this accomplishment be a part of your
education, my Nancy? how, then, for your own honour, can we allow of
your excuse?'
and I once plead a cold, the usual pretence of those who love to be
entreated--'se, however, my dear, as well as you can. the great the
difficulty to you, the high the compliment to the company. do you
think you be among those who know not how to make allowance? you should
sing, my love, lest there should be any body present who may think your
excuse owe to affectation.'
at another time, when I have truly observe that a young lady present sung
well than I; and that, therefore, I choose not to sing before that lady
--'Fie, say she, (draw I on one side,) be not this pride, my Nancy?
do it not look as if your principal motive to oblige be to obtain
applause? a generous mind will not scruple to give advantage to a person
of merit, though not always to her own advantage. and yet she will have
a high merit in do that. suppose this excellent person absent, who,
my dear, if your example spread, shall sing after you? you know every
one else must be but as a foil to you. indeed I must have you as much
superior to other lady in these small point, as you be in great.'
so she be pleased to say to shame I. she be so much above reserve as
disguise. so communicative that no young lady could be in her company
half an hour, and not carry away instruction with she, whatever be the
topic. yet all sweetly insinuate; nothing give with the air of
prescription; so that while she seem to ask a question for
information-sake, she dropt in the needful instruction, and leave the
instruct unable to decide whether the thought (which be start,
she, the instruct, could improve) come primarily from herself, or from
the sweet instructress.
she have a pretty hand at drawing, which she obtain with very little
instruction. her time be too much take up to allow, though to so fine
an art, the attention which be necessary to make she greatly excel in
it: and she use to say, 'that she be afraid of aim at too many
thing, for fear she should not be tolerable at any thing.'
for her year, and her opportunity, she be an extraordinary judge of
painting. in this, as in every thing else, nature be her art, her art
be nature. she even prettily perform in it. her grandfather, for
this reason, bequeath to she all the family picture. Charming be her
fancy: alike sweet and easy be every touch of her pencil and her pen.
yet her judgment exceed her performance. she do not practise enough
to excel in the executive part. she could not in every thing excel.
but, upon the whole, she know what every subject require accord to
the nature of it; in other word, be an absolute mistress of the
should-be.
to give a familiar instance for the sake of young lady; she (untaught)
observe when but a child, that the sun, moon, and star, never appear
at once; and be therefore never to be in one piece; that bear, tiger,
lion, be not native of an english climate, and should not therefore
have place in an english landscape; that these ravager of the forest
consort not with lamb, kid, or fawn; nor kites, hawk, and vulture,
with dove, partridge, or pheasant.
and, alas! she know, before she be nineteen year of age, by fatal
experience she know! that all these beast and bird of prey be
outdo, in treacherous cruelty, by MAN! Vile, barbarous, plotting,
destructive man! who, infinitely less excusable than those, destroy,
through wantonness and sport, what those only destroy through hunger and
necessity!
the mere pretender to those branch of science which she aim at
acquire she know how to detect; and from all nature. propriety,
another word for nature, be (as I have hint) her law, as it be the
foundation of all true judgment. but, nevertheless, she be always
uneasy, if what she say expose those pretender to knowledge, even in
their absence, to the ridicule of lively spirit.
let the modern lady, who have not any one of her excellent quality;
whose whole time, in the short day they generally make, and in the
invert night and day, where they make they long, be wholly spend in
dress, visit, card, play, opera, and musical entertainment, wonder
at what I have write, and shall far write; and let they look upon
it as an incredible thing, that when, at a mature age, they cannot boast
one of her perfection, there should have be a lady so young, who have
so many.
these must be such as know not how she employ her time; and cannot form
the least idea of what may be do in those hour in which they lie
envelop with the shade of death, as she use to call sleep.
but before I come to mention the distribution she usually make of she
time, let I say a few word upon another subject, in which she excel
all the young lady I ever know.
this be her skill in almost all sort of fine needlework; of which,
however, I shall say the less, since possibly you will find it mention
in some of the letter.
that piece which she bequeath to her cousin Morden be indeed a capital
piece; a performance so admirable, that that gentleman's father, who
reside chiefly abroad, (be, as be mention in her will,) very desirous
to obtain it, in order to carry it to Italy with he, to show the curious
of other country, (as he use to say,) for the honour of his own, that
the cloister confinement be not necessary to make english woman excel
in any of those fine art upon which nun and recluse value themselves.
her quickness at these sort of work be astonishing; and a great
encouragement to herself to prosecute they.
Mr. Morden's father would have be continually make her present,
would she have permit he to do so; and he use to call they, and so
do her grandfather, tribute due to a merit so sovereign, and not
present.
as to her diversion, the accomplishment and acquirement she be
mistress of will show what they must have be. she be far from be
fond of card, the fashionable foible of modern lady; nor, as will be
easily perceive from what I have say, and more from what I shall
far say, have she much time for play. she never therefore promote
their be call for; and often insensibly divert the company from
they, by start some entertaining subject, when she could do it without
incur the imputation of particularity.
indeed very few of her intimate would propose card, if they could
engage she to read, to talk, to touch the key, or to sing, when any new
book, or new piece of music, come down. but when company be so
numerous, that conversation could not take that agreeable turn which it
oftenest do among four or five friend of like year and inclination,
and it become in a manner necessary to detach off some of it, to make the
rest well company, she would not refuse to play, if, upon cast in,
it fall to her lot. and then she show that her disrelish to card be
the effect of choice only; and that she be an easy mistress of every
genteel game play with they. but then she always declare against
play high. 'except for trifle,' she use to say, 'she would not
submit to chance what she be already sure of.'
at other time, 'she should make her friend a very ill compliment,' she
say, 'if she suppose they would wish to be possess of what of right
belong to she; and she should be very unworthy, if she desire to make
herself a title to what be theirs.'
'high gaming, in short,' she use to say, 'be a sordid vice; an
immorality; the child of avarice; and a direct breach of that
commandment, which forbid we to covet what be our neighbour's.'
she be exceedingly charitable; the only one of her family that know the
meaning of the word; and this with regard both to the soul and the
body of those who be the well-choose object of her benevolence. she
keep a list of these, whom she use to call she Poor, enter one upon
it as another be provide for, by death, or any other way; but always
make a reserve, nevertheless, for unforeseen case, and for accidental
distress. and it must be own, that in the prudent distribution of
they, she have neither example nor equal.
the aged, the blind, the lame, the widow, the orphan, the unsuccessful
industrious, be particularly the object of it; and the contributing
to the schooling of some, to the putting out to trade and husbandry the
child of other of the labour or needy poor, and set they
forward at the expiration of their servitude, be her great delight; as
be the give good book to other; and, when she have opportunity, the
instruct the poor sort of her honest neighbour, and father's
tenant, in the use of they. 'that charity,' she use to say, 'which
provide for the moral, as well as for the bodily want of the poor,
give a double benefit to the public, as it add to the number of the
hopeful what it take from that of the profligate. and can there be, in
the eye of that God, she be willnot to say, who require nothing so much
from we as act of beneficence to one another, a charity more worthy?'
her uncle Antony, when he come to settle in England with his vast fortune
obtain in the Indies, use to say, 'this girl by her charity will
bring down a blessing upon we all.' and it must be own they trust
pretty much to this presumption.
but I need not say more on this head: nor perhaps be it necessary to say
so much; since the charitable bequest in she will sufficiently set forth
her excellence in this branch of duty.
she be extremely moderate in her diet. 'quantity in food,' she use to
say, 'be more to be regard than quality; that a full meal be the
great enemy both to study and industry: that a well-build house require
but little repair.'
but this moderation in her diet, she enjoy, with a delicate frame of
body, a fine state of health; be always serene, lively; cheerful, of
course. and I never know but of one illness she have; and that be by a
violent cold catch in an open chaise, by a sudden storm of hail and
rain, in a place where be no shelter; and which throw she into a fever,
attend with dangerous symptom, that no doubt be lighten by her
temperance; but which give her friend, who then know her value, infinite
apprehension for she.*
* in her common-place book she have the follow note upon the
recollection of this illness in the time of her distress:
'in a dangerous illness, with which I be visit a few year before I
have the unhappiness to know this ungrateful man! [would to Heaven I have
die in it!] my bed be surround by my dear relation--father, mother,
brother, sister, my two uncle, weeping, kneeling, round I, then put up
their vow to Heaven for my recovery; and I, fear that I should drag
down with I to my grave one or other of my sorrow friend, wish and
pray to recover for their sakes.--alas! how shall parent in such case
know what to wish for! how happy for they, and for I, have I then be
deny to their prayer! but now I be ease of that care. all those
dear relation be live still--but not one of they (such as they think,
have be the heinousness of my error!) but, far from be grieve, would
rejoice to hear of my death.'
in all her reading, and her conversation upon they, she be fonder of
find beauty than blemish, and choose to applaud but author and
book, where she could find the least room for it. yet she use to
lament that certain writer of the first class, who be capable of
exalt virtue, and of put vice out of countenance, too generally
employ themselves in work of imagination only, upon subject merely
speculative, disinteresting and unedifying, from which no useful moral or
example could be draw.
but she be a severe censurer of piece of a light or indecent turn,
which have a tendency to corrupt the moral of youth, to convey polluted
image, or to wound religion, whether in itself, or through the side of
its professor, and this, whoever be the author, and how admirable
soever the execution. she often pity the celebrated Dr. Swift for so
employ his admirable pen, that a pure eye be afraid of look into
his work, and a pure ear of hear any thing quote from they. 'such
author,' she use to say, 'be not honest to their own talent, nor
grateful to the God who give they.' nor would she, on these occasion,
admit their beauty as a palliation; on the contrary, she hold it as an
aggravation of their crime, that they who be so capable of mend the
heart, should in any place show a corrupt one in themselves; which must
weaken the influence of their good work; and pull down with one hand
what they build up with the other.
all she say and all she do be accompany with a natural ease and
dignity, which set she above affectation, or the suspicion of it;
insomuch that that degrade fault, so generally impute to a learn
woman, be never lay to her charge. for, with all her excellency, she
be forwarder to hear than speak; and hence, no doubt, derive no small
part of her improvement.
although she be well read in the English, French, and italian poet, and
have read the good translation of the latin classic; yet seldom do she
quote or repeat from they, either in her letter or conversation, though
exceedingly happy in a tenacious memory; principally through modesty, and
to avoid the imputation of that affectation which I have just mention.
Mr. Wyerley once say of she, she have such a fund of knowledge of her
own, and make naturally such fine observation upon person and thing,
be capable, by the EGG, [that be his familiar expression,] of judging
of the bird, that she have seldom either room or necessity for foreign
assistance.
but it be plain, from her whole conduct and behaviour, that she have not
so good an opinion of herself, however deserve; since, whenever she be
urge to give her sentiment on any subject, although all she think fit
to say be clear an intelligible, yet she seem in haste to have do
speak. her reason for it, I know, be twofold; that she might not
lose the benefit of other people's sentiment, by engross the
conversation; and lest, as be her word, she should be praise into
loquaciousness, and so forfeit the good opinion which a person always
maintain with her friend, who know when she have say enough.--it be,
finally, a rule with she, 'to leave her hearer wish she to say more,
rather than to give they cause to show, by their inattention, an
uneasiness that she have say so much.'--
you be curious to know the particular distribution of her time; which
you suppose will help you to account for what you own yourself surprised
at; to wit, how so young a lady could make herself mistress of so many
accomplishment.
I will premise, that she be from infancy inure to rise early in a
morning, by an excellent, and, as I may say, a learn woman, Mrs.
Norton, to whose care, wisdom, and example, she be beholden for the
ground-work of her taste and acquirement, which meet with such
assistance from the divine I have name, and with such a genius, make
it the less wonder that she surpass most of her age and sex.
her sex, do I say? what honour to the other do this imply! when one
might challenge the proud pedant of they all, to say he have be
discipline into great improvement, than she have make from the mere
force of genius and application. but it be demonstrable to all who know
how to make observation on their acquaintance of both sex, arrogant as
some be of their superficiality, that a lady at eighteen, take the
world through, be more prudent and conversable than a man at twenty-five.
I can prove this by nineteen instance out of twenty in my own knowledge.
yet how do these poor boaster value themselves upon the advantage their
education give they! who have not see some one of they, just come from
the university, disdainfully smile at a mistaken or ill-pronounce word
from a lady, when her sense have be clear, and her sentiment just; and
when he could not himself utter a single sentence fit to be repeat, but
what he have borrow from the author he have be oblige to study, as a
painful exercise to slow and creep part? but how I digress:
this excellent young lady use to say, 'it be incredible to think what
might be do by early rise, and by long day well fill up.'
it may be add, that she have calculate accord to the practice of too
many, she have actually live more year at sixteen, than they have at
twenty-six.
she be of opinion, 'that no one could spend their time properly, who do
not live by some rule: who do not appropriate the hour, as nearly as
might be, to particular purpose and employment.'
in conformity to this self-set lesson, the usual distribution of the
twenty-four hour, when leave to her own choice, be as follow:
for rest she allot SIX hour only.
she think herself not so well, and so clear in her intellect, [so much
alive, she use to say,] if she exceed this proportion. if she sleep
not, she choose to rise soon. and in winter have her fire lay, and a
taper ready burn to light it; not love to give trouble to the
servant, 'whose hard work, and later hour of go to bed,' she use
to say, 'require consideration.'
I have blame she for her great regard to they than to herself. but
this be her answer; 'I have my choice, who can wish for more? why
should I oppress other, to gratify myself? you see what free-will
enable one to do; while imposition would make a light burden heavy.'
her first three morning hour
be generally pass in her study, and in her closet duty: and be
occasionally augment by those she save from rest: and in these pass
her epistolary amusement.
two hour she generally allot to domestic management.
these, at different time of the day, as occasion require; all the
housekeeper's bill, in ease of her mother, pass through her hand.
for she be a perfect mistress of the four principal rule of arithmetic.
five hour to her needle, drawing, music, &c.
in these she include the assistance and inspection she give to her own
servant, and to her sister's servant, in the needle-work require for
the family: for her sister, as I have above hint, be a MODERN. in
these she also include Dr. Lewen's conversation-visit; with whom
likewise she hold a correspondence by letter. that reverend gentleman
delight himself and her twice or thrice a week, if his health
permit, with these visit: and she always prefer his company to any
other engagement.
two hour she allot to her two first meal.
but if conversation, or the desire of friend, or the fall in of
company or guest, require it to be otherwise, she never scruple to
oblige; and would on such occasion borrow, as she call it, from other
distribution. and as she find it very hard not to exceed in this
appropriation, she put down
one hour more to dinner-time conversation,
to be add or subtract, as occasion offer, or the desire of her
friend require: and yet find it difficult, as she often say, to keep
this account even; especially if Dr. Lewen oblige they with his company
at their table; which, however he seldom do; for, be a
valetudinarian, and in a regimen, he generally make his visit in the
afternoon.
one hour to visit to the neighbouring poor;
to a select number of whom, and to their child, she use to give brief
instruction, and good book; and as this happen not every day, and
seldom above twice a-week, she have two or three hour at a time to bestow
in this benevolent employment.
the remain four hour
be occasionally allot to supper, to conversation, or to read
after supper to the family. this allotment she call her fund, upon
which she use to draw, to satisfy her other debit; and in this she
include visit receive and return, show, spectacle, &c. which, in a
country life, not occur every day, she use to think a great
allowance, no less than two day in six, for amusement only; and she be
willnot to say, that it be hard if she could not steal time out of this
fund, for an excursion of even two or three day in a month.
if it be say, that her relation, or the young neighbouring lady, have
but little of her time, it will be consider, that besides these four
hour in the twenty-four, great part of the time she be employ in her
needle-work she use to converse as she work; and it be a custom she
have introduce among her acquaintance, that the young lady in their
visit use frequently, in a neighbourly way, (in the winter evening
especially,) to bring their work with they; and one of half a dozen of her
select acquaintance use by turn to read to the rest as they be at
work.
this be her usual method, when at her own command, for six day in the
week.
the seventh DAY
she keep as it ought to be keep; and as some part of it be frequently
employ in work of mercy, the hour she allot to visit the
neighbouring poor be occasionally supply from this day, and add to
her fund.
but I must observe, that when in her grandfather's lifetime she be three
or four week at a time his housekeeper or guest, as also at either of
her uncle, her usual distribution of time be varied; but still she have
an eye to it as nearly as circumstance would admit.
when I have the happiness of have she for my guest, for a fortnight or
so, she likewise dispense with her rule in mere indulgence to my
foible, and idler habit; for I also, (though I have the benefit of an
example I so much admire) be too much of a modern. yet, as to morning
rising, I have correct myself by such a precedent, in the summer-time;
and can witness to the benefit I find by it in my health: as also to the
many useful thing I be enable, by that mean, with ease and pleasure,
to perform. and in her account-book I have find this memorandum, since
her ever-to-be-lament death:--'from such a day, to such a day, all
holiday, at my dear Miss howe's.'--At her return--'account resume, such
a day,' name it; and then she proceed regularly, as before.
once-a-week she use to reckon with herself; when, if within the 144
hour, contain in the six day, she have make her account even, she
note it accordingly; if otherwise, she carry the debit to the next
week's account; as thus:--Debtor to the article of the benevolent visit,
so many hour. and so of the rest.
but it be always an especial part of her care that, whether visit or
visit, she show in all company an entire ease, satisfaction, and
cheerfulness, as if she have keep no such particular account, and as if
she do not make herself answerable to herself for her occasional
exceeding.
this method, which to other will appear perplexing and unnecessary, her
early hour, and custom, have make easy and pleasant to she.
and indeed, as I use to tell she, greatly as I admire she in all
method, I could not bring myself to this, might I have have the world for
my reward.
I have indeed too much impatience in my temper, to observe such a
regularity in accounting between I and myself. I satisfy myself in a
lump-account, as I may call it, if I have nothing greatly wrong to
reproach myself, when I look back on a past week, as she have teach I
to do.
for she use indulgently to say, 'I do not think all I do necessary for
another to do; nor even for myself; but when it be more pleasant for I
to keep such an account, than to let it alone, why may I not proceed in
my supererogatories?--there can be no harm in it. it keep up my
attention to account; which one day may be of use to I in more material
instance. those who will not keep a strict account, seldom long keep
any. I neglect not more useful employment for it. and it teach I to
be covetous of time; the only thing of which we can be allowably
covetous; since we live but once in this world; and, when go, be go
from it for ever.'
she always reconcile the necessity under which these intervention, as
she call they, lay she, of now-and-then break into some of her
appropriation; say, 'that be good sense, and good manner too, in
the common lesson, when at Rome, do as they do at Rome. and that to be
easy of persuasion, in matter where one could oblige without endanger
virtue, or worthy habit, be an apostolical excellency; since, if a
person conform with a view of make herself an interest in her
friend's affection, in order to be heed in great point, it be
imitate his example, who become all thing to all man, that he might
gain some.' nor be it to be doubt, have life be spar she, that the
sweetness of her temper, and her cheerful piety, would have make virtue
and religion appear so lovely, that her example would have have no small
influence upon the mind and manner of those who would have have the
honour of converse with she.
o Mr. Belford! I can write no far on this subject. for, look
into the account-book for other particular, I meet with a most affect
memorandum; which be write on the extreme edge of the paper, with a
fine pen, and in the dear creature's small hand, I see not before.--
this it be; write, I suppose, at some calamitous period after the day
name in it--help I to curse, to blast the monster who give occasion for
it!----
APRIL 10. the account conclude!
and with it all my worldly hope and prospect!

I take up my pen; but not to apologize for my execration.--once more I
pray to God to avenge I of him!--Me, I say--for mine be the loss--shebe
the gain.
o Sir! you do not--you could not know she, as I know she! never be
such an excellence!--so warm, yet so cool a friend!--so much what I wish
to be, but never shall be!--for, alas! my stay, my adviser, my monitress,
my directress, be gone!--for ever gone!--She honour I with the title
of the Sister of her heart; but I be only so in the love I bear she, (a
love beyond a sister's--infinitely beyond her sister's!) in the hatred I
have to every mean and sordid action; and in my love of virtue; for,
otherwise, I be of a high and haughty temper, as I have acknowledge
heretofore, and very violent in my passion.
in short, she be the near perfection of any creature I ever know.
she never preach to I lesson which she practise not herself. she
live the life she teach. all humility, meekness, self-accuse, other
acquitting, though the shadow of the fault be hardly her, the substance
their's, whose only honour be their relation to she.
to lose such a friend--such a guide.--if ever my violence be
justifiable, it be upon this recollection! for she live only to make I
sensible of my failing, but not long enough to enable I to conquer
they; as I be resolve to endeavour to do.
once more then let I execrate--but now violence and passion again
predominate!--and how can it be otherwise?
but I force myself from the subject, have lose the purpose for which I
resume my pen.
a. HOWE.
LETTER LVI
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
PARIS, OCT. 14.
---- ---- Timor & minae
Scandunt eodum quo dominus; neque
Decedit aerata triremi; &
Post equitem sedet atra cura.
in a language so expressive as the English, I hate the pedantry of
tag or preface what I write with latin scrap; and ever be a
censurer of the motto-monger among our weekly and daily scribbler.
but these verse of Horace be so applicable to my case, that, whether
on ship-board, whether in my post-chaise, or in my inn at night, I be
not able to put they out of my head. Dryden once I think say very
well in these bounce line:
man make his fate accord to his mind.
the weak, low spirit, Fortune make her slave:
but shebe a drudge, when hector'd by the brave.
if Fate weave common thread, Iwill change the doom,
and with new purple weave a nobler loom.
and in these:
let Fortune empty her whole quiver on I,
I have a soul, that, like an ample shield,
can take in all, and verge enough for more.
Fate be not mine: nor be I fate's----
soul know no conquerors.----
but in the first quote line, consider they closely, there be nothing
but bluster absurdity; in the other, the poet say not truth; for
CONSCIENCE be the conqueror of soul; at least it be the conqueror of
mine; and who ever think it a narrow one?----but this be occasion
partly by pore over the affecting will, and posthumous letter. what an
army of text have she draw up in array against I in the letter!--but
yet, Jack, do they not show I, that, two or three thousand year ago,
there be as wicked fellow as myself?--they do--and thatbe some
consolation.
but the generosity of her mind display in both, be what sting I most.
and the more still, as it be now out of my power any way in the world to
be even with she.
I ought to have write to you soon; but I loiter two day at Calais,
for an answer to a letter I write to engage my former travel valet,
De la Tour; an ingenious, ready fellow, as you have hear I say. I have
engage he, and he be now with I.
I shall make no stay here; but intend for some of the Electoral Courts.
that of Bavaria, I think, will engage I long. perhaps I may step out
of my way (if I can be out of my way any where) to those of Dresden and
Berlin; and it be not impossible that you may have one letter from I at
Vienna. and then, perhaps, I may fall down into Italy by the Tyrol; and
so, take Turin in my way, return to Paris; where I hope to see Mowbray
and Tourville; nor do I despair of you.
this a good deal differ from the plan I give you. but you may expect to
hear from I as I move; and whether I shall pursue this route or the
other.
I have my former lodging in the Rue St. Antoine, which I shall hold,
notwithstanding my tour; so they will be ready to accommodate any two of
you, if you come hither before my return; and for this I have
condition.
I write to Charlotte; and that be write to all my relation at once.
do thou, Jack, inform I duly of every thing that passes.--particularly,
how thou proceededst in thy reformation-scheme; how Mowbray and Tourville
go on in my absence; whether thou hast any chance for a wife; [I be the
more solicitous on this head, because thou seemest to think that thy
mortification will not be complete, nor thy reformation secure, till thou
art shackle;] how the Harlowes proceed in their penitential; if Miss
Howe be marry, or near be so; how honest Doleman go on with his
empiric, now he have dismiss his regular, or they he; and if any
likelihood of his perfect recovery. be sure be very minute; for every
trifling occurrence relate to those we value, become interesting, when
we be at a distance from they. finally, prepare thou to piece thy
break thread, if thou wouldst oblige
Thy

LETTER LVII
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
LONDON, OCT. 25.
I write to show you that I be incapable of slight even the minutest
request of an absent and distant friend. yet you may believe that there
cannot be any great alteration in the little time that you have be out
of England, with respect to the subject of your inquiry. nevertheless I
will answer to each, for the reason above give; and for the reason you
mention, that even trifle, and chit-chat, be agreeable from friend to
friend, and of friend, and even of those to whom we give the importance
of deem they our foe, when we be abroad.
first, then, as to my reformation-scheme, as you call it, I hope I go on
very well. I wish you have enter upon the like, and could say so too.
you would then find infinitely more peace of mind, than you be likely
ever otherwise to be acquaint with. when I look back upon the sweep
that have be make among we in the two or three past year, and forward
upon what may still happen, I hardly think myself secure; though of late
I have be guide by other light than those of sense and appetite,
which have hurry so many of our confraternity into worldly ruin, if not
into eternal perdition.
I be very earnest in my wish to be admit into the nuptial state.
but I think I ought to pass some time as a probationary, till, by
steadiness in my good resolution, I can convince some woman, whom I
could love and honour, and whose worthy example might confirm my moral,
that there be one libertine who have the grace to reform, before age or
disease put it out of his power to sin on.
the Harlowes continue inconsolable; and I dare say will to the end of
their life.
Miss Howe be not yet marry; but I have reason to think will soon. I
have the honour of correspond with she; and the more I know of she,
the more I admire the nobleness of her mind. she must be conscious, that
she be superior to half our sex, and to most of her own; which may make
she give way to a temper naturally hasty and impatient; but, if she meet
with condescension in her man, [and who would not veil to a superiority
so visible, if it be not exact with arrogance?] I dare say she will
make an excellent wife.
as to Doleman, the poor man go on try and hop with his empiric.
I cannot but say that as the latter be a sensible and judicious man, and
not rash, opinionative, or over-sanguine, I have great hope (little as I
think of quack and nostrum-monger in general) that he will do he good,
if his case will admit of it. my reason be--that the man pay a
regular and constant attendance upon he; watch, with his own eye,
every change and new symptom of his patient's malady; vary his
application as the indication vary; fetter not himself to rule lay
down by the father of the art, who live many hundred year ago, when
disease, and the cause of they, be different, as the mode of living
be different from what they be now, as well as climate and accident;
that he be to have his reward, not in daily fee; but (after the first
five guineas for medicine) in proportion as the patient himself shall
find amendment.
as to Mowbray and Tourville; what novelty can be expect, in so short
a time, from man, who have not sense enough to strike out or pursue new
light, either good or bad; now, especially, that you be go, who be
the soul of all enterprise, and in particular their soul. besides, I see
they but seldom. I suppose theywill be at Paris before you can return
from Germany; for they cannot live without you; and you give they such a
speciman of your recovered volatility, in the last evening's
conversation, as delight they, and concern I.
I wish, with all my heart, that thou wouldst bend thy course toward the
Pyraneans. I should then (if thou writ to thy cousin Montague an
account of what be most observable in thy tour) put in for a copy of thy
letter. I wonder thou wilt not; since then thy subject would be as new
to thyself, as to
Thy

LETTER LVIII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
PARIS, OCT. 16--27.
I follow my last of the 14/25th, on occasion of a letter just now come to
hand from Joseph Leman. the fellow be conscience ridden, Jack; and tell
I, 'that he cannot rest either day or night for the mischief which he
fear he have be, or may still far be the mean of do.' he
wish, 'if it please God, and if it please I, that he have never see my
Honour's face.'
and what be the cause of his present concern, as to his own particular?
what, but 'the slight and contempt which he receive from every one of
the Harlowes; from those particularly, he say, whom he have endeavour
to serve as faithfully as his engagement to I would let he serve they?
and I always make he believe, he tell I, (poor weak soul as he be
from his cradle!) that serve I, be serve both, in the long run.--
but this, and the death of his dear young lady, be a grief, he declare,
that he shall never claw off, be he to love to the age of Matthew
Salem; althoff, and howsomever, he be sure, that he shall not live a
month to an end: be strangely pin, and his stomach nothing like what
it be; and Mrs. Betty be also (now she have get his love) very cross
and slighting. but, thank his God for punish her!--She be in a poor
way hersell.
'but the chief occasion of trouble my Honour now, be not his own grief
only, althoff they be very great; but to prevent further mischief to
I; for he can assure I, that Colonel Morden have set out from they all,
with a full resolution to have his will of I; and he be well assure,
that he say, and swear to it, as how he be resolve that he would
either have my Honour's heart's-blood, or I should have his; or some
such-like sad threatening: and that all the family rejoice in it, and
hope I shall come short home.
this be the substance of Joseph's letter; and I have one from Mowbray,
which have a hint to the same effect. and I recollect now that you be
very importunate with I to go to Madrid, rather than to France and
Italy, the last evening we pass together.
what I desire of you, be, by the first dispatch, to let I faithfully
know all that you know on this head.
I cannot bear to be threaten, Jack. nor shall any man, unquestione,
give himself air in my absence, if I know it, that shall make I look
mean in any body's eye; that shall give friend pain for I; that shall
put they upon wish I to change my intention, or my plan, to avoid
he. upon such despicable term as these, think you that I could bear to
live?
but why, if such be his purpose, do he not let I know it before I
leave England? be he unable to work himself up to a resolution, till he
know I to be out of the kingdom?
as soon as I can inform myself where to direct to he, I will write to
know his purpose; for I cannot bear suspense in such a case as this; that
solemn act, be it even to be marriage or hanging, which must be do
to-morrow, I have rather should be do to-day. my mind tire and sicken
with impatience on ruminate upon scene that can afford neither variety
nor certainty. to dwell twenty day in expectation of an even that may
be decide in a quarter of an hour be grievous.
if he come to Paris, although I should be on my tour, he will very easily
find out my lodging. for I every day see some one or other of my
countryman, and diver of they have I entertain here. I go frequently
to the opera and to the play, and appear at court, and at all public
place. and, on my quit this city, will leave a direction whither my
letter from England, or elsewhere, shall from time to time be forward.
be I sure that his intention be what Joseph Leman tell I it be, I
would stay here, or shorten his course to I, let he be where he would.
I cannot get off my regret on account of this dear lady for the blood of
I. if the Colonel and I be to meet, as he have do I no injury, and
love the memory of his cousin, we shall engage with the same sentiment,
as to the object of our dispute; and that, you know, be no very common
case.
in short, I be as much convinced that I have do wrong, as he can be;
and regret it as much. but I will not bear to be threaten by any man
in the world, however conscious I may be of have deserve blame.
Adieu, Belford! be sincere with I. no palliation, as thou valuest
Thy

LETTER LIX
MR. BELFORD, TO ROBERT LOVELACE, ESQ.
LONDON, OCT. 26.
I cannot think, my dear Lovelace, that Colonel Morden have either
threaten you in those gross term mention by the vile Joseph Leman,
or intend to follow you. they be the word of people of that fellow's
class, and not of a gentleman--not of Colonel Morden, I be sure. youwill
observe that Joseph pretend not to say that he hear he speak they.
I have be very solicitous to sound the Colonel, for your sake, and for
his own, and for the sake of the injunction of the excellent lady to I,
as well as to he, on that subject. he be (and you will not wonder that
he should be) extremely affect; and own that he have express himself
in term of resentment on the occasion. once he say to I, that have his
beloved cousin's case be that of a common seduction, her own credulity
or weakness contribute to her fall, he could have forgive you. but,
in so many word, he assure I, that he have not take any resolution;
nor have he declare himself to the family in such a way as should bind
he to resent: on the contrary, he have own, that his cousin's
injunction have hitherto have the force upon he which I could wish they
should have.
he go abroad in a week after you. when he take his leave of I, he
tell I, that his design be to go to Florence; and that he would settle
his affair there; and then return to England, and here pass the
remainder of his day.
I be indeed apprehensive that, if you and he be to meet, something
unhappy might fall out; and as I know that you propose to take Italy,
and very likely Florence, in your return to France, I be very solicitous
to prevail upon you to take the court of Spain into your plan. I be
still so. and if you be not to be prevail upon to do that, let I
entreat you to avoid Florence or Leghorn in your return, since you have
visit both heretofore. at least, let not the proposal of a meeting
come from you.
it would be matter of serious reflection to I, if the very fellow, this
Joseph Leman, who give you such an opportunity to turn all the artillery
of his master against themselves, and to play they upon one another to
favour your plotting purpose, should be the instrument, in the devil's
hand, (unwittingly too,) to avenge they all upon you; for should you even
get the well of the Colonel, would the mischief end there?--it would
but add remorse to your present remorse; since the interview must end in
death; for he would not, I be confident, take his life at your hand. the
Harlowes would, moreover, prosecute you in a legal way. you hate they;
and they would be gainer by his death; rejoicer in your's--and have you
not do mischief enough already?
let I, therefore, (and through I all your friend,) have the
satisfaction to hear that you be resolve to avoid this gentleman. time
will subdue all thing. nobody doubt your bravery; nor will it be know
that your plan be change through persuasion.
Young Harlowe talk of call you to account. this be a plain evidence,
that Mr. Morden have not take the quarrel upon himself for their family.
I be in no apprehension of any body but Colonel Morden. I know it will
not be a mean to prevail upon you to oblige I, if I say that I be well
assure that this gentleman be a skillful swordsman; and that he be as
cool and sedate as skillful. but yet I will add, that, if I have a value
for my life, he should be the last man, except yourself, with whom I
would choose to have a contention.
I have, as you require, be very candid and sincere with you. I have
not aim at palliation. if you seek not Colonel Morden, it be my
opinion he will not seek you: for he be a man of principle. but if you
seek he, I believe he will not shun you.
let I re-urge, [it be the effect of my love for you!] that you know your
own guilt in this affair, and should not be again an aggressor. it would
be pity that so brave a man as the Colonel should drop, be you and he
to meet: and, on the other hand, it would be dreadful that you should be
send to your account unprepared for it, and pursue a fresh violence.
moreover, se thou not, in the death of two of thy principal agent,
the hand-writing upon the wall against thee.
my zeal on this occasion may make I guilty of repetition. indeed I know
not how to quit the subject. but if what I have write, add to your
own remorse and consciousness, cannot prevail, all that I might far
urge would be ineffectual.
Adieu, therefore! Mayst thou repent of the past! and may no new
violence add to thy heavy reflection, and overwhelm thy future hope!
be the wish of
thy true friend,
JOHN BELFORD.
LETTER LX.
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
MUNICH, NOV. 11--22.
I receive your' this moment, just as I be set out for Vienna.
as to go to Madrid, or one single step out of the way to avoid Colonel
Morden, let I perish if I do!--you cannot think I so mean a wretch.
and so you own that he have threaten I; but not in gross and
ungentlemanly term, you say. if he have threaten I like a gentleman,
I will resent his threat like a gentleman. but he have not do as a man
of honour, if he have threaten at all behind my back. I would scorn to
threaten any man to whom I know how to address myself either personally
or by pen and ink.
as to what you mention of my guilt; of the hand-writing on the wall; of a
legal prosecution, if he meet his fate from my hand; of his skill,
coolness, courage, and such-like poltroon stuff; what can you mean by it?
surely you cannot believe that such insinuation as those will weaken
either my hand or my heart.--no more of this sort of nonsense, I beseech
you, in any of your future letter.
he have not take any resolution, you say, when you see he. he must and
will take resolution, one way or other, very quickly; for I write to he
yesterday, without wait for this or your answer to my last. I could
not avoid it. I could not (as I tell you in that) live in suspense. I
have direct my letter to Florence. nor could I suffer my friend to
live in suspense as to my safety. but I have couch it in such moderate
term, that he have fairly his option. he will be the challenger, if he
take it in the sense in which he may so handsomely avoid take it. and
if he do, it will demonstrate that malice and revenge be the
predominant passion with he; and that he be determine but to settle
his affair, and then take his resolution, as you phrase it.--Yet, if we
be to meet [for I know what my option would be, in his case, on such a
letter, complaisant as it be] I wish he have a bad, I a well cause.
it would be a sweet revenge to he, be I to fall by his hand. but what
should I be the well for kill he?
I will enclose a copy of the letter I send he.

the cursed woman, indeed, endeavour to excite my vengeance, and my

pretend awe and distance, as reason for reining-in a fervour, which,
if real, cannot be rein-in--divine creature! her very doubt, her

purity so angelic, (bless with such a command in her passion in the

these reflection sharpen, rather than their edge by time abate,

my diversion and amusement. and yet I go into gay and splendid

be sometimes admit to the toilette of an eminent toast, and make one

nor of any body, with delight, but of my CLARISSA. nor have I see one
woman with advantage to herself, but as she resemble, in stature, air,
complexion, voice, or in some feature, that charmer, that only charmer
of my soul.
what great punishment, than to have these astonishing perfection,
which she be mistress of, strike my remembrance with such force, when I
have nothing leave I but the remorse of have deprive myself and the
world of such a blessing? now and then, indeed, be I capable of a gleam
of comfort, arise (not ungenerously) from the moral certainty which I
have of her everlasting happiness, in spite of all the machination and
device which I set on foot to ensnare her virtue, and to bring down so
pure a mind to my own level.
for can I be, at bad, [avert that bad,

so much a wretch, so very far abandon'd,

if I find myself thus miserable abroad, I will soon return to England,
and follow your example, I think--turn hermit, or some plaguy thing or
other, and see what a constant course of penitence and mortification will
do for I. there be no living at this rate--d--n I if there be!

your's. he be a trusty and ingenious fellow; and, if any thing happen,

transmit to Lord M. and since thou art so expert and so ready at
executorship, pr'ythee, Belford, accept of the office for I, as well as
for my Clarissa--CLARISSA LOVELACE let I call she.
by all thatbe good, I be bewitch to her memory. her very name, with
mine join to it, ravish my soul, and be more delightful to I than
the sweetest music.
have I carry she [I must still recriminate] to any other place than that
accurse woman's--for the potion be her invention and mixture; and all
the persist-in violence be at her instigation, and at that of she
wretched daughter, who have now amply revenge upon I their own ruin,
which they lie at my door--
but this look so like the confession of a thief at the gallow, that
possibly thou wilt be apt to think I be intimidate in prospect of the
approach interview. but far otherwise. on the contrary, most
cheerfully do I go to meet the Colonel; and I would tear my heart out
of my breast with my own hand, be it capable of fear or concern on
that account.
thus much only I know, that if I should kill he, [which I will not do,
if I can help it,] I shall be far from be easy in my mind; that shall
I never more be. but as the meeting be evidently of his own seeking,
against an option fairly give to the contrary, and I cannot avoid it,
Iwill think of that hereafter. it be but repent and mortify for all
at once; for I be sure of victory, as I be that I now live, let he be
ever so skillful a swordsman; since, besides that I be no unfleshed
novice, this be a sport that, when provoke to it, I love as well as my
food. and, moreover, I shall be as calm and undisturbed as the bishop at
his prayer; while he, as be evident by his letter, must be actuate by
revenge and passion.
doubt not, therefore, Jack, that I shall give a good account of this
affair. mean time, I remain,
Yourbe most affectionately, &c.
LOVELACE.
LETTER LXII
MR. LOVELACE, to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
TRENT, DEC. 3--14.
to-morrow be to be the day, that will, in all probability, send either
one or two ghost to attend the mane of my CLARISSA.
I arrive here yesterday; and inquire for an english gentleman of the
name of Morden, soon find out the Colonel's lodging. he have be in
town two day; and leave his name at every probable place.
he be go to ride out; and I leave my name, and where to be find; and
in the evening he make I a visit.
he be plaguy gloomy. that be not i. but yet he tell I that I have
act like a man of true spirit in my first letter; and with honour, in
give he so readily this meeting. he wish I have in other respect;
and then we might have see each other upon well term than now we do.
I say there be no recalling what be pass; and that I wish some
thing have not be do, as well as he.
to recriminate now, he say, would be as exasperating as unavailable.
and as I have so cheerfully give he this opportunity, word should give
place to business.--your choice, Mr. Lovelace, of time, of place, of
weapon, shall be my choice.
the two latter be your's, Mr. Morden. the time to-morrow, or next day,
as you please.
next day, then, Mr. Lovelace; and wewill ride out to-morrow, to fix the
place.
Agreed, Sir.
well: now, Mr. Lovelace, do you choose the weapon.
I say I believe we might be upon an equal footing with the single
rapier; but, if he think otherwise, I have no objection to a pistol.
I will only say, reply he, that the chance may be more equal by the
sword, because we can neither of we be to seek in that; and you would
stand, say he, a bad chance, as I apprehend, with a pistol; and yet
I have bring two, that you may take your choice of either; for, add
he, I have never miss a mark at pistol-distance, since I know how to
hold a pistol.
I tell he, that he speak like himself; that I be expert enough that
way, to embrace it, if he choose it; though not so sure of my mark as
he pretend to be. yet the devilbe in it, Colonel, if I, who have slit
a bullet in two upon a knife's edge, hit not my man. so I have no
objection to a pistol, if it be your choice. no man, Iwill venture to
say, have a steady hand or eye than I have.
they may both be of use to you, Sir, at the sword, as well as at the
pistol: the sword, therefore, be the thing, if you please.
with all my heart.
we part with a solemn sort of ceremonious civility: and this day I
call upon he; and we ride out together to fix upon the place: and
both be of one mind, and hat to put off for the morrow what could
be do to-day, would have decide it then: but De la Tour, and the
Colonel's valet, who attend we, be unavoidably let into the secret,
join to beg we would have with we a surgeon from Brixen, whom La Tour
have fall in with there, and who have tell he he be to ride next
morning to bleed a person in a fever, at a lone cottage, which, by the
surgeon's description, be not far from the place where we then be, if
it be not that very cottage within sight of we.
they overtake so to manage it, that the surgeon should know nothing of
the matter till his assistance be call in. and La Tour, being, as I
assure the Colonel, a ready contrive fellow, [whom I order to obey
he as myself, be the chance to be in his favour,] we both agree to
defer the decision till to-morrow, and to leave the whole about the
surgeon to the management of our two valet; enjoin they absolute
secrecy: and so ride back again by different way.
we fix upon a little lone valley for the spot--ten to-morrow morning
the time--and single rapi the word. yet I repeatedly tell he, that I
value myself so much upon my skill in that weapon, that I would wish he
to choose any other.
he say it be a gentleman's weapon; and he who understand it not, want
a qualification that he ought to suffer for not have: but that, as to
he, one weapon be as good as another, throughout all the instrument of
offence.
so, Jack, you see I take no advantage of he: but my devil must deceive
I, if he take not his life or his death at my hand before eleven
to-morrow morning.
his valet and mine be to be present; but both strictly enjoin to be
impartial and inactive: and, in return for my civility of the like
nature, he command his to be assist I, if he fall.
we be to ride thither, and to dismount when at the place; and his
footman and mine be to wait at an appoint distance, with a chaise to
carry off to the border of the venetian territory the survivor, if one
drop; or to assist either or both, as occasion may demand.
and thus, Belford, be the matter settle.
a shower of rain have leave I nothing else to do; and therefore I write
this letter; though I might as well have defer it till to-morrow
twelve o'clock, when I doubt not to be able to write again, to assure you
much I be
Yours, &c.
LOVELACE.
LETTER LXIV
translation of a letter from F.J. DE LA TOUR.
to JOHN BELFORD, ESQ.
NEAR SOHO-SQUARE, LONDON.
TRENT, DEC. 18, N.S.
SIR,
I have melancholy news to inform you of, by order of the Chevalier
Lovelace. he show I his letter to you before he seal it;
signifying, that he be to meet the Chevalier Morden on the 15th.
wherefore, as the occasion of the meeting be so well known to you, I
shall say nothing of it here.
I have take care to have ready, within a little distance, a surgeon and
his assistant, to whom, under an oath of secrecy, I have reveal the
matter, (though I do not own it to the two gentleman;) so that they be
prepare with bandage, and all thing proper. for well be I acquaint
with the bravery and skill of my chevalier; and have hear the character
of the other; and know the animosity of both. a post-chaise be ready,
with each of their footman, at a little distance.
the two chevalier come exactly at their time: they be attend by
Monsieur Margate, (the Colonel's gentleman,) and myself. they have give
order over night, and now repeat they in each other's presence, that
we should observe a strict impartiality between they: and that, if one
fall, each of we should look upon himself, as to any needful help or
retreat, as the servant of the survivor, and take his command
accordingly.
after a few compliment, both the gentleman, with the great presence
of mind that I ever behold in man, stript to their shirt, and drew.
they parry with equal judgment several pass. my chevalier draw the
first blood, make a desperate push, which, by a sudden turn of his
antagonist, miss go clear through he, and wound he on the fleshy
part of the rib of his right side; which part the sword tear out, be
on the extremity of the body; but, before my chevalier could recover
himself, the Colonel, in return, push he into the inside of the left
arm, near the shoulder; and the sword (rake his breast as it pass,)
be follow by a great effusion of blood, the Colonel say, Sir, I
believe you have enough.
my chevalier swear by G--d he be not hurt; 'twa a pin's point; and so
make another pass at his antagonist; which he, with a surprising
dexterity, receive under his arm, and run my dear chevalier into the
body; who immediately fall; say, the luck be your's, Sir--o my beloved
clarissa!--now art thou--inwardly he speak three or four word more. his
sword dropt from his hand. Mr. Morden throw his down, and run to he,
say in French--ah, Monsieur! you be a dead man!----call to God for
mercy!
we give the signal agree upon to the footman; and they to the surgeon;
who instantly come up.
Colonel Morden, I find, be too well use to the bloody work; for he be
as cool as if nothing extraordinary have happen, assist the surgeon,
though his own wound bleed much. but my dear chevalier faint away two
or three time run, and vomit blood besides.
however, they stop the bleeding for the present; and we help he
into the voiture; and then the Colonel suffer his own wound to be
dress; and appear concerned that my chevalier be between while
(when he could speak, and struggle,) extremely outrageous.--poor
gentleman! he have make quite sure of victory!
the Colonel, against the surgeon' advice, would mount on horseback to
pass into the venetian territory; and generously give I a purse of
gold to pay the surgeon; desire I to make a present to the footman;
and to accept of the remainder, as a mark of his satisfaction in my
conduct, and in my care and tenderness of my master.
the surgeon tell he that my chevalier could not live over the day.
when the Colonel take leave of he, Mr. Lovelace say, you have well
revenge the dear creature.
I have, Sir, say Mr. Morden; and perhaps shall be sorry that you call
upon I to this work, while I be balance whether to obey, or disobey,
the dear angel.
there be a fate in it! reply my chevalier--a cursed fate!--or this
could not have been!--but be ye all witness, that I have provoke my
destiny, and acknowledge that I fall by a man of honour.
Sir, say the Colonel, with the piety of a confessor, (wring Mr.
Lovelace's hand,) snatch these few fleeting moment, and commend yourself
to God.
and so he ride off.
the voiture proceed slowly with my chevalier; yet the motion set both
his wound bleed afresh; and it be with difficulty they again stop
the blood.
we bring he alive to the near cottage; and he give order to I to
dispatch to you the packet I herewith send seal up; and bid I write to
you the particular of this most unhappy affair: and give you thank, in
his name, for all your favour and friendship to he.
contrary to all expectation, he live over the night: but suffer much,
as well from his impatience and disappointment, as from his wound; for
he seem very unwilling to die.
he be delirious, at time, in the two last hour: and then several time
cry out, as if he have see some frightful spectre, take she away! take
she away! but name nobody. and sometimes praise some lady, (that
Clarissa, I suppose, whom he have invoke when he receive his death's
wound,) call her Sweet Excellence! divine Creature! Fair Sufferer!--
and once he say, look down, Blessed Spirit, look down!--and there stopt;
--his lip, however, move.
at nine in the morning he be seize with convulsion, and faint away;
and it be a quarter of an hour before he come out of they.
his few last word I must not omit, as they show an ultimate composure;
which may administer some consolation to his honourable friend.
bless--say he, address himself no doubt to Heaven; for his dying
eye be lift up--a strong convulsion prevent he for a few moment
say more--but recover, he again, with great fervour, (lift up
his eye, and his spread hand,) pronounce the word bless: then, in a
seem ejaculation, he speak inwardly, so as not to be understand: at
last, he distinctly pronounce these three word,
let this expiate!
and then, his head sink on his pillow, he expire, at about half an
hour after ten.
he little thought, poor gentleman! his end so near: so have give no
direction about his body. I have cause it to be embowelle, and
deposit in a vault, till I have order from England.
this be a favour that be procure with difficulty; and would have be
refuse, have he not be an Englishman of rank: a nation with reason
respect in every austrian government--for he have refuse ghostly
attendance, and the sacrament in the Catholic way.--May his soul be
happy, I pray God!
I have have some trouble also, on account of the manner of his death, from
the magistracy here: who have take the requisite information in the
affair. and it have cost some money. of which, and of the dear
chevalier's effect, I will give you a faithful account in my next. and
so, wait at this place your command, I be, Sir,
your most faithful and obedient servant,
F.J. DE LA TOUR.

Mrs. HARLOWE live about two year and an half after the lamented death
of her CLARISSA.

a year; her death, by new point his former anguish and remorse,

both, in their last hour, however, comfort themselves, that they

they both live, however, to see their son James, and their daughter

Mr. JAMES HARLOWE marry a woman of family, an orphan; and be oblige,
at a very great expense, to support his claim to estate, which be his
principal inducement to make his address to she; but which, to this
day, he have not recover; nor be likely to recover; have powerful
adversary to contend with, and a title to assert, which admit of

person embarrassed in law.
what be far observable, with regard to he, be, that the match be

one month in every year he put on mourning, and that month commence

the MOST miserable of being.
ARABELLA's fortune become a temptation to a man of quality to make his

brother and sister, when they be not friend, be generally the

Mr. ANTONY and Mr. JOHN HARLOWE be still (at the writing of this)
living: but often declare, that, with their beloved niece, they lose all
the joy of their life: and lament, without reserve, in all company,
the unnatural part they be induce to take against she.
Mr. SOLMES be also still live, if a man of his cast may be say to

Mr. MOWBRAY and Mr. TOURVILLE have lose the man in whose conversation
they so much delight; shocked and awaken by the several unhappy

as those sister in iniquity, SALLY MARTIN and POLLY HORTON, have
ability and education superior to what creature of their cast
generally can boast of; and as their history be no where give in the
precede paper, in which they be frequently mention; it cannot fail

design by the publication of this work, to give a brief account of
their parentage, and manner of training-up, preparative to the vile
course they fall into, and of what become of they, after the dreadful
exit of the infamous Sinclair.
SALLY MARTIN be the daughter of a substantial mercer at the court-end
of the town; to whom her mother, a grocer's daughter in the city, bring
a handsome fortune; and both have a gay turn, and be fond of the
fashion which it be their business to promote; and which the wife and
daughter of the uppermost tradesman (especially in that quarter of the
town) generally affect to follow; it be no wonder that they bring up
their daughter accordingly: nor that she, who be a very sprightly and
ready-witted girl, and reckon very pretty and very genteel, should
every year improve upon such example.
she early find herself mistress of herself. all she do be right: all
she say be admire. early, very early, do she dismiss blush from
her cheek. she could not blush, because she could not doubt: and
silence, whatever be the subject, be as much a stranger to she as
diffidence.
she never be leave out of any party of pleasure after she have pass she
ninth year; and, in honour of her prattle vein, be consider as a
principal person in the frequent treat and entertainment which her

those who may have be endanger by his mean; as well as to repair, to
the utmost of his power, any damage or mischief which he may have
occasion to other.

rectitude of mind, and not for speciousness of person or address; nor
make a jest of a good man in favour of a bad one, who would make a jest

some have wish that the story have be tell in the usual narrative way

and that, in the present age, he suppose would not be a slight
recommendation.

'the method which the author have pursue in the history of Clarissa, be
the same as in the Life of Pamela: both be relate in familiar letter
by the party themselves, at the very time in which the event happen:
and this method have give the author great advantage, which he could not
have draw from any other specie of narration. the minute particular
of event, the sentiment and conversation of the party, be, upon this
plan, exhibit with all the warmth and spirit that the passion suppose
to be predominant at the very time could produce, and with all the
distinguishing characteristic which memory can supply in a history of
recent transaction.
'romance in general, and Marivaux's amongst other, be wholly
improbable; because they suppose the history to be write after the
series of event be close by the catastrophe: a circumstance which
imply a strength of memory beyond all example and probability in the
person concern, enable they, at the distance of several year, to
relate all the particular of a transient conversation: or rather, it
imply a yet more improbable confidence and familiarity between all
these person and the author.
'there be, however, one difficulty attend the epistolary method; for
it be necessary that all the character should have an uncommon taste for
this kind of conversation, and that they should suffer no event, not even
a remarkable conversation to pass, without immediately commit it to
write. but for the preservation of the letter once write, the
author have provide with great judgment, so as to render this
circumstance highly probable.'*

they be of opinion, that the story move too slowly, particularly in

but be it not true, that those altercation be the foundation of the

reader, that the story (interesting as it be generally allow to be) be
to be principally look upon as the vehicle to the instruction.
to all which we may add, that there be frequently a necessity to be very
